U.S. Air Force expands tests of glider-based spy drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:51:33 UTC
15:51:33 KST

- The U.S. Air Force added $46.1 million to DZYNE Technologies' ULTRA operational assessment contract, raising its total value to $85.6 million.
- ULTRA is a long-endurance surveillance drone that can fly more than 80 hours, with testing planned in the United States and overseas.
The U.S. Air Force has more than doubled the value of its contract with DZYNE Technologies for operational testing of ULTRA, a glider-like surveillance drone that can stay in the air for more than three days, the U.S. Department of War announced.
The $46.1 million modification raises the contract’s total value to $85.6 million, up from $39.6 million. It covers operational assessment of the Uncrewed Long-Endurance Tactical Reconnaissance Aircraft, with work in the United States and at overseas locations through March 26, 2031. The Air Force obligated $12.3 million in fiscal 2025 research and development funds at award. The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center in Dayton, Ohio, is managing the contract.
ULTRA is built on the airframe of the Stemme S12, a German two-seat motor glider, fitted for remote operation. The Air Force Research Laboratory’s Center for Rapid Innovation began the project with DZYNE in 2019 and took it from concept to first flight in under 10 months.
The aircraft weighs about 1,360 kg (3,000 pounds) and has a wingspan of 25 m (82 feet). It can fly for more than 80 hours carrying over 180 kg (400 pounds) of cameras, signals-collection gear or other sensors, and it is controlled over satellite links. It cruises at roughly 130 km/h (81 mph) and needs a runway of about 1,500 m (5,000 feet). The laboratory says ULTRA can travel more than 3,200 km (2,000 miles) and still loiter over a target for a full day.
That endurance is what the Air Force is buying. The MQ-9 Reaper, the service’s main surveillance drone since 2008, spends much of its flight time getting to and from distant areas. The research laboratory designed ULTRA for long-range missions, pointing specifically to the Pacific.
ULTRA has already flown operationally. The Air Force deployed it to an undisclosed location in May 2024, and The War Zone reported that it was flying from Al Dhafra Air Base in the United Arab Emirates. Those missions reportedly complemented MQ-9s over the Middle East. The Air Force requested four ULTRA aircraft for $35 million in its fiscal 2025 budget.
DZYNE has since developed ULTRA Turbo, a version with a turbocharged engine for better performance at high altitude. The company said in April that the Air Force Research Laboratory had ordered three ULTRA Turbo aircraft, after a first flight above 5,500 m (18,000 feet). DZYNE has also reported a 60-hour mission-representative flight at 7,600 m (25,000 feet) and 185 km/h (115 mph).
Air Force budget documents cited by The War Zone show ULTRA Turbo is due for an operational assessment within U.S. Central Command’s area, the Middle East, starting in fiscal 2026 and continuing into 2027. The contract announcement does not say whether the new funding supports that effort.
DZYNE says the aircraft can also carry electronic warfare equipment, relay communications and launch other payloads. The company opened a 11,600 square meter (125,000-square-foot) facility in Irvine, California, in 2024 to build ULTRA and its other long-endurance drones.

Tusk Warns of “Critical” Winter as Russian Strikes Force Polish Border Evacuations

Tusk Warns of “Critical” Winter as Russian Strikes Force Polish Border Evacuations
Polish authorities temporarily evacuated two border crossings with Ukraine as Russian forces launched an intense wave of missile and drone strikes near the Polish border, Polish broadcaster RMF24 reported on September 24.
The evacuations happened alongside security measures in eastern Poland, where the government deployed military aviation and temporarily suspended flights at the Rzeszów and Lublin airports during previous Russian bombardments of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
During a joint press conference with Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev in Warsaw, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed the border disruptions, noting the proximity of the Russian strikes to Polish territory.
“It is a true drama of today’s times, because it is not the first time that when I talk to one of our partners here in Warsaw about how aggressive Russia’s behavior is and what a problem it poses for Poland, at that exact moment the Russians decide to prove it,” Tusk stated, according to RMF24.
“While we were talking just now, Ukraine was attacked again near the Polish border and we again had to evacuate border crossings in Hrubieszów, in Dorohusk,” he continued.
According to RMF24, the specific crossings at Dorohusk and Zosin were non-operational and evacuated for approximately 30 minutes around noon before normal border traffic was permitted to resume.
In response to the Russian strikes—which killed at least nine people across Ukraine’s Kyiv and Kharkiv regions—Poland’s Government Security Centre (RCB) issued two safety alerts to residents of the bordering Podkarpackie and Lubelskie voivodeships. The second alert remained active for several hours.
Additionally, Polish military aircraft were scrambled into the nation’s airspace to monitor the threat, marking yet another deployment of Polish aviation to secure the border during a Russian aerial assault, RMF24 wrote.
Pointing to the escalating proximity and intensity of the attacks, Tusk emphasized the urgent need for both national readiness and European cooperation as the year ends.
“The situation forces us to act very consistently here in Poland, cooperate with Ukraine, but also warn Europe and European partners that this time is truly difficult and that we must prepare well for the coming weeks and months,” the prime minister warned. “Autumn and winter could indeed be critical.”
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski had also recently stated that Poland will not escalate tensions over a recent airspace violation by a Russian military helicopter if Moscow formally apologizes and attributes the incident to pilot error.
Following a 42-second breach near Russia’s Kaliningrad region border, Sikorski clarified to reporters that while Warsaw won’t “make a big deal” out of a mistake, the military is fully authorized under the constitution to shoot down aircraft if a threat is deemed intentional.

Seven arrests at protest against refugee facility in Gelderland

Seven arrests at protest against refugee facility in Gelderland
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Police have broken up a protest in Gelderland against a planned asylum seekers’ centre after fireworks were thrown from the crowd.
Seven people were arrested as the demonstration outside the village hall in Kesteren threatened to turn violent at around 9pm. Police cleared the area by 11pm, taking some demonstrators away in vans.
Some 300 people responded to a call on social media to gather outside the building on Thursday after the local council banned demonstrations in the neighbouring village of Opleusden, where riots broke out a week ago.
Neder-Betuwe councillors were meeting in Opleusden to discuss plans to accommodate 132 refugees, including eight unaccompanied minors, in a former transformer station.
The meeting was moved forward from 8pm to 6pm and lasted just 17 minutes after all political parties agreed in advance to approve the plan, mayor Jan Kottelenberg said.
The area outside the town hall was subjected to an emergency order banning public gatherings after last week’s riots outside the previous council meeting, which led to 14 arrests.
Towns and villages across the Netherlands have been the scene of violent protests against asylum seekers’ centres across the Netherlands, often organised by far-right “Defend” groups.
A group calling itself We Are The People called an anti-asylum march in The Hague at the weekend that was cancelled by the mayor when participants chanted racist slogans, threw fireworks and traffic poles at police and refused to remove face masks.

Northrop’s F-16 jammer deal tops $1.9 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:43:26 UTC
15:43:26 KST

- The U.S. Air Force added $87.4 million to Northrop Grumman's F-16 electronic warfare suite contract, bringing its total value to $1.92 billion.
- The funding supports low-rate initial production of the AN/ALQ-257 system, with work in Rolling Meadows, Illinois, through 2029.
The U.S. Air Force has added $87.4 million to Northrop Grumman’s contract for the AN/ALQ-257 Integrated Viper Electronic Warfare Suite, a new radar-jamming and threat-warning system for the F-16 fighter, the U.S. Department of War announced.
The modification funds low-rate initial production, the first small production run before full-rate manufacturing. It raises the total value of the contract to $1.92 billion, up from $1.83 billion. Work will take place at Northrop Grumman’s plant in Rolling Meadows, Illinois, and is scheduled to finish by Dec. 31, 2029.
The Air Force obligated $79.4 million at award: $11 million in fiscal 2025 research and development funds and $68.4 million in fiscal 2025 aircraft procurement funds. The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, manages the contract. The announcement did not say how many systems the money will buy.
The system, known as IVEWS, warns F-16 pilots when enemy radars are tracking them, jams those radars and helps locate and identify the threats. Northrop Grumman says it covers an ultra-wide frequency range, including millimeter-wave radars, which operate at very high frequencies used by some modern missile seekers and fire-control systems.
IVEWS is built into the aircraft. Earlier F-16 self-protection jammers, such as the ALQ-131 and ALQ-184, hang in pods under the jet’s belly and take up the centerline weapons station.
The Air Force picked Northrop Grumman for the program in 2021. Two F-16 Block 50 jets flew more than 70 sorties and over 100 flight hours during a seven-month operational assessment at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, and Nellis Air Force Base, Nevada, which wrapped up in 2025. By July 2026, the system had logged more than 550 flight-test hours across 300 sorties, company officials said.
In September 2025, the Air Force issued an urgent operational need to get IVEWS into service with F-16 units in the Middle East. The next month, Northrop Grumman reported that the suite had been integrated with the APG-83 radar being installed on upgraded F-16s.
The first Air Force production batch will equip 72 F-16 Block 50 jets, Northrop Grumman vice president Jim Conroy told Air & Space Forces Magazine in October 2025. Up to 450 U.S. F-16s are to receive the system in the initial program, Militär Aktuell reported in January. Northrop Grumman is also offering IVEWS to foreign F-16 operators, whose fleets together with the U.S. total more than 2,800 aircraft.
Congress set aside $187 million in last summer’s reconciliation bill to finish development testing and begin initial production, Conroy said at the time. He said the fiscal 2026 appropriations bill, then still pending, included $250 million for the first full-rate production lot.
The F-16 is expected to remain one of the main fighters of the U.S. Air Force and dozens of allied air forces into the 2040s, alongside the F-35. IVEWS is one of several upgrades meant to keep the jet competitive, together with the APG-83 radar and Northrop Grumman’s LITENING targeting pod.

European FOMO while Trump-XI summit wraps in Washington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25

Good morning. Angela Skujins here on Friday newsletter duties. Let’s dive in.
Chinese President Xi Jinping will today wind-up a three-day summit with US President Donald Trump on American soil — the first in 11 years for Xi. Europeans are watching closely for any decisions that could directly affect their economic interests.
Not so heated rivalry: The world’s most powerful leaders tackled tricky issues such as artificial intelligence, the war in Iran and trade. On the latter issue, a fragile trade truce was set to expire in November, but the two countries agreed Wednesday to extend it for another two months.
Ian Lesser, Distinguished Fellow German Marshall Fund, just told Euronews’ Europe Today programme that the three-days of crunch talks was more about “managing the rivalry” between the duo rather than the blooming of a new friendship.
“There was nothing deeply negative,” he said. “On the other hand, there wasn't a lot of progress on a lot of the substantive issues of trade and tech and other things people were looking for.” Watch.
As my colleague Peggy Corlin writes, those on this side of the Atlantic are taking notes. Something else to be mindful of: any tension with the US might lead China to reroute more exports to Europe, which may not necessarily be a bad thing.
But the EU has its own deadline for closing an eye-watering trade deficit with China, set for the beginning of October. If not, there will be “harsher measures”, the European Commissioner for Trade Maroš Šefčovič previously told Euronews.
Fortifying Europe: Over a dozen EU ministers will descend on Munich on Saturday for a meeting aimed at supercharging migration priorities. Vincenzo Genovese reports that those in attendance include the European Commissioner for Migration and Internal Affairs, Magnus Brunner.
On the sidelines of the summit, ministers from Greece, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands are set to continue their discussion on return hubs, also known as third party deportation centres. At the beginning of September, the five ministers met in the Danish capital and agreed on a common model for deportation centres to be built outside of Europe.
But patience is a virtue: The first agreement with a non-EU government regarding these return hubs is expected around the New Year. But it is unknown who those international partners could be — beyond the rumblings.
Marion Maréchal, of the far-right European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) group, just told Europe Today that return hubs would strengthen Europe’s defences. She said in French that there are a range of proposals that should allow the bloc to more easily intercept and return undocumented migrants from European soil.
The French Member of the European Parliament, who hails from the Le Pen family, made the comments from Ceuta, a city that has come to represent Europe’s weakest migration point.
Spanish scrutiny: After the incident in July, which saw over 80,000 individuals from Morocco storm the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Rome rapidly reintroduced temporary border controls. It also offered a swift rebuke to Madrid over its apparent handling of the arrivals.
In the weeks that followed, Spanish socialist prime minister Pedro Sánchez was left notably isolated amongst a sea of right-leaning European governments when it came to the migration file. However, all eyes on an upcoming European Council summit next month, with migration set to take centre stage.
Danish security: At the tail-end of a competitiveness council in Brussels on Thursday, my colleague Lauren Walker spoke with the Danish Minister of Business and Competitiveness Martin Lidegaard. Their interview spanned critical rare earth minerals, Brussels’ favourite buzzword — competitiveness — but also the recently minted Washington-Nuuk-Copenhagen deal.
“There is a huge desire in Greenland to grow, to create new jobs, and also when it comes to mining, have a bigger sector than today,” Lidegaard said when asked about how other countries can access Greenland’s critical rare earth minerals in light of the agreement.
Win-win-win: “And I think that the Americans are very happy about the fact that they have a huge access to the Greenlandic territory when it comes to military bases, but also when it comes to minerals.” Watch.
Some news from the finance world: European Central Bank (ECB) board member Isabel Schnabel announced her resignation as of January 2027, my colleague Eleonora Vasquez reports. She accepted the role of Financial Counsellor and Director of the Monetary and Capital Markets Department at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Washington.
“This decision was not easy for me. Serving on the Executive Board of the ECB and working with all of you has been one of the greatest privileges of my professional life,” Schnabel wrote in an email to her colleagues seen by Euronews.
ECB President Lagarde thanked Schnabel for her “invaluable” commitment in her work, saying she played a key role in the ECB’s determination to stabilise inflation at the bank’s 2% medium-term target. Schnabel’s successor will be appointed by the European Council.
Why is this important? Schnabel's departure might be the beginning of a major ECB reshuffle, with Lagarde herself expected to step down before the end of her mandate. Meanwhile, other ECB leaders prepare to depart on schedule. Among them is Chief Economist Philip Lane, whose mandate ends in May 2027.
The musical chairs come in a moment of high uncertainty for the eurozone. The volatility of energy prices due to the ongoing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine is making the job hard for the ECB to keep inflation low.
On 10 September, Lagarde announced an interest rate hike to keep inflation low, and said that the ECB's 2% inflation target will not be met by the end of next year.
Brussels dials up pressure on Kyiv to speed up reforms amid budget crunch
Brussels is stepping up expectations on Kyiv to accelerate reforms indispensable for unlocking €20 billion in financial assistance, which the country badly needs as the budget deficit swells and Russia escalates the war.
EU officials have raised the alarm about the slow legislative pace in the Rada, Ukraine’s parliament, where several laws are stalled. Two separate payments, one of €3.9 billion and another of €2.9 billion, have been delayed as a result.
As my colleague Jorge Liboreiro reports, the situation stands in stark contrast with the public messages from Zelenskyy and his deputies, who are asking allies to mobilise additional resources to plug a €23 billion gap in the Ministry of Defence. Separately, the country faces a €32.6 billion hole in next year’s budget.
The Commission wants to refocus the conversation. According to Jorge’s must-read analysis, the EU executives are rephrasing it as a conversation in which reforms comes before any conversation about new cash.

Northrop gets $124 million for delayed F-35 radar parts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:37:41 UTC
15:37:41 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Northrop Grumman up to $123.8 million for long-lead parts for 67 APG-85 radars for U.S. F-35s.
- Delays to the APG-85 have forced U.S. services to accept new F-35s with ballast in place of radars.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Northrop Grumman up to $123.8 million to buy long-lead parts for 67 AN/APG-85 radars, the new radar meant for the F-35 fighter, as brand-new jets continue to reach U.S. squadrons with ballast in their noses instead of radars.
The contract, announced Sept. 24 by the U.S. Department of War, covers materials, parts and components for what it calls APG-85 Lot 7, supporting the delivery schedule for 67 production radars for the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Marine Corps and U.S. Navy. Long-lead items are parts that take years to make and must be ordered well before final assembly.
The U.S. Air Force is paying $66.5 million and the U.S. Navy $57.3 million from fiscal 2026 aircraft procurement funds, all obligated at award. Northrop Grumman will do the work in Linthicum Heights, Maryland, and is scheduled to finish in February 2031. The fixed-price incentive contract, with a firm target price, was not competed. Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, is managing it.
The APG-85 is an active electronically scanned array radar built with gallium nitride components. It is designed to replace the APG-81 that has flown on the F-35 for years and is a core piece of the Block 4 upgrade package. The F-35 Joint Program Office had planned to start fitting it to some jets in Lot 17, the aircraft production batch delivered from 2025 through September 2026.
The radar has not arrived on time. Lockheed Martin redesigned the nose structure of Lot 17 jets to hold the APG-85, and the new mounting cannot accept the older APG-81 without major structural rework. With no radar to install, Lockheed has been delivering jets with ballast in the nose to keep the aircraft balanced. Development problems with cooling and power consumption have contributed to the delay, Avionics International reported.
The first radar-less F-35B flew its acceptance flight in late February 2026. At a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on June 23, Lt. Gen. Gregory Masiello, head of the F-35 Joint Program Office, told lawmakers the U.S. Marine Corps had accepted six F-35Bs without radars. He said he would not count those jets as fully mission capable. The U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy were expected to start accepting aircraft in the same configuration later in 2026.
The jets can still fly and use their other sensors, including electro-optical systems, and they can receive data from other aircraft. They cannot search for, track or target aircraft on their own radar.
A fix on the production line is still years away. Lockheed has proposed a nose bulkhead that can take either radar, but it is not expected to be ready until Lot 20, whose deliveries begin in 2028, Breaking Defense reported. Jets delivered before then without radars are due to be retrofitted once APG-85s become available.
Export customers are not affected. F-35s built for foreign buyers, including Poland, still carry the APG-81, because the APG-85 is not being offered abroad.
The Marine Corps said the Block 4 schedule depended on developing several components at the same time and that delays to some of them disrupted the plan. It called that approach a calculated risk the program office needed to take.

NEW DELHI: Union minister Chirag Paswan on Friday urged the Election Commissioner to "firmly present its side" amid the ongoing row over the internal disagreements in the poll panel.Speaking to reporters, Chirag said the Election Commission must retain people's trust and address their doubts about the electoral process."If such questions are being raised against the Election Commission, I believe it is also the responsibility of the Election Commission, especially the CEC, to firmly present its side," the Union minister said.
"I don't care what the opposition says because it is their job is to do politics. The Election Commission must maintain the trust of the people because if doubts arise in the public's mind about the electoral process itself, that would be wrong. In such a situation, the Election Commission should firmly put forth its points so that no doubts arise in the people's minds," he added.This comes after the opposition demanded Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation after an Indian Express report highlighted differences among members of the EC over the SIR of electoral rolls.
The report said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi raised formal objections on at least 14 occasions over a 10-month period against decisions and orders related to electoral-roll processes.Earlier on Thursday, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi accused the CEC of "vote chori, kanun chori, sanstha chori (vote theft, law theft, institutional theft)", calling it an "act against the nation".
"The Election Commission is the institutional protector of the vote... I have shown it with proof, and there is already more than enough information to make this a 100% certainty that Indian elections, Lok Sabha elections, 2024 election, Vidhan Sabha elections are all being rigged," he said, addressing a press conference.The Election Commission, however, described the queries and observations raised by its members as part of its routine internal process. It said written notes, technical inputs and internal scrutiny were standard mechanisms to check legal compliance and protect voters' rights.The ECI further said all decisions taken by the Commission, including those related to SIR, had full legal backing and stressed that its final decisions were unanimous.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a tough election in October, yet in his speech at the UN General Assembly, he highlighted his close bond with U.S. President Donald Trump and lashed out at a range of perceived and actual enemies, reports Politico.
Netanyahu stated that Israel has no greater partner than the US and thanked Trump for his bold leadership. Despite mounting tension between the Israeli government and the Trump administration over a potential war with Iran, the conflict in Gaza, and violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the West Bank, Netanyahu offered warm words for the US president. Dissatisfaction regarding US relations with Israel is also currently growing among certain Republican groups.
Last week, US Vice President JD Vance—who has privately opposed a US-Israeli war against Iran—emphasized that the US must not subordinate its foreign policy to Israel. Trump, who a few months ago called Netanyahu “crazy” during a heated phone call, has not publicly endorsed Netanyahu’s re-election. Nevertheless, the words of praise directed at Trump signaled the high value Netanyahu places on his relationship with the American leader at a time when Israel faces growing international isolation—a situation for which many Israeli voters blame Netanyahu himself. Throughout his speech, he maintained a defiant tone, taking aim at everyone from European leaders to New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani. Netanyahu rebuked Great Britain and France for leading a group of US allies in imposing sanctions on goods from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. He portrayed them as hypocrites who accuse Israel of colonialism, despite having themselves popularized the term.
Netanyahu stated that
attacks by Israelis on Palestinians and their property had drawn excessive international attention,
and he downplayed the significance of the death toll resulting from such attacks. Addressing world leaders who had condemned this aggression, the Israeli Prime Minister declared that they did not understand what they were talking about. Many of the Israeli settlers are staunch supporters of Netanyahu’s right-wing government. At the same time, Netanyahu also sought to soften his rhetoric, stating that he would not condone vigilantism by settlers.
As Netanyahu began his speech, many delegations present walked out of the hall. This had also occurred in previous years as anger mounted over Israel’s actions in Gaza. Netanyahu accused these individuals of hypocrisy, calling them moral cowards and claiming that leaders from many of these nations had privately thanked him for thwarting Iran’s nuclear program. The Israeli Prime Minister criticized Qatar—which has sought to act as a mediator in talks between the US and Iran—as well as Turkey, whose relations with Israel have deteriorated significantly in recent years. He accused both countries of spreading antisemitic lies. Accusations of antisemitism were also leveled at the Mayor of New York, who allegedly maintains “chummy” ties with the terrorist group Hamas. Mamdani supports Palestinian statehood and, during his election campaign, pledged to execute the arrest warrant issued for Netanyahu by the International Criminal Court—though he later backed away from that promise.
Another target of Netanyahu’s ire was Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa. On the 23rdd of September, the Syrian criticized Israel for its occupation of southern Syria and stated that the Golan Heights must remain Syrian territory. Netanyahu responded on the 24th of September, saying that Jews had been in the Golan Heights since the time of Moses, and called on al-Shara to pick up a Bible.

U.S. arrests executives of Oxygen Forensics after company supplied smartphone-access tools to both ICE and the FSB
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:33:05 UTC
15:33:05 KST

U.S. authorities have accused executives of Oxygen Forensics, a company that sold software to the Pentagon and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), of concealing that the company was controlled by Russian citizens and that its software was developed in Russia.
CEO Lee Reiber and Chief Technology Officer Oleg Davydov were arrested in connection with the case. The Insider was able to confirm that Oxygen Forensics supplied software capable of accessing the contents of locked phones not only to U.S. law enforcement agencies but also to Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). The same software was used to extract data from the iPhone of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty journalist Alsu Kurmasheva.
According to U.S. prosecutors, 55-year-old Reiber, an American citizen and CEO of Oxygen Forensics, was arrested in Idaho on Sept. 20 and was later ordered released on bail. Davydov, a 52-year-old Russian citizen and co-founder and chief technology officer of the company, was arrested the same day at London’s Heathrow Airport as he was preparing to fly to Istanbul. The U.S. intends to seek his extradition.
According to court documents, Reiber told the U.S. government that Virginia-based Oxygen Forensics was not owned or controlled by foreign nationals, even though five Russian citizens, including Davydov, allegedly owned stakes in or helped manage the company through a Cyprus-registered holding company. Prosecutors also allege that Reiber falsely claimed Oxygen Forensics software was developed in the United States rather than Russia. A court in California, where the case will be heard, ordered the seizure of company accounts and more than 50 domains belonging to the business.
Court documents say that no later than March 2022, Reiber, Davydov, and others entered into a conspiracy to obtain contracts from federal agencies. The software they supplied is used to recover, preserve, and analyze electronic data from digital devices while maintaining original files in an unchanged state.
Oxygen Forensics was founded in Virginia in 2013 with the involvement of Moscow-born Davydov. Reiber joined the company two years later. In 2022, after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Oxygen Forensics executives decided to conceal information about the company’s Russian owners — references to them were removed from official corporate records, prosecutors said. Reiber was appointed CEO, president, and chairman of the board in March 2022.
How the FSB gains access to opposition figures’ phones
On June 2, 2023, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty journalist Alsu Kurmasheva was due to return to Prague from Kazan, where she had been visiting her sick mother. However, she was detained at the airport. Authorities seized her iPhone XR, and the FSB was subsequently able to access its contents, including WhatsApp messages. Her passports were also confiscated, and she was barred from leaving Russia. A year later, she was sentenced to 6.5 years in prison on charges of spreading “false information” about the Russian military under a law that is widely used against critics of the war.
According to the case materials, the FSB accessed Kurmasheva’s locked phone using a specialized program called Mobile Forensic Expert (or “Mobilny Kriminalist” in its Russian transcription), developed by Oxygen Software.
The program has long enabled the FSB to access locked phones, including newer models. Last year, for example, the FSB used the same software to unlock an iPhone 14 belonging to a Russian activist detained at the border (whose lawyers asked that his name not be published). In that instance, security officers were also able to access messages in several messaging apps.
Phone searches at the border have become routine in Russia. When the FSB takes particular interest in someone, authorities commonly detain the person on an administrative charge in order to gain access to their devices. Information found can then be used to open a criminal case.
Oxygen Software, which supplies effective software for unlocking iPhones, has therefore served both the FSB and U.S. security agencies.
A U.S.-Russian company serving the FSB
In 2000, two programmer friends, 28-year-old Oleg Fyodorov and 27-year-old Oleg Davydov, founded a company and gave it the name Oxygen (a play on “two Olegs,” which can be shortened to O2). They initially focused exclusively on foreign markets, but in 2007 they created a Russian version of the product called Mobile Forensic Expert (“Mobilny Kriminalist”). Its main purpose is to extract all available data from mobile phones.
In 2008, the two Olegs described the program on their website with pride: “Our clients include government agencies, police, the military, customs and tax services, and other government bodies. Since 2002, the program has been successfully used in more than 50 countries around the world.”
The business expanded, and by 2026 the company’s U.S. website said it was operating in 150 countries worldwide (the site is currently unavailable). Oxygen’s main selling point is its ability to retrieve information even from locked smartphones, including newer iPhone models.
Oxygen’s services have been used extensively by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency, which sharply expanded its activities after Donald Trump’s return to the White House in 2025. In its contract with Oxygen, ICE explicitly stated that there were no other products on the market offering comparable functionality. The U.S. Secret Service, which protects the president and vice president, also became an Oxygen customer.
The two Olegs did not publicize the fact that Oxygen and Mobile Forensic Expert were essentially the same program, but they did not go to great lengths to hide it either. Investigators with Pervy Otdel (lit. “Department One”), a Russian legal rights group, noted that both the Russian and U.S. versions received updates at the same time and had nearly identical interfaces.
The two Olegs later removed their portraits from the U.S. website, but as The Insider can confirm, they continued traveling to the United States until recently.

Australia pushes tougher AI safeguards after OpenAI agent breaches government portal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:29:54 UTC
15:29:54 KST

A rogue OpenAI agent’s unauthorised access to an Australian government Medicare statistics portal is adding urgency to Canberra’s plans for tougher artificial intelligence safeguards, while potentially testing the country’s already strained technology relationship with Washington.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Thursday that the incident, which occurred in June, was “unacceptable” and that he had expressed his “extreme concern” directly to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. The government has launched a forensic investigation with the Australian Signals Directorate.
The agent accessed public and non-public files on the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal after being blocked from obtaining certain information.
Australian officials said no individual’s Medicare data was accessed and described the impact as relatively minor, while stressing that the unauthorised access itself was a serious incident.
OpenAI said it discovered the incident in August and notified Services Australia in September. Australian officials have criticised both the delay and the way the notification was made.
Breach could shape Australia’s AI rules
The incident arrives as Australia develops national AI standards and considers broader regulation of the rapidly expanding technology sector.
Experts say the episode could strengthen calls for AI companies to report security incidents promptly, provide greater transparency around autonomous systems and face clearer responsibilities when their products interact with government infrastructure.
The government has already announced that the incident will be examined by a task force, with findings expected to inform its wider work on AI standards.
Australia has also maintained a tougher position on copyright than OpenAI and Anthropic have sought, requiring companies to negotiate with rights holders rather than receive a broad exemption for training on Australian creative content. Both companies recently urged Canberra to reconsider that approach.
Data centres face a new test
The fallout could also influence how Australia assesses the rapidly growing infrastructure needed to support AI.
OpenAI has partnered with Australian data-centre operator NextDC on a planned 612-megawatt facility in Sydney, while Anthropic has partnered on a proposed 2.16-gigawatt facility in Queensland. Both projects require government approvals.
The breach may increase attention on the concept of “social licence” — whether major technology projects provide sufficient benefits and protections for the communities where they operate.
Australia is already considering rules governing data-centre energy use, water consumption and the treatment of Australian content used to train AI systems.
Victoria state this week announced new data-centre rules that include renewable-energy requirements, water restrictions and community investment provisions.
US tensions add another layer
The regulatory debate comes against existing friction between Canberra and Washington over technology policy, including Australia’s restrictions on social media for under-16s and other proposed online-safety measures.
Australia’s decision to maintain its copyright rules has also frustrated OpenAI and Anthropic, which have argued for greater flexibility to train AI models on Australian material.
Technology policy experts say Australia now faces a broader choice over how aggressively it wants to regulate frontier AI while attracting investment in data centres and maintaining close ties with the United States.
For Canberra, the Medicare incident has turned that debate from a question of future safeguards into a more immediate test of how AI systems should be governed when they interact with critical public infrastructure.

Romania gets its first South Korean K9 howitzers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:27:23 UTC
15:27:23 KST

- Romania has received its first K9 howitzers, K10 resupply vehicles and K12 vehicles from Hanwha Aerospace under a nearly $1 billion contract.
- The order covers 54 K9s and 36 K10s, with most future vehicles to be built at Hanwha's new plant in Petrești, Romania.
Romania has received its first K9 self-propelled howitzers, K10 ammunition resupply vehicles and K12 vehicles from South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace under its tracked self-propelled howitzer program.
Romania signed a contract worth nearly $1 billion with Hanwha on July 9, 2024, for 54 K9 howitzers and 36 K10 resupply vehicles, along with ammunition and tracked and wheeled support vehicles. The deal includes 18,000 rounds of 155 mm ammunition. An initial batch of 18 K9s and 12 K10s is being built in South Korea, and the remaining vehicles are due to be produced in Romania.
The contract originally set the first delivery for early 2027. Hanwha said in July that the first vehicles would arrive in the second half of 2026 for testing and evaluation, with the rest of the initial batch following in early 2027. The first Romanian K9, named Tunetul, Romanian for Thunder, rolled off Hanwha’s production line in South Korea in April.
The K9 is a tracked howitzer that fires 155 mm shells from a 52-caliber barrel and can move off quickly after firing to avoid return fire. Romania is the tenth country to buy it and the sixth NATO member, after Türkiye, Poland, Norway, Finland and Estonia. The new guns will replace Soviet-era 152 mm artillery and older 155 mm systems still in Romanian service.
The K10 is built on the same chassis as the K9 and keeps the howitzer supplied in the field. It carries 104 shells and 504 propellant charges and transfers them automatically at up to 12 rounds a minute, reloading a K9 completely in about 37 minutes. Romania is the third K10 operator, after Norway and Australia.
Production is set to move to Romania. On Feb. 11, Hanwha broke ground on the Hanwha Armoured Vehicle Centre of Excellence Europe in Petrești, Dâmbovița County, northwest of Bucharest. It is the company’s first factory in Europe. The site covers about 181,000 square meters (1.9 million square feet) and will include assembly lines, testing facilities and a 1,751 m (5,744-foot) driving track. Hanwha aims to source up to 80% of the work from Romanian industry, with partners including Iveco and Pro Optica.
In July, Hanwha outlined plans to invest €1.3 billion ($1.48 billion) in defense production and technology transfer in Romania. The company says the Petrești plant could later build infantry fighting vehicles, long-range precision strike systems and unmanned ground vehicles, and estimates that expansion tied to an infantry fighting vehicle program could create up to 2,000 jobs.
Under the 2024 contract, all 54 howitzers and 36 resupply vehicles are due within five years of signing.

"The recovery in the Reform Party's rating is particularly noticeable among older voters. However, the polling data does not allow us to conclude that media coverage caused the increase in support," Voog said.
The non-parliamentary Parempoolsed recorded its best-ever result in September, with support rising to 10 percent. Support for Parempoolsed stood at 7 percent in August.
Center's rating falls for fourth consecutive month
In a month-on-month comparison, support fell the most for both Isamaa and the Center Party. Isamaa had the support of 24 percent of respondents in September and the Center Party 17 percent. A month earlier, support for each party was 2 percentage points higher.
"Support for the Center Party fell for the fourth consecutive month. Taking the margin of error into account, the Center Party and the Social Democratic Party are now tied for second and third place," Voog said.
Support for the Social Democratic Party stood at 17 percent in September, down from 18 percent in August, putting it level with the Center Party despite the slight decline. As recently as June, support for the Center Party stood at 22 percent.
EKRE was in fifth place with 13 percent support, up 1 percentage point from the previous month.
Eesti 200 had 2 percent support, while the Greens, ERK and Koos each had 1 percent.
Riigikogu opposition parties had the support of 71 percent of respondents in September, down from 74 percent in August, while the coalition parties had 17 percent support, up from 15 percent in August.
'Don't know' vote grows among non-ethnic Estonians
The share of respondents with no party preference, or those who answered "don't know," rose to 30 percent. The increase occurred primarily among respondents of non-Estonian ethnicity.
When respondents with no party preference are also included, Isamaa had 15.6 percent support in September, followed by the Social Democratic Party with 12.7 percent, the Center Party with 11.9 percent, the Reform Party with 10.1 percent, EKRE with 9.3 percent, Parempoolsed with 7.0 percent and Eesti 200 with 1.2 percent.
Among ethnic Estonian respondents, Isamaa ranked first in September with 27.5 percent support. It was followed by the Social Democratic Party with 19.2 percent, the Reform Party with 17 percent, EKRE with 14.3 percent and Parempoolsed with 11.2 percent. The Center Party had 6.2 percent support among ethnic Estonian respondents, while Eesti 200 had 1.7 percent.
Among respondents of non-Estonian ethnicity, the Center Party retained a clear lead with 63.9 percent support. The Social Democratic Party had 9.8 percent support among this group, Isamaa 7.5 percent, EKRE 6.9 percent, the Reform Party 3.4 percent, Eesti 200 2.7 percent and Parempoolsed 2.2 percent.
Among Tallinn voters, the Center Party was the most popular with 26.2 percent support, although its lead over the Social Democratic Party has narrowed. Support for the Social Democrats in the capital stood at 22.9 percent in September.
The Reform Party had 13.3 percent support in Tallinn, EKRE 13 percent and Isamaa, which holds the mayor's office, ranked fifth with 12.6 percent. Parempoolsed had 9.6 percent support in Tallinn and Eesti 200 1.4 percent.
The Center Party also held a clear lead in Ida-Viru County, while the Social Democratic Party ranked first in Tartu and Jõgeva counties for the first time. Isamaa ranked first in all other regions.
Men prefer Isamaa, women the Social Democrats
Among male voters, Isamaa ranked first with 29.9 percent support, compared with 18.9 percent among women. EKRE and Parempoolsed also had higher support among men than among women.
Among female voters, the Social Democratic Party was the most popular choice, with 23.1 percent support. Among men, support for the Social Democrats stood at just 10.8 percent. The Center Party, Reform Party and Eesti 200 also had somewhat higher support among women than among men.
By education level, Isamaa ranked first among respondents with both basic and secondary education. Among respondents with higher education, the Social Democratic Party was the most popular choice.
The Social Democratic Party ranked first in the younger age groups, those aged 18-24 and 25-34. In the oldest age group, those aged 75 and over, the Reform Party and Center Party were tied for first place. Isamaa ranked first among those aged 35-49 and 50-64. Among those aged 65-74, Isamaa and the Center Party were tied for first place.
Emor surveyed 1,535 voting-age citizens across Estonia online and by telephone from September 14–23. With a sample of this size, the maximum margin of error is ±2.2 percentage points. More information about the ratings is available on ERR's ratings page.

‘Orphan,’ the new film by László Nemes, tells a bleak story of a Jewish boy in 1950s Budapest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:22:14 UTC
15:22:14 KST

László Nemes burst onto the international movie scene with this first feature film, Son of Saul (2015), which told the story of a member of the Sonderkommando at Auschwitz, the unit tasked with disposing the millions of murdered bodies at the death camp.
It subverted every cliché of Holocaust filmmaking up to that point. Where most Holocaust dramas were slow-paced, and some, like Schindler’s List, even featured tasteful black-and-white cinematography and dialogue in English (one of the only European languages not spoken by a sizable percentage of death-camp inmates), Son of Saul went for grueling realism.
The movie is in color, and the Sonderkommando work at breakneck speed, as we know they were required to do from accounts of the few survivors.
But it had a deep emotional core, about a man who is shaken out of the numbness he has used to protect himself when he goes on a doomed quest to give a proper burial to a murdered boy he claims is his son.
It was such a perfectly conceived and realized movie that it won the Best Foreign Language Film Oscar, as well as the Grand Prix at Cannes, and dozens of other awards.
Few have ever made such a great film, and expectations were understandably, perhaps unfairly, high for Nemes’s subsequent movies. His follow-up feature, Sunset, was far more modest, and now he has a new film, Orphan, which opens Thursday in Israel.
'Orphan' is set on the backdrop of a crushed student uprising
Although it is set after the war, Orphan references the war in nearly every disconsolate frame, and captures the melancholy of trying to pick up the pieces after a tragedy of such a grand scale.
Much like Son of Saul, it subverts the cliches of stories about boys searching for their true father and wishing that this father was a great hero. Based on the story of Nemes’s own father, it is about a 12-year-old boy named Andor (Bojtorján Barabás) in Budapest in 1957.
A student uprising against the Stalinist regime was just crushed by the Soviets, and it’s a bleak, hopeless setting, which mirrors the bleakness of Andor’s life.
He is not an actual orphan but is one of the luckier Jewish children who survived the war in an orphanage and was reunited after the war with one parent, his mother, Klára (Andrea Waskovics). His father, Hirsch, whom he has always been told was a brave and brilliant man, perished in a death camp.
Andor treasures every scrap of information about his father, and clings to a vain hope that he might not really have died. He needs this fantasy about his father to help him get through his days.
His mother works in a state-run shop and barely has enough money for food. Just as bad, from her son’s point of view, she is depressed and careworn, with barely any energy for him. Andor spends much of his time avoiding bullies and trying various schemes to make a little money with his one trustworthy friend.
When a crude, obnoxious gentile butcher, Berend (Grégory Gadebois), who turns out to be not only rude but violent, rides up to their building on a motorcycle, acting like he owns Klára, Andor knows that their already struggling family is in even worse trouble.
'Orphan' has stylistic similarties to earlier works
Gradually, what we sense from this butcher’s first appearance becomes clear to Andor. Klára’s first husband may well have been a murdered hero, but it seems likely that Berend is Andor’s real father. It turns out that this married butcher hid Klára during the war and forced her into a sexual relationship.
She managed to escape his clutches once the war ended, but now that he has found her, he still considers her his, and wants her back, along with the boy he thinks of as his son.
Not only does his reappearance shatter Andor’s fantasies about his father, but it presents him with a terrifying problem: He must contend with this violent man who wants to come and live with him and Klára.
In Hungary in this period, there is nowhere for Klára to turn for help, especially since Berend is buddies with many of the local Communist Party functionaries.
The movie has some stylistic similarities with another, very different portrait of a troubled childhood, Francois Truffaut’s The 400 Blows, especially in its refusal to sentimentalize anything. Childhood is a time when children are at the mercy of the adults around them and have no one to turn to if those adults are brutal or neglectful.
Andor is not in a concentration camp, like Saul in Son of Saul, but he lives in a reality where he may be a victim of violence at any moment. Orphan vividly portrays that climate of fear.
Unbearable tension with no hope for anything better
While no movie could be harder to watch than Son of Saul, in some ways, somehow Orphan makes you long to flee the theater more than Son of Saul does. The bleakness of Andor’s life is so relentless, I found myself wishing the movie would end long before it did.
Son of Saul teased us with the promise that Saul would find some small measure of redemption in the end, and showed that he had achieved a kind of grace just by choosing to try to bury his son.
Here, there is absolutely no glimmer of hope, and nearly every scene involving Berend has the unbearable tension of a family gathering ready to explode into brutality, even death.
Cinematographer Mátyás Erdély has done a brilliant job of making the sepia-toned photography mirror the emotional barrenness of the world that Andor inhabits.
The cast is excellent, and Gadebois manages the almost impossible feat of giving us some glimpses of the butcher’s humanity: Despite his flaws, he does care for Klara and wants to raise this boy. But while Truffaut gave us hints that his abused hero would find a way out, Nemes gives us no such comfort.

Sinwar warned Israel of 'earthquake' weeks before October 7, former Fatah official reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:22:09 UTC
15:22:09 KST

Former senior Fatah official Sufian Abu Zaida said he relayed an unusual message from Hamas leader in the Gaza Strip Yahya Sinwar to Israel three weeks before the October 7 attack, he revealed in a documentary aired on Al-Ghad on Thursday.
In the interview, Zaida said that for more than a year he served as an intermediary in a secret channel between Israel and Hamas in an effort to advance a prisoner exchange deal.
The channel was opened in March 2022, after senior Hamas official Ghazi Hamad approached Zaida and asked for his help in advancing the talks. Zaida contacted a former senior Israeli security official and later met with Israeli officials.
According to Zaida, the contacts progressed to discussions over the names and lists of prisoners, but the sides did not reach an agreement.
As part of the talks, Zaida also met with then-Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) chief Ronen Bar. He said he presented Bar with the conditions Hamas had set for a deal. Among other things, Sinwar demanded the release of all female prisoners, prisoners under the age of 18, prisoners released in the Gilad Schalit deal who had subsequently been rearrested, and veteran prisoners, while giving priority to sick prisoners.
According to Zaida, the Israeli side offered extensive measures benefiting the Gaza Strip in exchange for resolving the prisoner issue, including increasing the number of Gazan workers permitted to enter Israel, rehabilitating the electricity grid and other infrastructure, and advancing reconstruction in the Gaza Strip.
Despite progress in the contacts, the sides did not reach an agreement.
Sinwar warns Israel that Hamas would put 'cards' on negotiating table
On September 14, 2023, Zaida met with Sinwar in Gaza. During the meeting, he said Sinwar asked him to relay a message to Israel that before the end of that month, Hamas would place “cards” on the negotiating table that would cause an “earthquake,” and that Israel should prepare for the “emptying of the prisons.”
Zaida said Sinwar dictated the message to him precisely and asked him to deliver it exactly as given.
Zaida transmitted the message to the Israeli side in both Hebrew and Arabic.
According to him, he was contacted less than half an hour later to verify that Sinwar had indeed intended to convey those words, and he was summoned to an urgent meeting the following morning.
At the meeting in Ashkelon, Zaida was asked what Sinwar meant by an “earthquake” and what the “cards” were.
Sinwar's message keeps security officials awake
According to Zaida, the officials he met told him that no one in the security establishment had slept that night because of the message.
Zaida replied that Sinwar had been calm when he conveyed it to him.
That was, he said, the final meeting held through the contact channel. Zaida returned to the Gaza Strip on October 5 and was scheduled to meet Sinwar again on October 8.
The meeting never took place. Twenty-two days after Zaida relayed the message, the October 7 attack occurred.

Colombia severs diplomatic ties with Iran
Bogotá cites links to terrorist groups and concerns over human rights and Iran’s nuclear program; consular relations remain in place
Colombia announced Thursday that it had formally severed diplomatic relations with Iran, effective Sept. 19, citing national and hemispheric security concerns and links between Tehran and terrorist and narcoterrorist groups.
The Foreign Ministry said it had also considered human rights violations in Iran, attacks on countries outside the Middle East conflict, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and what it described as obstruction of International Atomic Energy Agency efforts to assess Iran’s nuclear program.
Together, those issues had eroded Colombia’s trust in the Iranian government, the ministry said. The break does not end consular relations.
The move comes amid a shift in foreign policy under President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office in August. His government has restored ties with Israel after his predecessor, Gustavo Petro, broke them in 2024 over Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar welcomed Colombia’s decision in a social media statement provided for this article, praising de la Espriella’s leadership and calling for a united response to Iran. "I commend Colombia 🇨🇴 and the leadership of President @ABDELAESPRIELLA for severing diplomatic relations with the Iranian regime. This is a clear stand against terrorism, narco-terrorism and Iran’s dangerous nuclear ambitions. The free world must stand united against the Iranian regime."

Feature: Mooncakes bridge Chinese culture with Lao people's Mid-Autumn Festival celebration
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:15:54 CST
15:15:54 KST

VIENTIANE, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- When the Mid-Autumn Festival is mentioned, mooncakes are often among the first things that come to Lao people's minds. With their sweet, dense and rich flavor, mooncakes offer Lao people a simple yet memorable way to experience Chinese culture through taste.
Kham, a 32-year-old resident of the Lao capital Vientiane, told Xinhua on Friday that although she is neither Chinese nor of Chinese descent, she buys mooncakes every year ahead of the Mid-Autumn Festival, often giving them to elders or guests invited to dinner gatherings. For Kham, the festival is closely associated with the taste of mooncakes and the time spent with people close to her.
"Every year I host a small party for my friends and family to gather and have dinner together. After dinner, we eat mooncakes together. So when I think of the festival, the taste of mooncakes shared with the people closest to me always comes to mind first," she said.
For Kham, the mooncake has become more than a seasonal delicacy. Its taste is tied to memories of gathering with family and friends, giving her a personal connection to a Chinese festival despite not having a Chinese background.
Phonethida, a Lao vendor selling mooncakes, said the pastries appeal to customers not only for their taste but also for their distinctive and elegant packaging, which makes them suitable as gifts.
"When the Mid-Autumn Festival approaches, more Lao customers come to buy mooncakes. Some buy them for their families, while others buy them as gifts. I believe many Lao people are already familiar with mooncakes and have tasted them before," she said.
"Even when it is not the festival, some customers still ask for mooncakes. They tell us that they like the taste and want to eat them, especially with tea," Phonethida said.
The popularity of mooncakes among Lao people reflects how a traditional Chinese festival food has become familiar to some in their everyday lives, offering a simple way for people to encounter and exchange culture through taste.
Beyond the taste of mooncakes, the Mid-Autumn Festival also offers Lao people another way to encounter Chinese culture through learning and cultural experiences. For Lao students studying Chinese, traditional festivals provide opportunities to participate in activities that help them gain a deeper understanding of China and its culture beyond what they learn in the classroom.
Xayadeth, a 17-year-old student taking a Chinese language course, said he looks forward to Chinese festivals because they allow him to experience Chinese culture firsthand while learning new words and expressions related to each celebration.
He said his Chinese language institute organizes special activities for students during different Chinese festivals, giving them opportunities to learn about a wider range of Chinese traditions.
"I like learning through activities during festivals because they help us understand more about China and its culture. There are things that we cannot fully imagine just by reading books or studying in the classroom," he said.
The Mid-Autumn Festival, celebrated annually on the 15th day of the eighth month in the Chinese lunar calendar, falls on Sept. 25 this year. ■

Philippines tops global disaster-risk ranking

Unknown Publisher

15:15:51 KST

MANILA, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- The Philippines has again ranked as the country with the highest disaster risk in the world, topping the 2026 World Risk Index with a score of 46.69, according to local media reports on Thursday.
The index published by German institutes covered all 193 United Nations member states. India ranked second with a score of 44.97, followed by Indonesia at 44.63.
The World Risk Index assesses disaster risk based on two broad factors: a country's exposure to natural hazards and its societal vulnerability, including its capacity to cope with and adapt to disasters.
The Philippines has consistently ranked among the countries most exposed to disasters because of its geographic location.
Located along the Pacific Ring of Fire, the Philippines is vulnerable to earthquakes and volcanic activity. Its location in the western Pacific exposes it to frequent tropical cyclones, heavy rainfall, flooding and landslides.
The Philippines also ranked first in the 2025 edition, when it posted a score of 46.56. ■

traditional emirati patterns and craft frame al maktoum archives’ interiors in dubai
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:15:47 UTC
15:15:47 KST

Emirati heritage shapes the layout of Al Maktoum Archives
At Dubai’s Al Maktoum Archives, Kart Group brings the warmth of a traditional majlis into a government workplace. Palm-frond weaving, hand-tufted wool, and CNC-cut marble carry Emirati heritage into the interior, integrating cultural references into the everyday setting of the archive.
Designed by Mustafa Khamash and his team at Kart Group, alongside contractor EMKAY, the 8,000-sqft headquarters occupies Level 2 of Dubai’s Emirates Towers. The working institution safeguards historical records, private manuscripts, and cultural narratives documenting the Maktoum family’s lineage and the emirate’s evolution. The design combines the requirements of a contemporary workplace with references to this history.
The traditional Emirati majlis informs the furniture layout, with a seating suite positioned at the center of the space. Mashrabiya motifs from the Al Shindagha Museum provide another starting point, with their repeating geometry reconstructed from fundamental units and adapted to contemporary surfaces and fabrication methods.
Traditional motifs take on new forms across the interior
Geometric motifs are particularly visible in the custom carpet, hand-tufted from New Zealand wool. Its pattern aligns across the floor, extending the geometric composition beyond an individual furnishing. Al Khoos, the traditional palm-frond weaving craft, introduces another material reference through woven palm fronds, fine metal inlays, and stenciled wall coatings. At the principal feature wall, CNC-cut and engraved marble brings the heritage geometry to an architectural scale, with the pattern digitally redrawn for stone.
Each motif was adapted by Kart Group’s design team to its medium, from hand-tufted wool to furniture inlays and machine-cut marble. This allows the references to remain recognizable while responding to the different qualities and tolerances of each material.
Kart Group brings the traditional Emirati majlis into a government workplace
Wool, palm fronds, and marble anchor the workplace
Material selection balances longevity, texture, and cultural relevance. New Zealand wool provides resilience and softness underfoot, woven palm fronds maintain a connection to traditional making, and marble establishes a sense of permanence. Contemporary textiles from Romo, Dedar, and Kirkby Design sit alongside these materials.
The traditional majlis suite is complemented by an AJZAL Burj Rashid coffee table, while Herman Miller Aeron task chairs and Polflex leather armchairs support the workplace program. These contemporary elements keep the archive grounded in present-day use rather than historical reenactment.
The interior connects the archive’s institutional purpose with the continued use and adaptation of inherited patterns and craft traditions. Heritage extends beyond the collection itself into the materials, furniture, surfaces, and working environment surrounding it.

Moving target: Congo's North Kivu province becomes new Ebola hotspot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:12:15 UTC
15:12:15 KST

Moving target: Congo's North Kivu province becomes new Ebola hotspot
BUTEMBO, Democratic Republic of Congo, Sept 25 - All 29 beds were full this week at the Kitatumba Ebola treatment centre in Congos North Kivu province, where surging cases have overwhelmed health facilities even as the deadly virus shows signs of easing elsewhere.
In one room, a critically ill patient lay on oxygen support, crying out as medical staff in masks, gloves and plastic aprons rushed past him at the centre in Butembo, a city of 2 million people.
"Over the past two weeks, we've seen a very sharp increase," said Stephanie Hoffmann, project coordinator for the international medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) in the city.
"There are sometimes patients who know they have Ebola but cannot find a bed."
City authorities announced the opening of two new treatment centres this week to deal with the demand, bringing the total to four.
But some patients arrive so unwell, there is nothing doctors can do, said Hoffmann, speaking at the Kitatumba centre.
She described the case of a 10-year-old boy who died in triage before doctors could admit him to the facility on Tuesday.
The scenes underscore the difficulty of containing Ebola across a stretch of eastern Congo that is bigger than France – one where medical resources are stretched thin.
Researchers believe the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus was spreading for months before the first cases were confirmed in Ituri, a province that neighbours North Kivu, in May. Aid cuts, surveillance system gaps and the absence of approved vaccines and treatments hampered the response, along with armed conflict in the region.
As of Tuesday, Congo had confirmed 7,820 cases and 3,779 deaths, according to government data.
While Ituri remains the worst-affected province, North Kivu's share of new infections increased sharply this month, the data shows. The province now accounts for around a third of newly confirmed cases and deaths, the World Health Organization (WHO) said in a report on Sunday.
Last week, South Ubangi became the seventh province affected, another sign of what WHO described as a "pronounced geographic redistribution of transmission."
United Nations and Congolese government officials said last week there were signs transmission is slowing in some of the worst-affected parts of Ituri, where responders have been racing to set up treatment facilities, identify victims, trace contacts and educate people on how to protect themselves. But it remains a "massive" outbreak, UN Special Ebola Coordinator Julien Harneis told reporters in Geneva.
Frontline workers say cases continue to emerge in new and underprepared areas.
"Assuming the outbreak is under control because some Ebola treatment centres are admitting fewer patients would be a mistake," Anthony Kergosien, MSF's emergency coordinator in Congo, said in a September 18 statement. "The outbreak is not shrinking; it is moving."
DEEP MISTRUST
Interviews with residents, health workers and local leaders suggest shortages of funding and skilled personnel, together with deep-seated mistrust of Ebola responders, are making the virus difficult to contain in North Kivu.
Just over 60% of people diagnosed there are dying, significantly higher than the national average of 48%, the data shows. Medical staff say there has not yet been enough education about the virus, and patients are avoiding health facilities. That complicates efforts to identify cases and start treatment before the disease reaches its most dangerous stages.
By the time Ebola patients reach Dr Michel Paluku Mukuloli's hospital in Butembo, it is often too late.
"Patients think that if they arrive at the hospital, they will be immediately sent to the treatment centre to die," he said.
In Butembo, one of the region's largest cities and a major trading hub, there are few signs that mitigation measures are being widely adopted. Overcrowded minibuses criss-cross the city. Markets remain packed.
Some residents refuse to have their temperature checked or wash their hands at entry points to the city and outside public buildings, according to the head doctor in the Butembo health zone, Pablo Paluku Lwanzo.
Only two of the zone's nine health checkpoints are operating due to staffing constraints, he added.
Other residents question whether Ebola is real. One local welder said his 12-year-old son, who suffered from respiratory problems, died the day he was transferred to an Ebola treatment centre. Because none of the relatives and neighbours who accompanied the boy became sick, he became convinced doctors had wrongly diagnosed the case.
"For me, Ebola does not exist," the man told Reuters on condition of anonymity.
Frightened and angry residents have attacked teams sent to decontaminate their homes and safely bury people suspected of having died of Ebola.
One person "came at me with a machete," said Lambert Maboko, a member of a burial team, as he recovered at home from the attack, which fractured his knee.
Ahead of each deployment, members of the team hold a prayer session for their safety.
Earlier this month, residents set fire to a health post they accused of collaborating with Ebola responders, sending patients fleeing into the community, staff said. Microscopes and solar panels were lost in the attack.
"I'm at a loss for words," Kakule Mahamba, head of the Hope health post, said as he surveyed the charred wreckage. "Even the hospital beds were burned, as well as the medicines."
Congolese authorities and WHO say they are working on building trust through awareness campaigns, household visits and engagement with religious and local leaders.
Speaking after meeting with the North Kivu governor and WHO representatives on Wednesday, Congo's incident manager for the Ebola outbreak, Steve Ahuka, said authorities had gained more access over the past four weeks.
"While pockets of resistance remain, we believe that with the involvement of traditional, religious and neighbourhood leaders … we can make progress."
Responding to Reuters questions, WHO said cases declined in North Kivu in recent days after several weeks of marked increases. But funding and staffing constraints remain significant challenges across affected areas.
"The pressure is particularly acute in North Kivu, which … has seen a significant increase in transmission with limited bed capacity for patient care," the statement said.
MEMORIES OF PAST OUTBREAKS
North Kivu was the epicentre of three previous Ebola outbreaks, including one in 2018-2020, which until this year was Congo's largest and deadliest. Those outbreaks, however, were caused by a different type of Ebola virus, known as the Zaire species.
Much less is known about the Bundibugyo species. But responders say in the early stages of infection, patients often experience milder symptoms easily mistaken for more common diseases such as malaria and typhoid fever.
Unlike the more common Zaire species, there are no approved vaccines or treatments. That is contributing to suspicions the outbreak might be a hoax, according to local authorities.
"People remember the 2018 outbreak and ask why vaccines and treatments existed then but not today," said Pepin Kavota, a civil society coordinator in the nearby city of Beni.
Cases of sexual abuse and exploitation on the part of responders during the 2018-2020 outbreak, including some employed by WHO, further eroded public trust, Kavota added.
In the statement to Reuters, WHO said it recognises that "trust must be continually earned," adding it has significantly strengthened efforts to prevent and respond to abuses since the previous outbreak.
Last month, provincial authorities recruited pro-government fighters known as Wazalendo to help protect responders and improve adherence to prevention measures. On some roads leading to Butembo, armed men now operate handwashing stations.
A leader of the force warned that people who repeatedly refused to comply with Ebola control measures could be forcibly taken to treatment centres and whipped.
Others worry such coercive tactics could worsen the very problem they are trying to address: mistrust.
"We should not need to use the police or the army in a response," Lwanzo said. "The population must be sensitised and willingly adopt the measures that are being put in place to protect them." REUTERS

From tarantulas to a stork nest fire, Tallinn rescuers come to animals' aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
06:12:00 UTC
15:12:00 KST

From tarantulas to a stork nest fire, Tallinn rescuers come to animals' aid
While house fires and cats stuck in trees are more common, Estonia's rescuers have also responded to calls for everything from an abandoned tarantula to a stork nest fire.
There are usually several things you can do if you come across an animal in need, but Siim Palu, communications manager for the Estonian Rescue Services Agency's Northern Regional Rescue Service, said the simplest option is often to contact an animal shelter.
Even so, he said rescuers regularly respond to calls involving animals in trouble, and sometimes even take them in until a new home is found.
Someone in Tallinn once called emergency services over a tarantula found abandoned in a small terrarium in the middle of the street.
"They did the right thing," Palu stressed. "Lilleküla rescuers went and picked it up and took it to Paljassaare Animal Shelter."
Rescuers have likewise responded to several calls over a fox at Viru Shopping Center recently, including after it had made a den in the mall's parking garage. Rather than tear apart the walls, rescuers waited for the fox to emerge before trapping it and releasing it in the wild.
"As the city expands, it's inevitable that wild animals will eventually make their way into urban areas," Palu said. "If [that fox] comes back a third time, we'll just have to take it further into the woods."
Rescuers have also responded to calls about pythons more than once. Most recently, they caught one slithering around a grassy area outside an apartment building in Mustamäe.
"That one was a story in itself," Palu recalled. A Lilleküla Rescue Brigade member happens to keep exotic pets and builds terrariums as a hobby, and he was the one who ended up rescuing the python loose in Mustamäe.
"He even took it home temporarily until we could find it a new home," the communications chief said.
'We rescue them all'
Rescuers have also handled more typical pets, from rabbits to the stereotypical cats stuck in trees.
"That's a call we get often," Palu confirmed, adding that rescuers can reach the cat with a ladder if it can't or won't come down on its own. "We rescue them all."
Birds pose another recurring challenge, often seasonally. Rescuers have regularly helped storks that fell from their nests.
"One time, a stork nest even caught fire," he recalled. "The rescuers cut the power and rescued the stork."
People can call emergency services at 112 when a large wild animal such as a moose or bear is in trouble or posing a danger in a more densely populated area. For other animal-related calls, the state helpline 1247 can also help.
"Rescuers handle all these calls one way or another anyway," Palu said. "We go to the scene, assess the situation, catch the animal and, if needed, provide temporary shelter until it's found a new home."

Stepaņenko’s father added to Latvia’s list of undesirable persons
