Pope Leo heads to France with AI, apologies for clergy abuse on agenda
VATICAN CITY, Sept 25 - Pope Leo leaves on Friday for a weekend visit to France, where he is hoping to repair the Catholic Church's standing after abuse scandals and is expected to renew calls for global rules on AI development while laying out a vision for Europe's future.
Leo is likely to draw large crowds on the September 25 to 28 visit, which includes stops in Paris, at the famed Catholic shrine in Lourdes, in the southwest, and in Metz, a city on the German border central to the founding of the European Union.
Some 600,000 people have registered to join an outdoor Mass in central Paris with Leo on Saturday, with throngs expected to stretch down the famed Avenue des Champs-Élysées.
"Pope Leo's visit to France has sparked a real tidal wave" of interest, retired French Bishop Marc Stenger told Reuters.
AI AT TOP OF PAPAL AGENDA
Leading Leo's agenda on Friday are speeches to President Emmanuel Macron and other French leaders at the Élysée Palace and to staff at the headquarters of the UN culture and education body, UNESCO, which is facing budget shortfalls after US President Donald Trump withdrew from the agency in 2025.
The first US pope attracted Trump's ire earlier this year after criticizing the Iran war.
Leo, who has made the risks spurred by AI a major concern of his papacy and has called on world leaders for global rules to oversee the industry, is expected to address the issue at UNESCO.
In a speech at the Vatican on Thursday, the pope said AI could benefit humanity, but has introduced "new dangers to security and international peace". He urged global leaders to "govern wisely" in overseeing the technology.
Leo's visit comes as Catholic leaders in France have been at odds with the government over the 2024 enshrining of a right to abortion in the French constitution, a world first, and the passage of a law earlier this year legalizing assisted dying for adults with incurable illnesses.
The Catholic Church teaches that all human life is sacred and opposes abortion, assisted dying and capital punishment.
Leo will also lead a prayer service in Paris on Friday at the restored Notre-Dame cathedral, in the first visit by a pope since a devastating fire nearly destroyed the Gothic masterpiece in 2019.
POPE TO MEET ABUSE SURVIVORS
Leo is the first pope to make an official visit to France in nearly 20 years. Local Church leaders hope the trip will repair the Church's standing after a crushing 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades.
French bishops have since introduced compensation and safeguarding measures, but survivors have continued to press Church leaders to demonstrate accountability.
"Leo bears the immense responsibility of 'declaring enough is enough'," Alain Esquerre, 66, a spokesperson for victims at the Notre-Dame de Bétharram Catholic institution, told Reuters.
The pope will meet seven French victims of abuse by Catholic clergy on Sunday in Lourdes. The Vatican, which usually only issues statements about the pope's meetings with abuse victims afterwards, has not provided further details.
Leo's French tour will culminate in Metz on Sunday with a speech on "the roots of Europe for peace and unity".
Macron has invited leaders from all 27 EU member states to attend but it is unclear who will come.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy may attend, according to media reports. Zelenskiy's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. REUTERS

A week in diplomacy: Trump talks tough, and the world calls his bluff

News analysis
A week in diplomacy: Trump talks tough, and the world calls his bluff
- President Trump aimed to reassert US power with a tough UN speech and a summit with China, but faced growing resistance from world leaders amid his domestic and international challenges.
- The US-Iran war has stalled, raising global energy prices and dividing Trump’s base, while his midterm election outlook dims due to unpopular foreign policies.
- World leaders appear to be preparing for a time when the US president’s influence could begin to wane following the midterms, and with less than two-and-a-half years left in office.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – From his high-profile address to the UN General Assembly to his high-stakes White House summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump this week was looking to reassert himself on the world stage.
But Trump’s diplomatic flurry has done little to dispel the view among many analysts of a president beset by problems at home and abroad. Those include a widening Iran war that has driven up US petrol prices and cratered his approval ratings, while his relations with allies worsen and the AI challenge from China intensifies.
With the limits of his power exposed, Trump has begun facing pushback from world leaders on issues ranging from the crisis in the Middle East to Russia’s war in Ukraine, leaving the impression of a foreign policy agenda that has stalled.
This comes as Trump’s Republican Party faces midterm elections in November that could further constrain him politically.
Even so, Trump’s speech to the United Nations on Sept 22 was a stark reminder of how, since returning to the White House in 2025, he has shaken up the rules-based global order that Washington helped to create from the ashes of World War II.
Standing atop the rostrum of a world body dedicated to peacemaking, he issued a fresh threat to “annihilate” Iran if it does not agree to a deal, defended his coercive approach to OPEC member Venezuela by asserting “to the victor belong the spoils”, and signalled he may not be done deploying the US military to achieve his international aims.
Despite that strident stance, Trump’s talks with Xi on Sept 24 put the US president up against a Chinese counterpart who appeared to be in a stronger position, overseeing a surge in his country’s trade with the world while the US grapples with the economic fallout from the Iran conflict.
Limited results
That was the backdrop for a state visit by Xi that was heavy on pomp and ceremony but light on substance, despite a host of thorny issues such as AI, trade, Taiwan and Iran.
The most tangible outcome appeared limited to a two-month extension of a trade truce, originally due to expire in November, between the world’s two biggest economies.
While Trump showed little interest in publicly airing any differences between the two powers, Chinese state media reported that, behind closed doors, Xi urged him to oppose independence for Taiwan. The democratically governed island claimed by China remains the most contentious topic in relations between Washington and Beijing.
Trump’s seemingly non-confrontational attitude was a far cry from his previously hawkish, tariffs-driven approach, which has been tempered by Beijing’s control over rare earth minerals, a key input for technology and auto manufacturing that Beijing has shown the ability to withhold in retaliation.
“Trump sees himself taking us back to a world where might makes right,” said Brett Bruen, who was a foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration and now heads the Global Situation Room strategic consultancy. “But it’s noteworthy that he goes all wobbly when it comes to Xi Jinping and ascendant Chinese power.”
A White House official rejected the notion that Trump’s foreign policy has hit a wall and said his UN remarks “highlighted his various wins in advancing US interests around the world”, including preventing Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. Tehran has always said its nuclear programme is for peaceful purposes.
Iran war stalemate
Looming over Trump’s packed week of diplomacy was the war with Iran, which he started alongside Israel on Feb 28.
It has dragged on for nearly seven months, disrupting global energy supplies and spreading to other countries in the region, most recently to Yemen and the Red Sea shipping corridor.
Iran’s defiance, despite the economic and military beating it has taken, has become the most intractable foreign policy challenge of Trump’s second term.
Trump used his address at the UN to defend his attack on Iran and to declare that “America is back”, stronger than ever.
But after a string of early foreign policy achievements, including a Gaza ceasefire and the capture of Venezuela’s leader, Trump’s record in his second term in office is increasingly defined by stalemates.
With the Iran war deeply unpopular and dividing Trump’s political base, he could pay a price in the midterm congressional elections when his Republican Party’s control of Congress is at risk.
World leaders appear to be preparing for a time when the US president’s influence could begin to wane following the midterms, and with less than two-and-a-half years left in office.
Most European and Asian allies have already spurned Trump’s demands for assistance in an Iran conflict he launched without consulting them.
At this year’s UN gathering, some US partners took aim at Trump, though mostly without mentioning him by name.
France’s President Emmanuel Macron warned against a global “return to the law of the jungle”, saying countries faced a choice between a world governed by power and coercion, and a “civilised international society”.
In a rebuke to Trump, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva decried foreign interference in his country’s October election and insisted that “we do not need aircraft carriers patrolling our waters. We need cooperation to stem the flow of weapons and money that fuel crime”.
The White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Trump was “not concerned with posturing but about results”, and that some leaders’ public comments did not match what they told the president in private.
Resisting Trump
In another sign of diminished clout, Trump’s effort to pressure Ukraine and Russia to agree to even a limited energy ceasefire failed to gain much traction.
And while Trump touted a deal with Denmark and Greenland for an expanded US military presence in the vast Arctic island, it fell short of his initial demand to “own” the territory and his threat, if necessary, to take it by force from a fellow NATO member.
“A year ago, few countries dared cross Trump,” Ian Bremmer, president of the Eurasia Group, wrote on X. “Now, Canada, Europe, China, Iran, Russia and others are all more willing to say no.”
At one point, Trump himself seemed to wonder how much international sway he actually possessed.
In his speech, he told world leaders he wanted to rebrand AI as “super intelligence”.
“Let’s see if I have any power,” he said. “Maybe I do and maybe I don’t. We’re going to find out pretty soon.” REUTERS

Largely EU-funded Narva defense base delayed by political turmoil
Construction of the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) base in Narva will cost a little over €20 million and be completed six months later than planned, in summer 2028.
The cost rose by €5 million and the delay was caused by political turmoil in the eastern border town's government, which held up the allocation of land.
The base is largely funded by EU money and had originally been due for completion by the end of next year.
Ando Voogma, northern and northeastern portfolio manager at the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK), said construction costs were affected by the war in Iran and higher oil prices, while the EDF's requirements have also been refined.
"The previous situation in Narva politics and the city's administration prevented us from moving forward with the development of the base. I won't comment on all of it here, but until that decision was made, the process was effectively at a standstill. That's where we lost the time," Voogma said.
The land swap has now been completed and the construction contract could be signed as early as October, though main construction work will not begin until next year.
"The Defense Forces will get a command and headquarters building, accommodation buildings, catering facilities, a building for storing and maintaining equipment, a sports hall and the necessary infrastructure," Voogma said.
Until the permanent base is completed, the EDF is tol establish a presence in Narva at a temporary base using containers. Voogma said the procurement for this facility is in its final stages, with a contract possible in the coming weeks. Installation should begin at the end of the year, with the base to be ready in January or February.
The temporary base will accommodate a company-sized unit, while the permanent base once built will have indoor accommodation for up to 500 people plus tents for another 500. Around 200 personnel will be permanently stationed at the main base once it is open.
Of the total cost, about €19 million is to come from the European Union's Cohesion Fund.
Narva's city government was paralyzed for months in spring-summer 2026 due mainly to a power struggle between then-mayor Katri Raik and council chair Mihhail Stalnuhhin. The latter filibustered council sessions for 130 days and blocked no-confidence motions, while the opposition held a rival session and elected its own mayor.
Raik, who had previously been the town's mayor 2020-2021, was ultimately ousted in a no-confidence vote on July 25, and Jaan Toots (Center) took over as mayor. The land swap needed for the defense base finalization to go ahead followed this.

New map shows how oil slicks are smothering our oceans - with one hotspot in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:02:34 UTC
14:02:34 KST

More than 90 per cent of the estimated oil pollution in the oceans occurs within national waters – including in protected areas.
Oil slicks cover an estimated 1.58 million square kilometres of the world’s oceans each year, according to a new satellite analysis that exposes the scale of pollution at sea.
That amounts to an area about three times the size of Spain. Yet, unlike headline-grabbing spills such as the Deepwater Horizon crisis, much of the pollution appears as smaller oil slicks that draw little public attention.
The analysis by conservation technology nonprofit SkyTruth found that ships were linked to around 81 per cent of the oil slicks whose likely source could be identified. Oil tankers and cargo ships were the most common culprits, while offshore oil and gas infrastructure accounted for another 18 per cent of them.
“Oil pollution is a constant, global issue that happens far more often than the spills that make headlines,” says Karl Wuster, chief technology officer at SkyTruth.
Where is ocean oil pollution the worst?
Released on 23 September during Climate Week NYC, the analysis used satellite observations collected between 2023 and 2025 and data from SkyTruth’s Cerulean oil pollution monitoring system.
Researchers used the observations to model annual pollution from vessels and offshore facilities, accounting for differences in satellite coverage and vessel density.
More than 90 per cent of the estimated pollution occurs within national waters, often close to coastlines, they found. Some of the highest concentrations were seen in the Red Sea, Persian Gulf, Mediterranean and Black Sea, as well as waters off West Africa and around Indonesia.
The SkyTruth analysis also identified several repeat polluters.
Researchers repeatedly saw the same 16 vessels alongside oil slicks. Three of them – a Palau-flagged cargo ship, a Russian oil tanker and an Indonesian oil tanker – were spotted near slicks in more than one in five satellite images.
Some offshore facilities were also repeatedly linked to pollution.
Oil slicks appeared in nearly 29 per cent of satellite images of one facility off the coast of Indonesia and in about 24 per cent of another off the coast of Nigeria.
Protected waters are not immune from oil pollution, either. Although around 75 per cent of marine protected areas had lower concentrations of oil slicks than their surrounding waters, pollution was still detected in sensitive habitats – including the critically endangered Rice’s whale habitat in the Gulf of Mexico.
The researchers also warn that the true picture remains unclear, as satellite coverage is limited over the high seas and leaves large expanses of the ocean poorly monitored.
War, accidents and shipwrecks also threaten oceans
Oil pollution is not coming just from shipping and offshore operations.
In August, oil from a carrier struck during the war in the Gulf washed ashore on Iran’s Qeshm Island and reached its protected mangroves. A separate spill from a Russian shadow fleet tanker off Oman spread more than 2,000 square kilometres.
On top of conflicts embroiling the oceans, accidents pose another threat.
A mystery vessel that capsized off Tobago in 2024 covered beaches in oil and triggered a national emergency, while a passenger ferry that ran aground in Sweden a year earlier left a five-kilometre slick of fuel in the Baltic Sea that eventually reached the coast.
Even ships that sank decades ago remain risks to ocean health.
An estimated 8,500 potentially polluting shipwrecks, mostly dating from the two world wars, lie on the ocean floor. Some are already leaking oil as their hulls corrode.

Brussels dials up pressure on Kyiv to speed up reforms amid budget crunch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:00:46 UTC
14:00:46 KST

The European Commission in sounding the alarm over Ukraine's slow pace of reforms, which is complicating access to critical financial assistance.
Brussels is dialling up the pressure on Kyiv to speed up the reforms indispensable for unlocking roughly €20 billion in financial assistance, which the country badly needs as the budget deficit swells and Russia escalates the war.
"It is essential that Ukraine continues to deliver on the reforms and policy conditions jointly agreed with the European Union," a European Commission spokesperson said.
"Their timely implementation is key to enabling the Commission to proceed with the corresponding disbursements as planned."
It comes as the Commission is engaged in intense talks with the Ukrainian authorities to pin down the precise extent of the country's financial shortfall. The International Monetary Fund, which runs a separate assistance line, is also involved.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy initially flaggeda $27 billion (€23.75 billion) gap in the Ministry of Defence, a number that caught EU officials off guard and raised serious questions about its origin.
Separately, the country faces a $32.6 billion hole next year.
As a solution, Zelenskyy proposed to front-load a share of the EU's €90 billion support loan from 2027 to 2026. The loan is split into two halves of €45 billion each, which means any change to the timeline would leave less money for next year.
Zelenskyy also floated the idea of tapping into the immobilised Russian assets, a controversial project that the bloc tried and failed last year.
But Brussels contested the logic and stressed that before requesting additional resources, Ukraine should focus on completing the reforms that it has committed to approving and that are stalled in the Verkhovna Rada, the unicameral parliament.
The reforms are a precondition to accessing two financial envelopes: €13.5 billion from the support loan and €6.45 billion from the Ukraine Facility.
A combined payment of €2.9 billion was greenlighted on Thursday. However, the slow legislative pace has delayed a second one worth €3.9 billion.
The situation prompted Commissioners Valdis Dombrovskis and Marta Kos to send a letter to Ruslan Stefanchuk, the speaker of the Rada, alerting him of the stakes at play.
"Timely adoption of the necessary legislation is essential to secure available EU financing, to sustain momentum on Ukraine's EU accession path and to strengthen Ukraine's economy and public finances," they wrote.
"Continued dialogue with the European Commission remains crucial to ensure that the final law adopted is compliant with the EU requirements."
The letter, seen by Euronews, includes an annex of reforms "pending adoption" that Brussels wants approved and implemented in the short term.
Some laws, such as those related to SME insolvency, civil service and VAT simplification, are already under consideration in the Rada. Others, such as state aid, anti-money laundering and the disciplinary system for prosecutors, have not yet been submitted.
One piece of legislation, designed to remove the duty-free exemption for international parcels, has proven particularly contentious among Ukrainian legislators due to the popularity of Chinese marketplaces Temu and AliExpress in the country.
The bill was rejected twice in the Rada, earning a rebuke from Brussels. It was adopted on first reading last week, but another reading is still needed.
Further reforms are required to unlock the remaining €17 billion available for this year. The Rada is currently on recess until mid-October, though the speaker has said he is ready to call an extraordinary session as soon as the legislation is ready.
Ursula von der Leyen raised the issue of reforms when she met with Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York earlier this week.
Following a Bloomberg report that described the meeting as "tense", Zelenskyy said the talks with the Commission chief had been "absolutely positive".
The Ukrainian president asked Brussels to be more flexible about the timeline and take into consideration that the Rada's activity has been affected by airstrikes.
"Ukraine has demonstrated a remarkable capacity to pursue and implement far-reaching reforms in the face of Russia's war of aggression for more than four years. We recognise these considerable efforts, undertaken under extraordinarily difficult circumstances," the Commission spokesperson said in response to Zelenskyy's comments.
"At the same time, we continue to recall the importance of maintaining the momentum of reforms."

‘We wanted to prove we didn’t need air conditioning’: the airport cooled by natural ventilation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:00:41 UTC
14:00:41 KST

At the arrivals terminal at Roland Garros airport on Réunion island, visitors are greeted by floor-to-ceiling windows framing the lush green mountains of the French Indian Ocean territory.
What they may have also expected was the icy chill of air conditioning; this island just off Madagascar sits in the tropical zone to the south of the equator. But instead, the terminal is cooled by a light tropical breeze, the result of natural ventilation built into its unique design.
The genesis of the project was in 2016, as part of a wider effort by airport management to reduce its carbon dioxide emissions. Marc Delanoë, who was then leading the airport’s environmental and energy team, was determined from the beginning that the new arrivals terminal, which was being built completely from scratch, would not use air conditioning.
“I took on the responsibility to prove to my management that not using air conditioning was feasible,” said Delanoë, now the airport’s sustainable development director. “So, from the start, we never thought of this building having air conditioning being an option. It was a risky bet, but the further we went with our studies, the more we realised that we were right.”
The roof of the terminal, which opened in 2024, curves upwards from each of the rectangular building’s long sides in gentle waves. But, instead of meeting in the middle, the roofs end abruptly to form a “canyon”. The creation of an area of low pressure funnels wind into the building through vents on each side that are adjusted depending on the weather conditions.
Ceiling fans with a 7.5-metre (24.6ft) diameter help to circulate the air. In the 30C (86F) humid heat of Réunion’s wet summers, which last from around November to April, the resulting breeze reduces the perceived temperature by four to five degrees, to almost the same level usually set for air conditioning.
Less air is allowed to flow in during the island’s dry winters, when the coastal daytime temperature falls to 25C and below. During a cyclone, the entire building is closed up.
The building’s lead architect, AIA Life Designers, said it wanted to challenge the assumption that adjusting temperature was the only way for humans to cope with heat.
“It is precisely this pitfall – understanding summer comfort solely through the lens of indoor temperature – that we want to dismantle, a pitfall that traps us in the logic of air conditioning as the only answer to comfort requirements,” said Éric Bussolino, the firm’s engineering and environment director.
“Our objective is to maintain an indoor air temperature identical to the outdoor temperature while generating an airflow of 1 metre per second to reduce the perceived temperature for passengers.”
AIA, chosen for its expertise in designing airport buildings, partnered with a local architect, Olivier Brabant, who had the necessary expertise of designing buildings for the island’s tropical maritime climate, Delanoë said.
Local architects were already using natural ventilation on the island, in everything from offices and libraries to a university amphitheatre designed by Brabant. “We simply had to change the scale,” Delanoë said.
“You have to channel the air, play with the elements … That’s exactly what our ancestors did on La Réunion,” he said. “They built houses according to the direction of the wind, with a central corridor, and they opened the windows or closed the doors depending on the amount of air that they wanted to let in. If they were cold, they closed them; if they were hot, they opened them.”
Building the arrivals terminal cost €75m , of which €15m went on a new baggage sorting system and €60m on the building, said Delanoë. Since opening two years ago, the airport has saved €150,000 a year in energy bills, he said. AIA said this amounted to savings of about 60% compared with an air-conditioned building, while carbon emissions were lower by a factor of eight.
Delphine Robert, who leads the local tourism board’s welcome team, works in the terminal once a week and said she preferred it to other offices.
“It’s very airy. It’s comfortable – a lot of light, the ventilation is optimal,” she said. “I find it better working in this building, because I am often sick. And that’s the result of air conditioning, which is very strong in offices. So that’s why it’s more pleasant to work in a building where the air circulates, but it is natural.”
The lessons from the terminal’s natural ventilation will be harder to apply in large, polluted cities in mainland Europe, said Delanoë. “You will concentrate the pollutants inside – it doesn’t work,” he said. “We are lucky, we are on an island, there is no pollution around.”
Continental Europe, which is struggling to adapt to heatwaves being made ever more severe by the climate crisis, would also have to eschew air conditioning to make use of natural ventilation, Delanoë said.
“The problem is that if you have air conditioning at home and you have air conditioning in your car, when you get to the office, if you don’t have air conditioning, you’re going to be hot, he said.
“That is to say that if you reduce air conditioning throughout your life … when you get to 30 degrees in the office, you won’t be hot. In La Réunion, people are used to 30 degrees.”

Andy Burnham talks about ‘public control’ of the utilities but it’s a minefield. We can lead him through it | Will Hutton and Andy Haldane
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:00:41 UTC
14:00:41 KST

Andy Burnham came to power promising greater “public control” over the UK’s utilities, such as water and energy. His reasons for doing so were to cut what is described as the “privatisation premium” paid for public services by consumers, and to improve their quality. The plight of the stricken Thames Water exemplifies the scale of those problems.
Yet two months on, the government has failed to provide any real clarification of what it means by “public control”, beyond stating that this may not necessarily mean public ownership of these companies. One option under discussion is to build a network of regional political bodies to hold water companies to account. But such a step would not, by itself, confer the control needed to meet the prime minister’s objectives. Meanwhile, in a febrile environment for borrowers, uncertainty about “public control” is imposing real costs, both on those companies affected and the UK government.
As a result of this uncertainty, bond issues by utility companies that would have financed investment are being deferred and their costs are rising. Thames Water is in a state of suspended animation, in part because no one knows what its ultimate proposed ownership and regulatory structure will be. With public ownership not having been ruled out, its potentially significant cost is another factor adding to pressures in UK government debt markets.
In the face of these mounting costs, there is a strong case for the government to quickly clarify its intentions. What should it mean by public control of utilities, in order to secure the best possible services at a reasonable cost?
Good governance typically involves seeking an appropriate balance between incentives and expertise. For public services, this means a set of incentives well aligned with the interests of customers – namely, the general public – while having the expertise to deliver services effectively.
This underlines the perils of the privatised model. For example, Thames Water is owned by a consortium of investors, including highly leveraged hedge funds. This governance structure has no shortage of high-quality financial expertise. Unfortunately, this highly “innovative” (and leveraged) financing structure is singularly ill-suited to a low-risk public utility; investor incentives are horribly misaligned with the public good.
Full nationalisation faces the opposite problems. In this scenario, the company’s incentives would be aligned, by statute, with the public good. But without commercial discipline and expertise, there are fewer reasons to expect it to be run expertly and efficiently. Past experience – from British Rail to British Steel to British Leyland – demonstrates this risk.
For public utilities, then, “public control” should mean seeking governance structures with aims that are aligned with those of the general public. This should not be mistaken to mean that the public sector itself should necessarily play a central role in owning or operating the company. This erroneous belief is costing the UK (and the utilities) dear, and needs dismissing once and for all.
Having done so, what alternative governance structures strike a better balance than the extremes of nationalisation or privatisation? Aligning the incentives of utilities with those of the public could be done most easily and effectively by turning them into public-benefit companies with a primary, constitutional objective of delivering high-quality services, with profitability subordinate to that broader aim.
This has the advantage that it could be introduced within the current ownership and licensing regime. While not without potential legal challenge, in principle it would not require expensive compensation to shareholders who have already considered a level of regulatory risk when making their investment. The government itself could take a special or “golden share” at a nominal cost of £1, of the type used to maintain BAE Systems and Rolls-Royce (and latterly Royal Mail) in domestic ownership.
Importantly, the utility companies would go beyond “benefit” or B Corps (obliged to display high standards of social and environmental performance, transparency and accountability), and instead would have more demanding governance requirements, tailored to their needs and standards. These could be taken off the shelf – for example, Ofgem already requires energy companies to comply with certain international environmental standards – or alternatively, stakeholders could work together to develop industry-specific standards.
With this core structure, there are various ways the governance regime could be enhanced. For example, utilities could be required to have a minimum fraction of their shares publicly listed and traded, which would help transparency and market discipline. Publicly quoted utilities have tended to outperform the alternatives across all metrics.
To strengthen further public incentives, executive pay could be linked to public-benefit outcomes. This could also be achieved by requiring each utility to create an independent customer group and incorporating its views in all dimensions of the companies’ decision-making. There is good evidence across the utilities of customer involvement improving outcomes.
Lastly, this would imply a paradigm shift in the culture and architecture of regulation, currently alternating between regulatory capture and mutual distrust, which has palpably failed. Public-benefit utilities would be constitutionally obliged to want the same outcomes as public-interest regulators. Open-book accounting would be routine as regulator and regulated both prioritised the delivery of high-quality public services.
There is an urgent need for the government to clarify its intention around public control before uncertainty imposes further costs on fragile utilities and public finances alike. A public-benefit structure would, we believe, achieve a much better balance between public-good incentives and operational expertise at a much lower cost for consumers, investors and the government. It would be measured in single pounds rather than hundreds of millions. Burnham won power by daring to be different. Daring to be different – within practical bounds – should also inform his approach to public control of utilities.
- 
  Will Hutton is a journalist and political economist and host of the We Society podcast. Andy Haldane is president of the British Chambers of Commerce and a former chief economist of the Bank of England

Benjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for Belgian buns | The sweet spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:00:41 UTC
14:00:41 KST

Belgian buns are among a dying breed of bakes, forgotten about in favour of pretty cinnamon and cardamom buns and creative laminated doughs. I’d love to see more of these old-school, classic treats in bakeries, not least because they’re really simple to make. There are no twists or extra frills, just soft, buttery dough swirled with lemon curd and juicy sultanas. The icing glaze and cherry on top are essential, though, for maximum eating pleasure.
Belgian buns
Prep 5 min
 Prove 2 hr 30 min+
 Cook 1 hr 15 min
 Makes 8
320g strong white bread flour, plus extra for dusting
  40g caster sugar
  1½ tsp instant yeast
  ¼ tsp fine sea salt
  100ml milk, warmed
50ml water
  2 large eggs, 1 beaten for the egg wash
Zest of 1 lemon
  40g unsalted butter, softened
3-4 tbsp lemon curd 
  70g sultanas 
 For the glaze
120g icing sugar
  1-2 tbsp water
  8 glacé cherries
Put the flour, sugar, yeast and salt in a large bowl or stand mixer, and mix briefly to combine. pour in the milk, water, one egg, and the lemon zest, and stir until the mixture comes together into a shaggy dough. Knead by hand for eight to 10 minutes (or in a stand mixer for about five minutes), until you have a soft dough, then leave to rest uncovered for five minutes.
Pat the dough flat on a lightly floured work surface and smush the butter all over the top. Fold the dough over itself, then knead again; it’s a messy job, but use a dough scraper to scrape the surface often and it will eventually all come together. Once the butter is completely incorporated and the dough looks silky and shiny, put it in a lightly greased bowl, cover and leave to prove in a warm place for two to three hours, until puffy and nearly doubled in size.
Knock the air out of the dough, then tip it out on to a lightly floured work surface. Roll it out to a roughly 35cm x 25cm rectangle, then spoon the lemon curd on top and spread it out evenly. Sprinkle the sultanas all over.
Starting from one long side, roll the dough into a log and put it seam-side down on a work surface. Use a sharp, serrated knife to slice the log into eight pieces, then arrange these on a large, lined baking tray. Cover loosely with clingfilm and prove again for 25-35 minutes, until puffy.
Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Brush the tops and sides of the buns with a little egg wash, then bake for 10 minutes. Turn down the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and bake for another 10-15 minutes, until the buns are golden brown. Remove and leave to cool while you make the icing.
Put the icing sugar in a bowl and stir in the water a tablespoon at a time, until it’s a thick but pourable consistency. Spoon a dollop of icing on to each bun, letting it fall into the folds, then top with a cherry. Leave the icing to set before eating.

Capital gains tax: how it works, benefits and pitfalls of another hike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:00:40 UTC
14:00:40 KST

Recent data from HMRC showed revenue from CGT was up 89% in 2024-25 after changes in tax policy. Photograph: Mykhailo Polenok/AlamyView image in fullscreenRecent data from HMRC showed revenue from CGT was up 89% in 2024-25 after changes in tax policy. Photograph: Mykhailo Polenok/AlamyExplainerCapital gains tax: how it works, benefits and pitfalls of another hikeIncreasing the rate of CGT is one of the tax levers available to chancellor as he considers revenue-raising optionsCapital gains tax (CGT) has been widely cited as a possible revenue-raiser as the chancellor, John Healey, prepares to deliver a tough budget next month. How does it work, and what are the pros and cons of raising it further?What is CGT?When you sell an asset – whether it’s a share, a business, or a buy-to-let property – you pay capital gains on the uplift in its value since you bought it.It’s not quite that simple: you can reduce your CGT bill by deducting losses made on other investments, and the costs of investing in improving a property. But essentially, it’s a tax on the profits realised when an asset is sold.The rate of CGT is now 18% for basic-rate taxpayers and 24% for higher-rate taxpayers. There’s an even higher rate, of 32%, for City fund managers who take their earnings as a share of profits in a controversial system called “carried interest”.All those rates have gone up significantly since Labour came to power in 2024, as Rachel Reeves, the previous chancellor, chose to tax wealth more heavily – the basic rate was previously 10%, for example.Recent data from HMRC showed the take from CGT was up 89% in 2024-25 as a result of these and other changes, which have also included cuts to the tax-free personal allowance for CGT, begun under the last Conservative government.Who is calling for CGT to rise?Thinktanks and politicians across the left have argued that it is unfair to tax the gains from holding an asset at a lower rate than a salary that has been earned by working. (The basic rate of income tax is 20%, for example.)Another argument – advanced by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) – is that it distorts behaviour: incentivising people to hold on to assets inside a business, for example.Back in May, when Wes Streeting had his eye on the Labour leadership, he called CGT “the wealth tax that works” – in contrast with the prospect of setting up an entirely new tax.Given Streeting’s position towards the right of the Labour party, his backing for higher rates of the key tax underlined how widespread the view is within the party.The first secretary, Louise Haigh, argued in an article in the journal Renewal, before she took on her powerful role in Andy Burnham’s cabinet, that CGT rates should be “brought closer to income tax rates”.She said such a change was necessary to “shift the taxation burden away from punishing work, and towards unproductive capital accumulation which does little to grow the everyday economy”.Other advocates of equalising CGT and income tax rates include the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation at Warwick University (CenTax), the Resolution Foundation, and the TUC.What are the downsides?Business lobby groups argue that higher rates of CGT would disincentivise just the kind of productive investment the UK needs to generate stronger economic growth.As Lena Levy, the deputy director of policy at the British Chamber of Commerce, puts it: “Speculation over changes to capital gains tax in next month’s budget is only adding to the huge uncertainty for people looking to invest, grow or sell a business. The UK’s capital gains taxes are already above the OECD average of 20%.”The prospect of another rise – along with a slew of other tax reforms since 2024 – is also cited as one reason that high net worth individuals might choose to leave the UK.And there would be fears, too, that some wealthy individuals would be able to dodge the new higher rates through other forms of tax avoidance, undermining it as a revenue-raising strategy.Are the pitfalls avoidable?Fans of equalisation say yes: Prof Arun Advani, of CenTax, says there’s no point just raising CGT rates without reforming the “base” – the rules that determined what it is charged on.He suggests a package of reforms, to be implemented alongside a rise in CGT rates.As well as making the system fairer, the aim of these would be to prevent potential revenues leaking out – with an “exit tax” levied when wealthy individuals move elsewhere, for example, and by removing the exemption that now applies to inherited assets.And the changes would also be intended to incentivise productive investment better, by including an “investment allowance” that would mean CGT was only paid on gains made over and above the general rate of asset inflation across the economy.These and other CGT reforms have been widely discussed – a version of them was recommended in the IFS’s authoritative Mirrlees review of the UK tax system way back in 2011, for example.But in 2024, Reeves opted for the simpler halfway house of just raising the rates. Healey could do the same, or wait until the budget next spring to undertake more comprehensive reform.What are Healey’s other tax-raising options?The most straightforward would be the big money-raisers – income tax, national insurance or VAT. Income tax is expected to raise about £330bn this year, for example; capital gains tax roughly £22bn.Burnham has ruled out breaking the Labour manifesto promise to leave these untouched, however, so if Healey wants to raise taxes he would have to look elsewhere.Other much-discussed possibilities include a bank windfall tax, or tweaking Reeves’s upcoming “mansion tax” so that it applies to more homes, and/or at a higher rate.Does he have to raise taxes?It depends on how far off course the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) believes Healey is from meeting Labour’s fiscal rules, and how slim a margin against those rules he is willing to accept.And that depends crucially on how the OBR interprets a slew of recent data – in particular, eye-wateringly high energy prices that have also spooked government bond markets and driven up the cost of borrowing.Treasury insiders suggest the budget will be relatively narrowly focused – on fiscal devolution, for example – with some big decisions, such as when the UK should aim to be spending 3% of GDP on defence, deferred into 2027.But a particularly bleak fiscal forecast, or a decision to take more drastic action to cushion consumers from looming energy bill rises, could yet prompt a more radical statement on 28 October. In that case, CGT may seem like an obvious lever to pull.Explore more on these topicsCapital gains taxTax and spendingTaxJohn HealeyBudgetLabourEconomic policyexplainersShareReuse this content

Skylarks and sandwich terns among new birdies on reserve created from ‘boring old golf course’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:00:40 UTC
14:00:40 KST

There is no chance of a birdie or an eagle any more. But there are skylarks, short-eared owls, avocets and curlew.
Sandilands, a former golf course on the Lincolnshire coast, has been transformed by the National Trust into a 2km-long nature reserve with wetlands, wading pools, rough grassland and coastal scrub.
The new reserve opens to the public on Saturday but the birds have already flocked in: little ringed plovers and avocets nested this summer as soon as fairways and bunkers were turned into shallow pools and islands for shore and marsh birds. Marsh harriers have been hunting over the reserve, with water rail, sandwich terns and spotted redshank also flying in.
“It’s been super-exciting to see the transformation from a boring old golf course – sorry golfers,” said Katie Scott, an area ranger for the National Trust at Sandilands. “It was quite flat and the grass was cut when it was a golf course but now with all the mounds and undulations – and just by not mullering the grass – so many new plant species have come up. It just goes to show that nature is always there waiting to push through.”
Scott said there were a few local people who mourned the loss of the course, which was founded in 1894, but the private club went into liquidation in 2018 before the trust stepped in, ensuring the coastal site was not developed or turned into a caravan park. What was once a site only accessible to a few hundred golf club members is now open to everyone.
Sandilands is on the edge of Mablethorpe, a deprived seaside town, and the trust has been deluged with offers of support and help from local people, with 50 already volunteering on the new reserve.
“As soon as the office cabin was put on site, people came knocking saying they wanted to get involved,” said Anstee Stratigou, the community, participation and volunteering manager for the trust. “We’ve worked so hard with the local community talking about the work we’re doing and encouraging them.”
One volunteer, Sue Cushen, said: “What’s happened over the last few years here is remarkable and it is going to get better. I grew up around here and it was a pretty ordinary golf course to be fair. Now we’ve got really nice nature on this part of the coast and the birds are coming back. It’s great. It’s also hard work.”
As with many nature restoration projects, annual “weeds” such as thistle and ragwort are the first to colonise the disturbed ground and Cushen and fellow volunteers have spent much of the summer hand-pulling ragwort, “our nemesis” as she called it, to keep it under control.
Some local people complained about the number of thistles on the new nature reserve but Scott explained that they would boom for a year or two before being replaced by a natural cycle of perennial grasses and flowers. Green hay from a nearby Lincolnshire Wildlife Trust reserve has been spread to establish local native species including wild carrot, yarrow, yellow rattle and red clover.
“We left the thistles this year and we had a massive explosion of painted lady butterflies,” said Scott.
The coastal reserve, which includes a timber-framed community centre and cafe and an accessible pathway weaving through the long site, was originally coastal wetlands before the golf course was established, and as soon as shallow ponds were dug, reed and reed-mace sprouted up naturally.
The pools and marshes of Sandilands will become a mecca for birdwatchers with the reserve sitting within the internationally important “East Atlantic flyway”, one of Europe’s major migration routes. Every year, thousands of birds travel along Britain’s east coast between Arctic and northern European breeding grounds and warmer wintering areas farther south. Rare migrants blown into Sandilands will find shelter in some of the 36,000 native shrubs, including sea-buckthorn, blackthorn and gorse, planted by the volunteers.
The transformation was funded thanks to £2m from Mablethorpe Towns Fund, along with £1.5m from National Highways and £200,000 from the government’s shared prosperity fund, as delivered by East Lindsey district council.
Highland ponies will be introduced to the site to provide conservation grazing and the trust hopes to reintroduce the rare natterjack toad once the pond habitat is ready.
While the Guardian visited, a skein of pink-footed geese flew over, and birders reported seeing black-tailed godwits on the site, with gannets, red-throated divers and shearwaters passing just out to sea.
Martin, a day tripper visiting the new reserve from Melton Mowbray with his dog, Alma, said: “Walking between the pools and seeing all the wildlife is lovely, it really is. It’s so peaceful.”

‘Devastating’: council rejects Frome residents’ bid for regeneration project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:00:40 UTC
14:00:40 KST

A bold bid by residents of a progressive town in the English West Country who raised almost £1m to create what could have been the UK’s largest community-led regeneration project is in tatters.
More than 1,000 residents of Frome in Somerset had clubbed together with the aim of building homes, workspaces, a riverside park and a lido on a brownfield area in their town centre.
But rather than selling the 5-hectare (12-acre) site to the community-led Mayday Saxonvale project, Somerset council has agreed a deal with a real estate investment company based in Soho, central London.
The announcement of the preferred bidder’s identity at a packed meeting in Frome town hall was greeted with shouts of “who?”, “shame on you” and “stitch-up”. Some of those who had worked on the Mayday project for more than five years were in tears.
The Liberal Democrat-led council said it hoped the prospective owners would work with Frome residents but admitted the sale was unconditional.
Some local people fear that rather than providing the sort of mixed development with a generous proportion of affordable homes they envisaged, the prospective owners will be free to build expensive riverside houses and lucrative accommodation for elderly people.
“It’s devastating news,” said Sara Butler, a Frome town councillor. “So many people have worked so hard on trying to ensure this site is developed with the best interests of Frome. It’s been a town-wide mission and this is a slap in the face.”
Frome is famed for its independent, renegade spirit and the leader of the town council, Fiona Barrows, said the idea of the Mayday plan had been to create homes that local people could afford and places where they could work.
She said the town council would work with the prospective owners but criticised the transparency of the process. “Saxonvale is simply too important to Frome to be treated as an ordinary land disposal,” she said.
Susie Jenkins Temple, who had got together with friends to put money up for the Mayday project, said it had been an extraordinary effort. “Across Frome, people reached into their own pockets because they believe this place matters,” she said.
Many local people suspect Somerset council’s executive had decided who to sell the site to before it met at Frome town hall on Wednesday to hear last-minute appeals from the townsfolk.
The way the identity of the successful bidder was revealed added to residents’ suspicions that the meeting was little more than a PR exercise.
Within two minutes of Somerset council announcing the identity of the preferred bidder – Newcore Capital – at the end of an impassioned meeting, it had issued a full press release on the deal. Less than 15 minutes later, Newcore released its own press release.
Paul Oster, an executive director of Mayday Saxonvale community benefit society, said the chance to create the UK’s largest community-led regeneration project had been lost.
The council argued it could not be sure Mayday had the full funds for the project. However, as well as the money invested by local people, Mayday had secured £1.2m from the social impact fund Resonance – the largest investment it had offered. Mayday said it had other investors interested. It is thought the agreed sale price for land was about £3m.
Jon Rolls, the head of developing communities at Resonance, said that without local ownership there was a “real danger” that Saxonvale would become another regeneration scheme done to a community, rather than by and with that community.
He said: “The people of Frome haven’t simply expressed an opinion. They organised behind this vision and invested their own money.”
Other Newcore projects include a 3.2-hectare (8-acre) site in east London, where the plan is to build a new supermarket, community health centre and childcare facilities alongside 1,047 new homes, and a care home and retirement living apartments on a brownfield site in Cambridge.
In its statement, Newcore said it was committed to working closely with the people of Frome “to understand local aspirations, discuss the opportunities and constraints and work collaboratively to develop the plans in partnership with the community”.
It added: “Emerging proposals are likely to include a range of new homes, intergenerational accommodation, community facilities including space for local artists, open space and new car parking.”

Which European passports are the strongest for visa-free travel?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:00:18 UTC
14:00:18 KST

A new ranking compares passport strength based on how many destinations European travellers can visit visa-free, with an ETA or by obtaining a visa on arrival.
Travel can be stressful enough at the best of times, without having to add visa applications to the mix. Wrestling with lengthy paperwork and additional fees on top of air and hotel fares – who needs that hassle? That’s where visa-free travel helps ease that burden.
A study by Passport Reports has surveyed passport strength by country and how many destinations travellers can go to visa-free, with an electronic travel authorisation (ETA) or by obtaining a visa on arrival. The ranking also measured the number of destinations a passport holder needs to obtain a visa prior to entry.
In the latest ranking, two European countries feature in the top five, after the UAE and Singapore, which take first and second place respectively, while Malaysia is fourth.
Ranked as the strongest European passport for visa-free travel, and third overall, Spain was given a mobility score of 174. Spanish travellers have access to 121 countries visa-free and a further 42 can be visited with a visa on arrival. However, an ETA is needed in 11 countries and holders also require a visa to enter 24.
Meanwhile, Luxembourg scored 173 for mobility. In fifth place globally, passport holders can travel to 122 destinations visa-free and a further 41 countries are accessible via visa on arrival. An ETA is needed to visit 10 countries and a visa is required in 25.
Belgium and France rank equal sixth, with each scoring 173 for mobility. Their passport holders can access 121 countries visa-free and 41 with a visa on arrival. While an ETA is needed to 11 countries and visas required to 25.
Also scoring 173 for mobility, six European countries share seventh place: Denmark, Finland, Germany, Italy, Netherlands and Sweden. Passport holders from these six nations can travel to 120 destinations visa-free, 42 with a visa on arrival, ETA for 11, and visas required for 25.

LRT English Newsletter: America is back, for now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

LRT English Newsletter – September 25, 2026.
American troops are coming back to Lithuania following prolonged discussions over their future in the Baltic states. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda told Fox News he personally pleaded with his American counterpart, Donald Trump, to keep troops in the Baltics.
The announcement comes amid a spike in activity about the allegedly impending doom in the Baltics. The Danish intelligence services issued the bluntest warning yet, saying there was a low but growing risk of Russia moving troops into a NATO country along the lines of the earlier little-green-men scenario in Ukraine.
Interestingly, Baltic officials have been more careful in their warnings after spending much of the past decade calling out the growing threat from Russia. Their caution against panic is increasingly contrasting with the growing alarmism in the West, with Baltic officials saying panic would play into the Kremlin’s hands. There’s also nothing to suggest an immediate apocalypse anyway, they say.
For example, much of the international media found out about Lithuania’s wartime plan to evacuate vulnerable civilians (published in July), causing a flurry of reports. Vilnius also had such a plan in place from 2025. In any case, the Polish defence minister responded to a journalist’s question about it, confirming that Warsaw would help with evacuation if need be.
POTASH IS BACK?
Next to the announcement of two American battalions headed to Lithuania (and more troops to Estonia) came Trump’s message of a US deal to buy fertiliser from Belarus. Visibly, it caught Vilnius off guard, with officials saying they had no prior knowledge of any such deal and reminded of the existing EU sanctions that ban the transit of Belarusian potash via Lithuania. Recall, the US envoy to Belarus previously called on Lithuania to renew the transit of fertilisers – a cash cow for the regime – that travelled via Klaipėda.
Lithuanian officials maintain that nothing has changed in Belarus that would warrant a sanctions rethink. For example, smuggling balloons forced a brief closure of the Vilnius airport, again.
DRONE DEFENCES
Baltic states are seeking 500 million euros from Brussels to help with drone defences, saying the eastern EU members bear the brunt of Russia’s drone threats. Even as individual countries are footing the bill for beefing up defences, they need more to shield the skies over Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania – even if it’s naive to think that an airspace can be fully protected, one official said. The drone incidents are also prompting more Lithuanians to stock up on emergency go-bags.
MIGRATION, ISLAM, POPULISM
Intelligence services said there was no sign of the Muslim community posing a threat, but the migration topic is becoming increasingly politicised, with questions posed over the future of Lithuania’s growing muslim immigrant community.
This is prompting politicians to react as politicians do. The social democrat interior minister, who was formerly a member of a far-right party, announced Lithuania would be closing migration centres in some Muslim countries over an alleged terrorism threat.
Granted, other officials said, Lithuania needs to review its migration approach, with the country living through a period of increased immigration after decades of outward migration and even depopulation. The rising immigration, as well as the populism in response, is driving fears of radicalisation in society as a whole. A case in point: a Quran was burned on a Vilnius street.
EDITOR’S PICKS:
– Lithuania’s local elections have been confirmed for March 7, 2027.
– Lithuania mulls cutting public transport costs to address rising fuel prices.
– Politicians are having to defend against criticism for holding a 50,000-euro party at the Defence Ministry.
– Lithuania’s EU presidency begins in 100 days (ish).
– Lithuania will not boycott Eurovision over the Israel question.
– LRT back on agenda: the supervisory and politicised council issued a warning to the general director over an earlier decision that was backed by the very same council. If the director receives another warning, she’s out.

Macron says Russian drones could target sites in France
As reported by an Ukrinform correspondent, Emmanuel Macron said this in a joint interview with TF1 and France 2.
“Some information points to 300,000 additional troops. In any case, this is a scenario that seems plausible to us. There are several indications that Russia is preparing for this,” he said.
According to the French President, the Russian authorities were waiting for the State Duma elections to conclude before potentially making such a decision.
Macron stressed that the threat concerns not only Ukraine, against which Russia has been waging war since February 2022, and in fact since 2014, but Europe as a whole, where hostile actions have increased in recent weeks.
“Today, we need to be very clear: Russia considers Europe to be Ukraine’s strategic rear. Since Europeans are helping Ukrainians, while Ukrainians are striking oil refineries and other sensitive facilities in Russia to force it to end the war, Moscow believes that Europe could also become a target,” he explained.
Asked whether Russian drones could attack an aircraft or an airport in France, Macron said: “Yes.”
At the same time, he rejected media reports that U.S. intelligence had warned Paris that Russia was preparing a drone attack which could be launched from the sea against southern France.
“We can refute this information. The CIA did not inform French services of preparations for such an attack,” the Macron said.
He noted that France had not recorded attacks similar to the incident in Leipzig, Germany, where explosive-laden drones were discovered in early August and, according to available information, were intended to attack Ukrainian aircraft.
“The attack in Leipzig was extremely serious. It failed, but if it had succeeded, there would have been deaths on German territory. Yes, this is war. Period. These are hostile actions that can kill,” the French President stressed.
According to Macron, Russia has been attacking European countries in the information and cyber domains for years, and its actions are now becoming increasingly dangerous.
“Russia is multiplying hostile, and sometimes criminal, actions against European states,” he said.
Speaking about the situation on the battlefield, Macron noted that at the current pace of Russia’s advance, it would take another one and a half to two years to attempt to capture the entire Donbas, at the cost of enormous losses and further suffering for Ukraine.
“Our responsibility is to help Ukraine resist. That is what we have been doing from the very beginning,” the French leader stressed.
He recalled that during his recent meeting with Volodymyr Zelensky, a contract was signed to supply Ukraine with additional radars, and an agreement was reached on the supply of interceptor missiles to strengthen Ukrainian air defense.

Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
04:51:00 UTC
13:51:00 KST

Nepal paying the price of climate change, PM says
September 25, 2026
Four weeks after catastrophic flash floods ravaged Nepal, the small Himalayan country's prime minister stood at the podium of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) to warn leaders about the impact of a warming world.
"I wish I could stand here today simply to speak about development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation. Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions," Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in his UNGA address Thursday.
Nepal's leader calls for cooperation to protect the Himalayas
The Nepalese leader stressed that the perils of climate change transcend national borders as he made a case for greater international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas.
"The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet's life-support system," Shah said, proposing the establishment of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, which he said would be led by Nepal, India and China.
Shah elaborated that the mechanism would help countries share satellite data and expertise, as well as monitor glacial lakes that pose a threat. He also called for stronger joint early-warning systems and coordinated, cross-border assistance in the event of a disaster.
"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information," the prime minister said.
Nepal paying 'colossal' price for climate change
Shah noted that his country contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
"We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it," he said, adding that he was not blaming any individual nation or continent.
"We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield. We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity," Shah said.
Grants, not loans, necessary for flood recovery
The Nepalese prime minister emphasized the principles of responsibility, reparation and resilience as he called for grant-based support rather than loans.
Shah said vulnerable nations should not be forced to take on additional debt to recover from climate catastrophes.
"When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants. We need adequate grant-based support from the world," he said.
The 36-year-old Shah was the youngest head of government to speak at the 81st session of the UNGA.
Nepal-Tibet floods — the deadly 'Himalayan tsunami'
On August 26, a glacier collapsed near the border between Nepal and China's Tibet Autonomous Region, unleashing landslides and a flash flood that ripped through downstream valleys.
In the days after the disaster, the world watched powerful images of the widespread destruction emerge from Nepal.
Entire villages were flattened. In other visuals, people trapped in hydropower tunnels deep within the Himalayas were seen crawling away a thick sludge of mud to reach rescuers.
Over 6,000 people are still reported to be missing, with search and recovery efforts still ongoing.

Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin told world leaders at the UN General Assembly on Thursday that the international community had failed Palestinians, warning that continued violence and settlement expansion were undermining prospects for a lasting peace.
Addressing the 81st session of the General Assembly in New York, Martin said the international legal order was under “tremendous strain” and described the denial of fundamental human rights as one of the defining challenges of the era.
“We, the collective international community, have failed Palestine,” Martin said, referring to the continuing suffering of civilians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Martin said the first phase of the Gaza peace plan agreed by Israel and Hamas last October was welcome but had not fundamentally changed conditions on the ground.
He pointed to continued Israeli attacks, restrictions on humanitarian assistance and the ongoing suffering of civilians.
Martin warns two-state solution is being eroded
He also condemned the expansion of illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, saying developments there were damaging prospects for a just and lasting peace.
“What we are witnessing on the ground is a deliberate attempt by some to make the prospect of a two-state solution impossible,” Martin said, citing statements attributed to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu opposing the establishment of a Palestinian state and Israel’s approval of development in the E1 area.
The UN secretary-general has similarly warned that illegal settlement expansion and other developments in the occupied Palestinian territory are eroding the conditions needed for a viable Palestinian state and called for renewed efforts toward a two-state solution.
Ireland backs international legal accountability
Martin also reaffirmed Ireland’s support for the International Criminal Court, saying there could be “no impunity for war crimes” and calling for measures aimed at undermining the court to be withdrawn.
His remarks came amid broader debate at the UN over Gaza, Palestinian statehood and the future of the two-state solution.
The UN secretary-general has urged an end to the fighting, expanded humanitarian access and compliance with international law.
Martin said the international community would ultimately have to confront the record of what has happened in Gaza, warning that the consequences would carry a lasting moral and political weight.
Ireland has been among the countries advocating for Palestinian rights and a negotiated two-state settlement, while Martin’s address placed the issue at the centre of his appeal for a stronger international commitment to human rights and international law.

25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called for stronger international action on Palestine, Iran and the risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI), warning the UN General Assembly that the multilateral system was under growing strain.
Addressing the assembly in New York on Thursday, Albanese said Australia would continue to oppose illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank while rejecting any future role for Hamas in Palestine.
“We will continue to speak out against actions that damage that prospect of peace, including illegal settlements in the West Bank,” he said, adding that Canberra would also “continue to oppose any role for the terrorists of Hamas in Palestine’s future.”
Turning to Iran, Albanese said the conflict had taken “a severe toll on the Middle East” and caused a “devastating impact on the global economy.”
Australia, he said, was calling for a ceasefire, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and restoration of freedom of navigation and trade. He also urged Iran to halt “indiscriminate attacks” across the region and abandon any effort to obtain nuclear weapons.
Albanese devoted part of his address to artificial intelligence, saying the technology could transform health care, productivity and economic growth but posed significant risks without safeguards.
“We can’t ignore AI or prevent it,” he said, arguing that governments must “shape artificial intelligence development, rather than be passively shaped by it.”
He said an AI agent had recently infiltrated an Australian government website, calling the incident “unacceptable,” and cited Australian efforts to establish standards governing the technology.
Albanese also called for UN reform, stronger representation for small and middle powers and greater international action on climate change.
“Australia stands for a safer world, where no country dominates and no country is dominated,” he said, pledging to elevate Pacific nations’ voices on climate change, development and security.

Ahmet Salih Alacaci
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Republic of Ireland midfielder Jason Knight has become the first national team player to publicly say that the country should not play its upcoming UEFA Nations League match against Israel.
Knight expressed his personal opposition to the fixture following Ireland’s 1-0 defeat to Kosovo in Pristina on Thursday.
“I don’t think the game should be going ahead, but it is going ahead,” he said.
The 25-year-old Bristol City midfielder said the squad would hold more detailed discussions before deciding how to approach Sunday’s match in Debrecen, Hungary.
“We’ll have a deeper talk about it and what that means. We’ll get our thoughts as a group and go from there,” he added.
Ireland captain Dara O’Shea said earlier that the players would meet on Friday to discuss their views and whether to stage a collective protest during the fixture.
Potential measures could include refusing customary pre-match handshakes or post-match shirt exchanges, although the squad has yet to announce a decision.
O’Shea said the decision to fulfill the fixtures had been taken by the Football Association of Ireland (FAI), the Irish government and UEFA, rather than by the players.
The FAI has faced mounting pressure to boycott the two Nations League matches against Israel over the continuing genocide in Gaza.
More than 160 Irish athletes have signed an open letter urging the national team not to play, while the Stop The Game campaign has organized demonstrations demanding Israel’s suspension from international football.
Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson previously said some players felt “really uncomfortable” about the matches and described the team as playing “against genocide,” prompting a sharp response from the Israeli Football Association.
The FAI has said it opposes Israel’s continued participation and has lobbied UEFA for its suspension but decided against a unilateral boycott because of the possible sporting and financial consequences.
Its general assembly voted 75-38 to fulfill the fixtures after officials warned that withdrawal could cost Irish football at least €5.5 million ($6.5 million) and expose the association to further UEFA sanctions.
The first match will take place at the Nagyerdei Stadium in Debrecen on Sunday. The return fixture, officially Ireland’s home game, has been moved from Dublin to Backa Topola, Serbia, and will be played behind closed doors on Oct. 4.
The FAI will not provide tickets to Irish supporters for either match, while Irish national broadcaster RTE has said it will air the games without its customary studio coverage, punditry, advertising or its own commentary team.

MOSCOW, September 25. /TASS/. Russia’s Central Election Commission (CEC) will convene on Friday to establish the final results of elections to the ninth convocation of the Russian parliament’s lower chamber, the State Duma.
The commission will announce the exact distribution of all 450 mandates and sum up the results of over 2,200 lower-level electoral campaigns, also held on September 18-20.
The results of the vote were not immediately announced after the polls closed. CEC Chair Ella Pamfilova said that regional commissions were given time until September 25 to conclusively review all incoming complaints and requests, conduct the necessary inquires and only then establish the official outcomes of the campaigns.
Who will make it into the new Duma?
According to preliminary results, five parties crossed the five-percent threshold: the United Russia party, the Communist Party, LDPR, the New People and A Just Russia.
The 225 seats designated for party lists will be distributed among them. The other half of the State Duma will be determined by the voting results in single-seat constituencies.
The United Russia is poised to form the largest faction. Party Chairman Dmitry Medvedev said on September 24 that it is expected to secure 349 seats in total, according to preliminary allocation: 140 via the federal list and 209 in single-seat constituencies.
If the CEC confirms this distribution, it will mark the largest number of seats won by a single party in a legislative election in the entire modern history of the State Duma. The current record is also held by United Russia, which secured 343 seats in the 2016 elections. In 2021, it got 324 mandates.

End of the road for Finland's travelling Tivoli carnival after 138 years
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
07:41:07 EEST
13:41:07 KST

Finland's largest and longest-running travelling carnival, Tivoli, is to close after 138 years of operating.
Trips to the park, which was founded in 1888 by Johan Grönroos, became a staple of Finnish childhood traditions — with hundreds of thousands of people visiting the mobile amusement outfit across the country every year.
However, the company has run into serious financial difficulties in recent years, and 2026 marks Tivoli's seventh consecutive loss-making fiscal year.
In a statement, Tivoli noted that its operations were hit particularly hard by the effects of the Covid pandemic and the financial problems have continued since then, with rising inflation, increasing energy costs, changing consumer behaviour and Finland's sluggish economy all playing a part.
"When operating revenues do not cover costs over the long term and there are no visible signs that a return to profitability will happen soon, we have a responsibility to make the difficult decision," the statement said.
Tivoli's financial challenges have been evident for a number of years, and in July the carnival did not travel from Oulu to Kajaani as planned because it could not afford the relocation costs.
A 1988 Yle documentary — marking 100 years of the carnival — revealed Tivoli's colourful history and influence on Finnish society, from being denounced by priests as a "corrupting influence" in the 1930s to becoming the first Western carnival company to visit the Soviet Union.

Xi attends state dinner held by Trump
China
