Small public schools in rural areas are set to receive more state support as falling numbers of children put some schools at risk of closing.
The government is allocating 500 million DKK through 2030 to support small schools and slow further closures.
Minister for Economic and Interior Affairs Pia Olsen Dyhr from the Socialist People’s Party, is presenting the plan today at a visit to a school in Toksværd in Næstved Municipality, according to TV2 ØST.
“A school is a gathering point for parents, teachers, and students, and they help create local life and connection in our rural districts,” Dyhr said.
The initiative follows a commitment in the government’s platform from June to prevent a new wave of school closures. Small public schools in rural areas are also expected to receive greater financial support and more freedom.
One school facing possible closure is Vesterlandsskolen’s branch in Hyllinge. Only fifty-four students attend this school, and Næstved Municipality’s administration has proposed ending teaching and after-school care there from August 1, 2027.
Closing the branch would save 7.53 million DKK annually from 2028. The proposal has not been approved, and the city council is expected to adopt its budget on October 6.
School board chair Karina Wolan said additional state funding could help keep the Hyllinge branch open.
“If it means that the school can be allowed to exist, that would be wonderful,” she said.
It remains unclear how the 500 million DKK will be distributed, which municipalities will qualify and whether the funding is included in the government’s previously announced five billion DKK annual investment in children, daycare, schools and leisure.
Social Affairs Minister Monika Rubin of the Moderates says the government wants more freedom to change Denmark’s disability system after withdrawing from a political agreement reached two years ago.
The framework agreement was signed in May 2024 by the government and Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and the Social Liberal Party. It was not a formal political settlement with special rules governing withdrawal.
“With the framework agreement, one had bound oneself in a way that made it more difficult than it needs to be to cooperate broadly across the Folketing,” Rubin said, referring to Denmark’s parliament.
“The original agreement has outlived its potential,” she added.

Rubin’s Moderates also supported the agreement at the time.
Rubin now says she will work on initiatives involving “fundamental changes to the disability area,” with more trust, structure and coordination of professional expertise around people with disabilities.
The decision drew different responses from other parties.
Katrine Daugaard, social affairs spokesperson for Liberal Alliance, a Danish liberal party, accused Rubin of “running away from an agreement.” She said ending it risks “more uniform, mediocre public services, less specialization, and less freedom of choice.”
Torsten Gejl, political spokesperson for the Alternative, a Danish green party that was not part of the agreement, welcomed the decision.
“The framework agreement for disability, which has tightened the finances in the disability area and made people with disabilities feel like a cost-cutting exercise, was suddenly dropped this evening. That is fantastic,” Gejl wrote on X.

The leaders of Denmark, Greenland and the United States are expected to sign a security and defense agreement concerning Greenland on Tuesday.
The ceremony is scheduled for 10:30 a.m. local time, or 4:30 p.m. Danish time, at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office described it as “a joint agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic region.”
The agreement will be signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Jens-Frederik Nielsen, head of Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government.
Few details about the agreement have been released since it was announced Friday.
Trump said on Truth Social that the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen has said the agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We are not ceding sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I never will as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told Danish broadcasters DR and TV 2 on Monday.
She said sovereignty could be maintained alongside closer defense cooperation with other countries.

More than 20 percent of Nordic teenagers drink energy drinks at least once a day, according to a survey of 4,916 people ages 15 to 19.
The study covered Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. Six in 10 respondents drank energy drinks at least weekly.
Almost half said they could not get through the day without an energy drink or sometimes felt that way.
The report found that 46 percent began drinking energy drinks at age 14 or younger. One in 10 started before age 12.
Among those who consumed the drinks, 30 percent reported feeling unwell or experiencing other negative health effects. Heart palpitations and sleep problems were among the most common complaints.
“When a habit begins to affect sleep, well-being, or everyday life, there is reason to act,” said Sabina Litens Karlsson, a toxicologist at Livsmedelsverket, Sweden’s national food authority, which conducted the study.
Taste was cited by 73 percent of consumers, while 51 percent wanted more energy and 34 percent wanted to stay awake.
Weekly consumption was highest in Sweden at 75 percent and lowest in Denmark at 43 percent.
Norway has banned sales to people under 16. Denmark has no legal age limit, but its food authority advises children under 15 not to consume energy drinks.
Denmark now expects to complete the final compensation cases for the mink industry in the third quarter of 2028, at least six months later than previously planned.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority disclosed the delay in a briefing shared with the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“The decisions on compensation have unfortunately proven to be more time-consuming than assumed,” said Transport and Rural Affairs Minister Signe Munk of the Socialist People’s Party.
The authority previously expected the final cases to be completed during 2027.
The delay is linked to European Commission approval for state aid, which expires on April 1 and cannot be extended.
Officials must prioritize partial decisions determining whether applicants qualify for compensation before that deadline. Two teams have been reassigned to the Mink Secretariat unit preparing those decisions, leaving fewer employees to complete final compensation awards.
The delay could add about 40 million DKK in costs, the authority estimated.
At the beginning of 2026, the total expected cost of compensation, farm demolitions and administration was 29.1 billion DKK.
Denmark ordered all 15 million farmed mink killed in November 2020 over concerns about a mutated coronavirus.
When lawmakers agreed on compensation in 2021, the total bill was expected to be between 15.6 billion DKK and 18.8 billion DKK.

Seven emergency medical vehicles in Denmark’s Central Denmark Region will begin using direct blood pressure monitoring during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR.
The regional prehospital emergency service said the method could help staff adjust chest compressions and improve survival after cardiac arrests outside hospitals.
“With blood pressure measurements, we get a better idea of whether the cardiopulmonary resuscitation sufficiently drives the blood around the body, or whether we need to adjust and adapt the chest compressions,” emergency doctor Jesper Fjølner said.
Fjølner, who developed the project, said the method had already contributed to successful resuscitation in several cases.
The procedure, called invasive blood pressure measurement, involves placing a catheter with a monitor into an artery. Hospitals already use it to monitor patients in operating rooms and intensive care units.
Using the method outside a hospital is more complex and requires training, equipment and experience.
Chief physician Allan Bach said the service expects the procedure to help resuscitate more people without reducing patient safety or the quality of CPR.
The European Resuscitation Council, which prepares European guidelines for cardiac arrest treatment, recently recommended the method. The Central Denmark service said it is among the first in the world to introduce it.
About 5,000 people experience cardiac arrest outside hospitals in Denmark each year. Around 15 percent survive.
Diabetes patients taking a low dose of Novo’s experimental drug Cagrisema lost more weight than those taking a low dose of Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide in a new study.
Patients receiving 1 milligram of Cagrisema lost an average of 12.4 percent of their weight over 60 weeks, Danish pharmaceutical company Novo said.
Those receiving 5 milligrams of tirzepatide lost 9.1 percent during the same period. Tirzepatide is the active ingredient in Eli Lilly’s approved weight-loss drug Zepbound.
Cagrisema has not been approved. Novo expects the US Food and Drug Administration to decide on its application near the end of 2026.
The treatment combines semaglutide, the active ingredient in Novo’s Wegovy, with a newer substance called cagrilintide. Novo hopes the combination can produce greater weight loss than semaglutide alone.
Results from another study released in February favored tirzepatide. Participants taking tirzepatide lost 25.5 percent of their weight over 84 weeks, compared with 23 percent for those receiving Cagrisema.
Novo shares fell more than 16 percent after those earlier results.
The company released the new findings during its capital markets day. Novo shares were down more than five percent around 1:15 p.m. Monday, and the announcement did not significantly change the share price.
Drivers using Denmark’s Vejlefjord Bridge should expect daily queues and longer travel times while two expansion joints are replaced, the Danish Road Directorate said.
Preparation work will take place during the final two weeks of September. The main repairs will run from early October until early November, with work continuing seven days a week.
Two of the bridge’s five expansion joints in the southbound lanes will be replaced.
Expansion joints are movable sections that allow a bridge to expand and contract as temperatures change. The joints have repeatedly caused problems in recent years, leading to emergency repairs, delays and traffic queues.
The Road Directorate, the Danish government agency responsible for national roads, expects the work to reduce the need for emergency repairs in the near future.
Almost 100,000 vehicles cross the nearly 50-year-old bridge each day.
“When we take lanes for a work area, and road users only have one lane in each direction, queues will occur,” project manager Allan Højgaard Madsen said.
Queues are expected in both directions from about 7 p.m. and for several hours afterward throughout the repair period.
Morning and afternoon rush-hour traffic is expected to face delays only in the southbound direction.

Most Danes want the government to temporarily cut taxes on gasoline and diesel as fuel prices reach unusually high levels, a Voxmeter poll for the Danish news agency Ritzau shows.
In September, diesel reached a record 19.19 DKK per liter at gas stations.
The poll found that 53.8 percent supported temporary tax cuts, while 33.3 percent opposed them. Another 12.9 percent did not know.
Torben Kudsk, policy chief at FDM, Denmark’s main car owners’ organization, said rising prices were creating serious problems for motorists.
“Fuel is historically expensive. As far as we can see, prices have not been higher in recent times,” Kudsk said.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats said the government was monitoring the situation.
“If energy prices continue to rise, and the situation develops further, we are of course ready to do more,” he wrote on Facebook. He did not describe possible measures.
The poll also asked what should guide decisions on fuel taxes. A total of 39.2 percent said reducing motorists’ costs should come first.
Another 27.2 percent said taxes should remain because of climate and environmental concerns, while 25.9 percent gave both issues equal weight. The remaining 7.7 percent did not know.
The price increases have been linked to wars and conflicts causing a global fuel shortage.

Ukraine has obtained detailed Russian plans for strikes on its energy system this winter, including calculations for the types and quantities of weapons needed to destroy specific facilities, First Deputy Prime Minister and Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal told Ukraine’s Inter TV channel.
According to Shmyhal, the intelligence consists of two extensive Russian documents outlining planned attacks on electricity generation, heating, water supply, sewage systems and other critical energy infrastructure.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The plans also reportedly cover interconnectors through which Ukraine imports electricity from Europe.
“There are two large documents, written very coldly and very clearly – with tables and the amount of weapons needed for each facility to destroy it,” Shmyhal said, adding that the weapons range from ballistic missiles to jet-powered and conventional drones.
Russia targets winter resilience
The disclosure comes as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine’s energy and civilian infrastructure ahead of the heating season.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said this week that Russia will not end the war without stronger pressure and called for additional ballistic missile interceptors and sanctions against Moscow and those helping it generate revenue.
Ukraine has also been seeking a winter air-defense package from its partners as Russian forces expand their use of ballistic missiles and faster jet-powered drones.
Can Trump and Xi Turn Leverage Into a Russia Deal – and What Are the Stakes for Ukraine?
Fortifications and international mobilization
According to Shmyhal, Ukrainian authorities have constructed more than 200 protective structures around infrastructure sites considered priority Russian targets.
At the same time, Ukraine and its international partners are building equipment reserves to enable rapid repairs following possible strikes.
More than 40 countries have joined the Energy Ramstein initiative, while more than $2.1 billion has been raised for the Ukraine Energy Support Fund over the past three years.
Partners provided $545 million this year alone, with another €305 million in confirmed commitments. Since the fund began operating, more than 33,000 tonnes of critical energy equipment have been delivered to Ukraine, according to Shmyhal.
A difficult winter ahead
Shmyhal said the coming winter will not be easy, but government calculations indicate it should not be more difficult than the previous one.
Ukraine’s preparations follow another winter in which Russian forces systematically and repeatedly targeted energy facilities across the country.
A UN Human Rights Office report covering December 2025 through May 2026 found that Russian attacks damaged or destroyed electricity generation, transmission and distribution facilities and repeatedly disrupted heating and water supplies for civilians.
The attacks triggered emergency blackouts affecting millions and left hundreds of thousands without heating and hot water for extended periods as temperatures fell below minus 20 degrees Celsius.
The new intelligence gives Ukraine an important advantage in preparing physical defenses and positioning repair equipment before the next wave of attacks.

Report warns new Taiwan-US cables vulnerable to China gray-zone operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
04:16:20 UTC
13:16:20 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Three new undersea cable systems being built to connect the US with Taiwan are among the trans-Pacific systems most vulnerable to potential Chinese gray-zone operations, according to a report released Tuesday.
The report, commissioned by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC) and produced by the China Strategic Risks Institute, identified E2A, TPU, and ORCA among the 10 most vulnerable of the 32 trans-Pacific cable systems it assessed. All three are currently under development and are expected to enter service within the next three years.
The researchers used an index to assess the risks facing each cable system. The index considers factors including heavy maritime traffic, seabed conditions, and proximity to China’s maritime claims, such as Taiwan and areas within the nine-dash line.
The report also examined four existing cable systems linking Taiwan with the continental US, modeling the potential impact of a single cable cut on each system. Based on publicly available data, the researchers estimated that traffic demand would exceed the lit capacity of three systems, while the fourth, the Trans-Pacific Express, would have less than 20% spare capacity.
The findings come as Taiwan continues to face frequent disruptions to its submarine cable network. In the past four years, an average of seven to eight submarine cable incidents occurred annually in Taiwan’s coastal waters, with anchor dragging accounting for around 38% of the cases, according to a statement by the Ministry of Digital Affairs in April.
Andrew Yeh, a co-author of the report and senior director for Taiwan and the Indo-Pacific at the CSRI, said Taiwan has taken significant steps to protect its undersea cable network.
“Taiwan has done more than perhaps any other country to bolster cable security,” Yeh said, citing tougher laws and penalties aimed at deterring potential saboteurs.
Taiwan amended its law in 2023 to impose tougher criminal penalties for damaging critical telecommunications infrastructure, including submarine cables. Further amendments taking effect in January gave authorities the power to confiscate vessels used in cable sabotage and strengthened ship monitoring, according to the MODA statement.
MODA Spokesperson Wu Fang-ting (吳芳定) told Taiwan News that the government is developing a three-layer communications backup system using submarine cables, microwave links, and satellites to maintain connectivity when cables are damaged.
The report called for broader regional cooperation to strengthen cable security, recommending that Taiwan, the US, Japan, the Philippines, and other regional allies establish a joint maritime domain awareness platform to detect suspicious activity. It also called for wider use of technologies such as distributed acoustic sensing, synthetic aperture radar, and underwater drones.
Tu Chen-yi (杜貞儀), an assistant research fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, said improving shared maritime awareness is a challenge faced by countries beyond Taiwan.
“The factors contributing to these (cable) ‘accidents’ and their effects are complex,” she said. “Strengthening shared maritime domain awareness to improve navigational safety remains the most fundamental step.”

La Rábida monastery: where Columbus persuaded Castile to discover America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
04:12:22 UTC
13:12:22 KST

The discovery of America remains one of history's great exploits, where two cultures met. Before sailing, Columbus secured key backing at La Rábida from Franciscan friars and the Pinzón brothers.
On a small hillock in Huelva, at the point where the Tinto river meets the Odiel before flowing into the Atlantic, stands one of the most decisive sites in world history: the monastery of Santa María de La Rábida. Without its walls, its friars and the faith invested there, it is likely that Christopher Columbus's great venture would never have sailed from the nearby shores of Palos de la Frontera towards the New World.
The Franciscan presence here dates back to the early 13th century, when the first friars settled in this early hermitage on the Huelva estuary. For decades, La Rábida was a place of retreat and prayer, far from the hustle and bustle, until fate, and the persistence of a navigator, turned it into the epicentre of one of the most significant episodes ever experienced: the encounter between two worlds that until then had no knowledge of each other.
Today, visitors can walk on the very ground the navigator trod and pass through the doorway that sealed his fate. There, in La Rábida, the friars welcome us just as they welcomed Christopher Columbus more than 500 years ago.
A haven for a sailor down on his luck
When Columbus reached these shores, he had spent years trying to persuade a European crown to back his plan: a westward trading route to the Indies which, without him realising it, would lead to the encounter with a continent unknown to Europeans. Before arriving in Huelva, the navigator had sought support in Portugal, France and Italy, without success. He had also tried to conclude a deal with Castile and Aragon, but the monarchs were focused on the campaign in Granada to reconquer the last Muslim stronghold on the Iberian Peninsula after more than 770 years of reconquest.
It was in the convent of La Rábida that he found more than lodging: he found allies willing to believe in him and to support him before Queen Isabella I of Castile, the great sponsor of Columbus's project and defender of the Indigenous peoples who lived in the newly discovered lands. She herself asked that they be treated as Castilian subjects, free citizens protected from any abuse or enslavement. Even on her deathbed she did not forget these new Castilian subjects: the will of Isabella of Castile is considered a key legal milestone that anticipated the modern concept of human rights, by laying down the protection and freedom of Indigenous Americans.
The Franciscan friars, particularly Fray Juan Pérez, who had been the queen's confessor, listened to Columbus's proposal and decided to intercede at the court of the Catholic Monarchs. Thanks to that mediation, the pioneering navigator finally secured an audience which would lead to the backing of Isabella I of Castile, the visionary queen who agreed to finance the expedition that would change the course of history.
The Virgin who 'witnessed' the beginning of the voyage
Within the walls of this hermitage, the image of Santa María de la Rábida, also known as Our Lady of Miracles, is still kept today. According to tradition, it was before this statue that Columbus himself prayed moments before setting off into the unknown, on a voyage that many thought was madness and which would ultimately redraw the map of the world.
Visiting today the chapel where this image is kept is, in a sense, to stand in the exact spot where the journey was forged: a place where silence can be heard, a space that witnessed directly a decision that would shape the destiny of two continents.
The Pinzón brothers, the missing piece needed to sail to the New World
Winning over the Crown was not enough: Columbus needed a crew willing to embark on a voyage into the unknown that many sailors of the time saw as a one-way journey. At that point one of the most influential families in the seafaring world of Palos de la Frontera came into play: the Pinzón brothers.
Martín Alonso Pinzón, an experienced navigator and a highly respected figure in the town, put his reputation at the service of the project and helped recruit much of the crew, overcoming the misgivings of those who distrusted the navigator's plan. His involvement was so decisive that he ended up commanding the caravel La Pinta, while his brother Vicente Yáñez Pinzón took charge of La Niña. The third brother, Francisco Martín Pinzón, sailed as master (second-in-command) on La Pinta, rounding off a family presence that proved crucial on all three ships in the expedition, along with the nao Santa María, captained by Columbus himself.
Without the human and nautical support of the Pinzóns, it is unlikely that the venture would have managed to set sail from the port of Palos on 3 August 1492.
Today, replicas of these three vessels can be visited at the Wharf of the Caravels. There, the three ships offer a glimpse into the exploratory past of what was then Castile.
A legacy of light and shade
The discovery of the Americas, launched from this small monastery in Huelva, brought about the greatest cultural, economic and biological exchange in modern history. From that encounter came foods now considered essential in Europe, such as the potato, which centuries later would be crucial, for example, during the Irish famine, the tomato, sugar cane and coveted cocoa. At the same time, that feat was marked by episodes of violence and subjugation against Indigenous peoples, a reality that today is examined with a critical eye, though it is difficult to apply contemporary standards to the 15th century.
La Rábida is not only a religious building: it is the symbolic point of departure for a complex historical process, one that helps explain both the flourishing of a new relationship between cultures and the dark sides that the same process entailed.
Today, the Franciscan Convent of Santa María de La Rábida has become a leading tourist and cultural attraction for those who wish to retrace the steps that led up to the discovery of the Americas. Its rooms preserve documents, models and objects that recreate convent life in the 15th century, as well as the atmosphere in which Columbus worked out the final details of his expedition.
Strolling through its cloister under the sky illuminated by the Moon that inspired the navigator to set sail beyond the seas, contemplating the image of Our Lady of Miracles or looking out over the very landscape that watched the caravels depart is like travelling straight back to the origins of modern history. It is a place of pilgrimage not only for the faithful but also for anyone seeking to understand how a small monastery in Huelva ended up changing the course of the world.

Pope makes first official visit to France in 18 years, meeting abuse survivors and EU leaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
04:00:47 UTC
13:00:47 KST

The Pope is making the first official papal visit to France in 18 years, during which he is expected to meet survivors of sexual abuse, EU leaders and large crowds of worshippers.
Church bells will quite literally be ringing across France this Friday morning as Pope Leo XIV lands on the tarmac of Paris-Orly airport for the first official papal visit to the country in 18 years.
The Bishops’ Conference of France (CEF) described the decision to ring bells for seven minutes "as a simple and symbolic gesture" to mark the beginning of the Pope’s apostolic journey and allow people "to take part" from wherever they are.
From addressing EU leaders and meeting with victims of sexual violence within the Church to parading through Paris on his popemobile, the pontiff has a packed four days ahead of him.
The paternal grandmother of the Chicago-Born Pope Leo XIV — who is the first US pontiff — was born in France.
An operation heavy on logistics
Pope Benedict XVI’s September 2008 trip was the last papal trip to France classified as an official visit. While Pope Francis travelled to France on three occasions during his pontificate — Corsica, Marseille and Strasbourg — none of these trips constituted an official papal visit.
The cost of the Pope's trip to France is set to cost an estimated €27 million, with the Catholic Church in France covering the bulk of the expenses through donations. Meanwhile, the total cost incurred by French security forces — who have had to lay out a vast security apparatus — remains unknown at present.
Speaking to French broadcaster BFMTV on Wednesday, French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said no "specific threat" had been detected at the time of the interview.
“The police are always on high alert, and intelligence agencies, in particular, are monitoring the situation in advance. We haven't detected any specific threat, but there will be a major security operation in place,” he stated.
The Popemobile and Notre-Dame-de-Paris
After being received by the French President at the Elysée Palace, the Pope is set to deliver a speech at UNESCO's headquarters, addressing a number of topics — including artificial intelligence and global peace.
AI has become a central theme over the course of the Pope's pontificate, who published his first 42,300 word encyclical entitled "Magnifica humanitas**"** in May, focusing on the risks unchecked artificial intelligence pose for humans.
The pontiff will celebrate Vespers at the Notre-Dame-de-Paris Cathedral later on Friday before heading to the Stade de France in Saint-Denis for a major evening prayer vigil with young people.
The following day, crowds will gather for an open-air Mass at the Place de la Concorde and along the Champs-Élysées. French authorities have estimated that around 600,000 people are expected to attend the event and surrounding areas.
Over the course of the Pope's two-day Paris trip, a million pilgrims and visitors are expected in the French capital.
Meeting with sexual abuse victims and addressing EU leaders
After Paris, the Pope will travel to the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, one of the world's most renowned Catholic pilgrimage sites, located in southwestern France.
The popularity of Lourdes is intrinsically tied to the story of Bernadette Soubirous. Between February and July 1858, Soubirous — a young girl from a modest background, who suffered from asthma — reported 18 visions of a lady dressed in white in the Grotto of Massabielle near Lourdes.
The Catholic Church later recognised Bernadette's visions as apparitions of the Virgin Mary. Her accounts, along with the discovery of spring water believed by some to have healing properties, led to the construction of a sanctuary at the site. Millions of pilgrims have since travelled there to pray.
In Lourdes, the Pope will also meet with seven survivors of sexual abuse who were assaulted as children or adults. A 2021 report estimated that 330,000 children had been sexually abused over 70 years by church personnel in France.
Although many have supported the Pope's plan to meet with sexual violence victims, not all victims are convinced by the idea.
Among them is Arnaud Gallais, a child-protection activist and survivor of sexual abuse by a priest during his childhood, who has criticised aspects of the Pope’s visit while calling for the meeting with survivors to lead to concrete commitments from the Church.
He told Euronews that he was critical of the decision to give the Pope a ceremonial welcome, arguing that it is difficult to reconcile such displays with the scale of sexual abuse and the suffering experienced by victims within the Church.
"I can see that this meeting is important for the victims, but what I think should be really be a priority, is for the President of the French Republic to hold a diplomatic meeting with the Head of State of the Vatican to address the issue of sexual violence in the Church."
Macron will not attend papal masses
On Monday, the Pope is set to address EU leaders in the northeastern French city of Metz with a speech entitled “To the Roots of Europe for Peace and Unity."
He will deliver this address at the Robert Schuman Convention Center, named after one of the key figures behind the creation of the European Union. The Élysée Palace did not respond to a request regarding which leaders are set to attend.
The French president will not attend any of papal masses over the course of the trip.
In 2023, during Pope Francis' visit to France, he attended the mass held at the Stade Vélodrome, but did not participate in the Eucharist or receive communion. His presence drew criticism from figures on the left at the time, who accused him of disrespecting France's laïcité principle.
Green senator Mélanie Vogel took to X at the time to declare that "as the President of a secular country, you can go there as a Catholic, but not as President. That’s called secularism. You’re welcome."
Meanwhile, Bastien Lachaud, an MP from the hard-left France Unbowed party back then also accused Macron of mocking "secularism" and of trampling "on its principles — the separation of church and state, and the state’s neutrality toward religions."
Ahead of the Pope's visit, the Elysée stressed that France could embrace religious enthusiasm while remaining committed to secularism.
Macron will be represented by Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu as well as by his wife Brigitte Macron during the giant open air mass at the Place de la Concorde and adjoining Champs-Elysées on Saturday, according to the Elysée.
In Lourdes, the Pope is set to be greeted by a member of the government upon his arrival at Tarbes airport, but no officials will attend his Sunday mass at the Lourdes sanctuary.

Berlin’s new political star is offering something all of Europe needs – hope and housing | Fatma Aydemir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
04:00:38 UTC
13:00:38 KST

Hope is a fragile thing. You can only hold on to it as long as you find reasons to believe tomorrow can be better. A woman, for instance, who has the resources and opportunity to rent her own flat will be more likely to leave her abusive husband and recover. A pupil who has their own room and desk to do their homework might find more meaning in thriving at school. And an elderly person who can afford to live in a neighbourhood where they feel safe and connected is less likely to become isolated and depressed.
It’s not by chance that the examples above all revolve around the same topic. Affordable housing is possibly the most personal and most urgent social issue of our time. In Berlin, a city where 85% of residents live in rented accommodation, rents have risen by almost 70% in the past 10 years. And that is despite a rent control law that has been in effect since 2015. How? Loopholes and illegal practices have allowed property owners to continue putting pressure on the housing market. The social anxiety caused by this crisis, far from affecting just low-earners and single-parent households, affects vast parts of the middle class, too.
So what does a political party need to do to get into power in the state of Berlin? It’s really not rocket science: focus on the housing crisis, provide solutions and avoid distractions by political opponents. This is exactly what the leftwing party Die Linke has been doing for months. The result of last Sunday’s state election is striking: for the first time, Die Linke, with 25.7%, became the strongest party in Berlin. Not because everyone who voted for it suddenly agreed with everything else the party stands for. But because, more than any other party in this campaign, Die Linke made this issue unmistakably its own: the question of who gets to live in Berlin, and at what price.
The result is also remarkable because Germany is at a historic turning point: on the same day as the Berlin election, the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) emerged – with 38% – as the largest party in a state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Just two weeks previously, it had secured a victory in Saxony-Anhalt with almost 44%. While the centrist parties, in an attempt to win back their voters, are desperately mimicking the AfD’s ideas and rhetoric on migration, Die Linke could set an example in Berlin for the rest of the country: by actually listening to people’s worries and working on ideas to improve their lives sustainably, instead of scapegoating.
The party’s lead candidate, Elif Eralp, could become not only Berlin’s first mayor from the left since Germany’s reunification in 1990, but also Berlin’s first mayor ever with a migration background. Born in Munich, she is the daughter of Turkish socialists who fled following the military coup in Turkey in 1980. Eralp put housing at the centre of her campaign. For many weeks the whole city was flooded with giant portraits of the 45-year-old wearing an optimistic smile and a golden nameplate necklace with the word Mietendeckel (rent freeze).
Eralp’s programme was clear from the start: lower rents, more public housing and the implementation of Berlin’s 2021 referendum in which a majority voted for more public ownership of housing to alleviate the accommodation crisis. It’s not a completely new world that Eralp promises. All she had to do was simply speak about the one we are already living in.
But winning an election is one thing. Governing is another. Die Linke may have won the most seats, but it lacks a majority to run the state on its own. To turn its campaign promises into policy, Eralp has to negotiate with other parties, particularly the Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens. While Berlin’s Greens have already spoken out in favour of a progressive coalition, the SPD is deeply divided.
Die Linke’s top priority is a radical ambition: it would involve the compulsory purchase of the housing portfolios (which exceed 3,000 apartments) of large private real estate companies and their transfer into a democratically controlled non-profit, public body. The SPD’s approach is to regulate the housing market much more strongly, expand public housing and potentially introduce a rent cap. Which sounds like everything that has already failed in the last decade.
At the same time, Die Linke enters negotiations under a microscope. Political opponents are questioning whether the party’s positions are compatible with democratic values, while controversies surrounding antisemitism and parts of the party’s political culture have become a major subject of public debate. Antisemitism is, historically and today, a problem inherent in German society as a whole, one that also exists within Die Linke and should be combated more decisively. However, the uproar about antisemitic rappers and an organised crime member who was spotted at Die Linke’s election party seem like sham debates that overshadow the actual conflicts of interest.
Meanwhile, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has already stated, in response to the Berlin elections, that a federal law could be passed to prevent the expropriation of privately owned housing. Markus Söder, leader of the state of Bavaria, announced financial consequences for Berlin, if the “extremist”, “antidemocratic” and “antisemitic” Die Linke were to govern the capital. No such measures were announced for potential AfD-governed states, of course.
It is hardly surprising that conservatives are now foaming at the mouth, given that for decades they have been pursuing policies that benefit those who profit from the housing crisis. Yet, more and more Social Democrats are also up in arms, putting pressure on their party not to form a coalition with Die Linke.
And this is where hope becomes fragile again. Because Eralp now has to do something harder than naming a problem: she has to find coalition partners, and for that she has to compromise – without making her voters feel betrayed. Now that would be a radical act, indeed.
- 
  Fatma Aydemir is a Berlin-based author, novelist, playwright and a Guardian Europe columnist

A national project: what green hydrogen is and why Spain is backing it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
03:59:05 UTC
12:59:05 KST

Spain hopes to become Europe's green hydrogen leader, backed by its renewable resources. What is it, what is it for and what hurdles lie ahead?
For decades, Spain has relied on oil and gas from abroad. What was once an energy disadvantage could now turn into an opportunity. Sun, wind and plenty of room to generate renewable electricity on a large scale put Spain in a privileged position for a still nascent industry: green hydrogen.
"Spain has always had the disadvantage of not having oil or gas," Maarten Wetselaar, Moeve's chief executive, tells "Euronews". "But now it is Spain's moment because it has abundant solar power, very good wind resources and space to build large renewable parks."
The former Cepsa wants to make the most of that combination. The company has just begun in Palos de la Frontera, Huelva, construction of Onuba, the first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley: more than 1 billion euros of investment in a project that will start with 300 megawatts (MW) of electrolysis capacity.
The plan goes far beyond a single plant. Spain wants to use its renewable resources to build a new industry, cut its energy dependence and, in the longer term, become an energy supplier to other European countries.
But what exactly is green hydrogen? Why does Spain believe it can produce it competitively? And what obstacles still have to be overcome before that ambition becomes reality?
What is green hydrogen?
Although it is often described as one of the energies of the future, hydrogen is not a primary energy source like the sun or the wind. It is an energy carrier: energy has to be used to produce it.
Hydrogen has been used for decades in refineries, in the chemical industry and to make products such as fertilisers. The problem is that most of it is still obtained from fossil fuels. So-called grey hydrogen is mainly produced using natural gas, a process that generates CO2 emissions.
Green hydrogen changes how it is produced. Through a process known as electrolysis, an electric current splits water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen. If the electricity used comes from renewable sources such as solar or wind, we refer to renewable, or green, hydrogen.
And that is where Spain's first advantage comes in. Producing it requires vast amounts of electricity. According to Wetselaar, power accounts for roughly 70% of the cost of green hydrogen. "If you go to the place in Europe where (renewable electricity) is cheapest, which is the Iberian Peninsula, then your green hydrogen will be very, very competitive," the Moeve CEO says.
"Spain is a huge source of renewable energy and therefore can be and will be Europe's leading producer of green hydrogen," he adds. It is an ambitious forecast by the company, and there are still major hurdles before it can come true. But it helps explain why businesses and public authorities are channelling multi-billion-euro investments into this technology.
If we have renewable electricity, why do we need hydrogen?
This is one of the fundamental questions. Whenever it is possible to use renewable electricity directly, doing so is usually more efficient than using that electricity to make hydrogen and then using the hydrogen as an energy source. The aim is therefore not to replace fossil fuels with hydrogen across the board.
Its main potential lies in sectors that are hard to electrify directly. Certain processes in heavy industry, chemical production and parts of maritime and air transport need alternatives to fossil fuels that batteries cannot always provide in a practical way.
Hydrogen can also be used to produce derivatives such as ammonia or synthetic fuels.
Spain's prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, argued at the Huelva project launch that this technology can help cut emissions from activities that still depend on oil and gas. But he also framed the bet in economic terms.
"This transformation is therefore not only about protecting ourselves better against crises, which is also very significant. It is also about seizing a huge industrial opportunity," he said.
Huelva, a testing ground for Spain's bet
That opportunity is beginning to take shape in places such as Palos de la Frontera. Onuba will initially have 300 MW of electrolysis capacity and can later be expanded by another 105 MW. Moeve estimates it will produce around 45,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen a year.
The location is no accident. As well as having abundant renewable resources, Huelva has industrial activity, port infrastructure and potential consumers of that hydrogen relatively close to where it will be produced.
Moeve's ambition is subsequently to scale the entire Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley up to 2 GW of capacity, with facilities in Huelva and Cádiz. "By connecting Huelva with other industrial areas in Europe, whether through pipelines or maritime solutions, we will be able to expand this plant from the 300 megawatts we are currently building to 2 gigawatts and beyond," Wetselaar explains.
The aim, he adds, is to "truly create a new industry in Spain".
The big unknown: can it compete on price?
This is where one of the biggest obstacles emerges. Producing green hydrogen is still generally more expensive than obtaining conventional hydrogen from fossil fuels, although the gap depends on factors such as the price of gas, the cost of electricity, taxes on emissions and the specific conditions of each project.
Wetselaar argues that the current energy context is narrowing that gap. "Green hydrogen is competitive with grey hydrogen today, partly because the price of gas is very high," he says.
His bet is that the increase in production will bring down the cost of electrolysers and of the installations, in a similar way to what has happened previously with technologies such as solar and wind.
"As the cost of producing green hydrogen falls with the scaling up of the industry, those lines will cross and green hydrogen will become not only a clean energy source, but also highly competitive for Europe," he maintains.
But that trajectory is not guaranteed. For costs to come down, large-scale projects have to be built. And for companies to invest billions in such projects, they need to know there will be enough customers willing to buy the hydrogen they produce.
Safety and the risk of leaks
The move towards large-scale production of renewable hydrogen also raises questions about the safety of the facilities and, among them, the prevention and detection of possible leaks. Hydrogen is a highly flammable gas and, because of the small size of its molecules, requires particular attention to the tightness of equipment, pipes and connections. In enclosed spaces, a leak can also create a flammable atmosphere if it reaches certain concentrations.
Moeve says its strategy is precisely built around preventing such leaks from occurring in the first place. "We understand that the development of renewable hydrogen must go hand in hand with the highest safety standards, drawing on decades of real industrial experience in handling this molecule at the La Rábida Energy Park," María Olavarría, head of the Production Department at Moeve's La Rábida Energy Park, tells "Euronews". She explains that the new facilities are designed to be leak-tight and feature several independent layers of protection aimed at preventing incidents.
The company argues that this approach prioritises prevention over a strategy based solely on reacting once a leak is detected. "Our priority is that there are no leaks, rather than relying on detecting them afterwards," Moeve says. The firm adds that, as an additional barrier, it has automatic monitoring and detection systems designed to quickly identify anomalies during operation.
The government wants to turn it into a "national project"
Spain is not leaving the development of this industry solely to the private sector. The government has made renewable hydrogen one of the pillars of its energy and industrial strategy and has raised the electrolysis capacity target for 2030 to 12 GW.
Sánchez describes it outright as "a true national project". The prime minister said in Huelva that the government has allocated more than 3 billion euros to over 120 renewable hydrogen projects. Moeve's project alone has received more than 300 million euros in public support.
The strategy is also not just about producing the molecule. "We do not only want to generate molecules (...) of green hydrogen," Sánchez explained. "We aim for it to be produced with electrolysers, valves, compressors and the rest of the equipment manufactured here in Spain."
The goal is therefore to develop a value chain around hydrogen, from the equipment needed to produce it to the infrastructure required to store and transport it.
From importing fuels to exporting energy
There is another reason behind this race: energy security. The geopolitical crises of recent years have once again exposed how vulnerable Europe is when it depends on oil and gas from other countries. "What we need in Europe is European energy that is decarbonised, that is secure and that we produce ourselves," Wetselaar tells "Euronews".
For Spain, this ambition means reversing the traditional energy flow. Instead of importing fossil fuels, the country aims to generate renewable energy, convert it into hydrogen and its derivatives, and supply both its own industry and, eventually, other European markets.
"If this country can become, for the first time in its history, an exporter of energy, its relationship with the rest of Europe changes for the better," the Moeve CEO argues. Achieving that will require building infrastructure that does not yet exist at the necessary scale.
One of the key projects is H2Med, the corridor that aims to link the hydrogen networks of Portugal and Spain with France and, from there, with Europe's major industrial centres.
Can Spain really lead Europe's green hydrogen?
Spain has some obvious advantages: abundant solar and wind resources, the capacity to keep rolling out renewables, industry, ports and a strategic geographical position. There is also a strong public and private commitment. But leadership is not guaranteed.
Renewable hydrogen still accounts for a very small share of global production. Costs remain high, new transport and storage networks are needed, and sufficient industrial demand has yet to materialise to justify many of the investments announced.
It will also be necessary to produce much more renewable electricity. Green hydrogen can only contribute to decarbonisation if the vast amount of power it requires genuinely comes from new clean sources.
The construction of Onuba shows that some of Spain's major projects are starting to move from announcements to bricks and mortar. The hardest test now begins: proving that they can produce at scale, find enough buyers and do so at a competitive price.
If Spain manages to solve that equation, its sun and wind could allow it to turn one of its historic weaknesses (dependence on imported energy) into an advantage in the new European energy landscape.

Deutschland und Spanien zetteln Papierkrieg zu „Made in Europe“-Auslegung an
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
03:59:00 UTC
12:59:00 KST

Deutschland und Spanien zetteln Papierkrieg zu „Made in Europe“-Auslegung an
Berlin strebt einen breit aufgestellten Verbund von Handelspartnern an, während Madrid ein gestaffeltes System vorschlägt, bei dem in der EU hergestellte Waren Vorrang genießen.
BRÜSSEL - Deutschland und Spanien heizen den Streit darüber an, wie die Made-in-Europe-Regeln im Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) ausgelegt werden sollen. Beide Regierungen lancierten ihre gegensätzlichen Standpunkte über inoffizielle Diskussionspapiere (Non Paper) in Brüssel. Sie stellten damit die Weichen für harte Verhandlungen über das EU-Gesetz zur Industriepolitik.
Die Europäische Kommission hat den IAA im März vorgestellt. Er sieht unter anderem vor, staatliche Aufträge und Förderprogramme der EU-Länder für grüne Technologien, energieintensive Industrie und die Automobilbranche stärker auf Unternehmen aus der EU zu lenken. Dies soll ihnen im Wettbewerb mit Exporteuren aus China helfen.
Sechs Monate später ringen die 27 Regierungen der Union immer noch um eine gemeinsame Basis. Umstritten ist vor allem die Frage, ob Made-in-Europa-Privilegien nur für Firmen aus der EU, aus dem gesamten Europa oder auch für Länder gelten soll, die EU-Firmen ihrerseits Zugang zu öffentlichen Aufträgen gewähren.
Advertisement
In der EU geht es um Aufträge, die einen erheblichen Teil der Wirtschaftsleistung ausmachen. Von Windparks bis hin zu Stahl und Zement für den Bau von Autobahnen und U-Bahnen.
Deutschland, das Exportkraftzentrum der Union, dringt auf eine breiter angelegte „Made with Europe“-Definition. Dies entspricht auch weitgehend dem ursprünglichen Vorschlag der Kommission. Er sieht die Aufnahme von Partnern vor, die Freihandels- oder Beschaffungsabkommen mit der EU geschlossen haben oder einer Zollunion mit der Union angehören. Der Kreis könnte bis zu 80 Länder umfassen.
„Deutschland lehnt Protektionismus und Diskriminierung ab“, heißt es in dem deutschen Papier. „Die EU muss ein verlässlicher Partner für ihre Freihandelspartner bleiben und ihren rechtlichen Verpflichtungen nachkommen.“ Außerdem wird darin eine „Opt-in“-Möglichkeit gefordert, um Staaten einzubeziehen, die EU-Firmen eine entsprechende Behandlung gewähren.
Dem deutschen Papier haben sich bisher keine anderen EU-Länder angeschlossen. Frankreich, die zweitgrößte Volkswirtschaft der Union, dringt wie Spanien in die entgegengesetzte Richtung und plädiert für einen restriktiveren Ansatz.
Der französische Industrieminister Sébastien Martin bestritt zwar nicht, dass Europa gegenüber Handelspartnern offen bleiben müsse, betonte jedoch, dass öffentliches Geld in die Produktion in Europa fließen müsse.
„Auch in Zukunft wird es möglich sein, Produkte zu haben, bei denen ein Teil der Wertschöpfung aus anderen Ländern stammt, aber die Produktion muss in Europa stattfinden, damit sie für öffentliche Fördermittel infrage kommen“, sagte Martin bei seiner Ankunft zur Sitzung am Donnerstag in Brüssel.
Advertisement
Zwiebelsystem
Um das Konzept europäischer Präferenzen umsetzbar zu machen, hat Spanien laut seinem Papier eine dreistufige Struktur vorgeschlagen, bei der in der EU hergestellte Produkte die höchste Präferenz erhalten würden.
„Ein differenzierterer und risikobasierter Ansatz könnte sowohl die Wirksamkeit als auch die politische Akzeptanz des Textes verbessern“, heißt es in dem Dokument.
Die 27 EU-Mitgliedstaaten würden die erste Stufe bilden, während die zweite Stufe die Mitglieder des Europäischen Wirtschaftsraums und andere „vertrauenswürdige“ Partner umfassen würde.
Eine dritte Stufe wäre für Länder vorgesehen, die ein Freihandelsabkommen, eine Zollunion oder ein Beschaffungsabkommen mit der EU geschlossen haben. Ihr Status könnte auf die zweite Stufe angehoben werden, wenn sie ihre Handelsabkommen mit der EU vertiefen, heißt es in dem Papier.
Irland, das bis Ende des Jahres den Vorsitz im EU-Rat hat, bemüht sich, die Differenzen zu überbrücken. Dublin wird am 7. Oktober eine Sitzung der stellvertretenden Botschafter einberufen und plant, bis Mitte des Monats einen neuen Kompromissvorschlag vorzulegen, teilte Industrieminister Peter Burke seinen Kollegen am Donnerstag mit. Man hofft, im November eine Einigung zu erzielen.
Die Meinungsverschiedenheiten zwischen den EU-Regierungen ziehen sich auch durch die Parteien: Der deutsche und der spanische Flügel der Europäischen Volkspartei – der größten Fraktion im Europäischen Parlament – sind beim Industriegesetz ähnlich gespalten.
Advertisement
Die federführenden Abgeordneten des EU-Parlaments werden ihren Berichtsentwurf voraussichtlich am 28. September erörtern, während die Abgeordneten bis zum 7. Oktober Änderungsanträge einreichen können. Die Frist wurde auf Antrag der EVP um eine Woche verlängert.
Erst wenn Rat und Parlament ihre Standpunkte festgelegt haben, können Verhandlungen zwischen den EU-Institutionen aufgenommen werden. Das Ziel der Kommission, noch in diesem Jahr eine Einigung zu erzielen, erscheint zunehmend unrealistisch.
Die Debatte darüber, wer in den Club aufgenommen wird, wird in Großbritannien besonders aufmerksam verfolgt.
Der langwierige Gesetzgebungsprozess der EU erschwert die Bemühungen des Vereinigten Königreichs, seine Beziehungen zu Brüssel neu zu gestalten.
Die Regierung des neuen Premierministers Andy Burnham hat ihre Bedenken hinsichtlich eines Ausschlusses von „Made in Europe“ in die Diskussion eingebracht. EU-Vertreter haben darauf geantwortet, dass sie das Ergebnis des Gesetzgebungsverfahrens zum „Industrial Accelerator Act“ nicht vorwegnehmen können.
Dieser Text erschien zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO.

An array of liberal and left-wing Jewish groups took to the streets on Thursday to protest the arrival of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in New York City for his address to the UN General Assembly.
His arrival sparked a wave of demonstrations in Manhattan organized by groups spanning from liberal Zionist to anti-Zionist, as well as multiple Israeli expatriate groups.
“We are gathered here as American Jews, Israelis, New Yorkers, to say: You are not welcome here,” said Margo Hughes-Robinson, executive director of the left-leaning group New York Jewish Agenda.
She spoke at a protest in Dag Hammarskjöld Plaza, near the UN, sponsored by a host of liberal Jewish groups including hers, T’ruah, J Street, New Jewish Narrative, New Israel Fund, Smol Emuni and Partners for Progressive Israel.
“He is promoting a racist, destructive policy that is endangering both Palestinians and Israelis as well as others in the region,” Jill Jacobs, T’ruah’s CEO, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency in an interview.
New York rallies reflect political divide over Netanyahu visit
Democratic candidates for Congress spotted among the crowds included Brad Lander at the Israelis for Peace protest and Darializa Avila Chevalier at the Jewish Voice for Peace rally.
Counterprotesters attempted to drown out the gathering by blowing whistles and yelling into megaphones. They led chants of “Bibi!” and sang “Hatikva,” Israel’s national anthem, and “Am Israel Chai.”
Netanyahu’s visit marked the culmination of a back-and-forth between the prime minister and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who had vowed during his campaign to have him arrested. Netanyahu used part of his UN speech to attack Mamdani, whom he called “the antisemitic mayor of New York.”
Mamdani had acknowledged that he lacked the legal authority to carry out his campaign vow to arrest Netanyahu but has continued to call him a war criminal and the “architect of a horrific genocide of the Palestinian people,” and called for his International Criminal Court arrest warrant to be carried out.
As Netanyahu was scheduled to begin speaking on Thursday, Mamdani posted a video of himself planting an olive tree the previous night outside Gracie Mansion, the official mayoral residence, with Gazan families.
Jewish Voice for Peace praises Mamdani’s stance on Israel
Blocks away from Dag Hammarskjöld Plaza, at a demonstration by the anti-Zionist group Jewish Voice for Peace, JVP’s executive director Stefanie Fox told JTA that she has been “happy to see the mayor from his pulpit doing precisely what he should do to try to end the complicity of New York City and Israel’s war crimes.”
Dozens of activists were arrested at the JVP demonstration for blocking the intersection of 39th Street and First Avenue. A number of prominent progressives participated, including congressional nominee Darializa Avila Chevalier, City Council member Chi Osse and state Senate nominee Aber Kawas, as well as entertainers including Susan Sarandon, Hannah Einbinder and Caleb Hearon.
Three Democratic congressional nominees who are staunch Israel critics and were all endorsed by JVP — Melat Kiros from Colorado, Adam Hamawy from New Jersey and Chris Rabb from Pennsylvania — also appeared. Fox said their presence exemplified the “political earthquake” in Americans’ sentiment toward Israel and US support for it.
A number of speakers at Thursday’s demonstrations stressed that Israel’s elections, being held Oct. 27, offer a chance to remove Netanyahu from power.
UnXeptable, an Israeli expat group, held a rally of several dozen people in Union Square where they chanted, “Vote him out!” One woman held a sign reading, “I’m a Zionist Jew. I’m NOT the Israeli government.”
A passerby disrupted the demonstration, yelling “Free Palestine!” and “You guys killed thousands of babies!” The rally was the only anti-Netanyahu demonstration on Thursday where participants displayed Israeli flags.
Israeli activist criticizes Netanyahu government at NYC rally
Activist Ami Dror, who flew in from Israel, was one of a number of speakers on Thursday who cited reporting that Netanyahu had ignored a warning prior to Oct. 7, calling Hamas’ attack “the Netanyahu massacre.”
The Israeli government, Dror said in Union Square, does “not represent the people of Israel. It’s a criminal government, and they must go home.”
Rabbi Amichai Lau-Lavie of Lab/Shul commended those in the crowd at Dag Hammarskjöld who said they were traveling to Israel to either vote or support efforts to vote out Netanyahu.
Israelis for Peace and Friends of Standing Together, which supports an Israeli Jewish-Arab group that for a time considered a run in next month’s Israel elections, held a demonstration across from the Israeli consulate.
Brad Lander, the Jewish progressive and Democratic nominee for New York’s 10th congressional district, appeared at the rally, and also made stops at T’Ruah’s and JVP’s rallies. At the Israelis for Peace rally, Lander told reporters that both the US and Israel have big elections coming up, and that both congressional policy and Israeli policy “are going to have to change.”
In addition to the numerous protests, some political messages were displayed around midtown Manhattan. A man a block away from the UN held a sign that read “Israel’s killing Muslim children.”
More than 1,000 join pro-Palestinian demonstration in Manhattan
An 18-wheeler driving along Second Avenue featured a Palestinian flag design and the text “Free Palestine” on the side of its trailer.
A number of rallygoers trickled in from the T’Ruah rally to protest with Israelis for Peace. The expat group’s chants included, “He will burn the region down, Netanyahu out of town,” as well as “From the river to the sea, freedom and equality” — a take on the “From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free” chant that is commonly heard at pro-Palestinian protests.
More than 1,000 people joined a procession led by Palestinian Youth Movement and a number of anti-Zionist groups ater in the afternoon. Demonstrators marched from Bryant Park to near the UN, carrying “Free Palestine” signs and Palestinian flags. Some held Iranian or Lebanese flags.

Transport minister inaugurates 281km of highways, main roads in Sistan-Baluchestan
TEHRAN- With the presence of the Minister of Transport and Urban Development, 281 kilometers of highways and main roads in Sistan-Baluchestan province were put into operation. Of the inaugurated projects, 134 kilometers are in the south of the province, 89 kilometers in the north, and 58 kilometers on the North-South Corridor and coastal routes of the province.
According to IRNA, the deputy minister of transport and urban development said at the ceremony that inaugurating transport infrastructure is not merely a construction measure. He said that operating 281 kilometers of main roads and highways in Sistan-Baluchestan increases part of the province’s economic power and security.
Houshang Bazvand, while commemorating Sacred Defense Week, thanked the Minister of Transport and Urban Development for his attention to developing transport infrastructure in the province.
Referring to Sistan-Baluchestan’s capacities, he said: “With the measures taken and the governor’s follow-up, Sistan-Baluchestan can no longer be considered a remote region today, and this province has become an economic and trade gateway for the country.”

He continued: “This approach has been pursued at the national level, and the experience of war also showed the importance of this strategy and of attention to infrastructure.”
The CEO of the Construction and Development of Transportation Infrastructure Company also thanked the performance of the Directorate General of Transport and Urban Development of South Sistan-Baluchestan.

The CEO of the Construction and Development of Transportation Infrastructure Company stressed: “Corridors can play a role in the province’s economy and security, and operating these projects increases part of the province’s economic capacity.”
Bazvand thanked Farzaneh Sadegh, Minister of Transport and Urban Development; the governor of Sistan-Baluchestan; deputies and directors of the Ministry of Transport and Urban Development; the provincial deputy for development; governors; and all those involved in implementing the projects.
According to IRNA, Sistan-Baluchestan, due to its geographical expanse, the long distance between population centers, its location on important national and international corridors, access to open waters, proximity to Afghanistan and Pakistan, and its port, transit, mining, agricultural, tourism, and border trade capacities, needs a safe, fast, and standard transport network more than many other regions of the country.
In such a large geography, a highway is not only a construction project; it is part of the infrastructure for economic, security, social, and territorial development. Every kilometer of a four-lane route in Sistan and Baluchestan can reduce the distance between production and market, port and hinterland, city and village, border and the center of the country, and even economic opportunity and population.
A review of the 14th government’s two-year performance in the roads sector of Sistan-Baluchestan shows that the policy of developing communication infrastructure in this period has moved beyond the stage of defining projects and study promises and has reached the stage of implementation, completion, and operation in a significant part.
According to announced statistics, 59 highway and main road construction sites are currently active across the province, with 16 sites operating in the north and 43 in the south.
These sites have provided employment for about 6,000 people.
The activity of this number of sites, in addition to creating direct employment for executive forces, has significant indirect effects on the local economy. The activity of contractors, heavy machinery, material supply, transport, technical services, equipment repair and maintenance, and the supply chain of projects activates a set of dependent economic activities around construction projects.
From this perspective, highway projects can also be considered part of the province’s employment and economic prosperity policy.
The governor of Sistan-Baluchestan, referring to the completion of rail-laying operations for the Chabahar-Zahedan railway, stated: “Rail laying on the Chabahar-Iranshahr route has been completed, and the rail connection of this area has been made. Also, the number of project locomotives has increased from one to four, tamping machines from 2 to 3, and regulator equipment has also increased.”
The governor of Sistan-Baluchestan, referring to measures taken to supply the switches needed for the project, stated: “Fifty-five switches needed for the project have been purchased, 28 of which have been sent to the project so far, and the remaining 27 must be sent before 15 Mehr.”
He also announced an increase in ballast transport and production capacity and said: “The number of ballast transport wagons has increased from 17 to 70, and it is planned that this number will reach 105 wagons within the next 10 days. Also, daily ballast production has increased from 1,000 cubic meters to 2,500 cubic meters.”

The governor of Sistan-Baluchestan, referring to the schedule for operating the project, said: “A schedule has been prepared for the operation of this project by the end of Dey, and the remaining actions are being pursued according to this schedule.”
Farzaneh Sadegh, Minister of Transport and Urban Development, visited the Chabahar-Zahedan railway project during her one-day trip to Sistan-Baluchestan. With its implementation, the country’s only oceanic port will be connected to the national rail network.
The Chabahar-Zahedan railway project has a direct length of 630 kilometers, and its length, including branch lines, reaches 735 kilometers.
According to information about this project, the passenger transport capacity of the Chabahar-Zahedan railway is 2.2 million people, and its freight transport capacity is 7.7 million tons.
The project includes 39 tunnels with a total length of 17 kilometers, 201 intersections and special bridges, and about 2,000 culverts.
Also, in implementing the Chabahar-Zahedan railway project, 90,000 tons of domestically produced rail will be used, and the project has 33 stations.
The earthworks volume of this project is 70 million cubic meters, and its concrete pouring volume is 2.5 million cubic meters.
During this one-day trip, the Minister of Transport and Urban Development will also participate in the centralized inauguration ceremony of projects in the area of the Construction Company and Road Maintenance Organization, the operation of housing units for the disadvantaged, regeneration target projects, and the inauguration of port projects in Sistan-Baluchestan province.
A group of deputies of the Ministry of Transport and Urban Development accompanied the minister on this trip.
The Secretary of the Supreme Council of Free Trade-Industrial and Special Economic Zones, emphasizing the strategic capacities of Chabahar’s ports, described the development of port infrastructure and the strengthening of its commercial activities as requirements for the development of Makran.
According to Mehr News Agency, Hossein Forouzan, Secretary of the Supreme Council of Free Trade-Industrial and Special Economic Zones, during a trip to Chabahar, visited Shahid Kalantari and Shahid Beheshti ports and closely examined the operational capacities, port infrastructure, and the implementation process of development plans for these two ports.
During this visit, the existing capacities of Chabahar’s ports to support commercial and transit activities, the requirements for infrastructure development, and upcoming opportunities to increase the role of these ports in the regional economy were examined.
Shahid Beheshti and Shahid Kalantari ports in Chabahar, with their strategic location on the Makran coast and direct access to oceanic waters, have considerable capacity for developing trade, transit, and the country’s economic links with regional and international markets.
During this visit, emphasis was placed on the need to make maximum use of the port capacities and the Chabahar Free Zone and to strengthen coordination among relevant sectors to accelerate development projects and boost economic activities.

Scientists gave worms magnetic bacteria. They lived 43% longer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
03:52:22 UTC
12:52:22 KST

Scientists gave worms magnetic bacteria. They lived 43% longer
- Date:
- September 24, 2026
- Source:
- Hefei Institutes of Physical Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
- Summary:
- A magnet-producing bacterium extended the average lifespan of C. elegans worms by more than 43% while helping protect their neurological and intestinal health. Researchers traced much of the effect to suppression of ferroptosis, a damaging form of cell death linked to iron buildup and oxidative stress.
- Share:
Researchers led by Prof. An Xu at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have found that a magnetotactic bacterium (MTB) called Magnetospirillum magneticum AMB-1 (AMB-1) can extend healthy lifespan in the Caenorhabditis elegans model. The team also identified the main mechanism behind the effect -- suppression of a form of cell death known as ferroptosis.
The findings were published in Free Radical Biology and Medicine.
Magnetic Bacteria and Healthy Aging
Aging gradually reduces normal physiological function and raises the risk of many chronic diseases. Researchers have explored drugs and genetic approaches as possible anti-aging strategies, but questions about safety and practical clinical use remain.
Magnetotactic bacteria (MTB) offer a very different approach. These microorganisms contain specialized structures called magnetosomes and have shown good biocompatibility. They have already attracted attention for potential uses including drug delivery and cancer treatment, but their possible influence on aging has received far less study.
To investigate that question, the researchers tested the MTB strain AMB-1 in C. elegans, a widely used model organism for aging research.
Lifespan Increased by More Than 43%
Worms treated with AMB-1 lived substantially longer. Their average lifespan increased by 43.39%, and the treatment also helped preserve neurological function and intestinal integrity in older worms.
The team then examined whether magnetosome production was important to this effect. Their results indicated that the ability to produce magnetosomes played a major role in extending lifespan.
Wild-type AMB-1 produced a stronger longevity effect than reversibly non-magnetotactic RNM-AMB-1. In contrast, non-magnetotactic NM-AMB-1 did not extend lifespan.
Blocking an Aging-Linked Form of Cell Death
Further experiments offered clues about how AMB-1 produces its effects. The bacteria reduced iron buildup and lowered lipid peroxidation in the worms, changes that suppressed aging-related ferroptosis.
Ferroptosis is a form of cell death associated with iron accumulation and oxidative damage to fats within cells. Genetic analysis showed that several ferroptosis-related pathways were involved in AMB-1-mediated lifespan regulation, including the genes ftn-1, bli-3, and ads-1.
According to the researchers, the findings establish a new microbial strategy for anti-aging intervention and provide foundational evidence that could support broader use of MTB in geriatric medicine.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Hefei Institutes of Physical Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yuting Ding, Xinyao Huang, Yanan Zhao, Ruoyun Dong, Chenxi Zhou, Yuanyuan Wu, Hua Du, Juan Wan, Yun Liu, An Xu. A novel role for magnetotactic bacterium: Magnetospirillum magneticum AMB-1 prolonged healthy lifespan of Caenorhabditis elegans via regulating ferroptosis. Free Radical Biology and Medicine, 2026; 254: 434 DOI: 10.1016/j.freeradbiomed.2026.06.050

Overseas Lao workers send home 500 mln USD in first 7 months of 2026
China
Unknown Publisher

VIENTIANE, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Lao migrant workers sent home an estimated 500 million U.S. dollars in the first seven months of 2026, up 36.6 percent from 366 million dollars during the same period last year, according to the Lao Ministry of Labor and Social Welfare.
The ministry also reported continued growth in labor migration, with 350,567 Lao nationals working abroad between 2021 and 2025. By September 2026, a further 112,436 Lao workers had taken jobs overseas, according to Lao Economic Daily on Thursday.
The figures were presented on Tuesday at a meeting of the Steering Committee for the "TRIANGLE in ASEAN" project, which promotes partnerships for fair and effective labor migration across ASEAN.
Laos is strengthening measures to protect migrant workers and promote safe and legal employment abroad as the next phase of the TRIANGLE project gets underway in eight countries.
The 2026-2031 phase covers Laos, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Thailand and Timor-Leste. Building on lessons from the 2015-2025 phase, the project aims to promote safer migration, improve working conditions, strengthen skills and enhance protection for migrant workers. ■

Iran’s horticulture development adopts ‘Technology-Driven Development’ scenario
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
03:46:03 UTC
12:46:03 KST

Iran’s horticulture development adopts ‘Technology-Driven Development’ scenario
TEHRAN- According to the findings of the report "Future Studies of the Role of Research, Education, and Extension in the Development of Iran's Horticulture," the "technology-driven development" scenario was introduced as the proposed path for the development of Iran's horticulture in the horizon of Iranian calendar year 1420 (begins on March 2037).
According to Mehr News Agency, Iran's horticulture sector, with an annual production of 25 million tons of products and direct employment of more than 800,000 people, is one of the important pillars of the country's agricultural economy, but it faces challenges including limited water resources, declining productivity, and weakness in the knowledge transfer system.
This study was conducted with the aim of future-studies analysis of the development of Iran's horticulture and with emphasis on the role of agricultural research, education, and extension, and used data from the Statistical Center of Iran, the Ministry of Agriculture-Jihad, and the Customs of the Islamic Republic of Iran to design scenarios.
To quantify the consequences of each scenario, a Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) model, ARIMA time series models, and Monte Carlo simulation with 10,000 iterations were used.
According to the report's findings, in the "continuation of the existing trend" scenario, agricultural sector employment decreases from 2.07 million people to 1.94 million people, equivalent to a 6 percent decline. In this scenario, the trade balance of horticultural products reaches $4.7 billion.
In the "technology-driven development" scenario, two key assumptions were considered: increasing the research budget to 1.5 percent of the agricultural sector's value added and achieving 80 percent extension coverage of beneficiaries.
Based on the modeling performed, in this scenario, the value added of the horticulture sector increases by 61 percent, and 480,000 new jobs are created in the value chain. Also, agricultural sector employment will increase by 26 percent.
Another result of this scenario is a 78 percent improvement in water productivity, such that water productivity rises from 18.5 to 33 thousand rials per cubic meter.
Horticultural product exports in this scenario are also estimated at $12 billion, which is 94 percent more than the "continuation of the existing trend" scenario.
