Young men flee Tigray amid fears of forced recruitment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
03:45:06 UTC
12:45:06 KST

Young men flee Tigray amid fears of forced recruitment
Years after the war, unresolved tensions are again leaving young people fearful of being drawn into fighting.
Tigray, Ethiopia – Gebru, 27, says he was taken from his neighbourhood to a local administration office with other young men. His parents feared he would be sent to fight and searched for a way to get him out. They eventually paid to secure his release, he says.
“I was taken to the office with other young men. My parents found a way to get me released by paying 20,000 [Ethiopian] birr ($123) in cash.”
After he was released, Gebru left Tigray for Addis Ababa.
“My parents were afraid that if I stayed, I would be taken again. They told me to leave Tigray and save myself.”
Gebru is among young men who say they are leaving Tigray because they fear being forcibly recruited to fight as political and military tensions rise in the northern Ethiopian region.
Nearly four years after the November 2022 Pretoria Agreement ended the war between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), reports of forced recruitment and military mobilisation have raised fears among young conflict survivors that they could once again be drawn into fighting.
The African Union-brokered agreement ended two years of war in Tigray, but key issues – including contested territory, the return of displaced people and the disarmament of Tigrayan forces – remain unresolved.
Human Rights Watch reported in July that Tigrayan authorities and forces had forcibly recruited civilians, including children as young as 15, since at least April. The organisation documented cases involving former combatants and other men and boys who it said were taken from streets, homes, workplaces and gold-mining areas.
The allegations come as tensions between the federal government and the TPLF have risen, with both sides accusing the other of military mobilisation. Heavy fighting was also reported near Ethiopia’s border with Sudan in August.
For some young men, the response has been to leave.
Leaving before they are taken
Shewit, 24, had been trying to rebuild his life after the war. He was studying at Mekelle University, running a language-class business he had started about a year earlier and helping to look after his younger siblings.
But as reports of recruitment and military mobilisation increased, he said staying in Tigray began to feel unsafe.
“I had already survived one war. I didn’t want to go through another,” he told Al Jazeera.
He eventually left for Addis Ababa, leaving behind his family, his studies and his business.
“I left behind my siblings, who depended on me, and a business I had sacrificed so much to build.”
He says he does not want to return unless he can bring his family with him.
“I don’t want to go back. In fact, if I can, I want to bring my family and my siblings here with me.”
Those who remember the battlefield
Gebrehiwot, 28, is still in Tigray. He fought during the previous war but says he does not want to return to the battlefield.
He says the experience changed the way he viewed the war’s political and military leadership, particularly after seeing wounded fighters and families of dead soldiers struggle after the fighting ended.
“We were told that we were fighting for our people, but after the war ended, I saw wounded fighters and families of the dead being abandoned.”
He says reports that former combatants were being called back increased his fears.
“Former combatant friends were being called back to the army and I heard some had been taken away forcibly. I was afraid I would be next, so I left my hometown and moved to Mekelle, hoping I would not get identified here.”
Unlike Shewit and Gebru, he has not left Tigray. But he says his experience of the previous war makes the prospect of another mobilisation difficult to contemplate.
“I know what the battlefield looks like. I don’t want to go back there and risk not coming home.”
A wider pattern
Human Rights Watch says the recruitment allegations extend beyond former fighters to civilians and young people.
“We found that both former fighters but also civilians – young men, sometimes boys – were being abducted, detained,” said Laetitia Bader, the organisation’s Horn of Africa director. “Sometimes in the streets, in marketplaces, also in mining areas which is an important form of livelihood in the region.”
Bader said Human Rights Watch had documented cases involving minors as young as 15.
The organisation also said a mobilisation proclamation introduced in June criminalised desertion and attempts by relatives to prevent loved ones from being conscripted.
For young people who survived the previous war, Bader said, the reported recruitment was another reason to flee.
“The forced conscription continues to have an impact. Young people continue to try to flee the region not only because of the forced conscription but also the devastating humanitarian situation in the region,” she said.
The TPLF has disputed allegations of forced recruitment, saying young people were joining voluntarily. TPLF spokesman Michael Asgedom previously described the allegations as a “mistaken narrative”.
Al Jazeera contacted Asgedom for a response to the allegations in this story, but he did not respond to calls or text messages.
From recruitment to another war?
Muauz Gidey Alemu, an assistant professor of political science and lead researcher at the Tigray Institute of Policy Studies, said the recruitment should be understood within a broader political and security crisis that followed the Pretoria Agreement.
“The emergence of forced conscription at this particular moment should not be understood simply as a military recruitment exercise,” he said. “It is better understood as a symptom of the deeper political and security crisis that has developed around the incomplete implementation of the Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement.”
Gidey said the agreement had stopped large-scale fighting but had not resolved all the political and security issues surrounding the post-war period.
“The present situation demonstrates that Pretoria produced an effective cessation of large-scale warfare but an incomplete peace settlement,” he said.
He said continued mobilisation could create a cycle in which insecurity fuels military recruitment, which then deepens insecurity.
“Political insecurity generates military mobilisation; military mobilisation reinforces political insecurity; political insecurity then becomes an argument for further mobilisation,” Gidey said.
For the young men interviewed by Al Jazeera, however, the question is less about the political calculations driving mobilisation than about whether they can avoid being pulled back into war.
Gebru says leaving became his way of protecting himself.
“After what happened, I knew I could not stay there and live normally. I felt that the only way to protect myself was to leave.”
Shewit is now in Addis Ababa, separated from his family and the life he had been rebuilding.
“I didn’t leave because I wanted to. I left because I wanted to have a chance to build a future.”
Gebrehiwot, who remains in Tigray, says his hopes are simpler.
“I don’t want anything extraordinary. I just want to live peacefully, stay with my family and never have to pick up a gun again.”

Though CNN and MS NOW were back on the White House grounds Thursday, both news outlets said their journalists were denied access to Chinese leader Xi Jinping's state dinner arrival.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back into the White House on Thursday following a federal judge's order that the journalists have their access restored.
District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that revoking the White House press credentials of the three media outlets "likely violated their constitutional due process rights."
"The 'general rule' is that 'individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the Government deprives them' of a constitutionally protected interest," the judge said.
The three US outlets had been banned by US President Donald Trump from reporting from the White House for six days. They attempted to return to the White House early Thursday ahead of a visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping, but were initially turned away by the Secret Service.
But despite regaining access to the complex earlier in the day, CNN reported later Thursday that the White House had "denied two CNN journalists from covering Chinese leader Xi Jinping's arrival back at the White House for a state dinner."
The cable network reported that MS NOW journalists were also denied access to the arrival.
On a high-profile day when Xi was visiting Washington and attending a state dinner, no major American network was airing live coverage.
After the White House banned CNN from a rotation of five major US broadcast outlets who take turns shooting and sharing video, the other four — in a show of solidarity — were still declining to participate in the so-called video pool.
The White House Press Office accused CNN in a letter to the cable news outlet of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information," with similar accusations levelled against MS NOW and Politico.
The letter to CNN cited several stories about the US-Iran war and a story on Trump's plans to build a military bunker below the planned East Wing ballroom which allegedly "disclosed 'top-secret' construction details."

The pact stipulates that an attack on one of the three countries is considered an attack on all of them.
Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan have announced they are planning an urgent meeting of their chiefs of staff to discuss ways to support the kingdom under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
The announcement followed a meeting on Thursday in New York between Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, according to the Saudi Press Agency.

The statement did not say when the military chiefs would meet or what form of support could be considered.
Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7 to strengthen collective deterrence and expand defence cooperation.
The pact stipulates that an attack on one of the three countries is considered an attack on them all.
The three countries have since begun setting up mechanisms under the pact. Their foreign and defence ministers and military chiefs met in Istanbul on August 31 for the first meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee, agreeing to establish a secretariat in Saudi Arabia and to deepen military cooperation.
Thursday’s foreign ministers’ meeting also condemned attacks targeting Mecca as well as civilian and economic facilities in Saudi Arabia, and it affirmed the kingdom’s right to defend itself under Article 51 of the UN Charter.
The diplomatic moves came as Saudi Arabia reported a fresh wave of attacks from Yemen.
Saudi Arabia said its air defences shot down six ballistic missiles launched towards Taif and Yanbu on Thursday.
Major-General Turki al-Malki, the coalition spokesman, said further Houthi escalation would be “dealt with firmly”. Saudi Civil Defence authorities had issued alerts in several areas before later saying the danger had passed.
The Houthis separately claimed missile and drone attacks on a “sensitive target” in Riyadh and Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu.
France has also offered to provide defensive support to Saudi Arabia. President Emmanuel Macron said Paris would send military assets to help protect Yanbu.
“We are going to send military assets, meaning soldiers, radars and defence systems to protect this site,” Macron said in an interview with TF1 on Thursday.
Yemen clashes drive rising casualties and displacement
The cross-border attacks have coincided with some of the heaviest fighting inside Yemen since hostilities escalated again.
Fighting across several fronts in Yemen killed at least 150 Houthi fighters and members of government-aligned forces in the 24 hours leading into Friday, according to an AFP news agency tally.
The toll compiled by AFP included 98 fighters on the government side and 52 from the Houthis, with clashes reported around the Kahboub Mountains and areas between Lahj and Taiz overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The Houthis have also expanded their presence along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including by taking the port city of Mocha and strategic islands. The gains have strengthened the group’s position around Bab al-Mandeb, one of the world’s busiest shipping corridors. About 12 percent of global trade normally passes through the waterway, according to AP.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has urged greater international involvement, warning at the UN General Assembly that Houthi control around the strait poses a wider economic risk.
Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader Al Alimi-Bawzer accused the Houthis of using freedom of navigation as leverage, saying their actions were “taking hostage the entire global economy”.
The renewed fighting has forced more than 230,000 people from their homes since the beginning of September, according to UNHCR, as clashes spread across multiple front lines. The agency said the latest displacement has added to about 5.2 million people already internally displaced across Yemen.
UNHCR said families have been uprooted across governorates, including Hodeidah, Taiz, Lahj, Aden, Abyan, Marib, al-Dhalea and Shabwah, with many fleeing at short notice and leaving with few belongings.
Shelter, food, clean water, healthcare and protection services are among the most urgent needs, while host communities and displacement sites are becoming increasingly overstretched.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s presidential campaign has accused Donald Trump of wanting to “colonise” Brazil in order to capture its natural resources by meddling in next month’s presidential election.
The accusation came in a televised campaign advert that was broadcast on Thursday by Lula’s team amid growing fears over the impact alleged US interference could have on the vote.
The TV spot claimed the US president was trying to sway the election in favour of Lula’s far-right adversary in the election, Flávio Bolsonaro, in order to advance Trump’s interests in the South American nation.
“Flávio Bolsonaro is Trump’s candidate and what Trump wants is to colonise Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust,” the female narrator tells viewers in the minute-long video.
The state department has denied claims the US is meddling in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” it said last month in a statement.
Writing on X, Lula accused Bolsonaro of wanting to “hand our natural resources over to the United States”.
“If it’s up to him, Brazil will become a colony again,” the incumbent leftwing president added.
With just over a week to go until the 4 October first round vote, Lula and Bolsonaro are neck and neck in the polls. A second round run-off will be held on 25 October if no candidate secures more than half of the votes.
In recent weeks, there has been growing alarm – both in Brazil and overseas – about Washington’s apparent attempts to influence the result, with a campaign of diplomatic and economic pressure, including 25% tariffs on Brazilian imports.
Speaking at the UN general assembly in New York this week, Lula indirectly criticised the US’ perceived meddling, telling delegates: “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians.”
Earlier this week, dozens of Democratic party congresspeople wrote to secretary of state, Marco Rubio, to denounce the Trump administration’s “apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazil’s elections through what they called a “sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilisation in Brazil”.
The narrator of Lula’s campaign ad cited a series of recent media stories relating to alleged acts of US meddling.
They include reports about the alleged interference of Big Tech companies as well as a confidential document sent to electoral authorities by Brazil’s intelligence agency warning of a “critical level” of risk of US interference. The campaign video also highlighted recent claims about links between Bolsonaro’s campaign and the conservative donor network Rockbridge, which was co-founded by Trump’s vice-president JD Vance.
Éden Valadares, the communications secretary for Lula’s Worker’s party (PT), said the campaign ad was part of efforts to “alert the Brazilian people” to the ideologically-driven US campaign. “We don’t believe it will work but nor will we sit back and do nothing,” Valadares said.
“President Lula has instructed us … to mobilise Brazilian society … [and] to react in the streets,” added Valadares, who said a nationwide series of events were being planned for this Sunday.
Fears over US meddling are not confined to the Brazilian left. This week, another of the right-wing candidates in Brazil’s election, Renan Santos, also denounced Trump’s behaviour and said he did not want Brazil to become a US vassal state. “They want to interfere in Brazil’s elections to secure satisfactory contracts involving rare earths,” Santos claimed in a social media video.
Recalling the US invasion of Venezuela in January, Santos added: “I don’t want to see Latin America become an American protectorate.”
In the letter sent to Rubio on Friday, the Democratic lawmakers wrote that “rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy”, the US was “acting as an agent of interference and destabilisation – using diplomatic, economic and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil’s electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic US ally and trading partner”.
They asked Rubio if Trump’s administration would commit to respecting Brazil’s electoral process and requested a response by 1 October. The state department has not yet responded to a request for comment.

The 5th Global Digital Trade Expo (GDTE) kicks off today in east China's Hangzhou City. As China's sole national-level international professional exhibition themed on digital trade, the five-day-long expo puts artificial intelligence center-stage under the theme "Meet the AI Future at GDTE."
Across its 170,000-square-metre exhibition halls, the event links technological innovation, business matchmaking and international cooperation, mirroring the robust global expansion momentum of Hangzhou's AI industry.
Stepping into the sprawling venue, visitors are greeted with a strong sense of the future. The specially built Token Zone lays out a full-fledged innovation chain covering computing-power infrastructure, large language models, and industry-specific real-world applications. More than 200 AI large models are on collective display. Cutting-edge achievements such as brain-computer interfaces and embodied intelligence, once confined to research papers, are now demonstrated live for the general public.
Attendees may stop to observe how brain-computer devices rebuild bridges for people with disabilities to perceive the world. They can sit through simulated consultations powered by a traditional Chinese medicine large-model system, or get hands-on experience with service robots and smart wearable devices to see how technology transforms daily life. The Global Open-source AI Challenge and the Global Digital Trade Innovation Competition, which focuses on embodied intelligence robots, run concurrently. Developers from across the globe compete and exchange ideas, turning conceptual creativity into practical, real-world solutions.
Openness and connectivity lie at the very heart of the GDTE. Malaysia and Hungary serve as this edition's Guest Countries of Honour, with overseas exhibition groups larger than in previous years. Representatives from 121 countries and regions as well as 29 international organizations gather at the event.
Signature sessions including the Silk Road E-Commerce Day, the BRICS Special Economic Zones Hangzhou Dialogue and Africa Digital Trade Day are held successively. Participants sit together to exchange insights and advance pragmatic collaboration on Silk-Road-themed e-commerce, cross-border data flows and green digital trade.
Working together with five leading international authoritative institutions, the expo compiles and releases its flagship report, Global Digital Trade Development Report 2026, alongside several high-profile industry publications. These documents deliver valuable observations and reflections for the fast-evolving global digital-trade landscape.
Nearly 40,000 professional buyers and sellers take part in the grand gathering, among whom over 12,000 are overseas delegates. More than 1,300 business-matching sessions are held in orderly fashion, with AI assistants facilitating precise matchmaking for business opportunities.
Beyond the short-term offline exhibition, the upgraded Digital Trade Online platform creates a "never-ending digital-trade expo." It connects online cross-border-e-commerce platforms with offline specialized markets, extending trade engagement throughout the full pre-, during- and post-event cycle. Ticket interoperability has been realized between the GDTE, the APSARA Conference and the West Lake Conference, enabling mutual empowerment and amplifying the event's outreach.
Coinciding with the Mid-Autumn Festival, the expo also transforms into a lively digital carnival steeped in everyday charm. One hundred AI application scenarios, 100 premium digital-trade products and 100 consumer-experience spots are scattered across the venue.
An 800-meter-long bazaar brims with a rich array of exotic goods from around the world. Supporting services such as streamlined entry procedures and one-stop tax-refund processing for departing visitors are fully available. Guests from afar can fully immerse themselves in cutting-edge technology while strolling at leisure to savor the vivid delights of digital consumption.

In the first half of 2026, local core-AI-industry revenue reached 270.5 billion yuan, representing a year-on-year increase of 26%. Home-grown tech innovators are going global: dexterous humanoid robots are shipped worldwide, and rehabilitation exoskeletons cross oceans to help patients suffering from muscle weakness stand again. Cold hardware carries the warmth of human-centered care.

The China headquarters of the Arab Federation for Digital Economy will settle in Hangzhou, building a collaborative platform for Chinese and foreign enterprises to pursue joint-technology research and co-create products, so digital innovations originating in the East can benefit broader global markets.
As the Qiantang River's mighty tides roll onward, digital trade has become an undeniable force driving global-economic growth. At this expo, AI is far more than eye-catching technology. It acts as a bond linking enterprises, connecting markets and benefiting ordinary people. Drawing participants worldwide to Hangzhou, the expo fosters technical exchanges and business negotiations to jointly explore an open, inclusive, win-win development path for the digital age.

“We found something never seen before” – A dead star is producing a shock wave that shouldn’t exist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
03:19:34 UTC
12:19:34 KST

“We found something never seen before” – A dead star is producing a shock wave that shouldn’t exist
- Date:
- September 24, 2026
- Source:
- ESO
- Summary:
- A dead white dwarf with no detectable disk has somehow produced a powerful shock wave that appears to have persisted for at least 1,000 years. Its magnetic field may be partly responsible, but astronomers say an unexplained “mystery engine” may also be at work.
- Share:
Stars can produce powerful shock waves when gas and dust streaming away from them collide with material in the surrounding space. Astronomers have now captured a striking example around the dead star RXJ0528+2838 using the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (ESO's VLT).
The discovery is puzzling because, based on known mechanisms, this small stellar remnant should not be capable of producing the structure seen around it. The unexpected finding challenges current ideas about how dead stars exchange matter and energy with their surroundings.
"We found something never seen before and, more importantly, entirely unexpected," says Simone Scaringi, associate professor at Durham University, UK and co-lead author of the study published in Nature Astronomy.
"Our observations reveal a powerful outflow that, according to our current understanding, shouldn't be there," says Krystian Ilkiewicz, a postdoctoral researcher at the Nicolaus Copernicus Astronomical Center in Warsaw, Poland and study co-lead.
Astronomers use the term 'outflow' to describe material expelled from an object in space.
A Shock Wave Around a Dead Star
RXJ0528+2838 lies about 730 light-years from Earth. Like the Sun and other stars, it travels around the center of the Milky Way. As it moves through space, it encounters gas between the stars, producing a type of shock wave known as a bow shock.
Noel Castro Segura, research fellow at the University of Warwick in the UK and collaborator in this study, describes it as "a curved arc of material, similar to the wave that builds up in front of a ship."
Bow shocks are typically produced when material flowing away from a star slams into its surroundings. In the case of RXJ0528+2838, however, astronomers cannot identify any known process that fully accounts for what they observed.
A White Dwarf With No Disk
RXJ0528+2838 is a white dwarf, the leftover core of a dying low-mass star, and it is orbited by a Sun-like companion.
In binary systems like this one, material can be pulled away from the companion and transferred onto the white dwarf. That material often forms a disc around the dead star. The disc feeds the white dwarf, while some matter can also be thrown back into space in powerful outflows.
RXJ0528+2838 is different. Astronomers see no evidence of such a disc, leaving them without the usual explanation for the outflow and the surrounding nebula.
"The surprise that a supposedly quiet, discless system could drive such a spectacular nebula was one of those rare 'wow' moments," says Scaringi.
VLT Observations Confirm the Source
The unusual structure was first noticed in images taken with the Isaac Newton Telescope in Spain. Its strange appearance prompted the researchers to investigate it more closely using the MUSE instrument on ESO's VLT.
"Observations with the ESO MUSE instrument allowed us to map the bow shock in detail and analyse its composition. This was crucial to confirm that the structure really originates from the binary system and not from an unrelated nebula or interstellar cloud," Ilkiewicz explains.
The bow shock's size and shape suggest that RXJ0528+2838 has been producing a powerful outflow for at least 1000 years.
That creates another problem. Scientists do not yet know how a dead star without a disc could sustain such an outflow for so long, although the system's magnetic field may provide an important clue.
A Magnetic Field May Hold Part of the Answer
RXJ0528+2838 is known to possess a strong magnetic field, something the MUSE observations also confirmed.
Instead of allowing material from the companion star to settle into a disc, the magnetic field appears to guide that matter directly onto the white dwarf.
"Our finding shows that even without a disc, these systems can drive powerful outflows, revealing a mechanism we do not yet understand. This discovery challenges the standard picture of how matter moves and interacts in these extreme binary systems," Ilkiewicz explains.
The researchers suspect that the magnetic field could be connected to a hidden source of energy, which Scaringi describes as a 'mystery engine.' But the explanation remains incomplete.
According to the observations, the white dwarf's present-day magnetic field could sustain a bow shock for only a few hundred years. The structure appears to have existed for at least 1000 years, meaning the magnetic field alone cannot yet explain the full phenomenon.
Searching for the "Mystery Engine"
Astronomers will need to investigate many more binary systems to determine how these powerful outflows can form without discs.
ESO's upcoming Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) could play an important role by allowing scientists to study both known systems and much fainter examples in greater detail.
Scaringi expects the telescope "to map more of these systems as well as fainter ones and detect similar systems in detail, ultimately helping in understanding the mysterious energy source that remains unexplained."

Editor’s Notes: I believed in Israel’s third bloc until pollsters proved me wrong - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
03:17:24 UTC
12:17:24 KST

I was wrong about Israel’s third bloc. I also wanted it to succeed.
I wanted a political force strong enough to make the moderate parties of the Center-Right and Center-Left form a broad unity government. Enough seats to force politicians who could find endless reasons to avoid each other to discover reasons to sit together.
After the October 7 massacre and the war, I thought that was possible. I wrote columns explaining why.
The polling has forced me to reconsider. The independent camp I expected has failed to take shape. We are back to Bibi or no Bibi.
Wanting a broad government seems to me a perfectly reasonable position. Forecasting the emergence of a bloc that could force one into existence required evidence. I gave the possibility more weight than the campaign has justified, and I have to ask how much wanting that outcome influenced my judgment.
In August, I wrote about conversations around me in Gush Etzion, south of Jerusalem: at the kiddush after going to the synagogue, in the supermarket, at the park. People who had voted the same way for years were reconsidering their choices. They remained on the Right. Some were moving further Right. Their attachment to particular politicians had weakened.
My own thinking had changed, too. For years, I had argued that persuading haredi (ultra-Orthodox) men to serve in the military would achieve more than coercion. During the war, I came to support financial consequences for avoiding service. I knew how far I had moved on a question I had written about repeatedly.
I thought enough changes like these could produce a new political alignment. In that August column, I wrote: “Israel is going through the same thing with the lights on and pollsters in the room, failing to measure it.”
I was confident enough to suggest that the pollsters were missing something. Their numbers have since given me reason to question my own reading.
There was a leap in the argument. Dissatisfied voters still have to agree on where to go. Two reservists can agree about the unfairness of the burden they carry and disagree completely about who should be prime minister. A voter can lose faith in one right-wing politician and choose another who intends to join the same coalition. Changed loyalties can move seats around inside an existing camp.
The third bloc I imagined also had to do something quite demanding with those seats. It had to remain together, make a broad government a condition of its support, and leave the larger parties dependent on that support. Each step could fail. Even a respectable election result would have been only the beginning.
Those promising unity struggled to unite
Instead, some of the people promising unity struggled to unite with one another.
On September 4, Gilad Erdan withdrew his Unity party from the election, citing insufficient support and unsuccessful efforts to join forces with other parties. An N12 poll had put a potential combination of Unity and Benny Gantz’s Blue and White at 2.6%, below the 3.25% threshold for entering the Knesset.
Erdan said voters were primarily looking for an answer to “the question of who will be prime minister.” That was a fairly direct assessment from someone whose political offer had depended on voters giving a different question priority.
The negotiations also exposed a familiar problem. Asked by Walla why he insisted on leading a merged list, Gantz answered: “Because I need to lead this path.”
A project that asks parties across the political spectrum to compromise needs leaders capable of doing so themselves. The order of names on a list is a useful place to start. Those failed talks give us reason to examine the politicians’ decisions alongside the voters’ choices.
Some new lists remain. In the September 18 Maariv poll conducted by Lazar Research, Yoaz Hendel, and Yaron Zelekha’s joint list received four seats, as did Ofer Winter’s People of Israel. Both were narrowly above the electoral threshold. Winter’s seats were counted in the Netanyahu camp.
Four seats can matter enormously in a parliament of 120, where a majority requires 61. Those lists may yet affect who can form a government. The substantial independent camp I expected has nevertheless failed to emerge.
I also underestimated what the Netanyahu question would mean after October 7.
I had expected the scale of the catastrophe and the demands of the war to create pressure for a broad government. They could also make the choice of prime minister feel more consequential. A voter who holds Netanyahu responsible has a powerful reason to insist on his departure. A voter who trusts him most on security has a powerful reason to insist that he stay. The same war can deepen both convictions.
Mere calls for unity can not resolve disagreement
Calling for unity does very little to resolve that disagreement. Any party seeking to force a broad government has to explain whether it would serve under Netanyahu, what conditions it would set, and what it would do if those conditions were rejected. The answer could cost precisely the voters it was trying to bring together.
That is a harder problem than getting people to agree that the country needs unity. I gave too much weight to the apparent demand for a broad government, and too little to the compromises people would have to accept to produce one.
The election is still ahead. Polls can change, and small parties can cross the threshold or fall below it. But the weak numbers and failed attempts to build a common political vehicle are evidence I have to take seriously now. A columnist cannot keep extending the deadline for his own argument until it comes true.
I still want a broad government of the moderate Center-Right and Center-Left. I think it would give Israel a better chance of making decisions on military service, rebuilding, and responsibility for October 7 that could survive beyond one coalition.
The route I expected to get us there has failed in this campaign. A third bloc may have another chance in another election.
I would need to see leaders able to work together, voters prepared to accept the necessary compromises, and a credible way to turn their votes into a broad government. I owe readers that evidence before making the prediction again.

Pray for Leiter: The importance of supporting soldiers who protect Israeli life - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
03:17:11 UTC
12:17:11 KST

IDF reservist Neria Leiter was seriously wounded Wednesday when a Palestinian attacker rammed a vehicle into him at a checkpoint near Beit Horon on Route 443.
After hours of surgery at Jerusalem’s Shaare Zedek Medical Center, doctors said his condition had stabilized, but his life remained in danger. His family has asked the public to pray for Neria Dov ben Chana.
His father, Israel’s ambassador to the US, Yechiel Leiter, flew home from New York. At the hospital on Thursday, he spoke about a previous journey through grief. In November 2023, his eldest son, Maj. (res.) Moshe Yedidya Leiter, was killed fighting in Gaza.
“He died instantly,” Yechiel said. This time, he said, the family could gather at Neria’s bedside while doctors worked to save him, and they could pray together and ask others to join them. “His life is still in danger,” he told reporters.
There are many ways to describe this family. Yechiel Leiter left the United States for Israel at 18, making a deliberate choice about where to build his life. His children grew up here and made their own choices about service.
Neria returned to reserve duty after his brother's death
Moshe served for years, became a father of six, and was studying medicine when war called him back. After Moshe’s death, Neria returned to reserve duty.
Their father has spoken about other sons and sons-in-law who served on the front lines, of a son in a support role, and of another son who has Down syndrome, living through the war with the family. Each has a life beyond this accounting of service.
Neria described the decision to go back in a post this year. “As a bereaved brother,” he wrote, returning to the reserves “was not simple at all.” Losing Moshe had torn at him.
He also had opinions and criticisms about how the war and the country were being run. The question he posed, in translation, was: “What do I need to do? What is in my control?”
He could not sit at home while his friends reported for one reserve stint after another. His team included religious and secular men, husbands and fathers, alongside single men, from Israel’s center and its periphery. By then, the rounds of duty were too numerous to count. His closing words were about the privilege of defending home.
Israel's reservists carry an enormous weight for their country
Read the whole account, and its honesty becomes clear. A person can believe in his duty and feel the strain of carrying it.
He can disagree with those making the decisions and still answer the call. No country should mistake that resolve for an inexhaustible supply of time, health, or courage.
Israel has needed its reservists across multiple fronts since the October 7 massacre. Their families have lived with repeated departures, interrupted work, and the fear that accompanies every call.
The Leiter family’s name is known because Yechiel represents Israel in Washington. Countless families whose names never reach a newspaper have carried comparable burdens. They, too, deserve to be seen while they are serving and long after they return.
'Choosing life' means caring for the soldiers who protect it
Yechiel wrote after the attack that he believes prayer and national unity can bring miracles. “Neria needs a miracle,” he said, adding: “They choose death – we choose life.”
A father whose son is fighting for his life is entitled to speak with that force. For the rest of us, choosing life must also mean tending to those who protect it: giving wounded service members and their families sustained care, making repeated reserve service bearable, examining attacks seriously, and sharing the demands of defense as fairly as possible.
That requires support for families and employers long after the headlines have moved on. Officials must hear reservists who voice criticism, even when those same reservists continue to serve.
At Shaare Zedek, Yechiel’s daughter gave birth after visiting her brother. A new life began in one part of the hospital while doctors worked to save Neria in another. Nothing about that proximity tells us how Neria’s story will end. For now, the only ending to seek is his recovery.
The family has asked us to pray. We join that prayer. We should also listen to what Neria wrote when he was well enough to explain why he kept going – and make sure Israel lives up to the people who do.

Nine-year-old dies after contracting brain-eating amoeba after swimming in Kinneret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
03:17:09 UTC
12:17:09 KST

A 9-year-old boy died on Thursday after contracting encephalitis as a result of Naegleria Fowleri, also known as the 'brain-eating amoeba,' the Health Ministry announced.
The ministry first announced that the boy had been hospitalized with swelling in his brain and was subsequently sedated and ventilated in intensive care at Rambam Medical Center on September 6.
A sample was sent to the Health Ministry laboratory, which confirmed the cause as the amoeba the night before.
According to the ministry, an investigation found that the boy had been swimming at Kursi Beach in the Kinneret (Sea of Galilee) about a week before his hospitalization.
The microscopic amoeba is found in fresh and warm water sources and may cause an infection of the central nervous system if water containing the amoeba enters through the nose and the amoeba reaches the brain.
The ministry emphasized that the infection, while having a high mortality rate, is extremely rare and that it cannot be contracted from drinking the water or from another person.
There have been fewer than 500 cases worldwide, two of which were diagnosed in the US last year, and three of which were diagnosed in Israel in recent years.
Health Ministry advises public take care to mitigate risk while bathing in fresh, warm water
To reduce risk while bathing in fresh, warm water, it is recommended to avoid getting water in the nose as much as possible, especially when jumping, diving, or otherwise submerging one's head in the water.
The Health Ministry recommends closing one's nose or using a nose plug.
Additionally, avoid digging or stirring the bottom in shallow water, where the amoeba may gather in higher concentrations.
If symptoms, including fever, pain, significant headaches, nausea, or vomiting, especially combined with neck stiffness, confusion, unusual drowsiness, or a change in consciousness, appear, the public is urged to seek immediate medical attention and mention their water exposure.
Due to the amoeba's presence in warm water, swimming sports events have been postponed until the water temperature drops below 24 degrees, at which point the proliferation of the amoeba decreases significantly.

Abraham Accords countries hold first official meeting since Oct. 7 attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
03:12:00 UTC
12:12:00 KST

Abraham Accords countries hold first official meeting since Oct. 7 attacks
Ten blocks away from the United Nations General Assembly, U.S. diplomats quietly kickstarted the expansion of the Abraham Accords from the 43rd floor of a midtown Manhattan office tower.
On Thursday morning, State Department officials participated in the first official meeting of the Abraham Accords countries — the United States, Israel, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Morocco — since Oct. 7, 2023, when the Hamas attacks on Israel derailed the expansion of the Accords to more countries in the Middle East, Africa and Asia.
The Abraham Accords countries were joined Thursday for the first time by officials from Kazakhstan, which expressed an interest in joining the Accords last year.
The U.S. delegation was led by a senior State Department official, Under Secretary of Political Affairs Allison Hooker.
"Nearly three years after October 7, the Abraham Accords countries are back together," Hooker said, adding that President Trump brokered the historic agreements during his first term, and Thursday was an important signifier that the accords are "moving forward again."
The meeting was hosted by the N7 Foundation, a U.S.-based organization that has convened multilateral meetings of the Abraham Accords countries since 2021.
"The next phase is about deepening the relationships that already exist and identifying practical opportunities for countries to work together," said Jeffrey Talpins, founder of the N7 Foundation, who chaired the meeting.
Another senior administration official who was not authorized to speak publicly told CBS News that Secretary of State Marco Rubio's team and Steve Witkoff, the White House Special Envoy for Peace Missions, "are clearly prioritizing this effort."
Also present at the meeting were Aryeh Lightstone, special adviser to the Board of Peace, an international coalition dedicated to peace and reconstruction in Gaza, Ryan Arant, chief of staff to Under Secretary Hooker at the State Department, and Oren Eisner, president of the N7 Foundation.
The Abraham Accords are a set of agreements that normalized diplomatic relations between Israel and several Muslim countries. The first of a series of agreements was signed in 2020, toward the end of Mr. Trump's first term.
The UAE and Bahrain became the first two Gulf Arab countries to formally recognize Israel. Morocco soon followed.
Before the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks, momentum was building for Saudi Arabia and other Muslim countries to join the accords, but the attack and the wars in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran that ensued stalled further expansion.
President Trump announced Kazakhstan's intention to join the Abraham Accords during an Oval Office meeting with Kazakhstan President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in November 2025.
"We will soon announce a Signing Ceremony to make it official, and there are many more Countries trying to join this club of STRENGTH," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time.
An official with the Kazakhstan embassy told CBS News that Thursday's gathering was a tangible step in the direction of expanding the accords.
"We are very excited about joining the Abraham Accords and all the partnership can do," he said. "We are interested in collaborations in technology and transport. Together we can do more than each individual country could do alone."
Participants discussed next steps to formalize cooperation among Abraham Accords countries, according to a person familiar with the meeting.
"The Abraham Accords have demonstrated what is possible when countries come together around shared interests with a common vision for a more integrated and prosperous region," Talpins said.

1. Diplomacy or ‘diplotainment’?Senate Democrats criticised Trump’s summit with Xi, saying it prioritised pageantry over substance on the major issues. There was no sign a brief closed-door meeting yielded breakthroughs on the thorny issues of AI, trade, Taiwan and the war with Iran. Both countries agreed to extend until 10 January an agreement pausing their trade war, but experts said there were few other obvious tangible outcomes. Xi once again invoked the “Thucydides Trap”, an academic theory that competition between a rising power and an established one often results in war. Xi said the risk “can be overcome” and urged cooperation. After their meeting, Trump gave Xi a tour of the new helipad he had recently constructed on the White House’s South Lawn. “He loves good granite,” Trump told reporters, adding the two men had a “great meeting” without elaborating. Danny Russel, a former US diplomat serving in the Obama administration, expressed concern that the two leaders spent more time on social and ceremonial events than the actual meeting, which was about 90 minutes. “Pageantry and protocol don’t add up to progress. Pandas are cute, but what America needs are rare earths,” said Russel. “What we’re seeing isn’t diplomacy so much as ‘diplotainment,’ which won’t do much to solve the serious problems in the US-China relationship.”
 2. AI uncheckedAI analysts were forced to read between the lines to gauge the outcome of AI discussions between the pair. Trump had written in a Truth Social post on Thursday morning that he and Xi would discuss “super intelligence” (Trump’s newly coined term for AI) but suggested he had little interest in new regulations, despite concerns from industry leaders that AI could eventually pose a threat to humans. “Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is,” Trump wrote. “That is China’s position also.” During his comments on Thursday, Xi said both countries must “ensure that the development of AI is always under human control”. Analysts say intense competition between the two powers in AI is likely to limit the scope for anything beyond symbolic agreements.
 3. Taiwan and stalled $14bn arms dealDuring the afternoon discussion, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence,” according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua. The White House did not immediately provide its own summary. Xi was expected to press Trump to halt arms sales to Taiwan. In a statement signed by at least 19 of 47 members of the Senate Democrats caucus, seen by Reuters, Democrats on Thursday called on Trump to immediately deliver the security assistance package Congress has approved – $1.3bn in funds and the $14bn arms sale. China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has not ruled out using force to gain control over the island.
 4. Unusual airport greetingTrump greeted Xi on arrival with a red carpet on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, the first time a US president has welcomed a foreign leader there since Barack Obama met Pope Francis in 2015. Normally, presidents wait for state visit guests to arrive at the White House before offering a formal welcome. For months, Trump has derided Democrats as “communists”, but the president’s welcome for Xi included Chinese flags adorning the roof above the Oval Office alongside US flags. Despite the fanfare, Trump and Xi’s remarks during the trip were not carried live by any US television networks, which refused to provide footage in protest of the White House’s ban of CNN, MS Now and Politico.

Tech billionaires dine out at state dinnerThursday’s state dinner for Xi featured Washington powerbrokers and a cavalcade of billionaires, including: Apple’s Tim Cook, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Alphabet’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Tesla’s Elon Musk and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. In a continuation of Trump’s beef with certain media outlets, CNN and MS Now reporters were barred from attending. While outside the gate, a group of loud protesters shouted slogans like “China out of Hong Kong” that were clearly audible to the leaders as they posed for pictures on the red-carpeted White House steps.

12:00:00 KST

POLITICO et Cluster 17 s’associent pour publier un baromètre mensuel permettant de mesurer le niveau de rejet des principaux candidats à la présidentielle dans l’opinion. Et donc, en creux, leur véritable capacité de rassemblement au second tour.
“Je te hais, un peu, beaucoup, passionnément, à la folie…” Et si, pour les candidats à la succession d’Emmanuel Macron, l’enjeu était, in fine, non pas tant de susciter l’adhésion d’une majorité de Français, mais d’en être le moins rejeté ?
Tout le monde le sent, tout le monde le voit : quelque chose a changé. Mais peu ont mis des mots et des chiffres sur la chose. Pour Jean-Yves Dormagen, président de l’institut de sondage Cluster 17, l’élection présidentielle de 2027 a ceci de particulier qu’elle se déroulera dans un contexte où “le vieux réflexe consistant à considérer Marine Le Pen, la candidate du RN, comme l’issue la plus inacceptable, ne fonctionne plus automatiquement”. Il n’existe donc plus de “veto électoral” contre le parti à la flamme, ou du moins, plus dans les mêmes proportions. “En tout cas, pas plus que sur les autres, aujourd’hui”, observe-t-il. Et d’en conclure : “Personne, aujourd’hui, n’est potentiellement majoritaire.”
Pour aller plus loin, Cluster 17 a demandé à quelque 2 000 personnes d’estimer, sur une échelle de 0 à 10, quelle était la probabilité qu’ils votent “un jour” pour les personnalités politiques suivantes : Marine Le Pen, Edouard Philippe, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, Gabriel Attal, Marine Tondelier, Raphaël Glucksmann, Dominique de Villepin, Bruno Retailleau — 0 signifiant qu’ils l’excluent totalement, 10 qu’ils jugent “tout à fait possible” de le faire.
Advertisement
Tondelier et Mélenchon en tête
A ce stade de la campagne, c’est… Marine Tondelier qui remporte la palme du rejet, talonnée par Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Pas moins de 81% des sondés situent en effet entre 0 et 3 les chances qu’ils votent un jour pour la candidate Ecologiste. Ils sont 73% à en dire de même pour l’Insoumis, et même 98% à 100% chez les catégories de la population “réfractaires”, “autoritaires”, “anti-assistanat”, “traditionnalistes”, ou encore “libéraux”, selon la classification de Cluster 17.
Une différence majeure, toutefois, entre les deux principaux épouvantails de notre classement : là où seuls 9% de personnes interrogées jugent qu’il y a une probabilité forte ou très forte (entre 7 et 10) qu’ils glissent “un jour” un bulletin dans l’urne pour Tondelier, ils sont 19% à se voir probablement ou très probablement voter pour l’Insoumis en chef — soit l’équivalent des intentions de vote en sa faveur pour le premier tour de la présidentielle, à ce stade de la campagne et telles que mesurées par Cluster 17. Le socle de ceux qui adhèrent positivement aux propositions du candidat Mélenchon est donc nettement plus important. Et c’est particulièrement notable chez les jeunes : 42% des 18-34 ans jugent probables ou très probables (entre 7 et 10) les chances qu’ils votent pour l’Insoumis.
A noter : le fort rejet suscité dans une partie de la population par Marine Tondelier, notamment “dans tout l’espace conservateur”, a beaucoup à voir, selon Jean-Yves Dormagen, avec le “problème d’image” de son parti : “Les Verts sont très clivants sur les questions culturelles et sociétales, et l’écologie est devenue clivante aussi. Ils sont perçus comme très radicaux, promigrations, et ultraprogressistes”, note-t-il, soulignant que cette structure d’image est comparable à celle des Insoumis.
Le Pen et Philippe : même rejet
Autres enseignements majeurs de notre baromètre pour la présidentielle : les candidats les plus centraux ne sont pas en reste quand il s’agit de rejet. Les Français sont respectivement 68%, 72% et 66% à juger faible ou nulle la probabilité qu’ils votent pour Edouard Philippe, Gabriel Attal et Raphaël Glucksmann dans les temps à venir, et 69% pour le candidat des Républicains Bruno Retailleau. Et c’est bien Marine Le Pen qui est la moins rejetée : ils ne sont “que” 62% à déclarer que la probabilité qu’ils votent pour elle est faible ou nulle, contre 30% à l’envisager sérieusement (probabilité forte ou très forte, estimée entre 7 et 10).
Encore un peu plus dans le détail : 56% des personnes sondées jugent strictement impossible de voter pour Marine Le Pen (soit une note de 0 sur 10 ou une déclaration explicite de l’exclure), à touche-touche avec Edouard Philippe (55%), et à peine pire que Raphaël Glucksmann (53%). Ils sont en revanche respectivement 68% et 66% à l’exclure tout aussi catégoriquement quand il s’agit de Marine Tondelier et Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
La peur ou le rejet de l’Insoumis s’explique en partie dans le détail des traits d’image des candidats : Mélenchon est ainsi celui qui se voit le plus reprocher “un risque de dérive autoritaire” — le risque est estimé à 6,7 sur 10 en moyenne — devant Marine Le Pen, pour qui ce sujet est toutefois aussi un point faible (risque estimé à 5,6 sur 10 en moyenne).
Advertisement
Notons enfin que le tableau général n’est pas reluisant lorsqu’on demande aux sondés dans quelle mesure, selon eux, ces candidats seraient “capables de rassembler les Français” : aucun ne franchit la barre des 3 sur 10 (atteinte tout de même par Glucksmann et Philippe). Même chose quand on les interroge sur l’une de leurs principales préoccupations : Marine Le Pen n’apparait pas franchement comme “capable d’améliorer le pouvoir d’achat” des Français (3,3 sur 10)… alors qu’elle est en tête de tous les candidats testés. Même chose enfin pour la catégorie “comprend la vie des gens comme vous”, avec pourtant un faiblard 3,7 sur 10.
(*) Etude Cluster 17 réalisée auprès d’un échantillon de 2 045 personnes, représentatif de la population française grâce à la méthode des quotas, interrogées par questionnaire autoadministré en ligne, les 15 et 16 septembre 2026. Les données ont fait l’objet d’un redressement sociodémographique, à partir des données de l’Insee, ainsi que d’un redressement politique fondé sur la reconstitution des votes au premier tour de l’élection présidentielle de 2022 et aux élections européennes de 2024.

Newest AIM-9X Missiles Not Meeting Operational Availability Goal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
02:54:25 UTC
11:54:25 KST

One of the Air Force and Navy’s most common air-to-air missiles is falling short of a key readiness metric, and the services are ramping up stocks of a vital air-to-ground missile, according to recent Pentagon reports.
The Modernized Selected Acquisition Reports on the AIM-9 and the Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile, cleared for publication in July, lay out progress and shortfalls and provide a snapshot for the health of these key munitions.
According to the reports, the AIM-9X Sidewinder Block II is facing operational availability shortages. Operational availability is defined by the Warfighting Acquisition University as “the degree … to which one can expect a piece of equipment or weapon system to work properly when it is required.” The Air Force is at 58 percent operational availability for the latest version of the Sidewinder, and the Navy is at 78 percent—the requirement is 86 percent, the report says.
That shortage is forcing squadrons to face lower training asset availability, preventing fighter pilots from having the requisite number of Captive Air Training Missiles. Those CATMs have live seekers and guidance units that pilots use on regular training sorties to practice locking onto targets, tracking high off-boresight angles, and simulating missile shots.
When enough of the training pods are nonoperational, aircrews don’t have enough training rounds to fly daily air-to-air tactical training with realistic seekers.
The Air Force and Navy plan to buy more than 11,000 AIM-9X Block II missiles, which are infrared-guided, short-range, supersonic air-to-air weapons.
But reliability problems with integrating a new circuit processor into the latest configuration, the AIM-9X-4, have “impacted missile reliability and halted testing.”
As a result, a software update called Operational Flight Software 10.4, meant to integrate the advanced guidance control unit and inertial measurement unit hardware upgrades, will not be fielded.
Report authors note that the follow-on software that will fix the problem won’t be ready until September 2027.
AIM-9X maker RTX declined to comment on the report.
JASSM and LRASM Work
As the two services work out the air-to-air missile problem, both are seeking to expand their plans for the Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles and its cousin, the Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile.
Another shared munition between USAF and the Navy, the JASSM is a linchpin munition with multiple variants fielded and in production.
The AGM-158A JASSM is a 14-foot-long missile that strikes beyond 200 miles and has been a staple of U.S. aircraft use since 2001. The B-1B Lancer, B-2A Spirit, B-52H Stratofortress, F-15 variants, F-16 variants, and C-130 Hercules can carry it and its variants, and the F-35A Lightning II and B-21 Raider are planned to integrate it.
The AGM-158B JASSM-Extended Range can hit targets at more than twice the distance, with public reports showing ranges of more than 500 miles.
The AGM-158C LRASM has a range closer to the baseline JASSM but is equipped with radio-frequency seekers designed to strike large, moving targets such as ships.
According to the recent selected acquisition report, the joint program office between the two services had delivered 5,348 JASSM variants to the Pentagon as of April, according to the report.
Current production capacity sits at about 600 JASSMs annually, with near-term plans to reach 860 missiles a year.
More mid-term plans call for ramping up that production to 1,280 missiles annually by fiscal year 2030 and 1,880 by fiscal 2032, a spokesperson from Eglin Air Force Base in Florida told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email.
A March $52 million contract modification to LRASM will raise the missile’s production from 240 per year to 320 per year beginning in fiscal 2029, according to the report.
Lockheed announced a new JAASM option at AFA’s Air, Space, & Cyber conference earlier this month, the AGM-158 FLEX.
The company sees FLEX, a modular, designed munition which has swappable nose and launch options, as another way to offer a variety of strike options in the JASSM form factor.
“The AGM-158 FLEX airframe concept was driven by a strategic need to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats, insert emerging technologies quickly, manage obsolescence, and provide, at scale, a cost-effective missile family that can be repurposed for a wide range of missions while delivering timely, relevant capability to the warfighter,” a Lockheed Martin spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine via email.
The stockpile plus-up, however, will use current factory space via expansion efforts, the Eglin spokesperson wrote, and “will not require a new facility construction.”
Lockheed has an investment strategy that includes $8 to $9 million through 2030 to meet heightened munitions demand.
“We are expanding production and building and modernizing more than 20 facilities in Arkansas, Alabama, Florida, Massachusetts, and Texas,” Lockheed spokesman Scott Swofford told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email. “This includes upgrading existing facilities and incorporating advanced manufacturing techniques, production lines, tooling, and plant layouts to meet urgent production demand.”
Software, Paint, and Engines
Like the AIM-9X, the JASSM also faced software integration problems, specifically with its 54.0.02 flight software update. But an Eglin spokesperson said the software had received fielding approval since data for the selected acquisition report was gathered in April, and that “there are no impacts to combat readiness.”
The Air Force is also pressing to accelerate the integration of the Universal Armament Interface, a software architecture to standardize aircraft mission systems-weapons interface, but this has introduced “added software risk,” according to the report.
But the Eglin spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the UAI program has “made no changes to the delivery schedule” of the JASSMs.
“Integration activities remain on track to deliver planned capabilities as scheduled. Software risk is being actively managed through early software-in-the-loop integration, resource prioritization, and agile contract actions,” the spokesperson said.
Separately, the report noted that in an inspection of 1,356 JASSMs, inspectors flagged 49 missiles for depot-level maintenance and overhaul, mostly due to stealth coating defects. That issue won’t be resolved until 2029, the report says.
Lockheed switched from the flat gray paint scheme to a semi-gloss black coating to reduce radar and visual signatures. The new coating can absorb and deflect electromagnetic energy more easily during longer flight times used by the new, extended-range variants.
The shift began in 2021 as part of the Lot 19 contract award for the AGM-158B-2 variant.
The Eglin spokesperson said that both the program office and Lockheed Martin are “exploring contracting actions to increase repair capacity and return serviceable missiles to the field more efficiently.”
Beyond software updates, the Air Force also spent $200 million in fiscal 2025 to procure and mature a second-source engine for the LRASM and JASSM-ERs.
“Investing in a second engine source for the AGM-158 is essential to securing our supply chain and ramping up production of critical long-range strike weapons,” the Eglin spokesperson said. “By establishing a second production line, we eliminate manufacturing bottlenecks, drive competition, and secure deliveries of JASSM and LRASM to the warfighter.”

US tech titans attend Trump-Xi dinner. Who wasn’t invited?
Virtually all of America’s most powerful technology executives joined US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a lavish White House state dinner on Thursday, as AI emerged as a major theme of the Chinese leader’s visit.
The black-tie dinner in the White House East Room brought together more than 130 guests, including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, and Google CEO Sundar Pichai.
Apple chairman Tim Cook, AMD chief Lisa Su, Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon, Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra, Zoom CEO Eric Yuan, and Dell Technologies chief Michael Dell were also among those invited. Major finance and industrial executives, including JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon, BlackRock CEO Larry Fink, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser, and Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg, attended as well.
One notable Silicon Valley name was missing, however. Anthropic – the developer of the Claude AI models and one of OpenAI’s biggest US rivals – had no representative. CEO Dario Amodei has been among the industry’s more vocal advocates of tighter safeguards around increasingly powerful AI systems.
Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel was also absent, though he was in Berlin that evening receiving the 2026 Axel Springer Award. His CIA-seeded data-mining giant has grown into one of Silicon Valley’s biggest defense-tech players, supplying AI and analytics software to all six branches of the US military, as well as the FBI, NSA, and DIA. Its technology is also used by NATO and the Israeli and Ukrainian militaries, while the company has faced sustained criticism over its expanding role in surveillance and AI-enabled warfare.
Intel, IBM, and Oracle were also absent from the guest list, which otherwise featured most of America’s biggest technology and AI companies.
There was also a conspicuous absence on the other side of the table: No Chinese corporate executives were listed, despite earlier expectations that business leaders could accompany Xi. Instead, his delegation at the dinner was composed of senior Chinese officials.
The concentration of American tech executives came as Trump and Xi discussed the increasingly intense US-China competition in AI and advanced semiconductors.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi said both countries have a responsibility to ensure AI remains “under human control” and is developed for the benefit of people.
Trump said AI – which he has increasingly referred to as “superintelligence” – was high on the agenda of the summit, while reiterating his opposition to slowing development through extensive regulation. Washington has also proposed establishing a mechanism allowing the two countries to notify each other about serious AI-related incidents, an idea discussed by senior economic officials ahead of the summit.
The dinner followed around 90 minutes of talks between Trump and Xi at the White House, where the two sides also addressed trade, Taiwan, and the ongoing conflict involving Iran. Washington and Beijing agreed earlier this week to extend their existing trade truce by two months while negotiations continue.
Trump emphasized cooperation despite the rivalry, saying the two leaders represent “different systems” but can continue building a relationship promoting prosperity and security.

Ancient meteorites reveal a powerful force that helped build the Solar System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
02:45:24 UTC
11:45:24 KST

Ancient meteorites reveal a powerful force that helped build the Solar System
Ancient meteorite grains reveal that powerful magnetism may have helped shape the solar system from its very beginning.
- Date:
- September 24, 2026
- Source:
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- Ancient grains inside one of the oldest known meteorites reveal that a surprisingly strong magnetic field existed during the solar system’s first 200,000 years. The discovery suggests magnetism worked alongside gravity to help transform a vast cloud of gas and dust into the sun and planetary disk.
- Share:
About 4.6 billion years ago, the solar system began as an enormous cloud of gas and dust. Over the next several million years, this "solar nebula" changed dramatically. The cloud collapsed and flattened into a disk, eventually giving rise to the sun at its center and the planets that formed around it.
Gravity has long been considered the main force behind this transformation. New research from MIT, however, suggests that magnetism may also have been an important part of the process.
Scientists found evidence of ancient magnetic fields preserved in some of the oldest meteorite material ever identified. The researchers studied microscopic grains inside a meteorite discovered in Antarctica in 2008. Known as calcium-aluminum-rich inclusions, or CAIs, these grains formed during the solar system's first 200,000 years and represent the oldest known material from that period.
Their magnetic signatures indicate that a substantial magnetic field was already present during the solar nebula stage. The researchers estimate that this field was stronger than Earth's magnetic field today and may have helped move primordial material inward as the young sun formed.
"This transition, from a spherical cloud to a protoplanetary disk, is one of the most significant events in all of solar system history," says Benjamin Weiss, the Robert R. Shrock Professor of Earth and Planetary Sciences at MIT. "It has long been theorized that gravity caused this, but our measurements show magnetism likely played a role."
The findings were reported in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Along with Weiss, the study's MIT co-authors are first author Cauê Borlina PhD '22, Elias Mansbach PhD '24, and Nilanjan Chatterjee. Other collaborators include Xue-Ning Bai of Tsinghua University, Po-Yen Tung and Richard Harrison of Cambridge University, François Tissot of Caltech, and Kevin McKeegan of the University of California at Los Angeles.
How Early Solar Magnetism Could Have Worked
Magnetic fields arise when electrically charged matter moves. During the earliest stage of solar system formation, the collapsing cloud of gas and dust may have generated a plasma containing charged particles. As those particles circulated through the developing disk, they could have created and maintained a magnetic field.
If a magnetic field was present, Weiss and his colleagues reasoned, it should have left a lasting imprint on some of the material forming within the disk. As that material condensed, tiny magnetic minerals could have recorded the strength of the surrounding field. If those minerals survived for billions of years and eventually reached Earth, their "remanent magnetization" could provide evidence that magnetism existed in the young solar system and influenced its development.
The researchers had already found evidence of magnetism from about 2 million years after the solar system began forming. By that point, scientists believe the sun had already formed and the planets were beginning to assemble. That earlier work suggested magnetic fields may have contributed to planet formation.
"Nowadays people don't debate whether magnetism is present when planets are forming. But the debate is around the very early solar system, before planets are forming, when there's just a disk," says Borlina, who led the new study as an MIT graduate student and is now an assistant professor at Purdue University. "That's where the debate still resides, and that's where we're operating now."
A Meteorite With an Unusually Pristine Record
The latest study pushed the search even farther back in time, focusing on whether magnetism was present while the sun itself was still coming together.
The researchers examined samples from DOM 08006, a meteorite found in 2008 in Dominion Range, a mountain range along the East Antarctic Ice Sheet. Since its discovery, the meteorite has been studied extensively because of its unusually primitive composition.
DOM 08006 contains mineral grains from the earliest stages of solar system formation, possibly dating to before the sun had fully formed. Remarkably, the meteorite has retained much of its original mineral makeup despite surviving billions of years of solar system history.
"Other meteorites went through many different processes over this 4.5 billion year history," Weiss says. "They were formed in the solar nebula, then added to bodies with water, then got destroyed, moved to the asteroid belt, and then landed here. But somehow, DOM has experienced less alteration than any other meteorite."
That unusual preservation made DOM 08006 an especially promising place to search for evidence of magnetic fields from the earliest solar system.
If such a field existed, its signature might still be preserved in some of the meteorite's CAIs.
"We know they are the oldest things we have of the early solar system," Borlina says. "But CAI's are very complex and are not all the same, even within a 1-millimeter piece of the meteorite. So we have to carefully identify what types they are."
A Magnetic Field Stronger Than Earth's
Using small pieces of the original meteorite, the team separated tiny mineral grains and identified several CAIs containing naturally magnetic minerals, including iron. The researchers then carried out a series of tests to determine whether those grains still preserved ancient magnetism.
They found traces of a magnetic field recorded inside the minerals. From those measurements, the team estimates that the early solar system had a magnetic field measuring roughly 150 to 600 microteslas. That is about three to 12 times stronger than Earth's magnetic field today.
The result suggests that magnetism may have played a meaningful role in controlling how material moved through the protoplanetary disk as the sun was forming.
"We think these kinds of magnetic fields were helping to move gas from the protoplanetary disk, in toward this central star, the sun," Borlina says. "Gravity is also playing a role. But we are now showing that, if you want to fully understand how the sun and planets formed, you should include magnetic fields in the ingredients that make them."
This research was supported, in part, by NASA.

Materials provided by Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Cauê S. Borlina, Benjamin P. Weiss, Xue-Ning Bai, Po-Yen Tung, Richard J. Harrison, Elias N. Mansbach, Nilanjan Chatterjee, François L. H. Tissot, Kevin D. McKeegan. Paleomagnetic evidence for a nebular magnetic field from calcium-aluminum-rich inclusions. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2026; 123 (36) DOI: 10.1073/PNAS.2521660123
