Proof that Russia’s 2026 State Duma elections were the dirtiest parliamentary elections of the Putin era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:45:47 UTC
06:45:47 KST

Proof that Russia’s 2026 State Duma elections were the dirtiest parliamentary elections of the Putin era
The final results of the State Duma election are not in yet. Russia’s Central Election Commission still has not published returns from every precinct: as of the evening of September 23, data for the Leningrad region and the occupied regions were missing. Even so, the available figures show how this election differs from previous ones. It was the least fair Duma election of the Putin era, yet it looks more “normal” than the 2024 presidential election. And, surprisingly, United Russia’s support appears to have barely changed since 2021. Here is a closer look.
In March 2024, Meduza analyzed Russia’s presidential election in detail and found anomalies on an unprecedented scale. Huge spikes at round numbers were visible to the naked eye in the distribution of precincts by turnout and the winner’s vote share. The “normal” core of precincts with middling figures had disappeared, leaving a solid “comet tail.”
This Duma election produced a different pattern in the leading party’s result, turnout, and the distribution of votes. Presidential and parliamentary elections are not directly comparable, however: voters choose a person in one and a party in the other. What follows focuses mainly on comparing the 2026 election with earlier Duma elections.
One note before the charts: we use the terms “anomaly” and “falsification” in different ways. Both can, and often do, refer to the same event, but they describe it from fundamentally different perspectives. We mostly use “anomaly” here.
Here’s why
An anomaly is a statistical deviation from the voting behavior we expect to see. We can identify anomalies without knowing what caused them — provided, of course, that we agree on what counts as “normal” voting behavior. Russia’s Criminal Code defines falsification of voting documents and results in Article 142.
An anomaly alone cannot automatically be treated as falsification. More often than not, though, there is no mystery: clear anomalies in vote distributions really do reflect falsification. Such falsification can stop, for example, when an observer is present at a precinct that previously had anomalous turnout. But the link between an anomaly and falsification can be proven only in court, where statistical arguments are not accepted and only witness testimony counts — at least in theory.
The overall picture: The ‘tail’ became the ‘body’
The charts below show the distribution of party-list voting results in this State Duma election and the 2021 election. For this election, they show preliminary results from 82,124 precinct election commissions — about 85% of the total. Every precinct with published returns appears as an equal-sized dot. Its horizontal position shows turnout; its vertical position shows United Russia’s vote share there.
In the previous Duma election, most precincts clustered in a core where turnout was around 35–40% and United Russia received about 30% of the vote. The remaining precincts formed a “comet tail” extending up and to the right: as turnout rose, so did the ruling party’s vote share. The chart also shows a clear square grid, with turnout and vote shares clustering unnaturally at round numbers.
The main difference this time is that the “comet tail” grew much denser, forming a complex “body” of multiple clusters. The core survived — unlike in the presidential election — but became much smaller and thinner.
Despite those changes, the core has barely moved over the past five years; it has shifted only slightly upward. If we treat results at these precincts as “true” or “unfalsified,” we have to conclude that United Russia’s vote share has risen by about five percentage points since 2021, from roughly 30% to roughly 35%. That is a reasonable interpretation overall, but it comes with several qualifications, which we discuss below.
What did the same distribution look like in the presidential election?
The regional picture: The ‘Moscow column’
This election’s results contain another new feature: a sparse vertical “column” of precincts to the left of the main cluster. Highlighting precincts by region shows that these are Moscow precincts where people voted on paper.
The chart shows that Moscow’s distribution has changed completely since 2021: its symmetrical, rounded cluster shifted left and became a vertical “column.”
The shift toward lower turnout is easy to explain. Nearly 78% of Moscow voters cast their ballots remotely rather than at polling stations.
What the cluster’s uniform spread across vote shares means is less clear. It certainly is not the result of ballot stuffing, which would have stretched the cluster into a conventional “comet tail.” Nor are there signs that precinct returns were crudely altered to produce round numbers; that would create horizontal concentrations at those values. Manipulating precinct returns in the winner’s favor or government pressure on voters could explain the pattern. But the apparent uniformity of any such pressure and the absence of noticeable concentrations in the “Moscow column” require further study.
Hi, I’m Katya.
I’ve been running Meduza’s crowdfunding since 2021. Today, supporting Meduza is a crime in Russia. You can be sent to prison just for donating. We’re still able to do our work thanks to thousands of our Russian readers who now live abroad. But even they’re no longer safe.
Imagine you’ve left Russia, but then your mom becomes seriously ill. It could be your last chance to see her, so of course you go home. At the border, you’re interrogated. Officers hack into your phone and search for any trace that you’ve donated to Meduza.
The Kremlin is counting on that fear, and it’s working. People are afraid to donate. I’m afraid for our supporters, because any one of them could end up in prison. And I’m afraid for Meduza. Without crowdfunding, we simply can’t continue. So if you live outside Russia and don’t have to worry that donating to Meduza could keep you from going home to your family, I’m asking for your help. Please support our work.
The same chart shows substantial changes in other regions, too. In 2021, St. Petersburg and Moscow looked much alike in turnout, United Russia’s vote share, and the distribution of precinct results — hardly surprising for two similar major cities. In 2026, however, St. Petersburg moved in the opposite direction from Moscow: both turnout and United Russia’s vote share doubled. Small clusters of St. Petersburg precincts also appeared across the chart. Further research is needed to explain them.
Some regions remained stable. In Chechnya, for example, virtually nothing has changed in five years.
Year by year: The least fair Duma election of the Putin era
Comparing similar elections in the same regions matters, too: without that comparison, we would not know which results are “normal” and which are “anomalous.”
It is often said that only precincts within a normal distribution — a Gaussian bell curve — are “normal,” meaning free of falsification. Results from all other precincts are then attributed to falsification. On that basis, people usually conclude that the result in the comet’s core is the “true” result: the one produced by precincts without falsification.
That is not so.
Here’s why
The distribution of precinct results in a hypothetical country with honest elections could take any shape, not just a Gaussian one. A Gaussian distribution assumes that precinct sizes are distributed randomly and that individual voters’ choices vary randomly according to their own preferences.
Elections in other countries show that even when voting is fair, distributions of turnout and vote shares can differ sharply from a Gaussian curve because of a country’s particular characteristics.
In Canada’s 2011 parliamentary election, for example, the results had a distinctly bimodal distribution, with two clusters of precincts. English-speaking and French-speaking Canadians voted very differently because their attitudes toward the leading party differed sharply. In parliamentary elections that same year in Finland and Poland, turnout correlated clearly with the leading party’s vote share, though in different ways. Ballot stuffing, familiar to Russians, can produce a similar correlation. In those countries, though, the correlation reflected higher turnout among voters who favored the party in power — a pattern tied to local traditions and where people live.
Russia’s Central Election Commission also says that results outside a Gaussian distribution do not indicate falsification. But a historical comparison of Russia’s parliamentary elections undermines its argument. Even before falsification became widespread, the distribution of Russian election results showed a very slight rightward skew, with turnout correlated with the leading party’s vote share. That cannot explain what has happened now.
The chart below shows the last six Duma elections. It traces how the near-normal distribution of turnout and votes in 2003 first became a “comet” with a core and a tail, then something with no readily identifiable cluster of “Gaussian precincts” — a shape difficult to describe at all. Russia’s geography and population structure have not fundamentally changed over those years, but its vote-counting methods have.
Spikes at round numbers: There are many more of them
Spikes at “round numbers” are among the clearest statistical anomalies indicating that precinct returns have been rewritten. An honest ballot count cannot produce spikes of this size. More precisely, some spikes can occur because of the small number of votes at high-turnout precincts, but statistical methods can calculate a strict limit on their height. Above a certain statistical threshold, spikes clearly indicate interference with an honest count.
The chart below compares spikes in turnout (top) and vote share (bottom) in precinct-level results from this election and the previous parliamentary election. It shows that the “comet tail” has grown substantially thicker — especially in the vote-share distribution — and that spikes at round numbers have risen sharply, too.
Comparing this election with the 2003 vote shows what vote counting without doctored precinct returns should look like.
Using a method developed by Dmitry Kobak, Sergey Shpilkin, and Maxim Pshenichnikov and published in the journal Significance, we calculated the number of precincts with anomalously round turnout and vote-share figures. The number has almost doubled since the previous parliamentary election, rising from 1,300 to nearly 2,250 precincts. To repeat, that excludes the 15% of precincts whose returns are still unavailable or were unavailable until recently.

Xi, in lavish Trump summit, urges ‘human control’ over AI
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
WASHINGTON — China’s president issued a call from the White House on Thursday for artificial intelligence to remain “under human control” as the world’s two superpowers race for technological supremacy.
Xi Jinping’s remarks reflect growing concern within China over whether governments in Washington or Beijing will be able to contain a technology with potentially transformative capabilities, according to a U.S. official.
Lawmakers and AI industry leaders urged President Trump to use his summit with Xi this week to pursue a safety framework for AI, which researchers warn could soon surpass human understanding.
But Trump preempted the meeting with a post on social media stating he had no intention of negotiating limits on AI development.
“A big day with President Xi of China,” Trump wrote. “Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China’s position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ!”
After offering Xi a lavish welcome on the White House grounds, Trump made a passing reference to AI. “The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come,” he said.
But Xi gestured to substantial concerns, noting AI first among priorities to discuss between the two nations.
President Trump’s decision to greet Chinese President Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews just outside Washington rather than receiving him at the executive residence shows how far Trump is going to honor China’s leader as he makes his first state visit in more than a decade.
“Both China and the United States are leading nations in artificial intelligence,” Xi said. “We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good — and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control, and serves the well-being of the people.”
The two held a private meeting with aides in the Oval Office after participating in a military review in the Rose Garden and exchanging gifts in the Blue Room.
In the evening, a guest list of top banking and technology leaders — including AI industry executives — were scheduled to attend a state dinner in the East Room of the White House.
“Given Trump’s statements going into the summit about not wanting guardrails, I have tepid expectations about tangible outcomes” on AI, said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“The most likely scenario seems to be the establishment of a hotline — though how useful that will be depends on who will be staffing it, and how much each government prioritizes it,” Mehta added, “and likely some discussions about issues blocking cooperation, like distillation, with a promise to engage in ongoing dialogue.”
Earlier in the week, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met with his Chinese counterpart primarily to discuss AI development, according to U.S. officials.
“What we discussed was setting up a mechanism — so it’s going to be called the U.S.-China AI Dialogue. We’ve agreed to meet again,” Bessent said Monday. “The U.S. has proposed that we have a notification mechanism between the two countries, and we want a shared vision of common goals, and common threats.”
While Trump’s team has remained divided over whether — and how extensively — to regulate AI, Bessent has favored a cautious approach, advocating modest, voluntary guardrails that have shaped administration policy in recent months.
China, too, has shown increasing willingness to open channels of communication on AI, despite deep distrust between the two sides.
Two American AI companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, are widely viewed to be developing the most advanced AI models in the world, leading at the frontier of technological breakthroughs.
Both have begun to use their most sophisticated models to train the next generation, in a process known as recursive self-improvement. Researchers and industry experts believe the first company to master that process could set off an exponential cycle of progress, pulling so far ahead that competitors can no longer catch up.
But those same companies also fear what they’re creating: machines capable of continuously improving their own intelligence, pushing AI development beyond human control.
Leaders from the two companies have called on Beijing and Washington to cooperate, warning that geopolitical competition could thwart the two sides from preventing a human catastrophe.
In his remarks, Xi said that China and the United States “stand to gain from cooperation, and will both lose in confrontation.”
“We do not need to avoid mentioning competition, but our competition should be a healthy one, and should be kept within bounds,” the Chinese president said. “It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses. China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict, and no confrontation between us.”
“Our two militaries should maintain regular dialogue, and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention,” he continued, adding a historical reference to rising powers challenging established ones: “The Thucydides trap can be overcome.”
Xi’s trip to Washington follows just months after Trump traveled to Beijing for a state visit in May, where the U.S. president was greeted with a similarly imperial welcome.
The leaders emerged from that summit with few deliverables. But Trump left Beijing declaring the trip a success, emphasizing the importance of his personal relationship with Xi, China’s most powerful leader in generations.
A bipartisan group of Congressional leaders is pushing for a 20% federal tax credit for film and TV production, a move they say will help bring filming back to the U.S.
This time, Trump himself greeted Xi on the tarmac upon his arrival at Joint Base Andrews — a rare honor reserved in recent decades only for Catholic popes — before pulling out several red carpets and draped ceremonies for the Chinese leader.
The pageantry seen during the state visit has served China’s long-standing desire for respect and dignity on the international stage, said Jessica Chen Weiss, the director of the Johns Hopkins SAIS Institute for America, China and the Future of Global Affairs.
“Trump is someone who loves spectacle, and right now the spectacle is working in both leaders’ favor,” Weiss said.
For Xi, the ceremonies have offered a chance to demonstrate that relations with the United States remain under control and that China is being treated as a significant global power, she argued.
The state visit comes at a time when Americans are appearing to warm up to China, according to recent polls. A survey by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs recently found that a majority of Americans say the United States should have friendly engagement and cooperation with China.
“I tend to think we focus too much on the optics,” Weiss said. “But I also think treating China as a significant player on the world stage is not a concession. It’s appropriate if we want a stable relationship and is hardly something to worry about.”

AFU General Staff streamlines procedure for discharge from military service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:42:00 UTC
06:42:00 KST

AFU General Staff streamlines procedure for discharge from military service
This was stated in a comment to Ukrinform by Lieutenant Volodymyr Molodii, Spokesperson for the General Staff on human capital issues.
“As of today, the General Staff has streamlined the procedure for discharging service members from military service. All applicable legal provisions concerning discharge from service have been consolidated into a single practical instruction for officials involved in the discharge process. The document systematizes the sequence of actions to be taken by officials of military units, Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers (TRSC), healthcare institutions and other participants in the process. In other words, it determines who must take the necessary actions and at what stage,” Molodii said.
According to him, the main goal is to ensure a unified approach to organizing discharges, improve coordination among all the structures involved, and give service members a clearer understanding of what documents are required, what stages the procedure entails, and what actions must be taken by the officials responsible.
At the same time, the Spokesperson emphasized that the algorithm approved by the General Staff “does not establish any new grounds for discharge, but merely reminds officials how to proceed depending on the grounds already provided for by law.”
As Molodii explained, the first step is to determine the grounds for a service member’s discharge, as this determines the subsequent procedure, the required documents and the necessary formalities. The next step is to collect and prepare the documents and submit a report. Some documents may concern military registration, equipment and benefits, health status, and other matters.
The service member must then undergo the necessary procedures, which may include, depending on the grounds for discharge, a medical examination by the Military Medical Commission, preparation of documents for pension benefits, and other formalities.
The next step is for the military unit to formally process the discharge. After that, the service member must receive the documents and information needed following discharge, including information on further actions related to military registration. The final step is registration with a TRSC after discharge.
“After being removed from the personnel rolls of the military unit, a service member must report to a TRSC within five days and register for military service,” the Spokesperson said.
Molodii emphasized that during the discharge process, every service member can seek advice and assistance from various structures.
First and foremost, they can contact their commander, who can help properly prepare the report, explain the general procedure and direct the service member to the officials responsible.
They can also contact the personnel service, which will assist with processing the discharge. In addition, specialists in the civil-military cooperation office can provide information on rights, guarantees and benefits provided by law, including those available after discharge, and provide assistance through completion of the discharge procedure and removal from the military unit’s personnel rolls.
If the discharge is related to a service member’s health, the service member should contact a healthcare institution where matters related to the Military Medical Commission are handled, the Spokesperson said.
As reported by Ukrinform, the “Psychological Preparation for Combat Conditions” course was launched in the Army+ app. The course helps service members understand their own reactions to severe stress, manage their condition, and support a fellow service member in a difficult situation.

Demonstrators blocked an intersection several blocks from the UN building in a planned act of civil disobedience timed to coincide with Netanyahu’s speech, Maupin said.
RT footage showed protesters holding signs reading “stop settler terror” and “stop arming Israel.” Demonstrators also chanted “Netanyahu you can’t hide, we charge you with genocide” and “One, two, three, four, Gaza’s what we’re fighting for.”
“The protesters are expecting to be arrested. This is a planned act of civil disobedience timed with the Israeli prime minister’s upcoming speech,” Maupin said.
Another video showed detained protesters being loaded into an NYPD van. Some wore shirts bearing the slogan “fund people not bombs.”
US attitudes toward Israel have grown more negative in recent years, according to opinion polls. Some 62% of American adults had an unfavorable view of the Israeli government in May 2026, up from 43% in 2022, according to a Pew Research Center survey published in July. The share with a favorable view of Israel fell by 15 percentage points over the same period.
Israel’s actions in Gaza and the expansion of settlements in the occupied West Bank have also drawn international criticism.
“Settler violence has reached unprecedented levels,” senior UN official Ramiz Alakbarov told the Security Council last month.
The UN had documented more than 1,430 settler incidents resulting in casualties or property damage in the occupied West Bank this year as of August 10, affecting around 260 Palestinian communities, he said.
More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect in October 2025, bringing the total death toll since October 2023 to nearly 74,000, according to the Hamas-run Gaza Health Ministry.

Pentagon probing how shipment of F-35 fighter jet parts was diverted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:30:49 UTC
06:30:49 KST

Pentagon probing how shipment of F-35 fighter jet parts was diverted
The Pentagon is investigating how a shipment of F-35 fighter jet parts on its way to the U.S. from overseas was diverted, and the military is now trying to retrieve the parts, a defense official confirmed to CBS News.
A source briefed on the incident told CBS News a shipment was diverted to Hong Kong. According to Bloomberg News, the parts are now in China's hands, although the Pentagon declined to confirm this.
A defense official said in a statement, "The F-35 Joint Program Office and Department of War are aware of a shipment issue of unserviceable F-35 Lightning II components." The parts were in transit to the U.S. from Australia either for replacement or repair when they were diverted.
"We are actively working with U.S. authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence," the defense official said.
The F-35A Lightning II is the newest version of the plane and the most advanced fighter jet in the military's arsenal. It travels up to 1,200 miles per hour and can carry a payload of 18,000 pounds.
The missing parts are said to be related to the plane's canopy and weapons bay door. If this is the case, they do not contain the kind of advanced avionics that would be advantageous for an adversary to obtain. Nonetheless, they could provide information about the F-35's stealth technology: Even the canopy contains elements of the stealth systems — it's coated with radar-absorbent material that helps the plane hide from enemy radar.
It's not clear whether the U.S. raised the missing plane parts with China during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit with President Trump on Thursday, but military issues almost certainly came up during their meeting. Xi was expected to press Mr. Trump to curb U.S. support for Taiwan. China wants the U.S. to halt all arms sales to the self-governed island and oppose Taiwanese independence.
Doing so would effectively end the longstanding policy of strategic ambiguity, that is, refusing to state whether the U.S. would intervene militarily if China were to attack Taiwan.
After their summit in May, Mr. Trump said he had made "no commitment either way" on whether to move forward with a pending arms sale to Taiwan. Democratic and Republican lawmakers have urged him to approve the arms package, but it has remained in limbo since Mr. Trump and Xi last met.
On Wednesday, Republican Sens. Mitch McConnell, John Cornyn and Lisa Murkowski wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to ask why the State Department did not obligate $300 million in foreign military financing Congress had approved for 2026 and the Defense Department did not provide Taiwan with $1 billion appropriated by Congress for security cooperation. They also wanted to know why the administration did not approve the $14 billion in military sales to Taiwan that Congress passed earlier this year.
The senators said in their letter that the appropriations "are critical to the kind of deterrence by denial that will prevent conflict," and said "it is especially confusing that the Administration would withhold approval of the very arms purchases it aggressively pushed Taiwan to make."

China’s industrial strengths must also benefit its trading partners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:30:12 UTC
06:30:12 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
China’s industrial strengths must also benefit its trading partners
By shifting towards domestic consumption and exporting industrial know-how, Beijing can give global partners a genuine stake in its growth
3-MIN READ3-MIN
1
 Listen
Wang Huiyao is the founder of the Centre for China and Globalisation, a Beijing-based non-governmental think tank. 
The European Commission is pressing China for progress by next month to address the widening EU-China trade imbalance, and raising the possibility of new protectionist trade policy. The deadline raises a question: how should China and its trading partners address perceived economic imbalances while sharing the benefits of Chinese industrial competitiveness?
China’s merchandise trade surplus approached US$1.2 trillion last year even as other exporting economies press for controls. “Overcapacity” is accepted as the blanket explanation for China’s industrial success, with government support leading to a production glut.
But this framing obscures more than it clarifies. China’s success is multifaceted, given the vast scale of its ecosystem, intense domestic competition and dense supplier networks. An effective response must distinguish between genuine imbalances and the productive advantages that offer opportunities for cooperation.

Protecting Bab al Mandab shared regional, international responsibility — Yemen tells UNGA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:28:01 UTC
06:28:01 KST

Protecting the strategic Bab al Mandab Strait is a shared regional and international responsibility and should not be borne by Yemen alone, Presidential Leadership Council Vice President Abdullah al-Alimi said.
Al-Alimi told the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York on Thursday that Houthi attacks on maritime navigation have turned the security of one of the world's most important shipping routes into a tool of pressure and bargaining.
"The Houthis' use of maritime security as a tool of blackmail is not only a threat to Yemen, but is holding the global economy hostage," he said.
Al-Alimi said years of conflict had demonstrated that supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government and strengthening its economic, security and military capabilities amounted to an investment in international security and stability.
"Protecting this strategic passage is a shared regional and international responsibility that Yemen cannot bear alone," he said.
Al-Alimi said a secure Red Sea depended on a stable Yemen, while stability in Yemen required restoring effective state authority.
"There can be no sustainable peace as long as an armed militia remains above the state and outside the law," he said, adding that restoring the Yemeni state will contribute directly to regional stability and the protection of one of the world's most important maritime corridors.
'Iranian agenda'
He said the government had dealt "responsibly and positively" with regional and international initiatives and made major concessions in an effort to reach peace and alleviate the suffering of Yemenis.
Al-Alimi accused the Houthis of responding to those efforts with intransigence and using periods of a humanitarian truce to strengthen their military arsenal at the expense of Yemenis.
He also accused the group of rejecting peace initiatives and escalating attacks in the Red Sea and Bab al Mandab in service of "an Iranian agenda" extending beyond Yemen's national interests.
Al-Alimi said the threat posed by the Houthis is also being strengthened by "the absence of an effective and decisive international position."
He urged the international community to move toward a "strategic partnership" with Yemen to strengthen security and stability in the region, saying the government is capable of ending the threat posed by the Houthis.

Macron says France sees signs Russia is preparing to mobilize 300,000 more men
French President Emmanuel Macron told TF1 that tensions were rising across Europe as Russia stepped up hostile actions. “But yes, the situation really is growing more tense — for Ukraine, which has been at war with Russia since February 2022, and for us Europeans, because the number of hostile acts [by Russia] across Europe has risen sharply in recent weeks,” Macron said.
Macron said the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) had not provided France with information about an alleged Russian plan to launch drones from civilian ships to attack countries in southern Europe.
Journalists asked Macron whether France could be targeted by Russian drones, referring to Germany’s claim that Russia had been preparing to carry out sabotage at Leipzig Airport using drones.
“My answer is yes. Let’s be clear: Russia sees Europe as a strategic support base for Ukraine because Europeans are helping Ukraine. […] For years, we’ve been the target of information operations and cyberattacks. […] France has not seen attacks like those in Leipzig. But we must take a clear-eyed view of how the threat is evolving. We must prepare,” Macron said.
Macron also said France considered it plausible that Russia might decide to mobilize 300,000 people. He said there were “several signs” that Russia was preparing to do so. “The question is whether Russia will announce it publicly,” Macron said.
On September 18, Macron met with leaders of France’s political parties, then instructed the government to prepare a plan to protect critical infrastructure, including defense industry facilities, from drone attacks and cyberattacks. He accused Russia of trying to intimidate European countries and weaken support for Ukraine.

Insane catch helps South Africa beat Australia in one-day clash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:20:56 UTC
06:20:56 KST

A remarkable one-handed diving catch from all-rounder Marco Jansen has helped South Africa claim a 67-run win over Australia in a one-day clash in Durban.
Jansen was named the Player of the Match after scoring 75 off 59 deliveries with the bat before picking up one wicket with the ball. Mitch Marsh top scored for Australia with 60 off just 36 deliveries.
What's next?
South Africa leads 1-0 in the three-match series ahead of the second ODI in Johannesberg on Sunday night AEST.
Mitch Marsh could not hide his dismay at how Australia capitulated tamely in their opening ODI in South Africa, who were helped to victory by an incredible catch by Marco Jansen that needs to be seen to be believed.
The Aussies ended up succumbing to a 67-run defeat to the disappointment of their stand-in skipper after a succession of cheap dismissals in a sorry run chase in Durban.
Marsh himself seemed to have laid the foundations for victory with his blistering opening knock of 60, but after he had perished needlessly to the spinning wiles of Kehav Maharaj, none of his team could cement the partnerships to get them anywhere near the hosts' 298-run target.
After watching the world champs collapse to 230 all out off just 41.2 overs, Marsh sighed: "I'm pretty disappointed. South Africa outplayed us. It was a good game of cricket, but we fell well short.
"We had our opportunities. I am probably going to sound like a broken record speaking about having partnerships in our batting, but we weren't able to form many tonight."
The South Africans had set a challenging target after being inserted by Marsh, compiling 8-297 thanks largely to a brilliant 112 from Matthew Breetzke and a spectacular 75 off 59 balls from pace-bowling all-rounder Jansen.
Marsh, standing in as skipper again for the rested Pat Cummins, then led from the front in response with his 36-ball pyrotechnics, which featured three sixes, one of which sailed for 104 metres over the dressing room roof at Kingsmead and landed at the roadside.
He shared a blistering opening stand of 90 in just 9.2 overs with Travis Head, but like Head (36), Cooper Connolly, who'd looked supreme in making 38, and Matt Renshaw (44), he got out to an airy shot when the Australians were up with the required rate and under no real pressure.
The superb spinning of the two slow left-armers Maharaj (4-20) and Bjorn Fortuin (2-34) soon put them under that pressure, though.
Loading Twitter content
Discomfited, Josh Inglis got out to a poorly executed reverse sweep on the eighth ball he faced and Australia lost their last six wickets for just 54 to allow the Proteas to draw first blood in the three-match series.
The key moment may have been when Jansen took a sensational running, diving, one-handed catch in the outfield, stretching out his long telescopic arm to scoop up the ball just above the turf to get rid of key man Renshaw off Gerald Coetzee. It left Australia on 7-215, and there was no way back.
So, after the three-match sweep of the Zimbabwe series, this really did feel like a proper test of Australia with the defence of their 50-over World Cup in southern Africa just a year away.
The first part of the reconnaissance mission demonstrated just how much they still have to work on, and the weakness against spin was again shown up even while South Africa had five top-line pace bowlers sidelined through injury.
Man-of-the-match could easily have been Jansen, with his one wicket, four catches and big-hitting or the superb 36-year-old veteran tweaker Maharaj, but batting at No.4, Breetzke's superb 106-ball knock, before being run out by Connolly, deservedly won the day.
All-rounder Jack Edwards had an uncomfortable debut — 0-56 off 10 overs, followed by scoring five off 15 balls — but there was encouragement again in the display of paceman Nathan Ellis, who, fresh from his outstanding series against Zimbabwe, was again the bowling pick with 3-57.
All-rounder Cameron Green, back in the side after missing the series against Zimbabwe as he recovered from a shoulder injury, had a poor day with the bat, falling for five while trying to belt Maharaj over cow corner and getting caught in the deep.
The opening loss has really put pressure on Australia to turn the series round at The Wanderers in Johannesburg on Sunday, when Cummins is set to be recalled. They haven't won a bilateral series against South Africa since 2014.

Costa Rica’s foreign minister fired for attending Trump meeting
President Laura Fernandez claims unapproved participation in anti-cartel session inflicted ‘great strategic damage’
Costa Rica’s President Laura Fernandez on Thursday fired her foreign minister for attending a meeting on Latin America’s security led by US President Donald Trump without telling her.
Fernandez said she should have been the one to attend the meeting of Trump’s anti-cartel “Shield of the Americas” alliance in New York, and that Foreign Minister Manuel Tovar’s failure to consult her caused “great strategic damage”.
The meeting took place on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Tovar attended “without giving prior notice or informing” the president, a conservative Trump ally, of his participation, Costa Rica’s government said.

Finnish leader pleads with Musk to help Ukraine hit Russian missile launchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:11:49 UTC
06:11:49 KST

Finnish leader pleads with Musk to help Ukraine hit Russian missile launchers
NEW YORK, Sept 24 - Finnish President Alexander Stubb said on Thursday he pleaded with SpaceX owner Elon Musk to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage for Ukraine so it can strike Russian ballistic missile launchers located inside Russian territory.
With winter looming, Ukraine has an acute shortage of air defenses to repel Russian ballistic missiles, and Kyiv officials believe that turning on Starlink over Russian territory would help it target the Russian launchers that fire the missiles.
"That's why ... I plead that Elon Musk would give the Ukrainians the possibility to use Starlink in areas where there are ballistic missile launchers, either in the occupied territory of Ukraine or in Russia for strategic purposes because that would save lives," Stubb said.
The Finnish leader, a staunch ally of Ukraine who also has good relations with US President Donald Trump, made the remark in an interview with Reuters in New York where world leaders have converged for the annual gathering at the United Nations.
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy used the event to press hard for ceasefires that would cover strikes on targets related to energy infrastructure and vessels in the Black Sea. Russia has given no public indication it wants to see such arrangements.
Four-and-a-half years since the full-scale Russian invasion, the Ukrainians fear Moscow plans to systematically target and destroy power and heating sites in the depth of winter. Russia's use of ballistic missiles hit record levels this summer.
Only Ukraine's Patriot air defenses are able to intercept such missiles, but ammunition is severely depleted and it is unclear where new supplies could come from.
Musk switched on the Starlink satellite internet service over Ukraine shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. It has become the lifeblood of Ukraine's battlefield communications and a tool for piloting drones.
Starlink does not work over Russian territory, but Ukrainian officials believe turning it on for Ukraine's use inside Russia would allow its weapons to strike mobile ballistic launchers located within several hundred kilometres of the border.
Looking ahead to winter, Stubb said there were three things that Ukraine needed.
"One is air defenses and even Starlink would be to a certain extent a good air defense there. And the second one is energy installations for the winter."
"The third one is money. So those are the things that we're working on. We're working on putting up a winter package because I don't see the war ending, you know, before the winter."
Stubb said it was good that US-led peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine had restarted in August with the visits of US envoys to both Moscow and Kyiv.
"I still think that the easiest solution would be to call an unconditional ceasefire, basically stop the killing, as President Trump reiterated in his speech in the UN General Assembly," he said.
Such a step, he continued, would be followed by negotiations on security, territory, reconstruction and compensation and other topics.
The war could be frozen along the line of contact with 30-kilometre buffer zones east and west, he said, adding that the next best option was the idea of the partial ceasefire on energy and grain related targets. REUTERS

OpenAI’s agents went rogue — its human response caused the real damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:11:43 UTC
06:11:43 KST

If you’ve been forwarded this newsletter, you can sign up free here.
Confide in me: Send your tips to this generic inbox, [email protected].
ESSENTIALS
— It’s time to sort out human responsibility for AI agents
— China’s record nuclear expansion
— Whyalla steelworks: The distressed plant has repaid more than $5 million in government grants
Listen to Playbook’s Ryan Heath on ABC’s The Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and Clare Armstrong.
HEY, WHATEVER, WE LIKE HACKED MEDICARE OR SOMETHING, LOL.
When an artificial intelligence agent goes rogue and accesses Medicare statistics, who’s responsible? The answer under Australian law is probably “no one,” Paul Karp and Finn McHugh report.
The Australian government may still refer OpenAI’s unauthorized access to police, but rather than prosecutions, the main action is likely to come from a review coordinated by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet closing legal loopholes.
ONE RULE FOR HUMANS: “If a person hacked into a Medicare database they would be looking at years in prison, but if you are a big U.S. tech company, you don’t even get a slap on the wrist,” Greens AI spokesperson David Shoebridge told POLITICO.
“If a physical robot entered a Medicare office and broke into a safe, that would be a crime. Why is it that [when] a digital agent does this in a digital environment we treat that differently?” asked Olivia Shen, director of the Strategic Technology Program at the United States Studies Centre.
Breathe: We cover these nuances in more detail with Nicholas Davis of the University of Technology Sydney in the Playbook interview below.
NOT AN ISOLATED INCIDENT: This is the first publicly identified instance of rogue agents autonomously breaking into government systems, but it is not an isolated incident when it comes to agents out of control.
Step back in time: OpenAI rogue agents also attempted to break into at least two American government and university websites, government officials tell The New York Times.
THE NEXT WORLD-LEADING DIGITAL POLICY? Prime Minister Anthony Albanese didn’t engineer this, but he’s been spinning around to take advantage of it, and he will mention the incident in his general assembly speech later today to reinforce his view that AI needs more guardrails.
IT’S THE AFTERMATH, STUPID: The intrusion wasn’t sophisticated, no one was harmed, but it’s still a political timebomb. The problem is what comes next — when the same thing happens but then agents start colluding to take it further, and personal data is breached or systems are shut down.
Wow! OpenAI had no idea for two months, and then had no idea how to handle this with the Australian government. Ryan Heath explains each of the major mistakes, and why this drama is part of a long history of large tech companies not taking non-American markets and governments seriously.
THE EXCUSES DON’T WASH: In Australian dollars, OpenAI has raised around $175 billion, is valued at over $1 trillion, and seeks to reshape the world. If its agents can hack the Australian health system, Playbook would be shocked if its global workforce of highly qualified and highly remunerated humans could not find the mobile number of the Australian minister’s media team. They can literally get the office phone number in an online search.
Slow: How it takes three weeks to escalate a global-first government hack to OpenAI’s senior leadership and government relations teams is anyone’s guess.
Give me just a little more time: How one meets multiple Australian ministers in that period, but there’s no system to say something, is also a mystery.
THE BUSINESS MODEL IS A CHOICE: There is no resource problem at OpenAI or its competitors. They all have the resources to ensure effective human management of their products — choosing to allocate those resources elsewhere is exactly that: a choice.
Reality check: The other reality is that San Francisco-based startups and scale-ups are not focused outside of their investors and products, let alone a smallish foreign government like Australia.
I believe in you: Australia can choose many options in reaction to those realities, the biggest mistake would be denying these realities.
WHERE DOES THIS TENSION CRYSTALLIZE? If an AI company can’t reliably know what its agents are doing, stop them when they cross a boundary and promptly tell the affected party when they discover it, what does human control over autonomous AI mean?
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, a.k.a The One, said at the U.N. Security Council that “we will all be better off … if we can agree on what good oversight looks like.”
Hand on your heart: He may be getting the answer quicker than expected: It almost certainly involves government interference in the frictionless and low-regulation business model AI companies prize.
WHAT THEY’RE SAYING
“Damages [should be] payable by those who are most responsible,”
— Greens AI spokesperson David Shoebridge 
“The government should be throwing the book at them.”
— Independent Sen. David Pocock
“Exactly the kind of canary in the coal mine we need to prompt greater action on AI guardrails, governance and disclosures of incidents.”
— Olivia Shen, director of strategic technologies at the United States Studies Centre
“Australia has few levers to protect its national interest until we are materially embedded in the frontier AI supply chain. The starting point for developing safety standards on Australia’s terms is hosting frontier AI training onshore.
“Today, Australia is relying on volunteers in the U.S. to find out about incidents where Australia is exposed. We need to urgently build accident and incident reporting capability and position to shape global safety standards.”
— Anna-Maria Arabia, CEO of the Australian Council on AI Strategy
WHAT RICHARD MARLES SAID, AND WHAT HE MEANT
What he said: “Mis-aligned activity”
What he meant: A rogue AI agent hacking government websites.
What he said: “The way we regard this is taking this incident as a salutary warning”
What he meant: Whoa, we’re lucky we got away with this one.
What he said: “Very cooperative in terms of the engagement that we are having with them now”
What he meant: OpenAI is finally playing ball after months of not taking it seriously.
BACK IN SUPERPOWER LAND — THE U.S. CHINA AI DIVIDE: U.S. and Chinese officials remain starkly divided on AI safety. Beijing is open to restrictions. The Trump administration is shooting the idea down, saying national sovereignty must trump international bodies.
WHEN YOU BECOME THE PUNCHLINE … On a night like this with Capital Brief’s ideas editor James Hennessy comes a dire personal story.
NICHOLAS DAVIS — “WE HAVEN’T TESTED THIS EXACT SCENARIO IN AUSTRALIAN LAW”
An industry professor of emerging technology at UTS, Davis spoke with Paul Karp on the legal issues potentially arising from yesterday’s OpenAI breach.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Based on what we know so far about the incident, do you have a view about whether it breached any laws or AI guardrails?
If you conduct unauthorized access into a government system, the law says: There is criminal liability and corporations can be held to account for that as well.
So we do have laws in Australia that indicate on the surface, there would definitely be something to answer or investigate here. The trickiness and the ambiguity is that normally our laws and systems are focused on a human doing it and doing it with intent. In a situation where a company gets held liable for a human doing it, it is because of corporate culture, or acting as an agent, [the corporation] enabled it, or they were reckless in some way. We haven’t tested this exact scenario in Australian law, that I know of.
So, a genuine first?
It’s a first, that I know of, in terms of where there may not have been some kind of intent from an actor. Most of the time when we get hacks of this nature, even if they’re done by [AI] agents, they’ve been sent off to do it. Someone stands behind it saying “please go off and hack these systems.”
What level of culpability does the person who sets it off on the task have?
I don’t think we know exactly what instructions were given. I hope that’s something OpenAI can be clear about, because it gives us a much clearer idea about in the future, whether these agents are safe for organizations or you and me to use. If I’m a researcher at UTS, and I tell Claude or OpenAI to research health statistics, I don’t want to be on the line for hacking into a government server because it’s a bit aggressive.
What does this do for OpenAI’s credibility as they ask for other reforms on data centers and copyright?
I think it’s more a troubling indicator that OpenAI may not be treating this as seriously as they should. It seems strange to me that they do really care — and the Australian government cares — about getting the data center question right. We have OpenAI executives visiting Australia regularly, and an OpenAI team here in Australia as well, and yet the notification went to a generic public inbox at Services Australia. That’s an indicator they don’t have the monitoring or engagement with the government on these threats calibrated to the seriousness of the damage an autonomous agent could do.
3%: The pay rise members of the Australian Defence Force will receive between Nov. 3, 2026 and Nov. 3, 2027, per a Defence Force Remuneration Tribunal decision. It’s an interim rise because the broader three-year pay rise offer for civilian defense officials is due Oct. 13.
3.5%: Consumer Price Index to July 2026.
$319 million: The estimated cost of the 3% pay rise.
$14 billion: Additional funding for Defence over the next four years, to implement the National Defence Strategy.
3 years: The length of the usual pay arrangement. (Note: Not agreement. ADF members don’t get a say).
MIDDLE POWER COP: Don’t expect nail-biting, let alone successful major negotiations, at this year’s global climate summit — there’s no political appetite for it. We need to work on our preparedness, our knowledge, and our readiness so that our response in the event of a threat becomes a confident, almost natural response. ... (The guide) is intuitive, graphically accessible, and easily explains the basic principles of a safe place, both outdoors and indoors

Militech Group Launched Production of Composite Parts for Ukraine’s Defense Industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:09:43 UTC
06:09:43 KST

Militech Group has launched specialized contract manufacturing of composite products for Ukrainian defense companies.
Representatives of the company told Militarnyi about this.
The company notes that establishing in-house production for each individual component requires significant investment, specialized equipment, and a team of experts.
Therefore, Militech Group is developing a contract manufacturing model that enables small teams with their own technologies to create and scale complex products without having to build a complete production cycle.
Militech Group manufactures composite fuselages and other structural components based on the customer’s technical specifications.
The company handles process preparation, production, and delivery of finished products, while the customer can focus on research and development, engineering, and refining their own product.
Composite products most often use fiberglass, carbon fiber, and other fiber-reinforced polymer materials.
The main advantage of composites is the combination of low weight and high strength. This is particularly important for drones: a lighter airframe can mean greater payload, range, or flight duration.
This technology is not new to Ukraine. In 2019, Motor Sich manufactured helicopters made of composite materials.
According to the company, this model of collaboration is particularly relevant for young teams specializing in the development of unmanned systems.
Specialization makes it possible to shorten the path from prototype to mass production without having to expand one’s own manufacturing infrastructure. As a result, developers can direct more engineering resources toward creating and improving technologies for the Ukrainian military.
“The Ukrainian defense-tech sector is gradually shifting from a ‘everyone does everything on their own’ model to one of cooperation. Developers have more resources to work on creating technological breakthroughs, while delegating the production of individual components to specialized partners,” noted Vasyl Polishchuk, a representative of Militech Group.

‘Her mental health deteriorated’: family forced to wait years for autism diagnosis

For Rosalyn, the battle for an official autism diagnosis for her 14-year-old daughter, Imogen, has been intense, deeply frustrating and has lasted five and a half years.
That Rosalyn has three other children who have autism diagnoses meant she was acutely aware of the signs.
Rosalyn, 53, from Trafford, Greater Manchester, who works in the medical profession, was diagnosed aged 39. She noticed her youngest child’s problems with socialising and sensory issues at about the age of eight. “It wasn’t going to be unusual that she might also be autistic. We have a very strong family history of it,” Rosalyn said.
The school had noticed issues and agreed to start collecting information for a referral, which took about 18 months. It was sent off in the hope a diagnosis would be made before Imogen started high school.
Trafford Autism and Social Communication Pathway then “sat on the referral for a while”, said Rosalyn. There were multidisciplinary meetings to decide if they would accept the referral – which took months. Finally, two years later – on 27 March 2023 – Imogen was accepted on to the waiting list.
“And we waited. And we waited. I kept emailing every few months to say ‘Where is she?’ And they would say ‘Oh, it’s a 12-month waiting list’. And then after a year: ‘It’s an 18-month waiting list’. And then: ‘It’s a 24-month waiting list’.
“In this time, her mental health deteriorated. She started struggling with a lot of issues that she wasn’t struggling with at the time she was referred.
“I kept writing. The GP wrote several times. Nothing. The school wrote. Nothing. Eventually, about six months ago, I wrote a very strongly worded email.” Rosalyn then listed all the mental health problems her daughter had developed “particularly in the last 12 months”.
“They eventually agreed to expedite her, after three and a half years. They finally saw her about a week-and-a-half ago. But we haven’t got a result yet,” Rosalyn said.
Getting a diagnosis is important, she said. “It is helpful to understand who you are,” Rosalyn said. It also affects the support her daughter can access. “Quite a lot of doors are shut to you if you don’t have a diagnosis,” she added.
In school, Imogen does not have an education health and care plan (EHCP) used to access certain support in school. “If you don’t have a diagnosis, that undermines your evidence,” said Rosalyn. “It’s a catch-22.”
Without a diagnosis, she will not qualify for a disabled students’ allowance, which she will need if she goes to university. Or, should she require it, a personal independence payment. Some support groups “want evidence – the evidence is the diagnosis”, Rosalyn said.
“There is a lot of self-diagnosis now, and I think that is because people cannot access diagnosis. You are simply driving people towards self-diagnosis, which is then creating a health inequality.
“You’ve got wealthy people who can access [private] diagnosis. Great. And they are opening the door to all that diagnosis means. And you have people who can’t afford that never getting a diagnosis.”
Of her daughter, Rosalyn added: “She’s into her GCSEs now. Her mental health has massively deteriorated.” They have a “complex family situation”, she said, and Imogen is dealing with a lot of things “perhaps other kids aren’t dealing with”.
“There’s the circumstances around our family life, I accept that. But I think not having a diagnosis for her, she feels like a fraud. People go ‘Well. Do you have a diagnosis? No? Oh right. OK!’ Some people are very critical of self-diagnosis.
“Most people seeking an autism assessment are doing so because they’ve had years of wondering why they don’t feel like other people. Not because it’s trendy. Nobody wants to be autistic. I don’t want to be; I just am,” Rosalyn said.
Imogen’s siblings were diagnosed far more swiftly, partly because of the way referrals are now dealt with and partly to do with waiting times, Rosalyn said.
“With Imogen – six years younger – it’s become such a battle.
“It’s very distressing. She has a lot of issues around her behaviour, her sensory needs, her inability to socialise. She doesn’t leave the house. She’s 14. She should be out living her best life and she isn’t. And that makes me mad.”

The death toll from the sinking of the KM Virgo Transport 8 in Indonesia's Java Sea has risen to 42 after search and rescue teams recovered 14 more bodies from inside the vessel, media reports said Thursday.
The victims were retrieved during diving operations inside the wreckage, state-run Antara News Agency reported, citing Mohammad Syafii, the head of the National Search and Rescue Agency (SAR), or Basarnas.
“The joint SAR team's efforts have once again yielded results,” said Syafii.
He said divers from the Basarnas Special Group, the Indonesian Navy and other search and rescue units recovered all 14 bodies from inside the ship.
The bodies were initially transferred to the KN SAR Pacitan search and rescue vessel for emergency handling before being flown to Banjarmasin.
A Basarnas HR-3604 helicopter and an Indonesian Navy Panther helicopter were used to transport the victims, according to the Antara News Agency.
Upon arrival in Banjarmasin, the bodies were handed to the Disaster Victim Identification team and authorities for medical identification and additional procedures.
As of Thursday, authorities had found 150 people from the vessel's passenger manifest.
Of them, 108 survived, while 42 were confirmed dead.
Search and rescue operations are continuing for 93 people who are missing, according to the latest figures.

NHS bodies in England impose two-year minimum wait for ADHD and autism assessments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:00:30 UTC
06:00:30 KST

NHS bodies are forcing people with suspected attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism to wait at least two years before they can be assessed as they struggle to meet surging demand for diagnoses of neurodiversity.
Four NHS integrated care boards (ICBs) covering large regions of England have adopted the approach because they cannot afford the cost of the number of assessments that people are seeking.
Patient groups are warning that the “scandalous” delays such policies involve may damage children’s chances of succeeding at school, deny people the help they need to manage their lives, and increase the risk of suicide. The charity ADHD UK denounced minimum waits as “heartless and dangerous”.
In all, 15 ICBs, which between them cover 19 million people, have brought in various ways of rationing assessments for ADHD and autism to try to balance their books. These include limiting the number of assessments the ICBs will pay for in any given year and using “clinical prioritisation” criteria to restrict assessment to those with the most serious signs of neurodiversity.
Disclosure of the NHS’s widespread efforts to delay and deny access to assessments comes before the publication of a major government-commissioned review of the colossal increases in diagnoses of mental illness, as well as ADHD and autism, in recent years. It was ordered last year by Wes Streeting, the then health secretary, amid concern that the weight of requests for assessment, diagnosis and care was overwhelming the health service’s ability to meet demand.
The 700-page report of the review, led by Prof Peter Fonagy, was due to be published on Thursday but was unexpectedly postponed until early next month.
Sources familiar with the document told the Guardian that it painted a detailed picture of how the fast-rising demand for help with mental illness conditions, ADHD and autism has left those affected struggling to get rapid access to NHS care and increasingly reliant on private providers.
Fonagy’s report raises serious concerns about the sector, especially about the consistency and quality of the assessments it provides and the fact that there are “financial incentives associated with assessment activity”.
It also lays bare the scale of the challenge that the increasing number of diagnoses of mental illness, ADHD and autism pose for the NHS, as well as schools, employers and families, by highlighting up to 24-fold rises in the prevalence of neurodiversity in boys since 2000.
It reveals that the percentage of seven- to 18-year-old boys with autism rose from 0.2% in 2000 to 4.7% in 2025. Prevalence among boys aged six to 11 rose from 0.4% to 6.3% over the same period – a 16-fold jump.
Similarly, the percentage of seven to 18-year-old boys diagnosed with ADHD rose from 0.4% to 5.1% between 2000 and 2025 – an almost 13-fold leap – and from 0.7% to 3.8% – up five-fold – among boys aged six to 11, according to figures provided by the Clinical Practice Research Datalink.
“Minimum waits” after referral by a GP mean people in the areas affected cannot seek an assessment by a private sector provider. That is even though private clinics now undertake half of NHS-funded assessments of ADHD and a third of those for autism, because many patients exercise their legal right to choose non-NHS care, given the NHS’s own limited capacity to do the assessments.
Such curbs by the NHS are likely to force those who can afford it to pay a private provider for an assessment for themselves or their child, which can cost several thousand pounds. They are being implemented at a time when there are 960,000 people in England waiting for an ADHD assessment and another 295,000 awaiting one for autism.
West Yorkshire NHS integrated care board has introduced a minimum waiting time of two years from referral for anyone seeking an ADHD or autism assessment with an independent provider. That was in response to its bill for such assessments soaring from £7m in 2023-24 to £21m last year, it said.
The West Yorkshire ICB’s decision applies to the 2.4 million people for whom it commissions and pays for care in Leeds, Bradford, Kirklees, Calderdale and Wakefield. Its area includes the constituency of Pontefract, Castleford and Knottingley – the parliamentary seat of the health secretary Yvette Cooper.
Private providers that the North East and North Cumbria ICB funds to assess people “are working to an approximately 78-week minimum waiting time for an initial assessment”, it says.
Somerset ICB is operating a minimum wait of 52 weeks, while the equivalent in Devon is a lot lower, at 14 weeks. Kent and Medway ICB has also decided to impose a minimum wait.
This month, in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, assessment for ADHD and autism has been restricted to those patients who meet the ICB’s priority criteria.
“It’s scandalous that any NHS body should impose a two-year minimum wait for ADHD and autism assessments,” said Henry Shelford, the chief executive of ADHD UK.
“This is the health service denying people care they need, and care that is available, and slamming the door shut on people who need an assessment of their symptoms to give them a diagnosis and unlock essential care that helps people hold down jobs, stay in education and stay out of crisis services.
“A minimum wait is heartless and dangerous. It is institutionalised cruelty.’
A spokesperson for Finally Seen, which tracks NHS restrictions on the right to choose, said: “A two-year minimum wait is not a waiting list. It is a locked door with a date on it.
“The right to choose still exists on paper. In practice it is being rationed by the calendar, which is a blunt and bleak way to treat a legal right.”
The British Medical Journal recently revealed that 17 of the 36 ICBs had introduced minimum waits of 12 to 16 weeks before patients could have a new hip or knee fitted or cataract removed, even though the NHS is meant to give 92% of patients planned hospital care within 18 weeks.
Mel Merritt, the head of policy and influencing at the National Autistic Society, said: “Restricting access to autism assessments denies people support because, while it shouldn’t be the case, a diagnosis is needed to get help. For children, this can mean years of wasted school while they wait for an assessment and further waits to get a plan for support and adjustments to be put into place.
“A diagnosis doesn’t only confirm if people are autistic or not, but also their needs and what adjustments could make a massive difference to being able to participate and enjoy life. Longer waiting times and restricting access to assessments will only worsen challenges for autistic people, pushing them into crisis and increasing the number of people with urgent needs.”
The Independent Healthcare Providers Network, which represents many independent assessment services, urged the NHS to let private clinics offer as many appointments as were available.
Sean Phillips, its head of policy, said: “For someone struggling with suspected ADHD or autism, those extra months or years without diagnosis and support can have a profound impact on their mental health, education, work and family life.
“With more than a million people already waiting, we should be using all available capacity to get people the support and treatment they need as well as ensuring that their legal right to choose the best provider for them is being upheld.”
Rebecca Gray, the director of the NHS Alliance’s mental health network, said local NHS leaders were “keenly aware of the deep frustration caused by long delays and are doing all they can to address them.
“But the need to balance budgets and the pressures of soaring demand have – in some places – led to ‘minimum waits’ or even the closure of some waiting lists.
“The current situation is unsustainable and delivers a bad deal for patients and taxpayers.”

‘Send in the Clowns’: Viral video fuels claims Denmark trolled Trump and Rubio
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:00:16 UTC
06:00:16 KST

‘Send in the Clowns’: Viral video fuels claims Denmark trolled Trump and Rubio
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
A viral video claims Danish officials played Judy Collins’ “Send in the Clowns” as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived for a Greenland signing ceremony, sparking claims of Danish “trolling”. Our checks of separate livestreams confirm the song really played and the video was not manipulated. Denmark has denied choosing the music, while the UN says it did not organise the event. Whilst the song was real, there is no evidence Denmark selected it deliberately. Vedika Bahl fact-checks.
On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a deal Tuesday to expand Washington’s military presence in the Arctic territory. The agreement came after months of diplomatic tensions over Greenland, with Denmark also seeking to reaffirm its control over the island.
But an unusual song played before the signing has sparked a wave of speculation online.
A video circulating widely on social media claims Danish officials deliberately played Judy Collins’ version of the classic Broadway song “Send in the Clowns” as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived.
The clip has amassed more than a million views in a single post on X, with the footage also widely shared on Bluesky, Threads, Facebook and Instagram.
The song’s lyrics include the line: “Where are the clowns? Send in the clowns. Don't bother, they're here.”
Social media users quickly interpreted the music as a deliberate dig at the US delegation, with some praising Denmark for what they described as “epic trolling”. Others questioned whether the footage was genuine, while some went further, sharing AI-generated images depicting members of the US delegation as clowns.
The speculation raised a key question: did the song actually play at the ceremony, and if so, was it deliberately chosen by Denmark?
We checked footage from multiple livestreams of the event.
The original viral video carries the watermark of US-based outlet MAGNO News. In its Facebook livestream, just before the 11-minute mark, Rubio and other delegates can be seen entering as “Send in the Clowns” plays in the background. The Guardian’s livestream, filmed from a different angle, also captures the same song playing as the delegates arrive.
The evidence therefore confirms that the song really was played. There is also no indication that the viral footage was manipulated, but there's also no evidence that Denmark selected it.
Whilst the song played as Rubio entered, along with him entered the Ministers for Denmark and Greenland. If this was an attempt to "troll" a particular nation or send a message, it didn't go as intended as all countries representatives entered together.
A spokesperson for Denmark’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated that Denmark was “not involved in selecting the music for the signing”.
Fact-checking outlet Lead Stories also contacted the United Nations. The spokesperson for the UN secretary-general directed the outlet to the US mission, saying it had not organised the event.
It's possible the song was played by coincidence or accident, rather than as a deliberate message to any one country.
So while “Send in the Clowns” was genuinely playing before the Greenland deal signing began, the claim that Denmark deliberately selected it to mock the US delegation remains unsubstantiated.
