More than half of complaints against AFP 'finalised' without investigation, figures show
More than half of all allegations made against Australian Federal Police officers have been "finalised" without investigation due to the use of discretionary powers the national watchdog says pose a risk of "denying procedural fairness".
Figures released by the AFP to the national inquiry into racism, hate, and violence directed at First Nations people reveal the number of complaints made against officers in the last five years.
Since July 2021, 512 complaints have been made about AFP officers' conduct, with 1,213 individual allegations identified.
Of those allegations, 643 were "finalised", without investigation, using a broad discretionary power available to the AFP under section 40TF of the legislation.
Read the full story from national Indigenous affairs correspondent Dana Morse in the link below.
PM sidesteps questions on US banning diesel exports
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has sidestepped questions about the idea of the US banning diesel exports from the US.
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday, local time, he backed the idea of a ban on diesel exports from the US, which has been floated by some Republican politicians ahead of the midterm elections in November.
A leading energy analyst has warned that Australia could be looking at diesel rationing within weeks and prices topping $4 a litre.
Albanese has told News24 "trade between the United States and Australia is a good thing".
"That's why we have a free trade agreement. What happens with barriers impact the country and can hurt the country that's imposing them. But the United States domestic policy is, of course, a matter for the United States," Albanese says.
Albanese says digital duty of care will not shut down free speech
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has denied the government's digital duty of care legislation will shut down free speech.
Labor's proposed digital duty of care could let Australians opt in or out of algorithmically recommended social media content.
It also sets out expectations for all online platforms, including social media, AI chatbots and search engines, to proactively protect Australians from harmful content.
The Trump administration has warned the Albanese government that the policy would be "extraterritorial censorship of protected speech".
But Albanese says the digital duty of care is the opposite of the government getting involved.
"This is about giving Australians power and empowering them for them to determine what they receive on their device," Albanese says.
Australia must 'lean in' on artificial intelligence development: Albanese
Anthony Albanese says Australia can't be defined by its relationships with other countries and must speak up for the nation's interest.
Asked if he was concerned the US president isn't open to any further guardrails on artificial intelligence, the PM has sidestepped the question.
But he says Australia has to "lean in" on AI and its development.
"It is up to Australia to not be defined by our relationships just with other countries, to speak up for Australia's national interests and to engage constructively will continue to engage constructively, with both the United States and China," Albanese says.
"We want to be a part of the development, because what that will do is enable us to have a say in how this is rolled out."
PM defends timing of disclosure of OpenAI agent hack
The prime minister has defended the timing of when the federal government informed the public of the OpenAI agent hack.
Nationals frontbencher Bridget McKenzie suggested today that there were political reasons the PM announced the hack yesterday.
Anthony Albanese says that's "nonsense" and the government released the details as soon as it could.
"Imagine if we had said there's been a data breach, but we don't know what has been sourced. We don't know if your personal information is out there," Albanese says.
"That would have created a great deal of anxiety, which was unnecessary. We had to ascertain the facts. And then we made the statements as a matter of urgency. We also provided briefings to the opposition, as is appropriate."
No personal details compromised in OpenAI agent hack, Albanese says
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says personal details weren't accessed in the OpenAI agent hack revealed yesterday.
The OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia on June 18.
Speaking in an interview with News24 from New York, Albanese says there is no evidence of any harm being done in the incident.
"That doesn't mean that it's not serious, because it is an example of the implications that we have been warning of," Albanese says.
"Indeed, AI companies themselves have warned of that the potential for this new technology to go in directions without human direction, without human control."
Ayres defends work of AI Safety Institute
Tim Ayres has defended the work of the AI Safety Institute following the recent OpenAI agent hack on a Services Australia portal.
The institute was established to examine new artificial intelligence capabilities, along with emerging risks and harms.
Asked on News24 whether the institute was reactive rather than proactive, Ayres says it is responsible for securing AI investment in Australia.
The industry minister says the cybersecurity approach across government is a responsibility of departments and ASD.
"It is to secure onshore investment in AI training, in particular because that is an important sovereign capability for Australia, and that means questions like pre-launch testing," Ayres says.
Taylor indicates support for changing laws to charge OpenAI for breach
A taskforce has been assembled to review whether Australia can prosecute OpenAI after its agent breached a Medicare data portal.
So if the review suggests the law needs updating, would the Coalition agree to this? Angus Taylor appears open to it.
"We haven't seen any proposal yet for the government," he says.
"What I will say is that I've long believed that data breaches need to be dealt with in an appropriate way and those responsible for the data breaches need to be accountable for it.
"But we'll wait and see what the government has in mind."
Taylor questions timing of PM's reveal of OpenAI hack
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor is on the Gold Coast this morning, where he's again spruiking the opposition's plan to slash the fuel excise.
He stopped by a petrol station to fill up a car and used it as an opportunity to give the PM a whack for attending the UN General Assembly while fuel prices were so high.
The focus of the press conference quickly turns to the OpenAI agent hack of a Medicare data portal.
Taylor says the breach is "serious". But he questioned the timing of the prime minister's announcement.
"It seems to be terribly coincidental, doesn't it. He's swanning about New York at black tie dinner events, getting this Global Citizen of the Year award. And he wanted to say something, so he held off," the Liberal leader says.
"I mean, this stuff matters and it should be timely. The government should be talking about it as soon as it knows about it."
Albanese and his office were briefed on the hack over the weekend. The breach occurred in June, but Services Australia was not told by OpenAI until September 10.
Taylor also called on the government to start using AI to identify vulnerabilities in our cybersecurity defences.
Albanese meets with Greece's PM on sidelines of UN
Anthony Albanese has caught up with Greece's prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, on the sidelines of the United Nations.
The Greek PM delivered his speech to the UN General Assembly just before Albanese stepped up to the podium to deliver his address.
Key Event
Australia a 'reliable, practical and transparent' partner, PM says
In conclusion, the PM says Australia's geography gives the country a unique perspective as a Pacific nation connected to South-East Asia, the Indian Ocean and Antarctica.
Anthony Albanese says addressing climate change and accepting the science has been an entry point for engaging with the Pacific.
He says Australia is a "reliable, practical and transparent" partner.
"We listen with respect, we partner as equals, and we protect what matters most," Albanese says.
"We engage across regions, listen to different perspectives, and build trust.
"Australia helped create the United Nations to bring an end to an era of destructive conflict. And to build something better, for all of us."
Key Event
Albanese says decision to recognise Palestine was 'considered'
On Australia's decision to recognise the State of Palestine, Anthony Albanese says the decision was "considered" and in step with its partners.
Albanese says the decision was motivated by the "determination" to end the "cycle of violence".
He says Australia will continue to speak out against actions that damage prospects of peace in the region.
"We know the only viable path to peace and security in Palestine, in Israel and in the broader Middle East, is through a two-state solution," Albanese says.
"We will continue to speak out against actions that damage that prospect of peace, including illegal settlements in the West Bank.
"Just as we continue to oppose any role for the terrorists of Hamas in Palestine's future."
And on the conflict between the US and Iran, Albanese says Australia has been consistent in calls for a ceasefire and for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen.
PM reaffirms Australia's opposition to Russian invasion of Ukraine
Anthony Albanese has used his address to the United Nations General Assembly to reaffirm Australia's opposition to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
The prime minister says Australia this week endorsed the 2026 International Crimea Platform joint statement.
He says it reaffirms Australia's respect for Ukraine's sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity.
"We oppose Russia's continued illegal, unprovoked and immoral invasion of Ukraine and reiterate our calls for Russia's immediate, complete and unconditional withdrawal and an end to attacks upon civilians and civilian infrastructure," Albanese says.
Key Event
Albanese says AI must be subject of public discussion now
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says artificial intelligence must now be the subject of public discussion.
The prime minister says while it has the potential to improve people's lives and productivity, it carries risks.
He's also spoken about the recent OpenAI data hack that affected a Services Australia portal.
"Recently an Artificial Intelligence agent infiltrated an Australian government website. This is unacceptable. And it is why Australia has been leading the way in establishing Australian Standards for AI," Albanese says.
"Standards to ensure AI will work and deliver for people — not the other way around. We can't ignore AI or prevent it."
World must 'embrace change and reform', Albanese says
Anthony Albanese says the world must "embrace change and reform" to create a world of human dignity.
He says Australia doesn't believe in abandoning multilateralism, but rather reforming it to adapt to challenges ahead.
The PM says Australia seeks to amplify the voices of mid-sized states to ensure Security Council decisions are informed by a wide range of perspectives.
He says Australia stands for a "safer world" where "no country dominates, and no country is dominated".
"In our region, the Indo-Pacific, we are elevating relationships that help to build sovereign capability and offer nations sovereign choice, free from coercion," Albanese says.
"So that our partners can address the big issues confronting them: economic security, human development, energy security, transnational crime, sovereign capabilities, trade and investment, and science and technology."
Key Event
PM makes his pitch for Australia's seat on UN Security Council
The prime minister is now making his pitch for Australia's non-permanent seat at the UN Security Council from 2029 to 2030.
Anthony Albanese says Australia wants to respond to the world's challenges by partnering to make a difference.

"We will work to prevent crises, resolve conflicts and protect civilians through diplomacy, peacebuilding and practical action."
Key Event
Albanese says UN mission can't be entrusted alone by great powers
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says from artificial intelligence to climate change, the world is being confronted by challenges predecessors could never have imagined.
He says the world can rise to meet new challenges now to reaffirm national sovereignty and shared humanity.
Albanese says smaller countries need to take more responsibility for the world's challenges.
"We understand the UN mission cannot be entrusted solely to the great powers, or the biggest countries, or even the loudest voices alone," Albanese says.
"Nor can it be sub-contracted to the world's richest companies or dictated by the pace of technology.
"Then, now, and always, shaping a secure, peaceful and prosperous world is a task for all of us."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has just taken to the podium at the United Nations General Assembly in New York to speak.

Albanese has urged world leaders to "lean in" and strengthen and modernise the fundamental parts of the UN system.
"Sovereignty, prosperity and peace are never guaranteed—they must be created, nurtured and protected by each generation," Albanese says.
"We know that the surest way to minimise the potential for conflict is to create the prosperity, opportunity and economic justice on which lasting peace depends."

Norway to allocate $9B to support Ukraine in 2027
According to the Norwegian government's website, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere said this during a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Finnish President Alexander Stubb on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Ukrinform reports.

We will also continue to support efforts that pave the way for genuine negotiations between Ukraine and Russia," Stoere said.

Arab lawmaker criticizes exclusion of Arab lists from Israeli election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:56:22 UTC
05:56:22 KST

Khaled Yousef, Mohammad Sio
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Arab member of the Israeli Knesset Ayman Odeh on Thursday criticized the Central Elections Committee’s decision to bar Arab electoral lists from running in the Oct. 27 parliamentary election. 
Israeli Army Radio quoted Odeh as saying: “All the Kahanists are allowed (to run the elections), but representatives of the Arab population are prohibited from competing.” 
Palestinian citizens make up around 21% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million. 
The term “Kahanism” refers to a far-right Israeli ideology associated with Meir Kahane, an Israeli-American rabbi and politician who founded a movement known for its extremist views. 
On Wednesday, the Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify the Joint Arab List and the United Arab List, or Ra’am, as well as Knesset member Ofer Cassif and Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh from running in the election. 
Critics of the decisions say the exclusions are part of efforts by Israel’s right wing to prevent Arab parties from influencing the formation of the next government, as polls show neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing bloc nor the opposition securing the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority. 
By contrast, the Central Elections Committee on Thursday rejected a request to disqualify the far-right Otzma Yehudit party, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.  
Odeh expressed hope that Israel’s Supreme Court would overturn the disqualification decisions and allow the barred candidates and lists to contest the election. 
Earlier Thursday, Cassif also criticized both the government and the opposition in a post on US social media company X following his disqualification. 
“The Kahanists in both the government and the opposition are afraid of the power of our voice,” said Cassif, a lawmaker with the Joint Arab List. 
“Our voice is the only one that offers a genuine alternative to racist, militaristic and bloodthirsty discourse,” he added. 
Cassif is known for his opposition to the Netanyahu government’s policies toward Palestinians, particularly Israel’s genocide in Gaza since 2023. 
The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in 2024 over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. 
Netanyahu has headed the current government since late December 2022. He is also standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies.

European leader backs int'l courts at UN

05:51:47 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- European Council President Antonio Costa Thursday reiterated his support for the International Court of Justice (ICJ) and the International Criminal Court (ICC) in defense of international law.
In delivering his speech in the general debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, Costa said there can be no double standards in terms of international law and "we are witnessing deliberate violations of international law."
Following and defending international law is not an option but a responsibility, according to Costa.
"We stand firmly behind them and will uphold their independence, their integrity and their ability to fully exercise their mandate," said Costa, referring to ICJ and ICC.
"It is unacceptable to threaten or attack the International Criminal Court, its officials and its staff. Accountability cannot depend on political convenience," he added.
In August, Costa said on social media platform X that he stood firmly with the ICC, its president Tomoko Akane and officials working to uphold its mission.
Costa urged for strong, effective, representative and deliverable multilateralism in a bid to address challenges of today around peace, climate emergency, economic insecurity and artificial intelligence (AI).
Costa called for an accountable, transparent and regulated architecture on AI and its governance.
"We need an AI that serves humanity, not controls it," said Costa, who added that the United Nations must play a central role in setting global standards on AI governance.
Moreover, Costa stressed the need to reform the global financial architecture with an eye on sustainable development.
The 2027 Sustainable Development Goals Summit must be a "turning point" to correct course, regain momentum and meet the targets for 2030 and beyond, said Costa. ■

Yemen's Houthis claim missile, drone attacks on Riyadh, Aramco facility in Yanbu
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
04:51:29 CST
05:51:29 KST

SANAA, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Thursday evening that it had launched missile and drone attacks at a "sensitive target" in the Saudi capital Riyadh and an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, marking another round of long-range attacks amid an escalating confrontation with Saudi Arabia.
In a televised statement aired by Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV, the group's military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said the Houthi armed forces carried out two separate operations, one targeting a site in Riyadh and the other targeting an Aramco facility in Yanbu.
Sarea said the attacks were carried out with "a number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones," claiming that both operations "successfully achieved their objectives." He did not identify the target in Riyadh or provide details of any damage or casualties.
There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the two claimed strikes, and the Houthi account could not be independently verified.
Sarea said the attacks were launched in response to continuing Saudi air and missile strikes against Houthi-held areas in Yemen.
He claimed Saudi forces had carried out a total of 1,018 air and missile strikes since the latest escalation began, causing civilian casualties and damage to infrastructure.
The Houthi spokesperson vowed that the group would continue retaliatory operations as long as Saudi military action continued, reiterating what he described as an "escalation for escalation" policy.
The fresh announcement came only hours after the Houthis claimed a separate large-scale missile and drone operation against Saudi military positions in the southwestern border region of Jazan.
The latest Houthi claims also followed an announcement by the Saudi Arabia-led coalition earlier Thursday that its air defenses had intercepted and destroyed six ballistic missiles, thwarting attempts to strike Taif and Yanbu in Saudi Arabia.
The latest exchanges underscore the widening confrontation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, with both sides stepping up long-range attacks in recent weeks alongside intensified ground fighting in Yemen.
Yemen's conflict erupted in late 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

Trump and Xi Meet Ahead of State Dinner With Top A.I. Leaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:51:12 UTC
05:51:12 KST

Amid a fast-growing international debate over regulating artificial intelligence, President Trump and Chinese President Xi met at the White House for several hours on Thursday ahead of a state dinner where several of the biggest players in A.I. were set to attend.
“We had a great meeting,” Trump said later that afternoon at the Southern Portico, where he gave Xi a tour of the South Lawn Helipad.
“He’s an expert on stones, and he loves good granite,” Trump said of Xi.
The day began with remarks from both Trump and Xi at the grand foyer of the White House. Afterward, Trump and Xi participated in a military review at the Rose Garden and took part in hours of meetings before Trump led a tour of parts of the White House.
While both leaders mentioned AI in their opening remarks, Xi stressed that the development of AI always needs to be “under human control.”
Trump was set to host a state dinner for Xi Thursday evening, joined by a slate of tech leaders. Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla CEO Elon Musk were set to attend the dinner, a White House official confirmed.
According to Chinese state media, President Xi raised the issue of Iran during the bilateral meeting, saying that he hoped the US and Iran would resume negotiations and that China would support the two countries recommitting to the 14-point memorandum of understanding reached months ago.
On Taiwan, Xi said he hopes the U.S. would maintain its position of opposing Taiwan independence. The U.S. has not officially endorsed Taiwan's independence, but has previously sold weaponry to the island and is widely viewed as a key player if China were to ever invade the self-ruling island.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi urged more cooperation between the two countries. During his remarks, he called for more direct flights between the U.S. and China and invited 100,000 American students for cultural exchange in the next five years. And continuing a longtime diplomatic tradition stretching back to the Nixon era, he announced two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be delivered to Zoo Atlanta in the coming days.
“China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation between us, and we can certainly find the right path for two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home,” Xi said.
This is the first time a Chinese leader has made a second formal state visit to America. The last time Xi conducted a formal state visit in Washington, D.C. was at the invitation of President Obama in September 2015, three years after he succeeded as the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Trump and Xi first met in 2017, during Trump’s first term, at the President’s home base of Mar-a-Lago, Florida. The pair last met in May during a two-day state visit by Trump to Beijing, where the U.S. and China delegations discussed a range of topics including tariffs, rare mineral trade, as well as the Strait of Hormuz. The two leaders used the visit to announce the launch of a so-called Board of Trade intended to lower tariffs on products that aren’t considered a national security risk. In June, the Office of the United States Trade Representative asked the public to weigh in on which types of products would benefit from this new mechanism. The Administration has offered few updates on the board since then.

Feature: Chinese craftsmen turn press-on nails into high-value art in Milan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
04:50:51 CST
05:50:51 KST

MILAN, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- As the Italian model slowly moved her fingers under the spotlight, the green tourmaline stones on the translucent, green-gradient nails glittered, drawing the visitors' attention at Milan Fashion Week.
The showcase was part of a special event held Wednesday on the sidelines of Milan Fashion Week, featuring handmade nail art products -- specifically press-on nails -- from Donghai County in East China's Jiangsu Province.
Far from ordinary disposable press-on nails, the Donghai products combine art with techniques such as crystal carving, filigree and enamel work. Some elaborate sets carry price tags of thousands of U.S. dollars.
Li Xiao, general manager of Jiangsu Jingyiyi Supply Chain Management Co., Ltd., said a hand-painted Sun Wukong (Monkey King) press-on nail set brought to the event proved especially popular. A local tour guide spotted it on the first day and pre-ordered it.
Li said Sun Wukong's popularity overseas gives the design cross-cultural appeal. Since Donghai is closely associated with Huaguo Mountain, the legendary home of the Monkey King, designers drew inspiration from a story tied to the area and made this characteristic authentic creation.
"Handcrafting is central to the products' character," said Li. Painting, the layers of carving, and the placement of inlaid crystals all reflect the maker's individual artistry, while traditional techniques such as filigree have also been incorporated into modern nail art, giving the products their distinctive character and value.
"Unlike disposable options, these intricate press-on nails can be carefully removed, stored, and reused," Li noted. "This makes them a high-value alternative to traditional manicures done at a nail salon."
A Chinese press-on nail company told Xinhua that a hand-painted set can range in price from several hundred RMB to several thousand U.S. dollars. A set inspired by the famous Chinese painting A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains has been priced at 2,000 U.S. dollars. Some people have begun treating the nails as collectibles.
"I'm deeply drawn to Chinese press-on nail design. I think this is something novel for Italy, since designs like these are rarely seen on the market here," said Italian fashion blogger Katerina Kutsak, adding that the motifs incorporating Chinese culture felt especially distinctive.
Behind the products on display in Milan is an industry that emerged around 2019, after investors noticed that small crystal stones could be attached to artificial nails. The industry expanded rapidly, drawing on the crystal resources of Donghai, which is globally recognized as a World Craft City for Crystal.
Donghai has since become China's largest press-on nail production center, with its products exported to over 30 countries and regions, according to the county government. ■

Former Houthi spokesman tells i24NEWS he welcomes cooperation between Israel, Saudi Arabia ‘when it comes to defeating Houthis’

- The Houthi advance in Yemen may revive Israel-Saudi relations
The Houthi advance in Yemen may revive Israel-Saudi relations
In an interview with i24NEWS, former Houthi spokesman Ali al-Bukhaiti discusses Iran’s role in the group’s advance and the possibility of Saudi-Israeli cooperation
As the Houthis push toward the Bab al-Mandab Strait and continue to take ground from Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, the question of Saudi-Israeli cooperation against the Iranian-backed group is back on the table.
Riyadh and Jerusalem have quietly worked together before, and the Houthis' latest advance may give them good reason to do so again.
In a special interview, Ali al-Bukhaiti, a former Houthi spokesman, told me he knows of no publicly announced coordination between Riyadh and Jerusalem. But he doesn't see a problem with it.
"In my personal view, cooperation is not something wrong when it comes to defeating the Houthis," he said. "Just as Saudi Arabia cooperates with the United States and European countries. If it is possible for them to cooperate with the Israelis on this issue, personally, I don't see anything wrong with that."
Why the urgency? According to al-Bukhaiti, this is no longer just a Yemeni war. "I believe that the Battle of Bab al-Mandab is the first battle in which the Iranians and Hezbollah personnel are directly participating," he said. Not as fighters, but "in a management capacity. Intelligence management. Intercepting the communications of the other side. As well as coordinating between the fronts and information warfare."
For Tehran, the timing makes sense. Hezbollah is weakened, Assad is gone, and the Iraqi militias are weak. "Therefore, its winning card is the Houthi group," al-Bukhaiti said, "because of its proximity to the region's most important strait."
For more than two decades, the Houthis have built their entire identity around one slogan: "Death to America, Death to Israel." Yet now that they finally stand at the gates of one of the world's most important shipping lanes, with real leverage over American and Israeli interests, they are rushing to reassure both.
According to al-Bukhaiti, Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdulsalam said the Bab al-Mandab blockade targets only Saudi ships. American and Israeli vessels will be left alone.
"The Houthis' slogan for 20 years or more has been, 'Death to America, death to Israel.' But when they reached the Bab al-Mandab Strait, they said, 'We have nothing to do with either America or Israel. Our problem is with Saudi Arabia and the Muslims,'" he said.
So much for the resistance. The group that claimed to fight for Gaza and against "global arrogance" has, when it truly mattered, chosen to aim its guns at fellow Arabs and Muslims instead.
On the Saudi-backed side, one absence stands out. "The absence of the Southern Transitional Council has nothing to do with the defeat. There may be a connection to the absence of the UAE," al-Bukhaiti said. Abu Dhabi built the forces of Tariq Saleh along the coast and backed them with continuous air cover and naval vessels near al-Mokha. Without the Emiratis, that front didn't hold.
So the Houthis have spared Israel, turned their guns on Riyadh, and let Tehran run the show. If al-Bukhaiti is right, Saudi Arabia and Israel may have more in common in Yemen than either is ready to admit.

LONDON, September 24. /TASS/. About 60 commercial vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, transporting 22 million barrels of oil, the largest daily volume since the beginning of July, Reuters quoted an unnamed US official as saying.
The source also said that about 40 of these vessels coordinated their actions with the US military to ensure protection.
Reuters said it could not verify this data from independent sources.
Before the war with Iran began on February 28, about 125 large commercial vessels per day typically passed through the strait, including bulk carriers and container ships, tankers and gas carriers, which transported about 20% of the world’s daily supplies of oil and liquefied natural gas.
In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, on the night of July 8, the United States resumed large·scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the agreements on the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump Administration Proposes Ukraine-Russia Energy Ceasefire and Grain Corridor Deal
Unknown

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Trump Administration Proposes Ukraine-Russia Energy Ceasefire and Grain Corridor Deal
The US President Donald Trump administration is pushing a three-step diplomatic proposal aimed at de-escalating the war in Ukraine and reviving negotiations with Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Axios in an interview on September 23.
The US framework focuses on establishing an immediate ceasefire on energy infrastructure, reopening the Black Sea grain corridor, and convening a trilateral meeting between the US, Ukraine, and Russia, potentially in Abu Dhabi.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The diplomatic push follows recent discussions at the UN General Assembly in New York, where Zelenskyy indicated Ukraine’s readiness to halt energy strikes if Russia does the same.
He also floated the upcoming G20 summit in Miami as a potential venue for leader-level talks with the US, Ukraine and Russia.
According to Zelenskyy, the US is prioritizing the mutual halt to strikes on energy infrastructure—driven partly by Washington’s domestic economic interests, as Ukrainian attacks on Russian diesel fuel have contributed to rising global energy prices.
“On the table now there is a proposition: energy ceasefire. We are ready,” Zelenskyy told Axios, noting that Kyiv is open to the US proposal.
The US diplomatic effort accelerated following a visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe three weeks ago, followed by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveling to both Moscow and Kyiv. Following a three-hour meeting with Russian leader Vladimir Putin on September 5, the envoys briefed Zelenskyy in Ukraine.
Zelenskyy recalled that the US envoys were highly optimistic about Moscow’s willingness to negotiate.
“They said, 'We think that Putin is ready.' I said, 'Look, I’m not sure, '” Zelenskyy stated, Axios wrote.
According to the Ukrainian president, the envoys pushed back, telling him: “No, we are close.”
Despite Washington’s optimism, Zelenskyy remains deeply skeptical of Putin’s intentions, expressing doubt that the Russian leader will follow through with a trilateral meeting. The Kremlin publicly stated on September 23 that conditions are not ready for resuming peace talks and that there are no current prospects for high-level meetings, Axios wrote.
Underscoring that reality, Russia launched multiple ballistic missiles toward Kyiv minutes before Zelenskyy sat down for the Axios interview, and he received updates about the strikes throughout the conversation.
Regarding his September 22 meeting with President Trump in New York, Zelenskyy described the US leader as “very positive” about the diplomatic push.
Trump told him, “We will try,” according to Zelenskyy. “I said, 'Great, and really wish you not only to try [but] to succeed.'”
Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine wants to see concrete progress before the onset of winter, regardless of the US political calendar. US and Ukrainian negotiating teams—including Witkoff, Kushner, and national security advisers from France, the UK, and Germany—met on September 22to refine the proposals, Axios reported.
Ukrainian officials noted that elements of the plan will be developed over the next two weeks before American envoys present them to Moscow again.
Additionally, Zelenskyy noted he has discussed the ceasefire and grain corridor efforts with leaders from Turkey, India, the UAE, and Egypt, all of whom maintain back-channel communications with Russia.
“Everybody wants [a] ceasefire. The corridor has to work again. We support [it]. They speak with Russians, I know. We will see,” Zelenskyy told Axios.
Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev is expected to arrive in New York on September 24 to meet with Witkoff and Kushner to discuss the latest iterations of the US proposals, according to Axios.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had recently emphasized the severe difficulty of acquiring air defense interceptors, stating that Ukraine secures them in batches of just “one or two missiles at a time” rather than in hundreds or thousands.
Speaking at a briefing in New York, Zelenskyy explained that these scarce and expensive deliveries require direct approval from allied leaders, as lower-level negotiations yield no results. Identifying the US as the only nation capable of supplying missiles at scale, Zelenskyy is directly lobbying President Donald Trump to fulfill Ukraine’s needs despite global shortages driven by commitments in the Middle East.

UN education officials call for urgent action for Gaza children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:41:36 UTC
05:41:36 KST

Berk Kutay Gökmen
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Education officials at the UN urged governments and donors on Thursday to step up support for children caught in conflicts and disasters, highlighting the devastating effect of the war in the Gaza Strip on access to education.
Gordon Brown, the UN special envoy for global education, said hundreds of millions of children worldwide are being denied education because of conflict, displacement and climate-related disasters.
“Instead of the world developing only some of the potential of some children in some countries, we must be determined to develop the potential of all children,” Brown told reporters at a UN briefing.
He highlighted Gaza, where hundreds of thousands of children remain out of school, and tens of thousands of young children have no access to preschool.
Maysa Jalbout, director of Education Cannot Wait (ECW), which touts itself as the first global fund dedicated to education in emergencies, said the organization was committing $3 million in emergency funding for vulnerable children in Gaza, including those with conflict-related injuries and disabilities.
The program is expected to reach up to 13,000 children and will be implemented through local organizations.
Jalbout said Gaza has more child amputees per capita than anywhere in the world, underscoring the severe toll the conflict has taken on children.
ECW is also responding to disasters elsewhere. In Nepal, where floods and landslides recently damaged or destroyed 29 schools, the organization committed $1 million to help children return to learning.
Jalbout said the crises in Gaza and Nepal are different, but the consequences for children can be similar: “School stops, protection disappears, and the future is put on hold.”
ECW is seeking $600 million in new funding to reach 10 million more children affected by crises worldwide.

hundreds of feet of cable and steel reimagine rodin’s thinker for networked age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:35:32 UTC
05:35:32 KST

Kasey McMahon rebuilds The Thinker from steel and cable
Artist Kasey McMahon reimagines the contemplative figure for the networked age, constructing a life-size Thinker by hand from steel and hundreds of feet of network cable, the physical infrastructure through which contemporary information travels.
A nod to Rodin’s iconic contemplative figure, the work replaces the solidity of bronze with the tangled physical infrastructure of the networked world. McMahon began working with network cable as a sculpturalmaterial more than a decade ago, drawn to the idea of turning the infrastructure behind our digital lives into something physical.
all images by Aaron Wessling – Single File Studio unless stated otherwise
Hundreds of feet of network cable form The Human Figure
The Thinker is the fourth life-size human figure in that ongoing body of work and the first male figure. The sculpture began with a welded steel armature that established the anatomy and seated posture. Artist Kasey McMahon then wrapped and layered hundreds of feet of CAT5 and CAT6 network cable by hand until the figure took shape.
Rather than concealing the material, the construction leaves connectors, printed markings, and individual lengths of cable visible. Blue, gray and white dominate the figure, punctuated by strands of red. The work was fabricated in McMahon’s Portland-area studio, a converted 120-year-old garage. The process moved between welding and metal fabrication, anatomical adjustment, and the slower work of wrapping and layering cable to give the figure its final mass and gesture.
Kasey McMahon reimagines Rodin’s Thinker using network cable
The Thinker is a reflection on bodies, networks, and technology
The pose is familiar, but the material changes the question. The figure is unmistakably human, yet its body is made from the infrastructure through which human communication and information travel. The Thinker arrives amid an increasingly charged conversation about artificial intelligence and our relationship with technology. It doesn’t attempt to resolve that tension. The figure simply sits, and thinks. The sculpture was privately commissioned and is now installed in Austin, Texas.

Yechiel Leiter was born in Pennsylvania in the United States and immigrated to Israel after being deeply influenced by Zionist values. He was named after Rabbi Yechiel Michel Leiter, his great-great-grandfather, a prominent European rabbi and halachic authority who later immigrated to the United States and served as a community rabbi, where he wrote the responsa work “Darkei Shalom.”
Yechiel’s grandfather, Moshe, was a well-known Torah scholar. Beyond his extensive religious learning, he was also known as a public activist. He published articles in the Orthodox Jewish press and founded a refugee association and a Talmud study organization in Zurich.
Because he felt the positions of Agudat Yisrael were not sufficiently enthusiastic about immigration to the Land of Israel and Zionism, he left the movement and remained active in Mizrachi.
He later immigrated to the United States, where his father served as a community rabbi and where he also held a rabbinic position.
In 1925, he immigrated to the Land of Israel but returned to Vienna after several months. He lived in Vienna until 1938, when he fled the threat of the Holocaust and moved to the United States. He was appointed rabbi of the Ahavat Re’im synagogue.
The father of Rabbi Yechiel Michel, Rabbi Shalom Leiter, was himself a rabbinical judge and halachic authority. His children, in addition to Rabbi Yechiel, also served as rabbis, heads of rabbinical courts, city rabbis and public activists.

WASHINGTON, September 24. /TASS/. US activists have sued the administration of US President Donald Trump with a demand to recognize the war against Iran as illegal and stop it, President of the non-profit organization National Iranian American Council (NIAC) Jamal Abdi said.
The claim filed in the court of the Metropolitan District of Columbia is based on the constitution, which says it is not the president, but the Congress that has the authority to declare war.
"Congress formally declared that the war must end, and yet the war continues," Abdi said adding that Americans of Iranian origin have their "loved ones killed and traumatized illegally with our own tax dollars."
According to him, the plaintiffs will seek to have the court recognize the operation against Iran as a war "no matter how many times [Trump] insists it is just an excursion. The question the courts will have to answer is very simple: is this a war? Because if it is, it is unauthorized. It is illegal, and they must declare it as such. And if so, it must end."
In response to a question from TASS, Abdi said that NIAC intends to file an appeal and seek its consideration in higher courts, including the Supreme Court, if the lawsuit is dismissed in the district court.
"We're prepared to take this as far as we can, pursuing all options because these are unprecedented times," Abdi said, adding that "it's a moment to not just end this catastrophe but to set a precedent for the future so that presidents can't take our country into a war without any authorization."
Attorney Bruce Fein, who represents NIAC, acknowledged in response to a question from TASS that the US Supreme Court has been "reluctant to opine on the war power issue. But I think we live in unprecedented times, and I think, given the fact that uniquely, both the House and the Senate voted against the war, would create a dynamic that's been different and make the court more likely to take this case up."
Earlier, both chambers of Congress adopted resolutions demanding an end to military actions against Iran. Such documents have no legal force and are of a recommendatory nature; the executive branch of the US government has the right to ignore them.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, on the night of July 8, the US resumed large·scale strikes against Iran. Subsequently, the US administration effectively signaled the cessation of the use of large·scale military force against Iran and the shift to an attempt to economically strangle it through sanctions.

Mother of man wounded by ICE in Texas describes video call moments after shooting
BARQUISIMETO, Venezuela, Sept 24 - The last time Wilber Rafael Garces Perez's mother heard his voice was on Sunday afternoon, moments after he had been shot by a federal immigration agent in his car in Austin, Texas, she told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday.
"They crashed into my car and shot me," Flor Perez recalled her son telling her over a video call as she tried to calm him down from her home in Venezuela. Then she saw an officer pulling her son out of the vehicle by his arm.
Four days later, Garces Perez, 28, remains in detention with a bullet still in his back and his mother said she has not been able to speak with him.
Federal immigration agents have shot at least 20 people since Republican President Donald Trump returned to office, 7 fatally, sparking protests across the US. Critics contend that Trump's push to ramp up deportations has led to an increasing number of violent confrontations, and accuse the administration of resisting accountability for the agents involved.
The sequence of events leading up to Sunday's shooting remains unclear.
Garces Perez, who is from Venezuela, said he was working as a food delivery driver on Sunday when his car was sideswiped by agents with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). He said they did not identify themselves or turn on their emergency lights until after the collision.
ICE has not offered its own version of events or explained why Garces Perez was shot while sitting in his car. Its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, said in a Tuesday statement that Garces Perez was the subject of a "targeted vehicle stop" and that "resisting officers and evading arrest is dangerous for our officers, illegal aliens, and the public."
Videos of the incident do not show the shooting, but do show Garces Perez injured in the car. The federal officer who shot him was not wearing a body camera, according to a person familiar with the incident. The officer, who has not been identified, was hired by ICE last year and had formerly worked for US Customs and Border Protection, the person said.
After the fatal shootings of two men six days apart during July traffic stops in Texas and Maine, US border czar Tom Homan said ICE agents would be required to record vehicle stops with at least one body-worn camera. ICE's acting director vowed to equip each officer with a body-worn camera by the end of August.
Asked for comment about the officer involved and the account of Garces Perez's mother, DHS sent an information sheet that did not address Reuters' questions.
'INTENSE PAIN'
Speaking from her home in Barquisimeto in northwestern Venezuela, Flor Perez, 51, said she was sleepless worrying about her son, hoping he would be allowed to see a doctor to remove the bullet and relieve his pain.
"What matters to me is that they take him to a hospital and treat him," she said.
Garces Perez's wound is currently stuffed with gauze that fills with blood and has to be changed two or three times a day, causing him "intense pain," Democratic US Representative Greg Casar of Texas said at a press conference on Wednesday night, hours after visiting him at an ICE detention facility.
"If you saw Wilber, just like if you saw anybody that had been shot three days ago, you would say this person needs a doctor, not a deportation or a detention center," said Casar.
Video released by Austin police on Tuesday from a body camera worn by one of its officers who responded to the incident shows Garces Perez inside his car with two ICE agents standing nearby. Garces Perez tells them his shoulder hurts, whereupon he is told to exit the vehicle and placed in handcuffs. A police officer then uses shears to cut away his shirt, revealing a gunshot wound to his upper back.
In its information sheet, DHS said ICE "does not and would not advise, nor be the authority on, a medical procedure" and said Garces Perez was "receiving medical care around the clock."
Perez said her son entered the United States from Mexico in December 2023 using CBP One, an app used by former President Joe Biden's administration to allow migrants to lawfully cross the border by scheduling an appointment with CBP.
DHS has said Garces Perez's work permit expired in 2025, making him eligible for deportation.
Garces Perez's "dream" in the US was to earn money to support his 7-year-old son, who was born with cerebral palsy and requires costly treatment in Venezuela. The family has not yet told him about what happened to his father.
“We’re going to have to tell the boy little by little," Perez said, "because he asks to talk to his dad every day."
Garces Perez's attorneys have filed a legal petition asking that he be released from custody so he can participate in the investigation into the shooting and pursue legal status.
His first hearing before a federal immigration judge in Texas is set for next Wednesday. REUTERS

PsyPost deploys audit program to track retracted and corrected scientific studies in its archive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:30:00 UTC
05:30:00 KST

PsyPost, a psychology and neuroscience news website, has implemented a new automated Python program designed to monitor its archive for scientific studies that have been retracted, corrected, or flagged by publishers.
During its initial run against the databases of Retraction Watch and Crossref, the program reviewed PsyPost’s entire archive of more than 16,000 articles and identified six covered studies that had been retracted. Following this initial audit, the program now runs on a consistent schedule to answer one specific question: has any study covered by PsyPost been withdrawn or altered, and which articles are affected?
By automating this check, PsyPost aims to maintain the scientific integrity of its content, ensuring readers are informed when the status of previously covered research changes.
How the Program Works
The audit process runs weekly in four steps to translate publisher data into a direct checklist for the editorial team:
1. Import
The program scans PsyPost’s WordPress archive, looking for the scientific studies linked in each article, and pulls the Digital Object Identifier (DOI) for every study. Because publishers format links differently, the program uses specific rules to find DOIs whether they are clearly listed or embedded in the URLs of publishers like SAGE, Wiley, Springer, Frontiers, and PLOS. For sites that don’t display a DOI directly, like Elsevier, PubMed, or Nature, the program uses lookup tools from Crossref and the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) to find the correct identifier. The program currently monitors approximately 17,000 distinct scientific studies.
2. Check
The program cross-references these DOIs against two primary sources. First, it checks a local download of the Retraction Watch database—which has been made freely available through Crossref since 2023—to identify retractions and their corresponding reason codes. Second, it queries Crossref’s publisher update logs to find corrections and expressions of concern, which Retraction Watch doesn’t track comprehensively.
3. Triage
A raw check produces hundreds of records, many of which are administrative changes like minor typo corrections, updated links, or metadata glitches. The program sorts these events, separating retractions and expressions of concern from minor corrections. It also filters by timing, separating notices that existed before PsyPost covered the study from those that occurred after publication. The result is a concise table showing the affected study, the specific notice, and the exact PsyPost article that requires an update.
4. Close
Once an editor reviews the alert, a notice is placed at the top of the affected PsyPost article, explaining the retraction or correction to the reader. In the system, the event is marked as handled, and the next digest will only display new alerts.
Handling False Alarms
The program is maintained and refined by human oversight. When the system returns a false positive—such as a publisher temporarily pulling and reinstating a paper due to a formatting error—a developer reviews the issue and writes a new rule in the code to ignore that specific class of administrative error in the future. By fixing the class of error rather than just the single instance, the tool produces fewer false alarms over time.
“Science is a self-correcting process, and when the status of a study changes, our articles need to reflect that,” said Eric W. Dolan, the founder and editor of PsyPost. “By regularly checking our archive against Crossref and Retraction Watch, this program allows us to systematically apply those corrections and provide our readers with an accurate reflection of the current scientific record.”

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington D.C. has been filled with signs of American airpower: U.S. Air Force B-1 and B-2 bombers and F-22 fighters have all performed flyovers Sept. 23-24.
Xi arrived at Joint Base Andrews, Md., on Sept. 23, and was greeted planeside by President Donald Trump—an unusual occurrence—and a military honor guard. The Presidential Salute Battery of the Army’s Old Guard, formally known as the 3rd Infantry Regiment, conducted a 21-gun salute as part of the arrival ceremony, and two B-1B Lancers roared overhead as the national anthem played.
A day later, a single B-2 Spirit, flanked by four F-22 Raptors, soared over the White House to cap a morning of military pomp and ceremony for Xi and his wife, Chinese First Lady Peng Liyuan.
This is Xi’s first state visit to the U.S. since 2015.
First Lady Melania Trump’s office released a statement Sept. 21 saying the welcoming event would feature 479 military personnel from all branches of the U.S. military.
As they arrived, Xi and his wife were met with a full military honor cordon along the White House’s South Drive, which led to a display of the flags of the U.S. and China. U.S. Army Herald Trumpets presented a fanfare for the Xis, and the Army Old Guard Fife and Drum Corps, the Marine Corps Silent Drill Platoon, and the United States Marine Drum and Bugle Corps—known as “The Commandant’s Own”—performed military demonstrations, before the B-2 and F-22 flyover.
Military flyovers are not unusual for state visits. A few months ago, four F-35s flew over the White House in honor of King Charles III’s state visit. But the presence of bombers is less routine and somewhat reminiscent of an August 2025 flyover of Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska, that featured a B-2 Spirit and four F-35s.

France records nearly 7 times more burned land than usual this year

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
France has recorded 97,724 hectares (241,500 acres) of burned land since the beginning of the year, nearly 6.9 times the area typically burned by this point in the year, according to data published Thursday by FeuxFrance.
The area burned so far this year compares with 14,177 hectares (35,000 acres) in an average year as of Sept. 24.
The figure is also 49% higher than the previous record for the same date, set in 2022.
FeuxFrance said that by Sept. 24, an average fire season would have recorded 86% of its annual fires.
Based on the pace of previous fire seasons, the year could end with about 11,639 fires.
About 9% of fires are estimated to have natural causes, while the remainder are linked to human activity.
Around 30% are estimated to have been deliberately started.

Why Germany is stuck with Friedrich Merz, for now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:25:01 UTC
05:25:01 KST

Why Germany is stuck with Friedrich Merz, for now
September is proving a miserable month for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Two weeks ago, his Christian Democratic Union suffered a crushing defeat in Saxony-Anhalt, where the Alternative for Germany won 43.8% of the vote against just 17.2% for the CDU, then, on September 20, another humiliation arrived in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The AfD finished first there with 38.2%, while the CDU, one of the parties that built postwar Germany, received just 4.9% and failed to clear the threshold for representation in the state parliament. It was the party’s worst result in any German state election since the foundation of the Federal Republic, and it happened in Angela Merkel’s home state.
Things were hardly better in Berlin, which voted on the same day. There, the CDU was beaten not by the AfD but by Die Linke (The Left), which won 25.7%, while the CDU slumped to 18.8%.
Merz himself called the results a “disaster,” and if Saxony-Anhalt made discussion of replacing the chancellor respectable, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has made it unavoidable. Criticism is spreading through the CDU and German newspapers are openly discussing his future as potential successors are already being mentioned.
The Spectator’s Henry Donovan put it particularly brutally, describing Merz as “the most tragic chancellor in the young history of the reunified Germany” and declaring that his time was up, and there is certainly something tragic about Merz’s career.
He might have reached the chancellery more than 20 years ago, but his rise was blocked by Merkel, who displaced him as leader of the CDU parliamentary group. Merz eventually left parliament for business, but when Merkel announced her retirement, he returned to politics in 2018, only to lose two successive CDU leadership contests. He finally became party chairman at the third attempt.
Then, after winning the 2025 federal election, Merz achieved another distinction he probably didn’t want when he became the first candidate for chancellor in the history of the Federal Republic to fail to secure election by the Bundestag on the first ballot.
For a man who spent decades trying to reach the top, departing after little more than a year with his authority badly damaged would be a bitter conclusion, so Merz, unsurprisingly, has no intention of doing so. After the latest defeats, he made clear that he planned to remain chancellor and continue with his reform program.
That raises an obvious question: If his opponents want him gone, why can they not simply remove him? The answer lies in Germany’s Basic Law.
Unlike in Britain, where a prime minister can effectively be dispatched by his own parliamentary party, Germany deliberately makes removing a sitting chancellor difficult, meaning the Bundestag can oust Merz through a “constructive vote of no confidence,” but only by simultaneously electing somebody else with an absolute majority.
It has worked only once, when, in 1982, Helmut Schmidt was removed after the Free Democrats abandoned their coalition with his Social Democrats and joined the CDU/CSU in electing Helmut Kohl as chancellor.
Merz’s opponents face two problems in attempting something similar, and the first is arithmetic. CDU parliamentarians are traditionally disciplined, and assembling a majority against their own chancellor would be extremely difficult without a major rebellion or votes from the AfD. Any arrangement dependent on AfD support would immediately collide with Germany’s Brandmauer, or “firewall,” under which the established parties refuse political cooperation with the rising upstarts.
The second problem is simpler, in that there’s no agreed replacement. Names are circulating, but no candidate has emerged around whom a Bundestag majority could plausibly unite and under Germany’s constitution, disliking the existing chancellor is not enough, parliament must agree on the next one before it can dismiss him.
Leaving Merz in place carries risks of its own, however, as the AfD’s rise has coincided with growing dissatisfaction over the economy, migration, energy costs, and Berlin’s support for Ukraine. Merz came to power promising change, but his government is now pursuing painful economic and welfare reforms while insisting that Germans must accept sacrifices to restore the country’s competitiveness and finance its wider strategic ambitions.
Whatever the merits of those policies, the electoral results suggest that a substantial part of the public isn’t buying the argument, thus the danger for the CDU is straightforward, given every further defeat strengthens the AfD while making the firewall increasingly difficult to maintain. Merz originally presented himself as the conservative who could stop voters defecting to the party, but instead, the AfD has just helped to inflict two devastating defeats on his CDU in the space of a fortnight.
His colleagues will probably first try persuasion, such as change the rhetoric, modify unpopular policies, and somehow arrest the electoral decline before Germany enters another cycle of state elections, but if that fails, the pressure for more radical action will inevitably grow.
For now, Germany has a chancellor who doesn’t want to leave, a parliament that cannot easily remove him, and an opposition whose growing strength makes every conventional route to replacing him more complicated.
Merz spent more than 20 years trying to become chancellor, but his problem now is proving that finally getting the job wasn’t the high point of his political career.
This article was first published by the online newspaper Gazeta.ru and was translated and edited by the RT team

Macron says he pressed Trump not to ban diesel exports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:20:22 UTC
05:20:22 KST

Emmanuel Macron speaks during an interview with France 2 and TF1 at the Elysee Presidential Palace, in Paris on September 24, 2026. | Ludovic Marin AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday he told U.S. President Donald Trump that a 90-day diesel export ban being considered by the White House was a bad idea.
“I think all the experts around him and all the American refiners can only tell him the same thing,” Macron said during a prime-time interview. “This decision would be a bad one — not just for the rest of the world, but for the U.S. economy as well.”
The United States is currently the world’s largest exporter of diesel, according to ClearView Energy, and removing that supply from global markets would have far-reaching effects given how the conflict in the Middle East has already upended the global energy trade.
Advertisement
“There is a war in the Middle East, and we are paying the price,” Macron said.
The European Union has in recent months purchased more diesel from the U.S. to make up for lost supply that can’t get through the Strait of Hormuz, and shipments from across the Atlantic now make up more than half of all diesel imports to the bloc.
Macron last week announced plans to chair a G7 meeting to look at releasing strategic oil stocks and held talks with the leaders of hydrocarbon exporters to secure supplies from alternative sources.
During Thursday's interview, Macron said France would deploy the military to help secure the Saudi port city of Yanbu, from which more than 5 million barrels of oil are shipped daily, after it came under attack by the Tehran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
The French leader has also tried to lobby Brussels to ease EU rules on the make-up of fuel and on methane emissions to help keep soaring energy prices under control, and his government this week announced it would spend €450 million to extend fuel subsidies enacted in March through the end of the year.
But those moves have so far failed to move the needle, with diesel prices in France and the rest of Europe surging to record highs this week, according to analyses from Agence France-Presse.
France has little fiscal space to further cushion the blow given its anemic growth, stubbornly high budget deficit and massive pile of debt. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said last week the government would propose a €54 billion budget squeeze to contain the deficit.
Ben Munster and Geoffrey Smith contributed to this report.

Since the start of the war with Iran, Iranian television channels aligned with the Islamic Republic have broadcast nightly images and videos of rallies supporting the country’s leadership and armed forces, part of a sustained effort by state media to project national unity and public backing for the government.
The displays come as much of Iran’s population of about 92 million contends with a worsening economic crisis and severe government repression. But the Islamic Republic also retains a significant base of genuine supporters who continue to turn out for pro-government rallies.
Throughout recent months, whether amid talk of a possible return to negotiations between Washington and Tehran or during periods of heightened regional tensions, nightly gatherings have continued in public squares across Iranian cities.
Last week, Iran marked what state-affiliated media described as the 200th consecutive day of pro-government street gatherings, with events beginning Sept. 15 and continuing for several days in cities across the country. Iranian officials and state institutions used the milestone to praise participants and emphasize what they described as the population’s resilience and support for the government.
The Basij, the paramilitary force that played a central role in the violent suppression of mass anti-government protests earlier this year, issued a statement marking the 200th day.
“The Iranian nation will remain in the streets and squares for as long as necessary, and for as long as the interests of the regime dictate,” the Basij said.
Iranian military Chief of Staff Ali Abdollahi also praised the demonstrators.
“Dear Iranian people, I bring you news from the battlefield: Your presence and unity are what strengthened the morale of the fighters, enhanced national resilience and sowed fear in the heart of the enemy,” he said.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, described the public as the country’s most important national security asset, saying Iranians had “defended the homeland, its territorial integrity and its independence through their presence and resilience.”
One of the most prominent gathering points has been Tehran’s Revolution Square, known in Persian as Enqelab Square. In recent days, Iranian channels have continued broadcasting videos showing crowds there waving Iranian and Hezbollah flags, praying and singing.
Reporting from the square last Wednesday, an Iranian television correspondent described the gathering as the 200th night of what he called “spontaneous public gatherings.”
“People gathered here to demonstrate solidarity and unity,” he said. “Two hundred nights have passed since the first days of the ‘Ramadan War’” — the Iranian name for Israel’s Operation Roaring Lion — “but not a single moment has passed in which these people have not thought about the slain leader, Ali Khamenei. Mourning for the leader continues to be felt deeply in people’s hearts.”
The reporter said those gathered behind him had come to the square for 200 consecutive nights.
“They will not leave the square until the Zionist regime is destroyed,” he said.
Another event marking the 200th day was held last week in Tehran’s Abu Zar Square, where a statue of Amir Ali Hajizadeh, the former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Aerospace Force who was killed during the war, was unveiled.
Tehran Mayor Alireza Zakani attended the ceremony. Images from the event showed participants holding portraits of slain Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. The ceremony also featured fireworks, a display of a Zelzal rocket and balloons shaped to form the number 200.
The nightly gatherings across Iran have taken different forms in recent months, at times reflecting developments elsewhere in the region. Some have included demonstrations supporting Yemen’s Houthis during their escalation with Saudi Arabia.
Anti-American and anti-Israel chants have also remained a regular feature, much as they were during the war. Video published from Abu Zar Square on Sept. 15 showed demonstrators chanting “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.”
“Death to America” chants were also heard at Revolution Square that day, shortly after a mass wedding ceremony involving several couples from the pro-government community. The couples arrived at the square in vehicles decorated with flowers.
The nightly displays have not been limited to rallies and slogans. They have periodically included military exhibits. Iran’s Mehr news agency published videos Sept. 14 showing drones on display in Quds Square in Isfahan during a nighttime rally.
Iranian state news agencies have also reported that some participants in the rallies have joined what authorities call the “Sacrifice of Life” campaign. The government claims more than 30 million people have signed up and declared themselves willing to sacrifice their lives and “defend the country’s territory,” although it remains unclear what participation in the campaign entails in practice.
A drill involving male and female campaign volunteers was held in Tehran last Friday morning. Iranian media aligned with the government said many thousands participated, though images from the event appeared to show something closer to a mass procession.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian attended the event and was quoted as saying, “Unity and cohesion, on every issue, will shatter the enemy’s hopes.”
Iranian reports said similar exercises would be held in other cities.
Danny Citrinowicz, a former head of the Iran branch in the IDF’s Intelligence Directorate research division and now a senior researcher in the Iran and Shiite Axis program at the Institute for National Security Studies, cautioned against using the rallies as a measure of the government’s overall popularity or stability.
Iran faces mounting economic difficulties amid continued U.S. pressure and is still dealing with the aftermath of widespread protests earlier this year that were violently suppressed. Nevertheless, Citrinowicz said the government retains millions of supporters whose significance should not be dismissed.
“There is real distress in Iran, and it is very evident, including in the statements of President Pezeshkian, who sees himself as a representative of the population,” Citrinowicz said. “The situation is difficult, but at the same time, I would not dismiss these demonstrations. Ultimately, there is a significant core that supports this regime, even in the current economic situation and amid the economic and social complexity Iran is experiencing because of the war.”
Citrinowicz said the latest gatherings were a direct continuation of the demonstrations held during the war, when tens of thousands of people took to the streets each night in Iran’s major cities, including Tehran.
The rallies, he said, served two purposes: projecting an image abroad that the government retained the confidence of the Iranian public while sending a message to Iranians opposed to the Islamic Republic.
The message to government opponents, he said, was that “there is no point in going out” to protest, even if they were considering taking to the streets, because public spaces had already been filled by government supporters and the leadership retained enough backing to make an uprising appear futile.
“We are seeing the same logic in the current demonstrations,” Citrinowicz said.
He said the government’s promotion of the “Sacrifice of Life” campaign fit the same strategy.
“The regime’s entire focus right now is on demonstrating both the support it enjoys and the Iranian citizen’s willingness to make sacrifices, in the sense of, ‘You will not break us. People will be willing to fight if necessary,’” Citrinowicz said. “It all serves the same strategic purpose. Even when the numbers are exaggerated, I would not underestimate the base of support the regime has.”

'A horrific crime' — Ukrainian man kills 1, injures 4 in stabbing at Polish monastery
A Ukrainian man attacked five people with a knife at the Benedictine Sisters' Abbey in Jaroslaw, Poland on Sept. 24, killing one victim and injuring four others in what President Volodymyr Zelensky called "a horrific crime."
The town of Jaroslaw in southeastern Poland lies approximately 35 kilometers (22 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The attacker stabbed four men and one woman on the premises of the Benedectine Sisters' Abbey before police arrived at the scene the morning of Sept. 24, according to local officials. Three of the victims were members of the clergy. All were rushed to the hospital after the attack.
One man, a Catholic priest, died at the hospital due to the severity of his injuries. Two of the other victims are in serious condition, District Prosecutor Bozena Harasz-Woloszyn said.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk later confirmed that the assailant is a Ukrainian national and currently in police custody.
"The investigation is ongoing," Tusk wrote on X.
"The perpetrator is a Ukrainian citizen. He will be punished to the full extent of Polish law. My heart goes out to the loved ones of the victims of this brutal attack."
Authorities have not yet established a motive for the crime. The suspect, a 31-year-old Ukrainian national, is believed to have entered Poland from Germany overnight. He then drove toward the border crossing with Ukraine, but did not enter Ukrainian territory.
Zelensky also condemned the attack in a social media post on Sept. 24.
"A horrific crime at the Benedictine Sisters' Abbey in Jarosław, committed by a Ukrainian citizen. We are shaken by this evil," he wrote.
Zelensky extended condolences to the loved ones of the man who died and wished the injured a swift recovery.
"The perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility in accordance with the law. ... Justice must be done," he said.
The deadly knife attack comes during a period of strained Polish-Ukrainian relations, inflamed by high-profile diplomatic spats and the politics of historic grievance. A majority of Poles report more negative attitudes toward Ukraine and Ukrainians, and incidents of interpersonal violence are on the rise.
The Kremlin has seized on the dispute to amplify disinformation narratives, aiming to drive a greater wedge between the two nations, which remain staunchly allied in their stance against Russian aggression.

New York, Polymarket file dueling lawsuits amid illegal gambling claims
New York attorney general accuses prediction market platform of targeting ‘most vulnerable’ residents.
The US state of New York and prediction market company Polymarket have filed dueling lawsuits amid claims the betting platform is in violation of gambling laws.
In a lawsuit filed on Thursday, New York State Attorney General Letitia James said that Polymarket has been operating as an unlicensed gambling operation due to its failure to obtain a licence from the New York State Gaming Commission.

The move comes after James’ office launched similar suits against Polymarket competitors Kalshi, Coinbase and Gemini Titan.
“Our gambling laws exist to protect New Yorkers, prevent the potential harms of problem gambling, and ensure funding for educational and public benefit programs,” James said in a statement announcing the suit.
“By skirting New York’s laws, Polymarket is targeting the most vulnerable and depriving New York families of critical services and support. My office will never hesitate to take action to defend our laws and keep New Yorkers safe.”
The suit also alleges that the company encouraged gambling among young people.
It accuses Polymarket of targeting users as young as 18, while state law requires users to be at least 21 years old to take part in mobile sports betting.
“By running an unlicensed gambling operation, Polymarket has done more than just knowingly violate state law, they have put New Yorkers at risk, especially those underage who are most vulnerable to problem gaming,” New York Governor Kathy Hochul said in a statement.
The more than 30-page lawsuit claims that Polymarket, which is valued at more than $20bn, has advertised sports betting in particular since July 2025.
It pointed to a post on X from August 17, 2025, about the launch of its US mobile app that said it was “BAD NEWS (For sportsbooks)”.
Polymarket filed a countersuit hours later, arguing the federal Commodity Futures Trading Commission has exclusive authority to regulate prediction markets.
The betting platform said New York had left it with an “impossible choice” between obeying state regulators, or continuing operations and facing potentially “huge” criminal liability.
“This is an extraordinary assertion of state power squarely foreclosed by federal law,” Polymarket said in its lawsuit in Manhattan federal court.
Chief Legal Officer Neal Kumar said Polymarket tried to work out its differences with state officials, but “they preferred the media hit”.
“We chose to engage with them directly on the substance and address their concerns,” Kumar said.
Polymarket’s main rival Kalshi is facing similar allegations in New York.
Kalshi has been critical of reporting on lawsuits against it and allegations that it is akin to a sports betting or gambling platform.
Polymarket did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
The Polymarket lawsuit comes days after reporting from the Wall Street Journal that alleged a wave of users had linked stolen bank debit cards and then used them to make wagers, effectively draining the accounts.
According to the report, when CEO Shayne Coplan was made aware of the issue, he responded: “Just keep growing and pay a fine if regulators ever find out.”
Political pressure
Prediction markets allow users to wager on so-called event contracts, covering political events, sports, elections and even award shows.
Concerns about the role of prediction markets came to a head earlier this year when wagers were made in the hours before the United States and Israel first struck Iran, prompting widespread backlash in Washington.
New York’s lawsuit joins a growing list of states that have sued prediction market platforms, including Arizona, Massachusetts, Nevada and many others.
Those states are at odds with the federal government, as the Commodity Futures Trading Commission has claimed that the federal agency exerts authority over the regulation of prediction markets.
Polymarket has close ties with the family of US President Donald Trump.
The prediction market platform has investment from 1789 Capital, a venture capital firm backed by Donald Trump Jr, the president’s eldest son, who also serves on the company’s advisory board.
