Syria recovers 36 looted antiquities from US worth over $5M
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:47:59 UTC
04:47:59 KST

Laith Al-jnaidi, Lina Altawell
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
- Recovered artifacts include massive funerary relief from Palmyra, 14 rare mosaics looted from 
- Roman villa in Syria Damascus credits Syrian-US cooperation, efforts by Manhattan District Attorney's Office for return of cultural heritage
Syria recovered 36 looted antiquities from the US worth more than $5 million, including a massive funerary relief from the ancient city of Palmyra and 14 rare mosaics stolen from a Roman villa in the country.
The artifacts were returned during a ceremony in New York this week as part of efforts to combat the illicit trafficking of antiquities and recover looted cultural property, Syrian news agency SANA reported.
Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg, US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, and US Special Envoy to Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack attended the ceremony, along with Syria's charge d'affaires in Washington Mohammad Nasser Qanatri, its UN Ambassador Ibrahim Olabi, and other officials and diplomats.
“Repatriation ceremonies are a powerful reminder that preserving cultural heritage transcends any border or nationality,” Bragg said in a statement published by his office.
He described the investigation that led to their recovery as “incredibly complicated, multi-faceted.”
The return of the artifacts would not have been possible without “close partnerships that spanned the globe," Bragg added.
Among the recovered pieces are a massive stone relief looted from the archaeological site of Palmyra and 14 rare mosaics stolen from a Roman villa in Syria, he said.
Bragg said his office's Antiquities Trafficking Unit seized 31 antiquities from the Middle East and North Africa as part of the investigations.
The Palmyra relief was smuggled from its original site during a period when the terrorist group ISIS (Daesh) was responsible for systematic looting of archaeological sites in Syria, he added.   
Funerary relief from Palmyra
The Palmyrene funerary relief dates to the late second century and consists of a massive limestone sculpture depicting a reclining man surrounded by a woman and three children, according to the Manhattan District Attorney's Office.
The relief once decorated the wall of a burial chamber in ancient Palmyra and weighs more than 1,000 pounds (454 kilograms).
The artifact appears to have been carefully removed from the wall to avoid damaging the figures carved into it, according to the same source. 
Mosaic dating to 3rd century BC
The recovered collection also includes the "Telete and Eros" mosaic, a large section of a mosaic floor dating to the third century BC.
The piece depicts the mythological wedding of Telete and Eros, made from hundreds of small colored stone cubes known as tesserae.
The Manhattan District Attorney's Office said it seized the piece in July 2021 along with 22 other mosaics stolen from Syria and Lebanon.
The recovered antiquities also include three female "Syro-Hittite" figurines dating to the second millennium BC and made in northwestern Syria.
The three figurines first appeared on the art market in the late 1980s and early 1990s in the possession of New York art dealer Edward Merrin, who was later convicted in federal court of crimes related to antiquities trafficking, before they were sold to the collection of antiquities collector Michael Steinhardt, according to the source.
Bragg said four of the artifacts returned to Syria were among 180 antiquities worth a total of $70 million seized by his office from the Steinhardt collection following a years-long criminal investigation spanning several countries.   
‘Part of Syria’s history is finally returning home’  
“Through Syrian-American cooperation, a part of Syria’s history is finally returning home thanks to the efforts of the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office,” Qanatri said.  
“This achievement demonstrates how mutual respect and a shared commitment to protecting cultural heritage can build lasting bridges between our two countries,” he added.  
Syrian archaeological sites suffered widespread looting, trafficking, and destruction during years of civil war, including Palmyra, which is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site.  
In 2015, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2199, imposing binding measures to combat the illicit trafficking of Syrian antiquities and cultural property amid concerns that proceeds from such trade could be used to finance armed groups.  
The US imposed emergency restrictions in 2016 on imports of Syrian archaeological and ethnological materials illegally removed from the country on or after March 15, 2011, referring to the start of the long civil war.  
Washington said at the time that the measures were intended to curb the looting and trafficking of Syrian cultural heritage.  
The US restrictions cover objects made of stone, metal, ceramics, glass, ivory, bone, and textiles, as well as paintings, mosaics, and other Syrian cultural property.  
Palmyra was particularly subjected to looting and destruction during ISIS’ control of the city in 2015, while UNESCO later documented the destruction of the temples of Bel and Baalshamin, the Arch of Triumph, and parts of the city's museum and its collections.

Quote: "Last week, we received information from our intelligence services that they had obtained from the Russian side – the Russian terrorists' strategy for this winter.
Our partners, like us, were struck by its cynicism, by this cold terrorist calculation of how to destroy our energy sector."
Details: Shmyhal added that Russia's plans envisage comprehensive strikes targeting everything from heat and water supplies and sewage systems to power generation and interconnectors – both those bringing electricity into Ukraine from Europe and those crossing the Dnipro River.
Quote: "There are two large documents, written in a very cold and precise manner. They contain tables specifying the amount of weaponry needed to destroy each facility. The types of weapons range from ballistic missiles to jet-powered and conventional drones. Everything has been calculated, with the required strike packages – as they call them – set out for each facility. We understand how they are going to act."
Details: Shmyhal said Ukraine is making thorough preparations to protect itself.
Quote: "More than 200 shelters have already been built – permanent concrete structures over facilities that are priority targets for the Russians. Pre-detonation screens are also being installed, and we are introducing nets to protect against FPV drones."
Details: The minister added that Ukraine is working with its partners to stockpile equipment because "not everything can be protected with concrete".
Background: On 23 September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned at the UN General Assembly that Ukraine would make winter painful for Russia if it continued striking Ukraine's energy system.

U.S. troops help Ecuador arrest dozens linked to notorious Mexican cartel
U.S. troops helped Ecuador dismantle a local branch of Mexico's notorious Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), arresting more than 30 members, Ecuador's interior minister said Thursday.
Quito, a Washington ally, is enthusiastically cooperating with President Trump's crackdown on organized crime across Latin America.
Thursday's early-morning operation "was conducted jointly with U.S. troops and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA)," Ecuadoran Interior Minister John Reimberg wrote on X.
Over 30 Ecuadorans were arrested for allegedly belonging to the group with a "direct connection to the CJNG," he said.
The minister said the group was involved in trafficking cocaine from Colombia, the world's largest producer, to international markets via ports in southwestern Ecuador.
Some 320 Ecuadoran police officers and 50 uniformed personnel from the U.S. Southern Command took part in the operation spanning several cities, he said.
Reimberg also released photos and videos of the operation, showing officers conduct raids and arrests suspects.
The military offensive against criminal organizations in Ecuador has caused alarm among human rights organizations, which denounce cases of excessive use of force, torture and enforced disappearance.
Right-wing President Daniel Noboa brushed off those concerns during an address to the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday.
"We receive plenty of criticism regarding the fight against organized crime and very little concern about the number of victims we are seeing from organized crime," Noboa said.
Earlier this year, American commandos joined Ecuadorian troops in a joint mission aimed at dismantling a suspected criminal hub operated by an alleged narco-terrorist organization along the country's coast.
Ecuador has gone from being one of South America's safest countries to a cocaine trafficking hub in a few short years, plagued by gangs with ties to Mexican and Colombian cartels.
Criminal gang violence continues unabated in Ecuador following the recapture in June 2025 of the country's biggest drug lord, Adolfo Macías, who leads the "Los Choneros" gang, after his escape from a maximum-security prison in 2024. I Think I Found an AI Agent Worth the Risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:36:35 UTC
04:36:35 KST

One of the first things I did when I left my full-time job at WIRED was give Claude Cowork access to my email and calendar. After reporting on artificial intelligence for years, I was curious about what the technology could do for me. I had imagined Cowork as a hyper-capable digital assistant, but was let down to discover that it was more like interacting with a regular chatbot, albeit one with extra tools. What did I want it to do? I had no idea.
Then Instinct, an invite-only AI agent that communicates with users through iMessage and WhatsApp, started popping off in the Bay Area. It connects to your email, calendar, and messaging apps. Think of it as OpenClaw for normies. The company, which launched in private beta in February, is reportedly in talks to raise $1 billion on top of the $350 million it’s already raised, bringing its valuation to $10 billion, according to The Information.
Instinct’s moment in the spotlight comes as Meta is experiencing its own unexpected burst of popularity thanks to Muse, an AI assistant the tech giant launched earlier this month. As of writing, Muse is the most popular free app in Apple’s App Store, with more than 900,000 downloads, according to third-party estimates. The commentator class on X seems genuinely excited about it, despite the fact that it rolled out with a serious security vulnerability that would have “let attackers do ‘whatever’ they wanted on a victim’s Mac,” according to Ars Technica. I’m not about to give Meta a ton of my personal information, but if Muse can keep me logged into Bloomberg or unsubscribe me from Hot Yoga São Paulo, which has been emailing me once a week since 2017, I’ll reconsider.
Agent Provocateur
The divide between people who use AI agents for everything and those who have never tried one has never been wider. It explains, in part, why tech CEOs were largely caught off guard by the data center backlash. If you think agents can automate the majority of people’s administrative drudgery and turbocharge their productivity, the costs and disruptions associated with building data centers might look like an acceptable trade-off. But if you’re using chatbots as a fancy form of Google, that deal is probably much less appealing.
The overarching problem, as technology journalist Jasmine Sun writes, is that “most people’s problems are not software-shaped, and most won’t notice even when they are.” AI agents, like chatbots, still require a lot of input and direction from users. If you know what you want—help with your homework, a virtual girlfriend—the tools are eager to provide. But if you don’t, well, welcome to the permanent underclass.
I was eager to avoid such a fate. I may not be agentic, but I like to think I’m action-oriented. Surely I could identify a software-shaped problem in my life. I had used Claude previously to generate a few freelance invoices, saving me approximately 10 minutes. It was nice, but not life-changing. I decided to give Instinct a try.
If you talk to AI researchers about Instinct, you’ll hear the phrase “form factor” a lot. Instinct got the form factor right—no open text box, just iMessage, WhatsApp, and a few helpful prompts. It’s hard to overstate how important this is. Rather than trying to figure out for yourself how to make the chat experience more useful, you’re texting with an agent that’s suggesting things it can do for you, and then actually doing them. And unlike other agents in this space, it doesn’t text too much. I tried a competing agent called Lindy for a week and deleted it after it texted me each morning and started popping into Zoom meetings without my approval.
For its first project, I gave Instinct my itinerary for a work trip to Venice, Italy. I had it book reservations based on where I was going to be, including WhatsApping hole-in-the-wall spots. Success! Restaurant reservations appear to be a gateway drug for many agent-curious people, and I was no exception. (It’s worth noting that while Muse can also call restaurants to book reservations on your behalf, some of those calls are reportedly made by humans in call centers, according to reporting in 404 Media).
Next, I gave Instinct a more complicated task. I had already booked a trip to New York in November with my sister when WIRED asked me to attend the WIRED World Fair, which was taking place in Miami the day before. Unfortunately, I’d booked a saver fare, meaning I couldn’t move the ticket, and if I missed the first leg of the trip it would automatically cancel the whole thing.
Could Instinct cancel my trip and get a refund? To my surprise, it could. The agent detected that Alaska had moved my flight 90 minutes earlier, a fact I’d completely missed, which qualified me for a full refund. It canceled my ticket, saving me roughly $550, and rebooked my one-way return to San Francisco. I don’t know about you guys, but I’m starting to feel the AGI.
Unnatural Instincts
This is where I have to pause and acknowledge the risks of using Instinct. There are a lot. People have reported that when they tried to disconnect the agent from their email, they found out it was retaining a copy of their inboxes anyway. One venture capitalist said he was banned from Resy after the bot pinged its API roughly 200 times per hour while trying to make a reservation. Another tech investor said he deleted the app after determining that it would be trivially easy for Instinct to be phished.
Instinct’s Terms of Service are pretty far-reaching, allowing the company to use at least some of your conversations to train its AI models. I also experienced an annoying (if minor) snafu: One day, Instinct canceled a DoorDash order that was seriously delayed, forcing me to forfeit $64. (I’d explicitly told it to cancel only if I could get a refund.) This alerted me to another thing Instinct is very, very good at: profusely apologizing without offering to pay for its mistakes.
The company Instinct, which shares the same name as its flagship AI agent, did not respond to requests for comment from WIRED.
Instinct feels like a mildly chaotic personal assistant, and since I’ve never had a real human assistant, I’m sticking with it. Last week it told me “NOT TO OPEN” an email from a friend inviting me to a backyard BBQ—it turned out to be a phishing scam. Agents are a security nightmare. I get it! But I’m busy. I’m a mom. Everything feels like a security nightmare these days. For now, I’m willing to take the risk.
This is an edition of the Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

For the 17th or 18th time, Putin promised to take Donetsk “in a few months” – Zelenskyy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:36:05 UTC
04:36:05 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin has again told US officials that Russia can capture Ukraine’s Donetsk Oblast within several months, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Speaking to the UN General Assembly on 24 September, Zelenskyy said this was the latest in a long series of similar promises as Russia has spent nearly five years trying to seize the region. He said Putin has made such promises 17 or 18 times, repeatedly pushing the deadline further back.
He contrasted those promises with Russia’s heavy battlefield losses and relatively limited territorial gains.
Russia has paid a huge price for its Donetsk offensive
Zelenskyy said Russian forces suffered 248,964 troops killed or severely wounded between January and August 2026.
He said Russia had captured only slightly more than 1,000 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory this year, while Ukraine had already liberated a significant portion of those gains.
Zelenskyy presented the figures as the human cost of Putin’s continued attempt to seize Donetsk, arguing that Russia is paying an enormous price for relatively limited territorial gains.
“Always the same: ‘Just a few more months,’” Zelenskyy said, adding that Putin would again fail to meet his latest deadline.
The Russian offensive is also facing a recent setback in northern Donetsk. Ukraine launched Operation Vivaldi in September to clear Russian infiltrators and retake ground near Lyman, disrupting Russia’s plan to encircle the fortified cities of the Donetsk “Fortress Belt.”
Ukrainian forces have reported retaking several settlements and clearing up to 125 square kilometers in the operation, although the full scope of the offensive remains undisclosed.
Ukraine retakes ground in a region Russia has fought for years to capture. “Vivaldi” is only getting started but is already “one of the most important victories for Ukraine in 2026”
Zelenskyy also warned that Russia’s ambitions extend beyond Donetsk. After saying Putin would again fail to capture the region, he said Russia would continue seeking other Ukrainian cities, naming Odesa, Kharkiv and Dnipro, while also pointing to Russian pressure on Moldova and threats toward Poland and the Baltic states.
Russia continues to pour missiles and drones into Ukraine
The battlefield campaign has been accompanied by a sustained Russian long-range attack campaign against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
Since the beginning of 2026, Russia has launched more than 2,100 missiles against Ukraine, including more than 950 ballistic missiles, according to Zelenskyy.
Ballistic missiles are particularly difficult for Ukraine to counter because it has a limited supply of interceptors capable of engaging them. Russia’s heavy use of ballistic weapons is therefore contributing directly to civilian deaths and infrastructure destruction.
Over the first eight months of the year, Russia also used 63,000 attack drones of various types, Zelenskyy said. More than 7,700 were jet-powered Geran drones, which he described as particularly destructive and dangerous.
The newer jet-powered drones are faster and more advanced than earlier Shahed-type models, making them harder to intercept and adding to the pressure on Ukraine’s air defenses as Russia attacks cities and infrastructure.
Zelenskyy said Russia was using the drones continuously to disrupt economic activity and normal life in Ukrainian cities, including by making it harder for children to attend school.
The figures show the scale of the Russian campaign beyond the front line. Alongside its ground offensive, Russia is using sustained missile and drone strikes to kill civilians, destroy infrastructure, and exhaust Ukraine’s air-defense resources.
North Korean troops add to Russia’s war effort
Zelenskyy also highlighted North Korea’s direct involvement in Russia’s war, saying its troops have suffered heavy losses while gaining battlefield experience alongside Russian forces.
He said North Korea’s military capabilities were also benefiting from its cooperation with Russia, pointing to improvements in its ballistic missiles and drone capabilities.
Ukraine recently transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. Zelenskyy said capturing the soldiers alive had been difficult and described one prisoner’s attempt to take his own life after realizing he was about to be captured.
He said the soldiers had been conditioned to believe they had to die rather than surrender.
“Do you really want to give such a force more time to learn how to fight?” Zelenskyy asked.
Zelenskyy calls for de-escalation before winter
Zelenskyy separately warned that Russia could again target Ukraine’s energy and heating infrastructure this winter.
Russia has already intensified attacks on Ukraine’s energy system ahead of the cold season.
Russia has also explicitly threatened to “freeze” Ukraine this winter, with its Defense Ministry linking the threat to attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. The country spent much of the previous winter dealing with the consequences of Russian strikes on power and heating infrastructure, including blackouts and disruptions to heat supplies.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine expects the coming winter to be difficult but warned that if Russia continues attacking Ukraine’s energy and heating systems, Ukraine will make the winter painful for Russia as well.
He called for steps toward de-escalation before winter, saying that diplomacy and military strength were both needed to end the war.

US, Iran discuss phased deal to reopen Hormuz, end US blockade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:33:08 UTC
04:33:08 KST

Breadcrumb
US and Iran discuss phased deal to reopen Hormuz and end US blockade, sources say
US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran, sources close to the talks said.
The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the nearly seven-month US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran.
The talks face a big obstacle as neither side wants to be the first to surrender its leverage, according to comments to Reuters by two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomatic sources, but behind Iran's stance is a recognition of the economic cost of prolonged confrontation.
A senior Iranian official said the most plausible way to end the impasse would be a phased arrangement, with Iran allowing navigation through Hormuz in return for the US lifting its economic blockade and Tehran potentially gaining access to frozen assets.
"One way forward would be to solve the crisis in stages. The first would be to end the blockade and reopen Hormuz," he said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
That would involve US President Donald Trump accepting another temporary fix, after an earlier understanding collapsed in July. So a central challenge facing the negotiators is not just to sketch out a deal but also to ensure any concessions are durable enough for both sides to trust, the sources said.
Trump has said he thinks the US and Iran could reach a deal after midterm elections to Congress on November 3. A senior European official said the Iranians "have a very long list of demands."
A White House official said that while "Iran is desperate for a deal, President Trump holds all the cards and will make whatever decision is best for the United States."
Trump, he said, remained "open to talking with Iran under the right circumstances" but had no need to negotiate, and the US was in a "very strong position" with control of the Strait of Hormuz and an Iranian economy that was "collapsing."
The official said "crushing sanctions" and "one of the most successful blockades in history" have crippled Iran’s economy and left Iran completely broke. Trump was content to let the "inevitable Iranian collapse" play out rather than be "played" by Tehran, the official said.
Former US negotiator Dennis Ross said he saw only a 30% chance of an agreement being reached before the vote, but that both sides may have stronger reasons to make a deal before than after the midterms.
"The blockade is what's really squeezing the Iranians. It's strangling them," Ross said.
A deal before the midterms could benefit Trump, as reopening Hormuz could ease tensions in the Gulf, contain oil prices and help bring down politically sensitive US gasoline prices.
Iran's chances of gaining much-needed economic relief may be greater while Trump still has a greater political incentive to strike a bargain.
After the midterms, Ross said, Trump may face fewer constraints and be more willing to intensify pressure or consider military options.
LEVERAGE AS OBSTACLE?
The leverage that brought Washington and Tehran back to negotiations could also make compromise harder.
Washington controls the pressure that is hurting Tehran most, while Tehran controls access to a critical energy chokepoint. Neither side wants to surrender that leverage without extracting something tangible in return.
This means the midterms may be less a deadline for diplomacy than for preserving the conditions that make the diplomatic efforts possible. If Washington and Tehran cannot turn leverage into a deal before the midterms, the diplomatic window could narrow as the risk of escalation grows.
Even as it seeks a diplomatic off-ramp, Tehran is preparing for the possibility of renewed war with Washington, the Iranian official said, accusing the US of using the economic blockade and threat of force as tools of coercion.
"Our fingers are on the trigger,” said the senior Iranian official. “The Americans know what they need to do but, because of their excessive demands, the chances of diplomacy resolving this are extremely low.”
Regional sources said Tehran was willing to drop a demand for payment of transit fees to use the Strait of Hormuz from the main agreement and put the demand in a side attachment instead, as ending the blockade had become the more urgent priority.
Gulf states have rejected the proposal for payment of transit fees. Any arrangement would be temporary, not a formal abandonment of Iran’s position, the regional sources said.
The US has tightened the economic vice on Iran, layering new sanctions on top of a blockade that has choked off Iran's oil exports, an important source of hard currency.
This month, it targeted Iran's remaining commercial airlines and support networks as part of a campaign to sever the economic lifelines sustaining the government and the powerful Revolutionary Guards. Trump warned that Iran's economy could "rot" unless it reached a deal.
"Iran is not primarily focused on imposing tolls in Hormuz but on preserving its administrative control of the waterway,” he said. "Iran may be willing to defer the toll issue, but they are not going to give up administrative control of the strait.”
At the heart of the diplomacy in New York is a fundamental tension. Washington wants pressure to produce concessions, Tehran wants pressure removed before making them, and the Gulf states want the conflict resolved without allowing the region's strategic waterways to become enduring bargaining chips.
FEARS OF AN OPEN-ENDED CONFLICT
During a separate meeting with Trump in New York, Gulf leaders sought clarity on Washington's endgame beyond the midterms, including on whether the US would resume military action if Iran refused to return to negotiations.
They conveyed their collective rejection of any Iranian control of Hormuz, saying freedom of navigation must be restored and that the strategic waterway should not become a tool of coercion against Gulf states, regional sources said.
Yet alongside their warnings over Hormuz, Gulf leaders have pressed hard for de-escalation and a political process, reflecting the region's determination to stay out of any further conflict between the US and Iran.
"It's still not clear what Trump’s endgame is, or what the alternative to the pressure campaign would be," said Ebtessam al-Ketbi, president of the Emirates Policy Center think tank based in Abu Dhabi.
"The Iranians, by contrast, know what they want. They're reshaping the regional landscape through Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb with a clear objective while Washington has yet to define its roadmap," she said, referring to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
That uncertainty is also shaping Tehran’s calculations. Danny Citrinowicz, a regional analyst and former Israeli military intelligence officer, said the New York talks had not altered the basic positions of either side and that Iran was unlikely to retreat as long as it believed Trump wanted to avoid a wider escalation before the midterms.
“The blockade is hurting them, but rather than softening their position, it is likely to drive them to escalate because they believe that if they soften their position, they are dead," said Alan Eyre, a former US negotiator on Iran.
A Western official familiar with the talks added: "It is all about opening the Strait of Hormuz. We're all under pressure domestically and the Iranians know that."

Italy ministers agree to ban burqa and niqab in school and cap foreigners in class
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:32:59 BST
04:32:59 KST

Italy ministers agree to ban burqa and niqab in school and cap foreigners in class
- Published
The Italian government has approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools, along with a limit on the share of pupils who speak little Italian in any one class.
A 30% cap will be imposed on children without Italian citizenship or poor knowledge of the Italian language in the first year of primary, middle and high school.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the measures as "common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate".
Opposition parties accuse the government of pandering to the policies of the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party, ahead of a general election next year.
Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara has said the limit is "purely linguistic" rather than one of citizenship, while he has sought to frame the ban on the niqab and burqa as a matter of gender equality.
"You must go to school with your face uncovered," Meloni said while announcing the plans on Sunday, adding that no-one could decide that a young woman should hide herself in the name of tradition.
There were several drafts of the decree ahead of Thursday's council of ministers meeting, however the core details were clear.
The veil ban would apply to the burqa and niqab, but not the hijab, which leaves the face visible.
The niqab is a veil for the face that leaves the area around the eyes clear. However, it may be worn with a separate eye veil. It is worn with an accompanying headscarf.
The burka is a one-piece veil that covers the face and body. Often there is a mesh screen around the eyes to see through.
Non-Italian citizens make up 11.6% of pupils in Italy's schools, according to the research institution Fondazione ISMU.
The 30% limit on pupils who speak limited Italian will cover separate stages of education differently.
In primary schools, it would cover non-Italian citizens who have either not been born in Italy or who have not attended at least two years of nursery school.
In lower- and upper- secondary schools, it would cover pupils without Italian citizenship who have not successfully completed at least three years in the Italian school system.
Local school offices would be asked to spread pupils with little Italian language skills more evenly among nearby schools. Where that is not possible, exemptions would apply, with extra Italian teaching.
The aim was to avoid "ghetto classes", the education minister explained.
The draft also goes further on parents, according to the Ansa news agency. Schools would have to report to social services cases in which persistent language barriers among those with parental responsibility hinder a child's integration. Free Italian courses would be offered.
The measure is a decree law, meaning it can take effect immediately, but must be ratified by parliament within 60 days.
Italy already has guidance on Italian language at schools. A 2010 ministerial notice under then-Education Minister Mariastella Gelmini set a 30% limit "as a rule" on pupils without Italian citizenship. The new decree puts the limit into law.
The political opposition says the plan is as much about politics as schools.
Opponents accuse Meloni of pandering to Roberto Vannacci, a retired military general who leads the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party and is seen as a threat to the governing coalition's right flank.
The leader of the centre-left Democratic Party (PD), Elly Schlein, called the plan propaganda and impossible to implement. PD deputy and chamber vice-president Anna Ascani also accused the government of propaganda at the expense of schoolchildren.
Valditara, speaking by video link from New York at a press conference rejected the charge.
"We are not chasing Vannacci; if anything, he is chasing us," he said.
Vannacci said he agreed with the measures, but they should have come years ago.
The League's Matteo Salvini, who launched a separate package of measures on what he called "political Islam" on Wednesday, accused Vannacci of "continually voting against the government".
Salvini said he hoped Futuro Nazionale would back the League's new proposals.

Allegations of Israeli genocide in Gaza are not only false but “the biggest lie of the century”, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told world leaders Thursday in a defiant speech that asserted his nation’s right to wage war against Iran – and was not heard by scores of delegates who trooped out before he started speaking.
Netanyahu, his voice rising in emphasis, said attacking Iran “was one of the easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make” and denounced as “moral cowards” a mass of delegates who walked out of the UN General Assembly when he took the podium to speak.
“In defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall,” Netanyahu said. “In fact, I want you to know that many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran’s nukes.”
When Netanyahu walked to the rostrum, a mix of cheers, boos and mass walkouts erupted. Scores of delegates marched out and a majority of visible seats sat empty afterwards. “Order in the hall, please,” General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman said repeatedly.
“If there are any other moral cowards who have not yet left the hall, please do so now,” Netanyahu said.
Read moreLive: Israeli PM Netanyahu calls Gaza genocide allegations ‘biggest lie of the century’
His remarks – which at times sounded like a stump speech as Israel gears up for elections – came after a week filled with speeches by world leaders accusing Israel of genocide and war crimes in Gaza.
The Palestinian Mission to the UN said in a message to many of the 193 UN member nations to bring as many staff as possible to the assembly hall and “collectively walk out of the assembly” once the Israeli prime minister is announced.
“This will send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end,” the message said.
Israel rejects allegations that it committed genocide and war crimes and is illegally occupying Palestinian territory. All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law, but the Israeli government insists they are legal.
Read moreIsraeli policies threaten 'life and existence' of Palestinians, Abbas tells UN
Netanyahu, who is prone to using visual aids during his General Assembly speeches, at one point held up a pager while reminding the audience of September 17, 2024, when Israel remotely detonated thousands of pagers that had been distributed to the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group in Lebanon. The pager attack wounded more than 3,000 people and killed 12, including two children.
He reminded the assembly of the scale of the October 7, 2023, attack in which Hamas militants killed about 1,200 people. “This is equal to 40,000 innocent Americans slaughtered in less than 24 hours,” he said, or 16 times the death count on the 9/11 attacks that left nearly 3,000 people dead in New York.
Netanyahu thanked US President Donald Trump for taking decisive action against Iran, and he insisted Israel would prevail: “We will continue to win because we have no other choice.”
In past years, Netanyahu has used his General Assembly speech to both denounce the United Nations as biased and make Israel's case to world leaders. His address – scheduled for prime time in Israel – is the cornerstone of an abbreviated trip to the United States unfolding under the shadow of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani calling him a “war criminal” and pushing for his arrest.
Mamdani has acknowledged that New York does not have the authority to execute an International Criminal Court warrant but urged federal authorities to do so.

Netanyahu dismissed incidents of Israeli settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank as a “handful of young juvenile delinquents” throwing stones, chopping down olive trees and lighting fires.
“I can’t stand that. I won’t stand for vigilantism,” the prime minister said before accusing foreign leaders and the international press of distorting the scale of violence in the West Bank.
Netanyahu’s government is dominated by settlers and their allies, including the Cabinet minister who oversees the police. There have been few arrests of settlers involved in attacks on Palestinians.
Israel captured the West Bank and East Jerusalem in the 1967 war, and the Palestinians want both as part of their future state. The Palestinians and much of the international community view the settlements as illegal and as an obstacle to creating a viable, contiguous Palestinian state.

Netanyahu's transit through French airspace 'consistent' with international law despite ICC warrant, says France

Esra Taşkın
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
France said Thursday that allowing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s plane to transit its airspace did not contradict international law, despite an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for him.
Speaking to reporters, Foreign Ministry Pascal Confavreux argued that allowing Netanyahu's plane to travel through French airspace was "fully in accordance with international law."
Mentioning how France had allowed this before, Confavreux said the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC, does not impose an "obligation" on member states on the transit through their airspace of a state aircraft carrying a passenger who is subject to an arrest warrant.
Turning to the Middle East, Confavreux said the 1974 Agreement on Disengagement between Israel and Syria is still valid and that France has called on all parties, including Israel, to comply with it.
Also reaffirming France's support for the UN Disengagement Observer Force, a UN peacekeeping mission tasked with maintaining the ceasefire between Israel and Syria, he stressed that France expects "an end to all military deployments" in the buffer zone between the two countries.
Any military deployment in the area violates the 1974 agreement, he noted.
Earlier Thursday, the plane carrying Netanyahu to the US to attend the UN General Assembly used the airspace of Greece, Italy, and France despite the arrest warrant for him issued by the International Criminal Court.
According to flight-tracking website Flightradar24, his plane left Israel early Thursday for the US to attend the UN General Assembly and crossed the airspace of European countries that are members of the International Criminal Court.
All three countries are parties to the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC, and are generally required to cooperate with the court's requests to arrest and surrender wanted individuals found on their territory.

Netanyahu calls Israel’s war in Gaza ‘opposite of genocide’ in UN speech

Benjamin Netanyahu delivered an inflammatory address to the United Nations on Thursday, decrying what he said was a global anti-Jewish conspiracy and swatting aside criticism of Israel’s war in Gaza, as he faces down international isolation and a fight for political survival in upcoming elections in Israel.
As planned protests erupted on the streets of New York City, Netanyahu took aim at critics of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, the international media, regional leaders such as Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, the leftwing commentator Hasan Piker and the New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani in an address that doubled as a stump speech to ignite his rightwing base for the elections.
Invoking his late brother Yonatan Netanyahu, a commando killed in a 1976 raid to free Israeli hostages from a hijacked airliner in Entebbe, Uganda, he repeated the lines: “We are going to win. We have no other choice.”
Dozens of delegates, inspired by a Palestinian call, walked out of the General Assembly Hall of the UN headquarters as Netanyahu took the stage, leading a speaker to pound his gavel and announce: “I’m calling for order in the hall.”
Palestinian representatives organising diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech said they wanted to “send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end”.
“If there are any other moral cowards in the audience, I urge them to walk out,” Netanyahu said before launching into his prepared remarks.
The speech revealed little new in terms of Israeli policy over the war in Gaza, militant settler violence in the West Bank, or Israel’s plans to end other regional conflicts including its joint war with the United States against Iran.
But he argued that the world faced an existential threat from Iran, suggesting that several missiles from Tehran could have destroyed the UN, and cited quiet support from world leaders for Israel’s actions that could not be aired in public.
“Devastating Iran’s nuclear facilities was … very hard to do,” he said of launching joint US-Israeli strikes in February. “But for me, it was one of the easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make as prime minister. Because if we hadn’t done it, we’d all be dead.”
He branded Turkey’s Erdoğan as a “tyrant” who “hosts Hamas terrorists”, decried Mamdani as the “antisemitic mayor of New York”, and declared that Israel’s war in Gaza is not genocide – “it’s the opposite of genocide”.
“So, to all those spreading these lies about my country and about our brave soldiers, whether they sit in this hall or in the office of the antisemitic mayor of New York, I say this: shame on you!” he said.
Netanyahu delivered the controversial address to the United Nations on Thursday just hours after Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas said his delegation was “unlawfully” denied visas by the Trump administration to attend the meeting of world leaders.
In a video address from Ramallah, broadcast in the General Assembly Hall, Abbas condemned Israel’s policies in Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem as a “malicious colonial plan” to establish a “‘Greater Israel’ and erase the Palestinian presence”.
Citing the humanitarian crisis in Gaza and the violent expansion of settlements in the West Bank, Abbas said that the Israeli government “now threatens the very life and existence of the Palestinian people in their homeland”.
“Do not allow another Nakba and further massacres like those of 1948 to continue taking place,” he added, referring to the expulsion of Palestinians upon the founding of Israel.
For the second year in a row, the US state department denied visas to Abbas and the Palestinian Authority delegation, arguing that they had failed to live up to their commitments to seek peace with Israel.
“As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the state department said last week in a statement.
In his speech, Abbas said his delegation “[rejects] these unlawful punitive measures, as well as the accusations and justifications on which they were based”.
He said: “Preventing the Palestinian delegation from reaching United Nations headquarters is inconsistent with the obligations of the United States as the host country.”
As he spoke, protests were forming on the streets of New York near the United Nations headquarters in advance of Netanyahu’s arrival.
Hundreds of demonstrators crowded into the street on Manhattan’s east side in midtown and held signs that said “End the Genocide” and wore shirts reading “Fund people not bombs”. By the end of Netanyahu’s speech, more than 100 demonstrators, including several local elected officials, had been arrested by New York City police.
Earlier this summer, the mayor, Zohran Mamdani, had said that Netanyahu was “not welcome” in New York, and said he was reviewing whether Netanyahu could be arrested by city police under an international criminal court warrant for his arrest.
He has since tempered that stance, saying this week that he wouldn’t attend the protests but promising to protect their “right to [protest] in this city”.
Netanyahu is not expected to meet Donald Trump, who is in Washington to host the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, nor with other senior US officials, as he faces growing international condemnation over his hardline stance. Netanyahu has said that he needs to return to Israel quickly because of the election campaign and the holiday of Sukkot, which begins on Friday.

'The whole base knows her': Service dog helps autistic IDF soldier thrive in classified Air Force role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:24:48 UTC
04:24:48 KST

Pvt. A., 18, and her service dog have become well known in the Israeli Air Force’s Special Air Forces Wing, known as Wing 7. Everyone on base already knows Vali, the third service dog to complete basic training at the Mahane Alon base in the Galilee.
Pvt. A. serves in a classified role with Vali at her side as part of the IDF’s “Titkadmu” program, a unique enlistment track designed to integrate young men and women on the autism spectrum into military service.
From the first day of basic training, commanders made it clear to the company that Vali was a service dog with a job to do and was not to be touched or disturbed.
During formations, the dog sat or lay quietly, and at the basic training graduation ceremony she synchronized herself with A.’s movements, sitting at attention and lying down at rest.
“She took part in all the marches, including a night march, as well as field and camouflage exercises,” A. said. “The other girls in the company welcomed Vali with great enthusiasm and a lot of respect for her role.”
Maj. H. said the IDF’s attitude toward service dogs has evolved over time, particularly as awareness has grown of their importance for soldiers with disabilities.
Israel’s Equal Rights for Persons with Disabilities Law enshrines the right to bring service dogs into public places, and their use was later expanded to support people with post-traumatic stress disorder and autism.
“The trend increased significantly after October 7,” Maj. H. said. “Although A. was not allowed to bring the dog into the dining hall during basic training, at her permanent base Vali integrated very well and became part of the unit’s daily life. There are several career soldiers, including a lieutenant colonel, who serve with assistance dogs, as well as reservists with PTSD who come with their dogs.”
The road to Wing 7 was long and filled with bureaucracy.
“I arrived at the recruitment office with a regular first-call notice. Of course, I came with the dog,” A. said. “When they asked why I had a dog, I explained that she was a service dog because I have anxiety attacks. About half an hour later, the head of the mental health section came and said they don’t enlist soldiers with service dogs.
“At that moment, I insisted on going through the first-call process. The mental health officer gave me an exemption on the spot, and that is how I began the volunteer process and joined the ‘Titkadmu’ track.”
Pvt. A. eventually reached Maj. H., who told her he would support her.
“He said he thinks service dogs can help a great many people, and that he sees this especially with reservists, and he thinks it is a great idea,” she said.
In the end, Pvt. A. enlisted together with Vali and went through induction and basic training with her.
“The commander at the induction center asked to take a picture of Vali wearing an Air Force beret. So somewhere there is a picture of her with the beret,” she said with a smile.
Now, when A. sleeps at her permanent base, Vali sleeps beside her in her crate.
“The whole base knows Vali and says hello to her. She contributes to the atmosphere and helps reduce tension. I know there is a lot of work being done to encourage enlistment with service dogs.
“There are reservists with service dogs, with levels of experience and knowledge that no one else has, who are able to continue in their roles because of the dogs. The dog also helps the other soldiers in the unit.”
Vali’s training began when Pvt. A. was just 16. Dana Wilker, owner of a training and instruction center for assistance dogs, trained her.
“Service dogs work with and accompany the people who rely on them for about eight to 10 years,” Wilker said. “That is a significant period of time, especially for someone who received the dog at age 16, with so many changes and so much growing up.”
Wilker, who also researches the cognition of working dogs, said: “Over these years, I saw A. open up and, with impressive inner strength, help herself develop and move forward.
“During training, the dogs undergo intensive exposure to a wide range of situations intended to prepare them for anything, including loud noises and unusual smells, until the dog is able to remain calm and continue working and carrying out tasks for the person it assists even in unusual situations.
“That was the case, for example, over the past month, when Vali accompanied A. throughout basic training.
“Vali and A. demonstrated to the military system that it is both possible and worthwhile to integrate and enlist soldiers who are accompanied by assistance dogs.”

US rapper Macklemore announces Free Palestine tour after Ed Sheeran fallout

Grammy Award-winning rapper Macklemore has announced a string of shows in support of Palestine after he was controversially dropped from Ed Sheeran’s United States tour after speaking out against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
The 43-year-old American rapper, who has almost 40 million monthly listeners on Spotify, announced his Free Palestine Tour on Thursday, with shows set to take place in Dublin, Paris and London in late October.

The Senate on Thursday narrowly voted down a measure demanding an end to the U.S. war with Iran.
The chamber voted 49-50 on the resolution, the latest to call for an end to the war.
All but four Republicans voted against the measure despite concerns that GOP candidates will face fallout in November's midterm elections from the war's economic costs. Some Republicans running in tight races have recently broken with President Donald Trump and called for an end to the war to bring gas prices down, a sign of potential voter discontent over the war's impact on the economy.
The Republicans who voted for the resolution were Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Maine's Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky. Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania was the lone Democrat to vote against it.
Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., did not vote despite having been in the Senate earlier Thursday. Alsobrooks has previously voted for similar resolutions. But if she had again voted that way on Thursday, the resolution still would have failed.
"Senator Alsobrooks has voted 13 times to end the war in Iran. Unfortunately, she was dealing with an urgent family matter during today's vote so was unable to cast her fourteenth vote to end the war in Iran," Alsobrooks' spokesperson Meredith Happy said in a statement to CNBC. "She believes every day that this war rages on, Americans are paying for it at the gas pump and the grocery store—and too many American service members have paid with their lives. She continues to urge this President to end this war once and for all."
An affirmative vote on the measure, known as a War Powers Resolution, would have directed Trump to remove U.S. troops from hostilities in Iran unless Congress explicitly approves the war.
The Senate has voted repeatedly on similar measures since the war began, approving one of them. The White House has effectively ignored that vote, arguing that the War Powers Act is unconstitutional.
The measure voted on Thursday, which like the one adopted was a so-called "concurrent resolution," did not carry the force of law and is never signed by the president, making the vote largely symbolic even if it had passed.
The Democratic leaders of the legislative push, however, argue that the Constitution vests authority to declare war in Congress, not the executive branch, and that the president must abide by their disapproval whether or not he signs it.
"The president right now is in violation of the Constitution and the War Powers Act and the concurrent resolution that we've already passed," said Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., who has led a number of the votes to end the war.
"We shouldn't have to do a second one because the president should follow the law, but we are doing a second one on the theory that maybe after a number of months more people will join us, the American public is even more deeply opposed to this war."
The measure cleared the House in July and faced just a 50-vote threshold to clear the Senate. Democrats have seen an uptick in Republican support in recent votes to end the war, as the administration has blown through timelines to seek congressional approval for the conflict.
The war has also created a challenging political environment for incumbent Republicans, who could lose control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections that loom less than six weeks away.
Gas prices, which have spiked throughout the conflict, currently average $4.48 per gallon nationwide, according to AAA. Recently, runaway diesel prices have begun stressing farmers and truckers and have alarmed Republicans in midwestern states, who have begun to distance themselves from the White House and call for an end to the war.
Lawmakers are set to hit the campaign trail for nearly all of October, and will need to explain to voters what they are doing to bring down prices.
"There are a lot of good things we can talk about; the problem is what you did for me recently doesn't even hardly count," said Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., when asked about how Republicans can message to economically anxious voters. "The other thing that we get to talk about ... is that at least we're not socialists."

Xi and Trump discuss AI cooperation (VIDEOS)
US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, have discussed cooperation on artificial intelligence during talks in Washington, stressing the technology’s growing global importance.
The meeting came as the two countries compete for leadership in AI while negotiating over advanced chips and critical materials, which became key bargaining points in their trade dispute last year.
Welcoming Xi to the White House for a state visit, Trump said the talks would cover security, technology and “superintelligence” – his new term for AI.
“The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come,” the US president said.
Xi said China and the US “bear a historic responsibility to promote human development and progress.”
“Both China and the United States are leading nations in artificial intelligence; we have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people,” the Chinese president said.
Beijing and Washington stand to benefit from cooperation and lose from confrontation, Xi added, stressing that competition between the two countries should be a “race” rather than a fight “in which one either wins or loses.”
Earlier this month, Trump singled out China as Washington’s main rival in the AI race, declaring that “whoever wins AI, wins.”
Technology has increasingly become a source of friction between the two powers. Washington restricted exports of advanced chips to China last year before later allowing some sales to resume in exchange for a 15% share of the revenue. Beijing, meanwhile, imposed export controls on several rare earths and restricted their supply for foreign military use.
China has agreed to suspend some of the restrictions for a year following a Trump-Xi meeting in South Korea last October.
Ahead of Thursday’s summit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that Washington and Beijing had agreed to extend their tariff truce by another two months. The arrangement has kept tariffs well below the peaks reached during last year’s trade war, when US duties on Chinese imports climbed as high as 145% and Beijing’s levies on American goods reached 125%.

Priest killed and four injured in knife attack at Polish abbey
- Published
A priest has been killed and four other people injured in a knife attack in south-east Poland, officials have said.
A 31-year-old Ukrainian man was arrested after the stabbings on the grounds of a Catholic abbey in the town of Jarosław.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki said Thursday's attack "has shaken us all and demands a firm response from the state", while his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky said "we are shocked by this evil".
Reports in Polish media said the attacker first injured a priest in a nearby cafe, and then another four people inside the abbey itself. A police investigation into the attacker's motives is now under way.
Polish police said four men and one woman were stabbed in the attack on Thursday morning on the abbey grounds.
The name of the murdered priest has not been publicly released.
Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said psychological support was now being provided to all those affected by the incident.
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the perpetrator "will be punished with the full severity of Polish law".
Echoing his words, President Zelensky said "the perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility according to the law", adding that Ukraine was counting on "a quick and thorough investigation of all circumstances".
The Ukrainian embassy in Poland also condemned the attack.
In a statement, it said: "In such difficult moments, it is especially important to support each other, remain steadfast in respect for human life, and not allow pain to escalate into hatred or new violence. Responsibility for a crime must be based solely on the law."
Poland has recently seen a number of often violent incidents involving its citizens and Ukrainians, many of whom have fled their home country after Russia's full-scale invasion.

CNN, MS NOW, Politico allowed back in White House after judge’s order
- A federal judge ruled that President Trump's ban on CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House likely violated their constitutional due process rights, ordering their access to be restored.
- The White House accused these outlets of spreading falsehoods and leaking sensitive national security information, but the judge doubted these claims motivated the ban.
- Top US broadcasters paused White House pool coverage in solidarity, emphasising the public's right to independent and accurate government information without media restrictions.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back into the White House on Sept 24, six days after being banned by President Donald Trump, after a federal judge ordered that the journalists have their access restored.
District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled overnight that revoking the White House press credentials of the three media outlets “likely violated their constitutional due process rights.”
Reporters for CNN, MS NOW and Politico who attempted to return to the White House early on Sept 24 ahead of a visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping were initially turned away by the Secret Service but were allowed in later around midday.
Journalists from other outlets surrounded CNN’s tent on the White House driveway and filmed reporter Betsy Klein as she reported live following her return.
“Welcome back,” several journalists said.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico had requested an urgent court hearing on Sept 24 after their reporters were initially barred from the White House despite the judge’s order.
In his ruling, Kelly took issue with how the White House went about expelling the three news organisations.
“The ‘general rule’ is that ‘individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the Government deprives them’ of a constitutionally protected interest,” the judge said.
Trump has long attacked media that have aired critical coverage of him, repeatedly blasting the press as the “enemy of the people.”
The Republican president barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House on Sept 18 for distributing what he called “fake news” and “fiction and lies.”
They filed a joint lawsuit asking for a temporary restraining order against the ban on the grounds that it violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which upholds the right to a free press.
Ahead of the ruling, the Department of Justice had argued that Trump can “control reporters’ access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office.”
“Access to the White House is a privilege – not a right,” it said.
National security?
The White House Press Office accused CNN in a letter to the cable news outlet of “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information,” with similar accusations leveled against MS NOW and Politico.
The letter to CNN cited several stories about the US-Iran war and a story on Trump’s plans to build a military bunker below the planned East Wing ballroom which allegedly “disclosed ‘top-secret’ construction details.”
Kelly, who was appointed by Trump during his first term, appeared unconvinced.
“The Court is sceptical – at least on this record – that Defendants’ interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes,” the judge said.
In a rare move, the top five US broadcasters said that they were halting pool coverage of the White House – where a broadcaster films on behalf of all television outlets for the day – in solidarity with CNN.
“The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting,” ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said. AFP

Ed Miliband meets Iran’s foreign minister as Tehran gives US ultimatum on strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Iran said it has told Donald Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear program the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports in return, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some of Iran’s frozen assets.
The proposal is designed to accelerate the steps first laid down in the memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran in June, particularly by helping the talks on Iran’s nuclear program start much more quickly than previously agreed.
Iran says a deal on the temporary route through the strait of Hormuz has been agreed with Oman, describing it as a done deal, and is ready to register the details with the International Maritime Organisation.
Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, said he was waiting to hear a response from the Americans to the proposal. He added that he had consulted on the plan with China, which fully supported the proposal.
Saudi Arabia had been expected to endorse the Oman-Iran route through the strait last week, but pulled back partly due to anger that Iranian-backed Houthis had started attacking Saudi Arabia as part of their dispute over the future of Yemen.
Iran claims it has urged the Houthis to cease the attacks on Saudi Arabia but that it does not have control over Houthi decision-making.
Araghchi, speaking to reporters in New York, said: “We have introduced a plan to the US through the mediators that if certain conditions are met, the strait will be open within seven days and talks will start.”
He said the Iranian preconditions were not new, and were contained in the Islamabad memorandum of understanding that was signed by Trump.
The advantage of the proposal, apart from opening the strait and lifting the chokehold on the world economy, would be bringing the US to the talks on Iran’s nuclear program much more quickly. Talks on the nuclear program under the MoU would not have started for 60 days. Araghchi said he was staying in New York over the weekend to await an American response, but added he was not in a hurry.
Privately, Iranian officials believe they could reach a deal with the Americans, and the Saudi hurdle over aspects of the route could be overcome, but fear Israel will use its influence to pull the US president away from the proposal.
Araghchi added he would like the deal to go through before the midterm elections, by which he meant that the strait of Hormuz could be opened and energy prices thereby reduced, something Trump badly needs for the Republican party to survive a political mauling.
For the US, there are difficulties in the plan related to forcing Israel to end the war in Lebanon. Israel may object to giving Iran such clear control over the route through which ships would travel through the strait of Hormuz. Iran also wants to retain control of shipping to prevent some US military shipping going through the strait.
Issues such as whether tolls or navigational fees could be imposed by the littoral states Oman and Iran would be settled later in the process.
Earlier in the day, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, met Araghchi, his Iranian counterpart, for the first time in New York.
It was also the first meeting between UK and Iranian ministers for a year, and the first exchange since the UK in July proscribed the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organisation, a move that has worsened the already sour relations between the two countries.
Miliband made clear that the UK was committed to freedom of navigation in the strait and wanted a diplomatic solution, also stressing support for Saudi Arabia, a UK ally in Yemen.
He warned Iran about its behaviour in the UK, including threats to Jewish communities, and called for the UK to be given consular access to the British couple sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment in Tehran.
Araghchi and the US’s special envoy Steve Witkoff also met earlier this week on the sidelines of the general assembly to discuss Iran’s terms for reopening the strait and the speed at which that may happen, as well as the time the US had been given to respond.
A faction inside Iran is arguing that Tehran should seek to escalate the conflict with a vulnerable US president, rather than let the crisis drift in its current deadlock. Brent crude was trading at about $107 (£81) a barrel on Thursday.
Some IRGC officers have also linked the strait of Hormuz issue to the closure of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway close to the south-west of Yemen now under control of Iranian-backed Houthis.
Maj Gen Rahim Safavi, a senior Iranian military figure, said: “If the Americans start a new war, a new front centred on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait may open before their eyes. Are they ready to enter the battle on this front? This is a question that they should pay more attention to.”
Domestically, Pezeshkian’s defiant message to the UN general assembly on Wednesday was deemed a success overall in that it balanced a refusal to bend the knee to “the US bully” with a willingness to seek diplomatic talks.
He also proposed a new security architecture for the future in partnership with Gulf states, including those it has been bombarding in an effort to dislodge the US from its military bases.
Maj Gen Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the IRGC, praised Pezeshkian’s speech, saying: “We are not afraid of war. It is the loud and firm call of the Iranian nation – a call that resonated from the United Nations podium, through the words of the esteemed president, and reached the ears of the world.”

After the US and Israel launched the war against Iran on February 28, Pakistan helped secure a ceasefire on April 8 and later hosted more than 20 hours of talks between American and Iranian officials in Islamabad.
Following weeks of mediation, Pakistan and Qatar helped secure the June 18 deal, which provided the two sides with a framework and 60 days to negotiate a longer-term agreement aimed at ending the war.
However, the two sides soon resumed retaliatory strikes, with tensions continuing.
Xi also urged the US to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’” and handle the Taiwan question “prudently” to lay a solid foundation for bilateral strategic cooperation and relations.
Beijing’s position on safeguarding its national unity and territorial integrity is “crystal clear", he said.
China considers Taiwan a breakaway province, while Taipei has insisted on its independence since 1949.
Xi also said that building a constructive China-US relationship based on strategic stability is not an expedient measure nor something that can be achieved overnight, additionally calling for translating the new vision of a constructive bilateral relationship of strategic stability into action.
‘Great meeting’

Xi arrived Wednesday for a three-day state visit to the US, his first in more than a decade.
He is the first Chinese leader to make two state visits to the US since the two countries established diplomatic relations in 1979.
Then-US President Barack Obama hosted Xi for his first state visit in 2015.

UNGA Day 3: Netanyahu defends Israel as delegates walk out
