That's a wrap on Day 3 of UNGA
We're wrapping up for the day, with the third day's sessions of the 81st General Assembly now complete.
Gaza dominated the speeches today.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the assembly, denying that his country's actions in Gaza amount to genocide, an accusation leveled by several speakers on Thursday, including Palestinian Prime Minister Mahmoud Abbas.
Several delegates exited the hall as the Israeli prime minister began his speech.
Protesters had also gathered outside the UN Headquarters in New York ahead of Netanyahu's address, with some being arrested.
Before the session wrapped up, the representatives of Iran, Turkey and Qatar used their right of reply to lambast Netanyahu's address.
Join us on Friday, when Iraq, Lebanon, Pakistan, Egypt, Mexico, Haiti, Norway, Sweden and others are due to address the assembly.
Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change
Four weeks after catastrophic flash floods ravaged Nepal, the small Himalayan country's young prime minister stood at the podium of the UN General Assembly to warn leaders about the impact of a warming world.
"I wish I could stand here today simply to speak about development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation. Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions," said Balendra Shah as he began his address to the UNGA on Thursday.
Nepal's leader calls for international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas
The Nepalese leader stressed that the perils of climate change transcend national borders as he made a case for greater international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas.
"The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet's life-support system," Shah said, proposing the establishment of a "Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism," which he said would be led by Nepal, India and China.
Shah elaborated that the mechanism would help countries share satellite data and expertise, as well as monitor glacial lakes that pose a threat. He also called for stronger joint early-warning systems and coordinated, cross-border assistance in the event of a disaster.
"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information," the prime minister said.
Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change
Shah noted that his country only contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
"We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it," he said, adding that he wasn not blaming any nation or continent.
"We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield. We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity," Shah said.
Nepal seeks grants, not loans, for flood recovery
The Nepalese prime minister emphasized the principles of "Responsibility, Reparation and Resilience" as he called for grant-based support rather than loans.
Shah said that vulnerable nations should not be forced to take on additional debt to recover from climate catastrophes.
"When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants. We need adequate grant-based support from the world," he said.
36-year-old Shah was theyoungest head of government to speak at the 81st session of the UNGA.
'Hands off ICC,' Dutch PM says amid growing US pressure
Netherlands Prime Minister Rob Jetten, addressing the General Assembly on Thursday, said the International Criminal Court, which is based in The Hague, was "under attack."
Jetten did not name the US or President Donald Trump, who on Tuesday urged countries to leave the court, the latest move in his administration's campaign against the ICC.
"How can you possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes?" Jetten asked the assembly, drawing loud applause from the delegates.
"I believe there can be only one response. To say: hands off the ICC, and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order. Because the reality is that we still need to fight impunity."
Washington has imposed financial sanctions and visa bans on ICC staff, with officials reportedly preparing additional sanctions that could curtail the court's ability to operate.
Yemen, Kuwait stress freedom of navigation at UNGA
Yemen and Kuwait, both heavily impacted by the Iran war and its regional spillover, have used their General Assembly addresses to stress the importance of the freedom and safety of navigation, while condemning Iran and its proxies in the region.
Abdullah Abdulkader Al Alimi-Bawzer, vice resident of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, represents the internationally recognized government, which has been at war with the Iran-backed Houthirebels for more than a decade.
Alimi-Bawzer devoted his address to highlighting recent Houthi actions and their impact on global trade.
The Houthis' conflict with Saudi Arabia, which has led a coalition against them, has recently escalated, with the Yemeni rebels declaring a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial global shipping route. This has further squeezed the Saudi kingdom as Iran continues to block access through the Strait of Hormuz.
"Ensuring security at sea begins with eliminating the source of the threat on land," Alimi-Bawzer said, in an apparent reference to the Houthis.
Kuwaiti Crown Prince Sheikh Sabah Khaled Al-Hamad Al-Sabah stressed that freedom and safety of navigation, as well as the right of passage through the Straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, must be guaranteed.
"To inflict harm on the economies of the region and the world, and to disrupt global trade and oil markets, Iran is obstructing maritime navigation and closing the Strait of Hormuz, using it as a bargaining chip in the war, in violation of international law and relevant Security Council resolutions," he said.
Kuwait has been among the countries targeted by Iranian strikes since the start of the war, in retaliation for US and Israeli strikes.
Nigeria says don't 'surrender our technological future to paranoia'
Nigeria's Vice President Kashim Shettima addressed the assembly on behalf of President Bola Tinubu.
Among a range of issues, he weighed in on the question of AI with an appeal for an optimistic and proactive approach more than what he deemed undue caution.
"We refuse to surrender our technological future to paranoia," he said. "An invention can be destructive or beneficial, depending on the purpose it serves and the judgment of those who use it. A knife can take a life in the hands of an assailant, and can save one in the hands of a surgeon."
He said that while AI could be used to wage war, it could also "transform" an array of areas like healthcare, education and agriculture.
"Muhc of the anxiety surrounding AI reflects the distrust we have allowed to grow amongst us," Shettima said.
He said Nigeria wished to invite the world "to work with our inventive, resourceful and enterprising young people to direct AI towards humanity's advancement rather than its destruction."
Fiji calls for cheaper financial transfers for remittances, saying 'they are not aid'
Fijian President Ratu Naiqama Tawakecolati Lalabalavu addressed the chamber on behalf of one of the low-lying island nations at severe risk from climate change on Thursday.
He said that many of the UN's sustainable development goals remained off track with 2030 approaching and said that aid and financial assistance often did a poor job of reaching remote islands exposed to more natural disasters than average. But then he called for a wider financial system that would better enable Fijians to help themselves.
"There is one measure of delivery that reaches Fijian households directly," he said. "Remittances are now Fiji's third-largest source of foreign exchange."
Lalabalavu said these funds paid for school fees, rebuilt homes after cyclones and sustained families between harvests.
"Your excellencies, they are not aid. They are earnings of Fijians abroad, sent home. Yet Pacific corridors remain among the most expensive in the world through which to send money."
He noted how the chamber had in May committed to work to keep such transfer costs below 3% and to eliminate corridors costing more than 5% — he said that Pacific countries like Fiji wanted this to be "treated as an obligation and not an aspiration."
"Labor mobility must also not become a one-way transfer of the people that we have trained," the president said. "Fiji does not begrudge any Fijian the chance to build a life abroad. We ask only that those recruit our nurses, our teachers invest in the systems that recruited them."
Lalabalavu also alluded to Fiji recently declaring a national HIV emergencyand said that organized crime and drug trafficking was exacerbating this problem. He said that as a small impoverished country, Fiji had three requests for the international community:
"That treatment and diagnostics reach small states at prices we can pay. That the Global Fund and UNAIDS be resources at a level that does not force triage between regions, and that our partners treat Pacific narcotics interdiction as the shared security interest it is."
Netanyahu calls genocide allegations 'the greatest lie of the century'
The Israeli prime minister said allegations of genocide in Gaza leveled at Israel by various world leaders or groups were false.
"It will take time for the world to acknowledge what is so plain to see. That Hamas used Palestinian civilians as human shields. That it used hospitals, schools, mosques as terrorist command posts. That it sold much of the food we let into Gaza," Netanyahu alleged.
"And while Hamas did everything possible to keep Palestinians in harm's way — often at gunpoint — Israel did everything possible to get them out of harm's way," he said, listing measures like warnings to civilians.
"I want to ask you a question: what genocidal regime gives a million polio vaccinations to the enemy's population? What genocidal regime enables the distribution of 2 million tons of food into Gaza? Accusing Israel of genocide is the greatest lie of the century," he said.
He also called out New York's "antisemitic" mayor, Zohran Mamdani, as one of the people spreading this message. He said that since Mamdani's election "many Jews no longer feel safe in New York."
Netanyahu said the "simple truth" was not that Israel committed genocide but that it prevented one, saying "that's exactly what Mr. Mamdani's Hamas buddies would have done to us if we had not stopped them."
Netanyahu says he 'drew a red line' on same podium 14 years ago
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began his speech with a reference to his notorious General Assembly appearance in 2012, when he stood with illustrated graphics depicting how near to creating a nuclear bomb he thought Iran was.
"Ladies and gentlemen, 14 years ago I stood on this podium and I drew a red line," he said. "I vowed to prevent Iran's murderous dictatorship from developing atomic bombs. Nuclear weapons that could destroy the state of Israel, nuclear weapons that could threaten the whole world. That's exactly what we did."
Netanyahu said that while it was "very hard" to devastate Iran's nuclear facilities, he said it was "one of the easiest decisions" he'd had to make as prime minister, "because if we hadn't done it, we'd all be dead."
Iran contends that its nuclear program was for peaceful purposes like electricity generation, a claim that Israel and the US dispute.
Netanyahu also referred to Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa's call for Israel to pull back its forces in the Golan Heights border area, addressing al-Sharaa and saying "you should know that the Jews have been in the Golan Heights since the days of Moses," referring to the Old Testament prophet thought to have lived more than 3,000 years ago.
Delegates leave the chamber in large group as Netanyahu enters
As Israeli Prime Minster Benjamin Netanyahu's turn to speak at the UN General Assembly came, a large number of delegates from various countries stood up and left the chamber to cheers and jeering.
Only after repeated appeals for calm was it possible for him to begin his address.
"Before I begin, just a quick announcement: if there any other moral cowards who have not yet left this hall, please do so now. Thank you very much," Netanyahu said.
He returned to the issue of the walkout later when discussing his decision to target Iran and its nuclear capabilities.
"Now do you want to hear the ultimate irony? In defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall. In fact, I want you to know that many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran's nukes," he claimed, saying "it's hard to imagine more mind-blowing hypocrisy."
Protesters had also gathered outside the building in New York ahead of Netanyahu's address. Some were arrested by police. A Democratic nominee for New York's 10th congressional district in November's midterm elections, Brad Lander, also joined the demonstrators, albeit wearing a suit and tie rather than a slogan-laden T-shirt.
READ: Nigeria and US sign mining deal
On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Nigeria and the United States agreed to increase American investiment in the West African nation's mining sector.
Nigeria's Minister for Solid Minerals Dele Alake announced the deal on Thursday, a day after he signed the framework deal with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau.
"Nigeria cannot remain a source of raw materials while others capture most of the value. We want more local processing, quality jobs, stronger skills and greater opportunities for Nigerian businesses," Alake said.
Read more about the US-Nigeria mining agreement.
Abbas calls for saving two-state solution and Palestinian self-determination
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas used his remarks to implore nations to support the two-state solution, saying his people seek a non-militarized, democratic Palestinian state that can exist alongside Israel in peace.
He said the first step to preserving the idea of such a solution is to protect the lands upon which a future Palestinian state would be based, as well as protecting those people who have lived upon them for generations.
Abbas underscored the fact that the Palestinian people would not be displaced by "military occupation, nor settlement expansion, annexation, nor settler terrorism."
He further said that "no lasting security can be built upon the occupation of another people and the denial of its legitimate rights," adding that the Palestinians have their own plans for an independent state and emphasizing the need to end the Israeli occupation in order to negotiate a solution.
This plan, Abbas said, is based on protecting Palestinians from displacement, preserving their lands, democratically renewing political institutions and building a new sovereign Palestinian state — with east Jerusalem as its capital.
All of this, he said, would be carried out with a "commitment to international law" and the right to exercise self-determination with the aim of achieving security and peace with Israel to, "pave the way to regional integration, cooperation, prosperity and security for everyone."
Abbas concluded his remarks by thanking those 160 nations whom he said have recognized Palestinian statehood, calling for its inclusion in the United Nations.
Palestinian leader Abbas blasts US and Israel in General Assembly
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, addressing those gathered at the UNGA via video because the US State Department refused to allow the Palestinian delegation into the country, has rejected Washington's approach as "unlawful and punitive."
Abbas described the denial of visas as a US failure to live up to its responsibility as the host nation of the international body.
Abbas quickly pivoted to blast Israel's "genocidal war" in Gaza, as well as the sanctioned "ethnic cleansing" perpetrated by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Saying that Israeli violations of international law put the two-state solution at grave risk, Abbas described the situation in Gaza, the West Bank and east Jerusalem as part of a "malicious colonial scheme" and warned of a "new Nakba."
He also referenced attacks on Muslim and Christian religious sites by radical Jews as having the potential to transform the current security situation into a wider religiously fueled conflict.
Not only Middle East, rising sea level threat also on slate for day 3 meetings
Beyond AI and the headline-grabbing conflict in the Middle East, the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday will discuss another pressing issue that impacts the world’s citizens — rising sea levels.
A high-level meeting is slated to begin at 10:00 a.m. (1400 GMT) on Thursday as swelling seas redraw coastlines and pose existential risks for islanders and those who live in low-lying areas near the shores of the world's oceans and seas.
The UN says nearly 900 million people live in such areas, adding that another one million could be impacted by mid-century.
Rising sea levels, says the UN, threaten not only land but also livelihoods and even the existence of entire nations. In the words of UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, "Rising seas are sinking futures."
Israeli and Palestinian leaders set to address UNGA on day 3
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas are both expected to address members of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) on Thursday, with the issue of the Middle East writ large on the day 3 agenda.
Netanyahu, who is increasingly unpopular at home and abroad, will not meet with US officials or Arab leaders during his stay. His office cited a "tight schedule" as the reason, listing as many as nine meetings during his visit, including with the presidents of Argentina and Bolivia, the vice president of Colombia and the prime minister of Papua New Guinea.
The increasingly isolated Israeli leader's Palestinian counterpart, President Mahmoud Abbas, will also address the General Assembly. Abbas, however, will do so via video, as the US State Department refused to issue him an entry visa.
The broader subjects of Gaza's future and Palestinian statehood will also be topics of discussion. The UK will convene a meeting on Gaza's current and future status, and Saudi Arabia and Norway will host a ministerial meeting to hash out plans for the implementation of the so-called "two-state solution."
That's a wrap on Day 2 of the UNGA
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russian President Vladimir Putin for the ongoing war between the countries, calling him "patient zero."
The Ukrainian leader also announced new defense deals with Finland and Australia.
Elsewhere, Syrian leader Ahmed al-Sharaa called for the Israeli occupation of the Golan Heights to end, saying the territory belongs to Syria.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also addressed Israel, calling for what he described as the "genocide" in Gaza to stop.
This comes ahead of a speech by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the UN General Assembly on Thursday.

France on Putin at G20: U.S. to decide who is invited
As reported by an Ukrinform correspondent Spokesperson for the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs Pascal Confavreux said this in response to a question about an invitation for Putin to attend the G20 summit, which is due to be held in the United States later this year.
“This year, the United States holds the G20 presidency, and as the host country, it is responsible for organizing the discussions and determining the list of invitees,” the spokesperson said.
He declined to directly comment on the possibility of inviting Putin, instead stressing that France notes Russia’s growing international isolation.
“For our part, we would rather note Russia’s isolation, caused by one person’s decision to continue Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. This was also evident during yesterday’s UN Security Council meeting in New York,” the French Foreign Ministry representative said.
According to him, France’s current priority remains continuing and strengthening support for Ukraine so that its population can withstand Russian attacks, particularly ahead of winter.
The Spokesperson also recalled that France continues working within the Coalition of the Willing on reliable security guarantees for Ukraine.
“The continuation of Russian strikes on Ukraine in recent days, including last night, shows that at this stage Russia is in fact not ready to make peace and sit down at the negotiating table,” he added.
As Ukrinform reported, President Volodymyr Zelensky believes that the G20 summit in December could provide a platform for a substantive trilateral meeting between Ukraine, the United States and Russia.

The EU is considering accelerating the provision to Ukraine of €45 billion scheduled for 2027
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
22:09:38 EEST

The EU is considering accelerating the provision to Ukraine of €45 billion scheduled for 2027
Kyiv • UNN
The European Commission is considering moving up the second tranche of the loan for Ukraine to the first half of 2027 due to the budget deficit. Brussels expects reforms.
The European Commission is considering the possibility of bringing forward the provision to Ukraine of €45 billion earmarked for 2027 under the EU’s €90 billion loan program. Euractiv reports this, according to UNN.
"The European Commission is considering the possibility of bringing forward the second half of the €90 billion EU loan allocated for the whole of 2027 to the first half of the new year," the publication writes.
Brussels is facing calls to release the funds to Ukraine ahead of schedule, as, according to the government in Kyiv, the country is facing a budget deficit of €23.5 billion this year.
"To prevent a crisis and in view of the approaching harsh winter, Commission officials are now considering moving the bulk of the second tranche of €45 billion, intended for next year, to the first half of 2027 to meet Ukraine’s urgent needs," the publication adds.
According to Kyiv’s estimates, the budget deficit will amount to $32.6 billion in 2027.
According to an official familiar with the meeting, while the Ukrainian president insisted on accelerating deliveries of air defense systems, Ursula von der Leyen urged Zelenskyy to carry out reforms to unlock EU funds.
This year, Ukraine has not yet received a total of €37 billion in the form of an EU loan and funds from the European Peace Facility. At the same time, EU officials in Brussels are becoming increasingly frustrated by the slowdown in the pace of reforms in Ukraine.
It should be recalled
Canada is negotiating support for the EU loan to Ukraine, as Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks closer transatlantic ties to reduce his country’s dependence on the United States.

Türkiye's Fidan chairs OIC meeting, highlights Gaza and regional conflicts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:06:07 UTC
04:06:07 KST

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has chaired the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) Foreign Ministers’ Annual Coordination Meeting in New York, Turkish diplomatic sources said.
Thursday’s meeting was held on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly as Türkiye holds the rotating chairmanship of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers.
In his address, Fidan discussed Israel’s ongoing genocidal war in Gaza, as well as its occupation and annexation activities across Palestine and attacks on Syria and Lebanon, according to the sources.
He also addressed developments affecting the wider Islamic world, including the situations in Iran, Yemen, Libya, Sudan and Somalia.
Fidan stressed the importance of the OIC’s role in protecting the rights of Muslim minorities and communities.
Türkiye holds OIC chairmanship
Held annually during UN General Assembly week, the coordination meeting provides a platform for foreign ministers from OIC member states to exchange views alongside the organisation’s annual Council of Foreign Ministers meeting.
The Council of Foreign Ministers normally meets once a year but can also convene extraordinary sessions to address major issues affecting the Islamic world.
Türkiye assumed the rotating chairmanship after hosting the 51st session of the Council of Foreign Ministers in Istanbul on June 21-22, 2025, under the theme “The OIC in a Transforming World”.
Türkiye previously hosted Council of Foreign Ministers meetings in 1976, 1991 and 2004.

04:04:22 KST

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's cabinet adopted a decree law on Thursday banning burqas and niqabs in schools and capping the number of students with a poor command of Italian per class.
The measure comes amid wider restrictions on Muslim women’s religious attire across Europe, which rights groups and Muslim communities have criticised as discriminatory and as limiting freedom of religion and expression.
According to Meloni, the decree introduces "a 30 percent cap on the number of students in a class who do not have an adequate command of Italian, more tools for learning our language, and a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools,"
If a child seriously struggles to integrate at school, social services will be called and the parents will be obliged to attend free Italian lessons.
Failure to comply will be punished with a fine of up to $1,140 (1,000 euros).
Italy is a frontline country for migration and integration is a hot campaign issue ahead of next year's general election.
Save the Children warned that forcing children to change schools or enrol in a different institution from their peers simply because of their nationality or limited proficiency in Italian would "create 'first-class' and 'second-class' students".
But Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said, "inadequate language proficiency... hinders educational progress".
"Parental participation in their child's educational path is fundamental for academic success", he told journalists.
Valditara said there were 34,000 school classes in Italy in which over 30 percent of the students are foreign.
But most of those would be not be affected by the new law, which targets new arrivals rather than those born in Italy or who attended kindergarten.
The 30 percent limit on the number of foreign students per class was established in a ministerial memorandum in 2010.
But the limit was flexible, and could be raised in cases involving foreign students with adequate language skills, such as foreign students born in Italy, or lowered when foreign students have a poor command of Italian.
‘New witch hunt at expense of children’
Opposition leader Elly Schlein accused the government of "a new witch hunt at the expense of children".
The burqa ban was "a matter of security", Meloni said in a television interview after the cabinet meeting.
"When a woman—or worse, a young girl—is forced to cover her face, she is being denied fundamental rights and the very integration that is so often loudly championed," she said.
A crackdown on the use of burqas in schools was called for in July by the National Future (FN) party.
The FN, which is not part of the governing coalition, is further to the right than Meloni's and has emerged as a major challenger, rising sharply in the polls since launching in February.

On Thursday President Donald Trump’s pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration appeared before lawmakers for a crucial Senate confirmation hearing in which she repeatedly distanced herself from the president’s false statements about drugs and vaccines but declined to say the president was ever wrong.
Heidi Overton, a physician who currently serves as a White House health aide, told lawmakers at the hearing that the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is both safe and effective, as are all other vaccines that are currently recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. When questioned about the abortion drug mifepristone, she said the medication has met FDA safety and efficacy standards. She also said that she has seen no evidence that the use of Tylenol during pregnancy causes autism. All of that puts her at odds with the president.
Still, when asked if she believes it’s possible for the president to be wrong about something, Overton refused to answer directly, saying only that he “sets the policy directions, but he works with all of his advisers to get the best information.”

Trump nominated Overton to head up the FDA in August, just a week after she stood behind the president as he signed an executive order aimed at altering the childhood vaccine schedule. That order called for the MMR vaccine to be broken into three separate shots. During the signing ceremony, the president claimed, without evidence, that the vaccine can be “lethal” to children.

In 2023 Overton wrote in a policy position for the right-wing America First Policy Institute that the drug is “dangerous to women.”
On Thursday, however, she declined to say what her plans for the drug will be if her nomination is approved. Overton said that the FDA will continue to examine the postmarket safety of all medications.

Overton laid out one major priority for the FDA if she is approved: cracking down on illicit e-cigarette products. But she defended the agency’s recent decision to approve several flavored vape products, which have been criticized as appealing to minors, saying they can be effective at helping adults to quit cigarettes.

Mona got a scan while on holiday. It uncovered what had gone undetected for months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:03:38 UTC
04:03:38 KST

IN BRIEF:
- Pancreatic cancer is common but symptoms can be easily missed.
- Researchers say more funding is needed for better patient outcomes.
When Mona Thind went for a gastrointestinal scan in late 2024, she'd known something wasn't right for months.
At 52, she had been told by doctors that the pain she felt around her ribs and upset stomach was likely caused by constipation or poor diet, easily treated by upping her fluid intake.
Months later, the pain returned, and as she was setting off for a holiday to Byron Bay in northern NSW, her father raised concerns.
"As I was walking out of his house, he said to me, 'My heart tells me we should do a scan ... I feel it in my gut'," Mona told SBS News.
At the time, she recalled, she laughed about it, thinking he was a typical overprotective father.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
But at the upper gastrointestinal scan in Byron Bay, she knew the sonographer had found something.
"I saw the look on her face," Mona said. "I came home, and everything happened."
Mona had pancreatic cancer. In the 15 months that followed, she underwent six rounds of chemotherapy and major surgery, gruelling treatment which she pushed through.
"When I was first diagnosed, I didn't cry," she said. "I wasn't sad every day; I just went, this is what it is."
But on the day she was congratulated for beating cancer, she "fell apart" for the first time.
"My dad promised me that he would be there for every chemo treatment for me. And he died on my last chemotherapy day. He was there for every single treatment," she said.
"He was my pillar of strength."
A major disease, commonly undetected
Pancreatic cancer is the eighth most commonly diagnosed cancer in Australia.
It occurs when malignant cells develop in parts of the pancreas, and it's estimated that one in 70 people will be diagnosed with the disease by the age of 85, according to the Cancer Council.
Senior researcher at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research's Cox Lab, Dr Amelia Parker, says it's also one of the most understudied and complex cancers to treat.
"For pancreatic cancer, less than 13 per cent of patients will survive at five years, and part of the reason for that is that a lot of the symptoms associated with early-stage pancreatic cancer are largely vague or not readily diagnosed," she told SBS News.
"This means that patients often aren't seeking medical help until the cancer is much more advanced."
Like other cancers, once pancreatic cancer has spread to other parts of the body, it is much more difficult to treat, leading to lower survival rates.
"We're working very hard to improve our detection of those cancers so that patients who have that disease are diagnosed earlier and have all of the most effective treatments available to them," Parker said.
Parker believes research gaps driven by dwindling investment directly impact patient outcomes.
"There has been less investment in research funding historically. And that's really hampered our efforts to both understand the disease and use that understanding to develop new and better treatments."
She said her research was making "real strides" in improving understanding of the disease, and she hoped it would translate into better outcomes for patients.
"But for that to happen, for there to be innovations in treatment, we really need to invest in funding," she said, adding that funding for cancer research was "highly competitive".
"There's more research out there that would make a difference," she said.
Kerry Strydom, CEO of the Australian Cancer Research Foundation, hopes to change that.
"I'm absolutely convinced that funding is the way that we will advance breakthroughs," she told SBS News.
"You've seen how the pace of technology improvements has accelerated over the last few years — we need to get those tools, that equipment, the latest technology, into the hands of our scientists, and I'm convinced that it'll get us closer to a world free from the burden of cancer.
"It's really important that we continue to back brilliant researchers so that they can turn their promising ideas into breakthroughs."
Hope for future advancements
In August, the US Food and Drug Administration approved a new oral prescription medication, daraxonrasib, sold under the brand name Rasonque, for previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer.
Parker from the Garvan Institute says that this marks a significant step forward for people diagnosed with one of the toughest common cancers.
"We work closely with our international colleagues to make sure that Australian patients could potentially have access to the same quality of care as in other parts of the world."
But Parker's ambition was clear: "My overall hope is that we'll be able to develop new treatments that will mean a cancer diagnosis is not one that's met with a lot of fear and uncertainty, that it's easily treatable and patients can look forward to a very long life ahead of them."
"So in many ways, I hope that maybe I'm out of a job in the future," she said.
Mona is hopeful that more funding for cancer research in Australia and abroad will pave the way for new treatments.
"It's very important to get that research so that we can treat people," she said.
"But what it really translates to is hope ... It's that birthday that you would have missed because there's no treatment, that trip you would put off because you may not be here.
"It's not just about the treatment; it's what you're giving back to the patients and their families and their friends."

'Spinning out of control': What came before OpenAI’s Medicare hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:03:31 UTC
04:03:31 KST

IN BRIEF
- The Australian government says an OpenAI agent "scaled the fence" of a Medicare portal, accessing statistics but no patient records.
- One of the first known AI hacking incidents is known as the Hugging Face attack.
Just as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman finished warning the world about the dangers of AI at the United Nations, news broke closer to home: one of his company's own agents had broken into an Australian government portal.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that in June an agent linked to the ChatGPT developer gained unauthorised access to the public–facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service Portal.
Both OpenAI and the Australian government have said no personal information was accessed during the breach.
But the nature of the incident has raised some concerns.
According to Albanese, the hack occurred after OpenAI's research team utilised an internal model to conduct internet-based research on public spending in medicine.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"There's an AI agent looking for information, asking questions. There were blocks clearly, which were coming back telling the AI agent, no. The AI agent found a way around those blocks. Didn't accept no for an answer," Albanese said.
"One of the issues here is we could not find precedent for this. But others, there may be, but not that we're aware of."
Dominic Meagher, a research fellow at ANU's Crawford School of Public Policy, told SBS News that while "this particular incident hasn't made me feel panic, but it does reinforce what we've heard from a few other recent incidents".
He likened AI to "a car spinning out of control."
"This isn't someone trying to do something. This is a piece of technology that isn't behaving the way we expected. It's doing what it was told, and it's operating in its environment according to the laws of physics.
"I don't think there's any way that we're going to avoid some bizarre things happening in the next few years ... How we manage all this is going to be really important."
This is the first known case of an AI agent hacking into a government portal — but it is only part of a pattern of various AI models going rogue and hacking different networks with different intentions, on several occasions.
The Hugging Face attack
One of the most infamous AI hacking incidents is known as the Hugging Face attack, with some describing it as the first time AI escaped human control.
In July, about 700 OpenAI models that were under development started breaching internal company tools, gained access to the internet and eventually hacked Hugging Face, an online library for AI models.
Later, the Reuters news agency reported that Hugging Face was not the only target and that the models had also hacked into other companies.
"These AI models have really been selectively evolved rather than coded, which is why they don't always behave in the way you're expecting," Meagher said.
"It's quite a tricky thing that people are working on. It raises a whole lot of interesting questions that I think are unresolved."
Anthropic hacking incidents
In late July, just weeks after the Hugging Face attacks were announced, Anthropic, developer of Claude AI, announced that while its models were being tested by an Israeli start-up, Irregular, they had accidentally connected online and hacked three companies in January.
At the time, Claude said in a statement that "these are three isolated incidents and were not part of a controlled, experimental comparison. We must therefore be cautious about drawing conclusions from them".
Later this month, they confirmed a fourth company was also hacked during the time.
A 'similar behaviour by Meta'
In August, Meta joined the chain, with the company announcing that one of its AI models hacked another company during a cybersecurity test.
The company announced at the time that its model "exploited a security vulnerability in a third-party service, in a manner similar to previously reported instances with other companies".
Hacking a gym class
During the same time, Andrew Bird, an Australian working with OpenClaw, a popular AI agent software that runs through the Claude service, reported another AI hack incident — this time targeting a gym.
He asked the agent to book him a gym class; the class was booked out, but the AI agent found a solution: it kicked someone off the waiting list and added Bird's name.
"This is a case where [the AI agent] did what he was asked to do, but not what he [Bird] wanted, because that's an impolite way of behaving. And clearly the gym didn't intend for that to be available," Meagher said.
"But he [Bird] didn't specify not to do that because why would he? It would never have occurred to him that that was an option."
Google hacks
Google announced last week that its model Gemini hacked into three companies during a test of its cyber-security in May.
During the hacks, Gemini found public information online and guessed credentials to access three websites it thought were within the scope of its test, Heather Adkins, Google's vice president of security engineering, said in a statement.
In one case, the Gemini model guessed passwords until it gained access to a protected system. In the other two cases, the model found credentials in a public repository that let it access protected systems, according to the Wall Street Journal, which first reported the news on Friday.

French President Emmanuel Macron denied CIA warnings of a possible Russian drone operation targeting southern Europe and pledged Thursday to send "military assets" to "protect" the Yanbu site, a key component of Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure network on Thursday.
In a joint interview aired on broadcasters France 2 and TF1 he said "We can deny this piece of information, the CIA did not inform France of this information and the Italian defence minister said the same thing".
On Thursday, Spanish daily newspaper El Mundo published an article which declared that the CIA had alerted several southern European governments to a possible Russian drone operation targeting Spain, France and Italy.

Pledge to send military to protect Saudi Arabia on Red Sea oil route

He detailed that this would amount to "military assets, meaning troops, radar systems, and defensive systems to protect this site, but we will not be engaging in any conflict. Our aim is to help stabilise the oil market."
The pipeline has played a crucial role during the war in the Middle East, allowing Saudi Arabia to bypass the Strait of Hormuz to export its oil. It can transport 5 million barrels of crude oil per day, with the capacity to temporarily increase to 7 million barrels.
The port, which also houses significant oil storage and refining facilities, has become a target for Houthi forces in Yemen, backed by Iran, during the current conflict in the Middle East.
"As soon as one of these locations is relaxed, the immediate impact is seen at the gas pump," the head of state added. "You'll see it in two days."

Addressing Russia's ongoing and intensifying hybrid campaign against Europe, Macron referred to the drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport on the night of 4-5 August 2026, which German authorities have attributed to Russia.
Macron said France had not experienced a comparable attack so far but warned that one remained possible. "When you ask me, 'Could this happen?' my answer is yes," he said.
The French President stressed that Russia considers “Europe to be the strategic heart of Ukraine," while also saying that the possibility of Russia seeking to launch an attack against Europe was "plausible."
"It is clear that there have been several signs indicating that Russia is preparing to do this," he stated.
As speculation mounts over Russia’s possible mobilisation plans, Macron said that a new mobilisation of around 300,000 personnel was a “credible scenario” that was “often shared”.
The French leader said he viewed this as a sign that Moscow was prepared to "make even greater sacrifices to take over the entire Donbas", estimating that Russia would need to advance for “a year and a half, two years” at the current pace to conquer the territories it does not yet control in that region, “with terrible losses and suffering for Ukraine.”

Dmitry Glukhovsky’s new novel ‘Registration,’ about Russians seeking to cash in on the war, has been called an émigré’s rebuke to those who stayed behind. Is that fair?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:02:15 UTC
04:02:15 KST

Dmitry Glukhovsky’s new novel ‘Registration,’ about Russians seeking to cash in on the war, has been called an émigré’s rebuke to those who stayed behind. Is that fair?
On September 17, Dmitry Glukhovsky posted his new novel, “Registratsiya” (“Registration”), online for free. Set in wartime Russia in the 2020s, it follows the pregnant girlfriend of a contract soldier as she tries to marry him as quickly as possible to qualify for benefits. The book is still stirring debate on social media. Many readers fault Glukhovsky, who has lived outside Russia since 2022, for judging those who stayed so harshly while he himself is relatively safe. Literary critic Liza Birger examines whom Glukhovsky condemns, and why.
Warning: This article, like Glukhovsky’s novel, contains profanity.
In 1920, Nadezhda Teffi published the story “Ke fer?” (“What to Do?”) in the first issue of the Parisian émigré newspaper Posledniye Novosti. Amid snippets of Parisian conversation, she described a bewildered Russian general emerging onto the Place de la Concorde and repeating: “All this, gentlemen, is very well, of course. Very well indeed. But que faire? What do we do?”
More than a century later, Glukhovsky has written “Registration,” in which “What do we do?” again becomes the prevailing tone — merciless and deeply bitter. Beyond the painful bewilderment of the present day, there is real horror here, too: the story of an ordinary person turning into a monster.
Monsters have long been Glukhovsky’s central subject, well before he himself was cast as one in the eyes of Russian society: in October 2022, he was added to the “foreign agents” registry, and in 2023, he was sentenced in absentia to eight years in a penal colony for an antiwar Telegram post. No one has done more to find Stephen King–style everyday horror in Russian life.
Mutants inhabit a future subway system in “Metro 2033” (2002) — and, as history has shown, that was hardly the worst way things could turn out. In “Sumerki” (“Twilight,” 2007), an ancient Mayan curse creeps from the jungles of the Yucatán into a Moscow translator’s apartment. In “Tekst” (“Text,” 2017), the source of horror turns out to be an ordinary narcotics officer’s phone. And in “Post” (“The Outpost,” 2019–2021), madness crosses a bridge over the Volga, spread by the words of a “demonic prayer.” The only way to escape is to puncture your own eardrums — much as with Russian propaganda. The monsters almost always come from outside, while Moscow remains the center of the world — as though Glukhovsky cannot imagine it as a source of evil, though today we might argue otherwise. What frightens him much more is the horror and despair of the rest of Russia.
Stephen King wrote that a plot is a fossil waiting to be dug up, and that “we make up horrors to help us cope with the real ones.” Glukhovsky has found that in present-day Russia, there is no need to dig: monsters are literally around the corner. In this new world, we have to protect ourselves from ourselves above all.
“Registration” opens with a sketch of seemingly peaceful life in Vologda. Tatyana, whose son Sasha is a contract soldier, is getting their new apartment in order. While he is at the front, she uses his pay to cover the mortgage. Meanwhile, Sasha’s girlfriend Ulyana, a massage therapist at a small salon, vapes a strawberry-flavored e-cigarette with a friend (“Kristina laughed melon, Ulyana strawberry”) and dreams of the future: she has just learned that she is pregnant with Sasha’s child.
The opening pages are the novel’s best. Here Glukhovsky still has the energy to write beautifully: “Things grew orderly; things grew clean. Life was finally doing what Tatyana told it to. It obeyed her puffy, crimson hands, as if scalded, smoothing itself down and lining up in rows.” Later, horror displaces that beauty. Sasha, it turns out, has gone missing in the war. When he is found in a Moscow hospital without his legs, his mother and girlfriend begin fighting over the benefits while he is still alive.
So Ulyana travels from Vologda to Moscow. She urgently wants to marry Sasha because, with a child, she is entitled to two-thirds of the benefits. They face delays in registering their marriage, and someone demands a bribe. In Moscow, she stays with her aunt and uncle, Marina and Maksim, members of the city’s intelligentsia. Maksim runs a small bookstore beyond the Third Ring Road. He boldly keeps books by “foreign agents” on the shelves — until activists show up with prosecutors — reads Meduza through a VPN, and tries to keep his composure. Marina runs a decorating agency and takes contracts from the mayor’s office. To keep her business, she reluctantly puts portraits of “heroes of the special military operation” on bus stops for May 9. Their family has “crawled away” from the war. Their son Kirill has already gone to Georgia via the Verkhny Lars border crossing and come back because “it gets a little old,” and he keeps partying happily despite the draft summons hanging over him.
Bringing Moscow intellectuals and a massage therapist from Vologda together feels rather contrived. In real life, they are probably farther apart than the émigré writer is from his characters. But the contrivance lets Glukhovsky show a cross-section of society and leave no one in the story unstained. Émigrés come in for just as much criticism. Consider Kirill’s speech about how Muscovites brought Tbilisi “the best Moscow had to offer — matcha lattes, kink parties, and dog-walking services,” yet the Georgian capital still cannot measure up to the Russian one. Or Maksim’s school friend Mitya, who calls from Israel and says that once they dig all the “little Arabs” out of the tunnels in Gaza, there will be peace. “Isn’t that the same as what’s happening back home?” Maksim asks.
But gathering everyone in one place and giving each a line so no one remains innocent has a downside. For Glukhovsky, the world that willingly yields to evil and adjusts to it is, above all, a world of women. He does more than show how people adapt to evil: again and again, he shows women doing it faster and better. The picture is strange. Men started the war and men fight it, yet in Glukhovsky’s novel, it is mostly women who adapt to it, bargain, and inform on others. Women send men to war, too. And women are first in line for the benefits it brings.
Hi, I’m Vladislav Gorin.
I’m the host of Meduza’s daily Russian-language news podcast. This summer, the Russian authorities opened a criminal case against me — not for committing a crime, but for telling the truth about Russia and its war against Ukraine.
Because the Kremlin has branded me a criminal, I can’t go home. I also can’t safely travel to countries like Turkey — even though it’s a NATO member — because I could be arrested and extradited to Russia. I can’t even renew my passport at the consulate anymore.
None of this is going to stop me. I know there are hundreds of thousands of people in Russia who don’t want this war and who still believe in freedom and democracy, and they deserve access to independent journalism. Please support Meduza so I can keep reaching them.
Maksim, ever ready to discuss morality, “sniffed at it but ate anyway” — not always realizing that Marina’s city contracts largely supported the family. Eventually, he gives in, too, and takes books by his beloved “foreign agents” off the shelves: “Bykov and Ulitskaya gazed up at him from the box like kittens peering from the bottom of a bucket on their way to be drowned.” Sasha was a kind boy who felt sorry for slugs as a child. He went to war so no one, “not the cops, not anyone,” could “treat him like shit” anymore. But it is never entirely clear whether that was his own idea or whether his mother sent him to earn money. At the end, Tatyana remembers taking him to the military enlistment office and watching him look at her from the bus “as though it were a prank, as though any moment they’d call the whole thing off and let him go home for lunch.”
Men are “easy to transport by train,” Ulyana thinks when she sees a group of uniformed men of different ages at the station. “You can fit a lot in at once.” Tatyana’s husband Vitalya does little but grunt and wait for a drink to ease his hangover, and no one listens even when he tries to say something. In her fight for the benefits, Ulyana learns to use AI to write denunciations to the FSB and demands that her marriage to the dying Sasha be registered immediately. In the final scene, her transformation into a monster is complete.
“We’ll wait it out, we’ll sit tight, we’ll outlast them for sure. That one died, and this one will die too…” members of the underground scrawl on ads around the city in an act of covert defiance. “But will the people who make it through be the same people who hoped to wait it out?” Maksim wonders. That may be the most complete summary of “Registration.” The book is not really about the marriage registration Ulyana is pursuing. It is an urgent attempt to register — to record — the reality of waiting out the war, waiting for who knows what.
Nothing ages faster than language, which Glukhovsky has always treated as a key to making his work feel current and true to life. Yet his attempts to capture it do not always succeed. Tatyana’s Vologda habit of clearly pronouncing unstressed o’s, sayings like “dick-cunt-Dzhigurda,” and the endless Dovlatov and Bulgakov quotes Maksim seems to use in place of his own words already sound like relics of another time. “Registration” keeps reminding us that its events are happening right now — yet by the end, that “now” sounds a little like “yesterday.”
The decision to post the novel online seems driven by a need to join a conversation before it is too late, though that conversation is nearly over already. Glukhovsky himself tries not to see a divide between “those who left” and “those who stayed” — or, more precisely, any fundamental difference between them. But judging by readers’ first reactions, people inside Russia see the novel as an accusation, and an unfair one, precisely because they no longer recognize their country in this portrait.
Still, the novel should not be read as an accusation or a hatchet job. That is not what “Registration” is about. It is an émigré writer’s attempt to imagine life on the other side of Russia’s border. Is it hard to write a novel about Russia in the 2020s from afar? No harder than writing one about the 19th century or the year 2033. Besides, writers rarely leave home anyway; being away from the thick of events is perfectly normal for them. Whatever else it is, Glukhovsky wrote “Registration” to record and understand what is happening, not to condemn. The book is merciless to everyone, not just the so-called “stayers.” In interviews and essays, Glukhovsky often says “we,” repeating that evil can be found in each of us and that our defeat is collective.
That is also the subject of his book “My. Dnevnik padeniya” (“We: Diary of a Fall”), published by Vidim Books in 2024. It collects columns and essays dating back to 2012, along with retrospective commentary in which he sees them as telling the story of a catastrophe. “Registration,” too, is about any of “us” who tries to wait it out, look away, or somehow come to terms with the new reality. It is about those who cannot go on reading about horrors forever (“life now was not made up of ugliness alone, and it was impossible to look only at the ugliness without wanting to drop dead”) but have no idea what to do — ke fer?

Estudio Zero shapes pink Mexican co-living complex after sound wave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:00:27 UTC

Estudio Zero shapes pink Mexican co-living complex after sound wave
Mexican practice Estudio Zero has created a co-living apartment building rendered in pink-toned concrete with a series of arched forms informed by sound waves in Puerto Escondido, Oaxaca.
Known as Amplitude Coliving, the 390-square-metre complex was completed in 2025 on a 315.5-square-metre site in La Punta, a coastal neighbourhood known for small-scale, independent construction.
Estudio Zero, which is based in Querétaro, worked with the client to personify the idea of amplitude, the physical shape of sound waves and the way energy travels and grows in intensity.
"We took that literally and translated it into the architecture – you can actually read the waveform in the facade, in the way the arches and columns rise and taper," the studio told Dezeen, explaining that the design also represents the energy of the client.
"From there it became a shared language between client and studio – not just a form, but a way of thinking about how energy and community move through the building."
The complex is organised as a sequence of courtyards, open-air corridors and interconnected common areas that allow circulation to progress into levels of social interaction.
A courtyard sits at the centre of the plan with a pool, shared kitchen and dining area and serves as the social heart of the complex. In the co-living plan, individuals rent rooms and share the common spaces.
"That's the whole idea behind this coliving model," the studio said, "not to program those encounters, but to design a courtyard that gives people every reason to be in the same place and let the connection happen on its own."
Open-air balconies with scalloped railings line the courtyard and transition to three different apartment types – studios, larger units with private garden spaces and double-height loft units on the upper level of the main facade with alternative roof vaults.
Tied to the Oaxacan coastal landscape, the interior and exterior colour palette includes terracotta-pink, hand-rendered stucco, board-formed concrete and tropical hardwood doors, window frames and custom millwork.
The warm, natural materials contrast with glass block that filters light in the bedroom, delicate steel spiral staircases and cable railings that add a nautical touch to the mass.
"The tapered, hourglass-shaped concrete columns that flare out to meet the balcony slab. Visually, they read almost like a waveform, tying the structural language directly back to the 'amplitude' concept," the studio said, explaining that all of the details reinforce the idea of the building as something in motion rather than a static object.
Opposing openings, shaded open-air corridors, deep overhangs and spatial porosity keep air flowing through the building, while the thermal mass of the concrete and stucco moderates internal temperature swings.
Meanwhile, solar panels are paired with battery storage to keep the building running during tropical weather events.
Other recent projects in Mexico that deploy a similar pink scheme include a residential complex by V Taller in Tulum centred around a tower, blocky beach housing by Reyes Rios + Larrain in Dzemul and a renovated apartment building by Heryco in Queretaro.
The photography is by Alex Krotkov.

The EU has added former RT France chief Xenia Fedorova to its sanctions list, accusing her of spreading tKremlin’s propaganda in French media as part of Russia’s broader hybrid campaign against Europe.

Under the sanctions, her assets in the EU will be frozen, and EU citizens and companies may not provide her with funds or other economic resources.
As of Thursday, her listing brings the number of people targeted under the EU’s regime on Russia’s destabilizing activities to 81 individuals, along with 20 entities.
From RT France to expulsion order
As president and director of information at RT France – the French branch of Russian state-backed network RT – Fedorova helped spread the Russian state broadcaster’s editorial line, including pro-Moscow messaging about the war in Ukraine.

Russia Solved the Censorship Problem
Those views also covered Western support for Kyiv, NATO, and diplomatic relations between Russia and the EU.
In 2024, her French residence permit was extended for 10 years.

On July 29, France ordered Fedorova to leave the country and placed her under house arrest, requiring her to report to police daily.

Russia’s pressure on France

Latvia and Estonia responded by imposing national sanctions on both men, while the UK criticized the EU’s move and said it intends to keep their sanctions.
On Thursday, Marine Le Pen, the far-right National Rally leader and front-runner to succeed Emmanuel Macron in France’s 2027 presidential election, said she would end financial aid to Ukraine and denied France is at war with Russia.

Scientists probe connection between deadly frog disease and coal wastewater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Scientists probe connection between deadly frog disease and coal wastewater in national park
In short:
A study found higher amounts of chytrid fungus in a frog species exposed to coalmine wastewater compared to nearby unexposed sites.
The mine company said any causal link between altered water chemistry changes and severity of infection was speculative.
What's next?
Scientists said water quality monitoring programs should include factors like frog health.
Frogs in Australia's oldest national park have higher rates of a deadly fungus when exposed to wastewater from a coalmine compared to unexposed waterways, a study suggests.
The study, published in the Journal of Hazardous Materials Advances last month, looked at chytrid fungus levels in two species of frog in Royal National Park, downstream from the Metropolitan Mine, south of Sydney.
Lead author Shannon Kaiser, an ecotoxicologist from Macquarie University, said wastewater from the mine could not definitively be identified as the cause of the observed disease pattern.
"However, the association is concerning and suggests pollution and wildlife disease risk may interact in freshwater ecosystems,"
Mr Kaiser said water quality monitoring programs should be expanded to reflect the potential disease risk to animals from environmental changes.
Typically water monitoring measures things like pollution, temperature and oxygen.
"Our results suggest biological effects, including frog health and pathogen loads, should also be considered," Mr Kaiser said.
In response, a spokesperson for the mine's operator Peabody, said any causal link between water chemistry changes and frog infection intensity described in the study was speculative.
The study was undertaken between December 2022 and February 2023, a few months after unlicensed discharges of coal contaminated water from Metropolitan Mine overflowed into Camp Gully Creek.
The NSW Environment Protection Authority fined Peabody more than $500,000 and issued clean-up orders along with new regulatory conditions after the incident.
A Peabody spokesperson said it had invested more than $1.5 million in upgrades since 2022 to reduce discharge risk.
"Including expanded water storage capacity and [Metropolitan Mine] now publishes real-time water quality data on its website covering some of the parameters examined in the study," they said.
"Metropolitan separately funds a three-year program in the Royal National Park to support rehabilitation of the southern stuttering frog, a species affected by chytrid fungus."
What happened to the frogs?
Cooper Riach, from Sutherland Shire Environment Centre which funded the study, raised concerns about frog health after seeing the coal waste enter Camp Gully Creek in 2022.
"You could put your hand into the water and just swish your hand around a bit and all this oily, thick, viscous substance would come off the base of the creek," he said.
"We came across a little green frog, which had unfortunately gotten caught up in all this, and it had just got covered in this coal waste."
Mr Kaiser saw a photo of the frog and decided to study how exposure to wastewater might impact adult amphibian body condition, immunity, and disease outcomes.
Frogs were sampled from sites both exposed and unexposed to wastewater discharge from the coalmine.
Unexposed sites included other tributary creeks to the Hacking River, and points on the river before the mine.
There were 166 frogs found across 25 unexposed sites, and 180 frogs from 22 exposed sites.
Most of these frogs were either the leaf green tree frog (Dryopsophus phyllochrous) or the Stony Creek frog (Rhyaconastes lesueurii).
Forty-five of the frogs were swabbed to see if they had the chytrid fungus, which can infect their skin.
"Because frogs rely on their skin to regulate water and salts, heavy infections can cause the disease chytridiomycosis, which can be fatal," Mr Kaiser said.
Eighteen frogs tested positive for the fungus across both exposed and unexposed sites.
Leaf green frogs in exposed sites were more severely infected compared to unexposed sites.
"[Leaf green] frogs in exposed streams carried higher disease load," Mr Kaiser said.
"It dictates whether an infection remains harmless or becomes fatal. A frog can be infected, but not be lethally impacted."
Leaf green frogs that were dead or showing signs of late-stage chytridiomycosis were only found in exposed sites.
But the infection intensity did not differ greatly between exposed and unexposed sites for the Stony Creek frog.
The overall number of frogs across both species and their body condition did not differ significantly between sites downstream of the mine and areas that did not receive wastewater.
Could something else influence frog disease?
Mr Kaiser said there could be other reasons the frogs had an increased transmission rate of chytrid in tested exposure sites.
Most of the exposed sites were in the Hacking River where having a higher density of frogs, compared to smaller creek areas, could influence fungus spread.
"It could be that something else is entering that stream that we're not aware of from further upstream from beyond the coalmine," he said.
An EPA spokesperson said it received the frog study and acknowledged the value of emerging environmental research for understanding potential impacts from mine discharges.
They said it had recently required the mine to engage independent experts to undertake macroinvertebrate monitoring in Camp Gully Creek.
"The EPA is currently reviewing the monitoring results to determine whether any further studies or actions are necessary," the EPA spokesperson said.

Text description provided by the architects. In Peruvian construction, brick masonry is rarely left exposed: it is built, plastered over, and disappears beneath the finish. Casa Berna begins by reversing this practice. The brick walls remain exposed, finished with a lime wash that lightens the surface without concealing it. Consequently, the bond, the joints, and the irregularities of the bricklaying remain visible on the entrance wall, the garden-facing facade, and in the living room. This is a constructive decision rather than a formal one, and it defines the character of the project.

Ukraine strikes 'very important' deal on new batch of Patriot missiles, Zelensky says
Ukraine has made a "very important" agreement on an upcoming package of missiles for U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 24 at a meeting with representatives of the Ukrainian community in the United States.
The announcement comes as Kyiv faces a critical shortage of air defense munitions, particularly of Patriots — the only weapons capable of reliably intercepting Russian ballistic missiles.
Zelensky told leaders of the Ukrainian community in the U.S. that more Patriot interceptors would be heading to Kyiv soon, though he did not disclose the country that will be providing the missiles.
"Today we reached an agreement — I won't say with whom — on a shipment of missiles for the Patriot systems," the president said, according to the Ukrainian outlet European Pravda.
"It's an important decision, a very important one. We've achieved a result."
Zelensky did not say when the missiles would be delivered or how many Ukraine would receive.
The news comes during Zelensky's visit to the U.S., where he has addressed the United Nations General Assembly and met with various world leaders, including U.S. President Donald Trump. He and Trump spoke about Ukraine's urgent need for Patriot supplies as winter nears, but no concrete decisions were announced following their talks.
Congressional records dated Sept. 15 indicate that the U.S. is ready to greenlight a transfer of 10 Patriot interceptors from Germany to Ukraine, though it is unclear when exactly Kyiv would receive the shipment. The package is valued at $29.6 million.
The U.S. State Department then announced on Sept. 18 that it had approved a possible sale of air defense equipment for Ukraine worth $2.7 billion. The package includes S-300 Clone and GAM-67 missiles, radar systems for countering drones, range-extended laser-guided air defense systems, counter-drone radars, and mobile launcher modification kits.
Since Trump took office again in 2025, the U.S. has ended large-scale defense funding and arms deliveries to Ukraine, leaving Kyiv to rely on support from other partners to obtain key weapons systems.
Patriot interceptors have been even harder to come by as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has diverted supplies to the Middle East.

Tomorrow, school students in Germany will take to the streets in protest against compulsory military service. According to DW, around 100 demonstrations are planned, reports UNN.
Details
Student demonstrations will take place across Germany. According to the “School Strike Against Compulsory Military Service” initiative (Schulstreik gegen Wehrpflicht), around 100 protest actions are planned for that day.
A spokesperson for the initiative told the dpa news agency that the students intend to continue the strike until the issue of introducing compulsory military service is removed from the agenda.

"This requires urgent and responsible intervention by the United Nations Security Council," he said.
The UN Trade and Development warned Thursday that Gaza is currently going through the worst economic crisis ever observed.
In the West Bank, violence by extremist Israeli settlers has surged, prompting Britain, France and Canada to impose economic sanctions.
With 160 countries now recognizing a State of Palestine, Abbas called on the UN Security Council to intervene urgently and responsibly.
"Today we say to the world: saving the solution begins with preserving the land on which the Palestinian state is to be established and protecting the people who live on it," he said.
Abbas said that Palestinians were heading toward legislative elections on November 28 "followed by the completion of the renewal of the institutions of the Palestinian National Council, followed by the Palestinian presidential elections."
In a letter sent in June 2025 to French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Abbas pledged to hold legislative and presidential elections on a fixed timetable.
On Wednesday, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot urged that those elections be held, amid mounting concerns in the international community they will be postponed due to logistical difficulties.
Those challenges relate to delivering voting materials to the Gaza Strip as well as securing Israeli visas for international observers to reach the West Bank, as requested by the European Union.

Majority of AFP complaints dismissed without investigation, figures show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:51:47 UTC
03:51:47 KST

More than half of complaints against AFP 'finalised' without investigation, figures show
In short:
Figures show Australian Federal Police have used discretionary powers to dismiss hundreds of allegations against officers without investigating them.
The figures were revealed in answers to questions on notice from the national racism inquiry.
What's next?
The inquiry is due to report back to the parliament by the end of the year.
More than half of all allegations made against Australian Federal Police officers have been "finalised" without investigation due to the use of discretionary powers the national watchdog says pose a risk of "denying procedural fairness".
Figures released by the AFP to the national inquiry into racism, hate, and violence directed at First Nations people reveal the number of complaints made against officers in the last five years.
Since July 2021, 512 complaints have been made about AFP officers' conduct, with 1,213 individual allegations identified.
Of those allegations, 643 were "finalised", without investigation, using a broad discretionary power available to the AFP under section 40TF of the legislation.
The Commonwealth Ombudsman has reviewed the AFP's operations several times and repeatedly raised concerns that the agency leans on section 40TF too often, especially for complaints about officers using excessive force.
"We observed complaints that were finalised without relevant evidentiary material having been identified or reviewed, failures to appropriately document clear reasons for decision-making," the ombudsman's latest annual review says.
"Used appropriately, section 40TF of the AFP Act can support the efficiency of the AFP's complaints framework. However, using the discretion too readily risks denying procedural fairness and deprives the AFP of opportunities for improvement."
Of the remaining 570 allegations, 283 remain under investigation, 63 have been established and 215 not established.
Independent senator for Victoria Lidia Thorpe said she would like the racism inquiry to recommend an independent national body to hold police accountable and crack down on section 40TF rulings.
"We know that there's good cops out there, but there are also bad cops out there, and the bad cops are doing bad things. So there needs to be accountability for the bad cops. And that's why we need an independent police oversight body with genuine independence from police," she said.
"We need to review that legislation so that the people out there that are experiencing bad behaviour from bad cops have an avenue, where it's not just being dismissed by the top cop, which is what's happening in this circumstance."
The AFP has been contacted for comment.
Complaints of racist conduct
The figures also break down complaints about racist conduct. Over the same five years, people made 25 complaints about racist conduct by AFP officers, containing 47 individual allegations.
Section 40TF powers were used to close 13 of those allegations without investigation. Another eight were investigated but not established, and 18 are still being investigated.
Senator Thorpe believes the number of complaints about racist conduct are vastly underestimated.
"Those numbers are very, very light-on. In fact, they're so light-on that I feel like putting my own complaint in from being assaulted by the AFP on the front lawns of parliament for all to see," she said, referencing an incident involving AFP officers at a protest in March 2023.
"A lot of people don't complain, because if you complain about the cops, then you're going to become a target for the cops … particularly Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. They don't complain about the assault and the violence and the racism."
Seven of the allegations made against AFP officers related to racist language and behaviour at work, including in group chats. The AFP said those were established, and officers faced disciplinary action, according to its answers to the inquiry.
"Of the seven established complaints, the disciplinary action included remedial action and retraining for five AFP appointees, and two AFP Appointees receiving a Notice to Show Cause pursuant to section 28 of the AFP Act," the AFP's answer reads.
"The AFP's values require all people to be treated with respect, and the AFP does not shy away from addressing poor behaviour or conduct that does not align with those values."
The parliamentary inquiry into racism, hate, and violence directed at Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people will consider the answers provided by the AFP before handing down its final report at the end of the year.
