'No eligible elector will be left behind': Goa CEO clarifies on 97 missing voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:52:42 UTC
02:52:42 KST

NEW DELHI: The Office of the Chief Electoral Officer of Goa on Thursday clarified the controversy surrounding 97 voters who were not included in the final electoral roll published in February 2026, saying the cases were subsequently processed through house-to-house visits and that many of the voters have since been enrolled.In a press note shared on X, the CEO's office said the 97 cases were separately processed by Booth Level Officers (BLOs) for completion of Form 6, the application used for inclusion of names in the electoral roll.
"Many have since been enrolled, while the remaining cases are being processed," the office said, adding that no eligible elector would be left out.The clarification comes amid a controversy over the exclusion of the 97 voters following Goa's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
What happened to 97 voters
According to an Indian Express report, the 97 voters had initially been flagged during the SIR process for what the Election Commission described as "logical discrepancies" in the electoral database.These discrepancies could arise from issues such as mismatches while linking an elector to parents or grandparents in older electoral rolls.The affected voters were subsequently given an opportunity to submit documents and objections.
In Goa, 649 electors came forward, following which Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) and Assistant EROs examined their cases. Officials found 97 cases where the earlier decisions needed to be reversed and the voters were eligible for inclusion.
However, the final electoral roll published on February 21, 2026, did not include the 97 names.
Software row at centre of controversy
The issue subsequently drew attention to the Election Commission's ECINet electoral-roll software.According to an Indian Express investigation, the Goa CEO's office sent eight communications between February 11 and 17 seeking a rollback or reversion facility that would allow the earlier deletion decisions to be reversed.The controversy has also triggered criticism from opposition parties, which have questioned the functioning and centralisation of the electoral-roll system.

Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.

AI Arrived at the Worst Possible Moment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:49:04 UTC
02:49:04 KST

AI is not arriving in a world capable of receiving it. Instead, it is coming into a world that has spent the last two decades systematically dismantling the very foundations that would allow us to deploy such a powerful technology responsibly. Institutional authority, shared truth, and information integrity have been battered. We are building the most sophisticated cognitive technology in human history atop the most fractured trust landscape in modern memory.
If you wanted to design the worst possible moment for AI to emerge, you might create a moment like this one.
From post-truth to post-trust
A decade ago, we worried about living in a “post-truth” world. Oxford Dictionaries selected “post-truth” as its Word of the Year in 2016, defining it as circumstances in which objective facts are less influential in shaping public opinion than appeals to emotion and personal belief. Post-truth describes a world where facts still exist but are often overshadowed by emotional narratives.
What we are experiencing now goes deeper. I call this the “post-trust era:” a world where the very mechanisms that allow us to establish trust have broken down. It is not just that emotions sometimes trump facts. It is that we have lost shared foundations for deciding what counts as a fact in the first place.
Look at what has happened to our information ecosystem over the past two decades. We moved from a world in which truth was curated by editors, printed by presses, and distributed by a small number of recognizable intermediaries, to a world in which anyone can publish, amplify, distort, or fabricate. Data exploded, and social media fragmented audiences. Algorithms began optimizing for clicks, engagement, and sensationalism. The incentives shifted from accuracy to attention: virality over veracity, outrage over nuance, speed over scrutiny.
The numbers tell their own story. Nearly 8 in 10 people get directed to their news primarily through algorithmic systems such as social feeds, search engines, and aggregators, effectively outsourcing their information diet to systems they neither understand nor fully trust. In the United States, trust in the federal government has fallen from over 70% in the late 1950s to under 20% today. Confidence in mass media has dropped: fewer than one-third of Americans express even a “fair amount” of trust. Religious institutions, financial systems, healthcare organizations, and even science itself have seen trust erode.
Post-truth describes a distortion in how people weigh facts and feelings. Post-trust describes a deeper fracture: the loss of shared procedures for determining what is real.
When the first photographs appeared in the 1830s, people marveled at their fidelity. For nearly two centuries, seeing was believing. A picture was not perfect, but it was evidence.
In early 2023, an AI-generated image of Pope Francis wearing a stylish white puffer jacket spread across social media platforms. It was compelling because it sat in a narrow band between familiar and unexpected. The photo’s style, posture, and lighting borrowed credibility from decades of real photography. Many accepted it as real before they had time to question it.
Within two years, AI-generated images, voices, and video had become so pervasive and so convincing that the question was no longer “can you spot the fake?” but “can you trust anything you see?”
The ability to fabricate convincing “evidence” at scale has arrived just as our information ecosystem is most fragmented. Research from Duke and NYU shows that exposing people to opposing political views on social media can increase polarization rather than reduce it. A landmark study in Science found that false news spreads significantly faster and more widely than trustworthy news online. Neuroimaging research suggests that when people encounter information challenging their political beliefs, brain regions associated with negative emotion light up, while confirmatory information activates reward pathways. We are not only divided about facts. We are wired to process confirming and disconfirming information through different cognitive channels altogether.
That is the substrate into which AI arrives: a world where information is abundant, but trust is scarce, where consensus reality has splintered, and where the mechanisms for establishing shared truth have broken down.
A different kind of intelligence
Into this fractured substrate arrives something genuinely new. Not just another tool, but the first technology in history whose core competence is cognition.
Past technologies extended our capabilities while remaining subordinate to human thought. The printing press amplified the words we chose to print. Electricity transformed the energy we decided to harness. Combustion engines replaced the muscle power we used, and computers executed calculations we programmed. The internet distributed the messages we wrote.
AI breaks that pattern. It no longer merely executes tasks. It generates arguments, synthesizes information, makes recommendations, and produces creative work that feels, at a human level, like someone else’s thoughts. A single model can write an essay, summarize a legal transcript, translate a medical note, draft code, plan a marketing campaign, and compose music.
At the heart of most of these systems is an architecture that learns by predicting what comes next, a word, pixel, or token, in a sequence. These models do not know “truth” in the way humans understand it. They discover patterns, frequencies, and correlations in whatever data they are given.
And here is where the timing becomes critical: the data they are given is generated in a post-trust world.
AI is trained on our news stories, our social media feeds, our digitized books, our biased archives, our polarized debates, our conspiracy theories, our scientific breakthroughs, and our misinformation. It absorbs not only our knowledge but our distortions. It learns not only our facts but also our conflicts about those facts.
The result is a strange mirror. AI reflects us to ourselves, refracted through statistical patterns and scaled by computation. It gives us answers we cannot easily audit, based on training data we cannot thoroughly inspect, optimized for objectives we do not always control.
A new kind of cognitive infrastructure is emerging at the precise moment our social infrastructure for trust is under strain.
Excerpted from The Trust Code with permission from Tiffany Xingyu Wang.

Ukraine Opens Second EU Negotiating Cluster as Reform Delivery Shapes Further Accession Progress, KSE Institute Says

Ukraine Opens Its Second Negotiating Cluster, but Further EU Accession Progress Depends on Reform Delivery – KSE Institute
In Q3 2026, Ukraine continued to advance in its EU accession negotiations. On July 14, Cluster VI, “External Relations,” was formally opened, becoming the second open cluster. As of September 16, two of six negotiating clusters and seven of 33 chapters had been opened. At the same time, measurable progress in negotiations and legislation contrasted with slower delivery on rule-of-law commitments, according to KSE Institute’s Ukraine EU Accession Tracker for Q3 2026.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Hungary did not approve the opening of Cluster II, “Internal Market,” and Cluster III, “Competitiveness & Inclusive Growth.” Following the July government change, nine Ukraine Facility-linked bills were removed from the Verkhovna Rada’s agenda; seven have since returned, while two still have no replacement. The new government nevertheless remains committed to opening all six negotiating clusters and completing negotiations by the end of 2027.
Progress on rule-of-law commitments remains slow. Only one of the ten points in the Kachka–Kos plan has been fully completed. Six of the 11 priority laws identified by EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos have been adopted and signed, while two more are awaiting signature. Reforms concerning NEURC independence, state-aid control, and the restoration of civil-service competitions remain incomplete.
Putin Envoy Heads to New York as Washington Renews Ukraine Diplomacy Effort
Two of the EU’s three financing tracks are conditional on reform delivery. The Macro-Financial Assistance track totals €8.35 billion, but the next €3.7 billion installment has been delayed until at least Q4 because some conditions were not met by August 31. Following the revision of the Ukraine Facility, its total payment envelope increased to €40.9 billion, with 27 new reform steps added.
As of mid-September, Ukraine had received €21.6 billion in seven Ukraine Facility installments, while €1.7 billion from previous payments had been withheld due to unmet commitments. The €28.3 billion Ukraine Support Loan for defence is not conditional on reforms; €8.4 billion has already been disbursed. The further pace of accession will increasingly depend on completing prosecution and anti-corruption reforms, key legislative changes, and the conditions tied to European financing.

Pashynsky pleads guilty in seized petroleum products case, to pay UAH 1.1 bln to budget and Defense Forces
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:46:20 EEST
02:46:20 KST

The High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) has approved a plea agreement with the former acting head of the Presidential Administration in the case involving seized petroleum products, according to a post on the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) Facebook page, which did not specify the former official's last name.
"The case concerns events that took place between March and June 2014, during which the defendant abused his official position to appropriate seized petroleum products, resulting in serious consequences in the form of losses to the state amounting to over UAH 817 million. The defendant is also charged with participation in a criminal organization. Under the terms of the plea agreement, the defendant fully admitted guilt under Part 2 of Article 364 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine and Part 1 of Article 255 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine and agreed to provide incriminating testimony to the investigation," the statement reads.
As Interfax-Ukraine has learned from its own sources, the individual in question is Serhiy Pashynsky, who served as acting head of the Presidential Administration from March 5 to June 10, 2014. From 2006 to 2019, he also served as a member of the Verkhovna Rada during four (V-VIII) convocations.
"Under the terms of the agreement, the former acting head of the Presidential Administration is obligated to: reimburse the state for the damages determined during the court proceedings, amounting to UAH 600 million, by transferring funds to the general fund of the State Budget of Ukraine in installments over a period of two and a half years from the date the judgment takes effect; transfer UAH 400 million to the Come Back Alive Fund's account or ensure the delivery of military equipment, as specified in the Come Back Alive list of the same value, to the fund's balance sheet or directly to military units at the fund's direction, with delivery to an agreed-upon location within 6 months from the date of the judgment; Come Back Alive of the same value, either to the fund's balance sheet or directly to military units at the fund's direction, with delivery to an agreed-upon location within six months from the date the judgment takes effect; transfer UAH 100 million to the account of the Sternenko Community Charitable Foundation directly for the purchase of weapons for the Defense Forces of Ukraine within 30 days from the date the verdict takes effect," the SAPO said.
Under the terms of the agreement, the former official must also pay fines totalling UAH 850,000 as the principal penalty and UAH 17,000, accompanied by a one-year ban on holding office in state or local government bodies, as an additional penalty.
"Confiscation of the convicted person's property was not ordered, since this additional penalty under Article 255 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine was introduced by law in June 2020 – that is, after the crime was committed," the statement reads.
The High Anti-Corruption Court said it had reviewed the plea agreement for compliance with the public interest and approved it with its verdict. The Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) states that if the convicted person fails to comply with the terms of the agreement, it will file a motion with the High Anti-Corruption Court to overturn the verdict and have the case heard under the general procedure.
Charges were filed in February 2024 against members of the criminal organization for misappropriating seized petroleum products. On September 5, 2025, the High Anti-Corruption Court approved a plea agreement with another defendant in the same case, who was sentenced to 8 years of imprisonment but was released from serving the principal sentence with a 3-year probationary period and without confiscation of property; Under the terms of the agreement, he transferred UAH 40 million to the Defense Forces and is required to pay UAH 110 million to the state budget over a period of 3 years from the date the sentence takes effect.

Italy bans burqas, niqabs in schools under new decree
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:46:00 UTC
02:46:00 KST

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government adopted a decree Thursday banning burqas and niqabs in schools while imposing limits on the number of students with poor Italian-language skills allowed in each classroom.
It introduces "A 30% cap on the number of students in a class who do not have an adequate command of Italian, more tools for learning our language, and a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools," Meloni wrote on social media.
If a child seriously struggles to integrate at school, social services will be called and the parents will be obliged to attend free Italian lessons.
Failure to comply will be punished with a fine of up to 1,000 euros ($1,140).
Italy is a frontline country for migration and integration is a hot campaign issue ahead of next year's general election.
Save the Children warned that forcing children to change schools or enrol in a different institution from their peers simply because of their nationality or limited proficiency in Italian would "create 'first-class' and 'second-class' students."
But Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said, "inadequate language proficiency... hinders educational progress."
"Parental participation in their child's educational path is fundamental for academic success," he told journalists.
Valditara said there were 34,000 school classes in Italy in which over 30% of the students are foreign.
But most of those would not be affected by the new law, which targets new arrivals rather than those born in Italy or who attended kindergarten.
The 30% limit on the number of foreign students per class was established in a ministerial memorandum in 2010.
But the limit was flexible, and could be raised in cases involving foreign students with adequate language skills, such as foreign students born in Italy, or lowered when foreign students have a poor command of Italian.
Opposition leader Elly Schlein accused the government of "a new witch hunt at the expense of children."
The burqa ban was "a matter of security," Meloni said in a television interview after the cabinet meeting.
"When a woman – or worse, a young girl – is forced to cover her face, she is being denied fundamental rights and the very integration that is so often loudly championed," she said.
A crackdown on the use of burqas in schools was called for in July by the National Future (FN) party.
The FN, which is not part of the governing coalition, is further to the right than Meloni's and has emerged as a major challenger, rising sharply in the polls since launching in February.

Iranian-American group sues Trump over war
Plaintiffs have families in Iran who have been harmed by the US war, they say.
A group of Iranian Americans have filed a lawsuit against United States President Donald Trump, asking a court to order a halt to military action against Iran that they allege is harming them and their families and is in violation of constitutional war powers checks.
The complaint, filed in a Washington, DC, court on Thursday by the advocacy group National Iranian American Council (NIAC), argues the war will continue indefinitely and “cause imminent threats to the lives, limbs, health, property, and bare necessities” of Iranians, as well as Iranian Americans whom the organisation represents.

list of 3 items

Al Jazeera has a copy of the lawsuit.
The lawsuit details the impact the war, which has raged on for more than six months now, has had on several of its members, including US citizens and a US Army veteran, and their families who are still inside Iran.
The relatives of some plaintiffs were allegedly killed or injured in air strikes during the war, including while in their homes, or as they went about doing routine tasks.
The plaintiffs also allege greater effects on themselves and their families, such as economic difficulties caused by US sanctions, and the inability to access adequate healthcare, or travel amid an expanding sanctions regime.
Those still inside Iran, the lawsuit says, are in danger because the Trump administration is continuing the war without legal oversight or proper authorisation. Thousands of civilians, including hundreds of children, have been killed by the US in the war so far, according to the lawsuit, and others are at risk.
“They are all in imminent danger of harm to their persons and properties proximately caused by the unconstitutional war waged by defendant President Donald J. Trump,” the complaint says.
In September, a United Nations fact-finding mission said the US likely committed “war crimes” in Iran, including in air strikes that allegedly killed hundreds of civilians.
“No President should have the power to take this country into an indefinite war by himself,” NIAC President Jamal Abdi said in a statement on Thursday. “This lawsuit asks a fundamental question: can one person decide, on his own, to keep an entire nation at war?”
On Tuesday, Trump told world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly that he was considering whether to “annihilate” Iran if Tehran did not return to talks and reach a deal with the US to end the war.

02:44:15 KST

The European Union has approved nearly €3 billion in new funding for Ukraine, including nearly €800 million provided for the first time through the Ukraine Support Loan. The payment is the eighth regular disbursement under the EU’s Ukraine Facility.
The funding will support Ukraine’s budget, recovery, modernization, and reform efforts as the country continues to fight Russia’s full-scale war and pursue EU membership.
Ukraine meets 88% of targets due so far
The latest payment follows Ukraine’s completion of 10 targets under its Ukraine Plan, the roadmap for reforms and investments linked to the Ukraine Facility. Ukraine has now completed 84 of the 95 targets required under the plan so far, according to the Council of the EU.
Funding under the Ukraine Facility is tied to Ukraine meeting these targets. It is intended to strengthen Ukraine’s macro-financial stability, keep public administration running, and support recovery and modernization.
The Ukraine Facility entered into force in March 2024 and provides more than €50 billion in grants and loans for Ukraine through 2027.
Norway adds €92 million
The EU also amended Ukraine’s plan to include approximately €92 million in non-repayable support from Norway.
Norway is the first non-EU country to contribute to Pillar I of the Ukraine Facility, which provides support through Ukraine’s reform and investment plan.
Sweden has provided more than €253 million in additional voluntary contributions over the past year, while the UK recently contributed more than €17 million to Pillar II, the Ukraine Investment Framework.
Ukraine has received more than €32 billion
Following the latest disbursement, Ukraine will have received more than €32 billion through the Ukraine Facility since mid-2024.
More than €40 billion of the facility’s total funding is earmarked for reforms and investments under the Ukraine Plan, with payments tied to Ukraine’s progress toward the agreed targets.

constraints established in this regard by the Constitutional
Court.

law's framework fails to provide adequate, concrete guarantees
that a personalized palliative care pathway—along with other
support systems designed to prevent recourse to suicide—will be
effectively made available beforehand."
This point was underscored by the sources at Palazzo Chigi,
explaining why the Council of Ministers decided to challenge
Emilia-Romagna's law on end-of-life care.

notwithstanding the significant allocations made by this
government—which increased palliative care funding by €40
million, bringing the total to €140 million—many regions remain
far from meeting the targets for utilizing their allocated share
of these resources locally."

end-of-life laws.

people to commit assisted suicide in Italy since a landmark 2019
ruling by the Italian supreme court that stated assisted suicide
is legal in some cases.

their lives to the Dignitas Clinic near Zurich.
                                    
                                       
				The Constitutional Court ruling laid down strict markers on
cases in which assisted suicide is legitimate and called on
parliament to end a legislative vacuum at the national level on
end-of-life issues.
                                    
                                       
				So far it has failed to do so.

France says EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ law should not include the UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:42:23 UTC
02:42:23 KST

France is leading a push to exclude the UK from the EU’s “Made in Europe” policy that could result in British companies losing out in the race to supply European countries with low-carbon technologies and electric cars.
The plans were raised by Andy Burnham when he met the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, on the sidelines of the UN general assembly earlier this week.
The policy, still under negotiation, aims to protect European companies from intense and “unfair” state-subsidised competition from China. But the government fears British companies risk being collateral damage and resolving the issue has become one of Burnham’s top priorities for the EU-UK relationship.
One key EU proposal is the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), which would require authorities spending public money – awarding subsidies or public contracts – to favour European products in sectors such as renewable technologies and electric cars.
But there is an intense debate inside the EU on how to define “made in Europe” and how far to include countries such as the UK, Canada and Japan.
At a meeting of EU industry ministers in Brussels on Thursday, France pushed for a narrow definition, starting with the EU27.
“European taxpayers’ money should support [European] workers and European factories,” the French industry minister, Sébastien Martin, told reporters.
Asked about the UK, he said: “The United Kingdom made a choice a few years ago to leave the European Union.
“That doesn’t mean that we don’t discuss things or that we don’t trade, it doesn’t mean that there can’t be agreements in certain sectors, but fundamentally there are those who have chosen the European project and those who have decided to leave.”
France’s Europe minister, Benjamin Haddad, speaking in London, had few assurances to offer the Burnham government either.
Asked about the risks of pushing the EU’s like-minded trading partners away, Haddad said: “At the end of the day, if you are not part of the internal market and if you are not contributing to the financial capacity of the internal market, you don’t get the same kind of protection.”
Germany wants a broader “Made with Europe” policy that would include the UK and other allies. Germany’s economic affairs minister, Katherina Reiche, told her counterparts: “We must reduce unilateral and critical dependencies, but we must not isolate ourselves from the rest of the world. This means that partner countries must be included in the union-origin principle, in general and on the condition of reciprocity.”
This position gets broad support from Nordic countries, which traditionally favour open trade.
Sweden’s outgoing deputy prime minister, Ebba Busch, who leads on business policy, said “we always miss the Brits”. Sweden wanted “a good solution where there is balance, given that some European countries are not members of the European Union but still completely essential for a functioning European market”, she added.
The charged internal EU27 debate on Made in Europe raises questions about the timing of the EU-UK reset summit, which was postponed when Keir Starmer stood down as prime minister. Since Burnham took office, no date has been fixed for the talks which are meant to happen in 2026.
British officials expect the summit will take place in November, although an earlier 6 November date has been scratched out. By December the EU is expected to be embroiled in deeply difficult internal negotiations on the bloc’s next seven-year budget, which are likely to consume the political bandwidth of EU leaders.
EU insiders believe that a Made in Europe agreement is a top priority for the UK, but have cautioned this cannot happen before the union has finalised its own position.
One EU diplomat said it was a “big risk” if the UK government were to insist on a deal at an autumn summit. “It puts [the UK] in a corner, because this [Made in Europe criteria] is a process that is very difficult for the EU27 [to agree internally].”
The Republic of Ireland, which is chairing EU ministerial negotiations, hopes for an agreement in December on the IAA, including the Made in Europe provisions, between the EU Council and the European parliament. “There are a divergence of views on the Industrial Accelerator Act, on European preference, on working with trusted partners and third countries,” said Ireland’s enterprise minister, Peter Burke. “It is difficult, but we have a pathway in sight.”
Poland’s economic development minister, Michał Baranowski, said it was too early to say whether countries such as Switzerland, the UK, Japan, Australia and Canada would be in or out, adding: “All these countries are in the mix of the discussion.”
The UK, he said, should have clarity on its status when the EU act is passed, he said, adding: “We are in the last stretch, but this last stretch might take a while.”
A UK government spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and trusted European partner, committed to our shared security and economic cooperation.
“We will continue to engage with the EU on Made in Europe and work together, as like-minded partners, to boost growth and open up trade.”

Former Anti-Corruption Official Among Two Iraqi Lawmakers Jailed for Illicit Enrichment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:42:00 UTC
02:42:00 KST

Reported by
Iraq's Central Anti-Corruption Criminal Court has sentenced two lawmakers to seven years in prison each for illicit enrichment, tying their hidden wealth to an ongoing corruption probe into a senior oil official.
Alia Nassif Jassem Aziz Al Obaidi, known as Alia Nassif, an MP representing Baghdad who built a public profile on anti-corruption rhetoric, previously served as the first vice-chair of parliament’s Integrity Committee. She was transferred to the Finance Committee earlier this year and arrested on corruption charges on June 28, according to Iraq’s official news agency.
MP Ashwaq Salem Hassan has also been linked to the same corruption probe.
The current chairman of the Integrity Committee, Taha Al-Difai, told OCCRP that the sentences were based on the interrogation of detained Deputy Oil Minister Adnan al-Jumaili by an investigating judge. According to Al-Difai, al-Jumaili admitted to having illicit dealings with the two lawmakers.
Investigators subsequently uncovered unexplained cash and real estate wealth that neither woman had reported on their mandatory financial disclosures, which officials must file within three months of taking office.
“This indicated an illicit accumulation of wealth at the expense of public funds,” Al-Difai said.
The Integrity Commission said the court ordered Nassif to return 14 billion Iraqi dinars ($10.68 million) and an additional $12 million in illicit earnings. Judges also fined her an equivalent amount, bringing her total financial penalty to approximately $45 million.
Similarly, Hassan was ordered to return 2.11 billion dinars ($1.6 million) and $2.92 million, plus an equivalent fine, bringing her total penalty to roughly $9 million.
Authorities have not publicly released the full details of al-Jumaili’s statements implicating the two lawmakers, nor a list of the ill-acquired assets that formed the basis of the court’s decisions.
The judgments also included three-year sentences for each lawmaker for concealing information on their mandatory financial disclosure forms. Because the court applied only the harsher punishment, the final prison term for each woman remains seven years. The Integrity Commission said it retained the right to seek further damages after the judgments become final.
The convictions are part of a sweeping anti-corruption campaign that has been rocking Iraq since April, which also saw the June arrest of Ziad al-Janabi, who previously chaired the Integrity Committee.
The irony of Nassif’s situation did not go unnoticed by the Iraqi public. Her sentencing drew a wave of comments highlighting her previous public statements against government corruption.
Nassif and Hassan did not respond to OCCRP’s requests for comment.

I needed a physically well-developed midfielder — Maldera on calling up debutant Varfolomieiev
Kyiv • UNN
Maldera called up Varfolomieiev because of his physical strength and experience in the Championship. The 22-year-old midfielder will make his debut for the Ukraine national team.
Ukraine national team head coach Andrea Maldera explained why he called up Lincoln City central midfielder Ivan Varfolomiiev to the squad, noting that he needed a midfielder who was physically well developed, UNN reports.
Details
We were monitoring many players. Varfolomiiev was one of the possible players who play in central midfield. He plays in a league where there is a lot of battling and self-sacrifice. He plays in the Championship regularly and has a lot of match practice. We also have midfielders who are capable of making more passes. I also needed to have a midfielder in the squad who is physically well developed and can also play for other purposes. Even if he is suspended tomorrow and will not play
What is known about Ivan Varfolomiiev
On September 16, Ukraine national team head coach Andrea Maldera announced the Ukraine squad for the Nations League matches.
The first call-ups went to Polish Górnik winger Maksym Khlan, Artem Stepanov from Dutch club Utrecht, and English Lincoln midfielder Ivan Varfolomiiev.
Ivan Varfolomiiev is a product of Simferopol's Tavriya, which ceased to exist after the occupation of Crimea. In 2014, he moved to the academy of Lviv's Karpaty.
In September 2020, he joined another Lviv club, Rukh. He made his debut in the Lviv side's shirt on February 21, 2021, in a 0:2 away defeat in the 15th-round match of the Ukrainian First League against Donetsk's Shakhtar.
In the spring of 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Varfolomiiev unilaterally terminated his contract with Rukh and left Ukraine, signing an agreement with Slovan Liberec in July. Following an investigation, the Dispute Resolution Chamber of the Ukrainian Association of Football ordered the footballer to pay Rukh compensation of approximately USD 100,000. However, the Court of Arbitration for Sport) overturned the decision of the UAF Dispute Resolution Chamber and ruled that the player had committed no violation, also ordering FC Rukh to pay him the outstanding amount for the period worked.
On August 21, 2025, Varfolomiiev joined English club Lincoln City, which currently plays in the Championship (England's second-tier league — ed.).
Recently, Lincoln City announced that Varfolomiiev had extended his contract with the club until 2030.
This season, the 22-year-old Ukrainian, who received his first call-up to the national team, has provided 1 assist in 9 matches at club level.
Ukraine national team winger Andriy Yarmolenko said during a press conference: "Regarding the newcomers and young players — you were right to mention the nerves. Of course, I have spoken with them, Mister (Andrea Maldera — ed.) speaks with them as well, and the rest of the team speaks with them too. It is normal when you are 19 or 20, even 22 or 23. You receive your first call-up, and you feel nervous, so these are normal things. The most important thing is to cope with those nerves and gain confidence. And to gain that confidence, this is, in principle, what teammates and older teammates are there for — to help and share their experience, so that the nervousness goes away as quickly as possible."

Israeli convicted of killing Palestinian teen dies in prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:39:09 UTC
02:39:09 KST

Yosef Haim Ben-David, 42, the main defendant in the murder of East Jerusalem Palestinian teenager Mohammed Abu Khdeir, died Thursday. He was taken from Hasharon Prison to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
Abu Khdeir, 16, from Shuafat, was murdered in July 2014, and Ben-David was sentenced to life imprisonment plus 20 years.
Ben-David and two other teenagers who were convicted in the case abducted and murdered Abu Khdeir on the night after the funerals of three Israeli teenagers — Naftali Frenkel, Gilad Shaer and Eyal Yifrah — as revenge for their abduction and murder by Hamas in June of that year, before the launch of Operation Protective Edge in the Gaza Strip.
According to the conviction, late on the evening of July 2, after making preparations and equipping themselves in advance, the three set out to carry out a “revenge attack” in memory of the three teenagers.
For about three hours, they searched for a suitable victim in the Wadi Joz and Beit Hanina neighborhoods, and at around 4 a.m. they spotted Abu Khdeir, who had left his home and was walking toward a mosque to pray.
They forced him into a car. During the drive, the two teenagers held Abu Khdeir as he struggled with them.
Ben-David ordered one of them to “finish him,” and the teenager strangled Abu Khdeir until he lost consciousness.
When they reached the Jerusalem Forest, one of the teenagers complained that he and the other minor were “doing all the work.” Ben-David then took a crowbar and struck Abu Khdeir while invoking earlier Palestinian terror attacks against Israelis. “This is for the Fogel family,” he shouted, referring to the parents and three children murdered in their home in the West Bank settlement of Itamar in 2011. “This is for Shalhevet Pass,” he added, referring to a 10-month-old Israeli girl killed by a Palestinian sniper in Hebron in 2001. He continued striking Abu Khdeir until blood ran from his head.
He also kicked the teenager several times while shouting, “This is for Gilad, Naftali, Eyal.”
They then set fire to Abu Khdeir while he was unconscious and fled the scene.
They destroyed evidence in Jerusalem's Sacher Park, then drove to Ben-David’s home in the settlement of Adam, where they played guitars and went to sleep.
Following the murder, Abu Khdeir’s family sought the demolition of the killers’ homes, but the High Court of Justice rejected the petition, citing, among other reasons, the time that had elapsed since the killing.
His father, Hussein, criticized the judges’ decision at the time.
“If it had been an Arab who murdered a Jew, they would have demolished his house within days,” he said. “If they do not want to demolish the homes of Jewish terrorists, then they should not demolish homes anywhere. This is discrimination and racism. A decision like this encourages people to continue harming us under the protection of the state.”
About four years after the murder, the teenager’s family sued the three killers for about 5.5 million shekels ($1.8 million).
The lawsuit stated: “There is no adequate compensation for such a pointless and infuriating loss of a young person’s life, all while the defendants deliberately intended to harm the deceased, injure him and acted with indifference and cynicism toward the most terrible possible outcome — the death of the deceased in pain and suffering — while showing no mercy toward his parents, who were left with nothing after the death of their son.”

The Guardian view on a supersized El Niño: a natural phenomenon and human folly are a lethal combination | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:37:39 UTC
02:37:39 KST

Some warnings are so grave that it is almost impossible to fully comprehend them. The descriptions of a super-sized, “Godzilla-level” El Niño already heating our planet would sound hyperbolic were they not issuing from eminent scientists. They say that the weather pattern, which occurs roughly every two to seven years, may be the strongest in at least a millennium. With its peak yet to come, the temperature rise in the Pacific Ocean has already surpassed the previous high.
The consequence will be huge amounts of heat in an atmosphere already experiencing frighteningly higher temperatures due to the human-caused climate crisis. Next year is almost certain to be the hottest on record globally, breaking this year’s record. The World Food Programme has warned that 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger. Others estimate that the extra heat from El Niño alone will cause the deaths of 450,000 people by February, from Nigeria and Indonesia to the US. That extraordinary toll is in addition to those killed by the wildfires, droughts and floods it is likely to bring – and also to deaths caused by global heating.
While the weather system develops in the Pacific Ocean, its knock-on effects will be felt far away. It increases drought risk in a large swathe of the world, while increasing rainfall elsewhere. India has already experienced a 50% shortfall in essential monsoon rains this month, affecting crops. In Sri Lanka, reservoirs for drinking water are running dry. European countries may be indirectly affected, with a stormier autumn, but the primary impact for them is likely to be on food supplies.
While there is ongoing debate about the impact of global heating on the pattern itself, a major study published last month found that strong El Niños in recent decades have been supercharged by the overheating of the planet due to fossil fuels. It is beyond doubt that the effects of this natural phenomenon are compounded by human-made folly and injustice. Domestically and internationally, the poorest will be worst hit, due to factors such as living conditions and underlying health, while being the least able to pay their way out of trouble. At the same time, the wealthy few will continue to enrich themselves from an economic system built on pumping out more emissions. Defenders of the status quo will continue to insist that we cannot afford to clean up our act. It is more than ever evident that we cannot afford not to do so.
The UK foreign secretary’s warning to other countries at the UN on Wednesday that El Niño and the climate and nature crises threaten their national security and defence was welcome. Andy Burnham, as well as Ed Miliband, should be seizing the opportunity to make the political case for tough action on emissions, and accelerating efforts to prepare the UK for increasingly extreme weather. The Climate Change Committee, which advises the government, warned in a landmark report in May that the country is “built for a climate that no longer exists”.
Globally, boosting the loss and damage fund to ensure support for developing countries, which have contributed the least to the climate crisis but are likely to suffer most, should be a priority. This unprecedented El Niño poses an immense threat. It could also be a spur to action against global heating and its associated injustices, which otherwise will only deepen.

Ukraine's Zelenskyy broke confidentiality over North Korean POW disclosure: South Korea's Lee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:36:53 UTC
02:36:53 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy broke a confidentiality agreement by disclosing that Ukraine had sent North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, Seoul's president has said.
Thursday’s remarks by President Lee Jae-myung came after Zelenskyy told the United Nations that Ukraine had sent two North Korean soldiers to the South, adding they were "not easy to capture alive".
The revelation prompted South Korea's political opposition to criticise the Lee administration for allowing a foreign leader to inform them of the prisoners' arrivals.
"I do not know why the Ukrainian side broke the agreement and made the matter public, but it is very disappointing," Lee said on X.
"The issue of bringing North Korean prisoners to South Korea is a highly sensitive one that could have a major impact on diplomacy, security and the situation on the Korean Peninsula," he said.
Confidentiality dispute
Lee said there had been calls to disclose the arrivals, but "given the problems that could arise from making it public, we agreed that keeping it confidential was the right thing to do".
Zelenskyy's aide Dmytro Lytvyn told journalists that Ukraine was "an open country" and that it would have been strange to hand over the soldiers in secret.
"From the entire story - which is long and detailed - we reported only the fact itself, that they were sent to the Republic of Korea," he said.
Early last year, Ukraine captured two North Korean soldiers among Pyongyang's troops fighting for Moscow.
A South Korean lawmaker had previously said the pair wanted to live a "normal life" in the South.
Under South Korea's constitution, all Koreans, including those living in the North, are considered citizens, and officials have said this would apply to any North Korean troops captured in Ukraine.

Europe needs 'decisive change' in defence efforts to face Russia threat, EU agency says
BRUSSELS, Sept 24 - The European Union is not rearming quickly or effectively enough to meet its goal of being ready to defend against Russia by 2030, according to the executive summary of an EU report prepared for the bloc's leaders and seen by Reuters.
EU members' current plans "do not seem to meet" the goal of filling gaps in areas such as air and missile defence, ground combat, naval forces, munition stockpiles and drones, the European Defence Agency said in its first annual Defence Readiness Report.
“Tackling the challenges of a contested and deteriorating security environment and the threat posed by Russia’s aggression requires moving further and substantially faster than now to reach defence readiness by 2030,” the EU agency wrote.
ACHIEVEMENTS UNPRECEDENTED BUT 'NOT YET ENOUGH'
Leaders from the EU’s 27 countries ordered the report last year to assess progress in their drive to ramp up Europe's defences, reflecting fears fuelled by Russia’s war in Ukraine and calls by US President Donald Trump for Europe to do more for its own security.
Trump has also threatened to withdraw from the NATO alliance that has been the bedrock of European security for decades, although he recommitted to its mutual defence clause at a summit in Ankara in July.
Russia has denied it has any intention of attacking an EU member and accused the continent's leaders of fearmongering. But EU leaders have dismissed Moscow's assertions, pointing out it made similar comments before its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Against such an uncertain international backdrop, EU leaders last year set themselves the goal of making Europe ready to defend itself by 2030.
EU defence ministers are expected to discuss the defence agency's report in Brussels on Monday and it will then go to the bloc's leaders.
“The first Annual Defence Readiness Report shows progress in spending, capability development, and industrial readiness, supported by deepened partnerships, notably with Ukraine,” the summary seen by Reuters said.
“However, the current momentum and increased investment do not yet translate into sufficiently deployable, sustainable and interoperable forces, while critical capability gaps remain. What has been achieved so far, although unprecedented, is not yet enough.” REUTERS

The Guardian view on vocational GCSEs: why now? | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:35:58 UTC
02:35:58 KST

The first question that should be asked about plans to launch a batch of vocational GCSEs is: how will these differ from the roughly 50 similar courses that already exist? Is this primarily a rebadging exercise, aimed at boosting the qualifications’ status and name recognition, while signalling how seriously non-academic education is taken by Andy Burnham and his education secretary, Lucy Powell? Or is there something the matter with the existing courses that they want to put right?
The independent curriculum review completed last year recommended a moratorium on new technical awards, except where there is an “exceptionally compelling” case for change. It also proposed that the Department for Education analyse existing ones, including how well they prepare pupils for 16-19 education; no such research has appeared.
Last year, around 170,000 16-year-olds in England and Wales took a level 2 BTec qualification alongside GCSEs – the two most popular being health and sport and leisure. They are also studied by post-16 students at further education colleges. While the number of entries is dwarfed by the overall annual total of 5.7m GCSEs, it is not the case that all individual GCSEs have higher take-up. In 2024, for example, just 6,723 pupils took a GCSE in dance.
The fact that technical awards are not on the radar of many pupils and parents does not mean that they lack value. The low awareness of vocational options is widely recognised as a problem and was cited by Pepe Di’Iasio, the general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, in response to this week’s announcement. Clearer signposting is expected to be among the recommendations of a review chaired by Charles Clarke, a former education secretary, when it is published later this autumn.
The second question about vocational GCSEs is how they will relate to the plans for new V-levels (level 3 qualifications like A-levels), to which the government is already committed. V-levels are due to replace all existing vocational level 3s apart from T-levels, after ministers rejected a campaign aimed at saving some older courses. Will vocational GCSEs be viewed as stepping stones to the new V-level courses? If not, how will duplication and repetition be avoided?
For schools, the key issues will be practical. Construction is one of the new GCSEs promised. But there are already many vacancies for construction‑related college teaching positions and it is not clear where a workforce for teaching 14- to 16-year-olds building skills would come from – or whether training teachers for new subjects should take priority over existing shortages.
The government’s commitment to getting more young people into jobs is admirable, and ministers are right to push for more work‑experience opportunities. But given the difficulties in this area encountered by T-level students – which led to a watering down of the initial requirement for a placement – it is doubtful whether the aim of getting large numbers of 14- to 16-year-olds into workplaces is realistic.
There is nothing wrong with rebranding level 2 technical awards and reshaping them if they are shown to be deficient. But given their ambitious reboot of post-16 options, as well as hugely challenging reforms of the special educational needs system, ministers should beware of new GCSEs becoming a distraction. If they are serious about boosting vocational learning, it is the overlooked further education sector that needs attention.

‘NAZA’ documentary misrepresents Gaza targeting process, Military official tells i24NEWS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:35:11 UTC
02:35:11 KST

‘NAZA’ documentary misrepresents Gaza targeting process, Military official to i24NEWS
Targeting is a seven-stage process and the military official claims that the interviewees were all serving in the first stage with no access to later stages
A military official has given the core criticisms of the documentary 'NAZA' by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. They noted that although it had not seen the full film, its criticism is based on the accounts of viewers and a representative who was at the screening, as well as press coverage and the filmmakers' public statements.
The core issue they lay out is that the interviewees only had access to a single stage in the intelligence process and as a result can recount only the preliminary intelligence stage of the process.
Targeting is a seven-stage process and they claim that the interviewees were all serving in the first stage with no access to later stages.
The first stage is intelligence analysis: analysts gather and cross-reference a variety of intelligence sources. Then, in stage two, intelligence verification, a separate intelligence officer verifies the material and decides whether to designate it for targeting.
Stage three is operational planning, non-intelligence military staff decide on munitions, timing and desired effect.
Independent military legal advisers then review the plan and assess its legality, impose conditions, or return the plan for further planning. The legal review is stage four.
In stage five, the command decision, operational commanders weigh expected civilian harm against military advantage; they then approve, restrict, or reject the strike. The official clarified that "Analysts don't sit at his table."
In stage six, real-time assessment, additional surveillance or intelligence is checked before the strike and can lead to the strike being reworked or cancelled entirely.
Following the strike, a post-strike review is held. In stage seven, a separate unit, divorced from the previous stages, assesses the outcomes and provides reports on them.
A military official explained that an analyst in the initial stage may have a high estimate for civilian casualties and assume that a strike occurred on the basis of that figure, but that later steps can significantly reduce that estimate, such as "narrowing the target, changing the weapon or timing, or updated evacuation data after warnings."
They laid out three key issues with the methodology. First, there is no verification: the film provides no way to verify any of the information in it. The filmmakers failed to put their allegations to the IDF prior to publication, which denied the IDF a right of reply, and the filmmakers continued to refuse to provide the IDF with a copy or details about the incidents. The film also failed to provide any context or mitigation for its claims.
The official also laid out several responses to specific allegations raised in the film. The official said that no strike with 500 civilian casualties was ever planned, approved, or carried out. The official also disputed that there was a set number of casualties allowed for junior and senior commanders. The official clarified that the interviewee likely confused an authorization threshold, which requires higher command levels to sign off on a strike, with permission for that number of casualties.
The offical also said that AI is not used to produce lists of targets or approve strikes and that no strike was carried out "by algorithm." The official responded to several other allegations by saying that intelligence analysts would not have access to the later stages at all.

Sami Abu Shehadeh, who leads the Palestinian nationalist party, Balad, said Thursday that the Israeli Central Elections Committee’s decision to disqualify him from the upcoming Knesset election was “political,” as he vowed to continue challenging the ruling.
“We will fight until the end to defend our right as Arabs to choose our leadership,” Abu Shehadeh told Radio al-Nas, which focuses on issues concerning Arab citizens of Israel.
He said the decision to bar his candidacy was not based on legal considerations but was instead politically motivated.
Abu Shehadeh said some members of the Central Elections Committee, whom he did not identify, had announced their support for disqualifying him before hearing his position, arguing that this “strips the committee’s decision of legitimacy.”
The committee voted 31-4 on Wednesday to disqualify Abu Shehadeh from running in the Oct. 27 election. The decision is subject to review by the Supreme Court.
Abu Shehadeh also criticized National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose far-right Otzma Yehudit party submitted the petition seeking his disqualification, accusing him of exploiting those who were killed in the Oct. 7, 2023, events for political purposes.
Ben-Gvir is “the last person who can speak about human rights,” he said.
Abu Shehadeh also accused Democrats party leader Yair Golan of “racism,” saying he “wants to tailor Arab leadership to suit himself.”
The Central Elections Committee also voted to bar the Joint Arab List and the United Arab List, or Ra’am, as well as Knesset member Ofer Cassif from participating in the election.
The committee is largely a political body made up of representatives of parliamentary factions in the outgoing Knesset, with seats allocated according to the size of those factions. As a result, the governing coalition holds a majority on the panel, which currently has 34 members, according to the Haaretz newspaper.
The committee is responsible for ensuring that the electoral process is conducted properly and reliably from beginning to end in a way that reflects the will of voters in Israel, according to its website. The committee bases disqualification decisions on Article 7A of the Basic Law: The Knesset, which allows candidates or electoral lists to be barred on grounds including “denying Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state, inciting racism, or supporting armed struggle against Israel by an enemy state or an organization Israel designates as terrorist.
Under election rules, the disqualification of an individual candidate requires Supreme Court approval before taking effect, while decisions barring an electoral list can be appealed to the court.

Saudi oil exports hit new hurdle as insurance costs soar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:33:54 UTC
02:33:54 KST

Breadcrumb
Saudi oil export strategy hits new hurdle as Red Sea insurance costs soar
The cost of insuring an oil tanker loaded from Saudi Arabia's main Red Sea port has tripled in recent weeks, industry sources told Reuters, adding to the major crude producer's struggles to find a viable channel for its exports.
Saudi Arabia used its East-West pipeline to divert around 4 million barrels per day - 4% of global supply - to the Red Sea after Iran constrained Gulf exports via the Strait of Hormuz from March in response to US and Israeli air strikes.
The kingdom shut the pipeline on September 11 after drone attacks that it said came from Iraq, where Iran backs some militia groups. It is now building volumes back but loadings at the major port of Yanbu have yet to resume, according to industry sources, satellite images and shipping data.
Quoted war risk premiums for Saudi-linked tankers calling at Yanbu have risen to around 3% of a vessel's value, four industry sources told Reuters. They were less than 1% in early July, before London's marine insurance market designated that stretch of water as high-risk in response to Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis attacking shipping near the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
For ports south of Yanbu, including Jizan, around 50 miles (80 km) from the border with Yemen, quoted premiums - around 1% in early July - can rise as high as 7%, almost as much as transits through Hormuz, which range between 6% and 9%, the sources said, declining to be named due to data sensitivity.
"It's easier to do the Strait of Hormuz right now ... because at least in the Strait of Hormuz, the US is providing some cover. In the Red Sea, there's nothing," Pankaj Khanna, CEO of shipping group Heidmar Maritime Holdings Corp, told Reuters.
"If you have a Saudi connection, then you have a problem."
The Iran-aligned militants who seized swathes of the Yemeni coast and captured Perim Island in the middle of the Bab el-Mandeb strait this month have vowed to target only vessels linked to Saudi Arabia due to its backing of Yemen's government.
Tankers transiting the Red Sea without any Saudi connection typically pay between 0.2% and 0.3%, with additional discounts often available, the four industry sources said.
Khanna said any tanker docking at Yanbu will have a Saudi connection and hence be at risk of being hit. Heidmar is avoiding Saudi ports while remaining active in both Hormuz and the Red Sea, he said.
The Houthis have also targeted Saudi Arabia itself. The kingdom intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on Thursday, including towards the Yanbu area, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said.
Earlier this week, two trading sources said traders were getting ready for Saudi oil loadings in the Red Sea by moving tankers to Egypt's Mediterranean Port Said for ship-to-ship transfers.
That could allow them to sail south out of the Red Sea via Bab el-Mandeb instead of heading north through the Suez Canal and then - for Asia-bound cargoes - via southern Africa, a much longer and more costly route.
There is no public data for agreed rates in the marine insurance market, which could vary from those quoted by brokers and underwriters.
But the jump in quoted premiums shows that despite Saudi Arabia's investment of billions of dollars in infrastructure to provide an alternative export corridor, it now faces similar constraints as other Gulf oil producers relying on Hormuz.
"We have seen rates certainly north of 7% for all calls south of Yanbu," said David Smith, head of marine at insurance broker McGill and Partners.
Saudi Arabia's government media office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The US-Iran war has prompted some Gulf oil producers to rush to buy their own tankers to protect their oil exports, shipping sources say.
As a result, the average price of old tankers has soared to above $100 million, five sources said. Saudi Arabia this week denied allegations by Iraq that it had bought 25 oil tankers worth an estimated $4.5 billion, saying that the rise in oil transport costs was due to other factors linked to the war.
War risk premiums typically cover 7-day voyage periods and are reviewed every 24 hours, meaning a journey from Yanbu could cost $3 million, or some $7 million from other Saudi ports further south or via Hormuz, up from at least $100,000 before the war.
Oil producers also need to pay at least $500,000 a day for chartering a tanker, according to industry estimates, and bunker fuel costs during the voyage could add another $100,000 or more.
The US military has been providing some aerial support to ships sailing via Hormuz in recent months, sources have told Reuters. No such protection exists in the Red Sea, where the European Union provides security but says it needs more ships.
A US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the United States did not automatically provide protection when asked by private companies.
Saudi Arabia's crown prince sought US military help this month to counter the Houthis, sources told Reuters, and the Saudi cabinet has appointed the Saudi Reinsurance Company to lead the country's marine war risk insurance pool.
Corey Ranslem, CEO of maritime security group Dryad Global, said Bab el-Mandeb transits remained challenging, with tanker-only figures totaling "only a handful of vessels per day".
"What continues to move consists primarily of dry bulk cargo, certain products, and a limited number of tankers without Saudi affiliations."

Rutte says Putin is in a 'bad place' as he reassures NATO allies amid threat reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:30:49 UTC
02:30:49 KST

NATO chief Mark Rutte said the alliance was prepared to respond to Russian hybrid attacks against European countries following fresh warnings from Danish intelligence. Meanwhile, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth urged European allies to take greater responsibility for their own defence.
NATO is prepared to respond to sabotage and drone incidents across Europe and has plans in place to address such threats, Secretary General Mark Rutte said on Thursday.
"Russia is doing more and more when it comes to the cyber etc. domain, but... NATO is ready for this," Rutte said at an event in New York commemorating the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States.
"We have all these response options in place... when it comes to hybrids to make sure that we stay strong," he added.
Rutte argued that the growing number of hybrid incidents in NATO countries indicated that Russian President Vladimir Putin was losing the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
"Putin is in a bad place," Rutte said, adding that Russia is not winning the war in Ukraine and that citizens of the 32 NATO countries can remain calm.
He urged NATO members to provide "more support for Ukraine" if they "really want to give a signal to the Russians on every hybrid incident, hybrid attack."
"All the response options are there, and we will use whatever we need," Rutte added.
His remarks came after Danish intelligence on Thursday warned of a growing risk of Russian military action against NATO countries, including further hybrid attacks.
At the same time, Spanish media reported that US intelligence had alerted European countries to a possible Russian drone operation targeting Spain, France or Italy.
U.S. Defense Secretary urges Europe to take the lead on its defense
Meanwhile, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Thursday that European allies must take the lead in defending their continent, calling for NATO to become a "real hard-line military alliance."
Speaking at a meeting of NATO defence ministers, Hegseth proposed a "NATO 3.0" focused on strengthening military capabilities and deterring threats in Europe.
His comments came weeks after Washington informed its allies that it would no longer provide certain warships and aircraft in the event of an attack on a NATO member. European allies and Canada are now assessing how to address the resulting capability gaps.
"NATO 3.0 is post-Cold War recognition that (NATO) needs to go back to a real hard-line military alliance that has real military capabilities capable of deterring right here on the continent and taking the lead for the conventional defense of Europe," Hegseth said.
Under Article 5 of NATO's founding treaty, an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. However, the provision does not automatically require allies to provide military assistance.
The US, which has NATO's largest armed forces, is seeking to reduce its role in Europe's conventional defence. It does not plan to withdraw its nuclear weapons stationed in Europe, which remain a central element of NATO's deterrence strategy.

Vakulenko: Two-day NMT model and retakes under discussion, but challenges remain
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

20:29:59 EEST
02:29:59 KST

Kyiv. September 24. INTERFAX-UKRAINE – Director of the Ukrainian Center for Educational Quality Assessment (UCEQA) Tetiana Vakulenko states that a transition to a two-day model for the National Multisubject Test (NMT) and the possibility of retakes are currently under discussion.
"Several models for administering the National Multisubject Test are currently being developed, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that the testing process should be more accommodating to applicants living in difficult circumstances. Among the announced changes is the potential implementation of a two-day testing model, in which participants would take one section within two hours on one day and then two more exams on another day of testing," Vakulenko said at a press conference on Thursday in Kyiv, which was dedicated to the results of the 2026 admissions campaign.
She also said that applicants may be given the opportunity to retake the National Multidisciplinary Test if they receive an insufficient score and fail to meet the minimum passing score.
At the same time, she said that it is still too early to say exactly which model will be implemented. "Because despite the great flexibility of the Ukrainian Center and the education system as a whole, we must take the calendar into account; we must release the results within the admissions campaign timeline, and we must also take into account the specific characteristics of our network, particularly the presence or absence of shelters," Vakulenko added.
She recalled that earlier this year, there was a situation in Odesa where some applicants were unable to take the tests under adequate conditions due to a lack of shelters and a prolonged air raid alert.
"If we apply a two-day model to this, multiplied by the possibility of retakes, there will actually be more such problems, because there are still not enough shelters for us to support the entire assessment model," she said.
As previously reported, in early June, amid public debate over the National Multidisciplinary Test (NMT), Yulia Hryshyna, chair of the Subcommittee on Higher Education of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Education, Science, and Innovation, along with 50 deputies, introduced a bill (No. 15254-1) to reduce the number of subjects on the National Multidisciplinary Test (NMT) in 2027 and to make mathematics an elective rather than a required subject.

Here's how Ed Sheeran can find his spine. It starts with Kneecap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:29:47 UTC
02:29:47 KST

Breadcrumb
Here's how Ed Sheeran can find his spine. It starts with Kneecap
In the early days of grime and UK hip hop, artists who wanted to be heard lacked platforms. Pirate radio carried sets across the estates, clash DVDs were copied until the picture barely held, and MP3 tracks moved from phone to phone over Bluetooth. MCs built reputations by word of mouth, but no reliable, quick way existed to access some of the most magical moments of the early culture. That is, until Jamal Edwards launched SBTV.
Edwards filmed rappers on street corners on a camcorder and uploaded the footage to YouTube. SBTV’s audience grew because it was one of the few places to easily access UK grime and hip hop. The street-corner vibe, along with the home-video aesthetic, gave the channel what the mainstream lacked: authenticity.
This is where Ed Sheeran launched his career in 2010. His track ‘You Need Me, I Don't Need You’ quickly went viral, and the rest is history. Sheeran has acknowledged just how much SBTV changed his life.
Ironically, the very platform that propelled Sheeran to fame was built from below by artists who weren’t afforded space on mainstream channels. It featured testimony from the otherwise ignored, and the impact was transformative. As bell hooks put it, "within commodity culture, ethnicity becomes spice, seasoning that can liven up the dull dish that is mainstream white culture ".
The testimony of disenfranchisement can only go so far, though: to the point of actually accusing a perpetrator. Mainstream consumption wants to hear these stories but doesn’t want the systems of disenfranchisement named. In the case of Palestine, it’s the genocide perpetrated by Israel. This is where Sheeran now finds himself embroiled.
Controlling the acceptable
Sheeran built his career on a platform meant to give voice to people the mainstream would not host, and now he performs in rooms where the absence of that same voice is a condition of entry. The tragedy is not that he betrayed anything; it is that by the time you can fill a stadium, you no longer own the stage.
This was proven once again when Sheeran’s US Loop Tour was set to begin. Rapper Macklemore was removed from the line-up after the stadium owners warned that the shows would not take place if he performed. This followed his calls for a ‘Free Palestine’ at a prior show in New Jersey.
Sheeran’s apology, which came only after the backlash and once every remaining support act had withdrawn in solidarity with Palestinians, was also rightly criticised as carefully curated and as equivocating between both sides.
There was also an interesting admission nestled in Sheeran’s statement. Reportedly, it wasn’t just Robert Kraft but operators of other venues too: David Tepper, Arthur Blank and Jeffrey Lurie, who also pressured Sheeran to drop Macklemore.
The obvious point is that those with power and ownership get to dictate who gets access to their venues; they are the landlords, and the rest of us compete for media real estate to argue our views. It goes beyond simply allowing or banning free speech; these owners get to decide what is political and apolitical.
The framing creates a category with only one occupant; ergo, politics becomes whatever the landlords don’t already agree with. Macklemore, and anyone whose politics dissent, can be prevented from entering the venue with impunity. Not because they infringed free-speech laws (or any other laws) but because they didn’t agree to the house rules, which were never written down to begin with.
It is a secret menu of acceptability, coded into a culture that consumes stories from people at the bottom, refuses the ones that implicate anyone at the top, and calls the result universal.
Don’t mention genocide
During the last few years of Israel’s most recent genocide in Gaza, the backlash against artists who refused to ‘stay in line’ has been fierce and relentless.
For example, in 2025, Cornell University withdrew its invitation to Kehlani to headline its annual celebratory event, Slope Day, after pressure over her support for Palestine. This time, the enforcer was an institution that exists for debate. The language used to silence the artists was shrouded in ‘student safety’ and ‘belonging’.
That same month, Irish hip-hop band Kneecap projected messages about Gaza during their Coachella set. The British state responded with a counter-terrorism investigation; it charged one of the artists, Mo Chara, over a Hezbollah flag displayed at a London gig; festival appearances were subsequently withdrawn on police advice; and the musicians were banned from entering Hungary. The charge was eventually dismissed and the High Court rejected the prosecution's appeal in March 2026.
Bob Vylan was another band that received the weight of punishment reserved for artists who dared address the Gaza genocide when they led a chant about the IDF at Glastonbury Festival. Their American visas were revoked, their agency dropped them, and festivals removed them from bills. This is despite the fact that the artists were never charged with anything over their statements.
Of course each case of repression differs. For example, Kneecap's case involved a proscribed organisation's flag, which is a question of law rather than taste. Macklemore said that opposition to genocide is not an attack on Jewish people and called for a Free Palestine. They differ enormously in content, yet they barely differ in consequence.
A university, a government, a talent agency and stadium owners independently arrived at the same remedy, which was removal, and the severity of that remedy bore almost no relationship to the severity of the artists’ actions. Nobody organised this. There was no meeting. That is what makes it a structure rather than a conspiracy, and why the useful question isn't who gave the order, but what the limit is protecting.
Ed Sheeran went on stage in Philadelphia with no support act in sight. While he often performs alone on stage, this time the empty stage was not his choice. In some sort of cosmic symmetry, it mirrored his viral performance on SBTV, both performances were just Sheeran and his guitar. The former launched his career; the latter is putting serious strain on it; the loop, it turns out, closes (pun fully intended).
Beyond the obvious image of the empty stage, though, is the deeper point: when the people who supplied the room's meaning withdraw, what's left is the building. The art is hollow without our contributions.
It is worth remembering what the industry is actually selling. Not the stadiums, not the lighting rigs, not the sponsorship. It is selling stories, and the stories came from below. So, the question the Macklemore affair leaves us with is not what the landlords will permit. It is what we are prepared to give them.
Whether we follow the artists who walked off the tour or the stage they walked away from. Whether we pay for testimony in the rooms that let them finish the sentence, or in the ones that cut it short. Whether the next Jamal Edwards builds a room of his own, and whether we turn up to fill it. The choice is ours.
A cultural and economic boycott directed towards the venues and artists who don’t clearly stand with Palestine is achievable and effective. Just look at the cultural boycott of South Africa during apartheid. The stories we tell were never the industry's to begin with. They were lent, and a loan can be recalled.
Nadeem Dawud studied History at Oxford and King’s College London, where he completed a Master’s in World History and Cultures. His interests lie in decolonialism, anarchism, and building resilient communities. A long-time activist in the UK Muslim community, he now focuses on grassroots projects that speak locally but resonate globally, and he co-hosts the Boys in the Cave podcast.
