Ethan Hawke leads a tense, Depression-era thriller in  ‘The Weight’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:58 UTC
01:38:58 KST

In April 1933, US president Franklin D. Roosevelt signed an executive order banning the hoarding of gold and requiring Americans to deliver excess quantities to a Federal Reserve Bank by that May. The policy isn’t the subject of much discussion in the tense and earthy thriller The Weight, but it does set the stage for a heist, in which a group of work camp prisoners are assembled for a dangerous, off-the-books gold smuggling job, with Ethan Hawke leading the charge.
Hawke plays Samuel Murphy, a single father to a young daughter, Penny (Avy Berry), who is struggling to make ends meet four years into the Great Depression. Murphy is smart, capable and honest, which does not necessarily benefit him or his daughter in these greedy and violent times. They return from church one day to find they’ve been evicted from their apartment. On the search for a new one, some toughs give them a hard time. But self-defense excuses only go so far when the agitator you’ve punched in the face is a police officer. Soon, Murphy is being shipped off to a work camp. If he’s not out in time, Penny will become a ward of the state.
With a raspy voice and a world-weary look, Murphy tries to keep to himself at the camp. But he can’t help but distinguish himself as a resourceful problem solver, and the warden, Clancy ( Russell Crowe ), takes notice. Clancy isn’t your run-of-the-mill sadistic, mustache-twirling kind of warden. He can seem even a little likable at times. But he’s also the one with all the power: It’s hard to know if he can be trusted even if he gives the workers the occasional day off. Still, when Clancy promises that if Murphy pulls off the gold job, he’ll sign papers to free Murphy so that he can reunite with Penny, he decides it’s a bet worth taking.
Photo: AP
So Murphy puts together a team of fellow prisoners: Singh (Avi Nash), Olson (Lucas Lynggaard Tonnesen) and Rankin (Austin Amelio) to help transport heavy gold bars from point A to B through the wet Oregon wilderness (played by Bavaria). There are also a few deeply suspicious and ornery guys who are working for the ones planning the operation, and a Native American woman, Anna (Julia Jones), who joins the trek as well. It’s a big group trying to stay under the radar on this white-knuckle journey, in which they have to figure out how to cross a broken rope bridge with the heavy gold (it involves a very stressful tossing and catching scheme) and ford a river to cover their tracks. No one is sure they can trust anyone in the group. And then there’s the wild card terror of the giggly lone vagrant looking for something to eat and wondering what exactly is in all those heavy-looking bags.
Hawke feels natural in this environment, clad in denim workwear that may have been standard issue at the time but also looks like something your average Brooklynite dad would wear. And he’s believable as the guy whose brain gets him out of more scrapes than his brawn.
The Weight comes from director Padraic McKinley and writers Matthew Chapman, Matthew Booi and Shelby Gaines, who keep the momentum going at a rousing and confident clip.
It is very much a “dad movie,” which isn’t, in this case, a bad or even limiting thing. More than a few people have compared it to something Clint Eastwood might have done at some point — just a solid, hearty, meat-and-potatoes kind of movie.

Motorcycle training to be boosted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:55 UTC
01:38:55 KST

Five hours of practical training would be added to motorcycle rider training courses from Jan. 1 next year, including three additional hours of on-road training, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications said on Wednesday, adding that pilot on-road motorcycle license tests in selected regions will also begin in October next year.
The ministry since January has been redesigning licensing in a bid to improve drivers’ skills.
Although attending a training course is not required prior to taking a motorcycle license test, the Highway Bureau provides subsidies to do so.
Photo: CNA
In the first six months of this year, 784 motorcyclists died within 30 days of being involved in a traffic incident, accounting for nearly 60 percent of total deaths in the category, ministry data showed.
Highway Bureau data showed that 59,912 people obtained government subsidies to take motorcycle training courses last year, up from 40,378 in 2024.
The training course for a regular motorcycle license consists of six hours of classroom instruction and 10 hours of practical training.
Proposed amendments to the Regulations Governing the Management of Private Motor Vehicle Driver Training Institutions (民營汽車駕駛人訓練機構管理辦法) announced on Wednesday would increase practical training hours for license applicants to 15, effective from Jan. 1 next year.
The five additional hours would be two hours of motorcycle handling skills at the training venue and three hours of on-road training to improve field of vision awareness, recognition of road conditions and the judgement of when to use headlights, the ministry said.
In addition to the increase in practical training hours, the ministry also announced that it would begin a trial in October next year to conduct on-road tests for motorcycle license applicants.
People would be eligible for a NT$1,300 subsidy after applying through a driving school, paying the course fee, completing the training and obtaining a license within the subsidy period, the Highway Bureau’s Web site said.
People who undergo post-test road-safety training are eligible for a NT$1,200 subsidy, while those who undergo pre-test road-driving training can receive NT$2,500, it said.

US lawmakers urge Trump to maintain arms sales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:54 UTC
01:38:54 KST

Four US Senate Republicans as well as a bipartisan group of US representatives wrote letters to the White House on Wednesday calling on the administration to uphold US commitments to supply Taiwan with arms ahead of US President Donald Trump’s summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平).
Xi is expected to press Trump to halt Taiwan arms sales altogether during his three-day visit to Washington, sources briefed on the matter said.
The Chinese leader landed in Washington on Wednesday night and was after press time last night to hold talks with Trump.
Photo: Bloomberg
The Trump administration in December last year approved an US$11 billion arms package to Taiwan, the largest ever, but a second US$14 billion package has been on hold for months.
US senators Mitch McConnell, John Cornyn, Lisa Murkowski and Thom Tillis wrote to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth expressing concern about more than US$15 billion in stalled national security assistance for Taiwan.
The letter cites the US Department of State’s failure to move ahead with US$300 million in foreign military financing the US Congress appropriated for Taiwan, the defense department’s failure to obligate US$1 billion and the administration’s decision to withhold approval for a US$14 billion package of foreign military sales.
“We are concerned by President Trump’s description of Taiwan as ‘a very good negotiating chip’ in engagements with Xi Jinping and the Chinese Communist Party,” the letter said.
“It is difficult to imagine how the United States might credibly project influence deterrence in the Indo-Pacific if the price of keeping up diplomatic appearances is denying our partners key deterrent capabilities,” it said.
The state and defense departments did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Rubio, speaking to reporters in New York, said the administration had to balance broader needs.
“I know everyone’s focused on Taiwan, but I want you to focus globally for a moment. If we sell you something, we don’t have it anymore. Now, we may be able to make it in the future, but we don’t have it right now,” he said.
“Anytime we do any sales — not to Taiwan, to anybody — it is always balanced against what are our own needs in different parts of the world and whether we can afford to sell something, because we may need it for ourselves. So that’s going through that process,” he added.
Trump’s fellow Republicans in Congress rarely question his administration’s actions publicly.
Three of the senators who signed Wednesday’s letter — McConnell, Cornyn and Tillis — are leaving the Senate at the end of this year, with only Murkowski remaining.
In a separate letter addressed to Trump, a bipartisan group of seven US representatives urged the president not to consult China on arms sales to Taiwan.
They commended the administration for its “record-breaking arms package for Taiwan” announced in December last year, saying that this package, alongside other steps taken to deepen bilateral military cooperation, is successfully helping deter Chinese aggression.
“Increasing Taiwan’s self-defense capabilities, including through additional arms sales, is essential to US security,” they wrote.
The letter also pressed Trump to demand the release of wrongfully detained US citizens in China, called for expanded bilateral law enforcement cooperation to combat the fentanyl crisis and urged Trump to hold Beijing accountable for its weaponization of critical mineral supply chains.
The signatories were US representatives Young Kim, Ami Bera, Aumua Amata Coleman Radewagen, Gabe Amo, James Moylan, Michael McCaul and Ryan Mackenzie.

The Animal Protection Act (動物保護法) stipulates that owners can be fined NT$3,000 to NT$15,000 if they fail to register their cats or dogs aged four months or older.
Nearly 33,000 pet owners had entered the lottery as of Wednesday, Chen said.
Winners are eligible for one of 30,000 vouchers, as well as 100 pet health checkup reimbursement vouchers, the department said.
The NT$300 vouchers can be used to buy pet food or other supplies, or agricultural products at any of the 436 stores operated by collaborating businesses or associations, it said.
Winners of the checkup vouchers can take their dog or cat to a veterinary clinic for a health check or medical treatment, it said, adding that the voucher can be submitted to the department for up to a NT$3,000 reimbursement.
Lottery entries are open until Wednesday next week, it said.
The draw would be livestreamed on the YouTube channel of the ministry’s Animal Protection Information Network on Friday next week, it said.

====================================================================================================

Vessel donation to Manila would not harm fishers: OAC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

Ocean Affairs Council (OAC) Minister Kuan Bi-ling (管碧玲) on Wednesday said decommissioned coast guard vessels were given to the Philippines to enhance regional rescue capacity and would not affect Taiwanese fishers’ rights and benefits.
Kuan made the remarks after confirmation on Tuesday that a 500-tonne Coast Guard Administration (CGA) patrol and rescue vessel would be given to the Philippine Coast Guard.
The donation ceremony was reportedly done in Manila, but whether the vessel — previously numbered “CG123” and named Kinmen (金門) — has been handed over has yet to be confirmed.
Photo courtesy of the Ocean Affairs Council
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) on Wednesday criticized the donation for “taking the side of the evildoer,” China Central Television reported.
TAO spokesperson Zhu Fenglian (朱鳳蓮) called for cross-strait cooperation on safeguarding territorial sovereignty for “the Chinese nation,” it reported.
Zhu criticized the donation for “increasing the risk of undermining Taiwanese fishermen’s rights and benefits,” as the Philippines and Japan had initiated maritime boundary negotiations involving waters east of Taiwan proper, it added.
Kuan on Wednesday in a Facebook post said the donation aimed to boost regional rescue capacity and maritime safety.
Taiwan has the right to cooperate with nearby countries and dismisses Beijing’s uninvited opinions, she said.
CGA authorities have long supported local fishery workers’ operations, Kuan said.
That included expelling Chinese vessels that trespass into Taiwanese waters, delivering life-saving medicines to fishers in distant waters, and helping with marine emergencies such as fishing boat grounding, fires on the ship or crew members overboard, she said.
Neighboring countries could more promptly help rescue a Taiwanese boat that encounters danger within their rescue zone if they are equipped with better vessels and rescue capabilities, Kuan said.
International maritime search and rescue is mutual assistance as well as a humanitarian action, Kuan said, adding that to boost a neighboring country’s rescue capacity would enhance Taiwanese fishers’ safety.
To establish a transparent, reliable regional maritime order, Taiwan has signed the Taiwan-Japan Fisheries Agreement, as well as the Agreement Concerning the Facilitation of Cooperation on Law Enforcement in Fisheries Matters with the Philippines, she said.
In contrast, China constitutes a more urgent risk to Taiwan’s fishers, Kuan said.
It arbitrarily conducts military drills around Taiwan, approaches and inspects Taiwanese vessels for so-called law enforcement, and detains Taiwanese boats and fishers for long periods without a transparent handling process, she said.
The donation’s agreements specify that the vessel must not be used in law enforcement against Taiwanese fishing boats, Kuan added.

====================================================================================================

A roadmap for the next UN secretary-general
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:46 UTC
01:38:46 KST

Leading the UN has always been a balancing act, but the breakdown of the postwar global order has added a new dimension of complexity to the role. The next secretary-general, who is to take office next year, will fill the most prominent position in multilateral governance at a time when multilateralism is arguably at its nadir. To rebuild trust in international cooperation, the new leader must view this crisis for what it is: an unprecedented opportunity for fundamental reform.
Seven candidates are vying to replace Antonio Guterres, although the third UN Security Council straw poll has further narrowed the field (while indicating members’ willingness to respect the principle of regional rotation, according to which the next secretary-general will be from Latin America or the Caribbean). Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica and Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett of Guyana have emerged as the top two contenders, but the absence of a clear front-runner could encourage a late entrant.
Whoever is ultimately selected will need a transformative roadmap for the first 100 days — and beyond — to shape the UN’s trajectory and ensure that global governance is made fit for the 21st century. Cepei, the Bogota-based think tank that I head, has partnered with organizations around the world and convened regional consultations with leading academics, former diplomats, policymakers, practitioners and other stakeholders to reflect on the agenda and priorities of the next UN secretary-general and the future of UN leadership more broadly.
Illustration: Mountain People
These meetings show that expectations are high. Although the UN secretary-general’s independent powers are limited, an incumbent wields political capital, serves as the organization’s public voice, appoints senior officials and oversees management. So, the question becomes, how can the next secretary-general demonstrate leadership, credibility and direction in the first 100 days while operating within these limits?
For starters, the next secretary-general should focus on delivering consistent messaging and on using the largely predictable UN calendar to achieve some early wins. They should begin with political clarity, not thematic expansion; complete existing agendas, such as the Sustainable Development Goals and climate agreements; and shift the focus from proliferation to execution.
More fundamentally, the new head must also commit to making power more transparent; embed inclusion across the UN system; strengthen coordination with member states; and ensure that financing is aligned with governance.
That means rebuilding trust from within. When appointing the senior leadership team, the next secretary-general should select people who demonstrate political courage, independent judgement, discipline in setting priorities, a willingness to take risks and withstand criticism, and a renewed commitment to mediation.
Such leaders will be well-positioned in the long term to incentivize coordination, build coalitions that outlive their tenure, and pursue meaningful structural and organizational change backed by concrete accountability mechanisms.
Instilling a renewed sense of purpose in a workforce of about 120,000 people struggling with low morale and impossibly tight budgets will require a compelling diagnosis of the UN’s challenges, a vision for its future and priorities for action. The diagnosis should focus on political factors first and foremost, as many of its problems can be traced to choices made by member states, weakening consensus and shifting power relations. To be sure, this limits what institutional reform — or the secretary-general alone — can realistically achieve. But, more importantly, it suggests that the selection and transition agenda should address not only the expectations for the next secretary-general, but also what member states are prepared to provide in return.
The secretary-general will inherit the unfinished UN80 Initiative, which aims to improve efficiency, review implementation of the body’s mandates, and examine possible structural changes and program realignments. In the first 100 days, important decisions must be made about which parts of the reform agenda to continue, which to adjust, and which to abandon, while keeping in mind the need to avoid reform fatigue and ensure that the next phase is shaped and owned by member states.
At the country level, the secretary-general must also make difficult choices about activities the UN should no longer pursue, while improving delivery, localization and coordination. This requires greater clarity about where the UN adds value, focusing on its universal legitimacy, convening and norm-setting power, and, perhaps most importantly, mediation and “good offices.” The guiding principle should be differentiation, not withdrawal: continuing direct delivery where necessary while relying more deliberately on regional and national actors when they are better placed to act.
Lastly, to reduce the UN’s dependence on voluntary contributions and earmarked resources, often from a small number of major donors, the next secretary-general should begin engaging with member states to develop a more sustainable funding model. This means preparing to make strategic use of the organization’s existing levers of authority to align financing with governance, which would strengthen the system’s effectiveness and accountability. This could be accomplished by maximizing unearmarked voluntary funding and creating project-specific funding windows (where transaction costs do not distort governance), while also providing contributors with appropriate political recognition and greater transparency.
The new UN head’s broader agenda — restore peace, protect the most vulnerable, and convince the world to act on climate change and regulate artificial intelligence — represents a formidable challenge, especially as geopolitical upheaval impedes efforts to forge consensus or deliver long-term solutions. The UN has not adapted quickly enough to today’s multipolar reality in which influence is dispersed across many sites. Tokenistic engagement and negative narratives reinforce a sense of exclusion, deepening the legitimacy crisis.
However, the next secretary-general can change that trajectory. Although rebuilding legitimacy will not be easy or immediate, a leader who demonstrates strong management skills and a commitment to reform in the first 100 days will provide an important foundation on which to build a reinvigorated UN.
Philipp Schonrock is director of Cepei, a Bogota-based independent think tank that specializes in global governance and data and digitalization to accelerate sustainable development.

Taiwan yesterday thanked eight European and Indo-Pacific countries for opposing unilateral changes to the “status quo” in the Taiwan Strait in a joint statement earlier this week, as well as three of Taiwan’s allies for speaking up for the nation’s participation in the UN at the body’s General Assembly in New York.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) welcomed the support and expressed his appreciation for the countries’ stance, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.
Foreign ministers and senior representatives of Australia, France, Germany, Japan, New Zealand, Poland, South Korea and the UK issued a statement on Tuesday after meeting on the sidelines of the General Assembly.
Photo: AFP
“We emphasize the importance of maintaining peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific. We encourage dialogue and oppose any unilateral attempts to change the status quo across the Taiwan Strait,” the representatives said.
The ministry said it welcomed the continued attention from the international community and like-minded partners to maintaining peace, stability and the “status quo.”
In the face of growing geopolitical and regional challenges, Taiwan would bolster its self-defense and societal resilience, while deepening cooperation with democratic partners, it said.
Three of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies — Paraguay, the Kingdom of Eswatini and Palau — on Wednesday pushed for Taiwan’s inclusion in the UN when their leaders addressed the General Assembly.
The ongoing crisis in the Middle East was already troubling, but there could be an even more serious crisis in Taiwan, Paraguayan President Santiago Pena said in his speech.
“If oil was the fuel of the 20th century, chips are the fuel of the 21st,” he said. “What is at stake in this potential conflict is significant: the very future of humanity.”
Taiwan’s exclusion is “a stain on the United Nations,” Pena said, reaffirming Paraguay’s support for the full and meaningful participation of Taiwan in the UN and its specialized agencies.
Palauan President Surangel Whipps Jr said that his country chooses its partners “based on shared values of democracy, human rights and a rules-based international order.”
Those principles “underpin our friendship with Taiwan, a trusted partner that can contribute even more fully if given space to do so,” he said.
“We stand with like-minded partners in calling for the reversal of misinterpretations of rules and procedures that have constrained Taiwan’s meaningful participation in this body,” he added.
King Mswati III also expressed Eswatini’s support for Taiwan, which he said plays a vital role in global supply chains.
Taiwan “has much to contribute to the international community and can play a highly meaningful role in building a sustainable future for humanity,” he said.
President William Lai (賴清德) thanked the representatives in a Facebook post, writing that democratic unity is the only answer to global authoritarian expansion.
As a key link in global democratic and supply chains, Taiwan is keenly aware of its responsibilities, Lai said.
“We are not only on the front line of safeguarding freedom and democracy, but also a mature, responsible and trustworthy force for good in the international community,” he added.

Tyler Jones umpired the first game of this week’s series between the Toronto Blue Jays and the Baltimore Orioles and was napping the next day when his brother Austin called and told him that the middle game of the series was rained out.
A doubleheader on Wednesday meant that Austin Jones — who in addition to being Tyler Jones’ identical twin is also an umpire — was on his way to Baltimore to work the games alongside his brother.
“This is something we’ve dreamed about forever,” Tyler Jones said. “We were told last year: ‘OK, if we can make it happen, we’ll make it happen.’ And it didn’t. The schedules didn’t align. Even this year we weren’t even sure if it was going to happen or not, and then it was kind of a shock.”
Photo: AP
The 31-year-old twins called both ends of Wednesday’s doubleheader, each won by Baltimore by a 4-2 score. Austin worked first base in the opener and Tyler was at second. Then they swapped for the nightcap — although the numbers on their uniforms were the only easy way to tell them apart.
The two are on a list of Triple-A call-up umpires who fill in at the big league level for injuries, illnesses, vacations and other reasons of absence. There are typically five umpires on a crew for a doubleheader instead of four, so Austin Jones was added.
Austin Jones umpired his first MLB game in 2024, Tyler Jones last year. They had worked a game together in the Gulf Coast League and the Arizona Fall League, but never in the majors.
“We talk to each other daily, especially about baseball and about everything, what we go through on a day-to-day basis, but to be able to live it together, and come to the ballpark and see him in the locker room and play cards with him before the game and share that experience was probably the best part,” Tyler Jones said.
Tyler Jones jokes that he got into umpiring because “I was a really bad baseball player.”
They both started young, working youth games and earning some money when they were in high school.
“We did umpire school together and we roomed together,” Austin Jones said. “We had never really lived on our own, we were 18 years old. So it was our first time out of the house, doing things on our own, and we said: ‘Man, if this is kind of what life in professional baseball is like, this is pretty cool.’”

The dangers that come with having Chinese IDs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:44 UTC
01:38:44 KST

China’s “united front” tactics against Taiwan have long gone beyond slogans and propaganda, gradually extending into identity, the economy and everyday life.
Recent media reports said that some people in Taiwan are suspected of acting as intermediaries, urging other Taiwanese to travel to China to apply for IDs. While such activities are ostensibly packaged as convenient services, in practice, they might be using the IDs to gradually draw Taiwanese into China’s governance.
Once an issue involves organized recruitment, repeated assistance with applications, or direction or exploitation by foreign forces, it is no longer simply a matter of cross-strait exchange — it is a warning sign that Taiwan’s national security defenses must be taken seriously.
Under Article 9-1 of the Act Governing Relations Between the People of the Taiwan Area and the Mainland Area (臺灣地區與大陸地區人民關係條例), people of the Taiwan Area are prohibited from establishing a household registration in China or obtaining a Chinese passport. The Mainland Affairs Council has made it clear that Chinese ID cards and permanent resident certificates are subject to regulations governing household registration in China. Those who contravene these rules might lose their status as residents of Taiwan and the rights that come with it.
Since the legal red lines have long been clearly established, no one should be allowed to exploit gaps in public knowledge by packaging something with such severe legal consequences as a “document application service” or a “business convenience.” This raises concerns about the involvement of organized recruitment, exchanges of benefits or foreign intervention. If those being recruited include active-duty military or law enforcement personnel, civil servants, defense technology workers or others in sensitive fields, this issue cannot simply be treated as an individual choice regarding one’s identity. When one’s identity is intertwined with public authority, classified information and key positions, a personal risk can become a major vulnerability for the system.
Furthermore, national security defenses cannot wait until classified information has been leaked or an organized network has already taken shape before scrambling to patch the gaps. Any organized solicitation or agency work should not be investigated merely by asking whether it is a “private activity,” but by tracing who is providing the funding, resources and directives behind it. Only then can Taiwan ensure normal cross-strait exchanges while safeguarding national security.
An ID card might appear to be a personal choice, but behind it lie questions of identity verification, legal jurisdiction and national security. What needs to be severed is not normal exchanges between people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, but local networks that exploit Taiwan’s openness and freedom to build bridges and clear a path for foreign infiltration from within.
Yeh Yu-cheng is a secretary at the Pingtung County Public Health Bureau.

The case came to light on Aug. 10, when an unidentified user on Threads wrote that a fisher had found a rubber dinghy on a beach near the Port of Taipei in July, initially thinking it belonged to another fisher.
However, after inspecting the vessel more closely the next day, the fisher found life vests, Chinese-made fuel containers and rolls of toilet paper with writing in simplified Chinese, and reported the case to law enforcement, the user wrote.
Photo: CNA
After learning of the incident on July 24, the Coast Guard Administration (CGA) launched an investigation, and detained two Chinese men, surnamed Luan (欒) and Yu (于), at Chaoyang Forest Park in Taoyuan on July 30.
The two men were turned over to the Shilin District Prosecutors’ Office, which received court permission to detain the men incommunicado on Aug. 3.
On July 19, Luan and Yu set out by car from Qingdao in China’s Shandong Province, later purchasing an outboard motor for their raft in Jinhua in Zhejiang Province, prosecutors said in an indictment filed yesterday.
At about 4am or 5am on July 22, the two men launched their raft from the shoreline outside Fuzhou in China’s Fujian Province, crossing the Taiwan Strait and reaching the Port of Taipei’s northern jetty at about 2am on July 23.
After illegally entering Taiwan, Luan and Yu traveled to locations in New Taipei City, Taipei, Hsinchu, Taichung and Taoyuan, before being arrested by coast guard investigators on July 30, prosecutors said.
The indictment was based on suspect and witness statements, cellphone data, surveillance video footage and DNA analysis, prosecutors said.
Luan and Yu were charged with contravening the Immigration Act (入出國及移民法) and the Act Governing Relations Between the People of the Taiwan Area and the Mainland Area (臺灣地區與大陸地區人民關係條例), they said.
Prosecutors said they requested that both men be sentenced to two years in prison in light of the "substantive harm" Luan and Yu’s actions caused to Taiwan’s border control, coastal defense security and public order — as well as the "severe public anxiety" caused by their case.
The indictment’s strong language likely referred to public criticism the coast guard received for failing to detect the men’s raft, which led the agency’s director to apologize on Aug. 11, one day after the incident became public.

Photo: Lo Kuo-chia, Taipei Times

The first set of forums would be held in Hsinchu and Kaohsiung, while the second would be in Taipei and New Taipei City, they said.

“Lee is keenly interested in hearing the voices of young Taiwanese and will continue to engage in discussion with them,” they added.

Business confidence weakens: TIER
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:39 UTC
01:38:39 KST

Taiwan’s business confidence weakened across major sectors last month as Middle East tensions raised costs and uncertainty, although manufacturers remained broadly confident in the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research (TIER, 台經院) said yesterday.
The institute’s manufacturing business-climate gauge slid 0.49 points from July to 100.73, while the services gauge dropped 1.19 points to 97.30, extending its decline to a second month.
In addition, the construction gauge fell 1.89 points to 108.34, ending four consecutive months of gains.
Photo courtesy of the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research
Manufacturers became more cautious mainly because of Middle East tensions rather than growing concerns that the AI boom is losing steam, TIER Economic Forecasting Center director Gordon Sun (孫明德) told a news conference in Taipei.
Recent calls by some US AI industry leaders to slow the development of frontier technologies should not be taken as evidence that the boom is ending, Sun said.
The US has strong incentives to keep AI investment moving because data center construction can attract foreign investment and create jobs, while Washington is also seeking to maintain its lead over China in AI, he said.
TIER president Chang Chien-yi (張建一) said at the news conference that global technology companies are likely to keep pushing ahead with AI development, with the industry’s expansion unlikely to reverse.
“It is a matter of timing and pace,” he said.
Still, any significant slowdown in AI demand would have a major impact on Taiwan, where related technology has become the economy’s most important growth engine, Sun said.
While the institute’s survey found services sentiment also weakened last month, retailers remained relatively optimistic about the months ahead, with nearly 60 percent upbeat about their business outlook, it said.
Strong economic growth, robust earnings at major listed companies and gains in Taiwanese equities are also expected to support household spending, while cultural events and other activities could also draw consumers, the institute said.
The construction gauge fell after four straight months of gains, but the decline does not necessarily point to renewed weakness, TIER Taiwan Industry Economics Database director Arisa Liu (劉佩真) said.
The central bank’s decision this month to ease financing restrictions on second-home purchases and land loans should help improve sentiment, Liu said.
Housing transactions could rise modestly next quarter while prices remain broadly stable, with owner-occupiers likely to remain the main source of demand, she said.

Minister says rise in NHI premiums not necessary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:38 UTC
01:38:38 KST

National Health Insurance (NHI) premiums would not need to be adjusted next year if the minimum wage, salaries and government funding increase as expected, Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said yesterday.
Shih made the remark after the NHI Committee on Wednesday capped NHI spending next year at about NT$1.04 trillion (US$32.72 billion), the first time that the amount has exceeded NT$1 trillion.
The budget was recalculated based on the committee’s consensus that the collective NHI expenditure — by hospitals, Western medicine clinics, dental clinics and traditional Chinese medicine — would grow at a maximum 5.5 percent annually next year.
Photo: Taipei Times
The NHI budget would be NT$1.0434 trillion next year, NT$55 billion higher than this year, Shih told reporters on the sidelines of an event in Taipei.
Asked if the committee’s decision would trigger a premium rate hike, Shih said the ministry has assessed that NHI premium revenue could rise if the minimum wage, salaries across all sectors and government funding increase as expected.
With the supplementary premium revenue and an additional NT$60 billion allocated by the government to shore up the NHI system next year, it would have a reserve fund by the end of next year that could sustain the system for 2.3 months based on the wage-rise and funding forecasts, he said.
“If that is the case, there would be no need to increase health insurance premiums next year,” he said.
Reporters asked Shih about criticisms that the committee meeting has become little more than a rubber stamp, with members settling on the percentage of growth in NHI spending ahead of time, as well as calls for the meetings to be livestreamed to avoid questions about their legitimacy.
Shih said that negotiations before the meetings are necessary, as efficiency would be greatly compromised if everything were decided on the day.
Every meeting is convened according to administrative procedures, he said.
The agenda is made public seven days ahead of the meetings and all statements made at the sessions are disclosed to the public within 10 days, he said, adding that audio and video files of the meetings are preserved.
The ministry would discuss with members of the NHI committee whether the meetings should be broadcast live, he added.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:37 UTC
01:38:37 KST

Thai teenage guitar sensation Nene Royal on Wednesday won the US$1 million top prize on America’s Got Talent, capping a viral run that made the 16-year-old a national celebrity and drew support from across her home country.
Rattikarn Amloy, better known by her stage name Nene Royal, was crowned the winner during the live results show, beating nine other finalists after emerging as the clear favorite before the finale. During Tuesday’s final, she sang and played guitar on a rendition of Seven Nation Army by The White Stripes.
“You should win. Give her the million, America,” judge Howie Mandel said after the performance.
Photo: AFP
Fellow judge Melanie Brown praised Nene’s “mysterious, mystical stage presence” before adding: “You’re from the best place in the world, Phuket, Thailand. I love to go there.”
Her victory caps a rapid rise that began with a swaggering rendition of The Cranberries’ Zombie, in which she sang and tore through the song on guitar. The audition amassed more than 200 million views across the show’s official online platforms, more than any other act this season.
Nene’s run sparked an outpouring of support in Thailand, where her international profile drew backing from some of the country’s most powerful business and political figures.
Among her most prominent corporate supporters was billionaire Dhanin Chearavanont, patriarch of one of Asia’s wealthiest families. His Charoen Pokphand Foods rented space on a giant screen in New York’s Times Square to feature Nene alongside messages of support from Thai fans ahead of the live rounds.
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul also threw his support behind Nene, directing tourism officials to explore ways to promote the teenage guitarist. He also hosted her at the Government House, where she played guitar while he sang a Thai rock song.
Officials have discussed featuring her in campaigns promoting the country’s “Amazing Thailand” tourism brand.
Anutin, who is in New York for the UN General Assembly, congratulated Nene and thanked her for showcasing Thai talent to a global audience and helping promote a positive image of the country through music and performance.
“Nene’s success is proof that young Thais have the potential to compete with anyone in the world when they are given the opportunity, stay determined and continue to develop their talent,” he said in a statement.
The US$1 million prize marks a remarkable ascent from the Phuket night market where Nene once played for donations. She started playing at seven on a 1,600 baht (US$47.89) guitar, a considerable expense for her family at a time when her father earned just more than 10,000 baht a month. To help pay for lessons, he encouraged her to perform at the market.
After her performance in Tuesday’s final, Nene reflected on how far she had come.
“I was so young when I touched the guitar,” she said. “I was thinking, in my mind, I was like: ‘I really want to become a rock star.’ My dream comes true.”

Unearthed church sheds light on Greenland’s past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:37 UTC
01:38:37 KST

The discovery of a medieval church in Greenland has unveiled important clues about how Viking society on the island was organized more than 800 years ago, the National Museum of Denmark said yesterday.
Probably dating back to the 13th century, the church was built when the Vikings founded a colony on the vast arctic island, which ceased to be in the 1400s, under circumstances that remain mysterious.
“This is a sensation, it’s shedding light on the significance of this whole area,” said archeologist Christian E.K. Madsen, who led the research at Qinngua near Narsarsuaq in the south of the Danish autonomous territory.
Photo: Reuters
After the Vikings converted to Christianity from paganism, “churches were vital in Norse society,” Madsen said.
“When you build a church, you are making a claim for religious power, [which] is also part of your economic power, because then you get access to the church revenues,” he added.
The Vikings first colonized Greenland in the 10th century, several millennia after the island was populated by the Inuit of the arctic at least 3,000 years ago.
Having likely been built sometime before 1450, the church is believed to predate Denmark’s modern colonization of Greenland in the 18th century by nearly 300 years.
At least one grave lies next to the church, which measures about 8m to 10m long and 3m to 4m wide.
Surrounded by three farms, the building long eluded archeologists, but a clue found in the last hours of excavations carried out last year led to its discovery.
“It’s how villages started in Greenland: This is a proto village,” Madsen said, adding that the three farms probably shared fields and resources.
The settlers did not live solely from agriculture, he said.
“It’s a very marginal area for farming and the settlement was also about accessing the arctic resources,” he said, adding that they would have hunted for the teeth of walruses and narwhals alongside polar bear skins.
The resources would then be fed “back into the European markets and all the way to the Middle East and central Eurasia,” he said.
“Essentially the farms become a base for marine hunting in this area,” he said.
The discovery “should allow us to approach the story of how this particular settlement developed over time, how it was built and collapsed,” Madsen said.
“According to written sources, which turned out to be very reliable, the church was part of a network with smaller Catholic churches. They were the first Catholic churches on the North American continent,” he said.
“It’s telling us how people took Christianity there and kept and tried to hold up a life in the roughest place they could find to live in,” he added.

Minimum monthly wage to rise to NT$30,900
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:34 UTC
01:38:34 KST

Taiwan’s minimum monthly wage is set to rise to NT$30,900 next year from NT$29,500, exceeding NT$30,000 for the first time following a decision yesterday by the Ministry of Labor’s Minimum Wage Deliberation Committee.
The minimum hourly wage would also increase to NT$205 from NT$196, with both increases pending Cabinet approval.
The new rates are scheduled to take effect on Jan. 1 next year.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
According to the Ministry of Labor, around 2.61 million workers in Taiwan, including 414,400 migrant workers, are expected to benefit from the minimum wage hike.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) in April said that he could “guarantee” the minimum monthly wage would exceed NT$30,000 next year.
The minimum wage increases would not apply to migrant workers employed as live-in caregivers or domestic helpers, as they are not covered by the Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法).
The meeting, which began at 10am, continued until 5:30pm due to disagreements between labor and management representatives over the scale of the increase.
It was the second-longest minimum wage review on record, trailing only a nine-hour negotiation session in 2018.
The 4.745 percent hike marks the 11th consecutive year in which the minimum wage has increased.
Since 2016, the monthly wage has climbed 47.4 percent from NT$20,008 to the current NT$29,500, and the hourly wage has risen 63.3 percent from NT$120 to NT$196.
During the negotiations, the committee referenced a ministry research report that projected the consumer price index (CPI) would increase by 2.07 percent this year, while the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics had revised its estimate for the nation’s GDP growth this year to 11.05 percent.
Prior to the meeting, Chinese National Federation of Industries executive director Sam Ho (何語) cited customs export data to highlight a heavy imbalance in industrial development, saying that many sectors would struggle to absorb a uniform wage hike.
Chinese National Association of Industry and Commerce secretary-general Chiu Yi-cheh (邱一徹) urged the committee to base its decision on the CPI while considering the practical financial pressures faced by various industries.
However, Minister of Labor Hung Sun-han (洪申翰) said that the wage adjustment must reflect inflation to maintain the purchasing power and basic living standards of low-income workers.

ASIAN GAMES: Teams slam Games organizers over ‘chaos’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:32 UTC
01:38:32 KST

Several teams yesterday rounded on the organization of the Asian Games in Japan, with Thailand likening it to a “chaotic” game of “musical chairs” and South Korea saying “they deserve a failing grade.”
The biggest issue at the Aichi-Nagoya Games has been a shortage of rooms for the 17,000 participants, while some athletes have complained of cramped accommodation.
That was compounded by delays at airports and hours-long waits to board a cruise ship acting as a floating hotel. Erratic transportation services have seen competitors’ buses to training and venues turning up late or, in some cases, not at all.
No traditional athletes’ village has been built as a cost-cutting measure. Teams have instead been staying in temporary container-style huts, hotels and the Costa Serena cruise ship moored in Nagoya Port.
“It remains a problem from the beginning until now,” said Chalitrat Chandrubeksa, deputy secretary general of the National Olympic Committee of Thailand.
“The number of [rooms available on] cruise ships and hotels does not match our actual number of athletes. On the peak day, we required 201 beds on the cruise ship, but they provided only 170,” Chalitrat said.
“When athletes checked in and found their names missing from the list, they had to be placed somewhere else and when the new athletes arrived, the previous ones had to move out and look for other hotels,” he said.
“It’s like musical chairs,” he added.
Frustrated athletes have made their feelings known online, with complaints also about some of the food.
“We are solving the problem by finding replacement accommodations ourselves,” Chalitrat said.
The shortages meant the Thailand team had to put some staff far away from the Games epicenter in the city of Nagoya.
“Our medical team has to stay about one hour 30 minutes from Nagoya,” Chalitrat said. “We had to rent additional vehicles from Tokyo so they could travel to look after the athletes. “It has been chaotic.”
South Korea said that the problems were “affecting athletes’ performances,” Yonhap news agency reported.
“If I were to give them a grade, it would be an F,” South Korean Sport and Olympic Committee president Ryu Seung-min said.
Asian Games organizing committee spokesman Hiroshi Koshizuka told reporters that there had beem issues with transport, but added that “there had been no significant impact on the Games and no event has been delayed.”
“We have set up a system to respond to complaints and we will address them in a sincere manner going forward.”
However, the the complaints keep coming.
Taiwan’s Olympic committee spokesman Steven Chen said that experience prepared them for the worst.
They booked 100 extra rooms at hotels in case there was a shortage of beds.
“We were informed at the last minute before departure that there weren’t enough beds. That was a major blow to every country,” he said.
Chen said that the “biggest headache” was with transport, with schedules frequently changing at the last minute.
“When our team had an evening flight, they suddenly informed us that the afternoon bus to the airport was changed to pick us up in the morning, which caused us a lot of trouble,” he said.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:32 UTC
01:38:32 KST

The Taiwan Go Go political alliance yesterday called for greater electoral transparency, saying that 107 of the 14,100 candidates for borough and village wardens have criminal records.
Such information is not included in election bulletins, limiting public knowledge of candidates’ offenses, the alliance said.
New Power Party Chairwoman Claire Wang (王婉諭) cited as an example the candidate for Wufen Borough (五分) warden in Taipei’s Neihu District (內湖), Wang Chien-sheng (王健陞), who had been sentenced to one year and 10 months in prison for attempted sexual assault of a person who was incapacitated.
Photo: George Tsorng, Taipei Times
If a borough resident had not brought the matter to the party’s attention, voters would not have known about the candidate’s conduct, as it would not have appeared in the election bulletin, the chairwoman said.
The alliance investigated candidates in 20 regions, and identified 107 candidates with criminal records, she said.
Kaohsiung had the largest number at 22, followed by New Taipei City with 17 and Tainan with 11, she added.
Taiwan Statebuilding Party Taipei City councilor candidate Wu Hsin-tai (吳欣岱) said that as of Wednesday, election-related offenses accounted for the largest category at 36 cases.
Illegal claims for public funds or false reporting of campaign expenses, and violence or intimidation each accounted for 21 cases, followed by eight cases involving drunk or drug driving and traffic offenses.
Taiwan Obasang Political Equality Party (TOPEP) Taipei city councilor candidate Lee Hui-hsuan (李惠喧) said there were seven people involved in cases of attempted sexual assault, forced indecency, profiting from premises that provide prostitution, sexual harassment, and stalking and harassment.
At least four are sitting borough or village wardens, Lee said, adding that in two sexual harassment cases, the victims were minors, while one candidate was found guilty of 13 offenses involving the sexual harassment of children and adolescents.
Borough and village wardens depend on residents’ trust and candidates for such positions should understand and respect personal boundaries, Lee added.
TOPEP executive Chen Wan-yu (陳宛毓) said there were eight offenses involving bribery and 25 related to illicit relocation of household registrations.
Green Party Taiwan general convener Kan Chung-wei (甘崇緯) said 19 candidates were involved in 21 cases involving the misuse of public funds.
Of those, 11 took actions for their personal gain or to benefit others, while 10 involved falsified documents, Kan said.
Another nine cases involved falsifying documents to use public funds for ineligible people, he added.
Taiwan Go Go was formed last year to coordinate candidates and pool resources in elections.

Southwestern Mexico on Wednesday braced for heavy rain and mudslides after Polo, a powerful Pacific cyclone, became a major hurricane. Forecasters also warned another system headed for Hawaii could cause catastrophic flooding later in the week.
Hurricane Polo, an “extremely dangerous” storm, is expected to skirt Mexico’s Guerrero state, submerging coastal areas with 10cm to 15cm of rain through yesterday, the US National Hurricane Center said.
Guerrero has been repeatedly pummeled by hurricanes in the past few years.
Photo: AFP
Farther out in the Pacific, Tropical Storm Nolo was churning about 475km south of South Point, Hawaii. The storm was forecast to become a hurricane by last night and expected to approach the Big Island as early as today.
Hawaiian Governor Josh Green’s office said public schools and state and county offices on the Big Island would close yesterday and today, while Maui County would shutter them today ahead of the threat of heavy rain, winds and flooding.
Forecasters said the storm could drop up to 51cmof rain.
Concepcion Lopez Villegas was busily bolstering her seaside restaurant in Lazaro Cardenas, Michoacan, against the expected onslaught of rain.
Strong waves were already hitting some beaches and Lopez Villegas said she feared the storm could destroy the small business she worked decades to build.
“We’re worried and trying to protect our businesses,” she said. “And of course, we’re sad because it’s our heritage, our legacy that from one moment to another could be destroyed.”
Guerrero state was particularly at risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides, the hurricane center said.
In the resort town Acapulco, rough surf pounded the shoreline, rain swept across the bay and strong winds bent palm trees. Merchants reinforced stall roofs as boats remained anchored in the bay.
“As they gave us a warning yesterday, I started getting my documents in order and half-packed my things, just in case,” local resident Andrea Tenorio said.
A nearby elementary school had been opened as a temporary shelter, she said.
Asked whether she was afraid, Tenorio said memories of Hurricane Otis still haunted residents.
“With Otis, we were left with trauma,” she said. “We haven’t been able to overcome it.”
Hurricane Otis slammed into Acapulco in October 2023 as a Category 5 storm, killing dozens and flattening the coastal town.

Lessons from the Mataian disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:30 UTC
01:38:30 KST

On Sept. 23 last year, an overflow from a Mataian River (馬太鞍溪) barrier lake devastated Hualien County’s Guangfu Township (光復).
In the aftermath, tens of thousands of people boarded trains with their shovels, rain boots and tools to travel to the disaster site and help clear away the mud. The so-called “shovel heroes” quickly became one of the most celebrated and moving images of Taiwanese civil society. One year on, what the occasion calls for is not simply another celebration of that generosity, but an examination of how much has actually changed since the disaster.
The government has been reviewing its disaster preparedness and prevention systems based on lessons learned from the flood, rapidly expanding training programs for disaster relief volunteers, and making amendments to the Disaster Prevention and Protection Act (災害防救法) regarding responsibility management, local coordination and barrier lake risks.
However, the most pressing question still remains: When the next disaster arrives even faster and harder than the last, would we still be waiting on an organization of volunteers to rush to the scene, or have we found a way to harness civic power, such as those shown by the shovel heroes, into a mobilizable force of national resilience?
Guangfu showed us that Taiwan has the people. The next step is to prove whether it has the systems.
Extreme weather events this year have only heightened the issue’s urgency. Bouts of short, but intense rainfall have repeatedly broken records, while the limits of river dredgers, drainage systems, box culverts, water pumping stations and flood detention facilities are beginning to be tested.
The water management system’s measures for success can no longer just be about how much silt has been cleared and how many flood retention ponds have been built; we must start seriously stress testing for extreme climate conditions. When rainfall over 24 hours exceeds flood control standards, the government should be clear on which communities might experience flooding, which bridges might break, which power stations and cell towers might fail, and which hospital and care facilities need protection.
How we think about disasters must change: We need system-level thinking about drainage, water storage, flood detention and diversion and pre-emptive evacuations. True social resilience does not mean that cities would never flood; it means that when the limits of defenses are breached, the government knows where people should evacuate, supplies should be sent and equipment should be deployed, while ensuring essential services continue to operate.
Even more important to consider is the institutionalization of professional engineering capacity. In 2018, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) converted the Chinese People’s Armed Police Force Hydropower Corps into China Anneng Construction Group, a centrally owned engineering and emergency-rescue enterprise. Taiwan does not need to replicate that system, but it could learn from some of its strengths and establish a national engineering emergency response system compatible with a democratic system.
We already have a legal framework for requisitioning professionals, private vehicles and engineering equipment; the armed forces and reserve system also offer an institutional basis for supporting disaster prevention and response. What truly needs to be strengthened is the ability to use those resources when disaster strikes.
The central and local governments should establish a national engineering disaster response resource database, recording the locations and mobilization times of excavators, bulldozers, cranes, low-bed trailers, dump trucks, water pumps, generators and their operators. Personnel that specialize in engineering, communications, medical care, transportation, water, electricity, civil engineering and drones should also be incorporated into a reserve and civil coordination units.
Disaster response preparations should follow the logic of military operations: During normal times, resources are organized, drills are conducted, equipment are readied and chains of command are established, so that resources could be mobilized properly when a disaster strikes, instead of scrambling for personnel and equipment during the emergency.
The most precious lesson the Mataian disaster gave Taiwan is that the nation has a powerful societal capacity for spontaneous mutual aid. However, the state cannot treat people’s goodwill as a disaster response plan, nor could it expect another group of shovel heroes to swoop in each time a major disaster strikes.
On their first anniversary, we should turn the civic miracle of the shovel heroes into the starting point for reform. Taiwan should reassess capacity during extreme rainfall, establish specialized disaster response units, create a disaster mobilization database for civilian equipment, and connect volunteers, businesses, local governments, the armed forces and the central government’s disaster response system.
In the face of disasters, Taiwan last year saw that Taiwanese were willing to step in. Now, the state must demonstrate that before torrential rain falls, roads are cut off or infrastructure is damaged, it already knows what to do next. That is the true meaning of treating disaster response like combat, and what shovel heroes have left for Taiwan to fulfill.
Elliot Yao is a reviewer.

Brave Eagle AJT production completed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:30 UTC
01:38:30 KST

Taiwan has completed production of all 66 domestically developed Brave Eagle (勇鷹) advanced jet trainers (AJT), with Aerospace Industrial Development Corp (AIDC) chairman Tsao Chin-pin (曹進平) yesterday personally piloting one of the final two aircraft to the Air Force Academy in Kaohsiung’s Gangshan District (岡山).
The two aircraft, No. 1165 and 1166, took off at about 11am, circled Ching Chuan Kang Air Base (清泉崗基地) and made a low pass over AIDC’s Shalu plant in Taichung, where employees waved to the aircraft.
They landed at 11:36am, marking the completion of a nine-year program to develop and mass-produce the new trainer.
Photo: CNA
Although 66 Brave Eagles have been produced, the air force currently has 65 after one crashed into waters off Taitung County in February last year.
The pilot ejected safely from the aircraft.
The Brave Eagle is designed to replace the decommissioned F-5E/F and AT-3 aircraft, enabling the air force to adopt a “three-stage, two-aircraft” pilot training system that also involves the T-34 trainer aircraft.
The Brave Eagle serves advanced and operational flight-training roles, allowing pilots to transition more efficiently to frontline fighters such as the F-16V Block 20 and Block 70 aircraft.
The advanced jet trainer program was launched in 2017 through contracts involving the air force, government-funded weapons developer National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST) and the AIDC.
AIDC was the prime contractor, overseeing aircraft design, component production, assembly and testing, while more than 200 domestic suppliers participated in the program.
Derived from Taiwan’s Indigenous Defense Fighter (IDF), the Brave Eagle has more than 80 percent of its components redesigned from those of the IDF, with changes to its aerodynamics, exterior and fuselage. Its domestic content reached 55 percent.
The first prototype was unveiled on Sept. 24, 2019, and named Brave Eagle by then-president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文).
AIDC completed the aircraft’s design and conducted its first flight within three years and two months, the company said.
Mass production began in 2021, but was affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, international conflicts and geopolitical tensions that disrupted global supply chains.
AIDC said it overcame shortages of imported systems and key components by developing some of them domestically in cooperation with government research institutes and local manufacturers.
Despite those disruptions, AIDC delivered 14 Brave Eagles each last year and this year, it said.
Completing the program has also strengthened its experience and capabilities in aircraft development, systems integration, mass production and supply chain management, which would support future military aircraft maintenance, upgrades and logistics programs, AIDC said.
With the Brave Eagle production completed and plans for a next-generation primary trainer or fighter jet still undetermined, experts warned of a potential talent drain in the domestic aerospace industry.
Chi Li-ping (齊立平), former head of the institute’s Aeronautical Systems Research Division, urged the government not to repeat the mistake it made after the IDF program in the 1990s, when a halt in development led to a decades-long technology and talent gap.
Maintaining an indigenous aircraft platform is the lifeblood of national defense autonomy, Chi said, adding that while Taiwan could integrate its domestically developed missiles onto the IDF, the US would never open the interfaces of purchased F-16s or MQ-9B drones to accommodate Taiwanese weapons.
Institute for National Defense and Security Research research fellow Shu Hsiao-huang (舒孝煌) suggested that pivoting to develop advanced combat drones could be a viable path to sustain the local industry’s manufacturing capabilities, although it would require significant financial and personnel investments.

The Center for Countering Disinformation (CCD) of the National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) has documented the continuation of a disinformation campaign aimed at discrediting Ukrainians in Poland and provoking interethnic conflicts.
"Through a number of publications that regularly spread narratives in line with Russian propaganda, manipulative articles about Ukrainians are being injected into the Polish information space. In particular, narratives are being spread claiming that "Ukrainians are committing crimes against Poles on a massive scale," "are massively establishing criminal drug-production businesses," and so on," according to the center's statement on Telegram on Thursday evening.
According to the Center for Countering Disinformation, claims are also being circulated in the Polish information space that there is a "Ukrainian fifth column in Poland that is destroying the country from within." In addition, conspiracy theories are being spread claiming that Ukraine is contributing to the narrowing of "Poland's borders to the boundaries of the Duchy of Warsaw." "This campaign is designed to incite hatred toward Ukrainians among Poles, provoke interethnic conflicts, and hinder aid to Ukraine," the center said.

Retail, food, beverage sales hit record highs for August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:28 UTC
01:38:28 KST

Retail and food and beverage sales last month hit record levels for August, rising annually for the seventh consecutive month, although growth moderated from the previous month, data released on Wednesday by the Ministry of Economic Affairs showed.
Retail sales increased 6.5 percent from a year earlier to NT$416.8 billion (US$13.12 billion), as holiday purchases, new department store openings and sales of new mobile phones bolstered consumer spending, the ministry said.
Last month’s growth slowed from the previous month’s 7.8 percent, but was within the ministry’s 5 to 8 percent growth forecast.
Photo: CNA
Sales of cars, motorcycles, auto parts and accessories increased 5.8 percent, while purchases at convenience stores, big-box stores, department stores, e-commerce and mail-order platforms, and computer and home appliance stores grew from 8.4 percent to 10.9 percent from a year earlier, the ministry said.
Even with purchases of cars, motorcycles, auto parts and accessories excluded, retail sales still grew 6.6 percent annually last month — slightly higher than overall sales growth, indicating that consumer demand remained strong, it said.
In the first eight months of this year, retail sales rose 4.9 percent to NT$3.298 trillion, a record for the period, ministry data showed.
Food and beverage sales rose 1.8 percent to NT$95 billion last month, meeting the ministry’s 1 to 4 percent annual growth projection, but was lower than the previous month’s 2.5 percent increase, the report said.
In this sector, restaurants and beverage shops posted sales growth of 0.3 percent and 7.4 percent respectively, while sales of catering and group meal services providers increased 11 percent, it said.
From January to last month, food and beverage sales rose 3.7 percent to NT$737.2 billion, also a record for the period, ministry data showed.
However, firms expressed reservation regarding their business outlook this month, as consumer spending typically slows after the summer holidays.
The ministry’s diffusion index — a gauge of companies’ sales expectations for the following month — declined to 49.8 for the retail sector and 33.7 for the food and beverage sector, both of which were below the neutral threshold of 50.
As a result, retail sales this month are expected to grow 3.6 to 6.6 percent year-on-year to NT$410.4 billion to NT$422.3 billion, and food and beverage sales are projected to increase 3 to 6 percent to between NT$85.4 billion and NT$87.9 billion, the ministry said.

OpenAI agent hacked government health site: Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:26 UTC
01:38:26 KST

An OpenAI agent breached an Australian government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorized access to files, Australia said yesterday, in what could be the first known instance of an artificial intelligence (AI) agent hacking a government Web site.
The breach is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the US, coming on top of several recent breaches globally by rogue AI agents that have alarmed governments and companies.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he was extremely concerned about the June 18 incident in which the OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to the medical statistics portal of Medicare, Australia’s universal health insurance program, while conducting research on public medical spending.
Photo: EPA
The portal hosted aggregate data about health spending and drug subsidies and is popular with researchers and academics.
No personal information had been accessed, the government said.
Albanese made the breach public following a telephone conversation with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman. Both are in New York to address the UN General Assembly.
Altman was among heads of major AI firms who in speeches on Wednesday pleaded with the UN to save the world or at least its people by somehow regulating the fast-expanding technology that they have been designing.
“Today I spoke with ... Altman to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident,” Albanese told reporters. “I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred and the nature of the way that notification occurred as well was unacceptable.”
OpenAI notified Australia of the breach in an e-mail to a government department’s generic address on Sept. 10, he said.
OpenAI in a statement said it had reviewed activity involving several Australian government departments and discovered “our models took actions we did not intend.”
An inquiry looking into the security breach would examine whether OpenAI could be criminally charged, Albanese said, adding that three other government health-related Web site might have been affected.
The inquiry would also investigate how Australian security agencies failed to detect the breach before OpenAI revealed it.
Albanese said he assumed there were commercial reasons for the AI investigation of how much was being spent on particular medicines and where expenditures were changing.
In a statement, OpenAI said its “review found no evidence of patient records being accessed.”
It added that it “identified activity involving several Australian government Web sites and services as our models attempted to look up answers ... our models took actions we did not intend.”
The breach adds to tensions between Australia and the largest US-owned technology companies. Canberra has already drawn criticism from social media firms and Washington after introducing a world-first ban on social media for children younger than 16 and new rules that force tech firms to let users switch off algorithm-driven content on their feeds.
Australia considered the breach serious.
“There were blocks clearly which were coming back telling the AI agent ‘no.’ The AI agent found a way around those blocks — didn’t accept no for an answer,” Albanese told reporters.
Australian Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said the incident was the first time that an AI agent was known to have gained unauthorized access to the Australian government’s information technology systems.
“This is a warning about the technology being developed without safeguards and without guardrails in place,” Marles said.
OpenAI was engaging with the government, but the situation was “fundamentally unacceptable,” he said.
When the agent was denied information, it engaged in “misaligned behavior” to gain unauthorized access, he said.
Marles used an analogy of the information sitting behind a fence.
“It was not sitting behind a particularly high fence. This AI agent scaled the fence ... and the point is it was unintended. It wasn’t asked to. That’s our concern here,” Marles said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy on Wednesday told world leaders that Russian President Vladimir Putin is the only obstacle to ending “the ridiculous and never-ending war,” as he urged nations to pressure Putin for peace by choking the country’s revenues and impeding its war efforts.
“Our target is Russia’s ability to finance this war, to drag it out, to make it more brutal and more destructive,” Zelenskiy told the UN General Assembly’s annual gathering. “Russia’s finances and Russia’s production are what must be stopped if Putin is to be stopped.”
When Russia gets money from trade, “it always says no to diplomacy, so Russia’s revenues must remain a target,” he said.
Photo: Bloomberg
Earlier on Wednesday, Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs Sergey Lavrov clashed with Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha and his country’s European supporters at a UN Security Council meeting. Lavrov and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also met on the assembly sidelines and discussed the war.
Rubio later told reporters that Russia and Ukraine have expressed interest in a limited ceasefire that would halt attacks on grain shipments — both countries are major exporters — and on each country’s energy sectors, which have been targeted in escalating drone and missile attacks.
Reaching even a partial deal would be difficult but worthwhile, Rubio said, adding that Zelenskiy had publicly endorsed such a plan and the US would be willing to help make it happen.
Russia’s foreign ministry made no mention of a partial deal on grain shipments in a statement after the Lavrov-Rubio meeting. The statement reiterated that the root causes of what it calls its “special military operation” must be addressed.
At the Security Council, Lavrov said Russia would not “pause” its military action, claiming Europe would use it to “pump” Ukraine with weapons.
He also made no mention of any kind of grain and energy deal, called Ukraine’s government “terrorists” and said Moscow’s military operation aims to ensure Russia’s security and the rights of Russian speakers.
Zelenskiy cast doubt on Russia’s interest in ending the fighting.
“Something always seems to stop Putin from saying: ‘That’s it. Enough. Peace,’” Zelenskiy said. “Can you even imagine him without war? He is ‘patient zero,’ the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further.”
“The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else,” he said.
Zelenskiy also said in his speech that Ukraine had transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
“Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea,” he said. “These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself, and he was shocked that fate did not let him die.”
Zelenskiy did not provide more details about the return. Ukraine captured the two North Koreans in Russia’s Kursk region in January last year. They were the first North Korean soldiers to be apprehended alive since the country joined the Russia-Ukraine war in 2024.
South Korean Representative Yu Yong-weon yesterday told reporters that the two North Koreans had left Ukraine last weekend, transited through a third country and arrived in South Korea three to four days ago, Yonhap News Agency reported.
“While their exact location is unknown, I believe our intelligence agencies are protecting them,” Yu was quoted as saying.
Meanwhile, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian delivered his speech at the General Assembly, displaying images of the late Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict.
He said his country had been the “victims of terrorism” by the US.
“We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.”
Turning toward the US, Pezeshkian added: “Yes, they did hit us, but we did not bend the knee.”
Pezeshkian addressed world leaders a day after US President Donald Trump used the same stage to suggest that he might “annihilate” the Islamic republic if an agreement was not reached soon to end the nearly seven-month war.
