Pentagon probes how China got parts for F-35s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:21 UTC
01:38:21 KST

The Pentagon is investigating how parts of the US’ most advanced fighter jet ended up in Hong Kong, with a news outlet on Wednesday reporting that China has obtained the F-35 equipment.
The F-35 Joint Program Office said in a statement that it and the US Department of Defense are aware of “a shipment issue” with F-35 components.
“We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the office said.
Photo: AP
UPS was shipping a cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door from an Australian military F-35 that was being sent to the US for inspection and possible repair or disposal in late May, said people briefed on the incident, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.
Both parts, supplied by Lockheed Martin Corp, were coated with radar-absorbing material that enhances their stealth capabilities, two of the people said.
The plane stopped in South Korea en route to the US and from there it was routed to Hong Kong, one of the people said.
It is not clear why the plane stopped in South Korea or why it was diverted to Hong Kong, or whether the parts were intentionally diverted or by mistake.
The Chinese government later took possession of the parts, and has not returned them, two of the people said.
Australian Minister for Defence Richard Marles acknowledged that the jet components ended up in Hong Kong when responding to questions from reporters on Tuesday.
“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here or sensitive parts. Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred,” he said.
A Chinese embassy spokesman declined immediate comment, while the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs yesterday said it was “not aware of the situation.”
Disclosure of the incident comes at a politically sensitive time for the two countries. Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) arrived in the US on Wednesday evening for a state visit hosted by US President Donald Trump.
At least two congressional committees are investigating how the parts fell into Chinese hands.
China’s possession of the parts, the stop in South Korea and the fact that UPS was used to transport them had not been previously reported. Politico reported earlier that the parts had been unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong.
“The juxtaposition is hard to miss,” US Senator Elissa Slotkin said on Bloomberg Television’s Balance of Power. “The Chinese are holding some of our most sensitive technology and we are rolling out the red carpet for their president.”
Slotkin said she had not received a briefing on the issue.
“When it comes to intelligence and military issues, China is a competitor and an adversary. They are always seeking information about our military equipment, sensitive information,” she said.
China has for years targeted the F-35 in its espionage efforts. Concerns that China could learn valuable intelligence about the jet were one reason why a US bid to sell F-35s to the United Arab Emirates, announced in Trump’s first term, later collapsed.
The F-35 is “widely recognized as America’s best and most advanced fighter jet,” said Bradley Bowman, senior director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington-based think tank.
Bowman in November last year said that US military systems are constantly being updated and improved, counteracting any possible secrets stolen years ago.
Described as a fifth-generation fighter, the F-35’s technologies include stealth coatings as well as advanced radar and sensors, according to the Congressional Research Service.
The plane has advanced sensors to better detect enemies as well as networking capabilities to communicate with allied planes and ground forces during combat, Bowman said.
The Pentagon said it was working to retrieve the parts.
Officials “are aware of a shipment issue of unserviceable F-35 components. We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” it said in a statement.
A Lockheed Martin spokesperson in Australia yesterday said in a statement that “the components in question are unserviceable and deemed low risk for exploitation.”
“It’s always best when your adversaries have to guess at your capabilities,” said J.J. Gertler, a former aviation analyst for Congressional Research Service who is now director of The Defense Concepts Organization. “You never want to hand them evidence.”
UPS disclosed the incident to the US Department of State’s Directorate of Defense Trade Controls, which enforces export control laws, out of an abundance of caution. Company spokesman Malcolm Berkley declined to comment.
During a closed US Senate Committee on Armed Services F-35 hearing on June 23, defense department program office officials expressed their hope the components would be returned, people familiar with the exchange said.
The diversion is being reviewed by two House congressional panels — House Foreign Affairs and Armed Services committees.
House Armed Services Committee spokeswoman Heather Vaughan said the “committee is aware of this issue and we’ve received multiple briefings on it.”
The Senate Armed Services Subcommittee on Airland also “is aware of the reports and is currently looking into the matter,” spokesman Dave Vasquez said.

UN should abolish Security Council veto
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:18 UTC
01:38:18 KST

The tragedies of the past few years, including pandemics, energy crises, disruptions to supply chains and regional conflicts, have demonstrated that leaving the resolution of global crises to the will of a handful of capitals is no longer compatible with the realities of today’s world. The adaptation of global decisionmaking mechanisms to today’s circumstances can no longer be postponed.
The UN Security Council still reflects the structure of the post-World War II era. A more effective, equitable and accountable approach to representation has become imperative. This requires not only broadening representation, but also sharing leadership responsibility equitably. We must incorporate the experience, capacity and will of different regions into efforts to address global and regional challenges. In this respect, our call that “The world is bigger than five” is an invitation to embrace a broader understanding of responsibility.
It is now imperative to translate the need for reform into a concrete roadmap. At the heart of this roadmap should be abolishing the veto privilege. Adding new privileged members to the Security Council would not resolve the problem of decisionmaking power being concentrated in the hands of a few states; rather, it would expand the scope of the privileged structure. The abolition of the veto privilege should be both the starting point and the fundamental strategic objective of any meaningful reform. Reform cannot mean extending the same privilege to other states.
Within the UN General Assembly, a broad coalition should be built around the principle that no state should have the power to permanently obstruct the will of the majority of the international community.
The balance between the Security Council and the General Assembly must also be restored. The powers of the General Assembly should be strengthened, and the representativeness of the Security Council and its accountability to the General Assembly should be enhanced through a structure in which there are no permanent members, Security Council members are elected by the General Assembly on a rotational basis for fixed terms, and countries seeking to serve again are required to regain the confidence of the majority of member states through elections.
We cannot build the international order of the future by preserving the hierarchies of the past. The developments of the past quarter century — a relatively brief period in world history — have demonstrated that no balance of power and no international order are permanent. The system that promised humanity peace, stability and shared prosperity has failed to prevent new wars, reduce inequalities or respond to shifting balances of power.
As new centers of power have emerged across fields ranging from the economy and security to technology and diplomacy, international institutions have failed to adapt to this transformation at the same pace. Wars, the climate crisis, irregular migration and economic vulnerabilities have once again underscored the importance of states having strong institutions, resilient economies and deterrent defense capabilities. The security and sustainability of trade, logistics, transport and energy corridors have become increasingly decisive.
As Asia’s economic weight grows, Africa is also calling for stronger representation commensurate with its potential, while developing countries are voicing their own priorities more assertively. The growing influence of certain regional actors also brings greater responsibility to address challenges within their own regions. The issues facing each region cannot be resolved through methods imposed from outside. We believe that approaches grounded in the will of the countries concerned, local circumstances and shared interests will produce more lasting and stable outcomes. It is an unavoidable necessity for countries with diplomatic capacity, economic resources and the ability to communicate with different parties to assume more effective roles in establishing peace and stability.
Expectations that globalization would spread prosperity have not been fully met. As income inequalities have deepened, technological and economic dependencies have become new arenas of competition. In these changing circumstances, responsibilities must be shared equitably to ensure global justice, while developing countries’ right to development and access to the financing they need must be guaranteed.
Such a change requires international will on a broad scale. Tukey will continue to draw on its strong global relations and experience in multilateral diplomacy in support of this pursuit of reform. We support this effort to abolish the veto privilege, give elected members greater weight in decisionmaking processes and strengthen the role of the General Assembly. The convergence of countries from different regions around this common ground will strengthen the legitimacy and representative capacity of the international system.
It is clear that lasting peace in today’s world cannot be built through the multiplication of disconnected blocs that fail to engage with one another. For “a fairer world,” we must bring together the experience, capacity and resolve of different regions on common ground. With its deep-rooted tradition of statecraft, diplomatic capacity and strong ties across different regions, Turkey will continue to assume its share of responsibility in the pursuit of this reform.
Recep Tayyip Erdogan is the president of the Republic of Turkey. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. Liquefaction map update shows several changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:18 UTC
01:38:18 KST

The classification of soil liquefaction risk at several areas near major population centers has changed — some for the better and some indicating greater danger — updates to a map released yesterday by the Geological Survey and Mining Management Agency showed.
Liquefaction risk classifications have changed in about 17 percent of the regions surveyed, agency Director-General Hsu Ming-hong (徐銘宏) told a news conference in Taipei, adding that the changes reflect improved data, not changes in the soil itself.
The map — which is available at https://liquefaction.gsmma.gov.tw/gsmma/Web/Map.aspx — shows areas designated as high, medium and low potential for liquefaction in Taipei, New Taipei City, Taoyuan, Hsinchu county and city, and Yilan County.
Photo courtesy of the Geological Survey and Mining Management Agency
Areas at high and low risk both decreased, with most shifting to medium potential, Applied Geology Division section head Chen Po-tsun (陳柏村) said.
Swathes of New Taipei City’s Banciao District (板橋) were redesignated as low risk, while portions of Hsinchu City’s North (北區) and Siangshan (香山) districts were redesignated as high-risk areas, Chen said.
The agency created a new layer on the map showing soft soil distributions to provide engineering agencies information on potentially dangerous soft soil that requires additional monitoring and specialized construction techniques if they are developed, Hsu said.
The government launched the map to enhance safety and transparency in the aftermath of the deadly 2016 earthquake centered in Kaohsiung’s Meinong District (美濃), Hsu said.
The agency is building the digital map to provide more data to facilitate land management, urban renewal and real-estate utilization, he said.
The latest survey investigated a larger area than its previous iterations, added new data derived from drilling and combined information gathered by soil liquefaction monitoring stations, he said.
“The soil liquefaction trend map does not show danger zones, but rather marks the strength of quakes that could liquefy the soil in a given area to help surveyors, architects and developers mitigate risks,” he said.
This year’s survey analyzed data from 11,731 boreholes across 909.8km2, a three-fold increase in bores providing data and about a 96km2 increase in areas investigated compared with the 2021 map, the agency said.
Ten operational soil liquefaction monitoring stations have been established, with one operating on a trial basis, a system that keeps tabs on changes to strata and aquifers during tremors, it said.
Three more updates covering Taiwan proper’s central, eastern and southwestern areas are planned for release as the agency gathers more data, it added.

Trump’s shocking threat to annihilate Iran in UN speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:17 UTC
01:38:17 KST

US President Donald Trump has a habit of discomfiting delegates to the UN General Assembly — but this year, he might have upstaged the ghost of Nikita Khrushchev by openly contemplating the annihilation of a fellow UN member state.
Eleven minutes into a 40-minute address, Trump announced that he had “a big decision to make” over Iran, which has staged a much more determined resistance than he anticipated when he decided to go to war against the country in February.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild, and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” he asked. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”
Possibly not since Khrushchev, the late Soviet leader, brandished his shoe and allegedly banged it on a desk in 1960 in protest at a fellow delegate’s speech has the annual gathering witnessed such a display of bellicosity from a superpower leader.
But this seemed more shocking.
The world might have become inured to Trump’s dire threats to send Iran “to the stone age” or end its civilization — so often have they been issued, only to sometimes be followed by a ceasefire or negotiations. However, hearing them voiced in a forum created in the aftermath of World War II, with the explicit aim of preventing future conflicts, was disconcerting.
Iran was the focal point of much of Trump’s speech, which began with a catalogue of familiar boasts of his supposed achievements that seemed better fitted to a domestic audience.
Whether the latest threat should be taken literally, little of what he said about Iran seemed reassuring. He appeared to play fast and loose with the facts, consciously or otherwise.
Trump twice incorrectly asserted that the theocratic regime had held power for 51 years. In fact, the Islamic revolution that toppled the pro-Western former shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, and installed the current regime happened 47 years ago, in 1979.
Trump also cited apparently inflated figures for the number of Iranians killed in anti-government protests in January, weeks before the war.
“The same regime slaughtered over 72,000 of its citizens this year,” he said, in support of his oft-stated declaration that Iran should never be permitted to acquire nuclear weapons.
No definitive death toll has been established, but previous estimates of people killed in the brutal crushing of January’s demonstrations — even including those previously stated by Trump himself — have been much lower.
The ominous rhetoric was not limited to Iran.
Members of the Cuban delegation were seen leaving the hall as he predicted the imminent collapse of the country’s communist regime, which has been struggling to cope with a food security and humanitarian crisis amid tightening US embargoes.
“It’s an absolutely failed state, it’s failing like never before, and it will fall,” Trump said. “Marco Rubio [the US secretary of state] is handling a negotiation. He’s deep into negotiations with Cuba. Let’s see what happens.”
US actions in Venezuela, where special forces in January seized the strongman president, Nicolas Maduro, and spirited him to New York to face drug-trafficking charges, was also cited as an ominous warning to other adversaries — as well as a vocal statement of how the administration would behave in Latin America, Washington’s supposed “back yard,” if it felt its interests threatened.
“Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the western hemisphere, and, if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States,” Trump said.
He was brazenly unabashed in hailing a recent US oil deal with Venezuelan Acting President Delcy Rodriguez that he claimed put the US and Venezuela jointly in control of more than 60 percent of the world’s oil.
“It was perhaps the biggest deal ever made. To the victor belong the spoils — you’ve all heard that,” Trump said.
There was outright antipathy for the International Criminal Court, which Trump called an “out-of-control institution” and “an evil group of people.”
“We will never allow US service members or anyone else to be investigated or given show trials by an anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction over us,” he said.
Given his pugnacious stance toward US adversaries, it probably came as a relief to Washington’s traditional friends that Trump had relatively kind words for them. It was a far cry from his General Assembly speech a year earlier, when he warned European allies “your countries are all going to hell” because of immigration.
This time, in a pointed message, Trump praised NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte as a “great leader”— a marked departure from his previous denunciations of the military alliance as “obsolete” and a “paper tiger.”
He lauded Denmark as “an incredible, beautiful country,” just days after announcing an agreement with it over Greenland, following prolonged tensions over the territory, which Trump had previously threatened to annex.
With that issue seemingly settled— at least for now — the president declared his intention to flex his muscles on a new battleground: artificial intelligence.
Echoing recent social media posts, Trump likened recent calls to slow its development, on the grounds that its rapid development poses an existential threat to humankind, as a “globalist scheme” hatched by the same forces he blamed for warnings of climate change, a premise he has long erroneously labeled a “hoax”.
Part of the answer, he said, was to change its name. Henceforth it would cease to be called “artificial” — which he said “makes it sound fake — and it’s not fake” — and would be called “super intelligence” in all US government documents.
“Welcome to the new world of super intelligence,” he said. “Let’s see if that goes. It’s much more accurate. Let’s see if I have any power. Maybe I do, maybe I don’t.”

It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. The Executive Yuan yesterday approved a three-year, NT$3.6 billion (US$113.28 million) plan to increase the number of safety personnel at junior-high schools to 2,000 from 620.
Local governments would provide annual subsidies of NT$120 million to 966 eligible schools from Thursday next week to July 31, 2029, K-12 Education Administration Director-General Peng Fu-yuan (彭富源) told a post-Cabinet meeting news conference in Taipei.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) authorized the plan to help teachers handle safety-related tasks, emotional outbursts and behavioral issues, including the use of narcotics, he said.
Photo: CNA
Under the plan, one campus security person would be assigned to schools with six classes or less, two to schools with seven to 36 classes and three for schools with 37 classes or more, Peng said.
A dedicated force of personnel would be valuable in dealing with campus safety issues, student-on-student or student-teacher altercations, and post-incident liaisons with parents, allowing educators to focus on teaching, he said.
Local governments would be in charge of selecting and managing the personnel, with the Ministry of Education covering 86 percent to 90 percent of the costs, according to need, he said.
The ministry would also subsidize training costs, such as specialized courses on emergency response, drug abuse prevention, anti-bullying policy and laws governing schools, Peng said.
Taiwan holds training courses for campus safety officers each year and more than 7,000 people are licensed to work as school safety officers, Deputy Minister of Education Chang Liao Wan-chien (張廖萬堅) said.
Elementary schools are already expanding their counseling staff under a separate program, and senior-high schools are protected by more than 2,000 campus safety officers, he said.
A rise in safety incidents in junior-high schools, which have fewer resources than other levels of education, prompted an official policy response, Chang Liao said.
School administrators expressed support for the policy during meetings with educational officials as a measure that would help relieve the burden on teachers, he added.

New metrics reshuffle top 30 university rankings, expose globalization gaps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:14 UTC
01:38:14 KST

The top 30 of The Korea Times University Rankings 2027 remained largely stable — 28 of last year’s 30 universities held their places — but beneath that continuity, a revised methodology reshaped individual positions and exposed widening gaps in the quality and depth of internationalization at South Korean universities.
Seoul-based private universities dominated the top 30, though seven universities outside the capital region also made the cut. They included regional flagship national universities — Pusan, Kyungpook, Jeonbuk and Chungnam — as well as private institutions known for their internationalization efforts, such as Woosong, Handong Global and Yeungnam universities.
Yeungnam University and Kookmin University were the only newcomers, climbing three and four spots from 32nd and 34th last year to 29th and 30th, respectively.
Photo courtesy of Kookmin University
Yeungnam’s rise was driven largely by its strong performance in international research. The private university in Gyeongsan, North Gyeongsang Province, ranked ninth among the 60 institutions in the research category with 30.95 points, placing first in the share of internationally collaborative research papers and third in field-weighted citation impact.
Kookmin’s rise was driven largely by gains in international student retention, where its score increased by 2.55 points from the previous year — the biggest contributor to its climb. A higher score for the share of papers published in the top 10 percent of academic journals also helped propel the university into the top 30.
The biggest gains within the top 30 came from Sejong University and Woosong University, which both climbed six places to seventh and 20th, respectively. Handong Global University followed with a five-place rise to 23rd, while Incheon National University and Kookmin University each moved up four spots.
Graphic courtesy of The Korea Times
On the other end, Konkuk University and Soongsil University recorded the steepest declines, both falling five places to 17th and 26th, respectively. University of Seoul and Kyungpook National University dropped four spots, while Seoul National University of Science and Technology and Jeonbuk National University each slipped three places.
RETENTION INDICATOR
Behind those movements was a revised methodology that shifted emphasis to education-related indicators.
The change to the student retention indicator proved particularly consequential. Among the 54 universities assessed in both years, it was the largest positive factor for 13 universities and the largest negative factor for 25 — more than any other indicator in both directions. Universities that previously had high dropout rates among non-degree students tended to benefit from the revised calculation, while those with relatively high attrition among degree-seeking international students were more likely to lose ground.
Another key factor was the newly introduced indicator measuring the proportion of international full-time faculty, which showed the widest gap among universities across all 19 indicators.
The divide was particularly pronounced between public and private universities. The 14 public universities averaged just 0.95 points out of 10, compared with 4.05 points for the 46 private institutions — suggesting that private universities have moved more quickly to build a more international faculty.
The rankings were more spread out at the top but became increasingly tight toward the 30th-place cutoff. From 24th to 30th, several universities were separated by only fractions of a point, meaning even small changes in a single indicator could significantly shift their positions.
The results suggest that basic standards for managing international students have become widely established across the 60 universities assessed. Greater weaknesses emerged, however, in indicators reflecting the broader impact of internationalization, including the social impact of graduates and research funding from overseas sources.
Even among the top 30, strengths varied sharply by category. Handong Global University ranked second in student support but 44th in research, while Hankuk University of Foreign Studies placed 12th in education but 58th in student support.
This shows that a high overall ranking does not necessarily translate into strength across all four areas — and that universities are pursuing different paths to internationalization. For prospective international students, the results suggest that looking beyond the overall ranking to the areas that matter most to their studies and campus experience may prove more useful.

Taiwan’s Wang Yan-cheng finds his footing in South Korean baseball
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Wang Yan-cheng (王彥程) is enjoying a strong first season in the Korea Baseball Organization (KBO) League, where he has posted an 11-6 record with a 3.97 ERA, 100 strikeouts and a 1.52 WHIP. His 11 wins rank among the most by foreign starting pitchers in the KBO, while he has emerged as one of the top performers under the league’s newly introduced “Asian player quota.”
Quiet in conversation, but candid about his experiences in South Korea, Wang appeared firmly focused on his physical preparation for the Asian Games when he spoke with the Taipei Times in Daejeon earlier this month.
Wang is the second Taiwanese pitcher to play in the KBO, after Wang Wei-chung (王維中), 34, now with Taiwan’s TSG Hawks (台鋼雄鷹). Wang Yan-cheng signed on with Japan’s Rakuten Golden Eagles in 2019 and played there through last year. In Japan’s farm league, he compiled a 20-21 record with a 3.62 ERA and 248 strikeouts. Wang is currently with Taiwan’s national team at the 20th Asian Games in Japan’s Aichi-Nagoya.
Photo: Don Huh
Taiwan has advanced to the super round, where it is to face China today and Japan tomorrow. Wang has yet to play in the tournament; according to the Liberty Times (Taipei Times’ sister newspaper), he could start one of the two games. The medal games are scheduled for Sunday. The following interview has been condensed and edited.
Taipei Times: What is your motivation to come to South Korea to play baseball? What were you hoping to gain from the experience?
Wang Yan-cheng: During the 2023 Asian Games, we played against South Korea. I saw that their pitchers and batters were very good, so I wanted to come to this league and see how they play baseball here.
TT: When you first arrived in South Korea, what was the most difficult part of adapting?
WYC: I think the most difficult part was everyday life outside baseball. There were no Chinese characters around me, and everything was written in Korean. At some restaurants, even the menus did not have pictures, so it was quite difficult to get used to at first.
The cheering culture was also very different. The cheering is very loud, so that took some time to adjust to.
TT: You have played in Taiwan, Japan and South Korea. What are the biggest differences among the three in terms of baseball culture, training methods and style of play? Has your impression of South Korean baseball changed since you previously faced South Korea in international competition?
WYC: I am still observing and learning. I think I need to complete a full season before I can properly analyze the differences.
For now, the biggest difference I have noticed is the cheering culture. The batting styles are also different. However, because I have not yet completed a full season, I do not think I can make any definite comparisons.
My impression is certainly different now because my mentality is different, and the way I work with my catcher this year is also different from before.
TT: You currently have a 11 wins. How much confidence has this season given you? Was there a particular game or moment when you began to feel you could succeed in South Korean baseball?
WYC: I think confidence is something you have to build through your everyday practice.
TT: As a Taiwanese player competing in South Korea, have you had any particularly memorable experiences? How have your teammates, coaches and fans treated you?
WYC: Everyone has been very kind to me, and I get along well with everyone.
There have also been Taiwanese fans who came to South Korea to watch me play this year. I am grateful that they took the time to come and see my games.
TT: Now that you have been playing in South Korea, is there any particular experience you would like to mention about South Korean baseball or its players?
WYC: There have been Taiwanese fans who have come to South Korea to watch me play this year. I really appreciate them taking the time to come and watch my games.
TT: Is there a KBO League player who has particularly impressed you?
WYC: Doosan Bears pitcher Gwak Been has impressed me. His ability is among the best in the league. I like his pitching style, and I think he is a very talented pitcher.
(Note: Gwak leads the KBO-best a 2.26 ERA this season, with an 11-7 record and 186 strikeouts.)
TT: You are expected to compete in the Asian Games. How are you preparing for the tournament?
WYC: I am still playing here at the moment, so I am focused on how I am going to pitch in my next game and what adjustments I need to make.
TT: Apart from baseball, how have you adapted to life in South Korea? Were there any aspects of South Korean culture that took time to get used to?
WYC: My interpreter has helped me a lot with everyday life.
As for dining, drinking and other aspects of South Korean culture, I have not had any major problems.
Language can be more difficult when I am alone, but that is part of the job.
TT: Have language or communication differences made living in South Korea difficult? When you were playing for Japan’s Rakuten Eagles last year, you had several Taiwanese teammates, but here you are the only Taiwanese player; do you feel any difference? How have your South Korean teammates treated you?
WYC: I think it has been OK. When there are Taiwanese people around, I don’t feel there is much of a difference. Being on my own can be a little more difficult, but there is nothing I can do about that — it’s part of the job.
TT: Taiwan and South Korea are often regarded as sporting rivals. From your experience playing here, does that rivalry extend to players or fans? Have you ever felt uncomfortable as a Taiwanese player in South Korea?
WYC: I do not think so. Of course, we are competitors, and there will naturally be a certain degree of rivalry between competitors.
TT: What are your goals for the next stage of your professional career?
WYC: Right now, I am focused on each game. I think about what I need to do in the next game and what adjustments I need to make.

EDITORIAL: Vote buying undermines democracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:14 UTC
01:38:14 KST

With campaigns for the Nov. 28 nine-in-one elections in full swing, former Financial Times Taiwan correspondent Kathrin Hille’s statement in an interview last month that “all the votes are bought” in Hualien County has sparked concern over the elections and cast a shadow over Taiwan’s democracy.
Hille, who moved to Hualien after she retired, recounted instances of neighbors mentioning who came by and put cash on the table, and said that despite Taiwan’s long-established democracy, vote buying remains common practice in the county.
Taipei Times columnist and former American Chamber of Commerce president Courtney Donovan Smith shared a similar experience: A Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) politician he was working for in Changhua County years ago openly admitted to using cash to “buy votes.”
Taiwan’s democratization after the lifting of martial law in 1987 has widely won international acclaim. Taiwan has been named by the Democracy Index a “full democracy,” and has served as a model of a robust and well-functioning democratic system.
Taiwan also stipulates higher legislative penalties for electoral bribery than most mature democracies. Under the Public Official Election and Recall Act (公職人員選罷法) and the Criminal Code, vote buyers could be fined a maximum of NT$10 million (US$314,663) and imprisoned for three to 10 years. That is higher than the US’ maximum two-year prison sentence, Japan’s three years and Germany’s five years.
However, electoral bribery cases continue in Taiwan.
Among the 5,218 people prosecuted from 2016 to last year for contravening the election and recall law, more than 91 percent were convicted of vote bribery, data from the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office and the Ministry of Justice showed.
In the 2022 local elections, the victories of more than 180 officials and councilors were invalidated after they were convicted of vote buying.
Vote buying has been a long and systemic issue in Taiwan, intertwined with political and local factions, traditional social customs, economic inequality and enormous post-election interests. Local politics has long relied on networks of kinship, factions, religious organizations, hometown associations and “voter broker.” Politicians utilize those networks to disguise vote buying as personal relationships and daily interactions, such as attending weddings and funerals, or giving gifts. Those have all blurred the lines between legality and bribery.
Hualien has long faced an electoral bribery problem, evidenced by the high number of electoral investigations and convictions. A bribery case in 2018 involving a single vote purchase of NT$10,000, as well as a major crackdown during the 2022 local elections that searched 72 locations, summoned 147 people, detained seven offenders and seized more than NT$620,000 in bribes are a few examples.
The Changhua District Prosecutors’ Office said that it has already received more than 100 reports of suspected election bribery, including at least 10 cases involving vote buying with cash.
Even Changhua County Council Speaker Hsieh Dien-lin (謝典霖) and his parents were investigated and detained last week after they were accused of vote buying — a feast in June and gifts worth more than US$1,000 — and using the council’s funds to pay for the feast.
Another issue is escalating electoral interference from China, which has been offering free trips, financial incentives and political benefits to Taiwanese, and spreading disinformation. Such interference pose a threat to Taiwan’s security and democracy, and has been a significant challenge for many Western and Asian democracies.
On the eve of the 2024 presidential and legislative elections, the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office said there were 117 cases of people contravening the Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法), resulting in the prosecution of 287 people. Fewer cases were reported during the 2020 elections, making it clear that China’s electoral interventions have evolved and are now sweeping in.
To eliminate electoral bribery, the government has raised the reward for whistle-blowers to NT$15 million. However, the judicial authority also needs to improve law enforcement. Current legislation does not fully disqualify convicted vote buyers from seeking re-election, so civic groups are calling for greater transparency regarding electoral cases and convicts, so that voters are aware of candidates’ criminal records and election histories.
The most important, but also the most challenging, task is to raise the public’s awareness of electoral bribery. Taiwanese must understand the value of their votes and share in the responsibility of safeguarding the election’s fairness and justice. The concept behind vote buying deterrence should transform from “passively abiding by the law” to “actively defending Taiwan’s democracy.”
Taiwan’s democracy and high-tech economy play a crucial role in global affairs and are central to the world’s embrace of a raft of next-generation technologies, including AI. It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. Indeed, since 1979 it has been embedded in US law, with the Taiwan Relations Act (TRA) charging the US with helping to improve the island’s ability to deter an attack from
Academia Historica director Chen Tsui-lien (陳翠蓮), speaking at the handover ceremony for her new role on Monday, said that when she accepted the position, she knew that her peaceful life as a history professor was a thing of the past, and that from now on she would have to “wear a helmet.” A specialist in Taiwan’s post-World War II history and the 228 Incident, she has been accused of being politically divisive. Forty-five of the assembly’s 71 lawmakers joined the group, representing more than 60 percent of the legislature. Its members include National Assembly President Shirley

Industrial computer maker Advantech Co (研華) on Wednesday said that order momentum in the US should remain robust in the second half of this year, supported by continued growth in the healthcare, semiconductor equipment and robotics businesses.
The company’s US book-to-bill ratio currently stands at 2.15 and is expected to stay at about 2 throughout this year, well above the company’s overall ratio of 1.4, Advantech North America general manager Ween Niu (牛文中) told a news conference in Taipei.
Design wins in the US market in the first half of the year already surpassed the US$420 million it gained for the whole of last year, Niu said.
Photo: Fang Wei-chieh, Taipei Times
A design win refers to a customer’s decision to adopt a supplier’s solution for a new product development project, suggesting orders from the customer and revenue contribution in the future.
US design wins in the second half are expected to be flat or higher compared with the first half, with the full-year total at least double that of last year, Niu said.
They are expected to start contributing to revenue in 2028, he added.
The US market generated US$430 million in revenue in the first half, accounting for 29 percent of the company’s total, he said.
US revenue in the second half is expected to rise at least 50 percent from the first half, and lift full-year sales to US$1 billion, he said.
Regarding the company’s healthcare business, Niu said Advantech works with 28 of the 30 largest US medical equipment makers, providing customers with hardware and system integration related to surgical robots, medical imaging and surgical navigation.
Advantech aims to expand from individual projects and standardized products into multiple equipment platforms, he said.
Its semiconductor equipment business is also growing fast in North America, with the company working with the three largest US semiconductor equipment makers, Niu said.
Revenue from this segment grew 75 percent year-on-year in the first half and is expected to increase about 120 percent next year, he said.
In robotics, Advantech is in talks on more than 20 projects in the US, with more than five entering the contract-signing stage, he said.
As humanoid robotics development is still in the early phase, the company aims to expand its customer base first, he said.
To ease capacity constraints amid robust US demand, Advantech offers overtime incentives and is accelerating the transfer of about 32 projects from its manufacturing site in northern California to a new southern California site in Tustin, Niu said, adding that US capacity is expected to match demand in the second half of next year.
The Tustin site, which began small-volume production in May and is scheduled to enter full operations next month, is expected to contribute more than US$80 million in revenue this year and about US$300 million next year, Niu said.
The site is expected to account for about 40 percent of Advantech’s total US production capacity after 2028, he said.

Alexander Lukashenko pardons another 15 people, including 13 convicted of what Belarus calls ‘extremist’ crimes
Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko has signed a decree pardoning 15 people, according to BelTA.
Thirteen of them were convicted of what BelTA called “extremist offenses.” Ten of those pardoned are women. Their names were not disclosed.
BelTA noted that all 15 petitioned for pardons, admitted guilt, expressed remorse for what they had done, and “promised to lead law-abiding lives.”
Since 2025, Lukashenko has periodically released people convicted on political charges as part of an agreement with the U.S. to lift sanctions in exchange for their release. Those pardoned have included opposition leaders Viktor Babariko and Maria Kolesnikova, among many others. Hundreds of political prisoners remain in Belarus, however. The human rights group Viasna puts the number at more than 800.

Armiia+ app connected to NBU BankID system for user authentication
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:34:34 EEST
01:34:34 KST

The Armiia+ mobile app for military personnel has been directly connected to the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) BankID system for user authentication, the regulator's press service reported.
"One of the state's objectives is to ensure citizens have convenient, reliable, and secure access to digital services. Connecting the Armiia+ mobile app directly to the NBU BankID system is an important step in this direction, as it will make authentication even easier for military personnel," said Olha Vasylyeva, Deputy Director of the NBU's Payment Systems and Innovative Development Department.
Previously, authentication in Armia+ was carried out exclusively via the integrated electronic identification system of the Diia state portal.
The direct connection of the Armiia+ app to NBU BankID—implemented through cooperation between the National Bank and the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine—will reduce the time required for military personnel to authenticate.
According to the National Bank, as of July 1, 2026, the BankID system comprised 37 identification providers and 117 service providers (102 commercial and 15 non-commercial).

				"All international studies indicate that parental involvement in

parental non-compliance—removing the minor from the family home

Trump invites Putin to Miami G20: Why that matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:32:56 UTC
01:32:56 KST

Trump invites Putin to Miami G20: Why that matters
US Secretary of State Rubio said the summit would be an ‘opportunity’ for Putin to engage with other world leaders.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has announced that Washington has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to December’s G20 meeting in Miami amid efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
Following a meeting with Russian Foreign Secretary Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Rubio said the US remained open to speaking with Moscow about Ukraine.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3The view from Russia: ‘No party can be antiwar’ in parliamentary election
- list 2 of 3Trump-Xi summit: Here’s what’s on the agenda, and why it matters
- list 3 of 3China vs US: Who is winning the AI race, in four charts
“We’ve just invited President Putin to the G20. We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with the president but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept,” Rubio said.
Trump and Putin last met, face to face, in Anchorage, Alaska, in August 2025, but failed to reach any agreement over Ukraine. Putin has not visited the contiguous United States since he invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Here’s what we know.
What is the G20?
The G20, or Group of 20, is a forum bringing together the world’s major and emerging economies. A summit is held annually – this year in Miami, Florida, in the US.
Those countries or groups of countries are:
- Argentina
- Australia
- Brazil
- Canada
- China
- France
- Germany
- India
- Indonesia
- Italy
- Japan
- Mexico
- Russia
- Saudi Arabia
- South Africa
- South Korea
- Turkiye
- United Kingdom
- United States
- African Union
- European Union
While many G20 countries, such as Germany, France, and the UK, are allied with Ukraine, others have closer ties with Russia – including China and India.
If he accepts the invitation, it would be Putin’s first in-person attendance at a G20 summit since 2019.
In 2021, the Russian leader attended the G20 summit virtually and spoke by video feed, but in 2023, when the summit was held in India, Putin sent Lavrov in his place.
What has Russia said?
On Thursday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said no decision had been taken about Putin’s attendance at the December summit.
When asked what the two leaders might discuss, Peskov told reporters, “It is premature to speak about this right now.”
“No decision has been made yet. We certainly appreciate this kind invitation, we value it, and it will be reviewed and coordinated, after which an appropriate decision will be reached.”
The spokesperson reiterated that Russia is seeking a peace settlement, not a temporary ceasefire.
How are US-Russian relations?
While the US maintains contact with Moscow for dialogue over the war in Ukraine, relations between the countries are strained.
Last week, Trump signed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 into law, which grants the president sweeping powers to sanction buyers of Russian energy, in a bid to pressure Moscow to end the war.
The legislation, named after the late hawkish Republican lawmaker, also sanctions President Vladimir Putin, senior officials and oligarchs, along with Russian banks and financial institutions.
However, this week, Trump appeared to contradict this approach when he called on Ukraine to agree to an “energy truce” with Russia whereby both sides stop launching strikes on each other’s energy facilities and infrastructure. In comments to reporters at the UN headquarters, Zelenskyy said Kyiv would halt strikes on Russian energy facilities if Moscow stopped targeting Ukraine’s energy systems, as well.
Trump has blamed the Ukraine-Russia war for the current record rise in diesel prices in the United States, which has become a major issue as the country approaches midterm elections in November, adding that Ukraine’s strikes on Russian diesel facilities were “hurting the world”.
But observers said Trump is placing pressure on the wrong actor in the war.
“It is Russia’s – not Ukraine’s – responsibility to end the attacks,” Marnie Howlett, an associate professor of international relations in Eastern Europe and Eurasia at the University of Oxford, told Al Jazeera. “The Russian Federation has repeatedly broken ceasefire agreements, so the war will continue until it agrees to recognise Ukraine’s territorial sovereignty.”
“The ongoing sales of Russian fossil fuels continue to finance Russia’s war against Ukraine,” Amanda Paul, senior policy analyst at the European Policy Centre (EPC), said.
“Rather than putting the emphasis on the impact of Ukrainian strikes on fuel prices, Trump should be putting greater pressure on Russia to end its attacks and bring the war to an end,” she said. “Trump himself is responsible for stoking high energy prices, due to the repercussions of the US-Israel war on Iran and the subsequent blocking of the Strait of Hormuz.”
Was the G20 invitation for Putin expected this year?
Last month, US media reported that the head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), John Ratcliffe, travelled to Moscow for unannounced talks.
According to CBS News, news of his trip came only after an Air Force Boeing C-17 Globemaster III transport plane was spotted flying into a Moscow airport.
While the CIA did not comment on his trip, Peskov told reporters in Moscow that Ratcliffe had spoken to Russian intelligence officials, but did not meet Putin. Then, a senior Ukrainian official told CBS that Washington had told Ukraine that a US delegation would be travelling to Moscow and asked Kyiv to pause its attacks until the delegation left.
On Wednesday, citing two sources familiar with the matter, the Reuters news agency reported that Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev would go to the US to meet special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
According to one source, the visit aims to keep Russia-US dialogue and peacekeeping efforts going. Economic cooperation, energy issues and a peace settlement in Ukraine will also be on the agenda.
Will Putin’s visit trigger the International Criminal Court (ICC) warrant for his arrest?
No.
In March 2023, the ICC issued a warrant for Putin’s arrest for the alleged war crime of unlawfully deporting Ukrainian children to Russia.
Under the Rome Statute, the international treaty that established the ICC, signatories are obliged to carry out the warrant if a person with a warrant for their arrest enters their territory.
However, the US is not a signatory to the Rome Statute and will therefore not abide by it. Furthermore, the Trump administration is reported to be preparing sanctions against the ICC, which has also issued a warrant for the arrest of Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on suspicion of war crimes in Gaza. The US has previously also placed sanctions on ICC officials.
The new US sanctions would prohibit most transactions with the ICC after a grace period of six to seven months, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday. If imposed, the measures would bar US citizens and companies from providing the ICC with money, goods or services without a licence from the US Department of the Treasury. Banks and other companies often take an especially cautious approach to US sanctions because they rely on access to the US financial system.
On Thursday, Trump urged all countries that are members of the ICC to quit and said it was “out of control”.
“The United States is equally opposed to the out-of-control institution known as the International Criminal Court,” he told the United Nations General Assembly. “I call on all nations that are members of the ICC to officially resign from this rogue institution immediately.”
How have other countries responded to Putin’s invitation to the G20?
Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s high representative for foreign affairs, criticised the invitation and said she would raise it with other members of the G20.
“We need to discuss this together with colleagues, but it’s clearly, I think, the wrong path to normalise people who are starting wars, who are going against the UN charter, who are killing and giving orders to kill civilians, to ignore the international humanitarian law, to cause as much damage and suffering to people that they can,” she added.
“By normalising this, believe me, we will have more of it around the world.”
On Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, a Ukraine ally, said inviting Putin to the Miami summit could encourage Moscow to continue its attacks on Ukraine.
“If inviting Putin to the G20 could bring us closer to a just peace, I would be absolutely in favour of it,” Tusk told a news conference.
“However – and this is both my concern and what my experience tells me – at this stage, Russia might well view it as an encouragement to continue its aggressive policies. That is what I fear.”

UK PM informs Zelenskyy he will maintain sanctions against Russian oligarchs – Bloomberg

UK PM informs Zelenskyy he will maintain sanctions against Russian oligarchs – Bloomberg
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has informed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that he disagrees with the European Union's decision to lift sanctions against Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman.
Source: European Pravda, citing sources familiar with the situation quoted by Bloomberg
Details: According to these sources, Burnham made these comments during a meeting with Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this week.
The UK prime minister also informed Zelenskyy that the United Kingdom will not lift sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman, sources noted. He stated that Ukraine's allies should continue to maintain their sanctions to exert pressure on Russia to end the war.
A Downing Street statement on Burnham's meeting with Zelenskyy made no mention of the EU decision but noted that the prime minister spoke about the "need to keep increasing pressure on Russia through sanctions to ensure he came to the table".
This criticism points to a rare rift between the UK and the EU over sanctions against Russia, which had largely been aligned since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Both Fridman and Usmanov had interests in the UK. Usmanov is best known internationally for his investments in London's Arsenal football club, which he exited in 2018. Fridman moved to London in 2013 but left the country after sanctions were imposed against him.
Background: The Council of the EU adopted a final decision on 22 September to extend sanctions against individuals and entities responsible for undermining or threatening Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence for a further 36 months. However, it has removed two Russian oligarchs from the list.

Southern Israel high school principal arrested on suspicion of biting student during brawl
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:31:09 UTC
01:31:09 KST

Police arrested a high school principal in the Negev on suspicion of slapping and biting a student during a brawl. Following questioning, the principal was released to five days of house arrest under restrictive conditions. Police at the Ayarot station are continuing to investigate the circumstances of the incident. The case was first reported by Reshet News.
The principal was the one who called police more than a week ago to report the brawl. The investigation found that his son and nephew were also suspected of being involved in the altercation. Investigators took statements from those involved, with one student saying the principal shoved him, bit him and slapped him. The principal was questioned under caution and later released to his home.
The principal gave his account in a letter sent to fellow school principals. He said: "Several days ago, a 12th-grade student called my son at night and began making serious threats against him and me, while also hurling curses and insults at us. We did not understand the reason for his behavior. That same night, I contacted the student's parents but did not receive an adequate response. Immediately afterward, I reported the threats to Israel Police and requested a police presence at the school the following morning."
The principal continued: "The next day, despite an agreement with the parents that the student would be barred from school, he arrived at the school, ambushed my son and brutally attacked him solely because he is the principal's son. He later tried to reach my office to physically harm me, and only the quick thinking of teachers at the school prevented him from doing so. Police arrived only after the attack, and I filed a formal complaint. At the end of the school day, I was asked to come to the Ayarot police station to give a statement."
'Fingerprinting in a humiliating and degrading manner'
The principal, who is suspected of assaulting the student, said he was surprised to discover at the police station that he was being detained and questioned under caution.
"My cellphone was taken from me, and I was placed in a detention cell with other detainees," he said. "I underwent identification procedures, was photographed and had my fingerprints taken in a humiliating and degrading manner. Only during questioning did I learn that the student who attacked us had filed a baseless assault complaint against me. The investigator treated me dismissively and did not listen to my account."
The principal added: "At the end of the questioning, I was released on bail to five days of full house arrest, while the violent student remains free. The following day, when my two sons went to the police station to file a complaint, they were arrested and also placed under house arrest. After looking into the matter, I learned that someone had posted content criticizing the student on TikTok. The student demanded that I, as principal, remove the post. When that did not happen, he decided to take revenge on my children and me.
"I am now sitting at home with very difficult feelings. In dealing with the police, the Education Ministry, the Teachers' Association and the local council, I feel completely alone. We acted properly, followed the law and made all the required reports, but in the end, they turned us — the victims — into criminals. It is an upside-down world devoid of justice.
"After a quarter-century devoted to education, working day and night for the sake of our students, I have reached the painful conclusion that in today's crazy reality — with no institutional support and violence running rampant — it simply does not pay to be a school principal."

Russian budget deficit to be 2.2% of GDP next year — Finance Minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:28:53 UTC
01:28:53 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. The Russian federal budget deficit in 2027 will amount to 2.2% of GDP, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov said at a Russian government meeting.
"Expenditures will total 48.8 trillion rubles ($574.1 bln), while revenues will stand at 43.3 trillion rubles ($509.4 bln). The budget deficit is set at around 2% of GDP for the next three years. In 2027, the budget deficit will amount to 2.2% of GDP. In conclusion, I would like to note that the prepared budget is balanced, which is important for maintaining macroeconomic stability, lowering inflation and interest rates, and driving the growth of real disposable public income, which will reach 1.4% next year," the minister said.
A smooth transition to the fiscal rule will be achieved by 2029, Siluanov noted. During the transition period in 2027-2028, the maximum expenditure limit will exceed the structural level by 1.5 trillion and 0.5 trillion rubles ($17.6 bln and $5.8 bln), respectively, the minister added.
"The budget is resilient to various scenarios. Starting next year, the base price of Urals crude oil is factored in at $50 per barrel for a three-year period. This means all obligations will be funded at this oil price level. If market conditions are more favorable, we will replenish the National Wealth Fund," Siluanov said.

Decree for school system that integrates without abandoning rules says Meloni
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:28:07 CEST
01:28:07 KST

The government decree that sets a 30%
cap on foreign pupils in Italian classrooms and bans burqas and
niqabs from Italian schools is a measure towards a school system
that integrates without abandoning the rules, Premier Giorgia
Meloni said after the cabinet meeting that approved the decree
Thursday.
                                    
                                       
				"Today, the Council of Ministers approved the decree on
schools," Meloni said on social media.
                                    
                                       
				"A 30% cap on the number of students per class who do not have
an adequate command of Italian, more tools for learning our
language, and a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools.
                                    
                                       
				"These are common-sense measures that do not divide but rather
foster genuine integration, preventing the formation of 'ghetto
classrooms' and ensuring equal opportunities for all students.
                                    
                                       
				"This is the path we intend to continue following," she added:
"a school system that integrates without abandoning rules,
supports those facing the greatest challenges, and puts everyone
in a position to start from the same baseline."

Russia’s economy minister outlines key drivers of growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:27:44 UTC
01:27:44 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov, presenting Russia’s socioeconomic development forecast at a government meeting, described consumer demand as a key driver of economic growth and said it was expected to increase significantly, by 4.1%, in 2026. The minister also pointed to rising household incomes.
"Consumer demand remains a key driver of economic growth. This year, we expect it to increase significantly, by 4.1%. Consumer activity is supported by rising household incomes. The main sources of this growth are labor and entrepreneurial income, as well as the fulfillment of all social commitments. Real disposable incomes will increase by 0.8% in 2026 and 1.5% in 2027. By 2029, we expect their growth to accelerate to 2.8%," he said.
The minister added that, by sector, growth would be driven by industries focused on domestic demand.
"First and foremost, manufacturing, which will grow by around 3.5% annually. Pharmaceuticals and mechanical engineering, including railway and aircraft manufacturing and electronics production, will grow the fastest. Tourism, IT, and agriculture will also expand at above-average rates," he added.

U.K. prime minister teases possible return of booze to soccer matches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:27:19 UTC
01:27:19 KST

Could U.K. soccer fans get their beers back? Prime Minister Andy Burnham teases possible end of 40-year ban
London — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called the ban on alcohol in the stands at high-level men's soccer matches in the U.K. "discrimination," teasing fellow fans with a possible reversal of a more than 40-year-old ban.
"I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out," Burnham told reporters in New York on Wednesday, where he is attending the United Nations General Assembly.
He hinted at a trial to reintroduce alcohol consumption in stadium seating.
The U.K. government, under then-Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, banned alcohol in the bleachers at men's soccer games in England and Wales in 1985.
Home Secretary Leon Brittan said at the time that booze was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behavior" in soccer stadiums.
Since then, fans attending men's soccer games in the top five divisions have not been allowed to drink alcohol in view of the pitch. People can still buy and drink alcohol in the concourse before games and during halftime, but they cannot carry it back to their seats.
No other sports are subject to such a ban in the U.K.
At some older, less well-equipped soccer grounds, lines for pints of beer can get so long during halftime that fans will leave their seats before the referee blows the whistle.
In a statement, the Football Supporters' Association said Thursday that it has "always argued that it's unfair to criminalize football fans for having a pint while watching the match," and it argued that many clubs are in favor of a reintroduction of alcohol, adding: "We welcome the prime minister's comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated."
After a successful pilot run in the Women's Super League, the highest level of English women's soccer, fans of the women's game have been allowed to drink in the stands since the beginning of the current season.
Burnham, who's a season ticket holder at Premier League club Everton, criticized the restriction shortly before becoming prime minister.
Asked Wednesday if he still held the same view, he said: "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different … And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis."
"I'm not going to back away from what's been a long-held view of mine," he said. "I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently."
The ban was imposed with reason, however.
Soccer hooliganism in 1970s and 1980s England — sometimes referred to as the "English Disease" — involved fans in rival gangs linked to soccer clubs fighting each other and vandalizing areas in and around stadiums.
Several high-profile deaths linked to hooliganism, including that of a 14-year-old boy who died when fans were pushed into a wall by police after violence between Birmingham City and Leeds United fans, led to the alcohol ban.
Police have long supported the legislation.
"Other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behavior from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behavior," a spokesperson for the U.K.'s Football Policing Unit said, according to CBS News' U.K. partner network the BBC.
"It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games," they said, adding that it would be "incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area."
A fan-led review of U.K. laws around soccer in 2021 called for the legislation to be reviewed, however.
In Scotland, which also has a history of soccer-related violence, alcohol has been banned from soccer stadiums since 1981, but recent trials have seen it reintroduced, and fans can now buy booze at games at Hampden Park, the country's national soccer stadium.

Finland had planned to deport a Russian mother and son who helped Ukrainian refugees. Instead, it’s granting them asylum.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Finland had planned to deport a Russian mother and son who helped Ukrainian refugees. Instead, it’s granting them asylum.
Finland has granted asylum to Russian nationals Olga and Nikita Belov, former St. Petersburg municipal councilor Svetlana Utkina told TV Rain. Finnish authorities had planned to deport the mother and son to Russia this spring.
The Belovs left Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. Nikita Belov said he decided to leave after refusing to take part in an “unnamed secret project” at the I.P. Bardin Central Research Institute of Ferrous Metallurgy. He said the institute’s management assured him the project was unrelated to the war, but he later learned otherwise.
In Finland, the Belovs helped Ukrainian refugees through the volunteer organization FinEst Volunteers. In spring 2026, they were summoned to a police station and told they would be deported. In August, a court ordered a review of their case. The Belovs’ lawyer said the family had provided “a great deal of new evidence” that they could face persecution in Russia.

Trump, Xi to talk Taiwan, AI, trade and Iran as DC summit kicks off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:26:47 UTC
01:26:47 KST

President Donald Trump and Chinese Leader Xi Jinping are meeting at the White House on Thursday for high-stakes talks focusing on trade, artificial intelligence and the Iran war — in between displays of military fanfare and a lavish banquet.
Trump said in an arrival ceremony speech that the two countries have been "working to encourage a more balanced trading relationship," and that the leaders plan to discuss "pressing issues" around security, technology and AI.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday evening that the countries have agreed to extend their temporary trade truce, which lowered U.S. tariffs and suspended Beijing's controls on exports of rare earths and critical minerals, among other stipulations. That agreement, which was set to expire in mid-November, will be extended by two months to Jan. 10, Bessent told Fox News.
"The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come," Trump said in Thursday's remarks.
Xi joined in the bonhomie. "China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation," he said in his own remarks, which were translated live.
"We do not need to avoid mentioning competition, but our competition should be a healthy one and should be kept within bounds. It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses," he said.
Xi also engaged in the Chinese specialty of "panda diplomacy," announcing that two pandas will be coming to Georgia's Zoo Atlanta in the coming days.
While China analysts broadly predict the leaders' personal relationship and policy goals will result in a cautious summit that yields few major deliverables, their latest face-to-face nevertheless carries real geopolitical risk.
Pomp and circumstance
That significance was on display the moment Xi arrived Wednesday evening at Maryland's Joint Base Andrews, where he was greeted on the tarmac by Trump — who met him at the airplane stairs after walking down a red carpet that U.S. service members had rolled out. The White House arrival ceremony Thursday morning included military members lining the south portico stairs holding alternating U.S. and Chinese flags, while trumpets played a fanfare.
It was Trump's first time traveling to the base to welcome a foreign leader, a source familiar confirmed to CNBC on condition of anonymity to discuss the president's plans for the summit. The last president to make the gesture was Barack Obama, who greeted then-Pope Francis on the Andrews tarmac 11 years ago this week.
Before leaving the tarmac, Xi was treated to a military flyover of two B-1 bombers while cannons fired and a U.S. Air Force band played the national anthem.
Chinese media was blanketed with images of Xi's arrival, holding up the red-carpet treatment as further proof of Beijing's vaunted global standing.
The flattery extended to social media. "I met President Xi at the plane (Airport!) yesterday and he looks strong, vibrant, and fit - Better than ever," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday morning.
AI takes focus
In another Truth post, Trump confirmed that AI will be at the top of the agenda — but asserted that neither the U.S. nor China want to change how the rapidly growing sector is handled.
"Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion," Trump wrote, using the term he picked to try to rebrand AI amid a crescendo of concerns about the risks posed by the increasingly powerful technology.
"But I want to leave it exactly where it is," wrote Trump, who has bristled at calls to slow AI growth on the belief that the U.S. must beat China in the race to AI dominance.
"That is China's position also," Trump said in the post, suggesting Xi also opposes new AI regulations and apparently precluding any possibility of an agreement to strengthen safety precautions.
He added that the U.S. "guardrail" is the Department of Justice, reiterating the Trump administration's stance that sufficient regulatory safeguards are already in place.
But Xi has previously acknowledged the risks of AI and the importance of keeping it under human control.
In remarks after arriving at the White House, Xi said that the U.S. and China have "both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people."
China's Iran ties
Trump has also confirmed the Iran war will be a topic of discussion with Xi. "I'll be talking about that and many other subjects but it's all coming along, including that," he told reporters Wednesday evening after returning to the White House.
The U.S. last month launched "Operation Economic Outcast," its effort to harm Iran by targeting its financial enablers with secondary sanctions. The plan raised questions about whether the U.S. would take action against China, Tehran's top trading partner and oil buyer.
The Trump administration has said no country is exempt from potential sanctions, but it has not directly targeted Beijing.
Trump has also shied from unreservedly criticizing China over its reported Iran ties in the run-up to the Xi meeting. Asked about a Wall Street Journal report that Chinese entities supplied Tehran with satellite imagery that it used to carry out deadly attacks on U.S. troops in Jordan in July, Trump said of Beijing's surveillance activities, "They basically do what we do."
Summit schedule
On Thursday morning, Trump and first lady Melania Trump welcomed Xi and Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan at the White House for an arrival ceremony. It is Xi's first visit to Washington since September 2015, coming to the capital city right after the pope.
The leaders then headed to the Rose Garden for a military review, after which Trump and Xi will hold a bilateral meeting, while Melania Trump and Madame Peng branch off for a separate event.
In the evening, Trump and the first lady will host the Chinese delegation for a state dinner in the White House's East Room, with both countries' leaders expected to give remarks at the top of the event.
A slew of U.S. business executives are slated to join the dinner. Reuters had reported that Xi was expected to bring along his own crew of CEOs, but that entourage did not materialize. The South China Morning Post reported Thursday morning that a small group of Chinese CEOs flew to the U.S. separately from Xi, even though they have not yet found out if they will be able to join the events.
On Friday, the presidents and first ladies will hold a private tea at the White House, then take a tour of the National Archives before Xi's departure.
"President Xi hosted President Trump in China for a historic summit this summer, and President Trump is reciprocating his hospitality by welcoming the Chinese delegation for a reciprocal visit this week," White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly told CNBC in a statement.
This is developing news. Please check back for updates.
— CNBC's Eunice Yoon contributed reporting.
