Netanyahu steps into UN lion’s den after days of fierce criticism of Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:54:06 UTC
00:54:06 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu used a combative address to the UN General Assembly on Thursday to defend Israel’s conduct in Gaza and strikes on Iran, reject genocide allegations as “the greatest lie of the century” and lash out at foreign leaders, protesters and critics he accused of hypocrisy toward Israel.
Netanyahu said the strikes against Iran's nuclear program were necessary for Israel’s survival and accused foreign leaders who criticize Israel publicly of privately thanking it for acting against Tehran.
Returning to his famous 2012 UN presentation, in which he used a cartoon-like bomb diagram to illustrate Iran’s nuclear progress, Netanyahu recalled drawing a red line over Tehran’s nuclear program.
“Fourteen years ago, I stood on this podium and I drew a red line,” Netanyahu said. “I vowed to prevent Iran’s murderous dictatorship from developing atomic bombs.”
Netanyahu said the decision to strike Iran’s nuclear facilities was among the clearest he had faced during his years in office.
“Devastating Iran’s nuclear facilities was hard. It was very hard to do,” he said. “But for me, it was one of the easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make as prime minister. Because if we hadn’t done it, we’d all be dead.”
The prime minister argued that Israel’s military actions had protected not only Israelis but other countries, including some whose representatives left the General Assembly chamber during his address.
“In defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall,” Netanyahu said.
He then accused those governments of hypocrisy, claiming some of their leaders had privately expressed gratitude for Israel’s actions against Iran.
“Many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran’s nukes,” Netanyahu said. “It’s hard to imagine more mind-blowing hypocrisy, but that’s exactly what it is.”
Netanyahu also turned to Palestinian attacks in the West Bank, using the biblical name Judea for the territory.
“They try to murder our people in our historic homeland in Judea,” Netanyahu said. “By the way, that’s where the word ‘Jew’ comes from — Judea. That’s our land.”
He said there are thousands of attacks each year targeting Israeli families traveling on West Bank roads.
“They shoot at pregnant women. They shoot entire families,” he said, accusing international media and social media platforms of largely ignoring such attacks. “None of it is covered in the international press or on social media. None of it.”
Netanyahu also addressed settler violence in the West Bank, describing those responsible as a small group of about 150 young offenders and saying Israel would not tolerate vigilantism.
“A handful of young juvenile delinquents, about 150 in number, go and throw stones, chop down olive trees and occasionally set fires,” Netanyahu said. “I can’t stand that. I won’t stand for vigilantism. We’re a country of law, so we put our Shin Bet on them.”
The prime minister rejected international criticism of settler violence, arguing that such incidents were disproportionately emphasized compared with Palestinian attacks against Israelis in the West Bank.
“The number of casualties a year is maybe two or three,” Netanyahu said. “Compare that with the thousands of terrorist attacks against peaceful settlers — honorable, law-abiding people. What a distortion. It’s an obsession.”
He also criticized foreign leaders who have raised the issue.
“Leaders of countries seriously talk about this, and they say with such importance, ‘We can’t stand settler violence.’ You don’t know what you’re talking about,” he said.
Netanyahu directly addressed French President Emmanuel Macron, citing two recent Palestinian attacks in the West Bank. Macron had triggered a dispute with Israel over comments about Hamas during his address to the UN General Assembly, appearing to claim that the terrorist group had never operated there.
“I say this to my colleague Emmanuel Macron: Three days ago, a French citizen, Netanel Shukrun, a father of six, was gunned down when he visited a spring with his 16-year-old son,” Netanyahu said. “A Hamas terrorist in Judea and Samaria came and fired at him point-blank. His last words were, ‘Flee, flee, son. Save yourself.’”
Macron's remarks drew an angry Israeli response. A French diplomatic source later said the remarks had been mistranslated and that Macron meant Hamas had never governed the territory.
Netanyahu then cited the attack on Neriya Leiter, who was seriously wounded Wednesday in a Palestinian car-ramming attack near the Maccabim checkpoint in the West Bank. Leiter, a member of a police patrol crew, is the son of Israel’s ambassador to the United States, Yechiel Leiter. His brother, Maj. (res.) Moshe Yedidyah Leiter, was killed fighting in Gaza during the war.
“Two days ago, in Judea and Samaria, a reserve soldier, Neriya Leiter, was mowed down by a Palestinian terrorist,” he said. “He’s fighting for his life now in a Jerusalem hospital.”
The premier vowed to continue defending Israel.
“Israel is like no other country. It's a privilege to defend it. To Neriya and to all the heroes of Israel, I pledge a sacred vow: Your sacrifice will not be in vain,” Netanyahu said. “We will continue to defend our state. We will continue to win because we have no other choice.”
Netanyahu praised the IDF as “the most moral army in the world,” citing the scale of missile attacks Israel has faced and the diversity of those serving in its military.
“You can imagine, think about 1,000 gigantic missiles falling from the skies on your cities, on your homes,” Netanyahu said. “I salute the courage of the people of Israel.  I salute the courage of the people of Israel. I salute the courage of our brave soldiers, Jews, Christians, Jews, Muslim, the most moral army in the world, the IDF.”
Netanyahu then launched a sharply worded attack on Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, accusing Turkey of spreading antisemitism and criticizing Erdogan’s domestic and regional policies.
“The latest country to become a superspreader of antisemitic lies is Turkey,” Netanyahu said. “Erdogan is a tyrant. He also hosts the Hamas terror chiefs. He has murdered thousands of Kurdish civilians. He denies the Armenian genocide. He jails journalists and opposition leaders.”
The prime minister went on to accuse Turkey of expansionism, pointing to its presence in northern Cyprus and tensions with Greece and Syria.
“I think he holds the world record on this, and that’s a tough call. But I think he’s number one,” Netanyahu said, referring to the jailing of journalists and political opponents. “He illegally occupies northern Cyprus, an EU member, and he regularly transgresses against Greece, a NATO member. Now he wants to take over Syria. Well, that’s not surprising.”
Netanyahu also targeted Qatar, accusing the Gulf state of using its financial influence over universities and media organizations to foster hostility toward Israel and the West.
“Decades ago, it started massively funding American universities and toxic media outlets like Al Jazeera,” Netanyahu said. “They did the same in Europe, by the way. And their goal was clear: brainwash young minds to hate Israel, hate America, hate the West. This is the same Qatar that hosts the Hamas butchers of October 7.”
Netanyahu defended Israel’s conduct in Gaza, saying Hamas had deliberately endangered Palestinian civilians while Israel had sought to move them out of harm’s way.
“It will take time for the world to acknowledge what is so plain to see: that Hamas used Palestinian civilians as human shields, that it used hospitals, schools and mosques as terrorist command posts, that it sold much of the food we let into Gaza,” Netanyahu said. “While Hamas did everything possible to keep Palestinian civilians in harm’s way, often at gunpoint, Israel did everything possible to get them out of harm’s way.”
Netanyahu went further, claiming Israel’s efforts to limit civilian casualties were unprecedented in modern warfare.
“Israel has done more to prevent civilian casualties in war than any other military in history,” he said.
Netanyahu flatly rejected allegations that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, turning the accusation on Israel’s enemies.
“Israel didn’t commit genocide. Israel prevented genocide,” Netanyahu said.
He called the allegation “the greatest lie of the century” and invoked retired U.S. Army Col. John Spencer, who has publicly defended Israel’s conduct in Gaza.
“Accusing Israel of genocide is the greatest lie of the century,” Netanyahu said. “If you want to know how big a lie, if you want to know how absurd it is, listen to Col. John Spencer.”
Netanyahu also singled out political commentator and streamer Hasan Piker while criticizing figures he accused of sympathizing with Hamas and anti-Israel causes.
“You praise criminals convicted of supporting Hamas,” Netanyahu said. “You count as friends people like Hasan Piker, who said America deserved 9/11.”
Turning again to Iran, Netanyahu held up a Starlink satellite internet terminal, saying he would leave it with the president of the General Assembly to give to the Iranian delegation. He portrayed the device as a symbol of free expression in the face of Iranian government censorship.
“This is a communications device, Starlink, that allows people to access truth, to exercise choice, to exercise freedom of thought and freedom of speech,” Netanyahu said. “I’m going to leave this device with you so you can give it to the Iranian delegation. So when they inevitably defect, they too can share their story.”
Netanyahu also directly attacked New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, accusing him of hostility toward Israel and attempting to prevent the prime minister from visiting the city.
“Mr. Mamdani, you tried to stop me from coming here. You tried to silence me,” Netanyahu said. “Well, you can’t silence me. You can’t silence the truth.”
Mamdani has called Netanyahu a war criminal and the “architect of the genocide in Gaza,” allegations Netanyahu rejects, and has called for his arrest under the International Criminal Court warrant issued against him in 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. The United States is not a member of the ICC, and Israel rejects both the court’s jurisdiction and the allegations against Netanyahu. 
Netanyahu has accused Mamdani of hosting a Palestinian journalist who, he said, had filmed Hamas terrorists abusing Israeli hostages but withheld the footage to protect them. He also accused Mamdani’s wife of liking social media posts praising the Oct. 7 massacre and saying Tel Aviv should not exist, and criticized Mamdani for repeatedly accusing Israel of genocide.
Netanyahu concluded his remarks on Iran by predicting that its government would ultimately be overcome by its own people.
“Despite your silence, despite your hypocrisy, it’s only a matter of time before something incredible happens in Iran,” Netanyahu said. “The power of the people will overcome the people in power.”
Addressing Iranians directly, he added: “One day — and it may not be far away — the Iranian people will be free.”
Netanyahu also challenged protesters outside the UN and delegates who walked out of the chamber, accusing them of remaining silent over Iran’s crackdown on its own citizens.
“To the protesters outside, to the hypocritical delegates who left this hall, I ask: Where were you when the Iranian tyrants butchered and maimed tens of thousands of unarmed Iranian civilians?” Netanyahu said. “When they butchered and maimed thousands of their own people, where were you?”
Netanyahu also predicted the eventual collapse of Iran’s government, directly addressing the Iranian people and portraying its downfall as inevitable.
“I want you to listen to my words carefully. One day — and it may not be far away — the Iranian people will be free,” Netanyahu said. “Their murderous regime will be toppled by its lies, by its corruption, by its cruelty. This evil regime will fall, and we will all celebrate that day.”
Netanyahu also recalled Israel’s September 2024 pager operation against Hezbollah in Lebanon, in which thousands of pagers used by members of the Iran-backed group exploded almost simultaneously. A second wave of explosions involving booby-trapped walkie-talkies followed the next day.
“Hezbollah — you remember the beepers? Remember these things? Remember them?” Netanyahu said. “Well, I can tell you this: Hezbollah certainly remembers them.”
Netanyahu then pointed to Israel’s broader campaign against Hezbollah, which he said had destroyed the bulk of the terrorist group’s once-formidable rocket arsenal.
“Guess what happened to the bulk of Hezbollah’s vast arsenal of 150,000 rockets?” he said.
Netanyahu has previously put Hezbollah’s prewar arsenal at roughly 150,000 missiles and rockets and said in June that only about 8% remained following Israel’s military campaign, though that figure is an Israeli assessment.
Netanyahu's visit was scheduled to be unusually brief and was expected to last only several hours. His schedule is markedly thinner than during previous trips to the annual gathering, with no meeting planned with U.S. President Donald Trump.
Before leaving Israel, Netanyahu signaled that his speech would be confrontational.
“You hear the terrible lies being spread there; I will fight for the truth,” he said, adding that there would be “surprises.”
A senior Israeli official had said ahead of the speech that footage involving National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Jewish extremist violence in the West Bank had badly damaged Israel’s international standing. The official said there was a perception abroad that Netanyahu had lost control of events and was allowing far-right ministers to act without restraint. 
The speech comes at the end of several days in which Israel has repeatedly been the subject of criticism from the General Assembly podium, including from UN Secretary-General António Guterres, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Jordan's King Abdullah II, Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and Macron.
Israel rejects allegations that it has committed genocide in Gaza and says its military operations have targeted Hamas and other terrorist groups. It has also accused critics of minimizing the security threats it faces and, in some cases, ignoring Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel.
Guterres warns over Gaza and West Bank
Guterres, delivering his final General Assembly address before his term ends Dec. 31, condemned Hamas' Oct. 7 attack while sharply criticizing the scale of Israel's military response in Gaza.
He described the Hamas assault as “abhorrent” but said the ensuing Gaza war had brought a scale of death and destruction he had not witnessed during his years as secretary-general. He also warned that violence, Palestinian displacement and settlement expansion in the West Bank were eroding prospects for a two-state solution.
Guterres renewed his support for two states and called for international law to be upheld consistently, part of a broader address in which he warned that global institutions were struggling under the weight of wars, geopolitical divisions and declining trust.
Erdogan delivered one of the most forceful attacks on Israel, urging countries to increase pressure on Jerusalem over Gaza and calling on governments that have not recognized a Palestinian state to reconsider.
The Turkish president condemned the humanitarian situation in Gaza and accused the international community of failing to stop it. Turkey has repeatedly characterized Israel's campaign as genocide, an allegation Israel rejects.
Jordan's King Abdullah II also focused heavily on Israel, Gaza and the West Bank, accusing the Israeli government of policies aimed at changing realities on the ground and making a viable Palestinian state impossible. He pointed to settlement expansion, land seizures and settler violence in the West Bank while describing destruction in Gaza as part of a broader threat to Palestinian statehood.
Qatar's emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, accused Israel of “genocide in the fullest sense of the word” in Gaza and criticized Israeli policy in the West Bank and elsewhere in the region.
Macron said the humanitarian situation in Gaza was a “spectacle that shames us all” and criticized increasing settler violence in the West Bank, arguing that it was undermining Palestinian rights and prospects for a two-state solution.
The criticism has not been limited to Middle Eastern leaders. Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva accused Israel of genocide and warned of lasting trauma among Palestinians, while British Prime Minister Andy Burnham condemned Hamas' Oct. 7 attack and affirmed Britain's support for Israel's security but also criticized Israeli government policy in Gaza and the West Bank.
Abbas: Israel ‘destroying’ two-state solution
Hours before Netanyahu's scheduled appearance, Palestinian Authority Chairman Mahmoud Abbas addressed the General Assembly by video after the United States denied him a visa to travel to New York for the second consecutive year.
The General Assembly voted 152-3, with four abstentions, to allow Abbas and other senior Palestinian officials to participate remotely in UN meetings when U.S. visa restrictions prevent them from attending. Washington has cited Palestinian efforts to pursue Israel in international tribunals and what it describes as attempts to “internationalize” the conflict among its reasons for the restrictions.
Abbas accused Israel of waging a “genocidal war” in Gaza, seeking to forcibly displace Palestinians and protecting what he called “settler terrorism” in the West Bank.
He also argued that Israeli policy was destroying prospects for a two-state solution and warned against another Nakba — the Arabic word for “catastrophe,” used by Palestinians for the mass displacement surrounding Israel's establishment and the 1948 Arab-Israeli war.
Abbas also called on the international community to stop supplying weapons to Israel.
Israel rejects Abbas' accusations and maintains that its military campaign was launched in response to the Hamas-led Oct. 7 attack.
Iran takes center stage
Despite the focus on Gaza and the Palestinians throughout the General Assembly, Netanyahu devoted a substantial portion of his speech to Iran.
Trump used his own General Assembly address Tuesday to issue a stark warning to Tehran, saying the United States could “annihilate” Iran if a peace agreement was not reached while also saying he believed a deal remained possible after the November U.S. midterm elections.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, meanwhile, used his appearance at the gathering to criticize U.S. policy and question Washington's commitment to diplomacy. The continuing U.S.-Iran confrontation has been one of the dominant Middle East issues surrounding this year's General Assembly.
Lightning visit, no Trump meeting
The political backdrop to Netanyahu's speech is unusual in another respect: The prime minister is making one of his shortest U.S. visits in years.
He was expected to spend only about six hours in the United States, landing at a military airfield, traveling to Manhattan for the General Assembly and returning to the airport after his address.
Netanyahu was accompanied by his wife, Sara. Environmental Protection Minister Idit Silman and Education Minister Yoav Kisch were also at the UN in connection with their ministerial duties and were expected to attend his address.
Netanyahu, who typically releases a video before departing Israel, kept an unusually low profile ahead of the trip. The first footage released by his office showed his arrival at Stewart Air National Guard Base in New York, outside New York City.
Netanyahu will not meet Trump during the trip. Their schedules do not overlap, with Trump having left New York after his own UN appearances. Netanyahu is also not expected to meet Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
The Prime Minister's Office said Netanyahu's planned meetings include leaders from Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay, Panama, Ethiopia, Colombia, Greece, Slovenia and Papua New Guinea, although the compressed timetable leaves little room for the extensive bilateral diplomacy that traditionally accompanies his General Assembly appearances.
Earlier plans for the trip were considerably broader. Netanyahu had been considering traveling to Texas for a possible meeting with Elon Musk and a visit connected to SpaceX, but the stop was canceled. The proposed Texas stop reportedly encountered logistical difficulties involving the U.S. Secret Service and would also have required an additional refueling stop in the United States.
Israeli officials had also explored meetings with Gulf leaders, but none had been finalized as the visit approached.
Netanyahu’s office said numerous foreign leaders had requested meetings with Netanyahu but that the tight schedule and his need to return to Israel before the start of Sukkot meant he could accommodate only some of them. Media reports, however, cited additional concerns, including security considerations and anticipated protests against the prime minister.
Netanyahu ultimately opted for such a brief visit that he was not expected to stay at the Loews Regency, his usual Manhattan hotel. Israel had already reserved three floors there, however, potentially leaving the government with a substantial bill. Finance Ministry officials were expected to negotiate with the hotel for a credit toward a future stay, though it was unclear whether the hotel would agree.
Before his UN address, Netanyahu met Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis. According to the Prime Minister’s Office, Netanyahu stressed the importance of the countries’ strategic partnership for regional stability and welcomed Greece’s selection of Israeli defense systems. The two also discussed regional developments, energy cooperation and plans for another trilateral summit with Cyprus.
Netanyahu also met Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša. His office said Netanyahu welcomed the opening of Israel’s embassy in Ljubljana and thanked Janša for his strong support for Israel and a resulting shift in bilateral relations. The two discussed expanding cooperation, and Netanyahu invited Janša to visit Israel.
Protests and another possible walkout
Pro-Palestinian demonstrators protested in New York ahead of Netanyahu’s appearance, while Israeli anti-government activists and supporters of Israel also held rallies. Security was tightened around the UN complex as world leaders gathered for the General Assembly.
Several protesters were arrested shortly before Netanyahu’s speech, including Oscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon, “Sex and the City” star Cynthia Nixon and activist Linda Sarsour, an adviser to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani who was recently denied entry to Israel.
Israeli officials were also concerned that Mamdani’s administration could create logistical difficulties for the delegation, including potentially requiring Netanyahu’s official Wing of Zion aircraft to leave a New York airport after dropping him off rather than remain there until his return from the UN. 
Attention will also be focused on the General Assembly hall itself. Delegates staged a large walkout when Netanyahu addressed the gathering last year, and Israeli officials expect another hostile reception this time. Israeli officials later said 77 delegations were either absent from the hall or walked out at the start of Netanyahu’s address.

Government expands the list of permitted chemicals for storage in coastal areas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:52:34 UTC
00:52:34 KST

Official logo of the ministry of environment, forest and climate change (representative image)
NEW DELHI: In a move that may boost port-adjacent industries by allowing storage of specific chemicals in coastal areas, the govt has expanded the list of petroleum and chemical products permitted for storage in the coastal regulation zone (CRZ) by amending the existing CRZ notification, 2019.The amendment, published by the Union environment ministry on Thursday, now provides for storing 26 petroleum and chemical products in the coastal areas instead of 23 such products permitted earlier. The additional products are linear alkyl benzene, N-paraffin and carbon black feedstock.The list of 23 already permitted products includes crude oil, LPG, kerosene, aviation fuel, high-speed diesel, lubricating oil, CNG, naphtha, acetic acid, methanol, liquefied natural gas and furnace oil, among others.The amendment was notified to accommodate formal representations made by various State Coastal Zone Management Authorities to facilitate the industrial receipt and storage of these specific chemicals in coastal areas. The decision was finally taken after the sectoral Expert Appraisal Committee for CRZ clearances and the National Coastal Zone Management Authority gave their nod.
The ministry’s notification said that National Coastal Zone Management Authority, after due deliberation, considering the comparatively lower hazardous chemical characteristics of these products in relation to those already permitted, “unanimously recommended allowing the receipt and storage of Linear Alkyl Benzene, N-Paraffin, and Carbon Black Feedstock in CRZ areas”, excluding Coastal Regulation Zone-IA, through the necessary amendment.
It means these products will not be allowed for storage in the environmentally most critical CRZ-IA areas (like mangroves, coral reefs, and turtle nesting grounds) along the coastline. This zone plays a vital role in maintaining the structural integrity of the coast and acting as a natural defence against hazards like cyclones, storms, and tsunamis.
Vishwa Mohan is Senior Editor at The Times of India. He writes on environment, climate change, agriculture, water resources and clean energy, tracking policy issues and climate diplomacy. He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

At Trump meeting, Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:52:13 UTC
00:52:13 KST

Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan.
At the start of his summit meeting with Donald Trump in the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could steer the two competing superpowers away from future military conflict and on to a road of mutual gain.
Rather than confrontation, conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand” and should be the goal, Xi said, citing Trump’s political catchphrase.
“We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on.
“We should coexist in peace. China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.”
With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, refering to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power.
Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it.
His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other.
Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was president.
“President Xi and Madame Peng arrive at an important moment for America, the 250th anniversary of our founding,” he said.
Trump said he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balances trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.”
He said the current visit would include discussion overs security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday.
Xi also extolled his personal relationship with his American counterpart, saying: “President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.”
Addressing Trump directly, he said: “During your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course towards the future.”
The White House welcome ceremony came after Trump had taken the unusual step of going to Andrews air force base in Maryland the evening before to greet the Chinese leader and his wife on the tarmac.
Much of the same pageantry was repeated in Thursday’s ceremony, with both countries’ national anthems being played. Trump was flanked by his wife, Melania, while members of his cabinet and senior aides – including Natalie Harp, Trump’s dedicated assistant nicknamed “the human printer” by fellow staffers – looked on.
Trump and Xi held bilateral talks after the ceremony and the welcoming speeches.
Later on Thursday, Trump hosted Xi at the White House for a state dinner. Notable invited guests from the tech world included Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Apple chair Tim Cook, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
Trump gestured to the titans of the industry in his remarks to the dinner, recounting when Chinese diplomats first arrived in the US 158 years ago, meeting American intellectuals like Henry David Thoreau and prominent political figures.
“Tonight, we revive the spirit of that first encounter here on American soil as we are joined by some of the top leaders in business, culture and government from our own time,” he said. “On one side, China draws on thousands of years of history and tradition from Sun Tzu to Sun Yat-sen. For Americans, we inherit a legacy of faith from Jerusalem to Rome, democracy of ancient Athens, the triumphs of Sparta and the freedom proclaimed in Philadelphia 250 years ago.”
Trump also touted his relationship with the Chinese leader.
“President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,” he said.
Xi also addressed the dinner, saying talks with Trump during the visit had yielded “common understanding on many issues”, and suggesting the US and China find a new approach to working together.
“China and the United States must act as responsible major countries,” he said.
Despite the harmonious tone adopted by both leaders, analysts have voiced scepticism about the possibility of longstanding stable arrangements being arrived at over a host of issues.
In the race for AI, the US has placed strict export controls on microchips, semiconductors, software and chip-making equipment in a bid to slow China’s development.
A truce agreed between Trump and Xi in South Korea last year aimed at keeping tariffs lower had been due to expire in November but has now been extended until February, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent said.
Analysts believe the extension suggests Trump continues to be dissatisfied with Xi’s concession offers on trade and wants to keep the pressure on in the hope of getting a better deal if the two meet again at the G20 summit scheduled to be held in Miami in December.
Despite the trade war between the two countries, Chinese imports have continue to surge into the US. China is on course to run a $1tn trade deficit for the second year running.
Uwa Ede-Osifo contributed reporting

Morocco’s ruling party suffers election defeat as Islamists stage comeback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:51:56 UTC
00:51:56 KST

The party leading Morocco’s outgoing government suffered a sharp defeat in parliamentary elections, while an Islamist party that campaigned against the country’s ties with Israel staged a significant comeback, according to near-final results released Thursday.
The Authenticity and Modernity Party, known by its French acronym PAM, emerged as the largest party, winning 97 of the 395 seats in Morocco’s House of Representatives, according to preliminary official results announced by the Interior Ministry. The National Rally of Independents, or RNI, which led the outgoing government, fell to second place with 66 seats, while the conservative Istiqlal Party won 65.
The Justice and Development Party, or PJD, an Islamist party that led Morocco’s government before suffering a crushing defeat in 2021, rebounded from just 13 seats five years ago to 54, making it the fourth-largest party in parliament.
The results represented a significant reshuffling of Moroccan politics but are unlikely to fundamentally alter the balance of power in the North African kingdom, where King Mohammed VI retains broad authority, particularly over foreign affairs, security and major strategic decisions.
Morocco is a constitutional monarchy of about 39 million people. Under the constitution adopted in 2011 following Arab Spring protests, the king must appoint the head of government from the party that finishes first in parliamentary elections. PAM will therefore provide the next prime minister, though Mohammed is not required to select the party’s leader. The new prime minister must then assemble a governing coalition.
PAM’s 97 seats fall far short of the 198 needed for a majority. The three parties in the outgoing coalition — PAM, RNI and Istiqlal — would together hold 228 seats, enough to continue governing together, though tensions between PAM and RNI emerged during the campaign and the makeup of the next coalition remains uncertain.
The government that emerges will oversee Morocco’s day-to-day administration for the next five years and preside over major infrastructure development ahead of the 2030 FIFA World Cup, which Morocco will co-host with Spain and Portugal. The scale of the projects has led some Moroccans to dub the next administration the “World Cup government.”
The king’s powers mean the government has considerably less latitude in foreign and security policy. Cabinet ministers selected by the prime minister also require royal approval, while Mohammed presides over a separate Council of Ministers responsible for major strategic decisions
Who will become prime minister?
It was not immediately clear whom the king would appoint to lead the next government.
Among the names discussed during the campaign was Fouzi Lekjaa, president of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a prominent government official who recently joined PAM. Lekjaa’s public profile rose further after Morocco’s historic performance at the 2022 World Cup, where its national team became the first from Africa and the Arab world to reach the semifinals.
Another possible candidate is Fatima-Zahra El Mansouri, 50, the mayor of Marrakech, outgoing housing and urban planning minister and a senior figure in PAM’s collective leadership. If chosen by the king, she would become Morocco’s first female prime minister.
El Mansouri was recently pressed on her position toward Israel after a political opponent accused her of supporting it.
“Our party’s positions regarding the Palestinian issue are clear and well known, and they are reflected in the party’s statements and declarations — documents that can be consulted,” she said.
“They are explicit and leave no room for distortion,” she added. “My party and I serve our homeland, and our homeland alone, alongside its fundamental principles and state institutions. That is our only and greatest honor.”
Islamist comeback raises questions over Israel ties
The election’s implications for Morocco’s relationship with Israel remain unclear.
Morocco normalized relations with Israel in 2020 as part of the U.S.-brokered Abraham Accords. The relationship has been strained by the Gaza war and repeated large demonstrations in Morocco opposing Israel, even as official diplomatic ties have continued.
The PJD’s resurgence could add domestic political pressure over those ties, though foreign policy ultimately remains largely under the authority of the king and it is not yet clear whether the Islamist party will join the next government.
The PJD is led by former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane. His party headed the Moroccan government when relations with Israel were normalized in 2020, though Benkirane said during this year’s campaign that the party’s role in that decision had been a “mistake.”
At a campaign rally in Marrakech, Benkirane warned of what he called “the dangers of Israel and Zionism in Morocco” and urged supporters to make their opposition heard.
“If we work hard, the king will close the Israeli Embassy,” Benkirane said. “The king does not like to act against his people.”
The PJD’s result marks a dramatic reversal from 2021, when the party collapsed from 125 seats to 13. It remains well below its previous peak but has again become one of Morocco’s four largest parliamentary forces.
Among the PJD figures elected to the new parliament is Aziz Hanaoui, a prominent opponent of normalization with Israel.
Hanaoui serves as secretary-general of the National Action Group for Palestine and the Moroccan Observatory Against Normalization. About a month before the election, he helped organize a demonstration against a visit to Morocco by Transportation Minister Miri Regev. Protesters carried Moroccan and Palestinian flags and signs condemning Regev.
A complaint was also filed with Moroccan prosecutors several months ago accusing Hanaoui of defaming Jacky Kadosh, head of the Jewish community in the Marrakech region.
One Moroccan source, speaking to ynet on condition of anonymity, expressed alarm at Hanaoui’s election and the broader gains by politicians hostile to Israel.
“Aziz Hanaoui, who tramples on the Israeli flag, has become a member of the Moroccan parliament,” the source said. “The faction in Morocco that supports Iran and Hamas has entered parliament. At a time when extremists should have had their presence reduced and been stopped, they were rewarded with seats in parliament.”
The source said opposition to normalization was not limited to the PJD.
“Activists who support normalization and identify with Israel are being pushed to the margins,” the source said. “On the other hand, those engaged in antisemitism and burning the Israeli flag are being rewarded, as is happening with people of this kind in the current election.”
The characterization reflects the source’s view of Morocco’s political factions and not an official assessment of the newly elected lawmakers.
A second Moroccan source, who also requested anonymity, said the results must be respected but argued that they reflected broader dissatisfaction with Morocco’s political establishment.
“Accepting the election results is a democratic obligation, but their implications warrant examination,” the source said. “The results confirmed continued voter apathy, driven by poor political practice and a lack of trust.”
The source argued that the weak performance of the governing majority, particularly the RNI, had created an opening for the PJD to return.
“This result reflects the lack of discipline and responsibility among its rivals rather than its own strength,” the source said, adding that low participation should prompt political parties to reconsider how they operate and recruit candidates.
Turnout sinks to 38%
Perhaps the clearest sign of public disillusionment was turnout.
Only about 38% of registered voters cast ballots, down from more than 50% in 2021 and the lowest level since 2007. Nearly 6 million of Morocco’s 15.8 million registered voters participated.
The reasons voters stayed home vary and cannot be determined from turnout figures alone, but the election came amid widespread concerns over unemployment, inequality, health care, education and the cost of living.
Morocco has enjoyed economic growth, rising foreign investment and a booming tourism industry, but the benefits have been unevenly distributed. Youth unemployment reached about 37% among people ages 15 to 24 in 2025, compared with an overall unemployment rate of about 13%.
Those frustrations helped fuel unusual youth-led protests last year demanding better public services and economic opportunities. Demonstrators also targeted the government of outgoing Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch, a billionaire businessman and RNI leader.
Economic frustration has also contributed to migration pressure, particularly among younger Moroccans seeking opportunities in Europe. The election campaign unfolded after mass attempts to reach Ceuta, the Spanish enclave on Morocco’s northern coast, further highlighting the lack of opportunities cited by many young people.

Diesel fuel prices are rising—chemistry can help explain why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:51:52 UTC
00:51:52 KST

Diesel fuel prices in the U.S. are rising dramatically—much more so than gasoline prices. That's putting economic pressure on agriculture and other key industries—but the reason why has as much to do with chemistry as it does with supply or demand.
As of Thursday, the average diesel price in the U.S. is $6.5141 per gallon, roughly a cent lower than the all-time historic high set on Tuesday, according to American Automobile Association (AAA) data. Experts believe that unless something dramatic happens in the ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine, the price climb is likely to continue.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The reason diesel is more expensive than gasoline involves a combination of geopolitics, as well as the chemistry of the product itself.
Both gasoline and diesel are made from crude oil, but their chemical makeup differs in several ways. Diesel’s chains of hydrocarbons—organic compounds made up of hydrogen and carbon atoms—are longer, which makes the fuel around 20 percent more efficient than gasoline, explains Robert Farrauto, a professor at Columbia University’s department of Earth and environmental engineering.
“That’s the reason truckers use diesel,” Farrauto says. “You get much better fuel economy because it uses less fuel, because the molecules are bigger. You get more energy, which means you need fewer hydrocarbons in mixture with air in order to get mileage.”
The process needed to refine diesel is more intensive, however. That’s because of the type of oil used in its production. Unlike gasoline, which is primarily made out of “sweet crude”—a high-quality oil with relatively few impurities and shorter chains of hydrocarbons—diesel is made out of heavier oil with longer hydrocarbon chains, such as those produced in Canada’s tar sands or Venezuela’s oil fields. This can come with high levels of metals such as nickel and vanadium, which can damage engines, and sulfur, which can be poisonous to people. Because of environmental regulations, those contaminants need to be removed during refining.
“It’s called a sledgehammer-type process, where you have high pressure, high temperatures, and you break the nickel and the vanadium and the sulfur, and you get rid of them, but you also break a lot of the molecules,” Farrauto says.
Because so much material is removed, the amount of diesel fuel produced from a barrel of oil is lower than the amount of gasoline that can be produced from that barrel—that’s part of why diesel is so much more expensive than gasoline. But economic pressures are driving up the price even more, says Gregg Ibendahl, an associate professor of agricultural economics as Kansas State University. Gasoline prices have gone up about 40 percent over the past 12 months, whereas diesel prices have nearly doubled over that time, according to AAA. That’s because gasoline is more elastic, fiscally speaking, than diesel.
“People still drive a lot when gas prices go up, but consumers do vote with their pocketbook, and they will cut back on trips and stuff,” Ibendahl says. “When it comes to diesel fuel, though, it’s not that way at all. Diesel price is $2.50 higher than what it was in spring, but that’s not going to stop a single farmer from running their combine out there.”
While most diesel consumed in the U.S. is refined domestically, and the country produces a surplus, the fuel is still affected by global economic forces. Oil supplies coming through the Strait of Hormuz remain down as a result of the war with Iran, while Russia, a major diesel producer, has largely stopped making the fuel after Ukraine struck several refineries.
Biodiesel, which is produced from sources such as vegetables rather than petroleum, exists, but its share of the diesel market is far too small to influence overall pricing, Farrauto says.
“The bigger issue there is that vegetable oils are also a food source,” he says. “If you start using too much biodiesel, then what that means is that you’re not feeding people.”
If the Iran and Ukraine wars drag on, Ibendahl says, diesel prices are likely to stay above $6 a gallon “for quite a while.” Reports that the U.S. government may or may not be preparing to implement a 90-day export ban aside, that would be unlikely to have much effect on prices, Ibendahl adds, because global supplies remain tight.
“Companies like Walmart and the trucking companies and such are going to try to absorb that as much as they can, but eventually, they’re going to pass those costs on to consumers,” he says.

Flush with allies, Tigray's leaders face internal discord in new Ethiopia war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:51:52 UTC
00:51:52 KST

Flush with allies, Tigray's leaders face internal discord in new Ethiopia war
NAIROBI, Sept 24 - The last time the Tigray People's Liberation Front went to war with the Ethiopian federal government in 2020, it compensated for its isolation amid a sea of enemies with internal cohesion.
As the biggest political party in northern Ethiopia's Tigray region enters a new conflict with Addis Ababa following the outbreak of fighting on Wednesday, that dynamic has been turned on its head.
This time, the TPLF has no shortage of allies. On Sunday, it announced an alliance with six other Ethiopian armed groups aimed at overthrowing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government. Regional experts also widely believe it is receiving support from neighbouring Eritrea. Asmara denies this.
On the home front, however, the TPLF’s grip over Tigrayan society has weakened significantly. Since the end of the last war in 2022, it has faced protests over dire economic conditions, increasing competition from rival parties and defections of leading members.
Overnight, armed men detained four veteran military leaders who had expressed doubts about the new war, including the commander-in-chief of Tigrayan forces during the last war, Tadesse Werede, a member of Tadesse's family told Reuters.
"Previously, TPLF had very large support within the region, within the country, as well as from outside of the country, the diaspora. And they also managed to mobilize the local people to join TDF (Tigray Defense Forces)," said Jalale Getachew Birru, East Africa regional expert for the non-profit Armed Conflict Location & Event Data project.
"But this time... we don't see all these things."
Abiy's spokesperson declined to comment. A spokesperson for the TPLF did not respond to a request for comment.
'PATRIOTS' AND 'TRAITORS'
Wednesday's developments, in which Tigrayan forces seized control of the region's main airports and attacked federal forces in two neighbouring regions as part of what they called a defensive war in response to federal government aggression, shattered the four-year-old peace deal that ended one of the century's deadliest civil wars.
In that conflict, TPLF faced enemies on all fronts, including the federal government, Eritrea to the north and fighters from the Amhara region to the south and Afar to the east.
The former guerrilla movement, which had dominated Ethiopian national politics for more than three decades until Abiy was appointed prime minister in 2018, was able to harness widespread animosity across Tigray towards the federal government.
That allowed it to weather swift early advances by federal forces and contest a grinding, two-year war, although the federal government ultimately gained the upper hand on the battlefield before the African Union-mediated Pretoria Agreement was signed in November 2022.
After the war, political unity in Tigray frayed. Many Tigrayans criticised the TPLF-led authorities for failing to address continuing hunger and displacement. War veterans staged public protests, demanding compensation.
And TPLF hardliners clashed with more moderate party members, leading to high-profile defections and the creation of a rival armed force by former TDF generals.
In recent months, Tigrayan authorities have turned to forcibly recruiting young men into the defence forces, according to local and international human rights groups, opposition parties and multiple Tigray residents.
The TPLF has denied conducting forced recruitment.
As the new conflict got underway, the mood in Mekelle was very different from in 2020, three residents told Reuters.
"At the beginning of the previous war, despite political disagreements, there was a strong sense of collective mobilization around the defence of Tigray," said one of the residents.
"Today that social cohesion has been severely weakened. Tigray is politically polarized, and people are increasingly being divided into categories of 'patriots' and 'traitors.'"
OLD FOES UNITE AGAINST FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
Tigray's leaders have taken heart from their new alliance, which includes its former foe the Amhara Fano National Movement.
Since Wednesday, they have been fighting together in Amhara, where Fano, a coalition of armed groups, has been waging an insurgency since 2023, security sources told Reuters.
The federal government has accused Eritrea, which won its independence from Ethiopia in 1993, of providing financial support to the TPLF and other armed groups - claims that many Ethiopia experts say they believe.
Eritrea has repeatedly denied supporting armed groups in Ethiopia.
But the alliance's real-world effectiveness remains in doubt. Its members have diffuse – and sometimes directly contradictory – interests. The TPLF and Fano, for example, continue to stake competing claims to land Amhara captured from Tigray during the last war.
"The only issue joining them is their opposition to (Abiy's) Prosperity Party rule," said Kjetil Tronvoll, a professor of peace and conflict studies at Oslo New University College.
The federal government, for its part, has major tactical advantages over its opponents. In the last war, its widespread deployment of foreign-made drones helped turn the tide of the conflict after the TPLF advanced into Amhara.
Since then, it has bolstered its stocks of drones, including by starting domestic production, while the TPLF surrendered weaponry as part of the Pretoria Agreement.
It faces its own challenges, however. Prolonged fighting has strained morale and resources, while frequent drone strikes have not been enough to suppress the insurgency in Amhara, analysts say.
"The TPLF look weaker than previously as their forces are depleted since the end of the last war," said Magnus Taylor, a Horn of Africa analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank. "However, the alliances with other opposition groups, plus support from other regional states ... could offset this to some degree." REUTERS

00:51:19 KST

To his family, Lt. Col. Mahmoud Khairaldeen was a gentle man who always had time to listen, offer advice, and help those around him. To the Israeli public, he was known only as “Lt. Col. M.” Eight years after he was killed during a covert operation in the Gaza Strip, the man behind the initials is finally being remembered for more than the secrecy that surrounded his life and death: for the quiet devotion he showed to his family, his community and the country he served.
A center in Isfiya was opened in his memory to support young entrepreneurs in starting their own businesses, marking a major first for Israel’s Druze community. The center honors not only the sacrifices made by Khairaldeen, but also the extensive work he did to help young Druze gain admission to the military boarding school he once attended.
Khairaldeen had a long military career in the Paratroopers Brigade and later in Military Intelligence’s Special Operations Division. However, his commitment to his community extended well beyond his military service. In 2009, he established a nonprofit to support young members of his community, and partnered with Aharai!, a program designed to help teenagers build the resilience and skills needed to succeed in the military once they turn 18.
“He had a gentle smile that was truly defining, and even today that smile continues to guide our steps, even giving us strength, purpose, and comfort in everything we do. Mahmoud was not only an extraordinary officer and commander; he was deeply dedicated to education, leadership, and empowering youth,” Khairaldeen’s brother Mamduch told The Jerusalem Post. “We believe in quiet leadership, leading through actions, building bridges between communities, and ensuring that the next generation has every opportunity to realize their full potential. For us, honoring his memory means carrying forward what he lived by, investing in people, driving positive social change.”
Lieutenant M foundation facilitates community support
With the generous support of Prof. Meriam Adelson, the center opened an “accelerator” only weeks ago to help advance young Druze in the high-tech industry.
Mamduch explained that his family first opened the Lieutenant M Foundation to carry on Khairaldeen’s memory. They are now working on several projects, including a commemoration and heritage center with an educational space designed to share Khairaldeen’s story, values and devotion to Israel, as well as a community and parenting support center focused on empowering parents with the tools they need to nurture their children’s development.
Mamduch said the foundation was working in close partnership with the Association for the Advancement of the Druze Soldier, also known as the Druze Veterans Association, a nonprofit founded by Koftan Halabi to support and empower IDF Druze soldiers and veterans in Israel.
“Koftan Halabi chose to dedicate this inspiring venture to the memory of my brother Mahmoud. We, as his family, deeply appreciate this meaningful tribute and are proud to partner with the foundation and support this innovation,” Mamduch said. “It truly reflects everything Mahmoud stood for: empowering the next generation and opening doors for young talent by connecting peripheral communities directly to Israel’s high-tech ecosystem and providing young entrepreneurs with mentorship and professional tools. This innovation turns military leadership and resilience into real-world innovation.”

Knesset candidate Einat Wilf's day-after plan for Gaza, and why she believes everyone is dodging it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:50:47 UTC
00:50:47 KST

With elections bearing down and the whole country consumed by the race, diplomat and writer Einat Wilf sat down with Jacob Laznik to make a case that almost no one else in Israeli politics is making. Running third on the Reservists–New Economic Party list, an unaligned slate polling around four seats and openly determined to blow up the country's paralyzing bloc politics, Wilf argues that the real fight isn't over territory or coalitions at all, but over consciousness.
October 7, in her telling, was the day adversaries "emerged from physical and metaphorical tunnels to launch a global assault on Jewish life," and her central claim is that neither the government nor the opposition grasps the scale of that war of ideas, let alone how to fight it.
For a writer and former lawmaker who has spent two decades on exactly this terrain, the campaign is less about a seat than about forcing a conversation the political class keeps avoiding.
Moving the topic to the Gaza Strip
Where the interview gets passionate is Gaza. Wilf contends that Israel's leaders have left the single most consequential question of the postwar era: What actually happens the day after, which is almost entirely undiscussed. She then lays out a strikingly concrete alternative: Reinterpreting the Board of Peace's twenty-point framework so that "Gaza will not be a threat" means ideological disarmament rather than a few weapons stashed in a shed, and splitting the Strip into a "Gaza of war" and a "Gaza of peace" where residents must formally renounce refugee status and the right of return before any reconstruction money flows.
It's a vision that ranges from the granular, which includes cutting UNRWA cards, new documents, a new flag, to the sweeping idea of rebuilding not just a place but a people's self-understanding. Around it she threads the themes her readers will recognize: the "bigotry of low expectations," "Westsplaining," the "Zionism Is" project, and the "mass psychosis" she says drives anti-Israel activism from the Oxford Union floor to the street. Laznik, in turn, questions the logistics, the other players at the table like Qatar and Turkey, the risk that reopening a signed agreement reads as reneging, and the uncomfortable reality that Hamas keeps boasting it would do it all again.
Whether you come away thinking Wilf's plan is visionary or unworkable, you'll want to hear how she answers when pressed. Watch the full interview to see where it holds up and where it strains.
This is part one of The Jerusalem Post's interview with Wilf. Stay tuned for part two.

Washington attempts dealmaking, Moscow sticks with warmaking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:50:43 UTC
00:50:43 KST

Washington attempts dealmaking, Moscow sticks with warmaking
Russian President Vladimir Putin in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on Sept. 1, 2026. (Peter Kovalev / Pool / AFP via Getty Images)
Andrew Chakhoyan
Academic director at the University of Amsterdam
"I can't die now. I still need to do the Russia sanctions," Lindsey Graham joked hours before his passing.
Nine weeks later, the bill bearing his name became law with the U.S. president's signature. Reflecting the wishes of the American people, Congress placed a very large stick in the hands of the executive: tariffs of up to 100% on the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas.
It will matter only if Trump swings it.
The Senate passed the measure 86-11 and the House 262-159, a rare show of bipartisan resolve and the most significant Ukraine legislation since Trump returned to the White House.
Long overdue, the law also exposes a dissonance at the heart of American policy. Russia under Putin has been invading its neighbors for nearly two decades, as aggression went unpunished and victims left to fend for themselves. The war continues because of Moscow's belligerent revanchism, not because, in Donald Trump's words, "two people (Putin and Zelensky) that hate each other."
Russia invaded Georgia in 2008 and Ukraine in 2014, five years before Volodymyr Zelensky was elected president. By July 2021, Putin laid out his genocidal intentions in a 5,000-word essay, and seven months later came the full-scale invasion.
It is onto this record that the diplomatic track spearheaded by Steve Witkoff has now been layered. Lamentably, it accommodates the very pattern of Russian aggression that Congress is finally trying to arrest.
"Aren't you disgusted to be sitting at the same table with an international war criminal, the butcher of the Ukrainian people?" a journalist, Dmytro Gordon, asked Trump's envoys in Kyiv, where Witkoff and Kushner arrived after visiting with Putin in Moscow.
A question and an accusation packaged as one. But what did the Ukrainians expect? How could the White House stay engaged in high-stakes diplomacy without talking to Putin? How can American negotiators keep a channel open without protocol, decorum, and occasional displays of respect?
Defensible on the surface, this logic fails disastrously when assessed through a consequentialist lens. Pursuing a deal, Washington's emissaries have produced results diametrically opposite to their stated aims.
Soon after taking office, the Trump Administration put an unconditional ceasefire on the table.
Ukraine accepted within 24 hours in March 2025. Moscow rejected it then and every day since. The aggressor state has answered every diplomatic overture with more wanton violence. It is now raining missiles and killer drones on food storage facilities and passenger trains, committing ever more brazen war crimes in plain sight.
Today, Russia is helping Iran develop ramjet-powered supersonic cruise missiles to threaten U.S. aircraft carriers and penetrate the defenses of its allied military bases in the region. Make no mistake, these weapons are designed to target and kill Americans.
Jared Kushner has a theory of peace. "War is a negative sum, and everyone loses from it," he told Victor Pinchuk at the YES conference in Kyiv. "Economics, business, and peace are very positive-sum." The goal, he explained, is to find "the right formula that works for everyone."
This theory, too, falls apart on contact with Russian drone operators hunting Ukrainian civilians for sport, in what UN monitors have termed a "human safari."
Kushner and Witkoff are lifelong dealmakers, and, when all you have is a hammer, every problem looks like a nail. So they reach for the framework they know: build trust, find overlap, make the pie bigger, strike a deal. Kushner says the hardest issue is territory.
His solution? Negotiation and compromise, of course.
Russia's war is not a bargaining problem. Dealmaking does more than miss the point. It incentivizes and rewards predation.
What are Russians fighting for? According to British intelligence, Russia suffered 1.5 million casualties, half a million dead. The vast majority of the losses were incurred after January 2023 in exchange for 2% of Ukraine's territory.
Putin says he wants all of Donbas. Have American envoys asked why? The kinetic battlefield is in Ukraine, yet Moscow has long told its people that they are at war with NATO and that NATO is a fig leaf for American power projection.
Subverting Western institutions, fracturing the most successful military alliance in history, and making democracies abandon their principles and strategic interests serve a purpose for the Kremlin, which is much closer to home.
The primary aim of Moscow's war on Ukraine is, paradoxically, not in Ukraine. It is the survival of the "Russian Federation" itself, and the Kremlin's grip on the internal colonies that make it up. To an outsider, this may seem strange.
The USSR collapsed in 1991, Moscow shed 14 republics, and Russia, which was left, looked rock-solid.
From Moscow's vantage point, this is naivete wrapped in ignorance.
Anyone who sits on the Russian throne eventually grasps that this continent-sized Frankenstein state, spanning eleven time zones, is forever exposed to centrifugal forces pulling it apart. Moscow needs an enemy, a grievance, and a story of national greatness strong enough to justify its right to pillage Tatarstan's oil, Yamalo-Nenets's gas, and Yakutia's diamonds.
There is no conflict, no misunderstanding, no prospect of a win-win, when it comes to Russia's war of choice. None. It persists because Russia keeps waging it.
America can't resolve Moscow's need to sustain an extractive system of rule from Kaliningrad to Kamchatka. This is why the framework of a "deal" with the Kremlin is an error of first principles.
Reagan's doctrine of strength and moral clarity worked on Moscow. Attempts to sacrifice Ukraine on the altar of peace-through-weakness have had the opposite effect, costing America its reputation as a trustworthy, serious world power and Ukraine its bravest sons and daughters.
This compulsive dealmaking won't put an end to Russian warmaking.
To a Moscow-centered predatory empire, accommodation is encouragement.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

New nuke sub leaves yard and heads to Scotland for trials
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:48:18 BST
00:48:18 KST

Cumbria Police closed Michaelson Road Bridge in Barrow-in-Furness on Thursday morning, working in collaboration with BAE Systems, and told residents a further message would be published once the crossing reopened.
The force confirmed the closure at 9am and said the bridge would remain shut while the operation was carried out. An updated statement issued later said: “Michaelson Road Bridge has now reopened. Thank you for your patience.” The closure ran until around 11.40am.
The UK Defence Journal understands that the operation covered the departure of a submarine from the yard, and that the boat involved was HMS Agamemnon, the sixth of the Astute class, with people gathering along the dockside to watch her leave.
Agamemnon was commissioned into the Royal Navy on 22 September last year at a ceremony in Devonshire Dock Hall attended by the King. Around 500 guests were present, and on the same day the King conferred Royal Port status on the town while steel was cut for HMS King George VI, the fourth and final Dreadnought-class submarine.
She completed a three-day trim dive shortly after commissioning, submerging to around 15 metres to confirm the integrity of the pressure hull and to establish her centre of gravity, with crew and engineers moving 16 tonnes of lead weights around the boat to simulate different loading conditions.
Steel was cut for Agamemnon in July 2013 and she was launched in October 2024, making her construction the longest of any nuclear submarine built for the Royal Navy, a delay attributed variously to the pandemic, the diversion of resources to begin the Dreadnought programme and the complexity of the Astute design.
Michaelson Road Bridge carries traffic across the entrance to Devonshire Dock, and closures of this kind are a familiar feature of submarine movements at the yard, with the bridge having to be swung clear before a boat of that size can pass out into Walney Channel.
At 7,400 tonnes and 97 metres, the Astute class carries Spearfish heavyweight torpedoes and Tomahawk Block IV land attack missiles, and the boats protect the deterrent submarines and the carrier strike group while also conducting surveillance and intelligence work. Seven were ordered, with the final submarine still under construction in the same hall.
Barrow remains the only facility in the United Kingdom with the infrastructure, site licence and resources to design and build British nuclear submarines, and the Defence Nuclear Enterprise annual update to Parliament published this month recorded that the workforce there has grown by more than 1,800 under the current government.
The yard is also preparing for the programmes that follow, with steel due to be cut on the first British SSN-AUKUS submarine in 2027 and the concept design completed earlier this year for SMITE2, a new submarine propulsion testing facility at the site.

Russian Rental Rush Hits Georgia, Serbia, Armenia—Kazakhstan’s Expected Wave Never Comes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:47:49 UTC
00:47:49 KST

- Category
- World
Russian Rental Rush Hits Georgia, Serbia, Armenia—Kazakhstan’s Expected Wave Never Comes
Russian demand for rental housing rose sharply in Georgia, Serbia, and Armenia in late summer 2026, according to real estate agents interviewed by Meduza, while agents in Kazakhstan reported no comparable increase.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Meduza reported the trend on September 24 after speaking with real estate agents in Tbilisi, Yerevan, Belgrade, Novi Sad, and Almaty. The outlet changed the agents’ names at their request.
Their accounts reflect individual market experience rather than comprehensive official arrival statistics.
According to Meduza, rumors of a possible new mobilization have circulated in Russia since the summer of 2026. Vladimir Putin has dismissed the reports as “nonsense” and said there is currently no need for another draft.
Russia’s two largest emigration waves since the full-scale invasion came in 2022, first in February and March and again after Putin announced a partial mobilization in September.
Georgia
Anna, a Russian realtor who has worked in Tbilisi for nine years, told Meduza that she has received up to five inquiries an hour since late July.
She said many new clients are younger than 30, arrive without firm plans, and have rental budgets of around $500.
Rents have so far increased by about $50–$100, Anna told the outlet. Apartments in major residential districts that could be rented for about $550 earlier this year are now being offered for $600–$700.
She expects some properties currently listed at $600–$700 to reach $900–$1,100 within several months if arrivals and demand continue to grow.
Irina, another Russian realtor working in Tbilisi, told Meduza that good listings now remain available for only a day or two.
Apartments that rented for $600–$700 a month a year ago are now going for $800–$900 a month, she said.
However, Irina expects demand to ease within three to four months.
She told Meduza that many clients plan to remain outside Russia for only two or three months before either returning or moving elsewhere in Europe.
Georgia’s Interior Ministry recorded about 1.5 million entries by Russian citizens during the first year of the full-scale war, Meduza reported.
Georgia’s national statistics service classified about 62,300 Russians as migrants, while more than 37,700 Russian citizens were living in the country in 2026.
Serbia
Meduza reported a similar rise in rental demand in Serbia.
Andrei, a Russian realtor working in Novi Sad, said he now receives several requests for long-term rental viewings each day, compared with periods earlier this year when he sometimes went a week without inquiries.
According to Andrei, individual apartments now attract lines of Russian applicants, with some prospective tenants offering above the asking price.
He linked the increase to rumors of a possible mobilization after Russia’s State Duma elections and to recurring internet disruptions in Russia.
Prices in Novi Sad have not risen significantly so far, Andrei told Meduza. Monthly rents there currently range from roughly $455 to $795, below the $909–$1,136 levels seen during the 2022 influx.
The situation in Belgrade is more pronounced. Petr, a realtor in the Serbian capital, told Meduza that “a lot of Russians” have been arriving since the second half of August and that he had not seen comparable demand since 2022.
Petr said rental prices in Belgrade have risen by about 20–30% since late July, with apartments in the city center now costing roughly $682–$1,136 per month.
He also said many landlords refuse on principle to rent to foreigners, partly out of concern that local students could struggle to find housing amid the increased demand.
Serbia’s Interior Ministry registered more than 140,000 Russian citizens between February 24 and November 2, 2022, according to data cited by Meduza.
Nearly 70,000 Russians obtained Serbian residence permits between 2022 and 2025.
Armenia
In Yerevan, Russian realtor Alexander told Meduza that demand began increasing in the second half of July, with August and September proving particularly active.
According to Alexander, rents in Yerevan have risen by roughly 30–50% since the beginning of the year.
A good two-room apartment in the city center now costs around $1,000 per month, compared with approximately $700 in the spring.
Kristina, another Yerevan realtor interviewed by Meduza, said inquiries for long-term rentals are now roughly twice the level seen during winter and spring.
Many prospective tenants contact her while they are still in Russia and preparing to relocate.
She also described a shift in the profile of arrivals.
Unlike the predominantly remote workers who relocated in 2022 with established jobs and budgets, more recent arrivals include people hoping to find work in the service sector, with some traveling using credit cards to cover their initial expenses, Meduza reported.
Armenia’s Migration Service reported in August 2024 that about 40,000 Russian citizens held legal residence rights or valid residence permits in the country.
Yerevan realtors interviewed by Meduza expect rents to peak in October, although they cautioned that longer-term price forecasts remain uncertain.
Kazakhstan
Kazakhstan has so far seen no comparable rental surge, according to Meduza’s interviews with realtors in Almaty.
The country recorded about 406,000 Russian entries in September 2022, but later tightened migration and residence rules.
Tamara, an Almaty realtor, told Meduza that Russian arrivals and departures currently appear largely normal, with no repeat of the demand seen four years ago.
Another Almaty agent, Dmitry, said local realtors had expected more Russians to arrive amid reports of fuel shortages and rumors of mobilization, but the anticipated increase did not materialize.
Russians once accounted for about 90% of his clients, he said, but now make up no more than roughly 10%.
Almaty housing prices have nevertheless increased by approximately 10–20% in recent months.
Dmitry attributed the rise to the start of the academic year and an influx of students, rather than to Russian arrivals, Meduza reported.
The reported demand follows a run of earlier warning signs.
In mid-July, searches for apartments in Yerevan reached 5,200 in a single week, exceeding the level recorded in the first week of the full-scale war in 2022, and rents in the Armenian capital had climbed by around 30% in three months.
By late August, more than 113,000 Russians had crossed into Georgia through the Verkhny Lars checkpoint in a single week, including over 20,000 on August 20 alone.

Ukrainians in UK fear cut to funds for Homes for Ukraine hosts could make them homeless
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:47:39 UTC
00:47:39 KST

Ukrainian refugees in the UK fear they could be left homeless after the government quietly axed 70% of funding for hosts of the Homes for Ukraine scheme, reducing monthly “thank you” payments to them from £350 to £100.
The scheme was launched after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and has provided support for 181,000 of the 234,000 Ukrainians who have since sought sanctuary in the UK.
Now the government has said it will cut the hosting payments and reduce contributions to local authorities, which are paid a sum for each arrival to meet the costs associated with delivering the programme.
A written statement to parliament from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) on 15 September said funding would be reduced from £5,900 to £3,300. The changes will come into effect from 1 January 2027.
Tetiana, a 73-year-old Ukrainian refugee who has been hosted for two years and four months, said she was devastated to read the government’s letter circulated to hosts in the last few days informing them of the changes.
She said: “I feel that this financial change could impact on my host’s ability to host me. If the hosting comes to an end, I don’t know where I will go and how I can start again. I can’t work because of my age and because I have mobility problems.
“I fled from Kharkiv, which is close to the Russia frontline, so I can’t go back to Ukraine. I don’t know what I will do. I’m at a loss about what my options will be. This change has created a lot of uncertainty for me. I don’t know how I would be able to pay rent if hosting finishes for me.”
Nataliya Rumyantseva is hosting her mother, the first Ukrainian to arrive in the UK after the war started. She said the changes were likely to have a significant impact. “When refugees arrive here from Ukraine, they are shellshocked and need time to adapt and learn the language. If hosting changes to become a more commercial rental arrangement, I think that’s cruel.”
One host who lives in Greenwich said he did not know if he would be able to continue hosting because of the drop in payments. “I’ve been a sponsor since May 2022. I was dismayed to learn that thank you payments are reducing to just £100,” he said. “I lost my job within months of becoming a sponsor and these payments have become an absolute lifeline even though I did not volunteer for this scheme for the money. I genuinely worry about the consequences of this change for Ukrainians in the UK.”
One option the government proposes is that hosts can switch to landlord status and charge refugees rent.
A host who lives in Cardiff and is hosting a Ukrainian who has enrolled on a course of study said: “The situation feels like a cheap shot from the government. We, in good faith, opened our home to someone in need. That person, in good faith, planned for a life in the UK. And the government, in what seems like very bad faith, saw an easy way to claw money back from people who aren’t in a position to stop them.”
The government says it has so far provided more than £1.81bn for the scheme.
An MHCLG spokesperson said: “The UK’s commitment to supporting Ukrainians is unwavering and the Homes for Ukraine scheme remains open. As the scheme has evolved from an initial emergency response into a more established programme, these changes are designed to secure the scheme’s long-term future while maintaining support for sponsors, guests and councils.”

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
