NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Japan ended China's long dominance of the men's table tennis team event at the 2026 Asian Games on Thursday, winning a dramatic final 3-2 to claim its first title in 60 years, while China retained the women's crown with a 3-0 victory over Japan.
China had won the men's team title at eight consecutive Asian Games, but Japan ended that run after Sora Matsushima defeated Wen Ruibo 3-1 in the deciding match.
China had taken an early lead through world No. 1 Wang Chuqin, who recovered from two games down against Matsushima to win 3-2. Matsushima took the opening two games 11-5, 11-8 before Wang won the next three by identical 11-9 scores.
Tomokazu Harimoto responded by beating 19-year-old Wen 3-1, before Lin Shidong defeated Shunsuke Togami by the same score to put China 2-1 ahead.
Harimoto then faced Wang in the fourth match and gave the Chinese player no opportunity for another comeback, winning 11-7, 11-4, 11-9 to force a deciding match.
Matsushima completed Japan's victory by beating Wen 3-1, roaring in celebration after sealing his country's first men's team title at the Asian Games since 1966.
China coach Wang Hao had reshuffled his lineup for the final, moving Wen into the second singles position.
"The result of the event was not what we had hoped for, and there are certainly things I could have done better personally," Wang said. "But the tournament is not over yet. I hope everyone, myself included, can quickly regroup, put this result behind us and focus on the competitions ahead."
Harimoto said Japan had been prepared for different possible Chinese lineups.
"We didn't know whether Wen or Lin would play twice, but we felt it didn't really matter to us," he said. "Our preparation was to be ready for whoever we faced and focus on doing our own job well."
South Korea and Chinese Taipei shared the bronze medal.
In the women's final, China beat Japan 3-0 to claim its sixth consecutive Asian Games team title.
Sun Yingsha gave China the lead with a 3-1 victory over Hina Hayata, before world No. 1 Wang Manyu survived a stern challenge from Miwa Harimoto.
Their match went to a deciding game, where Wang held her nerve to win 12-10 and complete a 3-2 victory.
Kuai Man then defeated Mima Ito 3-0 to complete China's sweep.
"Our unity is also very strong. Everyone is working toward the same goal of winning," Wang said. "That invisible support gave us the confidence to believe we could win when we found ourselves in difficult situations."
DPR Korea and South Korea shared the women's team bronze medal.
In the women's doubles action, China's Kuai and Wang defeated Kazakhstan's Angelina Romanovskaya and Albina Zhaxylykova 3-0 to reach the last 16, while compatriots Fan Shuhan and Chen Yi beat DPR Korea's Kim Kum Yong and Cha Su Yong 3-1.
Japan's Harimoto and Hayata also advanced with a 3-0 victory over Thailand's Kulapassr Vijitviriyagul and Phatsaraphon Wonglakhon. ■

A welcoming ceremony is held at Vietnam's Can Tho Port for the first foreign trade vessel to sail through China's Pinglu Canal, Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Duong Huy/Xinhua)
CAN THO, Vietnam, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- A welcoming ceremony was held at Vietnam's Can Tho Port on Thursday for the first foreign trade vessel to sail through China's Pinglu Canal.
The container vessel departed from Nanning Port in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region on Sept. 16, sailed through the Pinglu Canal and arrived at Can Tho Port on Wednesday.
It carried 252 twenty-foot equivalent units of cargo, including wood panels, sodium sulfate and auto parts, mainly from western China.
Hu Huaping, chairman of Beibu Gulf Port Group, said the group will work with Can Tho Port and other partners to develop two-way cargo flows, improve services and enhance logistics connectivity.
The 134.2-km canal, stretching from Hengzhou in Guangxi to the Beibu Gulf, opened on Sept. 16. It is the closest maritime outlet for much of southwest China.
Designed for vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the canal shortens the inland waterway journey for goods from southwest China to the sea by more than 560 km compared with traditional routes through ports in Guangdong Province. ■

Unique pyramid-shaped Roman-era tomb discovered in SW Egypt
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
23:37:56 CST
00:37:56 KST

CAIRO, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- An Egyptian archaeological mission discovered a unique pyramid-shaped tomb dating to the Roman period (30 BC-395 AD) in the southwestern province of New Valley, the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities said Thursday.
In a statement, the ministry said the tomb, discovered at the Bir al-Shaghala archaeological site in Dakhla Oasis, was built of mudbrick and used to bury a man and his wife.
The tomb features distinctive architecture and rare funerary inscriptions that shed light on the oasis' burial practices and religious and cultural life during the Roman period, the statement said.
Among the finds were a stone funerary stele bearing a 19-line Greek-language lament, an offering table, a sandstone purification basin, pottery vessels and a bronze coin depicting Roman Emperor Constantine.
The tomb is accessed by a 14-step staircase leading to a sandstone entrance decorated with recessed hieroglyphic inscriptions and funerary spells. Its lintel bears a rare scene depicting the seventh hour of the "Amduat," a major ancient Egyptian funerary text that serves as a twelve-hour map of the underworld recounting the sun god Ra's nightly journey.
The entrance leads to a mudbrick vaulted hall and two burial chambers beneath the pyramid-shaped superstructure.
The funerary stele commemorates a man who may have served as a judge, according to the statement. ■

China Focus: Tech giant Tencent launches payment app for inbound visitors as "China Travel" surges
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
23:37:54 CST
00:37:54 KST

SHENZHEN, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- China's tech giant Tencent on Thursday launched TenPayGo, a payment app for overseas users traveling to China. This new platform is designed to make payments more convenient for inbound visitors as the country sees a growing number of international travelers.
The app supports bank cards issued overseas by seven major international card organizations including Visa and Mastercard, as well as Apple Pay and overseas e-wallets such as Starryblu, Tencent said.
After linking a payment method, users can scan and pay directly through TenPayGo, according to Tencent. The company unveiled the app at an international payment services launch event in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province.
TenPayGo will also enable overseas visitors to activate a ride code for Shenzhen's buses and metro, with no phone number or transit card required.
In addition, TenPayGo will further expand its in-app services, pledging to connect payment with consumption scenarios, such as departure tax refunds and AI-powered translation of menus, the Shenzhen-based company added.
Dong Ximiao, chief economist at Merchants Union Consumer Finance Company Limited, noted that TenPayGo allows inbound visitors to travel across China with a single smartphone, which is set to further improve their travel experience.
The launch of TenPayGo came after Tencent announced in May a landmark integration of its extensive payment network with PayPal, enabling U.S. visitors to pay like locals in China via QR codes. The partnership connects Tencent's cross-border payments platform TenPay Global with PayPal World, a global platform connecting the world's largest payment systems and digital wallets.
Tencent's WeChat, which serves as a multifunctional app beyond social media and messaging, offers digital payment services known as Weixin Pay in the Chinese mainland.
The launch of TenPayGo by Weixin Pay comes amid a surge in foreign visitor spending. Data from Weixin Pay showed that in the first eight months of this year, the value and number of overseas e-wallet transactions in China increased by 80.6 percent and 81.8 percent year on year, respectively.
The payment growth came as "China Travel" surged, driven by the country's measures to facilitate inbound tourism, including the expansion of visa-free policies and improved departure tax refunds.
Official data showed that foreign nationals made nearly 61.29 million border crossings in the January-August period, up 19.5 percent from a year earlier. Visa-free entries accounted for 23.72 million of the total, up 26.8 percent from a year earlier.
To better cater to the increasing payment demand, Tencent said it will carry out cooperation with domestic online payment-clearing house NetsUnion and work to connect more overseas e-wallets with its payment network, in a bid to enable more overseas users to scan to pay when traveling in China. ■

ADDIS ABABA, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- The African Union (AU) has called for utmost restraint and immediate de-escalation amid rising security tensions in northern Ethiopia.
In a press statement issued late Wednesday, the 55-member continental organization said AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf expressed "deep concern" over renewed tensions and military escalation in northern Ethiopia.
The AU highlighted the seizure and occupation of airports in the East African country's Tigray regional state, as well as the detention of federal personnel by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and the ensuing disruption of civilian air services.
The chairperson also voiced "grave concern" over reports of escalating hostilities in parts of Tigray and Afar regions, along with recent developments involving the formation of new political and military alliance that risks further destabilizing the situation and reversing the gains made to silence the guns since 2020, the statement read.
Youssouf reaffirmed that the Agreement for Lasting Peace through a Permanent Cessation of Hostilities, signed in Pretoria in November 2022 between the Ethiopian government and the TPLF under the auspices of the AU, remains "the cornerstone of sustainable peace, stability and reconciliation in Ethiopia."
He said the seizure and occupation of civilian airports in Mekelle, Axum, and Shire by Tigray forces is inconsistent with the commitments and obligations under the above agreement and risks eroding hard-won gains achieved in the pursuit of lasting peace and stability.
The AU Commission chief called for "utmost restraint and immediate cessation of all actions that could further escalate tensions," while urging the immediate resumption of direct talks within the framework of the Pretoria agreement.
He also called upon all neighboring countries of Ethiopia to refrain from actions that could contribute to further escalation and to actively support de-escalation, dialogue, and confidence-building.
The latest developments come amid heightened tensions in Ethiopia's northernmost Tigray region, following Sunday's announcement of a new alliance formed by seven Ethiopian opposition and armed groups, according to local media.
Amid rising security concerns, the national flag carrier Ethiopian Airlines temporarily suspended flights to Mekelle, Axum, and Shire, effective Wednesday, citing the "current situation" in the region.
Also on Wednesday, Getachew Reda, minister advisor to the Ethiopian Prime Minister on East African Affairs, said TPLF forces launched "an all-out offensive" against government positions in Afar and Amhara regions, adding that TPLF forces have taken over previously federally-controlled airports in Tigray.
Tigray was at the epicenter of a two-year conflict between Ethiopian federal forces and TPLF-loyal troops from November 2020 to November 2022, which left millions in urgent need of humanitarian assistance, before the two parties signed the landmark Pretoria peace accord. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Abuduaini Tuergong won the men's discus title at the Asian Games on Thursday, ending a 24-year wait for China to reclaim the gold medal in the event.
Abuduaini threw 64.26 meters on his third attempt to take the title, while his compatriot Wu Nanjun finished second with 61.58m.
The 29-year-old, a two-time Asian championships winner who broke the Chinese national record several times last year, was visibly emotional after the victory.
"It's been more than 20 years since China last won the title. Now we've brought it back," Abuduaini said. "I'll call my family and friends when I get back to my hotel, and then have a good sleep."
Abuduaini took bronze at the Hangzhou Asian Games three years ago. He said gaining more than 20 kilograms since then had helped improve his performance.
"I weighed around 113 to 114 kilograms in 2023, and now I'm 140 kilograms," he said. "I made that sacrifice to improve my performance. Adding more than 20 kilograms has made me more stable in all aspects."
Bahrain's Winfred Yavi, the Olympic and world champion in the women's 3,000-meter steeplechase, won the women's 10,000 meters in 32 minutes and 39.18 seconds for her first international major title over the distance.
The race was Yavi's first competitive 10,000 meters.
"It feels so special because it's my first 10k at the Asian Games and I did it for the first time in my life in a competition," Yavi said. "It felt so good, entering in such an event and getting a gold medal."
Yavi said she would gradually shift her focus from the steeplechase to the 5,000 and 10,000 meters.
Uzbekistan's Sharifa Davronova won the women's triple jump with a personal-best 14.35 meters, with China's Huang Yingying taking silver and compatriot Li Yi bronze.

"I am extremely happy now because I never expected to reach this result," the 20-year-old said. "My initial goal was around 10 seconds."
It was Boonson's second sub-10-second run of the season. He set his personal best of 9.94 seconds last year.

In the women's 100 meters, 17-year-old Chinese sprinter Chen Yujie won the first heat in 11.41 seconds to post the fastest time in the preliminaries.
Chen said she was not satisfied with the result after having targeted 11.40 seconds or faster before the race.
"Before the race, I had a conversation with the coach. I estimated that I would aim for a time of 11.40 seconds or less," she said.
Chen set an Asian junior record of 11.08 seconds at a domestic championship in August, also the fastest women's 100-meter time in Asia this season.
Defending champion Ge Manqi, another member of China's team, suffered leg cramps during the fourth heat and finished in 12.13 seconds, failing to advance. ■

Belarus president Lukashenko frees 15 more prisoners in wake of US talks
Sept 24 - Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko pardoned 15 prisoners in a decree on Thursday that follows talks last week with an envoy for US President Donald Trump.
Trump's envoy John Coale has been negotiating with Lukashenko for more than a year, so far obtaining the release of hundreds of prisoners including opposition figures, activists, journalists and lawyers, in return for removing some US sanctions.
Banned human rights group Viasna says 883 political prisoners remain in Belarus, convicted on charges such as extremist activity, incitement to hatred or insulting the president.
Lukashenko, a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin, has ruled Belarus since 1994. He denies there are any political prisoners in the former Soviet state, but has engaged with the Trump administration in order to get sanctions relief and ease his international isolation.
Lukashenko's office said the 15 newly pardoned people included 10 women, and 13 of them had "committed crimes of an extremist nature". It said the pardons were granted after they asked for clemency and expressed remorse.
The releases represented further gradual progress towards Coale's stated goal of freeing all the remaining prisoners this year.
During his visit last week, he won the release of 25 people including prominent journalists and activists — far fewer than the 250 who were freed during his previous trip in March.
Analysts say Lukashenko is taking a tougher line in the talks, frustrated that the removal of some US sanctions — especially on potash, a key export earner for Belarus — has not been matched by the European Union.
Lukashenko has also demanded the release of $43 million to $44 million of frozen Belarusian assets that he says are "stuck" in Citibank, and Coale promised last week to address this. Citi has declined to comment. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

The Story of Bhutan’s UN Membership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:36:00 UTC
00:36:00 KST

Aside from Bangladesh, the youngest nation of South Asia born in December 1971, Bhutan is the second-to-last state from the region to gain membership in the United Nations. India is a founding member of the U.N., followed by Afghanistan (1946), Pakistan (1947), Nepal and Sri Lanka (1955), and Maldives (1965). Bhutan finally joined on September 21, 1971.
Bhutan’s King Jigme Dorji Wangchuk had formally applied for U.N. membership on December 10, 1970, mainly seeking the sovereign equality the global body offers to small nations like Bhutan. In a letter addressed to then-U.N. Secretary-General U Thant, the king wrote, “The Government and people of Bhutan area acutely aware of the proven value of the United Nations Organization to small and developing nations off the world and consequently attach great importance to membership.”
Bhutan’s Permanent Mission to the U.N. holds the same attitude today. Its website says: “The United Nations, with its universal scope and global membership and the spirit of multilateralism that the United Nations fosters, forms an integral part of Bhutan’s foreign policy.”
Two months after Bhutan’s formal application to the U.N., on February 10, 1971, the U.N. Security Council unanimously voted to favorably recommend Bhutan’s membership at that year’s 26th General Assembly. Bhutan was thus formally recognized as a U.N. member state on September 21, 1971.
Bhutan’s accession to the United Nations in 1971 was a great diplomatic achievement for a small state in South Asia. In the same decade, forget joining the U.N., the Kingdom of Sikkim had lost its very nationhood and merged into India in 1975. In 1971, the same year that Bhutan became a U.N. member state, Pakistan lost the “East Pakistan” part of its nation, which became the independent state of Bangladesh. Amid the making and breakings of nationhood in South Asia in this tumultuous decade, it was a diplomatic victory for a tiny Himalayan nation like Bhutan to become a part of the U.N. body.
Despite the tensions in the region, Bhutan’s entry into the world body wasn’t a part of controversy like nearby Nepal’s. Nepal applied for membership in 1949, but its ambition was delayed for six years mainly owing to the Soviet Union’s veto. Moscow’s obstruction, however, wasn’t really about Nepal. The USSR was seeking a broader diplomatic deal to win approval for five new U.N. member states that were in the Soviet camp: Hungary, Albania, Romania, Bulgaria, and Mongolia.
This was not the case for Bhutan. In the February 10, 1971 meeting of the Security Council, Bhutan’s ally India spoke in favor of its membership application. To do so, India requested permission to participate in the UNSC discussion, as New Delhi was not a member at the time. India’s U.N. representative, Samar Sen, said that the Security Council’s “decision to support Bhutan’s candidature… was but a final manifestation of Bhutan’s independent stature and nationhood.” Sen also noted that India “had, at Bhutan’s request, given it as much help as possible regarding the application for United Nations membership.”
In the same meeting of the UNSC, China’s U.N. Representative Liu Chieh said he “had been happy to vote for the admission of Bhutan.” In Liu’s words, “Bhutan had had a long history of independence… although in foreign relations, it had agreed to be guided by India.” However, China here means the Republic of China (or Taiwan), not the People’s Republic of China. The PRC government would gain China’s seat in the U.N. in October 1971 – one month after Bhutan entered the United Nations. That means Bhutan has been a U.N. member longer than the PRC.
Pakistan, like India, requested and was granted the right to participate in the UNSC session. Its diplomat, Agha Shahi, also voiced his support for Bhutan’s membership and welcomed the country to the “mainstream of international life.” He added that “Bhutan, although smaller than the other countries of the region, played a valuable role and would, he was sure, maintain harmonious relations with its neighbors in the interest of peace and stability.”
Japan, which held a non-permanent seat on the UNSC at the time, also approved Bhutan’s U.N. accession, saying that “Bhutan and Japan were closely connected by ties of the Eastern Asian civilization,” especially Mahayam Buddhism.
Other members of the UNSC in 1971 to support Bhutan’s membership included Argentina, Belgium, Burundi, France, Italy, Nicaragua, Poland, Sierra Leone, Somalia, the Soviet Union, and the United Kingdom. The session was chaired by the U.S. representative, Charles Yost, who concluded the session by pointing out that Bhutan “had long prided itself on its cultural traditions and its strong sense of national identity.”
Bhutan thus became the 128th member of the United Nations, with support from rivals like the U.S. and the Soviet Union, as well as India and Pakistan. Today, the number of U.N. member states has jumped to 193.
Bhutan’s major achievements in the U.N. include its graduation from Least Developed Country status in 2023 and its emphasis on “gross national happiness.” Bhutan also has a reputation as a voice for green growth, thanks to its global image as a “carbon negative” nation.
Beyond the U.N., Bhutan’s global diplomatic engagements remain limited. Interestingly, Bhutan does not have formal diplomatic relations with any of the five permanent U.N. Security Council members: China, France, Russia, the U.K., and the U.S. Bhutan does maintain a Permanent Mission to the U.N. in New York, where its U.N. representative also serves as Bhutan’s ambassador to Canada and Brazil.
Meanwhile, only three countries operate embassies in Bhutan: India, Bangladesh and Kuwait. Bhutan doesn’t host an embassy of Australia, the nation where reportedly 1.5 percent Bhutanese have migrated.
In the second week of June 2026, I was in Thimphu on my first tour to the fellow Himalayan nation. I talked to some tourism entrepreneurs, political figures, and ordinary citizens I met there and found that none of them were concerned about the few embassies in the Buddhist kingdom of around 800,000 people.
“In the age of digital visa and hyperconnectivity, we don’t need physical embassies of all important nations,” said a hotelier based in Paro, Bhutan’s third largest city which hosts the international airport. He added, “Even the U.S. and China don’t have embassies in all United Nations member nations.”

PARIS — Bloquer les prix de l’énergie ne pose pas de risque de pénurie de carburants en France, a affirmé Jean-Luc Mélenchon lors d’un entretien à POLITICO.
“Vous pensez vraiment qu’une compagnie comme Total et les autres vont dire : je renonce au marché intérieur que représente la France ?”, a argumenté le candidat de La France insoumise à l’élection présidentielle, interrogé lors du sommet POLITICO Playbook Paris Live.
Le blocage des prix de l’énergie est une mesure phare et ancienne du programme de La France insoumise. Face à l’envolée des prix des carburants, depuis le début de la guerre au Moyen-Orient, Jean-Luc Mélenchon prône un plafonnement à 1,70 euros le litre.
Advertisement
Pour ses détracteurs, cette mesure entraînerait une pénurie, notamment parce que la France importe environ la moitié de sa consommation de diesel.
“Une bêtise”, selon Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Selon lui, les entreprises pétrolières n’auront d’autres choix que de baisser le prix de leurs produits raffinés, “parce que la Chine n’en a pas besoin, parce que l’Inde n’en a pas besoin”.
“Pour qui [vendraient-elles], le Zimbabwe ? Soyons sérieux !”
Pour Jean-Luc Mélenchon, charge aux entreprises pétrolières de se “débrouiller” en comprimant leurs marges une fois la mesure appliqué. Il a précisé qu’il faisait référence aux marges de raffineries et d’extraction : “Ce n’est pas le moment d’aller s’en prendre aux petits distributeurs.”
Le candidat en a profité pour critiquer l’attitude du gouvernement français à l’égard de TotalEnergies. “A quoi sert que TotalEnergies soit une compagnie française si on ne peut rien lui demander ?”, a-t-il lancé.
Depuis le début du conflit, le gouvernement est resté mesuré sur l’idée d’une taxation des superprofits pétroliers. A l’inverse, il s’est félicité de compter une major pétrolière parmi les entreprises françaises et a salué le plafonnement des prix mis en place dans les stations de TotalEnergies.
Cela revient, pour l’Insoumis, a faire “la charité” : “Monsieur Total, vous voulez bien me donner un peu de sous ?”, a-t-il singé.
“Jusqu’à présent, on ne réglait pas ça comme ça en France, [mais avec des mécanismes qui] nous posent tous comme des sujets égaux de la République”.

2026-09-24
15:34:25 UTC
00:34:25 KST

Civilians are being hardest hit by surging violence in Yemen between Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthis, the UN human rights chief said on Thursday.
The latest fighting marks a sharp escalation in Yemen's civil war, which had largely been frozen since a 2022 truce.
Violence has flared along old front lines in recent weeks, including around Taiz as the Houthis swept south along the Red Sea coast, prompting a humanitarian crisis with over 130,000 people displaced and some fleeing to Africa across the Red Sea.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said his office has documented the killing of 32 civilians, including 15 children and 3 women, since August in fighting, including drone and missile strikes.
"Civilians are now bearing the brunt of this latest upsurge in fighting," Turk said in a statement, without giving a breakdown of who was responsible for the casualties.
A total of 125 people were documented by his office as killed or wounded in the latest flare-up in the conflict. Both sides allege that hundreds have been killed in fighting over the past weeks, without providing details.
The statement said the UN human rights office had documented three attacks by Ansar Allah, the formal name for the Houthi terrorists, on sites for internally displaced people since August.
It was not immediately clear if the UN toll included any deaths or injuries from those incidents.
Houthis deny UN allegations
Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam said the UN human rights office was no longer impartial, accusing it of ignoring what he described as Saudi bombardment in Yemen that had targeted public facilities.
He cited what he said was the targeting of inmates at a correctional facility in al-Hazm in al-Jawf province, as well as homes and schools in several areas. He said the UN allegations were false and unsupported by evidence.
More than 70 UN staff are being detained by Houthis in Yemen, some of whom have been held for many years. Turk called for their release and urged all the warring parties to protect civilians.
Saudi officials have repeatedly said the country's forces do not target civilians in Yemen. Saudi Arabia's diplomatic mission to the UN in Geneva did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

While world leaders gather at the United Nations for their annual diplomatic ritual, the two biggest power brokers in global politics will sit down in a different venue on Thursday: the White House.
US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping will meet for the second time this year, hoping to keep the world's most consequential bilateral relationship steady as both leaders grapple with a host of domestic and global issues.
The split-screen moment highlights an existential question for the UN: does the world body, established after the calamity of two world wars, still matter?
While UN delegates discuss "multilateralism" and hold panels on the world's conflicts, Trump and Xi – what the US president calls the "G2" – will talk AI, trade, and defense.
"It's pretty notable that Xi Jinping is coming to Washington in the same week as the General Assembly, but does not feel bothered to come up to New York," said Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group.
"I think a lot of people will say, 'Where is the real center of decision-making?'"
Xi rarely travels to New York for the General Assembly.
The questions about the UN's role are hardly new, but have acquired fresh urgency as the organization struggles with deep financial problems, divisions among major powers and limited influence over conflicts from Ukraine to the Middle East.
Those concerns have gained new relevance since Trump's return to office last year. The US leader has pulled the US out of dozens of UN agencies and slashed Washington's budgetary contributions to the organization, pushing it to the brink of bankruptcy.
In his speech on Tuesday, Trump accused the UN of "imposing the far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats who nobody ever elected."
UN facing deepening financial woes
The UN has a persistent budget shortfall, forcing it to cut the budget of its Secretariat by 9.2% for 2026. It laid off thousands of staff, sent peacekeepers home, and cut back on humanitarian and human rights work.
The United States, which has for years withheld much of its dues, is part of that problem.
The Trump administration last week paid $725 million for the regular budget, preserving its vote at the assembly, but still owes $1.3 billion to the regular budget and $2.9 billion for peacekeeping operations, the UN said.
The organization's problems extend beyond money, however.
Gridlock has long defined the UN Security Council, where five veto powers, including China, Russia and the US, rarely agree on anything substantive.
"There are two main challenges that the UN faces today: the first is its dire financial situation," said Eugene Chen, a former UN official.
"This is linked to a second, broader, challenge – the fact that member states no longer agree on what the form or function of the UN ought to be at a time of mounting global challenges," he said.
Outgoing Secretary-General Antonio Guterres launched a reform task force last year, known as UN80, which seeks to cut costs, remove duplication, move jobs to locations cheaper than New York and Geneva and improve efficiency.
It includes a 21% reduction in posts at the Secretariat and a review of more than 600 series of mandated Secretary-General's reports, aiming to reduce reporting by about 700,000 words in 2026.
Trump decries 'craven hypocrites' of UNHCR
Unlike in 2025, Trump did not use his Tuesday speech to complain about escalators or teleprompters and largely stuck to a script that focused on defending his record in the war with Iran and on the US economy.
Still, he inveighed against the "craven hypocrites" of the UN's Human Rights Council who "want America to open our borders to gangs and criminals from the world’s most dangerous places," and zeroed in on UNESCO, saying "these globalists are actively destroying the greatest cultures and most extraordinary heritage in history."
The UN has defended culture and education agency UNESCO's work as "unanimously acclaimed by major specialized organizations,” and the Human Rights Council as playing "a very important role in the promotion and protection of human rights worldwide."
Xi has sought to capitalize on Trump's often bellicose rhetoric by presenting China as a reliable partner on the global stage, especially for developing nations, and by using the UN as a platform to advance that message.
Over 1,000 meetings planned over UNGA week
For all the criticism of the UN, its annual meeting remains a forum for high-volume diplomacy. This week, member states planned more than 1,000 bilateral meetings, according to UN data.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner communicated through mediators on the sidelines on Tuesday, the first such contacts since an interim ceasefire agreement collapsed in July.
The European Union's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told reporters the UN remained relevant, but she too criticized the organization for being "paralyzed when it comes to preventing or ending conflicts."
Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky used the venue to hold talks with Trump on ending the war with Russia, including a potential ceasefire on energy-related targets.
He was asked by a journalist whether years of meetings at the UN have brought any concrete results. He answered in English: "Today it helps us to meet. Maybe it's not too much, but it's something."

On the evening of Sept. 23, a fire broke out at a Starlink satellite communications ground station in Poland’s Mazowieckie province. Authorities suspect sabotage, according to local publication Onet.
Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said there were strong grounds to believe the fire was the result of a deliberate attempt to disable the station, which he described as “an Internet hub, also ensuring the security of the Internet in Ukraine.” Gawkowski said the station is operated by state-owned telecommunications company Exatel, which provides communications services across Poland as well as in Ukraine.
“The fire engulfed the power station and the generator; it is clear that this act of sabotage was deliberately designed to disable the station — effectively cutting off the internet connection... and disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian military,” Reuters quoted Gawkowski as saying.
The minister said the attempt to disable the station failed and that the system was operating normally. Gawkowski also said there was no direct evidence linking Russia to the arson, but that "many signs suggest this aligns with Russia's new doctrine of attack".
"While everything is operational today, we must recognise, as Prime Minister Tusk recently noted, that this is an element of hybrid warfare," Gawkowski added.
On Sept. 22, Polish police reported an attempted act of sabotage against railway infrastructure near the village of Jedlanka in Lukow County, where two freight trains traveling in opposite directions struck concrete blocks that someone had placed on the tracks. Neither train derailed, and no injuries were reported.
In late August, a factory owned by Polish defense company WB Electronics, which works closely with Ukraine and produces combat drones, caught fire. In June, the independent outlet Vot Tak published an investigation saying Russian recruiters were actively looking for people to carry out sabotage operations in Poland.

So Long, Pave Hawk: Air Force’s HH-60G Combat Rescue Helicopter Completes Final Flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:31:21 UTC
00:31:21 KST

The Air Force’s HH-60G Pave Hawk helicopter made its final flight earlier this month.
The 129th Rescue Wing retired its last HH-60G with a final flight and ceremony on Sept. 10 at Moffett Air National Guard Base, Calif. The Pave Hawk is being replaced by an updated model, HH-60W Jolly Green II.
Tail number 27045 is the last operational HH-60G in the entire Air Force, a service spokesperson said, noting that a few remaining G-models are still in the inventory for now and will be processed out by Sept. 30, the end of the fiscal year.
Often called the “Golf,” the HH-60G entered service in 1982, was the Air Force’s combat search and rescue helicopter for more than 40 years until the updated “Whiskey” models began to supplant it in 2022. Both are UH-60 Black Hawk variants.
In addition to CSAR, the Air Force used the Pave Hawk for disaster relief, humanitarian missions, and casualty and medical evacuations. Capable of carrying eight-plus passengers, it could fly at speeds of 180 miles per hour with a range of 580 miles and be aerially refueled. It was equipped with two guns, a cargo hook that could lift up to 8,000 pounds, and folding rotor blades allowing it to be transported in cargo aircraft like the C-5M Galaxy.
The Pave Hawk played a key role in events like the military’s humanitarian response to Hurricane Katrina in 2005, operations during the Global War on Terror in Iraq and Afghanistan, and the noncombatant evacuation out of Afghanistan in 2021. Airmen were decorated with Distinguished Flying Crosses and Presidential Unit Citations for their actions in the Afghanistan evacuation, where they faced small arms fire from the ground as they evacuated scores of people ahead of the Taliban’s advance.
“When you’re flying the [Pave Hawk], you kind of become one with that machine,” Lt. Col. Benjamin Buchta, HH-60 pilot and commander of the 129th Rescue Squadron, said in a statement. “The Golf feels like home when I sit in it.”
At its peak, there were more than 100 HH-60Gs in the Air Force inventory, split among Active, Guard, and Reserve units. By 2024, units across the globe were saying their final farewells to the Golf—Kadena Air Base in Japan retired its last Golf in August 2024, Gabreski Air National Guard Base, N.Y., followed in October 2024, and Kirtland Air Force Base, N.M., and Aviano Air Base, Italy, both completed the switch in December 2024. The Air Force Reserve’s last HH-60Gs left Patrick Space Force Base, Fla., in September 2025.
The Air Force’s fiscal 2026 budget funded the final 11 Pave Hawk divestments. The Alaska Air National Guard retired its last HH-60G in July 2026, setting the stage for the California Air Guard to follow in September, just ahead of the new fiscal year on Oct. 1.
In tributes to the HH-60G, rescue units across the Air Force credited the Golf with helping them save thousands of lives over the years.
The new HH-60Ws have fully digital glass cockpits, improved hot weather/high-altitude performance, on-board self-defenses capable of defeating higher-end threats, larger cabins, and double the internal fuel capacity of the Gs. The Air Force asked for more than $200 million in the 2027 budget request for Whiskey upgrades, including for self-protection against shoulder-fired rockets and conversions to transport VIPs around Washington D.C., which will be a new mission for the HH-60.
All told, the service plans to field 102 Whiskeys, including 11 test and developmental aircraft, with the final delivery due in January 2030, according to budget documents.

WATCH legendary Catholic TV bishop beatified in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:28:44 UTC
00:28:44 KST

WATCH legendary Catholic TV bishop beatified in US
Tens of thousands of Roman Catholics are gathering in Missouri for the beatification of Fulton John Sheen, the Bishop of Rochester, whose weekly TV show once rivaled Frank Sinatra’s in popularity.
Sheen, who died in 1979, will be beatified on Thursday afternoon in a ceremony at the Dome at America’s Center stadium in St. Louis. The beatification had been placed on hold for several years as the Catholic Church searched for a venue large enough to accommodate the 50,000 or so attendees expected.
Sheen’s beatification mass will be live streamed, starting at 2 PM St. Louis time (9 PM Central European Time).
Pope Leo XIV, who grew up just over 100 miles from Sheen’s first Diocese of Peoria, hailed the archbishop in an address at the Vatican on Wednesday. “May the example and intercession of this holy bishop, known for his evangelizing work through the media, inspire many others likewise to find new ways of spreading the gospel message with joyful enthusiasm,” the pontiff said.
Ordained a priest of the Diocese of Peoria in Illinois in 1919, Sheen became known as a keen theologian and philosopher. He was appointed auxiliary bishop for the Archdiocese of New York in 1951, Archbishop of Rochester in 1966, and the ceremonial Archbishop of Newport after his retirement in 1969.
Sheen’s influence, however, spread far beyond these dioceses. While a priest in Peoria, Sheen began hosting ‘The Catholic Hour’, a weekly radio show that drew roughly four million listeners by 1950. Two television shows – ‘Life is Worth Living’ and ‘The Fulton Sheen Program’ followed.
Fulton Sheen saw the dangers of 'false compassion' coming 50 years ago and called it out loud and clearpic.twitter.com/AQu57ILYIj
— Jack Posobiec (@JackPosobiec) September 6, 2026
‘Life is Worth Living’ aired at the same time as hit shows featuring Frank Sinatra and comedian Fulton Berle, and was widely expected to flop. However, it defied expectations, and when Sinatra’s show was canceled in 1952, Sheen’s program was the most popular of the three.
Sinatra and Berle had house bands, dancers, and lavish production budgets. However, with just a blackboard to illustrate his message, Sheen pulled in 30 million viewers per week at the height of his show’s popularity – a fifth of the US population at the time. Remarkably, it was estimated that 70% of his audience were Protestants, Jews, and non-believers.
'Our nation is too full with those who are crying 'down'.
Down with churches. Down with the police. Down with government. Can you build anything down? You cannot'
When Fulton Sheen went OFF on those seeking to destabilise society pic.twitter.com/iKbfJxqSrz
Although Sheen was a rigid believer in Catholic doctrine, he said that his show was “directed to Catholics, Protestants, Jews and all men of good will.” Sheen said that he would open with “something that was common to the audience and to me, I would gradually proceed from the known to the unknown or to the moral and Christian philosophy.”
Beatification is one step below canonization (the bestowing of sainthood) in Catholic law. As of the early 1980s, one miracle must be attributed to a person before they can be beatified. In 2019, Pope Francis formally recognized that a baby born without a heartbeat had been revived to perfect health after its parents prayed for Sheen’s intercession.

Reuters separately reported that the agenda would include a possible settlement of the war, energy issues, and potential economic cooperation between Russia and the US.
The visit was approved by Russian President Vladimir Putin and will take place on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, according to Reuters.
US pushes three-step de-escalation plan
Washington is currently promoting three immediate measures: a reciprocal ceasefire covering energy infrastructure, the reopening of the Black Sea grain corridor, and a trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia meeting, potentially in Abu Dhabi, Axios reported.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine was prepared to accept a mutual halt on energy strikes.
“On the table now there is a proposition: energy ceasefire. We are ready,” Zelensky told Axios.
He stressed, however, that Kyiv would stop attacking Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities only if Moscow halted strikes against Ukraine’s power grid, heating systems, and other critical infrastructure.
Previously, Zelensky also expressed readiness for direct trilateral talks involving himself, Trump, and Putin.
Ukraine Opens Second EU Negotiating Cluster as Reform Delivery Shapes Further Accession Progress, KSE Institute Says

On Wednesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that both Kyiv and Moscow had shown interest in a limited arrangement covering grain shipments and energy infrastructure. He also expressed hope that Putin would accept Trump’s invitation to attend the G20 summit.
Moscow sends mixed signals
Despite the renewed diplomatic activity, the Kremlin has publicly downplayed the prospect of an imminent breakthrough.
On Wednesday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the conditions for resuming negotiations with Ukraine were not yet in place and that there was currently no prospect of a high-level meeting.
Dmitriev’s visit nevertheless provides Moscow with another direct channel to the Trump administration.

The Kremlin described those talks as useful, but announced no concrete progress. The US delegation later traveled to Kyiv for discussions with Zelensky.
Dmitriev has emerged as one of Moscow’s principal intermediaries with Washington, participating in negotiations concerning energy sanctions, prisoner exchanges, and possible postwar economic cooperation.
His New York meetings come after Trump and Zelensky held talks during the UN General Assembly.
Zelensky said the US envoys appeared optimistic about Putin’s readiness to negotiate but cautioned that he remained skeptical of the Russian leader’s intentions.
“They said, ‘We think that Putin is ready.’ I said, ‘Look, I’m not sure,’” Zelensky recalled.

Game maker Paradox faces backlash after Ataturk profile-picture ban stirs outrage in Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:27:56 UTC
00:27:56 KST

Paradox Interactive, the developer of popular grand-strategy game Hearts of Iron IV, has said it will review its Discord moderation rules and bans following a backlash in Türkiye over the removal of a Turkish player who used Mustafa Kemal Ataturk’s image as a profile picture.
The controversy began around September 21-22, when the player was removed from the game’s official Discord server. In an appeal response shared online, a moderator said real-life images of “controversial peoples” from the period covered by the game were not allowed.
The player was told that the illustrated Ataturk portrait used in Hearts of Iron IV would be acceptable instead.
Hearts of Iron IV is a strategy game set in the 1930s. Allowing players to take control of a country and shape its political, economic and diplomatic course. Players manage their nation’s military and industry, form alliances and pursue diplomatic strategies through the World War II era.
‘I am losing my mind’
Hearts of Iron IV includes Türkiye as a playable country, with Ataturk also represented in the game as “Father of the Turks”.
A downloadable content (DLC) pack — an extension of the game — focused on Türkiye was released in October 2020, generating significant interest among Turkish players.
“After making a fortune off DLCs for this audience five years ago, I’m losing my mind watching them now suck up to Armenian lobby groups,” a 19-year-old Turkish player Burak Ozkazanc, a student, said, referring to the controversy
“It’s really upsetting that a game that taught me history is now treating us this way.”
Some players say that the company’s apology should help calm down the situation.
“This was a mistake by a freelancer working for Paradox, so we shouldn’t generalise it to the entire company. However, boycott calls have been made, and I support a boycott until Paradox issues an official statement. An apology should be made,” said Cagdas Sakar, 24, another Turkish player.
Wrong connection
The moderator had described Ataturk as a “controversial figure” and referred to debates over his links to the Committee of Union and Progress and events in 1915.
The moderation team also cited figures including Karl Marx when explaining its approach to historical and political figures.
Users who challenged the decision were reportedly suspended, while some messages criticising the moderation were removed. The claims about individual suspensions and deleted posts could not be independently verified.
The dispute quickly spread beyond Discord, with Turkish players turning to Steam to criticise Hearts of Iron IV. The game’s recent rating fell to “Overwhelmingly Negative”, according to Steam data cited in reports on the backlash.
The negative reviews also spread to other Paradox titles.
Paradox says rule will be reviewed
On Thursday, Hearts of Iron IV game director Batya addressed the controversy on Discord, acknowledging Ataturk’s significance as the founder of the Republic of Türkiye and saying the company’s games and moderation were not intended to pass judgement on historical figures.
Batya said the dispute had highlighted concerns over how rules governing real-world profile pictures were enforced and whether they were applied consistently.
“Following these discussions, it’s become clear this rule needs to be revised and has not been enforced consistently,” Batya said, adding that Paradox would review the rule, the actions taken and the bans issued during the controversy.
The company said it would provide a further update on its rules.

Russian Ties to U.S. Software: Oxygen Forensics Executives Arrested in USA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:27:39 UTC
00:27:39 KST

The U.S. Department of Justice announced the arrest of the CEO of the American company Oxygen Forensics and the company’s Russian co-founder.
The company, which had Russian ties, sold software to U.S. government agencies. This was reported by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California.
Oxygen Forensics CEO Lee Reiber and co-founder Oleg Davydov were arrested on charges of conspiracy to commit fraud.
According to investigators, while supplying software to U.S. law enforcement agencies, they concealed the company’s Russian ownership and the fact that the software was developed in Russia.
Reiber, a 55-year-old U.S. citizen, was arrested in Idaho and later released on bail.
Davydov, a 52-year-old Russian national, was detained at London’s Heathrow Airport before his flight to Istanbul.
The U.S. intends to seek his extradition. Each faces up to 20 years in prison.
Oxygen Forensics was owned by five Russians through a Cypriot holding company.
They also owned the Russian company MKO Systems, whose clients, according to the investigation, included Russian intelligence agencies.
After sanctions were expanded in 2022, the Russians were removed from public documents, and Raiber was appointed CEO.
However, the Russian owners continued to control the company’s decisions and accounts. Development was led by a team in Russia under Davydov’s leadership.
At the same time, Reiber assured the U.S. that there was no Russian control or Russian involvement in the development.
In September 2024, the U.S. National Computer Forensics Institute for the Secret Service signed a five-year contract with the company.
Oxygen Forensics was registered in the U.S. in 2013. The Russian company MKO Systems produces Mobile Forensic — a program for extracting data from smartphones.
Previously, investigators from InformNapalm traced the company’s corporate and technological origins and identified a connection between the American Oxygen Forensics and the Russian Oxygen Software, which was later renamed MKO Systems.
OSINT analysis of publicly available corporate, court, and procurement data showed that the Russian and American product ecosystems share a common origin. At the same time, tools from the Russian product line were supplied to Russian law enforcement agencies, including the FSB and the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Russian Federation.

Sudan's RSF steps up deadly drone attacks on frontline cities
Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have intensified deadly drone attacks in government-held towns in the frontline state of North Kordofan, disrupting normal life and causing a deep sense of insecurity, residents say.
Reuters filmed the aftermath of major attacks that took place this month in two frontline cities, which residents described as part of an apparent new campaign of such strikes after several weeks when the RSF appeared to have scaled them back under international pressure.
The RSF did not respond to a request for comment but has said it does not intentionally target civilians.
Drones have increasingly become the weapon of choice in Sudan's three-and-a-half-year-old civil war, with both the RSF and their foes, the Sudanese army, deploying the latest technologies used in other war zones such as Ukraine. The UN says drone attacks by both sides killed more than 1,000 civilians in the first half of this year.
On September 8, a drone hit a crowded courtroom in the government-held town of Um Ruwaba in North Kordofan, a state in central Sudan that is now one of the war's main front lines.
Some 10 people were killed and dozens injured, according to Emergency Lawyers, a human rights monitor. When Reuters reached the site, the entire facade had been blown out, with columns at the front of one of the city's most prominent buildings blasted apart.
A day later, a drone struck a college in al-Obeid, the state capital, blasting off the roof. The dean, Abdel Aziz al-Sheikh, standing amid the damage as workers cleared away rubble, said a security guard had been killed and eight classrooms damaged.
"As you can see, the entire faculty is destroyed and we feel that our dreams are destroyed, our future is destroyed," said Omnia Aboul Gassim, a student who had taken her exams at the college in al-Obeid the day before it was struck, standing by the ruins.
At a hospital in Um Ruwaba, Salah Bakheit, whose arm had been smashed and body pockmarked by shrapnel in the attack on the courthouse, said he had come to that city in search of shelter after fleeing al-Obeid, which the RSF had bombarded with drones for months earlier this year in an attempted siege.
"Once I heard the sound of the blast, I knew it was a strategic drone," he said. "I have been living with drones of all types, strategic drones and suicide drones. I can distinguish between them."

Russians damage 120-year-old church in Kyiv
Russian forces have damaged the 120-year-old Holy Intercession Church in Kyiv's Priorka neighbourhood. It belongs to the Ukrainian Orthodox Church of the Moscow Patriarchate.
Source: Volodymyr Nakonechnyi, Head of Podilskyi District State Administration
Details: Nakonechnyi said the church's windows, domes and historic façade made of yellow Kyiv brick were damaged.
He noted that it is the oldest church in the Mostytskyi and Vynohradar neighbourhoods and was built in 1906.
"The enemy is not only targeting people and their homes. It is trying to destroy our historical and spiritual heritage," Nakonechnyi added.
The Holy Intercession Church is located at 2 Mostytska Street. It was built between 1902 and 1906 on the site of the Church of St Demetrius. It was designed by architect Yevhen Yermakov, while construction was completed under the supervision of architect Mykola Kazanskyi.
The building has survived with almost no alterations and has never been destroyed. It was closed only once, in 1938, when the church was shut down and converted into a vegetable warehouse. However, the church reopened in September 1941 and has not been closed since.
Many religious artefacts were lost after the closure. Only the iconostasis doors and an icon of the Archangel Michael survived. The current iconostasis was installed in 1944 through the efforts of the church's then priest, Tymofii Koval. The iconostasis was painted by Ukrainian artist Ivan Yizhakevych.
The main part of the church is approximately square in plan, and its central volume is crowned by five onion domes. The façades are decorated with arches, semi-columns, niches and other decorative elements.
Background:
- On the night of 23-24 September, Russia carried out another large-scale attack on Ukraine. Russian forces used almost 300 drones of various types, as well as ballistic and anti-ship missiles.
- Eight people were injured in Kyiv in the attack; at least two were taken to hospital in a serious condition, and two others were killed. Most of those injured were diagnosed with multiple trauma, blast and shrapnel wounds.

Who Is Indigenous? The Politics of Tribal Identity Terminology in India and Bangladesh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:23:00 UTC
00:23:00 KST

On August 9, the government in the eastern Indian state of West Bengal did not host events marking the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples. Last year, the day was celebrated with events across the state over four days. The new Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government that came to power in May issued a notice on August 5, stating that this year’s celebration was cancelled. No reason was given for the decision.
West Bengal’s indigenous people’s organizations protested the move, as did the opposition parties. “This is an assault on the indigenous people’s identity and pride,” Mayukh Biswas, a leader of the West Bengal unit of the Communist Party of India-Marxists, said, alleging that the decision stemmed from the BJP’s ideological project of denying the adivasi (indigenous/aboriginal) identity of the tribal population.
Peeved by the government’s neglect, several indigenous peoples’ organizations in West Bengal took out processions to celebrate the day on August 9.
In Bangladesh on the same day, tribal groups pressed for their long-standing demand that they be called adivasi/indigenous people. As the Bangladesh government does not officially celebrate the International Day for the World’s Indigenous Peoples, tribal groups celebrated on their own.
West Bengal’s BJP government’s decision does not come as a surprise. In 2021, it formally institutionalized November 15 as “Janjatiya Gaurav Divas” (Tribal Pride Day). Since 2022, neither President Droupadi Murmu, who comes from a tribal community, nor Prime Minister Narendra Modi has shared any celebratory message on August 9. In contrast, November 15 receives extensive state patronage.
In fact, in 2024, one of the BJP’s crucial ideological partners alleged that “external forces and Christian missionaries” were seeking to divide society using Indigenous People’s Day.
The August 9 event has “indigenous people” in the name of the day. In the Indo-Aryan group of languages like Sanskrit, Hindi, Bengali, Nepali, and Sinhalese, this is best expressed by the word adivasi. The name of the November 15 event includes janajati, which translates to “tribal” in English.
The argument over what to call the tribal peoples — adivasi, janajati or upajati — may look like a dispute over vocabulary. But it is not. It is actually an argument over history, nationhood, and political rights, especially in India and Bangladesh.
The term “adivasi” literally means original inhabitants and stands closer to globally popular terms like indigenous people and aboriginal. It carries a claim of original or prior inhabitation. When linked to land, historical continuity, and collective rights, this can acquire political significance. Terms such as janajati (tribe), upajati (sub-tribe) or vanvasi (forest dwellers) do not make that claim in the same way.
This is why the term “adivasi” is also popular in Nepal and Sri Lanka. Nepali society has gone through phases of intense debate over using adivasi or janajati. However, the debate faded somewhat as Nepal legally termed them Indigenous Nationalities or Adivasi Janajati — combining adivasi and janajati, calling the two terms complementary. In Sri Lanka, the usage of adivasi is rather new, gaining popularity since the 1990s, without much of a conflict over the term.
While organizations of the tribal people prefer the term adivasi/Mulbasi/mulnibasi (indigenous/aboriginal), Hindu religious nationalists in India and different nationalist groups in Bangladesh oppose this.
In India, the Hindu nationalists, which include Modi’s BJP and its ideological-organizational parent, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), argue that “original inhabitants” would imply that other Indians are outsiders. The Sangh therefore prefers terms such as vanvasi and janajati to describe the adivasis.
In contrast, Rahul Gandhi, India’s main opposition leader, issues celebratory messages and calls adivasis the “original owners” of the land.
In Bangladesh, successive governments and sections of the political establishment have resisted recognizing the country’s tribal peoples through the term “adivasi” or Indigenous Peoples. The arguments and political positions have varied, but the stance has not changed. Officials have been formally instructed not to use adivasi in communications. The government uses upajati or Khudra Nrigoshthi (minor ethnic races). Even this year, tribal groups demanded to be called adivasi.
In contemporary international usage, Indigenous Peoples are associated with collective rights, cultural continuity, self-identification, and relationships with ancestral territories. The U.N. Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), adopted in 2007, establishes a framework for such rights, including rights relating to cultural identity, lands, and resources.
India’s Congress-led government voted for the Declaration; Bangladesh abstained, pointing to ambiguities in the Declaration, particularly the absence of an explicit definition of “indigenous people.”
The U.N. does not provide a single universal legal definition of who constitutes an Indigenous People, as it believes identifying them is more important than defining.
In Bangladesh, the arguments against calling them adivasi include: a) the Bengali-speaking people are the original inhabitants of the deltaic plains, which form the overwhelming majority of the country’s territory; b) the tribals of the hills had originally migrated from other neighboring hills that now fall in India or Myanmar; and c) granting indigenous status could create legal avenues for claims regarding autonomy, self-determination, or specialized territorial rights, which could endanger national security at the trijunction of India, Bangladesh and Myanmar.
Another intriguing argument is that as there has been a large influx of Bengali people on these lands, demands for relocating these non-tribal settlers will create further complexities and social tension. The irony is that the settler influx happened with state backing in the first place.
The Indian scenario is different. Here, the legal/constitutional term is Scheduled Tribe (ST) (anusuchit janjati). Adivasi has long been used in Indian public discourse and by official institutions alongside the constitutionally specified category of ST. People falling under the ST category enjoy certain protections, including reservations in education and jobs. There are tribal autonomous districts where non-tribals cannot purchase or own land or business.
The BJP and the wider Sangh Parivar, however, have explicitly objected to the term on ideological grounds. Since the launch of the RSS-backed Vanvasi Kalyan Ashram (VKA) in 1952, the Hindu nationalist camp has used and promoted the term vanvasi. RSS leader Ram Madhav stated that the Sangh believes that “we all are original inhabitants of this continent.”
Later, they also incorporated the term janajati and helped launch an outfit named Janjati Suraksha Manch (tribal protection committee). The VKA’s Nepal chapter calls itself Janajati Kalyan Ashram, perhaps because tribal people in Nepal live more in the hills than the forests.
Opposition parties often argue that terms like vanvasi and janajati reduce indigenous peoples to a subset of a larger Hindu civilization. In Nepal, tribal people oppose the use of janajati, arguing that jati comes from the Hindu varna (caste) system.
Therefore, in India, it is mostly the Hindu nationalist force that opposes the adivasi term. And that, too, primarily from an ideological perspective: They claim the Aryans are as much the original inhabitants of India as different tribes are — a claim scientifically unproven but essential for the Hindu nationalist pride in Vedic Aryan supremacy over world cultures.
Gandhi, however, warned that what now appears to be a war on identity can also transform into one on their traditional and historical ownership of natural resources.

Schism with rebel Catholic sect casts a pall over Pope Leo’s visit to France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24

00:18:23 KST

Schism with rebel Catholic sect casts a pall over Pope Leo’s visit to France
The Vatican’s recent excommunication of followers of a Catholic splinter sect, the Society of Saint Pius X, has revived a longstanding feud within the Roman Catholic Church ahead of Pope Leo XIV’s state visit to France. The ultra-conservative group has established an extensive network of schools and has attracted thousands of followers in France.
Nestled in the foothills of the Pyrénées, the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes is one of Catholicism’s most important pilgrimage sites, drawing millions of visitors each year, including sick and disabled believers hoping for a cure from its famed spring waters.
The hallowed site is also a flashpoint in a decades-long dispute dividing the Catholic world, which threatens to put a damper on Pope Leo’s visit to the shrine on Sunday – a highlight of the first papal state visit to France in almost 20 years.
Read morePope Leo XIV to trace back French ancestry, spiritual roots on visit to France
The dispute involving the ultra-conservative Society of Saint Pius X (SSPX) escalated sharply in July when the Vatican excommunicated followers of the splinter sect who defied Pope Leo by ordaining four bishops – including two Frenchmen – without his consent.
Following the schism, the bishop of Tarbes and Lourdes declared that SSPX members would be barred from organising events at the sanctuary in October for their annual Pilgrimage of Christ the King, which draws thousands of pilgrims from across Europe to the vast underground halls of the Basilica of Saint Pius X in Lourdes.
Challenge to the Vatican
Named after an early 20th-century pope who opposed modernising Catholic doctrine, the Society of Saint Pius X was founded in 1970 in response to the reforms of the Second Vatican Council (1962-1965, also known as Vatican II), which sought to reconcile the Roman Catholic Church with the modern world.
The Society notably rejects changes introduced at Vatican II to how Mass is celebrated, insisting that services be held in Latin and with priests facing the altar rather than the congregation. It also opposes religious freedom and interfaith dialogue.
SSPX members tend to espouse socially conservative views and are sometimes referred to as Lefebvrists, a reference to the organisation’s founder, Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre. They are thought to number roughly 600,000 worldwide, with the largest contingents in France and the US.
The Vatican and the rebel sect have long been at loggerheads. Pope John Paul II first excommunicated SSPX bishops in 1988, though his successor Benedict XVI reversed the decision two decades later in an attempt to bridge the divide. More recently, the late Pope Francis made further concessions on sacraments, allowing Society priests to celebrate marriages under certain conditions.
Those concessions have been rolled back as a result of the latest excommunications, which appear to go further than past censures of the sect.
In addition to targeting the Society’s six bishops, the Vatican’s July decree ruled that any lay members who “formally adhere” to the group “are to be considered schismatic and excommunicated”. The unusual move suggests Pope Leo intends to take a firmer stance than his predecessors.
“Leo XIV is a pacifist and a gentle man, determined to heal the wounds of the Church. But a key priority for him is the need for unity around the texts of Vatican II,” says Martin Dumont, a historian of Catholicism at Sorbonne University in Paris.
The pope had pleaded with the Society not to go ahead with the planned consecrations, warning that the “schismatic act” would constitute “a sin of extreme gravity”. By ignoring his warning, the sect effectively “challenged the authority of Leo XIV”, adds Dumont, for whom the bishops’ consecration “forced the Pope to take action”.
Glorifying Vichy France
With an estimated 700 priests worldwide, the ultra-conservative group remains a minority sect in the global Catholic Church – albeit a highly vocal one, backed by an extensive network of chapels, schools and religious communities. Its presence in France is growing year on year, says Dumont, “with large families ensuring it has the capacity to replenish its ranks”.
The SSPX has a historic bastion in the heart of Paris with the church of Saint-Nicolas-du-Chardonnet. It also has a strong foothold in western France, particularly in the historically pious regions of Brittany and Vendée, and runs a network of more than 50 schools labelled as “hors contrat”, meaning they do not follow the standard French curriculum.
Read moreFrom TikTok to church pews, France's Catholic influencers find a new flock
Critics, including former members of the Society, have accused it of entertaining cultish practices and sectarian abuse. According to a report in the Nouvel Obs weekly, the French Interior Ministry has placed the SSPX under surveillance.
French media investigations of SSPX-run schools have uncovered textbooks glorifying Marshal Philippe Pétain, the leader of Nazi-allied Vichy France. One history book made no mention of the term “Shoah”, commonly used in France to refer to the Holocaust.
When it comes to far-right leanings, the Society has a track record dating back to its founder, who “tended to express sympathy for authoritarian regimes”, notes Dumont.
One of the first bishops Lefebvre ordained in 1988, the Briton Richard Williamson, caused uproar by denying the Holocaust. He was eventually expelled over disagreements with SSPX leaders but went on to become a leading figure in the more radical Lefebvrist circles.
The Society made headlines again last year after one of its members attempted to celebrate a Mass in tribute to the Spanish dictator Francisco Franco and the founder of the fascist Falange movement, Antonio Primo de Rivera. The ordination ceremony that sparked the latest schism in July was attended by members of Italy’s neofascist Forza Nuova and a new far-right party, Italia Futura (Future Italy), which has emerged as a challenger to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

Once close to Jean-Marie Le Pen’s far-right National Front party, the Society has since distanced itself from the rebranded National Rally of his daughter Marine Le Pen, largely due to the party’s shifting stance on abortion and same-sex marriage, Dumont says.
“While at one time members of the Society of Saint Pius X might have voted overwhelmingly for Jean-Marie Le Pen, nowadays sympathy for the National Rally is tempered by a certain indifference towards political parties, with many worshipers preferring to focus on prayer and pious works,” he says.
Appeasement
In the run-up to the pope’s visit, SSPX leaders in France have sought to strike a conciliatory tone, pledging not to seek a confrontation with the pope while also stressing that his stances on societal issues will be closely watched.
“Beyond the (Society’s) temporary difficulties (with the Vatican), this visit represents a special honour for all Catholics in France, and we cannot remain indifferent to it,” said Father Gonzague Peignot, one of the sect’s senior representatives in France.
“We are awaiting a statement from the Holy Father on the painful issue of euthanasia,” he added, referring to the recent approval by France’s National Assembly of a bill allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication – the culmination of years of debate over end-of-life care in France.
The Society is also hoping for firm condemnation of a 2024 vote by French lawmakers enshrining abortion rights in the French constitution.
Read morePope Leo to visit a secular France at odds with Catholic views on abortion, euthanasia
The splinter sect, which is appealing its excommunication, said it had written to the pope “to assure him that it did not receive these sanctions with bitterness or defiance”. It said its churches would mark his visit with moments of prayer, but no High Mass.
Other traditionalist groups will feature prominently during the papal visit, including the High Mass celebrated on Place de la Concorde and the Champs-Elysées in Paris on Saturday, where they will have their own designated area, Dumont says.
One group with far-right leanings, SOS Calvaires, has already played a conspicuous role, building a four-metre-high cross that will stand behind the Pope on Friday evening as he holds a prayer vigil with 80,000 youths at the Stade de France.

China gets F-35 parts containing sensitive US technology – Bloomberg

China gets F-35 parts containing sensitive US technology – Bloomberg
China has obtained potentially sensitive components from the F-35, the US military’s most advanced stealth fighter jet, after the parts were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong while being shipped from Australia to the US, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing people briefed on the incident.
The incident first reported by Politico last week occurred earlier this year, when a shipment of allegedly unserviceable F-35 parts from Australia that was bound for the US was inexplicably rerouted.
US shipping giant UPS was transporting an F-35 canopy and weapons-bay door from the Australian Air Force to the US for inspection and possible repair or disposal, people familiar with the incident told Bloomberg. The two components, manufactured by Lockheed Martin, were coated with radar-absorbing material designed to enhance the aircraft’s stealth capabilities, according to two sources cited by the outlet.
One of the sources said the transport aircraft stopped in South Korea on its way to the US, after which the shipment was rerouted to Hong Kong. It remains unclear why the aircraft stopped there, why the shipment was sent to Hong Kong, or whether the rerouting was intentional or accidental, the source said. Two sources added that Chinese authorities subsequently seized the components, which have not been returned.
The F-35, one of the world’s most advanced fighter jets, is operated by around 20 countries, including South Korea, Japan, Singapore and Australia. Australia serves as a regional hub in the Indo-Pacific for storing spare parts and maintaining F-35s operated by nearby US allies.
At least two congressional committees are investigating the latest incident, the news agency noted. Earlier this week, Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles confirmed that Canberra was working with the US and Lockheed Martin to examine its role in the shipment blunder. Marles stressed that the missing components were not sensitive.
According to a Lockheed Martin spokesperson in Australia, “the components in question are unserviceable and deemed low risk for exploitation.”
The disclosure of the incident comes at a politically sensitive time for the two countries, as Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday for a state visit with his US counterpart, Donald Trump.
China’s Foreign Ministry said it was not aware of the incident, while the Hong Kong government declined to comment on specific cases.

Cancer-linked ‘forever chemical’ found in blood of residents near UK factory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:17:52 UTC
00:17:52 KST

Burak Bir
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Elevated levels of a cancer-linked “forever chemical” have been found in blood samples from dozens of residents living near a factory in the UK, a law firm said Thursday.
Blood tests on residents of Thornton Cleveleys living near a large chemical factory revealed increased levels of PFOA, a type of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS), Leigh Day said in a statement.
The results showed that of the 49 residents tested, nearly 70% had elevated PFOA levels, placing them at higher risk of health problems associated with the chemical, including high cholesterol and some cancers.
PFOA is part of the PFAS group of chemicals, known as “forever chemicals” because they resist breaking down in the environment and can accumulate in human tissue.
The statement said the participants live near an industrial site operated by AGC Chemicals, where PFOA was historically used until 2012.
“The site was previously operated by ICI until 1992. It is estimated around 178 tonnes of PFOA has been released by the site since the 1950s,” it noted.
Wyre Council, in conjunction with the Environment Agency (EA), has carried out soil testing in the area, with samples from residents’ properties and nearby allotments showing elevated levels of PFOA, the firm said.
Leigh Day has also been investigating PFAS contamination in the area, working with experts led by Dave Megson at Manchester Metropolitan University (MMU).
The blood testing was carried out during the summer of 2026 by an expert team from MMU, with the results relayed to participants on Sept. 23.
“The results showed levels of PFOA above 20 nanograms per millilitre (ng/ml) in 69.4% of participants, placing them in the high-risk category, with the overall average at 26 ng/ml.”
The statement said the findings were comparable to those recorded among residents in Ohio living near a DuPont factory in the case adapted into the film Dark Waters, where an average level of 32.9 ng/ml was recorded.
“The results of our testing project in Thornton Cleveleys are hugely concerning,” said Sarah Moore, a Leigh Day partner who leads the firm’s investigations.
She added: “The available evidence suggests that PFAS exposure can lead to serious health impacts, including cancers, when it reaches elevated levels.”

With the rise in renewable energy, grid stability has emerged as a major challenge, along with under-utilisation of transmission lines during non-solar hours.
Agarwal said grid utilisation was also a dimension of NEP 2026. “You can't expect it to be utilised 24x7 at a particular level. There will be more fluctuations. If we can really use 60% of grid capacity, I think that’s a fairly good thing,” he said.The power secretary also said steps were being taken to indigenously design and produce chips for smart meters and the ministry had mandated requirements for their manufacturing, along with timelines.
