NATO defense forces on Thursday failed to intercept a single Russian war drone penetrating the air frontier of the member state Romania, in the second day in a row of unimpeded violation by Kremlin military aircraft of Atlantic Alliance airspace.
A Russian Geran strike drone entered Romania from Ukrainian airspace near the northern Romanian region of Botoșani on Thursday morning, at or shortly before sunrise. A major Russian missile and drone attack against Ukraine with more than 200 weapons, including hypersonic missiles, ballistic missiles, strike drones and decoy drones, had been in progress at the time.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to a Romanian Defense Ministry statement, Romanian military air defense radars first tracked the drone above Ukraine and heading towards the Romanian city of Botoșan. Two Romanian F-16s scrambled from Borcea airfield, a major Romania/NATO air defense base in the southeast of the country. The Russian drone flew in Romanian airspace for about four minutes before crashing in a forest near the village of Solca, Suceava County, that official statement said.
Defense Minister Radu Miruță subsequently told Digi24 television that the drone “did not pass through Moldova” and entered Romanian airspace from Ukrainian airspace.
A Russian Geran-2 drone flying into Romania from Ukraine via Botoșani would probably transit between 30 and 80 kilometers (19 and 48 miles) of Romanian territory before reaching Solca, and would have been in Romanian airspace possibly longer than the four minutes claimed by the Romanian Defense Ministry, Kyiv Post review of probable flight paths and typical Geran-2 cruising speeds found.
Ukraine’s Draft 2027 State Budget Envisages UAH 1.67 Trillion Deficit, KSE Institute Says
The Romanian F-16 fighter jet air base Fetești, near Borcea, is some 350-380 kilometers (217 and 236 miles) from Botoșani and Solca. Depending on the speed chosen by the pilot, an F-16 on an intercept mission would typically cover that distance in 10-20 minutes – possibly not fast enough to have intercepted the single drone flying towards Solca.
Following the crash, the Romanian Air Force launched an IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter from Bacău Air Base 95 “to monitor the situation in the area,” the Defense Ministry statement said.
A report by the major Romanian television channel Digi24 said that Russian military violations of Romanian airspace had tripled since 2025. Acting Minister of Defense Radu Miruță, in an interview aired Thursday by the channel, said that “it was an intense night from the perspective of the Romanian Army’s missions…Eight fighter jets were scrambled last night, from midnight until this morning, which is not a usual thing and is not something that is normal to happen.”
In Romania’s north-eastern Bucovina region, local residents recorded and uploaded to the internet video of a single, slow-moving propeller drone with a bat-wing silhouette and lawn mower engine sound consistent with a Geran drone, flying unimpeded in gray skies. Local chat groups reported loud noise similar to an explosion before the drone crashed, News Bucovina reported.
Journalists from News Bucovina and other media outlets reached the crash site prior to officials to film drone debris and the crash scene before officials arrived. Debris images published by Romanian media showed inscriptions in Russian.
The major Romanian news and information site, news.ro, reported Defense Ministry officials launched an investigation “immediately after the drone crash” and had sent specialists to the scene where they found dozens of fragments, and that an investigation was ongoing.
The Romanian Air Force’s failure to intercept the drone was the result of “dynamic” circumstances and peacetime rather than wartime rules of engagement, Miruță said.
“The Romanian Army and Romania are in a time of peace. Those who carry out such activities in violation of airspace, in violation of international law, must realize that it is not allowed,” Miruță said in part. “We, at the military level, have a responsibility to do everything we can with what we have at our disposal to defend the Romanian population.
Across north-eastern Romania, following the night-time air raid alert, schools in the Solca, Arbore, Botoșana, Cacica areas decided to suspend classes temporarily, until a 10 a.m. all clear.
Across the border over Ukraine, on the night, Russia, per Ukrainian Air Force counts, launched a 300+ weapon strike against Ukraine using anti-ship missiles, ballistic missiles, and 282 drones, including the Geran-2 that flew into Romania.
Within their own national airspace, per those Kyiv official claims, Ukrainian air defenses shot down four “Zircon” anti-ship missiles; three Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles; one “Banderol”/“Dan-T” cruise missile and 219 out of 282 Geran-type unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). By the standards of the Russo-Ukraine war, it was a mid-sized air attack by Russia whose most massive missile+drone raids have saturated Ukrainian air defenses with more than 100 missiles and 1,000 drones in a single night.
The single Russian drone violation of Romanian airspace was paralleled during the night of Sept. 23-24, by a drone or drones detected by Romanian air defense networks flying north of the village of Chilia Veche, over Ukrainian territory in the Danube delta region, where that river is the international border with Romania. Two Spanish F-18 fighters launched from the 57th Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base, near Constanza, but per news and official reports found no targets over Romania to intercept.
Ukrainian civilian air watch networks on the night reported tracking four Russian drones crossing Moldova from Ukrainian airspace, and that two of the aircraft appeared to have crashed in Moldova’s Sholdaneshtsky and Floreshtsky districts, in the central part of the country.
The other two drones flew on into Romania, those Ukrainian sources said, citing military air tracking data. Moldovan and Romanian official and media sources did not confirm the Ukrainian claim that two more Russian drones had passed into NATO airspace, in this case from Romania, without being stopped by NATO air defenses. Kyiv Post was unable to reconcile the conflicting reports.
Less than 24 hours before the Russian drone violations of Moldovan and Romanian airspace, on Wednesday, a Russian air force Mi-8 helicopter launched from an airfield in the Kaliningrad region flew into Polish airspace for about 42 seconds, penetrating about 300 meters (984 feet) into NATO nation territory, Polish air defense forces reported. The chopper returned to Russian airspace without hindrance.
“The flight of the machine was observed by the radio-location systems of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Poland. Fighter aircraft were scrambled, and ground-based forces and assets remained on standby. The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defense. The crews of the Republic of Poland’s air defense systems conduct round-the-clock observation, remaining in constant readiness to ensure the safety of Polish airspace,” an official Warsaw statement said.

Countries rush to fight diesel shock amid possible US ban, surging prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:51:30 UTC
22:51:30 KST

The US is reportedly preparing to impose a 90-day ban on diesel exports to bring down soaring energy prices, and several countries are gearing up for the domino fallout.
Politico reported on Thursday that the White House is trying to reduce high fuel prices that are weighing on Republicans ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
US fuel producers are opposed to the ban and have warned federal officials that "any short-term benefit would be outweighed by higher fuel prices in the future."
If the ban is enacted, it would be the first restriction on US energy exports since the Obama administration lifted a decades-old ban on oil exports in 2015, according to the report.
Diesel prices are currently at record highs around $6.52 per gallon compared with $2.83 per gallon last year, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).
Domino effect
The report said the steep increase is due to the US war against Iran in addition to Ukraine's attacks against Russian refineries.
But heading into the midterms, in which Republicans are trying to maintain majority control in both the US House and Senate, high energy prices are hampering Republican candidates trying to seek reelection, which is why sources told Politico that President Donald Trump is trying to implement the ban.
An industry executive told Politico that Trump is inclined to announce a ban by the end of the week and said the president considers any blowback "a December problem".
Industry experts said a diesel ban would have a domino effect on the rest of the world, noting that "countries around the world have grown more dependent on US diesel."
China
China's gasoline and diesel inventories have fallen to their lowest levels in more than a decade as exports surge and domestic demand recovers seasonally, according to GL Consulting.
Low stock levels appear to have raised Beijing's concerns, increasing the prospect of tighter export controls in October, according to Rystad Energy. 
GL Consulting said it expects exports to fall in October as state refiners prioritise domestic energy security.
Commercial gasoline inventories have hit their lowest level since 2011, while diesel inventories have fallen to their lowest since 2015, according to data provided by GL Consulting, a consultancy owned by Mysteel, a leading commodity information provider.
EU
The European Commission also expressed concern over reported US plans.
“The European Union views with concern the reported US plans to ban diesel exports, including to the European Union,” commission spokesperson Olof Gill told reporters at a daily briefing.
“EU-US cooperation in the field of energy is strong, stable, and mutually beneficial. Any disruption would risk negatively impacting both sides,” Gill said, adding that high-level contacts with the US administration were ongoing.
“We expect close partners to consult each other before taking measures that affect shared markets,” he said.
Asked whether the proposal could affect broader EU-US energy arrangements, Gill stressed that the plans remained unconfirmed. “Nothing is decided yet,” he said, adding that the EU was telling US counterparts at the highest level that it considered a ban a bad idea.
The US accounted for around 50 percent of EU diesel imports in August.
The EU’s Oil Coordination Group is due to meet next Tuesday to review the situation across member states.
Serbia
Serbia will release around 5,000 tonnes of diesel from state reserves, the energy minister said, hoping to ease shortages.
The Balkan country's oil market is also under pressure from months of record-low Danube water levels, which have hit river imports, and the looming threat of sanctions returning on its sole refinery over majority Russian ownership.
"The state is taking the necessary measures to protect citizens so they do not feel the consequences," Energy Minister Dubravka Djedovic Handanovic said.

Syria unveils plan to close all camps for IDPs by 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:48:20 UTC
22:48:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria presents plan to close all camps for internally displaced people by September 2027
The Syrian government has placed displacement and the need for people to return to their homes at the heart of its activities during the United Nations General Assembly meetings in New York, aiming to become "a Syria without camps" by September 2027.
Syrian officials called on the international community to fund rehabilitation in affected areas rather than limit funding to humanitarian response inside the camps.
During a high-level session organised by the Syrian mission to the United Nations under the title "Regional stability, security and sustainable return: The imperative of a Syria without camps", Minister of Emergency and Disaster Management Raed Al-Saleh said closing the camps should not become a process of moving people from tents to areas without the basic conditions for life.
Al-Saleh added, according to SANA, on Thursday, 24 September, that the return of displaced people should be voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable.
He stressed that "providing an alternative must precede the removal of tents", referring to the need to rehabilitate homes, roads, water and electricity networks, schools and health centres, as well as clear mines and war remnants.
Al-Saleh announced on 11 September that more than 200 camps had been closed, and about 141,000 families still lived in camps.
He said the Syrian government was working to close all camps by September 2027, and that about 20% of camp residents had returned to their areas since the formation of the government committee tasked with implementing the plan.
According to figures presented by the minister, Idlib has 786 camps housing about 458,250 people, while there are about 391 camps in Aleppo province. More than 40% of camp residents live in concrete-built housing, making some of them suitable for conversion into more stable residential communities.
According to Al-Saleh, the government is organising daily return convoys and preparing a convoy comprising between 4,000 and 6,000 families, while more than 200 camps have been closed since implementation of the plan began.
He also said about 3 million cubic metres of rubble had been removed during the first eight months of 2026, out of an estimated 50 million cubic metres across the country.
The launch of the plan in New York coincided with the continued return of Syrians from abroad and from areas to which they had been displaced inside the country.
According to the latest update from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, 1,795,641 Syrian refugees had returned from neighbouring countries to Syria by 3 September, including 718,611 returnees from Lebanon, 704,378 from Turkey and 296,156 from Jordan.
The UNHCR also estimated that 2,009,506 internally displaced people had returned to their areas of origin during the same period.
For his part, United Nations Development Programme Administrator Alexander De Croo said during the New York session that returning home should be the beginning of a recovery process.
He pointed to the start of work to remove rubble and mines and restore health services in areas of Syria.
De Croo noted that there are about 2 million internally displaced people, in addition to millions of Syrians who have returned from abroad, and stressed that implementing the vision of a "Syria without camps" requires investment, policies and a long-term programme, particularly on mine clearance.
Meanwhile, UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs Tom Fletcher expressed the international organisation's readiness to help turn the vision of "no camps and no tents" into practical steps.
UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih said about 1.8 million Syrian refugees had returned from neighbouring countries.
Salih called for financial pledges made by donors to be converted into concrete projects that help residents rebuild their areas, while stressing the importance of cooperation with the World Bank, the United Nations Development Programme and the private sector in providing the resources needed for economic recovery.
The Syrian government in recent months begun projects to prepare sites for the return of residents, as large areas still require rubble removal and infrastructure rehabilitation, and the ability of humanitarian aid programmes to continue at previous levels is uncertain.

Defense Ministry won’t appeal court rulings in cases involving deaths of military personnel
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:46:12 EEST
22:46:12 KST

The Ministry of Defense of Ukraine will not appeal court rulings in cases related to the death or disappearance of military personnel, the ministry's press service reports.
As noted in a Telegram post, this applies to cases involving the declaration of a serviceman as deceased, the establishment of the fact of a serviceman's death, the establishment of kinship and paternity, and the establishment of facts necessary to obtain payments and benefits linked to a serviceman's disappearance or capture.
"For families, this means fewer unnecessary court procedures and less waiting. They will be able to proceed more quickly with processing the payments, benefits, and other social guarantees to which they are entitled," the message reads.
At the same time, the ministry noted that the decision not to appeal will not be automatic. Each case will be reviewed individually, taking into account case materials, the official position of the military unit, and other relevant evidence.
For instance, in cases regarding the declaration of a serviceman as deceased, consideration will be given to the military unit's position and the materials of the internal investigation, the unit's participation in the proceedings, and the court's compliance with legislation and Supreme Court practice. In cases establishing the fact of a serviceman's death, account will be taken of the fact that the serviceman is listed as missing under special circumstances. Court rulings, establishing a family relationship, will not be appealed if family members petitioned the court due to inaccuracies in a surname, first name, or patronymic; in cases establishing paternity, they will not be appealed if molecular-genetic testing confirms the probability of biological paternity regarding the child on the part of the deceased or fallen servicemember.
Rulings establishing facts required to obtain payments and benefits related to a servicemember’s disappearance or capture will not be appealed if the case materials confirm the servicemember's status and identify the individuals entitled to payments, provided the military unit is a party to the proceedings.
"If necessary, you can contact the Ministry of Defence hotline at 1512," the Ministry emphasized.

Inside the bunker: How a Zelensky aide struggled to explain away corruption
A senior official in Vladimir Zelensky’s office frantically tried to reconcile her official annual salary of $12,500 with what surveillance records suggest was $30,000 per month in cash payments received from her new boss, a former head of Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR), according to a new investigation.
In records published by veteran investigative journalist Vladimir Boyko, Irina Mudraya, a former deputy justice minister serving as deputy head of Zelensky’s office, allegedly confided in her property magnate accomplice: “Who will ever believe me that I live on 50,000 hryvnia [$1,100] a month? Who?”
Mudraya was fired in August after being accused of laundering millions through Ukraine’s banking system to bail out one of Zelensky’s energy ministers, who himself had been arrested in a separate case involving the Ukrainian leader’s long-time associate Timur Mindich.
Boyko has been publishing pages of what he says are transcripts of surveillance recordings produced by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) between January and June as detectives followed Mudraya and her partner, former MP Maksim Mikitas.
Who is tasked with countering corruption in Kiev?
NABU and its sister agency, the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), established after the armed coup of 2014, have repeatedly clashed with Zelensky’s cabal. Last year, the Ukrainian leader attempted to place them under his control, but reversed course after Western donors threatened to suspend all aid.
Most recently the agencies exposed a massive scam-call center protection racket that was run through the office of Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, who then fled abroad under the false pretense of attending a conference in Paris.
Earlier this month, HUR agents engaged in a gunfight in Kiev with agents from the rival Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), which some news outlets linked to the fight for protection money from the scam-call criminal businesses.
Aside from NABU and SAPO, the National Agency on Corruption Prevention (NAPK) obliges hundreds of thousands of civil servants to submit annual finance and property declarations.
What did Mudraya have to worry about, according to the transcripts?
According to the transcripts, Mudraya received some $30,000 a month in cash payments from a man she called “Kirill Alekseyevich.”
Zelensky appointed Kirill Budanov, whose patronymic is Alekseyevich, as head of his office in January, replacing Andrey Yermak. Yermak resigned last year as initial news broke of Zelensky insiders syphoning some $100 million through energy contracts.
Mudraya appeared to seek advice from her partner Mitkas on hiding her ill-gotten riches from NAPK.
“You can declare the Bvlgaris and at least the Van Cleef. But no way can you declare the earrings,” the man said. “I’ll put you in touch with a man who will handle the income issue.”
Buying a Van Cleef piece during the war with Russia was “f**ked up,” Mudraya admitted.
The exchanges, which Boyko has staked his reputation on, suggest senior officials were flying under NAPK’s radar.
Mudraya and Mikitas discussed securing a highly paid sinecure that could cover for her enormous under-the-table income. She mentioned her envy of Zelensky’s adviser on sanctions policy, Vladislav Vlasyuk, who she said officially earned $335,000 a year as a member of the oversight committee of state-owned Sense Bank.
Sense Bank is the former Ukrainian branch of Alfa Bank, nationalized in 2023 under Kiev’s anti-Russian sanctions and through which Mudraya allegedly laundered cash by having the bank’s anti-fraud team suspend their digital monitoring platform.
While Mudraya said netting a job like Vlasyuk’s would not be legally possible, Mikitas suggested that a teaching position at a private institution could serve the same purpose. He offered to speak to a friend who headed a construction university, but Mudraya said she would look ridiculous teaching anything other than law.
Does the corruption link reach upwards?
According to the recording, Mudraya’s new boss personally delivered her first “salary,” unlike his predecessor who had a “specially trained girl” to carry cash. The payout turned out to be larger than expected:
“It was 30 [thousand dollars]. I went to him and said: ‘Kirill, it’s too much.’ Brought the hat with me. He says: ‘You said 30.’ I say: ‘No, I said I used to get 30. But we agreed to 20, not 30.’ He said: ‘Well, I won’t take it back.’”
Subsequent transcripts suggest the higher monthly payments continued and that Mudraya received an additional $20,000 bonus in May.
“He values you a lot,” Mikitas concluded. “Mark my word, in two months you’ll become first deputy prime minister,” he added, saying he expected “Kirill” to become the new cabinet chair.
What could the leaks mean for Budanov?
Some Ukrainian media have argued that NABU is targeting Zelensky’s inner circle to leverage reforms demanded by the EU.
Bloomberg reported that European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had a “tense meeting” with Zelensky this week, conditioning further financial support on implementing the changes Kiev had promised to Brussels.
Reform would give more power to NABU and SAPO and introduce oversight by EU-aligned experts for appointments of senior officials, curbing Zelensky’s extensive influence and the corrupt network he runs through his inner circle.
NABU and SAPO accused Yermak of involvement in a major money-laundering scheme in May and leaks to pro-EU media implicated Zelensky himself.
No formal charges can be filed against Zelensky as long as he holds presidential powers, which he has attempted to retain under martial law since his term expired in 2024.
Replacing Zelensky’s personal friend Yermak with Budanov, who has extensive contacts among Western special services, seems to be consistent with the EU’s goals.

ADHD and autism diagnoses have surged. A massive study may help explain why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:45:17 UTC
22:45:17 KST

ADHD and autism diagnoses have surged. A massive study may help explain why
- Date:
- September 24, 2026
- Source:
- Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal)
- Summary:
- A large Danish study found that children diagnosed with ADHD or autism today more closely resemble their peers in the general population than those diagnosed 10 years ago. The shift suggests that rising diagnosis rates may partly reflect broader identification and changing diagnostic patterns, rather than only an increase in the underlying conditions.
- Share:
New research suggests that the characteristics of children and teenagers receiving attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnoses have shifted over the past decade.
The study, led by the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal), a centre supported by the "la Caixa" Foundation, and Aarhus University, found that young people diagnosed with ADHD or ASD in Denmark now more closely resemble the broader population than those who received the same diagnoses 10 years earlier.
The findings suggest that the increase in ADHD and ASD diagnoses may partly reflect changes in who is being identified and diagnosed, alongside any possible changes in the underlying likelihood of developing these conditions. The research was published in JAMA Psychiatry.
Tracking changes in ADHD and autism diagnoses
Previous studies have identified several characteristics that occur more often among people diagnosed with ADHD or ASD than among the general population. These include being born prematurely or at a low birth weight, having parents with lower levels of education or lower household income, having a parent with a history of psychiatric disorders, and making greater use of healthcare services before receiving a diagnosis.
Researchers wanted to know whether those patterns had changed as ADHD and ASD diagnoses became more common.
To investigate, the team analyzed information from more than 2.1 million children and adolescents in Denmark. The researchers compared more than 71,000 young people diagnosed with ADHD or ASD between 2012 and 2022 with more than 713,000 individuals who had not received either diagnosis.
Differences narrowed over 10 years
Young people diagnosed with ADHD or ASD were still more likely than their peers to have many of the characteristics previously linked with these conditions. However, the size of those differences steadily declined during the study period.
Low birth weight provides one example. At the beginning of the study period, children born with low birth weight were 54% more likely to later receive an ADHD or ASD diagnosis than children born at a normal weight. By the end of the study, the difference had dropped to 17%.
Researchers found comparable declines in the associations involving premature birth and several measures of socioeconomic disadvantage.
"The key message is not that these risk factors are no longer important," says Magnus Elias Tarp, PhD student at Aarhus University and first author of the study. "What we found is that people diagnosed in recent years resemble the general population more closely than those who received the same diagnoses a decade ago."
A different way to understand rising diagnoses
Much of the research surrounding ADHD and ASD has examined why diagnosis rates are increasing or which factors are associated with a greater likelihood of developing these conditions. The new study approaches the trend from another direction by asking whether the population receiving diagnoses has itself changed.
The researchers say several developments could potentially contribute to the shift. Awareness of ADHD and ASD has increased, healthcare and education systems may be identifying cases more effectively, access to diagnostic evaluations may have expanded, and the point at which neurodevelopmental characteristics are considered clinically impairing may have changed.
The study cannot determine how much each of these factors contributed. However, the findings indicate that rising diagnosis rates should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that the underlying occurrence of ADHD or ASD has increased by the same amount.
"Our findings help us better understand why ADHD and autism diagnoses have increased so markedly in recent years," says Oleguer Plana-Ripoll, researcher at ISGlobal and Aarhus University and senior author of the study. "They do not show that these conditions are being overdiagnosed or that they have become less severe. Rather, they indicate that the population receiving these diagnoses has changed over time, and this needs to be taken into account when interpreting current trends. Further research in other countries would be needed to determine whether these findings can be replicated elsewhere," he adds.
What the findings could mean
Researchers say the results could affect how scientists interpret changes in the prevalence of ADHD and ASD. They may also be important for planning healthcare, education, and social services for people with these diagnoses.
The findings could also influence how researchers interpret reports of improving outcomes among people with ADHD or ASD. Some apparent improvements may result partly from changes in the characteristics of the population now receiving diagnoses, rather than from an improvement in the prognosis of the conditions themselves.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Magnus Elias Tarp, Mette Lise Lousdal, Charlotte Ulrikka Rask, Kathrine M. Keyes, Tomáš Formánek, Isabell Brikell, Xiaoqin Liu, Genona T. Maseras, Oleguer Plana-Ripoll. Changes in Characteristics Associated With ADHD and ASD Diagnoses Over Time. JAMA Psychiatry, 2026; DOI: 10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2026.2722

États-Unis. Amnesty International demande la suppression de l’ICE après avoir établi les violations généralisées des droits humains lors des opérations anti-immigration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:43:18 UTC
22:43:18 KST

In a new report released today, Amnesty International documented widespread human rights violations committed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and other federal agencies during the Trump administration’s large-scale, militarized immigration enforcement operations in Chicago, Minneapolis-St. Paul, New Orleans and Washington, DC.
The report, “We Had Whistles, They Had Guns”: Human Rights Violations in U.S. Immigration Enforcement Operations and the Case to Abolish ICE, demonstrates that the Trump administration is implementing a mass detention and deportation system, fueled by racist, xenophobic and false narratives, whose objective is to detain and deport as many migrants, asylum seekers and refugees from the United States as possible and spread fear throughout immigrant communities more broadly.
“Our report documents a chilling pattern of human rights violations across the U.S. intended to instill fear within migrant, asylum seeker and refugee communities,” said Nadia Daar, Executive Director, Amnesty International USA. “ICE’s record of violating human rights is nothing new, but our report shows many of these abuses have reached a perilous new level.”
Our report documents a chilling pattern of human rights violations across the U.S. intended to instill fear within migrant, asylum seeker and refugee communities.”
Nadia Daar, Executive Director, Amnesty International USA.
The Trump administration has committed a host of human rights abuses, including unlawful killings, some of which may amount to extrajudicial executions; arbitrary and discriminatory incommunicado detentions, including possible enforced disappearances, in some cases in conditions of confinement that may violate the prohibition on torture; violent repression of peaceful protests, and more. Based on these findings, Amnesty International is joining the chorus of community voices calling for ICE to be abolished, immediately.
ICE must be abolished
Amnesty International’s findings demonstrate that the violations documented across the four operations were not isolated or exceptional incidents, but part of recurring patterns of abuse with devastating consequences for immigrants and entire communities.
“Masked and armed federal agents attacking people in the streets with impunity doesn’t make our communities safer — it puts everyone in danger,” said Daar. “ICE is fundamentally broken and cannot be fixed. For the U.S. government to have an immigration enforcement system that complies with international human rights law and standards, ICE needs to be abolished and we need to start over.”
ICE is fundamentally broken and cannot be fixed. For the U.S. government to have an immigration enforcement system that complies with international human rights law and standards, ICE needs to be abolished and we need to start over.”
Nadia Daar, Executive Director, Amnesty International USA.
ICE was created in the wake of the September 11, 2001 attacks, and an extremely problematic security framework was adopted in the years following. Amnesty International and other organizations have documented human rights violations committed by ICE and a troubling lack of oversight and accountability since its creation in 2003. However, the scale and horror that we have witnessed since January 2025, fueled by billions of new dollars and persistent impunity, has reached new levels.
Human rights violations
The four operations resulted in human rights violations against immigrants, asylum seekers and refugees, people profiled as immigrants, Black and Brown communities, and those who came to their aid and challenged the conduct of the Trump administration. They also created a pervasive climate of fear that extended throughout entire communities.
Across all four operations, Amnesty International documented:
· Racially discriminatory immigration enforcement operations and arbitrary detention
· Harassment, intimidation, degrading treatment and unjustified use of force by federal agents
· Use of lethal force and unlawful killings by federal agents, which should be investigated as extrajudicial executions
· Repression of protests and use of less lethal weapons, including tear gas
and pepper spray, by federal agents
· Unlawful surveillance and facial recognition technology
· Inhumane detention conditions and denial of due process, which should be investigated as torture
· Unlawful incommunicado detention and possible acts of enforced disappearance
As the report documents, ICE agents operated within an institutional environment – openly supported and expanded by the Trump administration – in which violent and racially discriminatory immigration enforcement practices were encouraged by senior government officials, including President Trump. Agents frequently operated with masks and without identification; safeguards intended to prevent and address misconduct were weakened or dismantled; and human rights violations were rarely followed by meaningful investigation or accountability.
The report details an account from Minnesota State Representative Liish Kozlowski, who is Obijwe-Latine, who said: “My cousin was in her car going to work with her husband. ICE rolled up, literally looking for Black and Brown people. They smashed her window at gun point. They roughed her up; she was pregnant. Her husband yelled ‘She’s Native American, here’s her Tribal ID card’. An ICE agent responded, ‘That doesn’t [expletive] matter, this is our land now’.”
“My cousin was in her car going to work with her husband. ICE rolled up, literally looking for Black and Brown people. They smashed her window at gun point. They roughed her up; she was pregnant. Her husband yelled ‘She’s Native American, here’s her Tribal ID card’. An ICE agent responded, ‘That doesn’t [expletive] matter, this is our land now’.”
This is just one example from dozens in the report where ICE agents appeared to be engaging in explicit racial profiling.
“Racially profiling and snatching people off the street, separating families and arbitrarily detaining people are not only unlawful, cruel practices, but profoundly damaging,” said Ana Piquer, Americas Director at Amnesty International. “These practices violate human rights and cause fear and psychological distress and long-lasting health concerns to children, other family members and entire communities.”
Racially profiling and snatching people off the street, separating families and arbitrarily detaining people are not only unlawful, cruel practices, but profoundly damaging,”
Ana Piquer, Americas Director at Amnesty International.
The report also highlights how communities came together to resist and protect one another. These networks played an essential role in documenting human rights violations, and being there for their neighbors, through mutual aid networks, constitutional observer trainings, rapid response networks, walking school buses, and more in order to stand by and protect those most directly impacted. Protests were one important tool of resistance, but were frequently met with additional acts of lawlessness by ICE and Border Patrol agents.
For example, in Chicago, the Broadview facility became a focal point for protesting against ICE and Border Patrol’s actions in the city. Reverend David Black, who frequently went to the Broadview facility to do ministry, said, “The escalation of violence by ICE and CBP at Broadview when we were just praying and chanting was terrifying.” During one ministry service he led at the facility, Reverend Black, who was dressed as Clergy, was calling on three federal agents who were standing on the facility’s roof to repent, when the agents suddenly shot him in the face, arms and torso with exploding pellets of pepper spray. He is one of the numerous people whose experiences are documented in the report.
The report highlights numerous additional human rights violations during these cruel immigration enforcement operations. Amnesty International researchers interviewed 154 people across the four locations, allowing the organization to analyze how immigration enforcement operations affect diverse communities across different political, legal, and historical contexts, and to conclude that the human rights violations documented reflect broader national patterns rather than being isolated local incidents.
“It is heartbreaking to see the pain and suffering caused by this Administration as it criminalizes and demonizes immigrants,” said Daar. “I’m also hopeful – communities have rallied around those targeted and in some instances forced the Trump administration to back down. We must hold accountable those government officials responsible for this reign of terror, and we must keep fighting for an immigration system that is grounded in human rights and dignity, not cruelty.”
It is heartbreaking to see the pain and suffering caused by this Administration as it criminalizes and demonizes immigrants. Fears of return to war as Tigray rebels launch offensive against Ethiopian army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:43:09 UTC
22:43:09 KST

There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by fighters from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara and the formation of a new rebel alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed.
About 600,000 people died between 2020 and 2022 during a devastating war between the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict.
On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including the TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, the TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”.
The TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border.
Flights to the historic Ethiopian town of Lalibela were also suspended on Thursday because of nearby fighting, while people in Tigray stocked up on food and cash, with one resident telling Reuters that people there feared they could face siege conditions similar to those during the previous war.
A resident of Adigrat, a city close to the Eritrean border, described panic-buying and shops emptying. “Food shortages are worsening as market shelves sit empty … Essential medicines remain scarce and astronomically expensive,” he told Reuters. “Daily survival has become a constant calculation.”
The TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara.
The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital.
In its first public comments on the fighting, Ethiopia’s army said on Thursday it had foiled the attacks and killed, wounded or captured more than 500 enemy fighters.
Analysts say the TPLF has support from Ethiopia’s neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea. The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.”
The current fighting reflects shifting dynamics from the civil war, when Eritrea and Fano, an insurgent group that is now part of the new alliance, both fought with the government against the Tigrayans.
Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, the Ethiopian president, Taye Atske-Selassie Amde, decried “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”. He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours.
Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, said members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while with the financial backing of Eritrea. Eritrea has repeatedly denied similar accusations.
The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, eventually triggering the civil war.
The renewed fighting marks the most serious challenge yet to the 2022 Pretoria agreement, which ended the civil war and maintained an uneasy calm until late last year, when clashes resumed.
It raises fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across and further destabilise a region already strained by war in neighbouring Sudan and tensions along the Red Sea.
On Wednesday, the African Union chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, urged “utmost restraint” from the warring parties and resumption of direct talks. An EU spokesperson called for “immediate de-escalation” and a recommitment to the Pretoria agreement.
In the 2020-22 war, Tigray was largely cut off from the outside world as communications were severed, and access to food, cash and medicines was severely restricted, pushing hundreds of thousands of people into famine-like conditions.
AFP and Reuters contributed reporting

US no longer ally it once was, Belgian foreign ministry document says: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:42:29 UTC
22:42:29 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Belgium's foreign ministry said in an internal document that the US is “no longer the ally it has been in the past,” the Financial Times reported Thursday.
The paper, prepared by the ministry's Americas and Caribbean unit in October 2025 and seen by the newspaper, calls for a “thorough re-evaluation” of Belgium's and the EU's relationship with Washington.
It also warns that developments in the US could compromise vital Belgian and EU interests.
The document recommends maintaining engagement with the Trump administration while calibrating Belgian officials' visits and public actions to protect the country's interests. It says Brussels should seek areas of cooperation without being seen by Washington as hostile.
Contacts with US states and major cities should be “significantly reinforced,” the paper says, while also recommending continued discussions with Democratic politicians, engagement with Congress and efforts to identify emerging figures in both parties who could influence future US policy.
The document notes that Trump respects royal families. Since it was drafted, Belgium's King Philippe has visited the US, while Queen Mathilde accompanied Belgian ministers to New York for this week's UN General Assembly, according to the FT. 
Trade, defense, security
The ministry identifies economic relations, military spending, migration and cooperation against drug trafficking and organized crime as key issues in managing ties with the US.
On trade, the document warns that deeper engagement could leave Belgium more exposed to disputes and possible US protectionist measures.
“Diversifying our partnerships is more essential than ever,” it concludes.
The document says purchases of American weapons are viewed favorably by the Trump administration but recommends increasing purchases of European military equipment as well.
It identifies the fight against drug trafficking and organized crime as a promising area for cooperation. Belgium is a major entry point for cocaine trafficking through the port of Antwerp, according to the EU Drugs Agency.
However, the leaked document also raises concerns about differences between US and European approaches to drug gangs, surveillance and counterterrorism. It warns that US foreign aid cuts could strengthen criminal organizations by reducing other sources of employment, according to the report.
A Belgian foreign ministry spokesperson told the FT that the paper was an “internal working document” and should be distinguished from an agreed government strategy.
Assessing how changes in US policy affect Belgian interests is part of the ministry's regular work, the spokesperson added.
The White House did not respond to the newspaper's request for comment.

Israel offers cash to firms hit by trade ban; Europe dithers on new rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:42:05 UTC
22:42:05 KST

Israel offers cash to firms hit by trade ban; Europe dithers on new rules
Israel hopes to redirect goods from illegal Israeli settlements towards markets in Asia and South America. But the effect of European bans on trade itself is under question, with many nations yet to implement them.
The Israeli government plans to pay companies in illegal settlements up to 200,000 shekels ($54,000) following a commitment by European countries to ban their goods amid escalating human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
Roey Fisher, head of Israel’s Foreign Trade Administration at the Ministry of Economy and Industry, told Israeli media outlet Calcalist that it has set up a “dedicated team” to help companies operating in illegal settlements find “alternative markets”, including the Philippines, India, the United Arab Emirates, Chile and Argentina. The assistance also covers exporters of fresh produce, and more than 25 applications for assistance have already been submitted by companies expected to be affected, the report added.

list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Far-right UK activist Daniel Thomas arrested after slashing dinghy
- list 2 of 4Morocco’s elections: Fragmentation, disengagement and PJD’s major comeback
- list 3 of 4Tyson Fury to face British rival Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on December 11
- list 4 of 4Tunisia fuel strike highlights growing economic and political anger
Fisher, however, played down the immediate reach of the bans. “Not everyone is boycotting us,” he told Calcalist, pointing to differences between European countries. “Right now, Spain and the Netherlands are among the only places in Europe where there is an effective boycott,” he said. “The countries that have announced boycotts, including England, have not applied them to all Israeli exports.”
Julie Norman, an associate fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera the grants would provide a “significant lift” for exporters seeking new markets, but said the financial impact of the bans remained “uncertain”. She said the grants were unlikely to fully offset lost sales in the short term, with the UK and EU together accounting for “over a third of Israel’s exports”.
But Norman said the government support highlighted a broader challenge for countries seeking to economically target settlements. “The question of the grants highlights the challenge for states like the UK or European states when trying to target the settlements, when the settlements themselves are still supported by the Israeli government,” she said.
Shamiul Joarder, director at Friends of Al-Aqsa, a UK-based nonprofit, told Al Jazeera that government support helping exporters find alternative markets could “cushion the commercial impact” of the bans. “This demonstrates why targeting settlement goods alone is insufficient, as the settlement economy can simply redirect its trade elsewhere,” he added.
Which import bans are actually in force?
While a growing number of countries have pledged to restrict trade with Israeli settlements, far fewer have actually put those measures into force. On September 8, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom issued a joint statement saying they intended to introduce national restrictions, support restrictions at the European level or were considering such measures.
But among those countries, only a handful have enacted restrictions. Spain and Ireland have introduced measures targeting imports of settlement goods, while the Netherlands brought its ban into force on September 22.
The Dutch measure goes further than some others. It prohibits the import, purchase and sale of goods from illegal Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territory, as well as services facilitating that trade and attempts to circumvent the restrictions. Its significance also extends beyond the Dutch market, with the Netherlands serving as a major gateway for goods entering the rest of Europe.
Elsewhere, measures remain at various stages and are not yet operational. Belgium’s cabinet approved a draft measure on July 18 that would systematically refuse import permits for goods identified as coming from Israeli settlements. But the proposal includes a 120-day transition period and was sent to the Council of State for an opinion, meaning cabinet approval alone did not bring it into force.
Norway has put forward draft legislation that would go further than an import ban, prohibiting both imports from and exports to illegal Israeli settlements. But the legislation has yet to enter into force, with the Norwegian government listing it as still under consideration.
France and Canada have pledged national measures that have yet to take effect. Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Poland, Portugal and Sweden signed the joint statement, but none has announced that a national ban on settlement goods has entered into force. Sweden has instead proposed restrictions at the EU level, including higher tariffs on settlement goods and new export-certificate requirements.
Meanwhile, in the UK, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the legislation would be introduced within six to nine months, leaving a gap between the government’s pledge and any ban taking legal effect.
Norman said the UK’s six-to-nine-month timetable could give officials time to work through the practical details of implementing the ban. “I think that is to just work out logistics, and for UK firms to adapt so they don’t hurt their own domestic businesses,” she said.
The delay could also allow the government to wait for Israel’s elections, she added, “and see what the outcome is there, and how a new government approaches settlement expansion”.
Even in the United States, Israel’s closest ally, a group of senators has introduced a separate bill seeking sanctions against people involved in constructing Israel’s E1 settlement project in the occupied West Bank. It remains a proposal rather than a trade restriction in force.
But Israeli media reports suggest the country also sees the US as a potential avenue for relief should the import bans come into force, with lobbyists reportedly pushing for sanctions relief. There have also been warnings that the bans could trigger sanctions from US states under anti-boycott legislation.

Trump swoons over strongman soulmate Xi – are you feeling jealous, Vladimir?
David Smith
One is an authoritarian who represses the media with a strong allergy to democratic elections. The other is head of the Chinese Communist party.
Donald Trump welcomed the Chinese president, XiJinping, to the White House on Thursday, setting the stage for a scene quite unlike anything the august old building has seen over more than two centuries.
And while Chinese state media had been welcomed onto the White House grounds, many US journalists had not, thanks to Trump’s ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico. Michael McFaul, a former US diplomat, described the vivid contrast as “wrong and embarrassing”.
That was hard to deny, given that China ranks 178th in Reporters Without Borders’ press freedom index, ahead of only North Korea and Eritrea (the US, for the record, is down to 64th). But it also made perfect sense because, whereas past presidents sought to make China more like the US, Trump evidently aspires to make the US more like China.
The deference was deafening. On Wednesday night he and his wife, Melania, travelled to Joint Base Andrews in Maryland to greet Xi off his plane – a schlep that US presidents rarely make for foreign leaders – and rolled out a literal red carpet for his strongman soulmate.
Chuck Schumer, the Democratic minority leader, observed on X: “If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll roll out the red carpet for you…”
Vladimir, are you feeling jealous yet?
Xi is such a star that he got two welcomes. On Thursday morning, there were more flags, more trumpet blasts, and another red carpet as the Trumps emerged from the White House south portico to greet Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan.
Then it was on to the grand foyer for statements – with no reporter questions allowed, of course – before the two delegations, sitting in neat rows. Trump went first. You can tell when he’s on his best behaviour because he (mostly) sticks to the teleprompter.
But it was Xi, speaking more substantially, who looked like he owned the place. Trump, sitting behind with hands clasped together, had the appearance of junior partner. Xi said he was ready to work with the president to “steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course toward the future”.
Then he got to the meat in the sandwich, insisting that the countries can “co-exist in peace” and their competition “should be a healthy one”. “The Thucydides trap can be overcome,” Xi declared, in a tacit acknowledgement that China is threatening to displace the US as the world’s superpower.
But with more flattery, he added:
Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand.
None of this was covered by the usual cable news networks because they were boycotting shared coverage, in solidarity with the banned outlets.
Trump then sat down with the world’s biggest jailer of journalists for bilateral talks. Perhaps he was seeking tips.
When they met face to face, was this a Reagan-Gorbachev style summit of great historical import, discussing guardrails on AI and other ways not to destroy the world? Maybe not.
By the afternoon, some of the banned reporters had been allowed back on to the White House campus after a judge found Trump’s action to be unconstitutional. It must have been a tricky one to explain to Xi. He remains the master of repression; Trump is merely The Apprentice.

Denmark warns Russia could escalate hybrid attacks against NATO in coming months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:40:25 UTC
22:40:25 KST

Russia is likely to intensify its hybrid campaign against NATO and Western countries in the coming months, carrying out more frequent attacks with potentially greater consequences, Denmark's military intelligence service warned on Sept. 24.
The Danish Defence Intelligence Service (DDIS) said Russia had become increasingly willing to take risks as the security situation in Europe deteriorates.
"Russia will intensify its hybrid war by carrying out more frequent attacks against the West and NATO, with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past," the agency said in its latest threat assessment.
The attacks could include destructive cyber operations targeting critical infrastructure as well as sabotage carrying a significant risk of casualties, according to the assessment.
DDIS also warned of a "low but growing risk" that Russia could carry out a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia, even while the war in Ukraine continues.
"A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia's part" and could take place "in the coming months," the agency said.
Such an attack could involve isolated drone or missile strikes against infrastructure supporting Ukraine, with Russia potentially claiming that the weapons crossed into NATO territory because of Ukrainian electronic warfare, according to the assessment.
DDIS also said Russia could stage a false-flag attack using Ukrainian-made drones or deploy a limited number of troops, potentially without national insignia, into a NATO country bordering Russia.
The purpose would be to divert European resources away from Ukraine and test whether NATO members could agree on a collective response, according to the agency.
The warning comes amid a rise in suspected sabotage and other hostile activity across Europe. DDIS cited an attempted drone attack on Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport, which German authorities have attributed to Russia, as well as warnings from Denmark's domestic intelligence service that Russia is preparing sabotage against Danish defence companies.
It also pointed to increasingly aggressive encounters between Russian and NATO forces in the Baltic Sea region. On Sept. 14, a Russian frigate off the Danish coast fired flares toward a Danish military helicopter sent to photograph the vessel, an incident DDIS described as the most serious involving Danish forces to date.
The assessment said Russia is currently under greater pressure than at any previous point in its war against Ukraine, citing heavy battlefield losses, Ukrainian long-range strikes and mounting strain on the Russian economy.
At the same time, DDIS assessed that Russian President Vladimir Putin remains unlikely to compromise on Moscow's core war aims and may see the next several years as a "window of opportunity" before European military capabilities grow significantly stronger.
Despite the increased risk of escalation, DDIS said it saw no indication that Russia was preparing a full-scale invasion of a NATO country. Such an invasion remains "highly unlikely," according to the assessment, although the agency said it could not be ruled out entirely.
The intelligence service estimated that Russia would need at least six months to prepare the forces required for an invasion.
Its previous assessment, published in February 2025, estimated that under certain conditions Russia could become capable of fighting a local war against a neighboring country within about six months, a regional war involving several Baltic-area states within roughly two years, and a large-scale European war within around five years.

Russia’s state-backed messaging app Max can secretly change how it surveils individual users, researchers at InterSecLab find
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:40:22 UTC
22:40:22 KST

Russia’s state-backed messaging app Max can secretly change how it surveils individual users, researchers at InterSecLab find
The Kremlin-backed Max messenger has broad capabilities for tracking users, but their configuration can vary from account to account and is controlled by its developer, the Russian social media company VK. That’s according to a new report from the digital security lab InterSecLab, which Meduza has reviewed. For nine weeks, the report’s authors observed how the messenger worked using real accounts, intercepted its network traffic before the point of encryption, and checked each observation against the app’s code. Here are the key findings from the lab’s report.
Key finding: Max behaves differently depending on the user. VK can activate specific features for individual accounts without updating the app or changing its interface.
Max has no end-to-end encryption, and VK can access the contents of users’ correspondence. In the messenger’s “secret chats,” messages aren’t encrypted: they are simply deleted on a timer. The researchers say the term “secret chat” is deliberately misleading in Max’s case, since Telegram uses the same term for a mode of correspondence that does have end-to-end encryption.
Max can be configured individually for each account to: decrypt voice messages on VK’s servers, block message sending when a VPN is detected, collect data on the user’s actions within the app, and send information about the user’s identity to third-party services. The researchers also found a feature that was not active during testing: it would let Max obtain information about all the apps installed on a user’s device.
Every time Max launches, it sends VK a single report on the user’s network environment: public IP address, mobile carrier information, VPN activity, and the availability of other internet services. VK updates this report each time the app opens. The researchers say the IP address alone is enough to determine a user’s approximate location.
Max uploads a user’s entire address book to VK’s servers in unencrypted form. The app matches the names in it to phone numbers and syncs the data every time changes are made. In the process, VK gains access to the numbers of people who never registered with Max. One earlier analysis of the app claimed that numbers were hashed before being uploaded, but InterSecLab’s researchers disproved this.
A phone number alone can reveal a great deal about a Max user. In response to a request, Max returns the account ID, display name, and account creation date, then within 15 minutes sends information on when the user was last online. The person being searched for receives no notification of any kind, and the researchers found no limit on how many such requests can be made.
Max stops working if it detects a VPN, requiring users to turn it off before they can send a message. The restriction can be bypassed by moving the VPN to the router, the researchers wrote, though not all users know this workaround.
New Max accounts receive a curated list of 25 recommended channels before users make a single search query. The list includes state media outlets, officials, and pro-war journalists, including accounts for the Russian state news agency RIA Novosti, the Russian television channel NTV, Izvestia, Vladimir Solovyov, and Dmitry Medvedev.

POCSO case cannot be quashed on settlement, says Delhi HC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:38:59 UTC
22:38:59 KST

“POCSO offence cannot be quashed on basis of compromise”, says Delhi High Court
NEW DELHI: The Delhi High Court has held that proceedings under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act cannot be quashed on the basis of a compromise between a child victim or the victim's family and the accused.Justice Sachin Datta made the observation while dismissing a petition seeking quashing of an FIR and related proceedings on the basis of a settlement allegedly reached with the victim with the intervention of her family, according to news agency ANI.The court noted that the case involved allegations of aggravated penetrative sexual assault against a child by a person allegedly in a position of trust or authority. It observed that such offences are heinous and have a serious impact on society.The high court relied on a Supreme Court judgment which held that while a high court has inherent powers to quash criminal proceedings in appropriate cases where parties have settled their dispute, such powers must be exercised after considering the nature and gravity of the offence.
The Supreme Court has held that heinous and serious offences, including rape, ordinarily cannot be quashed merely because the victim or the victim’s family and the accused have reached a settlement, as such offences are not private in nature and have a serious impact on society.
Applying the principle, the Delhi high court held that an offence under the POCSO Act cannot be compromised by the child victim or the victim’s family. It said quashing the proceedings at this stage on the basis of a compromise would defeat the object of the statute and the ends of justice.

How Türkiye is helping take Iraqi oil to international markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:38:37 UTC
22:38:37 KST

Türkiye is emerging as an increasingly important route for Iraqi crude to reach international markets as disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz continue following the US-Israel war on Iran.
Iraq is currently exporting around 2.6 million barrels per day (bpd) from its southern ports and producing more than three million bpd from southern fields, Bassem Abdul Karim, head of the state-run Basra Oil Company said on Thursday.
Around 250,000 bpd of Basra crude is now being transported overland to Kirkuk before entering the northern pipeline network and reaching Türkiye’s Mediterranean port of Ceyhan.
The volumes remain relatively small compared with Iraq’s overall oil production, but the shift has brought renewed attention to the decades-old Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline as an alternative export corridor.
From Basra to Ceyhan
Iraq launched a pilot operation in September to transport crude by road from its southern oilfields to storage facilities in Kirkuk.
The operation, run by Iraq’s KAR Group, uses tanker trucks to carry crude north before it is pumped through the northern pipeline network and onwards to Türkiye.
During an initial two-day trial, 209 tanker trucks transported more than six million litres of crude from southern Iraq to Kirkuk.
The operation builds on efforts that began earlier this year.
Around 90,000 bpd of Basra crude was being transported north by April. The target increased to 140,000 bpd in May before reaching around 250,000 bpd by September.
The rapid expansion highlights Baghdad’s efforts to connect its major southern oilfields with a northern export corridor that bypasses the Gulf.
At the centre of the route is the Iraq-Türkiye Crude Oil Pipeline, commonly known as the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline.
Built in the 1970s, the pipeline connects northern Iraq with Ceyhan on Türkiye’s Mediterranean coast. Its design capacity has reached as much as 1.6 million bpd, although actual flows have historically remained far below that level.
Ceyhan’s location gives Iraq an important advantage: tankers departing the terminal can enter the Mediterranean directly without passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
Türkiye and Iraq deepen energy ties
Ankara and Baghdad have also taken steps to expand the corridor.
On August 1, Türkiye and Iraq signed a one-year agreement aimed at maximising use of the pipeline while negotiations continue over a longer-term energy framework.
The agreement followed talks between Turkish Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar and Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair.
Under the arrangement, Iraq committed to increasing pipeline flows from around 220,000 bpd towards a guaranteed capacity of 750,000 bpd as production around Kirkuk expands.
Bayraktar said the pipeline had become increasingly important for regional and global energy security, describing Türkiye’s role as extending beyond simply transporting Iraqi crude.
The cooperation also goes upstream. Turkish Petroleum Corporation, or TPAO, has secured a partnership stake in Iraq’s BP-operated Kirkuk oilfield, extending bilateral energy cooperation into upstream production.
Iraqi officials have floated an even more ambitious target of eventually supplying Türkiye with up to one million bpd.
Ceyhan's growing role
The expansion adds to Ceyhan’s existing importance as an international energy hub.
The Turkish port is already the Mediterranean endpoint of the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline, which carries Azerbaijani crude through Georgia and Türkiye.
Growing production from Türkiye’s Gabar oilfield has added another domestic source of crude flowing towards Ceyhan.
Turkish officials have also discussed expanding cooperation with Iraq beyond oil into natural gas and electricity, while Ankara sees the corridor as complementing the wider Development Road Project connecting the Gulf with Europe through Iraq and Türkiye.
Transporting hundreds of thousands of barrels by truck is considerably more complicated than moving crude directly by pipeline, making further infrastructure investment important if volumes continue to rise.
Nevertheless, the changing flows underline Türkiye’s growing importance to Iraq’s energy strategy.
A route created nearly half a century ago is once again providing Baghdad with access to the Mediterranean, while Ceyhan is strengthening its position as a gateway connecting Iraqi crude with international markets.

US steps up military activity near Iran – media
The US has stepped up military activity around the Strait of Hormuz, with reconnaissance aircraft spotted near Iranian territory and additional fighter jets reportedly deployed to the region, RIA Novosti reported on Thursday, citing sources.
US reconnaissance aircraft were observed overnight near the Iranian islands of Qeshm and Hengam, while aircraft and small drones were also seen over Kermanshah Province in western Iran, according to people familiar with the matter.
Washington has also reportedly transferred 12 F-16 fighter jets from Spangdahlem Air Base in Germany to the region, the source said, adding that the increased activity could signal a possible escalation.
The reported activity comes as oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has risen sharply. TankerTrackers, a vessel-tracking service, said this week that crude flows across the US Navy blockade line have doubled in less than a month to around 13 million barrels per day (bpd). It estimated actual Hormuz transits at about 10.35 million bpd after excluding exports from Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates and Mina al-Fahal in Oman.
The numbers have doubled in less than a month.
The total crude oil egress via the USN-BL is now 13 Mbpd, with estimated SoH transits at 10.35 Mbpd given that Fujairah and Mina al-Fahal together account for around 2.65 Mbpd on average.
This is partly attributed to Saudi Arabia… https://t.co/ZffcwAhQ4J
The Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy routes, has been a major flashpoint since the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran in February. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) moved to restrict shipping through the waterway following the initial strikes, while Washington later imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports. Oil flows through the strait fell from 21.6 million bpd in the final quarter of 2025 to 4.9 million in the second quarter of this year, according to US government data.
The tracking service attributed the increase partly to Saudi Arabia redirecting exports through the Persian Gulf following disruption to its East-West pipeline, as well as to daytime Hormuz crossings under additional US Central Command protection.
The East-West pipeline carries Saudi crude to the Red Sea, allowing exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. It had been transporting around 4 million bpd after the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted shipping through the strait, but was shut earlier this month following drone attacks that Riyadh said originated in Iraq, where Iranian-backed armed groups allegedly operate.
Saudi Arabia restarted the pipeline at a reduced rate this week, although a return to normal flows could reportedly take several weeks.
The developments follow renewed threats from US President Donald Trump against Tehran. Addressing the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said he faced a “big decision” between reaching an agreement with Iran and “annihilat[ing] the Islamic Republic.” He also called on other countries to join Washington in economically isolating Iran.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian responded by saying Tehran remained open to talks but would not negotiate under pressure.
US and Iranian officials also resumed contact on the sidelines of the General Assembly, with Tehran conveying its conditions for peace through Qatari mediators. They include an end to hostilities and the US naval blockade, the release of frozen Iranian assets, and arrangements for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei reportedly told Iranian state television that Tehran would not resume negotiations with Washington until its conditions are met.

Defence spending with Scottish industry rises above £2.5 billion

    Government investment in Scottish defence sector rose by 13% in real terms to £2.53 billion in 2025/26, marking the highest level of industry investment since records began.
- 
    Substantial investment translates to £460 for every person living in Scotland up from £390 the previous year.
- 
    Part of Government’s work to rebuild the nation’s defence industrial base, boosting defence readiness and the reindustrialisation of Britain.
Communities across Scotland are feeling the benefit of the government’s drive to strengthen Britain’s defence industrial base, new figures reveal.
In a significant boost to the Scottish economy, the figures, which cover the 2025/26 financial year, show a 13% increase in real terms spending, taking the total to £2.53 billion.
As the government accelerates efforts to reindustrialise Britain and strengthen deterrence, there has been a significant boost in investment in the electronics sector by 33%, ensuring UK industry can deliver at scale the modern capability and resilience the armed forces depend on.
The figures demonstrate how the government is placing the defence industrial base at the centre of national renewal, with rising investment generating jobs and opportunities in towns and cities across the UK, lifting living standards and increasing household incomes.
Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting MP, said:
  We cannot strengthen our deterrence without a strong, sovereign defence industry here at home, and Scotland is at the heart of that.
That’s why we are unashamedly backing British, using the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War to back jobs and skills in Scotland to build the capability and technology we need to keep us safe in a more dangerous world.
Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander said:
  The UK Government is delivering a defence dividend for Scotland. Scotland’s defence sector is a powerhouse of innovation and expertise and a key driver for economic growth. The figures mark a significant increase on the previous year, representing the highest level of Scottish industry investment since records began. This significant spending equates to £460 for every person in Scotland, up from £390 the year before.
The Ministry of Defence maintains a substantial footprint in Scotland, supporting 12,200 jobs. Scotland is home to a significant defence industrial base, with major employers including BAE Systems, Babcock International and Rolls-Royce, alongside key military hubs HMNB Clyde and RAF Lossiemouth.
The news builds on the work of the Defence Investment Plan, which commits £298 billion to UK defence over the next four years. The plan will drive sustained investment across British industry, ensuring the UK’s defence sector remains a cornerstone of the country’s economic renewal.

Excavations at Türkiye's Aspendos reveal settlement dating back 6,000 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:37:06 UTC
22:37:06 KST

Süleyman Elcin, Beril Çanakcı
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Recent excavations at Aspendos have revealed that the site was inhabited as early as 6,000 years ago.
Located in the Serik district of Antalya province, Aspendos, an ancient city in southern Türkiye known for its exceptionally well-preserved theater and aqueducts, was one of the important cities of ancient Pamphylia. Excavations are being conducted under the direction of Mustafa Bilgin, an associate professor at Afyon Kocatepe University, as part of the Culture and Tourism Ministry's Heritage for the Future Project.
The ancient city is best known for its nearly 2,000-year-old Roman theater, considered among the best-preserved ancient theaters in Anatolia. It also features aqueducts, an agora, a monumental fountain, a temple, stadium, council building and an ancient theater street.
Recent excavations have also uncovered a depiction of the river god Eurymedon dating to the third century, adding to the site's archaeological significance.
The discoveries have pushed the known history of settlement at Aspendos back well before the Iron Age.
Bilgin told Anadolu that the ancient theater was a rare example in Anatolian and Mediterranean archaeology because it has retained nearly all of its architectural elements.
He said most of the structures are standing almost to roof level, while monumental structures reflecting the landscape of the period can still be seen on the acropolis.
"Through our recent excavations, we understood that the history of the ancient city dates back 6,000 years from today," said Bilgin.
"This fertile geography was not an area that had only been settled from the Iron Age onward. We realized this, and it was an important archaeological finding for us," he said.
Archaeologists found evidence dating to the Late Chalcolithic Period in soundings beneath the floors of two-story shops, said Bilgin.
"Plates, bowls and various tools from that period revealed that the historical past of Aspendos' acropolis dates back to 3500-4000 B.C.," he said.
Bilgin described Aspendos as a "multilayered archaeological site," noting that most of its structures have survived in a form consistent with their identity in antiquity.
"This makes Aspendos an important destination in terms of tourism and archaeology," he said.
The site has also drawn increased visitor interest since the Culture and Tourism Ministry introduced night museum visits.
"Visiting the ancient theater and monumental structures at night, in that atmosphere, is very enjoyable for visitors," he said.
