For dessert, the guests will be treated to vanilla cremeux with sour cherry confit and walnut frangipane, as well as ice cream with honey from the White House bee hives.
The guest list includes Silicon Valley titans like Apple's Tim Cook, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, Alphabet's Sundar Pichai, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Tesla's Elon Musk and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
"I would say you have the entire tech world, the entire banking world and a lot more," Trump told reporters earlier in the week.
US, Iran should return to talks under memorandum of understanding, Xi says
Chinese leader Xi Jinping said he supported the US and Iran's memorandum of understanding to end the Iran war, Xinhua state agency reported.
Xi said he expressed hope that the US and Iran would return to resolving issues through dialogue and negotiation under the agreement as soon as possible.
Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have held lengthy indirect talks with Iranian officials during the UN gathering earlier this week.
US and Iranian negotiators were exploring a phased path out of the war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran, Reuters reported.
Melania Trump, Madame Peng head to Asian art museum
First Lady Melania Trump and Xi's wife Peng Liyuan left their husbands behind to tour one of the largest Asian art museums in the US.
The visit to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art in Washington was supposed to celebrate cultural ties between the US and China.
Both wives are known for their focus on soft power and cultural issues, one is a former fashion model and the other a soprano.
A choir of young school children from the Hope Chinese School sang to the duo as they toured the building, singing famous Chinese folk songs including "Song and Smile" and "Jasmine Flower."
It's the first public meeting between the two spouses in nearly a decade, since a 2017 encounter in Beijing. A crowd had gathered on the sidewalk across from the museum, some waving Chinese and American flags.
Trump says the pair had a 'great meeting,' takes Xi inside presidential helicopter
Trump's first comments to reporters after the talks were brief in the extreme.
In response to shouted questions as he took Xi to board the Marine One presidential helicopter for a brief tour, he told reporters, "We had a great meeting."
Images from the meeting showed that Chinese Vice Premier Hi Lifeng and Foreign Minister Wang Yi attended at least part of the talks, as did US Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
Xi left the White House after the meeting, but will be back later for the state dinner.
Xi tells Trump China's position on Taiwan and territory is 'crystal clear'
China's Xinhua news agency is reporting comments it says Xi Jinping relayed to Donald Trump during their talks in the Oval Office.
Xi said he hoped the United States would continue to oppose "Taiwan independence" and handle the question of Taiwan with "prudence," according to Xinhua.
He reportedly told the US president that China's position on safeguarding its national unity and territorial integrity was "crystal clear."
The US holds a complicated position when it comes to Taiwan. On the one hand, it is the small island nation's most important security guarantor. However, it has no formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan and does not recognize it as an independent country as part of its adherence to the so-called "one China" principle Beijing insists upon from all partners.
Xi also reportedly told Trump that China would support the US and Iran returning to negotiations "as soon as possible" as their naval standoff in the Persian Gulf drags well past the six-month mark.

DW explores fears over cybersecurity threats, autonomous AI behavior and even bioterrorism, while explaining why both Washington and Beijing see AI as a strategic priority.
With calls mounting for international oversight, what stance will US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping adopt?
CNN, MS NOW, Politico journalists are back at White House
Hours after a federal judge ordered Trump to lift the ban, US news outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico announced that they had been granted access to the White House.
Trump and Xi begin talks in Oval Office
After delivering their opening remarks and reviewing the military troops in the Rose Garden, Trump and Xi proceeded to the Oval Office for discussions.
Other US and Chinese officials joined them.
China to send two pandas to Atlanta zoo, Xi says
Speaking at the White House, Xi Jinping announced that a pair of pandas will soon make their home at Zoo Atlanta.
This isn't the first time Chinese pandas have been sent to a U.S. zoo. It's also an example of what's known as "panda diplomacy." Through this program, China lends the animals to select zoos around the world.
Xi also revealed that Beijing plans to invite 100,000 young Americans to visit China for cultural exchange and study over the next five years.
Xi thanks Trump for 'warm hospitality,' seeks to 'expand cooperation'
China's President Xi Jinping in turn thanked Donald Trump for his "warm hospitality," after the US president last night went to greet the Chinese leader and their wife on the tarmac at the airfeld.
In his opening remarks, as rendered by his interpreter, Xi said he was visiting the US to "carry on our friendship, expand cooperation and promote well-being of both our peoples."
He said that both the US and China were great countries with great people.
"I'm very glad to pay a state visit to your beautiful country, the United States of America," Xi said. "Thank you President Trump and Mrs. Trump for the warm hospitality that you have extended to me and my wife."

Trump hosts Xi for state dinner with tech CEOs

- Donald Trump and Xi Jinping and their wives attended a state dinner hosted in honor of the Chinese leader.
- State dinner featured a tech-heavy guest list, with Sam Altman, Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Nvidia chief Jensen Huang in attendance.
- Trump and Xi held a bilateral discussion this afternoon where Xi urged the US to oppose "Taiwan independence," according to a readout from Xinhua.
- In remarks after Xi's arrival on Thursday, Trump emphasized his "truly great friendship" with Xi.
Follow along here for live updates on Xi's state visit to the US:
What you need to know about Xi's meeting with Trump in Washington so far
US President Donald Trump on Thursday rolled out the red carpet for China's Xi Jinping on the Chinese president's first state visit to Washington in over a decade.
Ahead of the meeting, Xi said the US and China "should be partners rather than rivals," while Trump hailed his "truly great friendship" with the Chinese president. However, no breakthrough was expected in the trade tensions between the world's two largest economies.
The talks centered on the Middle East, Ukraine and the Korean Peninsula, according to a statement by Beijing. The US has not provided details about the meeting.
After the talks, Xi attended a lavish state dinner with Trump and US tech executives, including Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and Tesla's Elon Musk.
Trump described the event as the "hottest ticket in town" and said the "entire tech world" and "entire banking world and a lot more" would attend.
On Friday, Xi is scheduled to visit the National Archives, where the US Declaration of Independence, Constitution and Bill of Rights are held.
Protesters gather in downtown Washington to protest Xi's visit
A few hundred protesters gathered near the White House to rally against Xi Jinping's visit to the US.
Protesters highlighted a number of issues, from calls for religious freedom and autonomy in Tibet, Hong Kong and the Xinjiang region to demands that China refrain from interfering in Taiwan.
Protesters gathered in Lafayette Park, north of the White House, while other groups gathered outside the Chinese embassy. Pro-Xi rallies were also held in Washington.
Trump says he and Xi have 'never gotten along better' at dinner toast
US President Donald Trump continued to heap praise on his guest, Chinese President Xi Jinping, during a White House state dinner on Thursday.
"President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we've never gotten along better," Trump said during his toast, adding that "together, we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."
Xi noted in his own toast that "President Trump has pledged to make America great again" and that "China is committed to achieving great national rejuvenation."
"These two goals are both ambitious and can surely be mutually reinforcing," Xi said.
Earlier discussions between Xi and Trump touched on tensions over Taiwan, trade and artificial intelligence.
State dinner includes tech-heavy guest list, but Chinese CEOs are missing
Apart from the heads of state and their spouses, the list of invitees to the state dinner included a host of big tech names.
Industry titans including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman, and Dell Technologies chairman and CEO Michael Dell were all in attendance.
If this sounds familiar, it's because a similar group of tech leaders also accompanied Trump on his state visit to China in May. Names such as Nvidia's Jensen Huang, former Apple CEO Tim Cook, and once again Musk, were hosted by the Chinese president at a state dinner in the Great Hall of the People.
But Chinese CEOs are conspicuously missing on the guest list this evening in Washington as bringing Chinese firms to the US may raise more questions than it answers, experts said.
The Associated Press reported that US and Chinese planners did discuss including notable Chinese companies, but that one obstacle was that the US side was slow to suggest protocols and what roles the Chinese CEOs would have in the state visit.
Just like on Thursday, despite the star-studded business attendance, few major deals were announced during Trump's visit to China.

Has China received US F-35 parts by diverting an Australian shipment?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:36:22 UTC
22:36:22 KST

Has China received US F-35 parts by diverting an Australian shipment?
Australia and US investigate F-35 parts mistakenly sent to Hong Kong amid concerns over sensitive military technology.
The United States is investigating reports that parts of its advanced F-35 stealth fighter jet programme were diverted to Hong Kong while being shipped from Australia to the US.
The incident last week has prompted questions over whether China may have gained access to components of one of Washington’s most sophisticated weapons systems.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2US military says F-35B jet fighter crashes in California, pilot safe
- list 2 of 2Trump administration approves sale of F-35 jets to Saudi Arabia
There has been no suggestion so far from US or Australian authorities that Beijing deliberately diverted the shipment or accessed the technology.
On Tuesday, Australia’s Defence Minister Richard Marles said the components involved were not “sensitive”. China’s Foreign Ministry says it was not aware of the incident.
So, what happened and how serious was this incident?
What do we know?
On Saturday, US media outlet Politico reported that a consignment of F-35 components, including a cockpit canopy designed with radar-deflecting technology and a weapons-bay door, was unexpectedly rerouted to Hong Kong after leaving Australia.
The Pentagon’s F-35 Joint Programme Office said it was aware of “a shipment issue” involving components from the fighter jet and was working with US authorities and industry partners to recover them.
“We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the office said.
Marles confirmed the incident and revealed that Australia was helping the US and Lockheed Martin, the F-35’s main contractor, to investigate what happened. “We are examining very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end,” he said. “Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Australia has 72 F-35s and is one of seven countries outside the US which share a global pool of spare parts. A warehouse at Williamtown, north of Sydney, serves as an Asia-Pacific hub supporting the warplanes.
Why was the shipment diverted to Hong Kong?
It is unclear. Neither the Pentagon nor Australian authorities have publicly explained why the shipment went to Hong Kong and there is no evidence showing that China was responsible for its diversion.
While Lockheed Martin manages the global spare-parts programme, two sources told the AFP news agency that the programme itself is controlled by the US military. Australian defence officials have previously said Canberra does not control or direct the export of F-35 components from the Williamtown warehouse.
Alex Gatopoulos, Al Jazeera’s defence editor, said the international nature of the programme makes its logistics somewhat complex.
“The F-35 programme, whilst American, is supplied by subcontractors from 11 countries. Thirteen countries, apart from the US, fly the F-35, so the logistics network supplying each air force is vast,” he said.
Lockheed Martin Australia declined to discuss specific shipping procedures for security reasons but said every shipment is handled with “utmost diligence” and in accordance with US regulations.
How serious is this?
The incident is serious enough to warrant a Pentagon investigation to try to recover the components.
However, Australian Defence Minister Marles played down the security implications of the incident. “We’re not talking about sensitive equipment here or sensitive parts,” he said.
The concern stems from the F-35’s status as a fifth-generation stealth fighter incorporating stealth coatings, advanced radar, sensors and networking capabilities. More than 1,200 have been built, with 19 countries placing orders, according to the US Congressional Research Service.
China has also previously been accused of seeking information about the programme. A US Defense Science Board report released in 2013 alleged Chinese cyberattacks had accessed information from several Pentagon programmes, including the Joint Strike Fighter programme.
For years, US officials have warned about what they describe as an espionage threat from the Chinese state, while prosecutors have brought criminal cases against intelligence operatives from Beijing accused of stealing classified government material and proprietary commercial data, including via unlawful cyber intrusions.
In January, a former US Navy sailor received a prison term of more than 16 years after being found guilty of selling technical and operational manuals for vessels and naval systems to an intelligence officer acting on behalf of China.
However, Al Jazeera’s Defence Editor Alex Gatopoulos cautioned against assuming that possession of individual components would provide Beijing with any major technological advantages.
“Whilst China has a reputation for intense industrial espionage, its own stealth fighter jet programme is advanced, with sixth-generation prototypes coming online,” he said. “It’s debatable how much actual information China would glean from smaller, non-essential parts from an F-35.”

Fifth West Nile virus death confirmed as number of cases rises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:35:33 UTC
22:35:33 KST

Fifth West Nile virus death confirmed as number of cases rises
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A fifth person has died after contracting the West Nile virus since the turn of the year, while the number of confirmed infections has increased to 44.
The public health agency RIVM said another 16 patients had been detected since the last update a week ago. The agency has stressed there is no risk of a pandemic because the virus cannot be transmitted from person to person.
Doctors, vets, virologists and other specialists are monitoring the spread of the disease and deciding if extra precautionary measures need to be taken.
The virus, which is transmitted by mosquitos, causes no symptoms in 80% of people who contract it. but West Nile fever leads to neurological problems in around 1% of cases and in exceptional cases it can be fatal.
Following the death of a hospital patient in Utrecht, the RIVM said last month that the virus was now circulating in the Dutch mosquito population. Previous deaths had been limited to people who were infected while travelling abroad.
Around half the infections reported to the RIVM this year have been in Zuid-Holland province, with other cases in Utrecht, Noord-Holland and Noord-Brabant, Gelderland and Overijssel.
West Nile virus can also be contracted by other species such as birds and horses, but they cannot transmit the infection to humans. The RIVM has recorded 136 positive tests in horses and 171 in birds so far this year.

2026-09-24

22:35:00 KST

Alar Karis: UN Charter principles must not be trampled underfoot
At this difficult junction, the UN needs a strong and principled leader with an impeccable record of defending and advancing international law, human rights and the principles of the UN Charter. Estonia believes that after 81 years, it is time for a woman to lead the UN, President Alar Karis said in Estonia's national statement at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
Last year, speaking from this podium, I described the United Nations as an idea of a better world. It is a carefully crafted agreement to safeguard peace and security, promote development and uphold human rights. I still believe in that promise, enshrined in the United Nations Charter.
But the world around us is changing and not for the better. Over the past year in particular, it has become increasingly clear that the multilateral world order, with the UN and its Charter at its core, is at a profound turning point. Blatant disregard for international law and the principles of the Charter, reinforced by a sense of impunity, too often dominates over adherence to the rule of law and cooperation between countries for a better future. Mutual dependence has come to be treated as a critical vulnerability. Aggression, wars and conflicts risk becoming the new normal.
Millions of people are suffering in Ukraine, Gaza, Sudan, Haiti, Myanmar. Sometimes we tend to forget that behind the numbers there are always human beings – families separated, children affected, homes destroyed and lives disrupted by conflict. Over the past three years, more than 1,000 humanitarian workers have lost their lives. And beyond ongoing wars and conflicts there is the looming crisis brought on by climate change; one in which time is running out for us to act. Indeed, the time to act is now. Estonia, for example, is contributing its share: we have reduced our emissions by 66 percent over the past 35 years while transforming our energy system.
Yes, the world is on fire; troubles and problems are mounting before our eyes. The cooperative spirit in the international relations that emerged after San Francisco and that was clearly present after the end of the Cold War is fading away. The UN is suffering because of it. But it is also true that the UN requires profound reforms to be able to tackle the challenges of the 21st century. As such, the question really is this: do we let the United Nations, together with its aims and founding principles, just slowly fall apart? Or do we start facing these challenges with a sense of common responsibility and genuinely try to reform the UN and start to use the only global framework we have in a responsible and sensible way? The stakes are high. The choice is ours.
For Estonia, and I believe for the great majority of UN Member States, upholding the principles of the UN Charter is of vital interest. But we are also conscious that in order for those principles to remain valid and respected, we need to invest in them – as much with our words as with our actions.
One of the biggest tests for the UN's relevance is Russia's aggression against Ukraine. For more than 12 years now, since the illegal annexation of Crimea and occupation of Eastern Ukraine in 2014, a permanent member of the Security Council — the Russian Federation — has been perpetrating a war of aggression at the very heart of Europe. That aggression disregards the principles of the UN Charter to its very core: it violates the respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states and the prohibition on the use of force against another state.
The consequences of Russia's aggression, however, extend far beyond Ukraine and Europe. For example, by increasingly targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, commercial shipping, grain infrastructure and alternative export routes, Russia is putting global food security at grave risk.
As such, this is a concern for all of us, and rightly so. Russia's actions have been condemned by a large majority of this Assembly. But condemnation is not enough: we need to collectively force Russia into peace in Ukraine, to force it to the negotiation table by raising the cost of its aggression. For this we can and should use the diverse instruments at our disposal, be they economic, diplomatic or political. I strongly encourage more of my fellow heads of state and government to use this occasion to call on Russia to cease its aggression. Those of you who have done so already, be it in the Global South or North — you have my appreciation. The principles of the UN Charter cannot be trampled on. It is our collective task to stand up for them.
We should also support the efforts of international mechanisms to document war crimes, ensure accountability and provide assistance to those whose rights have been violated. Estonia is doing its part: we have completed all national procedures and taken the lead in discussions in Strasbourg to establish the Special Tribunal as soon as possible. A UN Member State whose armed forces have been repeatedly cited in the UN secretary-general's reports for grave violations against children and conflict-related sexual violence should have no place in UN peacekeeping operations. This is a matter of ensuring that a perpetrator's actions have consequences. But it is equally a matter of retaining trust in and the integrity of UN peacekeeping. I therefore call on the UN to stop reflecting and instead take appropriate action immediately.
Ukraine requires assistance in defending itself, but also in rebuilding the country. Estonia, together with its partners, has worked closely to support Ukraine's cybersecurity and resilience in responding to evolving threats through the Tallinn Mechanism and the IT-Coalition. Estonia is also proud to be hosting the Ukraine Recovery Conference in 2027, organized in cooperation with our closest friends in the Nordic-Baltic region. Building on the outcomes of earlier conferences, next year's event will be advancing in practical terms long-term international support for Ukraine and its recovery. As such, it will be a multilateral effort and example of true cooperation for international peace and security.
While it is the situation in Ukraine and Ukraine's security that affects Estonia most directly, we are neither indifferent to nor unaffected by the impact of other wars, threats and conflicts.
The situation in the West Bank and Gaza remains of great concern. Innocent civilians and children must not bear the devastating human cost of the war. Estonia has consistently called for upholding international humanitarian law and ensuring safe, rapid and unhindered access to humanitarian aid for those in need. We remain a stable donor to UNWRA and are committed to a credible political process leading to a negotiated two state solution, with Israel and Palestine living side by side in peace, security and dignity. We have provided food aid to hospitals in Gaza and stand ready to offer our digital transition expertise in its future reconstruction.
Estonia has consistently condemned the attacks by Iran against our close partners, the Gulf states, and has shown its readiness to contribute to ensuring freedom of navigation in the region. This is an issue that affects us all.
We also see the instrumentalization of migration as a means of exerting pressure on countries, whether on the European Union's eastern and southern borders or elsewhere. Irregular migration is increasingly becoming a security issue and it requires a coordinated international response.
If we want a United Nations that is more effective in terms of decision-making, more efficient in managing available resources and up to date on technological developments, we adopt it as our shared task to readjust the structure of the UN around all three pillars, as well as to reassess how the United Nations operates.
Estonia supports the system-wide reform of the UN80 and Humanitarian Reset, which are both well underway and have already delivered some encouraging results. Now is the time to build on this momentum and to move decisively forward with the reforms. We need ambition. For example, the humanitarian sector, alongside stronger data harmonization, could move towards a shared interoperability model that allows many systems to coexist while quickly and safely exchanging data.
Estonian humanitarian organizations are already testing these solutions, from Palestine to Sudan. We also need determination. Above all, we need action – action that strengthens the UN as the main actor responsible for multilateral cooperation and that prepares it for future challenges.
This year, the United Nations is set to make arguably one of its most consequential decisions: the selection and appointment of its next secretary-general. As an active member of the Accountability, Coherence and Transparency Group, Estonia has stood for a transparent, fair and inclusive process. At this challenging time for the organization, we need a strong and principled leader with an impeccable track record in championing and upholding international law, human rights and the principles of the Charter. Estonia also feels that after 81 years, it is time for this organization to be led by a woman.
Allow me to take this opportunity to commend and express our gratitude to the current Secretary-General, Mr António Guterres, for his steadfast commitment to the principles of the UN Charter, including his support for a just and lasting peace in Ukraine.
With regard to the Security Council, it must be said that its inability to take timely and decisive decisions on some of the worst crises we are seeing today risks rendering the United Nations irrelevant. We have not seen unified and decisive Council action on Ukraine, Sudan or Myanmar. The use of the veto and the threat of its use continue to loom over the Council and paralyze any of its attempts to take action.
Estonia has strongly advocated for permanent members to refrain from vetoing resolutions aimed at ending mass atrocities, in line with the France-Mexico proposal and the ACT code of conduct.
It is also important to call on the Security Council members to start fully implementing Article 27 (3) of the Charter once again and to abstain in cases where members of the Council are a party to a dispute.
The General Assembly resolution "United for Peace" gives this most representative and democratic body of the UN a toolbox to act on matters related to international peace and security when the Council is unable to deliver. In concert, we must reinforce the role of the General Assembly when it comes to peace and security, as this will help us in collectively finding solutions where the Council is powerless.
Estonia firmly believes that respect for human rights is a prerequisite for peace, security and prosperity. We stand firmly behind the United Nations human rights system and will continue to defend and strengthen it. As one of the first supporters of the Global Alliance for Human Rights, Estonia feels that human rights should once again be at the center of the world we choose to build.
Estonia is a member of the UN Human Rights Council for the period from 2026 to 2028 and is currently serving as Vice-President of the Council. As a country ranked among the world's top three for press freedom, we are committed to promoting media freedom, protecting journalists and enhancing media literacy.
We will continue our strong commitment to women's rights and gender equality, including sexual and reproductive health and rights. Together with New Zealand and Colombia, Estonia is leading negotiations on the Human Rights Council on the resolution on preventing maternal mortality and morbidity. Maternal survival is a question of justice and human rights, not only healthcare.
Estonia stands firmly for ending all forms of violence against children. One of the gravest aspects of Russia's war against Ukraine is the mass deportation and forced transfer of Ukrainian children, which is a systematic and deliberate attempt to erase their Ukrainian identity. It is a war crime and a crime against humanity. We therefore reiterate the call of the General Assembly resolution adopted on December 3, 2025, and demand that the Russian Federation ensure the safe, immediate and unconditional return of all forcibly transferred and deported Ukrainian children. We thank all of our international partners working to reunite these children with their families, in particular US First Lady Melania Trump for her remarkable humanitarian initiative.
Artificial Intelligence is here to stay and to be used to assist us as has been the case with every major new technology throughout human history. Like any new technology, AI poses risks and brings challenges. But with knowledge, wisdom and unity, we can put it to use in service of humanity. As a co-chair of the first UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance alongside El Salvador, Estonia has proudly brought its knowledge and experience in service of the UN and its Member States.
Personally, I had the honor of becoming one of the commissioners of the AI for Good Global Commission this summer. For me, this role means both trust and responsibility: to help ensure that AI serves people, that its use is secure and reliable and that its benefits reach as many countries and communities as possible.
As the current president of the UNICEF Executive Board, Estonia has been paying particular attention to the topic of innovation in education, notably how to advance — in a responsible way — safe, inclusive and child-centered learning with the support of AI. In Estonia we have introduced a massive educational innovation program we call the "AI Leap" whose aim is to assist schools — students and teachers alike — to adapt to the age of AI and to foster meaningful learning. Artificial intelligence should empower teaching and learning, rather than replace them. Under the auspices of the UN, notably through close cooperation with UNICEF, we are bringing our experience and best practice to the global scene, ensuring that AI creates equal opportunities for all humanity.
We know for certain that digitalization, which has now been reinforced by AI, has enabled our small country to grow, innovate and connect globally. This is why we have shared our experience with around 150 other countries worldwide. And this is also why Estonia has nominated a candidate for the position of director of the ITU Development Bureau. You can trust us to work to turn connectivity into lasting capability and to ensure that no country is left behind in the digital transformation. We hope to count on your valuable support.
The very fact that we are gathered here today should give us hope that we still share a commitment to the UN Charter and to multilateral cooperation. Otherwise, why would we keep coming to New York year after year? Let us preserve what matters, adapt where we must and design the future — together. We have a choice: to shape change or to be shaped by it. And we can only shape it if we stand together.
--

Heatwave to cost Swiss economy CHF 400 million

Heatwave to cost Swiss economy CHF 400 million
The hot summer of 2026 caused economic damage amounting to CHF400 million in Switzerland.
And weather events could also result in high costs next year, according to a study by the credit insurer Allianz Trade.
Labour productivity also suffered as a result of the extreme heat this summer – longer breaks were necessary, and there were absences due to illness.
According to Allianz Trade, the economic losses amount to CHF400 million, which corresponds to around 0.05% of gross domestic product. The credit insurer is working with Allianz to analyse the impact of extreme weather events on the economy.
The findings are to be published annually from now on in the Allianz Climate Risk Tracker study.
More
Switzerland’s worst-case climate scenario now more likely, say scientists
“Climate change is increasingly becoming an economic factor,” said Jan Möllmann, CEO of Allianz Trade in Switzerland. Following the hot summer, the next climate phenomenon – the already very strong El Niño – is just around the corner.
This could cost the global economy around $451 billion in 2027. China, the United States and India would collectively bear almost 60% of these losses. For Europe, including Switzerland, a net loss of around €21 billion is expected.
The study concludes that adaptation and preparedness are crucial for economic resilience. Countries with established early-warning systems, risk maps and clearly defined responsibilities are better prepared for climate risks.

Germany pledges to phase out fossil fuels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:33:22 UTC
22:33:22 KST

Germany pledges to phase out fossil fuels
Germany has presented a roadmap for completely phasing out fossil fuels by 2045. The government is sticking to its green transition policy, despite Chancellor Friedrich Merz earlier acknowledging that the country is going through “an energy crisis.”
Germany abandoned Russian pipeline gas, on which its energy-intensive manufacturing sector had been built, after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022. The US-Israeli war on Iran this year, which led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, accounting for some 20% of global crude oil trade, has further complicated the situation for the country’s businesses and households.
The German economy contracted in both 2023 and 2024, marking its first back-to-back annual decline in more than two decades, while 2025 only saw a weak growth of 0.2%. Over the past few years, leading German companies such as BASF, Bosch, and Volkswagen have been forced to shut down factories or announce major staff cuts.
In the document released on Wednesday, Merz’s government for the first time explicitly promised to get rid of coal, oil, and gas altogether. Previously, it only committed itself to “carbon neutrality.”
According to the roadmap, the proportion of renewable energy obtained from windmills and solar panels should increase from 55% to 80% in electricity generation by 2030.
It also envisages a reduction of methane emission by 30% by 2030 in line with the global methane pledge signed by Berlin in 2021.
The plan to phase out fossil fuel is being rolled out at a time when Merz’s approval ratings sank to a record low of 10%, with even the majority of supporters of his own Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party disapproving of his policies, according to the latest polls.
Speaking about the roadmap at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider called the 19-year deadline feasible, saying that the plan “combines independence, affordability, and climate protection.”
“Our roadmap is intended to set an international example. I am sure that many other countries will follow,” Schneider insisted.
Germany is only the third country after France and the Netherlands to publish such a plan.
Greenpeace energy expert Mira Jager welcomed the roadmap, but noted that “at the same time, the federal government is subsidizing the oil industry, breaking the heating transition, and slowing down the expansion of renewables,” as cited by Deutsche Welle.
The right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD), which delivered crushing defeats to the CDU in two local elections this month, warned in a post on X on Wednesday that “the German middle class dies” if the fuel price climbs from the current €2.3 ($2.6) per liter to €3 ($3.4).
“We demand the reduction of EU energy taxes as well as value-added tax. In addition, the immediate abolition of the CO2 levy on gasoline and diesel,” it said.
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel, who has been a strong opponent of Germany’s green transition, previously called wind turbines “the windmills of shame.” She also repeatedly argued that restoring economic ties with Moscow and bringing back Russian gas is key to reviving the German economy.

In Ukraine, the additional payment for teachers in frontline areas has been retained — how much educators will receive

The government has retained the monthly additional payment of UAH 2,600 for 23.6 thousand teachers in 614 schools. UAH 731.1 million has been reallocated for the payments.
The Cabinet of Ministers has retained a separate monthly supplement of UAH 2,600 for teachers in frontline areas who work in person or in a mixed format. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi reported this, according to UNN.
Despite limited financial resources, the government has retained a separate monthly supplement of UAH 2,600 for teachers in frontline areas who work in person or in a mixed format. It is provided for 23.6 thousand teachers in 614 schools
He noted that, for these purposes, the government redistributed additional funds that will allow full payment to be made for the time actually worked during the previous academic year in communities where there was still a need for funding, and ensure that the payment is made by the end of the year.
Supplement
According to government resolution No. 1078, from September 1 until the end of the calendar year in which martial law is terminated or lifted, teachers in frontline areas receive an additional payment for working under unfavorable conditions.
This applies to teachers working in certain districts of the Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Sumy, Kharkiv, Kherson, and Chernihiv regions.
The Ministry of Education and Science reported that the government redistributed UAH 731.1 million for this need.

UN rights chief says civilians are bearing the brunt of fighting in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:31:57 UTC
22:31:57 KST

UN says Yemen violence struck camps and health centres
GENEVA, Sept 24 - Displacement camps and health centres have been attacked during surging violence in Yemen between Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthis, UN agencies said on Thursday, deploring a growing civilian death toll which includes children.
The latest fighting marks a sharp escalation in Yemen's civil war, which had largely been frozen since a 2022 truce, as well as a widening of the conflict that has grown out of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Violence has flared along old front lines in recent weeks, including around Taiz as the Houthis swept south along the Red Sea coast, prompting a humanitarian crisis with over 130,000 people displaced and some fleeing to Africa across the Red Sea.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said his office had documented three attacks by Ansar Allah, the formal name for the Houthi movement, on sites for internally displaced people since August.
He said these attacks on August 7, September 7 and September 9 in the Marib region caused dozens of casualties and killed five children.
Overall, Turk's office has documented the killing of 32 civilians, including 15 children and 3 women, since August in fighting, including drone and missile strikes. They were among 125 people killed or wounded in the latest flareup in the conflict - a figure his office said was likely an undercount due to access constraints and insecurity.
"Civilians are now bearing the brunt of this latest upsurge in fighting," Turk said in a statement.
The World Health Organization said some health facilities had been "directly attacked" and an ambulance driver and a medic were killed in Lahj on September 18, without attributing blame.
INFLUX OF DISPLACED CAUSES NEW ACUTE AID SHORTAGES
Both sides allege that hundreds have been killed in fighting over the past weeks, without providing details.
Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam said the UN human rights office was no longer impartial and that its allegations were false, accusing it of ignoring what he described as Saudi bombardment in Yemen that had targeted public facilities including a correctional facility and homes and schools.
More than 70 UN staff are being detained by Houthis in Yemen, some of whom have been held for many years. Turk called for their release and urged all the warring parties to protect civilians, saying the government warnings of attacks did not remove the protections they should have.
Saudi officials have repeatedly said the country's forces do not target civilians in Yemen. Saudi officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Aid groups are ramping up their response to the crisis in a country where 18 million people, or roughly half the population face acute food insecurity.
The World Health Organization has stepped up distribution of medical supplies, including blood bags as well as trauma and surgery kits, and is deploying emergency teams as injuries rise, the statement said.
But many people lack support and a UN refugee agency plan for Yemen was less than 20% funded before the renewed violence caused a surge in needs.
An internally displaced mother of four, Aisha Ahmed, told Reuters in the Taiz camp that the influx of people in recent weeks is causing shortages. "We need water and everything else, we have nothing," she said. REUTERS

'No anti-incumbency against BJP?' Party counters Rahul Gandhi with Tamil Nadu, Bengal poll history

BJP counters Rahul Gandhi with Tamil Nadu, Bengal poll history
NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi's claim that anti-incumbency has “disappeared” for the BJP because of its alleged collusion with the Election Commission drew a sharp response from the ruling party. BJP national spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi cited the Congress's electoral record in states including Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Odisha to hit back at leader of opposition in Lok Sabha.Rahul Gandhi, speaking at a press conference in New Delhi on Thursday amid the ongoing row over the Election Commission and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, questioned how anti-incumbency could seemingly affect successive governments but not the BJP.Responding to Rahul's remarks, BJP MP Sudhanshu Trivedi questioned his understanding of Indian electoral history and argued that the stronger long-term anti-incumbency trend was against the Congress."From a political point of view, his wisdom is zero, his knowledge is zero," Trivedi said, launching a personal attack on Rahul.Trivedi then pointed to states where the Congress has not returned to power for decades.
"Yes, anti-incumbency is indeed very strong and consistent against Congress," he said.
On Tamil Nadu, Trivedi said the Congress had not returned to power since 1967, arguing that the BJP was not even a significant political force in the state at the time. In West Bengal, he said, the Congress had not returned to government since 1977.The Election Commission's statistical reports list assembly elections across the states and provide the historical electoral data on which such comparisons can be made.The BJP spokesperson also cited Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Odisha, saying there had been no Congress government in Bihar after 1990, no Congress government in Uttar Pradesh after 1989 and no Congress government in Odisha since 1999."Ever since transparent elections have taken place, CCTV cameras have come in, and independent media has arrived, they've started finding it difficult to come to power," Trivedi said.
What Rahul Gandhi said
Earlier in the day, Rahul held a press conference in which he cited former PM Indira Gandhi as an example, saying she was at the height of her popularity after the 1971 Bangladesh war but faced "massive anti-incumbency" within a year or two."The same thing happens to leader after leader, to Congress leaders and to regional parties. But, for some reason, it does not happen to PM Modi, Amit Shah and the BJP," Rahul Gandhi said.He also pointed to electoral changes in Haryana, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh, arguing that these states had historically seen voters shift between parties."Haryana swings from one party to another for 50 years, but suddenly anti-incumbency disappears. Maharashtra swings; suddenly that disappears. Uttar Pradesh swings, from the Samajwadi Party to the Bahujan Samaj Party, that also disappears," he said.
Rahul said the question had been a "fundamental" one for the Congress until the party arrived at what he described as the answer: "vote chori".His remarks came as he stepped up his attack on the Election Commission over the SIR exercise. He accused chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of undermining the electoral process, demanded his resignation and alleged that the destruction of votes would ultimately undermine the Constitution and institutions."From vote chori comes kanoon chori, and from that comes sanstha chori," he said.

GENEVA, September 24. /TASS/. Russia’s parliamentary elections, successfully held despite Ukraine’s attempts to disrupt them, enraged Vladimir Zelensky, permanent representative to the OSCE Dmitry Polyansky said.
He said that Zelensky, as the events on the battlefield unfold badly for him, is trying to draw the EU and NATO into a military conflict with Russia at any cost.
TASS has compiled the key statements by Russia’s permanent representative to the OSCE.
Elections to the State Duma
The parliamentary elections, which Russia has successfully carried out despite Ukraine’s attempts to disrupt them, enraged Vladimir Zelensky: "Zelensky and his clique were particularly enraged by the elections to the State Duma of the Federal Assembly of the Russian Federation, which took place last week. For the first time in the history of modern Russia, these elections were held amid a special military operation -- and for the first time, residents of the Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics, as well as the Zaporozhye and Kherson regions, took part in them."
Kiev attempted to disrupt the elections through terror against the civilian population: "The Kiev regime, realizing that it cannot prevent the expression of will by our citizens through political means, sought to disrupt the voting through terror. But it miscalculated."
Attempts to draw the West into the conflict
As events on the battlefield develop badly for him, Zelensky is trying to draw the EU and NATO into a military conflict with Russia at any cost: "Zelensky no longer has any interceptor missiles, which are in short supply on the global arms market. Yet, he continues to provoke Russia and tries to escalate the situation at all costs in order to drag Europe and NATO into a direct conflict with our country."
"War hysteria" among European political elites
The gap between the EU elites, who are inclined toward war with Russia, and ordinary citizens of the member states has become a "fundamental characteristic of modern Europe": "European political elites are consistently stoking military hysteria, preparing their countries for a direct confrontation with Russia, and doing so in defiance of the sentiment of their own people, who want peace, not war."
The EU authorities carefully conceal from the people Moscow’s regular denials of having any plans to attack Europe: "The intensified militarization of Europe and its preparation for war are accompanied by ever-new scare stories about an allegedly inevitable Russian attack." At the same time, information about Russia’s regular, high-level confirmations that a war with NATO and Europe is not part of our plans does not reach the average European citizen."
European elites carefully screen the information coming from Russia: "All information is carefully filtered; Russian media in EU countries have long been blocked so that nothing hinders the indoctrination of ordinary Europeans."
The situation in Ukraine
Amid Zelensky’s ongoing provocations, Ukraine is losing what remains of its industry as winter approaches. "As a result, Ukraine is losing the last remnants of its industry and infrastructure; experts are increasingly warning that the country is facing a complete energy and transport breakdown on the eve of winter."
Zelensky is not concerned about Ukrainians, but about the opportunity to siphon money from the budget: "The expired Ukrainian president doesn’t care about his citizens; he only cares about how much money the corruption system he created can still siphon from the country, around which more and more scandals are erupting."
Germany’s involvement in corruption schemes
The secret unit "Sonderstab Ukraine" within the German Defense Ministry creates an enormous scope for corrupt schemes between the Kiev regime and German defense contractors: "I would like, in particular, to draw attention to the information disclosed by the Financial Times about the existence of a top-secret unit within the German Defense Ministry -- Sonderstab Ukraine -- which is engaged in arms procurement for Kiev while bypassing all usual procedures. It is noteworthy that this structure operates without oversight by German auditors or parliament. As critics note, this creates enormous scope for corruption and kickbacks between the Ukrainian leadership and German military contractors."
Provocation in Bucha
A report "Heirs of Goebbels: The Falsification of Events in Bucha and the Bloody Staged Performances of the Kiev Regime," prepared by the International Public Tribunal on Crimes of Ukrainian Neo-Nazis, will be distributed within the OSCE framework: "We will circulate this report at the OSCE in the near future so that everyone should have the opportunity to read it and draw one’s own conclusions."

Gaza economy has entered world's 'most severe crisis on record': UN report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:31:02 UTC
22:31:02 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Gaza's economy has entered the world's "most severe crisis on record," with recovery and reconstruction needs reaching $71.5 billion amid widespread destruction of productive capacity, according to a UN report.
The report by the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) said the assessment was based on the peak-to-trough decline in real GDP per capita and the projected duration of recovery.
Gaza's annual real GDP per capita stood at just $212, or $0.58 per day, in 2025, equivalent to just 17% of its already low 2022 level.
Israeli military operations since October 2023 have left 92% of Gaza's economic establishments damaged or destroyed, "bringing productive activity to a near-total halt across all sectors," the report said.
Agricultural and industrial output each plunged 94% compared with 2022, while construction output collapsed by 99%.
The labor market has also been devastated, according to the report, with only 123,300 Gazans employed in 2025, leaving more than 90% of the working-age population without work.
Prices in Gaza remained 274% above 2022 levels in 2025, with food prices "spiraling." Potatoes, for example, cost more than 20 times their pre-conflict level.
Physical infrastructure damage was estimated at $35.2 billion, more than 2.5 times the pre-conflict real GDP of Gaza and the West Bank combined, alongside $22.7 billion in economic and social losses.
UNCTAD said total recovery and reconstruction needs had reached $71.5 billion by early 2026 and "will continue to increase until a sustainable ceasefire is achieved."
Gaza's share of the Palestinian economy had fallen below 4% by 2025, while GDP per capita stood at just 5% of the level in the occupied West Bank, down from near parity three decades ago.

How Gaza's dental crisis is putting treatment out of reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:31:00 UTC
22:31:00 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza's dental crisis: Families forced to choose between treating their teeth and feeding their children
For many families in Gaza, a visit to the dentist is no longer simply about treating a painful tooth. It has become a question of whether they can afford to pay for treatment or whether that money is needed for food, shelter and other basic necessities as Israel's genocidal war continues across the Strip.
As a dentist, I see this every day at the International Dental Centre in Al-Nuseirat refugee camp, one of Gaza's busiest and most crowded camps, where displaced Palestinians are supposed to be safe.
One of the patients I see is 38-year-old Maha El Masry, a mathematics teacher who previously worked on a temporary contract with UNRWA.
When I examine her painful teeth, I can see the exhaustion on her face. But instead of asking whether her teeth can be saved, she asks me one question: how much will the treatment cost?
Maha lost her job after UNRWA contracts were suspended during Israel's war. She has also been displaced from Sheikh Radwan to Deir al-Balah, while several of her teeth have begun causing her severe pain.
"My family partly relies on financial assistance from one of my siblings abroad. But restrictions on banking services and money transfers mean that the money may arrive only once every six months. When it does, it may cover little more than two months of the family's expenses," Maha tells The New Arab.
I know that Maha's teeth can still be saved through root canal treatment followed by crowns, but the estimated cost is around $1,200.
For her, that is far beyond what she can afford. "I am forced to consider a cheaper alternative: extraction," Maha notes.
'My daughters come first'
Maha's situation is similar to that of many other patients in Gaza. They come to the clinic needing treatment, but the cost forces them to think about what else their families need before deciding whether they can afford to save a tooth.
Forty-year-old Mahmoud Al Ataar from Al-Nuseirat lost his front teeth, from canine to canine, as a result of the war and needed urgent dental treatment.
He required dental implants, which cost around $4,000, or a fixed bridge costing about $1,650, but neither option was possible for him.
When Mahmoud learned how much the treatment would cost, he knew he had to put his family first.
"My daughters come first, and keeping a roof over their heads to shelter and protect them is all that matters to me," he says.
In the end, Mahmoud chose a removable denture costing around $165. Its quality does not match that of a fixed bridge, but it improved his appearance and helped him eat. It was the option he could afford in his family's circumstances.
Even getting the denture was not straightforward. One of the few dental laboratories still operating needed plaster and acrylic, two materials that have become very difficult to obtain. It took about two weeks just to find them.
Before Israel's war, the same denture cost around $100 and could be completed in about five days.
The problems Mahmoud faced with his teeth are also part of a much wider struggle. His house was damaged in a previous bombardment, and he suffered an injury that led to the amputation of several of his fingers.
After part of his home was destroyed, Mahmoud initially moved into a tent. The harsh conditions eventually led him to repair what he could of the house and cover it with tarpaulins.
"They provide my family and me with much better protection than staying in a fragile tent," Mahmoud explains.
Mahmoud has two daughters, ages 7 and 13, and four sons. With the family struggling financially, he says much of his time is now spent moving between organisations and charities looking for basic assistance.
"I spend my entire days moving between organisations and charities, trying just to secure a food coupon to feed my family," Mahmoud adds.
For him, paying for dental treatment was another expense to weigh against his family's basic needs.
"The choice was not between treating my teeth or leaving them; it was a critical choice between treating myself or meeting the basic needs of my daughters and family," he says.
'My grandchildren need milk first'
The same problem is visible with other patients around the besieged enclave, who sometimes choose to treat only the tooth causing the most pain while leaving other dental problems untreated.
One of those patients is 50-year-old Um Ahmed, who needed three dental crowns costing around $500. She did not have enough money to pay for them.
Um Ahmed called her son, Ahmed, before deciding what to do. He told her that the family could not afford the full cost and asked her to treat only the tooth causing her pain, at the lowest possible cost.
She followed his advice and treated just one tooth after her circumstances were taken into account and the price was reduced.
The single tooth was saved, but her other dental problems were left untreated.
For Um Ahmed, the family had more urgent needs. She has been a widow for five years, and her home was bombed during the Israeli invasion of Deir al-Balah, forcing her to flee.
"I didn't have a single shekel to treat my teeth. At the same time, my son Ahmed was struggling to provide milk for his infant and desperately needed to buy a tarpaulin to cover our tent and protect us from the upcoming winter rains. How could I think of my teeth when my grandchildren need milk first?" Um Ahmed shares.
Um Ahmed now lives in a tent inside a shelter in Al-Nuseirat with her eldest son, Ahmed. Her three married sons all lost their jobs during the war and now rely on working at street stalls to provide for their families.
She has no income herself and relies entirely on the charity of others.
Smiles hidden behind masks
For younger patients, the same financial pressure seems to affect their decisions about dental treatment.
One of them is 30-year-old Fedaa, who needed cosmetic fillings costing around $330. When she learned the price, she decided she could not afford the treatment.
"When they told me the cost, I was shocked. This amount would require about two months of hard, continuous work for me to save. My siblings are far more important than my teeth and my appearance. Putting them before myself is not a sacrifice; it is my duty. Now, I prefer to wear a mask all the time to hide my smile rather than deprive them of anything," Fedaa says.
Fedaa lost both of her parents during the war and is now responsible for her younger siblings. She lives in a tent in the Mawasi Khan Younis area with three of them, aged between 14 and 20.
She does not have a high school diploma, so she found work at a hairdresser's to help support her siblings.
She receives some limited assistance from her uncle, who also supports his own family. This means the money Fedaa earns from working is spent on feeding and clothing her siblings.
For Fedaa, spending money on cosmetic dental treatment is therefore not something she can justify.
A severe shortage of supplies in clinics
The stories of Maha, Mahmoud, Um Ahmed, and Fedaa show how difficult it has become for families to afford dental care. But the problem is not only the lack of money.
Inside Gaza's dental clinics, I am also dealing with shortages of materials, damaged facilities and rising costs.
Since Israel's war began, I have watched the cost of dental treatment rise sharply at my dental centre in Al-Nuseirat camp.
The rise in treatment costs is directly linked to the severe restrictions on the import of dental materials into the Gaza Strip.
Since the beginning of the war, new supplies of dental materials have been largely blocked by Israeli authorities from entering the Strip, leaving dentists to rely on what was already available before.
The supplies have also been affected by poor storage conditions, damage to dental supply warehouses and the destruction of facilities.
Together, these problems have reduced the amount of usable material by nearly half.
This shortage is evident in the cost of even basic dental treatment. A filling that once cost between $23 and $33 now costs between $66 and $83, while root canal treatment has risen from around $33 to approximately $100.
As prices have gone up, fewer patients have been able to afford treatment. The number of patients coming to my clinic has fallen to around a quarter of what it was before Israel's war.
The financial pressure has also affected the dental centre itself. I struggle to pay staff salaries, while some dentists have left their jobs to look for other sources of income.
The dentists who have stayed have also seen their share of earnings fall. In some months, fixed prosthetic treatments had to be halted because dental laboratories could not operate or obtain materials such as zirconia, acrylic, and dental plaster.
The clinic itself has also been damaged. A nearby bombing damaged the premises, leaving dental chairs and other equipment unusable.
These shortages affect the treatment patients receive. What their teeth need is only part of the decision; what they can afford has become just as important.
The remaining supplies are also being used by licensed dentists and dental students from Al-Azhar University and the University of Palestine.
With so many people relying on the same limited stock, the materials have become increasingly hard to find.
Some dentists have tried to bring supplies in from outside the Gaza Strip. But these materials often have to be obtained through expensive arrangements, and suppliers sell them to dentists at prices far higher than before the war.
The higher cost then reaches patients. Dentists have to pass on a significant part of the increase, which pushes up treatment fees and makes procedures that were once routine too expensive for many people.
The result is a chain of problems: restrictions limit supply, shortages drive up prices, and patients end up bearing the financial burden.
Ultimately, as a dentist working in Gaza, I see how the war has turned dental care from a basic need into a luxury, with patients delaying treatment, choosing cheaper options or living with pain because food and shelter come first, leaving me to see not only damaged teeth but also the economic and psychological scars of war.
For many of these patients, the shortage of dental materials and rising costs are forcing them to live with problems that could otherwise be treated, as families are left choosing between looking after their health and simply having enough to survive.
Dr Liza Hassouna is a dentist and writer based in the Gaza Strip. She has previously worked with UNRWA and now practices at a dental centre. She has also written for Al Jazeera Blogs, documenting the human toll of the war on healthcare in Gaza

====================================================================================================

Constitutional Reform as the Lee Jae-myung Administration’s Political Watershed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:31:00 UTC
22:31:00 KST

On September 18, President Lee Jae-myung convened a press conference. Unlike his other public appearances, this one was devoid of smiles. There were no pleasantries floated. He just trudged to the podium in his crisp dark navy suit, his presence and the ambience made heavier by the royal blue of the presidential office draped in the backdrop.
“I have been lacking fear and humility,” he said. “I shall revive the fear for the people and tackle every task more meticulously and fiercely, from a lower position of service.”
The administration’s poor performance in opinion polls prompted this sense of crisis and humble words. Lee’s approval ratings have been taking a steady dive since the June local elections.
Until late August, the two main factors behind the slide had been the government’s controversial housing policy and the Democratic Party’s much more controversial judicial reform, which entrusts all investigative powers to the police. That change seems premature, or even inappropriate, given the recent barrage of anecdotes of police corruption and incompetence.
In September, Lee’s approval ratings plummeted still more following his ill-fated Cabinet nominations. Back in 2021, Kim Seung-won, Lee’s pick for the justice minister, allegedly streamlined the drug approval process for a pharmaceutical company on behalf of his friend. This allegation resurfaced during nomination hearings.
Meanwhile, Lee picked Yong Hye-in, the only parliamentarian from the Basic Income Party, to lead the gender equality ministry. Yong’s insistence on holding both positions, however, garnered opprobrium.
As opposed to constituency legislators – those who won the most votes from their districts – proportional representatives like Yong owe their positions to their parties. South Korea’s proportional representation ballot, designed to give minor parties a chance at lawmaking, accounts for 46 out of the National Assembly’s 300 total seats. Legislators in these seats are expected to resign when they take up another government job since someone else from their party can replace them without tarnishing the voters’ mandate. It seemed apparent that Yong had no other reason to retain her legislative seat than to enjoy the perks of being a lawmaker.
Kim and Yong both withdrew from their ministerial nominations after much damage to the Lee administration. And now they are both under investigation, the former for alleged sexual harassment of his former staff and the latter for allegedly funneling her political funds to her husband.
The public smarts all the more to questionable behavior by liberal figures. Lee’s approval ratings in major polls hit a nadir in mid-September, dropping to 33.8 percent in a poll by Realmeter and 37 percent in another by Gallup.
So, Lee’s press conference was a revolving door of apology and resolution to do better on all the factors shaving his approval ratings. But the most emphatic point he made – and the one that received the most headlines – was his assertion that “I have no intention whatsoever for a second presidential term.”
The Problematic Presidency
The current South Korean constitution allows the president to serve a single five-year term. In 2025, when Lee was running for the snap presidential election following Yoon Suk-yeol’s impeachment, one of his campaign policies was to amend the constitution so that the president can serve two four-year consecutive terms. At the time, almost two thirds of the voters approved of such reform.
South Korea’s system of a single five-year term for the president has come under much flak. The populace has to wait too long until they can pass judgment on the president through ballots. Besides, without the prospect of another term, the incumbent president has no incentive to behave responsibly when it comes to their government. How frequently the people can make their voices heard through voting and how much accountability with which the president leads the country determine the soundness of democracy. And South Korea has been poor in this aspect.
On top of that, the strong, centralized nature of South Korea’s presidency – often called an “imperial presidency” – has exacerbated the problem. Consider the president’s monopoly on administrative decisions; the government’s monopoly on funding for the rest of the country; the president’s power to appoint some 10,000 top government agency and QUANGO posts; the president’s authority to wield some $400 billion through their budgetary decisions; their decrees overriding local government ordinances; and the National Assembly’s inability to monitor and check the president’s executive arms.
Yoon’s presidency manifested everything that could go wrong, from rampant corruption due to lack of auditory mechanisms to toxic control over law enforcement. South Korea’s presidency depends too much on the good will of that one person at the top.
Naturally, constitutional reform to trim down the imperial presidency and beef up the parliament and local government has been expected to materialize sometime soon. But the speaker of the National Assembly sparked an intense controversy in late July when he said that “the question of allowing the incumbent president to serve consecutively is ultimately up to the public.” The opposition People Power Party (PPP) immediately raised the possibility that Lee could be plotting “treason” by assuming another term.
In fact, the current constitution bars any constitutional reform – whether that’s to prolong the presidential tenure or introduce multiple terms – from applying to the incumbent president. Immediately after, the speaker admitted his error in legal interpretation.
The presidential office also clarified to the press that, when it comes to Lee running for re-election, “our constitution doesn’t allow it, the people won’t condone it, and it’s realistically impossible.” Lee, while visiting France on September 10, mentioned again that “the constitution clearly confines my term.”
Still, the controversy had gained enough traction to drag down his approval ratings ever since. Hence Lee’s forceful, articulate reminder during the September 18 press conference that the notion of him serving consecutive terms “is not only constitutionally impossible but also never have I thought of it.”
Lee then proposed to collaborate with the National Assembly to amend the constitution to allow for consecutive presidential terms – for future presidents, not for himself – and more even distribution of powers among the parliament and the central and local governments. He also didn’t fail to point out that this would require “bipartisan discussion and public opinion and ideas.”
Political Opposition
Despite Lee’s fairly categorical stance, the PPP is deliberately incredulous. “Lee says he has ‘no intention’ of serving another term. Why is it so hard for him to say ‘I will not serve another term?’” wrote Jang Dong-hyuk, the PPP leader, on his social media. To him, Lee didn’t promise anything, therefore “he hasn’t given up the dream of a second consecutive term.”
The PPP floor leader, Jeong Jeom-sig, also made it clear that the PPP wouldn’t partake in any discussion for constitutional reform during the Lee administration. “The PPP is telling you now: There will be no constitutional reform during this administration,” he said to much applause among fellow PPP legislators. Like Jang, Jeong suspects that Lee has an ulterior motive to amend the constitution and run for a second term. (The president is immune from indictment, which is why the trials in various legal cases against Lee are currently on hold.)
But the real reason behind the PPP’s refusal to hash out a constitutional reform could be that it can’t take the lead in remolding the constitution to its taste. Constitutional amendment requires 200 votes in favor. The PPP only commands 109 out of 300 parliamentary seats. Meanwhile, the liberal camp comprises more than 180 seats, with the DP holding the parliamentary majority alone with its 161 seats. The PPP would manage to eke out only a piecemeal compromise at the negotiating table.
Besides, history would only remember the Lee administration, not the PPP, for having reformed the constitution. The PPP is loathe to serve Lee and the DP such an enormous political cachet on a silver platter.
In spite of the PPP’s intransigence, the DP is plowing ahead. On September 20, the DP launched a constitutional amendment committee. “It’s time to stop picking at diction but start discussing constitutional reform,” said Kim Min-seok, the DP’s new leader.
Granted, the timing is convenient for the Lee administration. Public discourse and political haggling over constitutional amendment could overshadow any other agenda. In the process, the government’s sore spots could be covered and even forgotten.
Plus, constitutional reform is not a distant possibility. Although the PPP opposes talk for tweaking the constitution, the conservative bloc is fractious anyways. Quite a sizable pocket despises Jang and the PPP leadership. Breakaway participation and votes are possible for constitutional amendment. Hearsay has it that some in the PPP are already stirring to join the discussion for constitutional amendment.
Notably, Kim Tae-ho, a four-term PPP legislator, sounded the bugle of reason this time after Lee’s press conference. “We should end this war of attrition over this consecutive terms controversy,” he said on his social media, alluding to the PPP’s pathological distrust of Lee. He then underlined the need to reform the constitution “in order to disperse the authority channeled into the president and overcome the political polarization.”
But in the end, it is this “political polarization” that will be hindering the very first step needed to heal this polarization. According to Realmeter’s September 22 survey, 5 out of 10 South Koreans were still dubious about Lee’s true intentions for wanting to introduce a consecutive presidential tenure. No matter how well-meaning and earnest the government may be about reforming the constitution and the polity, if the public isn’t convinced and comforted, no talk of constitutional reform, nor any resulting constitution, would be viable.

EU to condemn war in Ukraine at G20 even if Putin attends
September 24, 2026
The European Union said on Thursday that it would continue to condemn Russia's war in Ukraine at the G20 summit in Miami scheduled for December.
It said that it would do this regardless of whether Russian President Vladimir Putin attends after being invited by this year's hosting country, the United States. The Kremlin has said that Putin would "consider" Washington's invitation.
The Russian leader did not attend the G20 summit in 2023 in New Delhi, India and the 2022 summit on the Indonesian island of Bali despite being formally invited by the hosting countries.
Also on Thursday, eight people were killed in a wave of Russian strikes on Ukraine.
What did the EU say about Putin's possible attendance at the G20 summit?
The EU said it would continue calling for an end to the war in Ukraine.
"Since 2022, the EU has consistently and forcefully used G20 meetings to condemn Russia's full-scale invasion [of Ukraine] and to call for it to end," EU spokesman Olof Gill said.
"What I can say today is that this approach, from the European Union perspective, will continue, irrespective of the participants at any G20 meeting."
Gill said that Russia remained a member of the G20 group and that it had "the right to participate" in its meetings.
Both the European Union itself and three of its individual member states — France, Germany, and Italy — are members of the G20 group.
What is the US position on Putin's attendance at the G20?
Ukraine's allies — including G20 members France, Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom and Canada — have called for Russia's exclusion from the group since Moscow launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Washington was inviting Putin after his meeting with his Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
"We think it's an opportunity for him to engage not just with [US President Donald Trump], but with other world leaders," Rubio said on Wednesday. "We hope that's an invitation he'll accept."
Putin's last visit to the United States was to attend a summit meeting with Trump in Anchorage, Alaska in August 15, 2025, also marking his first visit to a Western country since the start of the war in Ukraine.
Russian strikes kill 8 in Kharkiv, Kyiv
At least six agricultural workers were killed and 12 others were wounded in a strike on the northeastern Ukrainian region of Kharkiv, Interior Minister Ihor Vyhivskyi said.

Meanwhile, at least two people were killed across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, Prime Minsiter Serhiy Koretsky said.
Strikes were also recorded in and around the southwestern port city of Odesa, with officials reporting they sparked a fire at a shopping mall.

Court overturns Trump’s ban on certain media outlets at the White House

22:29:35 KST

A federal judge has ordered US President Donald Trump’s administration to restore White House access for journalists from CNN, MSNBC, and Politico, noting that the ban likely violates the Constitution, Reuters reports.
US District Judge Tim Kelly dealt a significant blow to Trump in his battle with the media by ruling to restore their access to the White House. CNN, MSNBC, and Politico filed a lawsuit after Trump issued an order on the 18th of September banning journalists from these outlets from the White House.
Kelly ordered the Trump administration to immediately return the press passes of journalists from CNN, MSNBC, and Politico and barred the imposition of new restrictions for 14 days. The judge rejected the government’s arguments that the ban was implemented in the interest of national security. He stated there was a lack of factual evidence showing that revoking the journalists’ passes would protect the country, or that restoring them while the legal proceedings are ongoing would compromise national security. Kelly added that Trump himself had cited a lack of truthfulness and negativity in the coverage by these specific media outlets as the reason for the ban. Trump wrote on social media that CNN, MSNBC, and Politico should not be able to constantly publish fabrications and lies, while Department of Justice lawyers sought to justify the ban based on national security interests.
On the 21st of September, CNN, MSNBC, and Politico filed a lawsuit against Trump and his administration
in a federal court in Washington, arguing that the ban violated First Amendment rights regarding freedom of speech and the press, as well as the right to due process.
The legal action was initiated just over a month before the midterm elections scheduled for the 3rd of November, which could prove to be a serious test for the Republicans. Trump’s approval ratings have also dropped to record lows, and citizens are increasingly concerned about the cost of living and the war in Iran.
On the 23rd of September, Kelly stated that two legal precedents clearly indicate that journalists are entitled to due process before their White House press passes are revoked. The judge added that it did not appear the White House had given the media an opportunity to contest the decision. A media lawyer told Kelly that the ban imposed on CNN, MSNBC, and Politico was enacted without the legally required prior warning or opportunity to challenge the decision, describing it as an unprecedented, unjustified, and severe penalty. Meanwhile, a Justice Department lawyer pointed out that the Trump administration had provided a sufficient explanation regarding the revocation of press passes in letters sent to the media on the 22nd of September. The judge viewed this statement skeptically, noting that the explanatory letters were sent after the passes had been revoked and after the media had already filed a lawsuit.
In a legal filing on the 22nd of September, the Justice Department emphasized that access to the White House is a privilege, not a right, and that the President has the authority to revoke it.
