A Starlink satellite ground station, which provides internet access to users in Europe—including Ukraine—was likely set on fire in Poland.
This was reported by Reuters, citing Polish Minister of Digital Affairs Krzysztof Gawkowski.
The fire occurred in the Polish village of Wola Krobowska in the Masovian Voivodeship.
The fire broke out late in the evening on September 23 in an electrical distribution cabinet to which the station’s antennas are connected. A power generator was also damaged.
According to RMF24, while inspecting the scene near the burned-out distribution cabinet, law enforcement officers discovered a bottle containing a flammable substance.
It is believed that this may indicate the use of a homemade incendiary device. As a result, Polish authorities are investigating the possibility of arson.
Police officers and agents from the Polish Internal Security Agency are working at the scene. Law enforcement officials are determining the circumstances of the incident and identifying possible suspects.
Gawkowski stated that the nature of the damage and the circumstances of the incident point to a deliberate attempt to disable the station. According to him, this could have led to an interruption in internet connectivity for various institutions, including the Ukrainian military.
In addition, Deputy Minister of National Defence Cezary Tomczyk, in an interview with an RMF FM reporter, called for the possibility of sabotage to be considered.
At the same time, Polish authorities have not yet reported identifying a suspect nor have they claimed that Russia was involved in the incident.
The ground station in Wola Krobowska is part of the Starlink infrastructure in Central and Eastern Europe. The facility is operated by Exatel, a Polish state-owned telecommunications company.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that the German Federal Ministry of the Interior intends to develop a set of measures to counter Russian sabotage, particularly cyberattacks.

Sudan slams US challenge to government’s legitimacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:28:40 UTC
22:28:40 KST

Sudan slams US challenge to government’s legitimacy
Sudan’s army-backed government has rejected US remarks questioning its legitimacy, insisting that efforts to end the country’s civil war must respect its sovereignty and national institutions.
US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said on Tuesday that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces nor the rival Rapid Support Forces (RSF), or their leaders, “represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan.” He said “the conduct of each leader of the warring factions renders them ineligible to govern the country,” adding that Washington seeks “to restore peace and give power back to the Sudanese people.”
In a statement on Wednesday, Sudan’s Foreign Ministry said Khartoum “strongly rejects” the State Department’s remarks and “calls for positive engagement with the Sudanese government.” It warned that negotiations must not legitimize territory taken by the paramilitaries or “reward the rebellion for its crimes against civilians and state institutions.” It demanded the dissolution of militias and exclusive state control over weapons.
The dispute comes as Washington has reportedly withheld a visa for Sudan’s transitional leader, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, to attend the UN General Assembly in New York, making his attendance conditional on accepting a 90-day ceasefire, according to Reuters, citing sources.
Three years of war Sudan has been at war since April 2023, when a power struggle between Burhan and RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo erupted into fighting. Burhan’s government relocated to Port Sudan on the Red Sea coast after fighting engulfed Khartoum. Prime Minister Kamil Idris announced its return to the capital earlier this year, following the army’s recapture of the city in 2025.
The army controls Khartoum and eastern Sudan, while the RSF dominates much of the western Darfur region. The paramilitary group and its allies established a rival administration last year in Nyala, South Darfur, with Dagalo heading its governing council and Mohammed Hassan al-Taishi serving as prime minister. The conflict has displaced millions of people and pushed parts of the country into famine. Repeated ceasefire efforts, including US-Saudi talks in Jeddah, have failed to halt the violence.
Mediation difficulties Burhan rejected a US-led proposal last November as “the worst yet,” arguing it would dismantle state security institutions while leaving the RSF in place. The Quad – comprising the US, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the UAE – proposed a three-month humanitarian truce followed by a political transition toward civilian rule. The RSF said it accepted the truce.
The UAE’s involvement in mediation remains a major point of contention. Sudan’s army-backed government severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi in May 2025, accusing it of supporting the RSF. The UAE denies supplying weapons to the paramilitaries.
On Wednesday, the Sudanese Foreign Ministry said peace remains the government’s “choice and strategic goal.” It affirmed Khartoum’s readiness “for positive and responsible engagement” with the US and other partners, including Russia, who it said are “working sincerely and impartially” to achieve stability in Sudan, “far from dictates and external interferences.”

When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:28:15 UTC
22:28:15 KST

When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
- Date:
- September 24, 2026
- Source:
- Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory
- Summary:
- The brain may have a built-in way to quickly settle disagreements between regions processing the same scene. Researchers found that matching signals between two visual areas lasted longer, while conflicting signals rapidly faded away. This “consensus building” mechanism could help explain how the brain turns many specialized inputs into one unified view of the world.
- Share:
Sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense. A shadow can briefly resemble a face, or one object can momentarily be mistaken for another. New research suggests that the brain may resolve these visual conflicts by allowing different regions to compare their interpretations until a more consistent picture emerges.
In a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R. Stebbins Fellow Mitra Javadzadeh and collaborators at the University of Cambridge and University College London examined how two neighboring regions of the visual cortex interact. They found that when activity in the two regions matched, the shared pattern persisted. When the regions produced conflicting patterns, however, the disagreement faded within a fraction of a second.
The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.
How Specialized Brain Regions Work Together
Different parts of the brain are responsible for processing different streams of sensory information, yet our experience of the world usually feels unified rather than fragmented. Understanding how those specialized systems coordinate with one another is a major challenge in neuroscience.
"We are trying to understand how you can have such a high level of specialization between these different blocks, yet always have a consistent holistic outcome," Javadzadeh says.
The researchers focused on two well known visual processing regions in the brain's neocortex: the primary visual cortex (V1) and the lateromedial visual area (LM). Visual processing does not simply move in one direction from one region to the next. Instead, these areas continually exchange information with each other.
Testing What Happens When Visual Areas Disagree
To explore that communication, Javadzadeh and her colleagues trained mice to tell the difference between two visual patterns tilted in opposite directions. The animals received a reward for recognizing only one of the orientations.
During the task, the researchers temporarily silenced either V1 or LM and watched how the remaining region behaved without its usual partner. The team then used those observations to create an artificial neural network model of the V1-LM circuit. With that model, they could test how the system might respond when particular neurons were altered.
The results revealed a striking pattern. Activity that conflicted between the two brain regions quickly disappeared, while activity shared by both areas lasted longer.
"We find that over time, these types of connections between areas implement a mechanism we call consensus building," Javadzadeh explains.
A Possible Brainwide Consensus Mechanism
The study examined only two regions involved in vision, but the researchers are now investigating whether the same process may operate more broadly across the neocortex.
"For example, when what you see contradicts with what you hear, do you still use the same kind of mechanisms to reconcile these two?" she wonders.
If dynamic consensus building turns out to be widespread, it could help scientists better understand how the brain combines competing signals into a stable interpretation of the world. It could also shed light on what happens when different brain regions fail to arrive at the same conclusion.
The idea may even have implications beyond neuroscience. Similar principles could help researchers think about how artificial intelligence systems might handle conflicting streams of information and decide which signals to trust.
"While we understand individual building blocks of the brain, what is the glue that puts them together?" Javadzadeh asks. "Knowing that can finally help us understand how the brain works as a whole."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Mitra Javadzadeh, Marine Schimel, Sonja B. Hofer, Yashar Ahmadian, Guillaume Hennequin. Reciprocal connections dynamically build consensus between neocortical areas. Nature Neuroscience, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02437-3

Rail Baltica delays leave local communities disappointed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24

22:28:00 KST

Rail Baltica delays leave local communities disappointed
Businesses and residents in the settlements along the planned Tallinn–Pärnu section of Rail Baltica are disappointed, as the state is once again breaking its promise and the completion of the new railway may be delayed by up to eight years.
A large BLRT foundry will soon open in Kohila, and the choice of location was influenced by the possibility of transporting goods by rail. Local residents and companies are eagerly waiting for the railway, but now no one knows when it will be finished.
"Speaking with company leaders, all have confirmed that the Rail Baltica line starting in 2030 is not only meant for passenger transport — freight transport has also been factored into their business plans. This means that our main interest and wish is that at least passenger transport to Pärnu should begin in 2030. Freight transport is just as important," said Kohila municipality development adviser Aivar Roop.
From Kohila, the new train would reach Tallinn in less than half an hour.
"Estonia has 78 municipalities, and 11 of them are showing growth today. Kohila is one of them — the only municipality outside the golden ring — that is growing in population. And this has a direct connection to Rail Baltica, because our first residential real‑estate developers have already arrived," Roop said.
No train has run to Pärnu for eight years. Sari Sopanen, head of Brackmann Arendus, which is developing a large hotel and conference centre near Pärnu beach, said rail service would benefit their business.
"It's not the reason we're building the complex there. But accessibility is very important for tourism. It would certainly help if the train connection existed and the railway connection existed. I especially think about how great it would be if Pärnu were connected to two international airports. That would be fantastic for our field," Sopanen said.
According to former Pärnu mayor Kristel Voltenberg, Pärnu was initially promised the railway already for this year, but then the deadlines began to shift.
"New promises were made for 2030. All Pärnu residents, our entrepreneurs — which is very important — and the entire city planning have actually been tied to that date. Now we see from public sources that this date is again turning into a promise that can be deflated with a snap of the fingers. We cannot be satisfied with this in Pärnu," Voltenberg said.
"In Estonia, it is possible to complete the Tallinn–Pärnu section first, so that domestic rail service can begin. We will still discuss this during budget negotiations, but it will certainly come before the completion of the entire route," said Minister of Infrastructure Kuldar Leis.
The government will discuss the completion schedule of the railway sections on Thursday.

Ukrainian POWs reportedly transferred from Makiivka penal colony in occupied Donetsk Oblast to Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:27:00 EEST
22:27:00 KST

Ukrainian POWs reportedly transferred from Makiivka penal colony in occupied Donetsk Oblast to Russia
All prisoners serving sentences in penal colony No. 32 in the city of Makiivka, in the temporarily occupied part of Donetsk Oblast, are to be transferred to prisons in Russia, with Ukrainian citizens being moved first.
Source: a local media outlet Novyny Donbasu (Donbas News)
Details: The first six prisoners – one civilian and five Ukrainian service members sentenced by the Russian-appointed occupation authorities to 10-17 years on serious charges including extremism, terrorism and espionage – were transferred in August.
A further 24 Ukrainian civilians, who were unlawfully sentenced to lengthy prison terms on similar charges, are now being prepared for transfer.
In total, Novyny Donbasu reported that more than 30 Ukrainian prisoners are to be transferred to Russia. Many of them have been held by the occupation authorities since 2017-2019.
Some of those being transferred require constant medical supervision.
Some prisoners could have been released within just one or two years, but their transfer to Russia could delay the process.
The greatest concern for those being transferred and their relatives is the uncertainty, as prisoners are not told where they are being sent.
Of the six people already transferred, only one has managed to make contact. He said he is currently being held in a pre-trial detention centre in the Russian city of Krasnoyarsk and that this was not his final destination. The whereabouts of the other detainees remain unknown.
The official reason given for moving prisoners out of Makiivka penal colony is the inability to provide adequate detention conditions, including water supplies and coal for heating.
Novyny Donbasu suggested there may also be an economic motive, noting that the number of penal colonies in Russia is declining as some inmates are sent to fight in the war and never return.
As a result, prison staff are being left without work. Novyny Donbasu suggested that transferring prisoners from occupied Ukrainian territories to Russia could be intended to prevent some Russian penal colonies from closing.
Novyny Donbasu also reported that after the prisoner exchange on 14 August 2025, more than 35 Ukrainian citizens, including five service members, are still being held in Makiivka penal colony No. 32.
Their relatives fear that those transferred to Russia could be placed in prisons operating under a "special regime", meaning conditions there are even harsher than those in high-security facilities.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said it has not had unrestricted access to Ukrainian POWs in Russia and temporarily occupied territories for two years.
As of February 2025, more than 180 penal colonies in Russia were reported to be holding Ukrainian citizens. However, ICRC representatives can access only some of them.
Novyny Donbasu also reported that Russian authorities allow the international organisation to see only prisoners who are in relatively good condition, while those who are ill or severely weakened are kept from view.

Operation Vivaldi: Ground Robots Cleared 30 Kilometers in Two Nights Without Losses
Ukrainian ground robots cleared 30 kilometers of routes in the Shandryholove sector in two nights during Operation Vivaldi, Militarnyi reported on September 24.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Third Army Corps told Militarnyi that unmanned ground systems completed the difficult demining task entirely on their own.
The corps estimated that two sapper companies would have needed about a week to complete the same work, whereas using robotic systems resulted in no sapper losses.
Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, commander of the Third Army Corps, said the corps sends unmanned systems ahead of infantry during assault operations.
“During assault operations, UAVs and ground robotic systems always go ahead of the infantry,” Biletskyi stated, according to Militarnyi.

The outlet added that the platforms also support assault operations, replacing servicemen on some of the most dangerous sections of the front.
According to Militarnyi, the corps also uses the systems for several other tasks:
- remote mining of routes used by Russian forces to advance, with one crew able to lay mines across up to 200 meters of terrain per day;
- frontline logistics, including evacuating wounded troops and delivering food, construction materials, and other equipment.
The demining effort follows the recapture of Shandryholove and Derylove and the establishment of full control over Drobysheve during the second phase of Operation Vivaldi.
The Third Army Corps says more than 125 square kilometers have come under Ukrainian control since the offensive began in the northern Donetsk region.
Days earlier, heavy bomber drones flown by the Third Assault Brigade delivered attack ground robots more than 10 kilometers behind Russian lines, in what was billed as a world first.

Suspected Sabotage Targets Starlink Ground Station Serving Ukraine in Poland

- Category

Suspected Sabotage Targets Starlink Ground Station Serving Ukraine in Poland
A fire broke out at a Starlink ground station in Poland that provides satellite internet connectivity to parts of Central and Eastern Europe, including Ukraine, with Polish authorities investigating possible sabotage, Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said.
According to RMF, the fire occurred late on September 23 at a facility in Wola Krobowska. The owner of the property where the Starlink infrastructure is located alerted emergency services after antennas caught fire and a power generator was damaged. Firefighters subsequently extinguished the blaze.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Together with a similar ground station near Kaunas, Lithuania, the Wola Krobowska facility provides internet access to a significant part of Central and Eastern Europe, RMF reported.
Preliminary findings indicate that unidentified individuals may have deliberately set fire to an electrical distribution panel at the site. Investigators are also considering a short circuit in the electrical system as a possible cause.
“The fire engulfed the power station and the generator; it is clear that this act of sabotage was deliberately designed to disable the station—effectively cutting off the internet connection and disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian military,” Gawkowski said, according to Reuters.
The incident also highlights Ukraine’s reliance on Starlink connectivity during Russia’s full-scale invasion. Poland spends around $50 million annually to finance half of the approximately 42,000 Starlink terminals used in Ukraine.
That reliance recently became a point of contention after Poland was removed from Starlink’s European roaming zone, prompting Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski to criticize Starlink owner Elon Musk amid concerns over the potential impact on satellite communications for Ukraine’s military.
Concerns over the Starlink station fire come amid heightened scrutiny of sabotage and other hybrid threats across Europe. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed a NATO-style mechanism on September 16 to help EU countries coordinate their response to sabotage, drone incursions, and other forms of non-military aggression.
Under the proposed “counter-hybrid playbook,” any EU member state targeted by such activity could initiate emergency consultations with other members, allowing the bloc to coordinate its response, deterrence, and mitigation measures.

Reporters from three news outlets banned from the White House by President Donald Trump were back on the grounds Thursday afternoon, hours after a federal judge ordered the administration to reinstate their access.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists were allowed back in, the latest development in an extraordinary showdown between Trump and media outlets whose coverage he dislikes.
The reporters were barred from the White House on Thursday morning despite a federal judge ordering US President Donald Trump to restore their access immediately, saying his ban on the three media outlets was likely unconstitutional.
The ruling appeared to be a major setback for Trump in one of his biggest battles with the media. US District Judge Tim Kelly issued his order in a lawsuit that the news organisations filed contesting the ban that the Republican president announced on September 18.
Read moreTrump bans media outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House
Trump had said on social media that the three outlets "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES", and Justice Department lawyers had sought to justify the ban on national security grounds.
After being denied access to the White House, CNN, Politico and MS NOW asked the judge who issued the ruling to hold an emergency follow-up hearing. Journalists from the three media outlets were then allowed entry on Thursday afternoon.
'Trump TV'
Journalists for the three news organisations were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday and had their passes confiscated in the latest flare-up of the 80-year-old Republican president's years-long assault on the mainstream US media.
In a previous case involving CNN during Trump's first term, Kelly, a Trump appointee, ordered the White House to temporarily restore the White House access for a CNN reporter whose pass had been revoked.
In a rare move, the top five US broadcasters said on Monday that they were halting pool coverage of the White House – where a broadcaster films on behalf of all television outlets for the day – in solidarity with CNN.
"The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting," ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said.
The White House Correspondents' Association and nearly 50 news organisations also filed a brief with the court calling for the bans on CNN, MS NOW and Politico to be reversed.

Gabriel Attal : “150 milliards d’économies, c’est une base”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:24:10 UTC
22:24:10 KST

PARIS — Lors d’un grand entretien au sommet Playbook Paris de POLITICO, Gabriel Attal a décliné jeudi les grandes orientations de son plan budgétaire à court et moyen terme.
Le candidat Renaissance, qui se targue d’être celui parmi ses concurrents qui a “donné le plus de détails sur sa feuille de route budgétaire”, considère que 150 milliards d’euros d’économies sur cinq ans seraient nécessaires pour amorcer le rééquilibrage des comptes publics. Mais que ce montant n’est qu’une “base” et qu’“il faudra probablement aller plus loin”.
L’ex-Premier ministre s’est engagé à ramener le déficit public de la France sous la barre des 3% du PIB avant 2032, tout en visant un retour à l'équilibre strict (“zéro déficit”) à l’horizon 2030.
Advertisement
Face au spectre d’une crise de la dette, Gabriel Attal, qui s’est entretenu mercredi avec plusieurs économistes (Xavier Jaravel, Natacha Valla ou encore Olivier Blanchard), a annoncé qu’il préparait “un plan de secours au cas où la situation se dégraderait à très court terme”.
Sans décliner l’ensemble de son plan d’économies, Gabriel Attal a évoqué ses principales pistes, dont une réforme des retraites, un serrage des dépenses sur la sphère sociale et sur les effectifs de l’administration grâce à l’intelligence artificielle. Le candidat va en outre dévoiler prochainement “une refonte globale de l’organisation des pouvoirs publics”, et compte réduire “d’une strate” le millefeuille administratif.
Interrogé par POLITICO sur le projet de loi de finances 2026, l’ex-ministre du budget ne s’est guère aventuré davantage, en attendant sa présentation par l’exécutif début octobre.
En revanche, Gabriel Attal s’est opposé à l’idée d’une baisse de la contribution française au budget de l’Union européenne. “Ça ne me satisfait pas”, a-t-il réagi. Toutefois, il s’est montré ouvert à ce que “éventuellement” les amendes payées par les géants du numérique puissent être redistribuées aux Etats membres.

After €4mn transformation, Pullman Riga Old Town GM Pawel Panczak says: 'The larger ambition goes beyond the building'  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:23:14 UTC
22:23:14 KST

Following a €4mn transformation, Pullman Riga Old Town is setting its sights on becoming the rate leader in Riga’s five-star hotel market and using international conferences to strengthen winter demand. General Manager Pawel Panczak tells The Baltic Times how the 151-room hotel preserved the character of its 1789 building, rebuilt the infrastructure guests never see and why people, costs and air connectivity remain the hospitality sector’s greatest challenges.
Pullman Riga Old Town underwent a major renovation in 2025. What were the most important changes, and how much was invested?
This was not a cosmetic refresh – we rebuilt the hotel with an investment of €4mn. All 151 rooms were stripped back and redone, the lobby and the entire ground floor were reconfigured, the conference area was built from scratch, and the wellness and pool floor on the seventh level was fully reworked.
A large share of the budget went into things a guest will never notice: air conditioning, lifts, fire safety systems, soundproofing and IT infrastructure. It is not the glamorous part of a project like this, but it determines whether a five-star hotel still works properly ten years from now.
How did you modernise the hotel while preserving the character and architectural identity of its historic Old Town setting?
The building dates from 1789 and stands in a protected part of the Old Town, which made the project a close collaboration with the heritage authorities from the very beginning. Preserving the façade, the rhythm of the windows and the proportions of the public spaces allowed us to celebrate the building's remarkable character. At the same time, we had the opportunity to completely reimagine everything behind it, creating a contemporary experience while remaining true to the spirit of the place.
We are fortunate in the layout: the property is really three buildings joined together – the historic house and two contemporary structures alongside it. That allowed us to place the demanding modern functions – the conference floor, the technical plant and the wellness area – in the newer parts, and let the historic building stay calm and residential in feel.
Inside, the design language is deliberately Nordic-Baltic: oak, linen, stone and muted colours create an atmosphere that reflects the region's heritage and natural surroundings. A guest should be able to tell from the room which country they woke up in.
What distinguishes Pullman Riga Old Town from other five-star hotels in Riga, particularly those in or near the historic centre?
Three things, I would say.
First, the address and the building. We are inside the Old Town, a few steps from the Saeima (Parliament), the National Theatre, Dome Square and the Freedom Monument. Guests walk out of the door and they are already where they wanted to be. And the door they walk out of belongs to a protected house from 1789, with genuinely modern conference and leisure infrastructure inside. Very few hotels can offer both on the same site. Usually, you choose one or the other. Here, you do not have to.
Second, the scale. With 151 rooms and eight meeting spaces for up to 200 people, we can host a full conference or an incentive group and still run the hotel normally for everyone else. Most five-star addresses in the centre are boutique properties of 40 to 70 rooms, which they do beautifully, but group business of that size is simply outside what they were built for.
Third, Harper Woolf. It is not a hotel restaurant in the usual sense. The kitchen is led by Maksims Kolomaznikovs, and the menu is built around shared plates, so the whole table orders together and tries a bit of everything. With up to 60 seats, it handles a group dinner easily, but it is just as good for two. An anniversary, a promotion or just an ordinary Tuesday: at Harper Woolf, every reason to come for dinner is a good one.
Which guest segments are most important – international leisure, corporate, conference delegates, or Baltic and Nordic visitors?
We deliberately do not lean on a single one. The mix is well balanced and shifts with the season, and that is the point – Riga is too seasonal a market to be a pure leisure hotel or a pure business hotel.
Geographically, the UK, the Nordics and Poland are our strongest inbound markets, with steady corporate demand from Lithuania and Estonia. The Nordic weekend guest brings particular value to the destination: the journey is short, communication is easy, and these stays often extend beyond the room itself, with guests enjoying dinner and making full use of the hotel’s facilities.
The segment I am giving most attention to at the moment is international MICE – associations, corporate meetings and incentives. That is where the Pullman flag genuinely helps, because it puts us on the radar of planners in France, the United States and Canada who would most likely never have considered a hotel in Riga otherwise.
How have occupancy levels, average room rates and guest demand developed since the renovated hotel reopened?
The first months after a reopening are never the real picture. You are still carrying construction noise in the reviews, the sales pipeline is empty and the online ratings start again from zero. About six months in, the curve began to look the way it should.
Occupancy is well above where the hotel stood before the renovation, and more importantly, we are achieving rates we simply could not have asked for with the old product.
What I follow even more closely than occupancy is our index against the competitive set – whether we are taking more than our fair share of the market. We are above that benchmark, and guest satisfaction scores have improved steadily every month since reopening.
How important are conferences, corporate events and business travellers to the hotel's overall revenue, and what facilities do you offer to this market?
Meetings and events account for roughly 25% to 30% of total revenue, and their real value is greater than that share suggests, because a conference fills rooms on precisely the nights leisure demand does not – Tuesday to Thursday, October to March.
We have eight meeting rooms, the largest for 200 people, all located in the modern part of the building, so delegates are not moving through the lobby past leisure guests. Alongside that, we run a full banqueting operation, and the restaurant, bar and cigar lounge give organisers somewhere to take an evening programme without leaving the hotel.
Riga's hotel sector experiences strong seasonal fluctuations. How does the hotel attract guests during the quieter autumn and winter months?
Winter demand has to be built around something other than the weather.
In practice, that means three things. Conferences and corporate meetings, which we pursue hardest in exactly those months. Short city breaks packaged for Baltic and Nordic guests, where the hotel itself is part of the reason to travel. And food and beverage: our immersive dining concept, Le Petit Chef, together with the seasonal programme in the restaurant, gives people a reason to come in December or February, when a city break on its own is a harder sell.
December largely takes care of itself thanks to the Christmas market – Riga does that very well. The months we have to solve are November, January and February, and that is where the meetings business and our restaurants earn their keep.
What role do the restaurant, wellness facilities and other services play in attracting local residents as well as overnight guests?
A hotel restaurant that serves only hotel guests is a missed opportunity. Ours has to work as a Riga restaurant first.
Harper Woolf is open to the city, and a meaningful share of the covers is local – that is the standard we hold it to. Le Petit Chef has been particularly effective in that respect: it is an occasion, so people book it for birthdays and company dinners, and most of those guests are Latvian rather than visiting. The cigar lounge and the wellness area follow the same logic on a smaller scale.
There is a commercial reason and a cultural one. Commercially, local business fills the shoulder periods. Culturally, a hotel that residents never walk into feels closed off, and international guests sense that immediately. When people from Riga use the building, the atmosphere is simply better.
What are the biggest challenges currently facing Riga's five-star hospitality sector?
People, first and by some distance. Latvia's working-age population is shrinking, and we compete for the same staff with the Nordic countries, where they can earn considerably more. Retention, training and offering people a career rather than a shift have become a central part of the job rather than an HR topic.
Cost is the second. Payroll is rising, and energy and food costs have not returned to their earlier levels. At the rate levels this market supports, you cannot simply pass all of that on to the guest.
Third, connectivity. Demand in Riga follows the route map from the airport very closely, and every new long-haul or Western European connection is worth more to this city's hotels than any marketing campaign we could run on our own.
I see competition as a positive force. A strong and diverse hotel landscape makes Riga an even more attractive destination for travellers and showcases the city's growing appeal on the international stage.
What are your principal targets over the next three years, and are further investment or expansion projects being considered?
Three targets. To establish the hotel as the rate leader in the Riga five-star market, measured against our competitive set rather than against our own last year. To keep guest satisfaction improving month on month. And to grow international meetings and incentives to the point where group business carries the winter reliably rather than occasionally.
On further investment, the core product is complete, so the next phase is smaller and more precise rather than another construction site. At the moment, we are working on the furniture in the restaurant and the cigar lounge, and that will be finished by the end of September.
The larger ambition goes beyond the building. Riga is still undersold as a city-break and conference destination compared with Tallinn or Vilnius, and that is a marketing question rather than a product one. We are now in a position to be part of solving it.

Russia threatens Armenia to halt all gas supplies from November 1 - media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:21:09 EEST
22:21:09 KST

Russia threatens Armenia to halt all gas supplies from November 1 - media
Kyiv • UNN
Sources report that gas supplies may be halted after November 1 due to Moscow's political demands. Yerevan is seeking alternatives.
Until September 25, gas supplies from Russia to Armenia have been temporarily suspended due to scheduled maintenance, while domestic demand is being covered by stocks in storage facilities. According to sources at the Armenian newspaper Hraparak, a major "accident" may occur or force majeure may arise on November 1, after which gas supplies will not be restored, UNN reports, citing DW.
Details
According to the publication's sources, Moscow may take such a step if Yerevan fails to meet four of its political demands. The list includes refusing to discuss the fate of the Russian military base in Gyumri and taking action against companies with Russian capital, as well as ending the criminal prosecution of politicians oriented toward Russia and appointing a deputy prime minister whose candidacy would be acceptable to the Kremlin.
According to Hraparak, another demand from Moscow is that Armenia choose between the EAEU and the European Union. In particular, Yerevan must either repeal the law launching the European integration process or set a date for a referendum on the matter.
It should be added
After Yerevan's decision to apply for EU membership, relations between the two countries became more strained. At the same time, Armenia remains almost entirely dependent on gas supplies from Russia and imports it at a preferential price.
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan noted that, regardless of Moscow's decisions, Yerevan would seek other sources of gas supplies. On September 16, Armenia's Security Council stated that the republic was capable of replacing Russian supplies with purchases from Azerbaijan, Turkey, and Iran.

Most Spaniards say Morocco triggered Ceuta crisis, poll shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:20:57 UTC
22:20:57 KST

MADRID, September 24. /TASS/. More than 82% of Spaniards believe that Morocco triggered the migration crisis in the autonomous city of Ceuta, according to a poll published by 20 Minutos newspaper.
According to the newspaper, 6.5% of respondents disagree with this view, while about 11% were undecided. More than 63% of those polled also believe that the Spanish government has not taken a firm enough position on protecting its sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla. Meanwhile, 82.7% of Spaniards believe that Madrid and the European Union should impose some form of sanctions on Morocco over its hypothetical involvement in the crisis.
More than 1,000 people took part in the poll, which was conducted from September 16 to 21.
In late July, tens of thousands of illegal migrants managed to reach Ceuta by swimming and wading around the breakwater separating the city from Morocco. Amid the crisis, Madrid decided to deploy military personnel to help ensure security in the city.

Meta removes post about Meta glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:19:23 UTC
22:19:23 KST

Meta takes down Dutch satirist’s film made with Meta glasses
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Instagram removed a video by Roel Maalderink in which the satirical journalist films himself asking the employees of parent company Meta how they feel about the controversial camera glasses.
In the short video, which can still be seen on Alphabet-owned YouTube, Maalderink dons the so-called “pervert glasses” and quizzes staff after instructing the device to start recording.
The gadgets, the most popular version of which is sold by Meta, look like normal glasses but allow users to film and take photos covertly.
The employees, all of whom have their features blurred and are unrecognisable, are not pleased about being recorded.
The video, made together with digital rights organisation Bits of Freedom, was removed from Instagram over what Meta said was “bullying and harassment”.
“I’ve been making satirical videos about everything for 10 years now: Gaza, Ukraine, refugees,” Maalderink said in a statement. He added that this was the first time he had had a video taken down.
Bits of Freedom said that this behaviour shows the company’s power. “Meta determines what becomes publicly discussable and how the debate unfolds. Apparently, there’s no room for criticism directed at Meta itself,” the organisation said.
Earlier this week, Dutch privacy watchdog AP warned that sharing images made with camera glasses violates GDPR rules unless permission is given by everyone in the image.

Ukrainian carries out attack at Benedictine monastery in Poland; Embassy strongly condemns incident
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:18:01 EEST
22:18:01 KST

An armed attack took place at a Benedictine monastery in the town of Jarosław, in Poland's Subcarpathian Voivodeship, on Thursday morning. A 31-year-old Ukrainian citizen attacked five people—four men and one woman—with a knife, polsatnews.pl reports.
"Four men (including three priests) and one woman were injured. All were taken to the hospital. Initial reports indicated that three of them were in critical condition. It was later revealed that one of the priests had died," the report states.
According to reports, the attack occurred before a mass scheduled to begin at 10:00 a.m.
The Ukrainian man who carried out the attack is in police custody. The Embassy of Ukraine in Poland has strongly condemned the attack.
"We consider any acts of violence unacceptable. It is particularly painful that this tragedy occurred in a place meant to be a sanctuary of prayer and mercy. Our thoughts and prayers today are with everyone affected by this tragedy. We extend our sincere condolences to the family and loved ones of the deceased. We wish the injured a speedy recovery. There can be no justification for violence or attacks on people," the Embassy said on Facebook.
The Embassy expressed its gratitude to law enforcement officers, medical personnel, and all services that responded to the incident and are providing necessary assistance to the victims.
"We are confident that the competent authorities will thoroughly and objectively establish all the circumstances of the tragedy, and that those responsible will be held accountable in accordance with the law. In such difficult moments, it is especially important to maintain mutual support, remain steadfast in our respect for human life, and not allow pain to turn into hatred or further violence. Accountability for the crime must be based solely on the law," the Embassy of Ukraine in Poland emphasized.

China to ease market access, boost digital trade: Premier Li
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:17:25 CST
22:17:25 KST

Chinese Premier Li Qiang addresses the opening ceremony of the Fifth Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, Sept. 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Ding Haitao)
HANGZHOU, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- China will further ease market access and improve policies for cross-border e-commerce retail imports, Premier Li Qiang said Thursday, pledging to share opportunities in its market with other countries.
Addressing the opening ceremony of the Fifth Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, Li said the rapid growth of digital trade had created new opportunities, but had also brought widening development gaps, new trade barriers and gaps in international rules into sharper focus.
Li called for closer international cooperation to strengthen digital connectivity and advance the alignment and mutual recognition of standards.
The international community should enhance North-South cooperation in the field of digital trade, and provide more support to developing countries in terms of technology, infrastructure and personnel training, he said.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, and Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers of Kyrgyzstan, Adylbek Aleshovich Kasymaliev, also addressed the opening ceremony, which was attended by more than 1,200 representatives from nearly 50 countries and regions, as well as international organizations.
The expo, an event dedicated to promoting digital trade and industrial cooperation, is running until Sept. 27, with artificial intelligence as its main theme.
China's digital trade has expanded rapidly in recent years. The country's digitally deliverable service trade value expanded at an average annual rate of 11.2 percent between 2016 and 2025, outpacing the global average by 1.8 percentage points. ■

Asian Games | China's weightlifter He sets snatch world record in men's 65kg
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:17:15 CST
22:17:15 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Yang Yang won the men's 60kg weightlifting gold on Thursday, giving China first medal in the sport at the 2026 Asian Games, while the day's highlight came from a snatch world record from China's He Yueji in the mens' 65kg division.
In the 65kg final, He managed a new snatch world record of 152kg, but had to settle for a silver as he had only 175kg in the clean and jerk. The title went to DPR Korea's Pak Myong Jin.
Pak, who took the 61kg silver at the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023, lifted 146kg in the snatch and 182kg in the clean and jerk for a total of 328kg. Vietnam's Tran Minh Tri had the bronze with 309kg.
In the men's 60kg, Yang, 23, lifted 138kg in the snatch and 166kg in the clean and jerk for a total of 304kg, a Games record. All six of his attempts were successful.
"My legs were shaking when I watched my opponent's final lift," the Games debutant said. "I was more nervous than when I was on the platform by myself."
Yang built an 11kg lead after the snatch, then applied a steady game plan in the clean and jerk.
"Our coach told us to play it safe, step by step," he said. "The tactics worked really well. I just treated this like a regular training session," added Yang.
Pang Un Chol of DPR Korea took silver with 301kg, while Thailand's Theerapong Silachai, the 2024 Olympic silver medalist, finished third on 299kg. Both failed in their final attempts when challenging world records. ■

Economic Watch: Young travelers drive China's county tourism boom
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:17:10 CST
22:17:10 KST

XI'AN, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- For Zhang Chengyong, a college student spending the summer working behind a coffee counter at a resort in Ningshan County, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, the job has offered more than a break from campus.
He serves more than 100 cups of coffee a day, and over 200 when visitors surge. Most customers are young travelers seeking experiences beyond city life, giving the sophomore tourism management major a glimpse into his future career.
One such visitor, a tourist surnamed Zhang from the provincial capital Xi'an, found the resort online and booked a three-day family getaway, spending more than 3,000 yuan (about 445 U.S. dollars) during her stay.
She chose the resort for one simple reason: it offered a break from the city and more time outdoors for her child.
Unlike conventional homestays, the resort combines accommodation and dining with hands-on cultural and nature-based activities, from making crested ibis-themed souvenirs to plant printing and painting traditional lacquer fans.
"Most rooms were booked throughout the summer. Young people are less interested in highly commercialized attractions, but are willing to pay for the relaxed atmosphere of the countryside," said Xue Rong, the resort's manager. About 80 to 90 percent of its visitors come from Xi'an, she added.
The resort reflects a broader shift in young people's travel preferences. Instead of rushing from one landmark to another, many are seeking nature, local culture and hands-on experiences, and are increasingly willing to pay for them.
Cheng Chaogong, chief researcher at Tongcheng Research Institute, said county tourism is gaining popularity because counties combine rich natural landscapes, distinctive local culture and rural tourism resources, offering experiences that large cities cannot easily replicate.
That shift is reflected in spending data. Meituan, a major local services platform, said spending in counties by visitors from outside their home areas rose 14.1 percent year-on-year in the first half of 2026. Average spending per transaction reached about 58 yuan, roughly 50 percent higher than that of local residents, while experience-based spending continued to grow.
The trend is spreading beyond Shaanxi, with counties across China turning local culture and traditions into tourism attractions.
In Sandu Shui Autonomous County in southwest China's Guizhou Province, for example, traditional horse racing has evolved into a popular tourism brand, attracting visitors to watch races, ride horses and experience Shui ethnic embroidery.
The county recorded 3.22 million tourist visits in the first half of 2026, up 11 percent year on year, while tourism revenue reached 3.3 billion yuan, up 13.1 percent, according to local authorities.
Policy support is also helping accelerate the trend. A set of measures released by the Ministry of Commerce and eight other government departments in August called for deeper integration of commerce, agriculture, culture, tourism and sports, as well as the development of distinctive rural tourism destinations.
Improved infrastructure is making more of these destinations accessible to travelers. By the end of 2025, high-speed rail covered 97 percent of Chinese cities with urban populations of more than 500,000, while 97 percent of county-level regions had A-rated scenic areas during the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025).
The expansion of county tourism is part of a broader effort to make culture and tourism stronger drivers of domestic consumption and economic growth.
China's newly released 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for cultural and tourism development calls for making the sectors pillars of economic development while improving people's livelihoods and sense of well-being.
Chinese tourists spent 6.3 trillion yuan on domestic trips in 2025, according to official data. The Ministry of Culture and Tourism expects the figure to reach 7.7 trillion yuan by 2030. ■

Polish Deputy PM on Starlink station fire: Russia tries to deprive Ukraine of internet access at front
Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Digital Affairs Krzysztof Gawkowski made the statement to journalists in Warsaw on Thursday, Ukrinform reports.
According to Gawkowski, Polish services are currently at the site of the fire at a SpaceX station leased by an American company from Polish government institutions.
Gawkowski said that everything that had happened at the site indicated that it was likely an act of sabotage, possibly carried out by Russia. He said the incident was apparently intended to disrupt internet access for Starlink terminals, which could have deprived Ukrainian forces of internet access on the front line. He added that the Polish authorities were aware of the threat and were taking steps to protect the infrastructure.
He noted that the facility is private infrastructure and had only video surveillance, without physical security, which should be provided for vulnerable sites of this type.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Polish authorities are investigating a fire at a Starlink satellite communications ground station in the Masovian Voivodeship in eastern Poland.
Meanwhile, the head of the Polish government said on Thursday that "strange incidents" occur in Poland, drawing attention to the previous day's fire at the Starlink ground station in the Masovian Voivodeship.
He said the situation "looks very bad," while emphasizing that there is not yet 100% certainty that it was an act of sabotage.

Swimming roundup: Ohashi sets WR, Bahrain breaks through as China's Zhang seals six-gold haul
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:16:59 CST
22:16:59 KST

by sportswriters Zhang Can and Liu Yichun
TOKYO, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Japan's 17-year-old Shin Ohashi shattered the men's 200-meter breaststroke world record on Thursday, while Bahrain celebrated its first swimming gold of the 2026 Asian Games and China's Zhang Zhanshuo took his gold-medal haul to six.
Ohashi clocked 2 minutes, 4.83 seconds to become the first swimmer to break 2:05 in the event, lowering the previous world record of 2:05.48 set by China's Qin Haiyang at the 2023 World Championships.
It was the first swimming world record of these Games.
"I am very happy to achieve the goal I've had for a long time, which is to break the world record," Ohashi said.
The teenager had already emerged as one of Japan's brightest swimming prospects. World Aquatics ratified his world junior records in the 100m and 200m breaststroke in 2025, and he had already won the 100m breaststroke title at the Asian Games.
Ohashi said his confidence grew after he clocked 2:09.00 in the morning heats.
"After the heats, I thought, maybe I really can do it," he said.
Ohashi, who said he had initially targeted a time in the 2:03 range, has set his sights on winning gold at the 2027 World Championships before turning his attention to the Olympics.
"I hope I can swim 2:02.00, or even 2:01.00 in the future," he said.
Earlier, Bahrain's Mikhail Arkhangelskiy produced another landmark performance, winning the men's 50m butterfly in 22.91 seconds to equal his own Asian record and claim Bahrain's first swimming gold at an Asian Games.
The 21-year-old, who was born in Russia and raised in France, began representing Bahrain this year after spending 16 years swimming in France and later competing at college in the United States.
"I found the energy, I found the confidence to win, and that's really something I'm proud of for my country," Arkhangelskiy said.
He said Bahrain's investment in swimming and the training conditions it offered played a role in his decision to represent the country.
"It's a big achievement, and I feel more confident, happier," he said. "I'm really proud and happy that Bahrain gave me the chance."
Arkhangelskiy will next turn his attention to the World Championships in Budapest next year.
China again claimed the largest share of the night's gold medals, with Zhang winning twice to take his tally to six titles.
The 19-year-old first defended his men's 800m freestyle title in an Asian Games record before returning to help China win the men's 4x100m freestyle relay alongside Zhao Jiayue, Wang Haoyu and Pan Zhanle in an Asian record 3:10.60.
Zhang has won six of the seven events he has entered and has the men's 400m freestyle remaining on his schedule on Friday.
"The schedule may look quite brutal from the outside, but for me there was a long break in between," Zhang said of racing twice on Thursday.
Reflecting on the relay victory, Zhang said he was pleased to have shared the title and Asian record with his teammates.
"I think today was a relatively good result. I'm very happy that I could win this valuable gold medal with my teammates and break a new Asian record," he said.
Wu Qingfeng added another Chinese gold in the women's 50m freestyle, winning in an Asian Games record 23.98 seconds, just 0.01 outside the Asian record held by Liu Xiang.
Siobhan Haughey of Hong Kong, China, took silver in 24.32, with China's Cheng Yujie third in 24.46.
"I feel it is a little regrettable," Wu said, pointing to a slow reaction at the start and an imperfect finish. "If I can do these two details better, I can go even faster."
China also dominated the women's 4x200m freestyle relay, leading from start to finish to win in 7:49.37 and claim its eighth consecutive Asian Games title in the event.
Japan's Kotomi Kato won the women's 200m breaststroke, ahead of South Korea's Park Sieun and China's Zhu Leiju. ■

Beijing requires topped-out structures for new home presales
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:16:54 CST
22:16:54 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- The city of Beijing requires new commercial housing projects to complete main-structure topping-out before applying for presale permits, and prioritizes completed-home sales, according to a guideline issued by the Beijing Municipal Commission of Housing and Urban-Rural Development and three other municipal departments Thursday.
For new commercial housing projects after Aug. 28, each building must have its main structure topped out before presale is allowed to proceed, according to the guideline.
Presale revenue for these projects will be put under supervision.
Starting Aug. 28, sale of completed homes are prioritized in new projects, the guideline says. It says in the mode of completed-home sale, developers may first sign deposit contracts with buyers after obtaining construction permits, with deposits generally capped at 1 percent of the total home price.
Buyers may terminate the deposit contract if developers fail to deliver homes on time, according to the guideline.
To ease developers' funding pressure, land transfer payments may be paid in installments, according to the guideline. ■

Distant time crystals can somehow fall into the same rhythm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:16:41 UTC
22:16:41 KST

Distant time crystals can somehow fall into the same rhythm
Physicists have discovered that separate time crystals can synchronize across surprisingly large distances inside a semiconductor.
- Date:
- September 24, 2026
- Source:
- TU Dortmund University
- Summary:
- Researchers have shown that multiple time crystals inside a semiconductor can synchronize their oscillations, much like pendulum clocks gradually falling into the same rhythm. The coupling is carried by spin-polarized electrons, allowing time crystals separated by up to 40 micrometers to lock to a common frequency. The discovery reveals surprisingly long-range connections between these exotic spin systems and could help researchers develop future spin-based devices.
- Share:
Physicists at TU Dortmund University showed in January 2024 that a continuous time crystal could persist inside a semiconductor, with its oscillations remaining stable for hours. Now, in a new study published inNature Communications, Prof. Alex Greilich and his colleagues have found that multiple time crystals can emerge within the same material and synchronize their electron-nuclear spin oscillations.
Time crystals are unusual physical systems whose internal behavior repeats in a regular rhythm over time, even though they are not being driven by a repeating external signal.
In the TU Dortmund experiments, the time crystals form inside a semiconductor made from gallium arsenide with small amounts of indium and silicon. These added elements create localized electrons within the material. At temperatures close to -270 °C, each electron interacts with roughly one million nearby nuclear spins.
To initiate the process, the researchers use a pump laser to align the electron spins. The electrons then transfer their polarization to the surrounding nuclear spins. When a weak magnetic field is applied, the polarization of those nuclear spins begins to rotate.
Feedback between the electron spins and nuclear spins keeps the oscillations going. A second laser allows the researchers to monitor how those oscillations develop over time.
Separate Oscillations Fall Into Sync
Different regions of the semiconductor are not perfectly identical at the microscopic level. Because of these local variations, time crystals that form in separate areas would normally oscillate at slightly different frequencies.
That changes when the researchers illuminate many regions at once with a broad laser beam. Under those conditions, the separate oscillations can lock together and begin operating at the same frequency.
The effect is reminiscent of an observation made by Christiaan Huygens in 1665 involving two pendulum clocks. Huygens noticed that clocks attached to the same support could gradually synchronize because of the weak mechanical interaction transmitted through that shared structure.
In the semiconductor, the connection works differently. Instead of mechanical vibrations, the time crystals become coupled through the movement of spin-polarized electrons.
Synchronization Across Surprising Distances
The team found that time crystals located as far as 40 micrometers apart could still synchronize. That distance is more than one thousand times greater than the characteristic size of a single oscillator.
Once the separation becomes larger, however, the individual time crystals no longer lock together and instead continue oscillating independently.
The findings demonstrate non-local coupling between spatially separated spin systems. They could also help lay the groundwork for future networks of controllable spin oscillators, potentially opening new possibilities for spin-based technologies.

NEW YORK - The Committee to Protect Journalists said on Sept 24 it had removed 22 people from its list of media workers killed in the Gaza war after a review triggered by Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad obituaries identified some as combatants, although it still named Israel the world’s leading killer of journalists.
With the reclassifications, the committee now concludes that Israel is responsible for the deaths of 191 journalists or other media workers in Israel or the occupied Palestinian territories since the start of the war, sparked by Hamas’s bloody Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel.
The New York-based group that defends media rights is barred like other journalists and researchers from entering the Gaza Strip independently, but says it reviewed published work, social media posts, photographs, videos, and statements of deceased journalists and other published materials before enlisting an outside auditor to assess the process.
“The accuracy and credibility of CPJ’s research are fundamental to our mission and to efforts to seek accountability and justice for journalists and media workers around the world,” the group’s CEO Jodie Ginsberg said in a statement.
The CPJ said it has continuously revisited tallies as new evidence emerges since it began tracking the killings of media workers in 1992.
“We base the determinations we make solely on whether individuals meet our definitions of who we consider to be a journalist, not an individual’s affiliation or views, nor in response to pressure or intimidation from any government or interest group,” Ginsburg said.
Israeli forces “remain responsible for by far the majority of killings of journalists and media workers worldwide since 2023,” the CPJ said in a statement.
The group said it was taking 22 people off its list of slain media workers in the conflict, bringing to 36 the net total removed.
The committee also reinstated four people it said had been wrongly removed from the tally.
It separately also reclassified two Israelis killed in the Hamas attacks on Oct 7 as journalists.
The changes came in part after the committee decided it will now exclude anyone who is actively part of the military arm either of a country or a non-state actor such as Hamas.
It had earlier included journalists in military media units if they were not known to have actively engaged in combat.
Israel has repeatedly dismissed criticism of its killings of journalists, saying either that Gaza media workers were part of Hamas and therefore combatants, or that they were not the intended targets.
Hamas and other militants carried out the deadliest ever attack against Israel on Oct 7, 2023, killing 1,221 people and dragging 251 others as hostages into Gaza, according to Israeli official figures.
Israel’s retaliatory offensive has displaced virtually the entire population of Gaza, damaged or destroyed the vast majority of buildings and killed more than 73,900 people, according to the Gaza health ministry, which operates under Hamas and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations. Family of Iranian twins sentenced to death and decades in jail ask UN for help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:15:48 UTC
22:15:48 KST

The family of 21-year-old twins who have been sentenced respectively to death and decades in jail for protesting against the Iranian regime have appealed to the United Nations for help.
A formal “submission of information” relating to the case of Taraneh and Romina Rahimi has been submitted by British human right lawyers on their family’s behalf.
The move could lead to the UN’s human rights council opening talks with the Iranian regime about resolving the case if it is found to involve human rights violations.
The president of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, told the UN’s general assembly in New York this week that the country was “ready for dialogue and diplomacy”.
Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were taken from their beds by men from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps eight months ago after they joined nationwide protests against the regime.
They were tried over charges that included moharebeh (waging war against God) for taking to the streets of Isfahan, in central Iran, on 8 and 9 January.
At the end of August, Taraneh, along with nine others, was sentenced to death. Romina received a 25-year prison sentence.
The girls’ family are seeking to appeal against the sentences but human rights groups have raised concerns that Taraneh’s execution could be fast-tracked.
The women are being held in Dowlatabad prison in Isfahan, where the twins’ family claim that Taraneh was threatened with being forced to watch the rape of her sister if she failed to sign a confession to her alleged crimes.
The sisters have been held in isolation but are said to have been able to hear each other’s screams as torture was inflicted upon them.
Neither of the women have been seen by their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, or other members of the family since their sentencing.
After the Guardian highlighted the case, the women’s cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, an IT engineer who lives in the US state of Utah, said Taraneh was told she would only be allowed to eat leftovers of other prisoners’ meals as punishment.
Nourmohammadi, 43, said he had turned to the UN out of desperation.
Taraneh is said to be in need of surgery due to injuries inflicted during interrogation.
Nourmohammadi said: “Turning to the United Nations is not something I ever wanted to have to do. I am simply asking the international community to help ensure that Taraneh and Romina receive the basic rights that every human being is entitled to: a fair process, protection from torture and abuse, access to medical care and legal counsel, and the right to have their cases genuinely reviewed.
“Taraneh is facing the death penalty, and Romina is facing decades in prison. They are young women who should be thinking about their futures, not whether one sister will be executed and the other will spend the best years of her life behind bars.
“They are my family and I will continue to use every peaceful and legal avenue available. I ask the United Nations to stand with them before it is too late – especially for Taraneh.”
A submission to the UN through its “special procedures” can lead to a formal request by the international organisation to a member state for an explanation and action.
Iran has executed more than 500 people this year, including at least 16 women. Hundreds of protesters have been sentenced to death or are facing charges which could carry the death penalty, including more than 70 in Isfahan.

A prominent anti-migrant activist has been arrested after an alleged boat slashing incident in the Channel earlier this week, UK media reported Thursday.
It came as the interior ministry confirmed 781 people arrived in Britain on Wednesday after crossing the busy waterway from France aboard small boats—a daily record for this year.
The annual arrival of tens of thousands of migrants on the boats has become highly contentious in the UK, seized upon by the hard right and helping to fuel growing anti-immigration sentiment.
The arrest of Daniel Thomas, a longtime ally of far-right figurehead Tommy Robinson—real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon—comes after he spearheaded several demonstrations involving black-clad masked men, some of which turned violent.
Thomas, 37, was arrested late Wednesday on suspicion of destroying ships or endangering people's safety and criminal damage with intent to endanger life, British media reported.
Hampshire Police in southern England confirmed the arrest of a 37-year-old man but did not name him, in line with UK policing protocols.
"A man has been arrested after a boat that had an emergency responder on board, was damaged in the English Channel," the force said in a statement, adding he remained in custody.
Thomas, better known by his nickname Danny Tommo, livestreamed Tuesday from a boat in the Channel, on a self-proclaimed mission to track small boats bound for Britain.
Footage later emerged online appearing to show him slashing an inflatable craft, apparently with a French rescuer still on board.
"This is English territory. It's not France anymore," Thomas shouts in the video, before repeatedly yelling "get off the boat" at someone dressed in the orange uniforms worn by staff from France's SNSM lifeboat service.
Yaxley-Lennon emailed supporters on Thursday appealing for donations to help his former right-hand man.
Meanwhile, interior minister Shabana Mahmood has ordered an urgent review after two small boats avoided border forces and landed on southeastern English beaches this week.
Successive UK governments have grappled with how to curb the crossings.
Wednesday's 781 new arrivals meant 32,184 people had arrived via the route so far this year, down 42 percent year-on-year.
The centre-left Labour government has said the reduced numbers vindicate its strategy of targeting the criminal gangs facilitating the perilous journeys and working in closer collaboration with European neighbours.

Trump-Xi Meeting Live Updates: AI, Trade on the Agenda at US-China Summit

====================================================================================================

Chinese analysts say Trump should "understand pressure doesn't work" on Xi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:12:11 UTC
22:12:11 KST

Chinese analysts say Trump should "understand pressure doesn't work," as he and Xi tackle thorny issues
Hong Kong — It was 11 years ago that Chinese President Xi Jinping last visited the U.S. capital, for a 2015 White House meeting with then-President Barack Obama. As he returns for a meeting on Thursday with President Trump, both Xi and China's role in the world have changed dramatically.
China is now regarded as America's chief geopolitical rival, and Xi arrived back in Washington Wednesday night projecting confidence and authority.
"I think after all these years, Americans should understand pressure doesn't work," Zhao Hai, an expert in Sino-U.S. relations and vice president of the Chinese Institute of Hong Kong, told CBS News ahead of the leaders' summit in Washington. "It doesn't work on Xi. It doesn't work on China, and it doesn't work on the Chinese people."
When President Trump visited Beijing in May, he and Xi agreed to pursue what they called "constructive strategic stability" — political-speak indicating a commitment to improve the world's most important bilateral relationship despite deep mistrust, suspicion and intense competition.
Four months later, Chinese analysts see little reason to hope for any major breakthroughs, and they say the bilateral relationship, far from easing, appears as strained as ever.
Extending the trade war truce
Xi will be keen to secure an extension of the fragile economic truce that has walked the world's two biggest economies back from last year's damaging trade war.
In late 2025, Mr. Trump backed down from threats to impose 100% tariffs on some Chinese imports after Beijing threatened to limit supplies of vital rare earth materials.
Later agreements reached during the summit in May, on the sale of U.S. soybeans, other agricultural products and Boeing aircraft to China, are likely to come up.
Beijing insists the relationship cannot be one-sided, and Xi is likely to push Mr. Trump to open up the U.S. market to more Chinese goods, potentially to Chinese electric vehicles.
In 2015, Xi traveled to the U.S. with the leaders of 15 Chinese companies, including Jack Ma, the boss of online retail giant Alibaba, and executives from tech giants Tencent and Baidu.
Professor Wu Xinbo, who advises China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, told CBS News he believed Xi had intended to bring a similar contingent with him to Washington this week, but that the U.S. did not approve visas for some Chinese business leaders ahead of the trip.
As a result, Wu said China decided not to send a business delegation this week. China's state television network CCTV listed the members of Xi's entourage, and it included his wife and a number of high-ranking Chinese Communist Party officials, but no corporate leaders.
The AI race
Safety concerns over the breakneck pace of artificial intelligence advancement are also expected to feature prominently in the leaders' discussion, following warnings from industry leaders that the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity.
Many Chinese firms agree that AI must be regulated, Leia Wang, a nonresident scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for Peace, told CBS News recently.
Yi Zeng, the dean of the Beijing Institute of AI Safety and Governance, wrote in a research paper shared with CBS News, meanwhile, that "the catastrophic risks posed by AI, and the hidden danger of human extinction, are growing by the day."
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has spoken out against regulating AI development, said in April that it was essential for U.S. and Chinese researchers to engage in dialogue, and he warned that such bilateral coordination by AI industry leaders "is glaringly missing because of the current [U.S.] attitude about China as an adversary."
Zhao also questioned Washington's commitment to engage in any genuine cooperation with its strategic competitors.
"This is not an American issue or a Chinese issue, this is a humankind issue, and it's very threatening," he told CBS News, adding that, in his view, "the Chinese government is much more concerned about the negative side of AI development and has more measures and tools to regulate AI development."
President Trump made it clear just before his meeting with Xi that he was not in favor of any guardrails on AI development despite concerns about the possible emergence of superintelligence - a theoretical AI agent smarter than any person — and he said China's leader was in agreement.
"Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China's position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ," Mr. Trump said in a social media post.
Taiwan
Xi is expected to press President Trump to limit U.S. support for Taiwan — the Chinese leader's top priority. He's widely expected to urge Mr. Trump to halt all arms sales to the self-governed island and oppose Taiwanese independence.
That would effectively end the longstanding policy of refusing to state whether the U.S. would intervene militarily if China were to attack Taiwan, a practice known as "strategic ambiguity."
After their last summit in May, President Trump said he had made "no commitment either way" on whether to move forward with a pending arms sale to the island. Democratic and Republican lawmakers urged the arms package to be approved, but it has remained in limbo since Mr. Trump and Xi last met.
"This relationship is far from stable"
Mr. Trump, who has rejected multiple reports that Beijing supports Iran in its ongoing war with the U.S., is expected to again seek Xi's assistance in resolving the conflict and ensuring the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. How he does that could determine the outcome, according to Zhao.
"If the American side is only thinking about pressuring China, and particularly using financial tools to pressure China, I think that will be a deal breaker," he told CBS News.
"We should not be too ambitious about this trip," added Wu, calling the bilateral meeting taking place at all an achievement, given the two nations' differences.
Wu attributed the lack of progress on the key issues thus far, in part, to what he called a big disconnect between what Mr. Trump says, and what his administration actually does.
He pointed, as examples, to the Pentagon placing 54 Chinese companies on a blacklist over the last two months; the Department of Homeland Security placing Chinese universities (including the one where Wu teaches) and other institutions on a watchlist, and the Federal Communications Commission imposing new regulations on Chinese robotics and other electronics.
Those measures were taken "all to gain leverage for these talks," Wu argued. "So, basically, beneath the surface, this relationship is far from stable."

Croatian court allows extradition of Nord Stream blast suspect to Germany, media reports

Croatian court allows extradition of Nord Stream blast suspect to Germany, media reports
Sept 24 - A Croatian court has ruled that a Ukrainian man suspected of being involved in the 2022 Nord Stream pipeline blasts can be extradited to Germany, Ukraine's Suspilne news portal reported on Thursday.
German prosecutors have said the man — identified as Vladimir Z. — was a scuba diver who was part of a group behind the blasts, which followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine earlier that year.
The explosions — described by Russia and Western countries as sabotage — damaged the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, a vital route for Russian gas exports to Europe, as well as the Nord Stream 2 branch, which had yet to enter service.
Vladimir Z.'s lawyer, Mykola Katerynchuk, dismissed the court ruling, made on Friday last week, as biased and political and said there would be an appeal, according to the Suspilne report.
German courts have treated the case as falling within their jurisdiction because the damaged pipelines terminate in the German state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, and their destruction affected Germany's energy security and internal safety.
Vladimir Z. was arrested in August in a hotel in the Croatian coastal city of Pula on a European arrest warrant. He has denied any involvement, his lawyers have said.
Another suspect in the case, former Ukrainian army officer Serhii K., was charged by prosecutors in July with orchestrating the blasts while acting on behalf of Ukrainian state entities.
That man — who was arrested in Italy in August 2025 and transferred to Germany in November — has also denied any involvement in the blasts near the Danish island of Bornholm.
The County Court in Pula confirmed on Thursday it had made a ruling, but said it could not go into details until the parties had decided whether to appeal. REUTERS
