Judge Orders White House to Restore Access for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. What Happens Next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:18:51 UTC
21:18:51 KST

CNN, MS NOW, and Politico reporters were allowed back into the White House Thursday after a federal judge ordered President Donald Trump to immediately restore their press access.
The re-entry came after a chaotic morning, during which the three outlets filed an emergency request for a hearing, accusing the Trump Administration of having “repeatedly violated” the court order and refusing several reporters access to the White House grounds. "This morning, journalists from each of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico attempted to enter the White House and were turned away, and Secret Service agents confiscated the hard pass of journalists whose hard passes had not previously been confiscated," the outlets said in the court document.
Judge Timothy Kelly had given the Trump Administration until 12:30 p.m. ET to respond to the outlets' filing.
In a court filing of its own, the White House said it "began the process" of reinstating press badges shortly at 7:25 a.m. ET and laid out a timeline of what followed. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Early Thursday, in a District of Columbia court, Judge Kelly issued a temporary restraining order of 14 days against the ban, saying it “likely violated” the media outlets’ “constitutional due process rights.” He ordered that journalists from the banned media outlets should have their White House access reinstated “until further order of the court or the expiration of this temporary restraining order.”
In a statement to TIME, Ted Boutrous, the lawyer representing the news outlets, said “this is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.”
The order came in response to a lawsuit filed against the Trump Administration by CNN, MS NOW, and Politico on Monday, in which the outlets argued the ban was a “direct assault” on the First Amendment and violated their Fifth Amendment due process rights.
Outlining his ruling, Kelly said the outlets had “shown a likelihood of success, at least on their Fifth Amendment procedural due process claim.” The Fifth Amendment protects Americans from being “deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law.” Kelly determined that the outlets were “likely to succeed in showing that their hard passes were revoked without constitutionally adequate due process.”
The judge also rejected the Trump Administration's assertion that the media ban was motivated by “national security” concerns. “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ plaintiffs from the WhiteHouse—instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly wrote, referencing Trump’s “fake news” reasoning.
The Justice Department, in a legal filing on Tuesday, said the outlets had “received adequate notice” of the ban (a point contested by Kelly) and insisted “the President’s actions are lawful under the First Amendment.”
What happens next?
Ahead of Thursday’s order, Trump dismissed the legal challenge over the ban and indicated he regretted appointing Judge Kelly in 2017.
Vowing to fight any legal block on his ban, Trump insisted: “Almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal, because fake news people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our national security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the [Oval Office].”
However, in the court filing, Kelly stated that “temporary restraining orders are generally unappealable.”
Instead, during the 14-day period, the court “will set a schedule for expedited briefing on a motion for a preliminary injunction,” allowing Trump and the media outlets to submit further evidence for Kelly to consider.
“Either the preliminary injunction will be issued or denied,” says Eugene Volokh, a law professor at UCLA who specializes in the First Amendment. “The temporary restraining order would then lapse, and whichever side loses can then appeal to the D.C. Circuit.”
Instead of an appeal, Trump could file for emergency relief from the D.C. court, similar to how CNN, MS NOW, and Politico did Thursday, according to experts.
But “emergency relief is usually harder to get than a resolution through appeal,” says Volokh.
Trump has a turbulent history with the media. In 2018, he revoked the White House press credentials of Jim Acosta, who was then a CNN correspondent, after a tense exchange during a news conference.
CNN challenged the decision in court and it was Judge Kelly who ordered the White House to reinstate the reporter’s press pass.
Volokh says that legal precedent in the D.C. Circuit, used in both the ongoing case and that of Acosta, has “already been set” for areas of the White House usually open to the media, including the press briefing room.
“The government can't exclude reporters based on viewpoint, and cannot take away a press pass without due process, without some sort of hearing opportunity to be heard, an explanation of what it is that they supposedly did wrong, what rules they violated,” he says.
In light of this, an appeal from the Trump Administration after a preliminary injunction would likely be rejected in the D.C. Circuit, he argues. However, the President may find a better chance in the Supreme Court.
“Generally speaking, the First Amendment does not secure a right of access to government office buildings,” says Volokh, once again noting the exception of areas usually granted access for press. "The same position could be taken by the Supreme Court, and [it] might say: 'Look, the government can pick and choose whom to allow on its property,'" he says.
Media bands together in solidarity against Trump's ban
There has been an outpouring of solidarity among other media outlets in light of the ban.
CNN, one of five U.S. news outlets in the White House press pool that rotates responsibility for pooled live video coverage, was scheduled to cover Trump's trip to the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Monday. When they were restricted from doing so, other major television networks declined to replace CNN’s pool crew.
In a rare joint statement, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC said: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No Administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”
In a further show of support, some media publications—including the New York Times and Washington Post—announced they would hold off on publishing or distributing still photographs taken as part of the White House pool coverage.
On Wednesday, 49 media organizations filed a legal brief voicing their support of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. “Stripping journalists and news outlets of their rights because of perceived editorial viewpoint violates decades of Supreme Court jurisprudence and is impermissible in any type of forum, including the White House,” the brief argued.

How Israel is trying to bar Palestinian Israelis from taking part in elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:17:18 UTC
21:17:18 KST

Israel's claim to its “democratic” credentials has long rested on the fact that its Palestinian citizens can vote and elect representatives to the Knesset.
But ahead of the October 27 election, Israel's political system is threatening to strip hundreds of thousands of Palestinian citizens of meaningful political representation while Israel continues its genocidal war on Gaza as the Central Elections Committee (CEC) has voted to bar both major electoral lists led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, as well as two prominent individual candidates.
On September 23, the committee voted to disqualify Ra'am, led by Mansour Abbas, and the newly reconstituted Joint List, made up of Hadash, Ta'al and Balad.
It also voted to bar Hadash lawmaker Ofer Cassif and Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh. The decisions are not necessarily final: the individual disqualifications require Supreme Court approval, while the parties can appeal their exclusion to the court.
Israel's October 2026 election comes after nearly three years of Israel's genocidal war in Gaza.
If the exclusions were ultimately upheld, a large part of Palestinian citizens' established political representation in the Knesset would disappear from the ballot.
Palestinian citizens of Israel make up roughly one-fifth of the population. Their parties have historically held 10–15 seats and can influence coalition arithmetic in a fragmented system.
Who is being targeted?
The CEC voted to bar Ra'am, or the United Arab List, which is a pragmatic, Muslim-leaning party that previously joined the 2021–22 Bennett-Lapid “government of change” — the first party representing Palestinian citizens of Israel to enter an Israeli governing coalition. It has focused on crime, infrastructure, and civic issues in Palestinian Israeli communities.
The petitions against it were brought by Likud, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party; Otzma Yehudit, the party led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
The central accusation is that Ra'am supports, or is insufficiently opposed to, armed struggle by terrorist organisations.
Ra'am rejects that allegation.
Its legal response says the petitions contain no evidence that the party supports armed struggle or otherwise meets Section 7A's disqualification requirements.
The party's stated programme includes a Palestinian state, an end to the occupation and illegal Israeli settlements, recognition of Palestinian citizens of Israel as a national minority, and greater equality in education and economic development.
The second target is the Joint List, an alliance of Hadash, Ta’al, and Balad, led by Yousef Jabareen. These parties emphasise equality, an end to the occupation, and transforming Israel into a “state of all its citizens” rather than a strictly Jewish state.
Again, Likud petitioned to disqualify the list.
The accusations include alleged support for positions said to undermine Israel's status as a Jewish state and alleged support for armed struggle.
The response from the Joint List's legal team is that much of the evidence is old, recycled material that has already been considered in previous disqualification proceedings.
The committee nevertheless voted 18-5 to disqualify the list.
The case against Cassif is particularly significant because he is Jewish lawmaker known for sharp criticism of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and the occupied West Bank
Likud sought his disqualification, arguing that his political activity amounted to support for an enemy or armed struggle against Israel.
Cassif's response is that criticism of Israeli military conduct and advocacy for Palestinian statehood cannot legitimately be transformed into support for armed violence. His lawyers also challenged what they described as distorted quotations.
The most direct case against a Palestinian political leader concerns Sami Abu Shehadeh, chairman of Balad and a former Knesset member.
Otzma Yehudit and Ben-Gvir sought his disqualification, accusing him of supporting armed struggle and of rejecting Israel as a Jewish state.
These are the primary vehicles for Palestinian-Israeli representation.
The CEC, dominated by representatives of the outgoing Knesset parties, with the coalition holding significant weight, approved the bans by margins such as 18–5 for the lists and larger majorities for the individuals.
What is being used to disqualify them?
The legal mechanism is Section 7A of Israel's Basic Law: The Knesset.
It allows a party or candidate to be barred if their objectives or actions include denying Israel's existence as a Jewish and democratic state; inciting racism; or supporting armed struggle against Israel by an enemy state or “terrorist organisation”.
But no evidence against the candidates and parties being opposed has been provided.
Israel's CEC is itself unusual. Although it is an independent statutory election-management body headed by a Supreme Court justice, its voting plenum is political and reflects the composition of the outgoing Knesset.
For the 2026 election, 18 of its 31 members represent the governing coalition, giving the coalition a majority in the body. The Israel Democracy Institute notes that this combination of political composition and quasi-judicial powers is “highly unusual” by international standards.
So essentially, the body deciding whether political competitors can appear on the ballot is, in effect, partly composed of representatives of the political parties competing for power.
What has happened so far is that the CEC has only accepted petitions alleging that their statements or activities meet the statutory threshold for electoral disqualification. The Supreme Court still has a decisive role.
The legal battle therefore continues.
Parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel and candidates have repeatedly faced disqualification attempts before Israel's CEC. Balad was disqualified in 2003 and 2009; Haneen Zoabi in 2013 and 2015; Ra'am-Balad and Ofer Cassif in April 2019; and Hiba Yazbek of the Joint List in March 2020. In many of these cases, the Supreme Court overturned the CEC's decision.
What would this mean for Palestinian citizens?
Palestinian citizens of Israel make up roughly one-fifth of the country's population and have historically used both parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel and, to a lesser extent, Jewish parties to participate in parliamentary politics.
The 2022 election provides an indication of the scale of Palestinian-Israeli political representation: Ra'am won five Knesset seats, while Hadash-Ta'al won five. Balad narrowly failed to cross the electoral threshold.
Palestinian-Israeli political participation has also been closely connected to turnout. In 2022, turnout among Palestinian and Druze citizens was 53.2 percent, and Palestinian lists won 85.7 percent of the vote cast in Palestinian localities.
That means removing established lists led by Palestinian citizens of Israel from the ballot could have consequences beyond the number of candidates directly excluded. It could affect whether Palestinian citizens see the election as offering meaningful political choices at all.

OpenAI agent hacks Australian government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:16:41 UTC
21:16:41 KST

OpenAI agent hacks Australian government
An OpenAI artificial intelligence agent “infiltrated” an Australian government health portal in what is believed to be the world’s first publicly reported AI-led hack of a state website. The IT giant kept the breach quiet for nearly three months after its agent accessed restricted files, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has claimed.
An AI agent is a software system that can independently carry out tasks on a user’s behalf, making decisions and taking actions with limited human supervision.
The OpenAI agent hacked the public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal on June 18 while researching Australian spending on medicines, Albanese said. The portal, widely used by researchers and academics, hosts aggregate data on health spending and government drug subsidies.
The prime minister disclosed the breach in New York on Wednesday after a telephone conversation with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Both are attending the UN General Assembly, where Albanese said he had a “very frank discussion” with the tech executive over the company taking “too long” to report the breach.
The agent repeatedly tried to obtain information from the portal and, after being blocked, found ways around the restrictions. It ultimately accessed restricted files, but officials said there is no evidence that personal Medicare records were compromised.
“The AI agent found a way around those blocks. Didn’t accept no for an answer, if you like,” the Australian prime minister told reporters.
OpenAI, however, did not tell the Australian government about the breach for nearly three months. The company claimed it became aware of the incident only in August during an ongoing review of “misaligned model activity” and eventually notified Australian officials on September 10. The portal has since been shut down and its data moved to more secure systems.
Albanese said he had expressed “Australia’s extreme concern about this incident” and warned there would “obviously be legal consequences.” Altman acknowledged there were “issues with protocols” at OpenAI, according to the prime minister.
A “forensic investigation” led by the Australian Signals Directorate will examine whether OpenAI could face criminal charges, whether other government systems were affected, and why Australian security agencies failed to detect the intrusion. Albanese suggested the agent may have been examining Medicare spending for “commercial reasons,” including expenditure on particular medicines.
Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said it was the first known case of an AI agent gaining unauthorized access to Australian government IT systems.
This is not the first time OpenAI has been accused of covering up rogue agent activity. The company reportedly kept unauthorized activity quiet for months after its agents bypassed restrictions and used more than ten previously undisclosed websites to communicate. On Germany’s DseWiki alone, they made over 15,000 edits and exchanged tactics for evading safeguards and detection.
In a more serious breach in July, OpenAI agents circumvented safeguards during cybersecurity testing, reached the open internet and gained unauthorized access to systems belonging to Hugging Face, a major AI platform. The incident showed that rogue agent behavior could spill beyond controlled tests and compromise real-world systems. OpenAI acknowledged the breach, calling it a “warning shot” over the risks posed by increasingly autonomous AI.
Other developers have reported similarly troubling behavior in controlled tests. Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4 resorted to blackmail when threatened with replacement in simulated scenarios, while other agents covertly altered code, facilitated fraud and manipulated records – behavior researchers call “agentic misalignment.”

Delivered to the Wrong Address? F-35 Parts Re-routed to Hong Kong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:15:00 UTC
21:15:00 KST

Last summer a shipment of F-35 parts was reportedly re-routed to Hong Kong from its intended destination in Australia. Australia is a partner in the F-35 program; the People’s Republic of China is not. U.S. authorities are reportedly trying to recover the parts and prevent future breaches. The incident has caused consternation in the United States and Australia, both of which have effectively committed to the F-35 as the foundation of their future airpower. And yet the mis-shipment has made clear a fundamental contradiction at the heart of the F-35 project; high tech proprietary classification does not go well with an aggressive policy of export and offshoring.
In short, it’s hard to keep aspects of the F-35 secret when the United States is aggressively trying to sell the aircraft abroad.
We do not yet fully understand whether this was an innocent (if catastrophic) error, or if it was the result of a complex and successful Chinese espionage operation. If the latter, we don’t know if Chinese intelligence has been able to exploit the shipment, though it appears that Beijing is in possession of the errant parts. But even if the diversion of the shipment to Hong Kong was accidental and not part of an espionage operation, the incident highlights some of the contradictions inherent in the F-35 program.
The F-35 is a supremely advanced fighter aircraft with many proprietary components that would be of immense value to several foreign intelligence services. It is also a consumer product that the United States has been trying to aggressively export over the past two decades to most every country in the Global North and a few in the Global South. Jonathan Caverley has called the F-35 “America’s Belt and Road,” because of both its substantial expense and because of its integrated production over several countries and integrated maintenance over several more. Work in all of these countries is spread among dozens of contractors and subcontractors, each of which offers a potential weak link in terms of keeping the parts of the aircraft secret and secure.
There are a limited number of countries that could usefully exploit the technology in the shipment, and China is one of them. Of particular concern is the canopy, which represents an enormous technological and financial investment and which could conceivably benefit China’s aerospace industry. As with most such cases, the issue here is less that Chinese engineers could copy the equipment and then integrate it into their own aircraft (modern industrial aerospace techniques are remarkably complex) but rather that careful study could reveal vulnerabilities or characteristics that could eventually give Chinese pilots a tactical advantage.
It’s worth noting that the F-35 is no longer a youthful aircraft. It has been in active service for more than a decade, flies for 12 different countries (and often for more than one air force per country), and boasts some 1,200 operational units across the world. It has flown in combat for Israel and the United States in several wars. Given this record, there’s only so much that can be done to keep the details of the aircraft’s manufacture and performance secret from China or Russia. China has its own fifth-generation fighters and has already worked out many of the problems associated with the critical technologies. Indeed, both China and the United States have moved onto sixth-generation programs. Thus, the availability of the canopy of the F-35 may be important, but it’s hardly critical. That said, while entrusting important components of a mainline fighter aircraft to UPS may be unwise, it was also probably inevitable given the nature of the project.

Ukrainians accused of training Myanmar rebels get bail in India
Six Ukrainian nationals accused of providing drone warfare training to armed groups in Myanmar were freed on bail in India after the country’s counterterrorism agency failed to file terror charges within the mandatory 180 days of their arrest.
The immigration charges against the Ukrainians – Viktor Kaminskyi, Petro Hurba, Taras Slyviak, Ivan Sukmanovskyi, Marian Stefankiv, and Maksim Honcharuk – were also settled before the Foreigners Regional Registration Office. However, they will have to remain in Delhi while the investigation is ongoing.
The six, arrested by India’s National Investigation Agency (NIA) in March along with American national Matthew Aaron VanDyke, had allegedly trained members of Myanmar-based ethnic armed groups, including the Chin National Front and Kachin Independence Army, in drone warfare, operations, assembly, and jamming technology.
However, the agency’s initial chargesheet filed on September 8 accused the seven foreigners of only relatively mild illegal entry and visa violations under the Immigration and Foreigners Act – and no charge was brought under India’s primary anti-terror law, Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA).
The same Delhi court had last week given bail to VanDyke for the same reasons.
The NIA says anti-terror charges could still be added against them if further evidence emerges. The agency says it has established links between the accused and Myanmar-based armed groups; no conclusive evidence has so far emerged that they acted against India or trained Indian insurgent organizations.
The seven were described as “mercenaries” and were alleged to have participated in combat operations and in a drone attack on a Burmese passenger plane. UAVs and related equipment detained by Indian customs authorities were later seized during the probe.
Indian investigators arrested them after alleging they had entered the country on tourist visas, traveled through the northeastern state of Mizoram without mandatory permits, and crossed into neighboring Myanmar illegally.

'Artificial' is out: Trump orders officials to call it 'super intelligence' instead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:11:50 UTC
21:11:50 KST

The US president has decided the word "artificial" makes intelligence "sound fake," so the State Department is now telling its diplomats to call it "SI" instead.
The State Department's international organisations bureau has instructed staff to stop using the term "artificial intelligence" and use "super intelligence" instead.
The order arrived in an email sent earlier this week by Michael Drager, the bureau's deputy assistant secretary, titled — appropriately enough — "Change in Nomenclature AI to SI".
"Following the president's remarks at the GA today, please change all references of 'Artificial Intelligence' to 'Super Intelligence' in our documents and positions," it read, adding that "SI" would be used in "all remarks, positions and press elements moving forward".
The email, obtained by the Associated Press on Wednesday, gave no indication whether other State Department bureaus were expected to follow.
Renaming things has become something of a habit for Trump since he began his second term.
He signed an executive order in January 2025 rebranding the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America," and in August this year issued another renaming Lake Ontario, shared with Canada, as "Lake America" amid a trade dispute with Ottawa.
Neither change has been recognised by other countries, though Google and Apple updated their maps to reflect the Gulf rename.
'It's not fake, it's super'
Addressing the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Donald Trump decided that "artificial" was doing the technology a disservice.
"The use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake, it makes it sound fake and it is not fake. It's actually amazing," he told the assembled world leaders, announcing that US government documents would "from this point forward" swap "artificial" for "the much more accurate term super".
There was no suggestion the remarks were intended as a joke, and the bureau overseeing US missions to the UN and other multilateral agencies did not treat them as one.
The consequences reach beyond paperwork.
Trump announced an "AI Force" over the weekend and if the new terminology holds, that presumably becomes the "SI Force".
US representatives have already started using the term "SI" at a UN Security Council meeting on the risks of artificial intelligence, where the chief executives of OpenAI, Anthropic and Hugging Face urged the world's most powerful diplomatic body to rein in the technology.
Renaming it does not slow it down
The new vocabulary arrives alongside starker warnings from elsewhere in the industry.
Anthropic's Dario Amodei has said poorly managed AI could pose a risk to humanity as a whole.
Lawmakers, including Senator Bernie Sanders, have raised alarm about the technology outpacing human control, and researchers have documented AI agents behaving in ways their own developers did not intend.
None of it has shifted Trump's underlying position.
He has consistently rejected calls for tighter government oversight, arguing that regulation would blunt the US's edge over China.
"I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution, or the internet, itself," he wrote on social media on Monday, alongside a claim that the US is comfortably ahead of Beijing in the field.
The timing puts the new terminology to an immediate test: Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday for a state visit, with AI high on the agenda.

Czech PM Andrej Babis reiterates importance of NATO for his country but rejects calls to increase defense spending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:11:00 UTC
21:11:00 KST

Czech PM Babis under fire for missing NATO spending targets
September 24, 2026
The Czech Republic "must remain committed to increasing defense spending," Matthew Whitaker, the US envoy to NATO, demanded in Prague last week. "We expect our allies to step up," he said.
The call is nothing new. As warnings about the threat emanating from Russia increase, and Washington demands European allies take greater responsibility for security, NATO has raised its target for defense spending from 2% to 3.5% of GDP, and pressure on those lagging is rising.
Czechia, alongside Slovenia and Albania, has yet to meet the old target. But Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, whose government cut the defense budget for 2026 to around 1.7% of GDP when it took office late last year, pushed back against the latest barb from Washington.
While reiterating that NATO membership is crucial for Czechia, the premier bluntly stated that the government cannot afford to accelerate spending. He has pledged to hit the 2% target in 2027 but plans no further increases.
That leaves the populist billionaire hoping that a personal rapport with US President Donald Trump will protect the country amid the burgeoning row.
Warnings of a growing threat
Whether Trump will protect Czechia from the threat of Russian hybrid warfare targeting Central European NATO allies is another question.
A growing wave of stray drones and Russian intelligence operations — suspected bombings, sabotage and cyber warfare — have spread alarm in the neighborhood.
Germany and Poland — key Czech partners — have reported high-profile incidents and linked them to attempts to intimidate Ukrainian allies.
Czechia should understand the threat better than most, having been among the first to experience such an attack.
Czechia's Security Information Service (BIS) reported in 2021 that the bombing of a depot storing weapons linked to Ukraine seven years previously had been carried out by Russia's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Security Service (FSB).
Babis, then in his first stint as PM, responded by expelling around 100 Russian diplomats and embassy staff, freezing relations with Moscow.
The BIS remains in step with other intelligence agencies across the region in warning that the threat from Russia is growing.
However, like its predecessors, the Babis government has failed to keep pace in terms of the national defense budget, even as neighbors have leapt into action.
Prague spent just 1.86% of GDP on defense last year; Poland and the Baltic States have already met the new NATO target and will hit 5% next year.
Prague's priorities
Babis has made it clear this approach will not change. However, his claim that Czechia can't afford to boost defense spending is at odds with the 2027 budget his government approved on September 22.
The fiscal plan will expand expenditure generously and targets Czechia's second-highest deficit ever at 386 billion Czech crowns (€15.8 billion or $18 billion).
While finally catching up to the old NATO target will account for some of that spending, most of the increased outlay will reflect the coalition government's domestic political priorities.
The plan clearly reflects the election campaign promises of Babis's ANO party and its junior partners, the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) and radical-right Motorists for Themselves party. They all say defense can't be allowed to disrupt the urgent need to spend on pensions, education, healthcare and infrastructure.
"The claim that the country cannot spend more on defense is primarily rooted in domestic politics," Ales Michal, a political scientist at Prague's Charles University, told DW. "The major priority is investment in the social system."
That will be welcomed by supporters of the governing parties, who skew older and less well off, and resent the support being given to 300,000 or so Ukrainian refugees.
"None of the governing parties promised voters higher defense spending," in campaigning for last year's election, Michal notes.
Critics, however, say that's because the government is downplaying the threat from Russia. The government's spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
'We don't want World War III'
The reticence to raise defense spending also reflects political narratives around the war in Ukraine.
Two days after Whitaker's rebuke, Babis appeared in a video dressed in a T-shirt emblazoned with the words "No War" in blue and yellow letters. While he noted the threat from Russia, he called for greater efforts to find peace.
"We don't want World War III, do we?" he pronounced, repeating his claim that Europe should work harder to end the conflict.
It was a performance echoing the stance of Europe's radical right-wing, and the sort that has seen the Czech PM labelled "pro-Russian" in some international media.
The truth is more mundane. Babis is a pragmatist. The ANO electorate is populist and anti-Ukrainian, but also strongly pro-Western. Surveys show that the plan to keep defense spending at 2% of GDP precisely matches its views.
Yet Babis's divisive personality leaves the party dependent on extremist partners for enough support to govern, and so he must also try to speak the anti-system, pro-Russian language of the SPD, which, despite controlling the defense ministry, was pushing to cut spending further in the 2027 budget.
"A critical stance towards Ukraine also shapes the government's position on spending," said Michal. The pro-peace stance downplaying Russia's aggression moves ANO "closer to the European radical right," he notes, but Babis is "guided by opinion polls," and must try to find a "balance between two polarizing positions."
Strategic understanding
The opposition sees this dichotomy as the government's Achilles' heel.
Martin Kupka, leader of the center-right Civic Democrats (ODS), welcomed Babis's reiterated NATO commitment before asking the PM: "When will you get rid of the Kremlin fifth column, which you took into the government and even entrusted with the Ministry of Defense?"
However, although the ODS-led government that held office between 2021 and 2025 offered fervent support to Ukraine, like all its predecessors, it also failed to meet the NATO spending target.
"Our partners may be unhappy about the approach to spending, but it's the reality of the political situation in our country," Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW.
However, he added that while weak defense spending growth "is not optimal," the biggest issue is a lack of strategic understanding regarding the military's size and role.

Exclusion of Arab lists from Knesset election is ‘surrender to Kahanism’: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:08:52 UTC
21:08:52 KST

Khaled Yousef and Ikram Kouachi
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Israeli daily Haaretz on Thursday criticized a decision by Israel’s election authority to exclude Arab lists from the parliamentary elections scheduled for next month, calling it evidence of “surrender to the rule of Kahanism.”
Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted Wednesday to exclude the Joint Arab List alliance and the United Arab List party, as well as Knesset member Ofer Cassif and Sami Abu Shehadeh, who is running for the elections.
In its editorial, the newspaper said that “both the disqualification and the vitriol it sparked are a document of surrender to the rule of Kahanism and reflected obedience to its rules.”
The term “Kahanist rule” refers to the Israeli political establishment’s submission to the far-right ideology associated with Meir Kahane, a radical Israeli-American rabbi and politician who founded the far-right fascist ideology known as Kahanism.
Kahane was born in New York in 1932 and assassinated there in 1990, and is considered the spiritual father of far-right religious Zionist currents active in Israel today.
“This policy is encouraged and fueled by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who reaps political capital from it,” the newspaper added.
It said that “Netanyahu’s greatest achievement, which benefits him politically, has been to make even the opposition view Arab voices as criminal.”
The newspaper called on Israel’s Supreme Court to overturn the Central Elections Committee’s decision and protect Arabs’ right to vote and run for the Knesset.
The Central Elections Committee is primarily a political body made up of representatives of parliamentary blocs in the outgoing Knesset, with seats distributed according to the size of those blocs’ representation. As a result, the governing coalition holds a majority on the committee, which currently has 34 members, according to Haaretz.
The committee is tasked with ensuring a proper and credible electoral process from beginning to end, reflecting the will of voters in Israel, according to its website.
The election is scheduled for Oct. 27, with 38 lists registered to compete, while opinion polls project that 13 lists will enter the Knesset.
Netanyahu has headed the current government since late December 2022, which is described as the most right-wing in Israel’s history.

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. The Russian Defense Ministry has patented and tested a new artillery smoke shell, eliminating the shortcomings of its French counterpart for the Caesar self-propelled howitzer, according to a document reviewed by TASS.
"The invention relates to the field of military technology, specifically to field artillery munitions of various calibers that can be used in aerosol-generating shells designed to create smoke screens, obscuring (blinding) fire control and optical systems, command and observation posts, and optoelectronic reconnaissance, target acquisition and weapon control systems operating in the infrared wavelength range," the patent description states.

Putin’s Sochi residence was demolished and rebuilt from scratch. A contractor linked to his friend Arkady Rotenberg is behind the project, BBC’s Russian Service reports.

Putin’s Sochi residence was demolished and rebuilt from scratch. A contractor linked to his friend Arkady Rotenberg is behind the project, BBC’s Russian Service reports.
Construction of a new Bocharov Ruchey residence for Vladimir Putin is nearing completion in Sochi: the old buildings there were demolished in 2024, and by the fall of 2026 new ones had already gone up in their place. The general contractor for the construction is the Crimea-based Transstroyinvest Group of Companies, which is tied to Putin’s friend Arkady Rotenberg, BBC Russia reports.
A classified state defense contract for the FSO covers the reconstruction of the Bocharov Ruchey residence, but journalists found the contract’s 25-digit identifier in court records. The digits show the contract covers 2023–2027, that it was awarded without competitive bidding or an auction, and that its price was fixed.
The general contractor is the Transstroyinvest Group of Companies, whose beneficiary is believed to be developer Alexei Fomenko. Russian media have linked Fomenko to Arkady Rotenberg. The company also built dachas in occupied Crimea for Vladimir Putin and Alexander Bortnikov, director of Russia’s Federal Security Service, and carried out the reconstruction of the Artek children’s camp.
BBC could not determine the total cost of the contract to reconstruct Bocharov Ruchey, but the scale can be gauged from publicly available job postings for individual construction subcontracts. Those postings listed work budgets of 90, 150, 250, 400, and 500 million rubles.
Workers for the construction site were recruited through social media and job-listing websites. The postings described the site as a “strategic facility” and warned candidates that they would face strict background checks. Builders were promised piece-rate pay in cash, three meals a day, and accommodation in a “hostel with a pool.”
BBC says construction at Bocharov Ruchey has continued even though Putin has visited Sochi far less often since Russia’s full-scale war in Ukraine began. According to calculations by the Financial Times, he visited there 24 times before the full-scale war, 13 times in 2022, and only twice a year in both 2024 and 2025, as Ukrainian drones increasingly reached the Black Sea coast.

'Pope fever' takes hold as Pope Leo visits France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:03:00 UTC
21:03:00 KST

'Pope fever' takes hold as Pope Leo visits France
September 24, 2026
France is gripped by "Pope fever." Since the 1905 French law on separating church and state, the country has embraced secular traditions. But over the next few days, the streets will tell a different story.
From Friday, Pope Leo XIV will spend four days in France, visiting Paris, Lourdes and Metz. All his public events have been sold out for weeks. Organizers expect around 1 million people to fill the streets of Paris on Saturday for a massive open-air mass at the Place de la Concorde.
"The pope is popular among both believers and nonbelievers," political scientist Olivier Roy told DW. He added that Leo XIV's conflict with US President Donald Trump in particular had lent him "a moral standing that extends far beyond the Catholic Church."
Paris gears up for influx
Massive crowds are expected for the pope's visit. Some 600,000 people who were able to get tickets will fill the entire Champs-Elysees, going right up to the Arc de Triomphe. Many more are expected to show up without tickets.
Authorities have announced that a number of metro stations will be closed. Across the city, churches have been draped with large portraits of the pope and Vatican flags. Security forces are gearing up for a major challenge.
With France's presidential election just over six months away, the visit comes at a delicate time. The left, Roy said, "appreciates Leo's personality but is skeptical about the state's involvement in organizing the reception."
Those on the far right, he continued, welcomed the visibility of Catholicism but had objected, for example, to an interfaith meeting planned in the eastern city of Metz, which they say places Islam on an equal footing with Christianity.
Because of the separation of church and state, the president will not be able to attend the large public Masses.
Leo's visit is likely to boost the pope's profile in the country, which last saw a papal state visit in 2008 when Benedict XVI traveled to Paris and Lourdes, the world-famous pilgrimage site in the country's southwest. He drew smaller crowds than those expected for Pope Leo.
His successor, Pope Francis, visited Strasbourg in 2014 and Ajaccio in Corsica in 2024 on one-day trips, and in 2023 he spent a night in the Mediterranean port city of Marseille. But each time, he came for a specific occasion rather than visiting the country as a whole. In his speeches to the European Parliament and Council of Europe in Strasbourg, Francis criticized the migration policies of what he described as an "aged and weary" Europe.
Roy described the contrasting perspectives of recent popes. He said John Paul II, pope from 1978 to 2005, viewed Christianity as "primarily European," while Francis saw it as "more shaped by the Global South."
This, Roy argued, explained Francis' "certain disregard for Europe." Leo was likely to assume the middle ground, while extending his predecessor's message, Roy said.
"He affirms the universality of the Catholic Church, while also recognizing Europe's weight within that universality."
Europe's key role for the pope
For Augsburg-based church historian and papal expert Jörg Ernesti, Europe has remained "the most important political point of reference for popes since the late 19th century," despite the growing internationalism of Catholicism. Ernesti pointed to the demographic shift: In 1900, more than two-thirds of all Catholics lived in Europe, he said; today, the figure is only around 20%.
This internationalization had also shaped the College of Cardinals, albeit with a time lag. "While Europeans have historically always made up the majority, they now account for just 39%," he said.
During his four-day visit, Leo is scheduled to deliver 15 speeches and homilies. Most of those in Paris will be aimed at wider French society and its political leaders, while the large Masses and events in Lourdes will focus primarily on France's Catholics.
The most keenly awaited speech is one scheduled for the final day in Metz, which French President Emmanuel Macron will introduce. It is titled "To the roots of Europe for peace and unity."
The choice of Metz itself is symbolic. Once a center of the Carolingian Empire, the city has changed language and allegiance several times over the centuries, at times being German, at others French.
While at the Robert Schuman Convention Center, Leo will be able to invoke the name of the man behind the building. Born in Luxembourg in 1886, Robert Schuman was a French statesman who had inherited his father's German citizenship at birth. In the aftermath of World War II, Schuman was an early advocate of Franco-German reconciliation. He pushed for a new, united Europe and in 1958 became the first president of the newly established European Parliament. After his death in 1963, he was buried in a small church in Scy-Chazelles, near Metz.
For Pope Leo, Roy said, "Europe is a real entity that must be sustained and developed beyond nationalism." That, he said, "has always been the message of the Catholic Church since World War II. It is Schuman's message."
Roy will be watching closely to see whether, and how openly, Pope Leo criticizes populism and nationalism in his call to strengthen the EU and whether he will speak about a form of nationalist Catholicism found in France. He said that defenders of the traditional Latin Mass were not infrequently "identitarian nationalists or even close to far-right circles."
Leo to meet abuse survivors
It's hard to imagine a papal trip without mention of the long-running issue of abuse. When Pope Benedict visited France in 2008, he did not take the chance to meet any survivors of sexual abuse in the French Catholic Church. His successors did, though the institution has been slow to confront its past amid a spate of new scandals.
This time, a meeting with survivors is on the pope's agenda in Lourdes. But something else has changed. During the pontificates of Benedict and Francis, those who met with them were usually not named. At times, it appeared that access to the Vatican came in exchange for silence. In France, the seven survivors who will meet Leo have spoken out together ahead of the meeting, with five of them also making their names public.
"Dialogue does not mean approval," they said. "Being received does not mean giving up our demands." The issue is likely to remain a thorny challenge for the Catholic Church — in France and elsewhere for a long time to come.

The Russian Aerospace Forces have received two new Su-57 fighter jets as part of the second 2026 batch, the Russian United Aircraft Corporation (UAC) press service reports.
The aircraft were handed over at the airfield of the Komsomolsk-on-Amur Aviation Plant named after Yuri Gagarin (KnAAZ).
Before being handed over, the fighters underwent tests to confirm their claimed specifications.
The delivery of the second batch at the end of the year is unusual for Russia’s aircraft industry. The delay may have been caused by a fire that broke out in April 2026 at the KnAAZ facility, which is owned by JSC Sukhoi Company.
The fire engulfed a workshop specializing in the production of polymer matrix composite (PMC) components for the Su-57.
The workshop produced around 300 types of components, about 100 of which were large-sized. These included aileron, air intake, flaperon, and floor panels, as well as outer wing panel tips.
Despite this, production of this type of fighter remains relatively slow. In September 2025, Militarnyi reported that Russia had received only 16 fighters for combat units since 2019.
Including the batch delivered in February 2026, the total increased to 18 aircraft. This production rate remains very slow.
Based on the tail numbers, the Russian Aerospace Forces operate at least 16 fighters of this type. According to available information, they are stationed at the Akhtubinsk, Znamensk, and Aksyonovo airfields.
Thus, the aircraft can be divided into two categories. The first includes Su-57s assigned to the 929th State Flight Test Center in Akhtubinsk. These are aircraft with the following tail numbers: ‘01’ Blue, 81774, ‘02’ Red, and ‘11’ Red.
The second category includes aircraft spotted at airfields alongside operational combat aircraft — in Znamensk and Aksyonovo. A total of 13 Su-57s with the following tail numbers have been identified there.

Greek-operated air defence system shoots down ballistic missile, drone over Saudi

EU grid power struggle: capitals push back against Brussels tariff rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:01:32 UTC
21:01:32 KST

European Union governments are pushing back against a Brussels drive to reshape electricity network costs, watering down plans for coordinated tariffs as the fight over the bloc’s expensive and congested power grids becomes increasingly political.
European Union governments want to weaken a proposal that would hand Brussels greater control over the bloc's power grid, preferring to retain control of how electricity networks are paid for and managed, according to a Council document seen by Euronews.
Political talks over who will pay for the modernisation of the bloc's power grid, a crucial step in meeting the EU's 2050 climate neutrality goal, are underway in Brussels just as electricity moves to the centre of the bloc’s economic strategy.
The EU wants homes and businesses to switch from fossil fuels to electricity, while manufacturers, data centres, heat pumps and electric vehicles are all expected to drive up demand. But the cost of expanding and operating energy grids is increasingly showing up in electricity bills.
Grid charges and taxes combined often outweigh the price of the electricity consumed. Network charges accounted for 27% of household electricity bills and 21% for businesses, while national taxes and levies added another 24% for households and 16% for firms, according to EU data.
Europe's rising electricity bills prompted the European Commission to propose new rules in July designed to slash energy bills amid a growing crisis triggered by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The Commission also introduced an electrification plan setting a 46% goal by 2040 for the Union.
The Irish Presidency — the rotating chairmanship of the Council of the European Union — is seeking to keep the Commission's broad ambition of making electricity cheaper and easier to adopt, while also giving national governments and regulators more room to decide how the rules work in practice, the document reveals.
The Irish Presidency, which is tasked with mediating negotiations between the Commission, the Council and the European Parliament, is proposing a sweeping overhaul of network charges, requiring tariffs to encourage consumers to reduce peak demand, use electricity at different times and take account of where new connections are located.
But the latest preparatory talks held on 23 September by EU ambassadors suggest governments are reluctant to let those tools become one-size-fits-all requirements.
"The rules on the application of a reference tariff methodology for electricity shall allow regulatory authorities to deviate from the reference tariff methodology in duly justified cases," reads a Council document dated 16 September and seen by Euronews.
Poland, Italy, Czechia, Luxembourg, Lithuania and Latvia want regulators to use tools such as cheaper off-peak electricity or incentives to locate new projects where the grid has spare capacity and only when suitable for an individual country's power system, rather than imposing these rules across the EU.
Spain, the Netherlands, Sweden and Cyprus have raised stronger concerns about the effectiveness and possible social consequences of these tools and measures.
Francesco Sassi, Assistant Professor at the University of Oslo, told Euronews that a centralised control by the Commission could "work towards easing the isolation of the Iberian Peninsula or drive more investments in low-carbon energy interconnections in Eastern and Southeastern Europe".
"These [countries] are showing increasing unease about ceding power to Brussels amid the second energy crisis under the presidency of Ursula Von der Leyen and repeated market shocks the European Commission appears unable to control," said Sassi.
National flexibility versus EU coordination
For the Commission, common rules are a way of making the bloc's fragmented power market more transparent and efficient. But EU countries are resisting anything that could force them to redesign national tariff systems that reflect very different grids, industries and consumer bases.
The clearest battleground is a provision that would allow the Commission to establish a common structure and reference methodology for electricity tariffs.
The Irish Presidency stresses that this would "harmonise the methodology" not the actual tariffs and that national regulators could depart from the reference approach where justified.
But several major EU members are still unhappy.
France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Finland, Spain and the Netherlands want the Commission's powers significantly reduced or removed. They argue that the emerging preference is for guidelines rather than a binding approach. Ultimately, the decision will come down to how the costs of the EU's energy transition are distributed.
"The elephant in the room that nobody wants to discuss directly, preferring to debate techno-economics applied to grid systems, grid control, interconnections, and tariffs, is that the nature of these issues is intrinsically political and geopolitical," Sassi added.
The fight over who gets the grid first
The political stakes become even clearer when it comes to new grid connections.
The EU is facing growing queues for grid access as factories, renewable projects, data centres and other electricity-intensive investments compete for limited capacity. The proposed rules would allow EU countries to establish priorities when there is not enough room on the network.
The latest compromise would strengthen the role of member states in setting the general policy direction, leaving regulators the freedom to implement the rules.
A large group of countries — including Germany, France, Spain, Portugal, Poland, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, Belgium, Lithuania and Latvia — broadly support giving governments a stronger role.
They argue that deciding which projects get scarce grid capacity is not merely a technical exercise, it involves political choices about industrial competitiveness, energy security and social priorities. The Commission argues that setting technical criteria and network charges is fundamentally a regulatory task.
Denmark has recently announced an emergency grid law that gives data centres the lowest priority for grid connections, after Copenhagen was forced to stop new connections early in the year because of a surge in data centre applications.
Several EU countries fear that the rapid expansion of data centres, which Brussels aims to triple capacity for across the bloc by 2035 as part of a push to reduce reliance on Big Tech and develop Europe's own AI capabilities, could strain electricity grids and drive up domestic energy prices.

Britain’s elites want you ready to die for a war they keep imagining
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:01:18 UTC
21:01:18 KST

Britain’s elites want you ready to die for a war they keep imagining
Great Britain is going through a war scare. Or to be precise, its combined political and media establishment is subjecting its people to a relentless propaganda (in up-to-date NATO-speak “cognitive warfare”) campaign to create a sense of impending war against Russia.
As you would expect, that war is, of course, framed as strictly defensive. In propaganda textbook manner, the message is both very simple and very repetitive: The UK is in great danger of a Russian attack, and its whole population must prepare itself to withstand and resist it.
It goes without saying that Moscow’s repeated declarations of having no such intention make no difference.
Britain is certainly not alone in its establishment-induced hysteria. Much of NATO-EU Europe is undergoing, in essence, the same treatment. In France, for instance, President Emmanuel Macron has called a theatrical all-manicured-hands-on-deck meeting to give what can only be called a national scare talk about “Russian hybrid warfare”; in Germany, Berlin and its mainstream media won’t stop stirring the pot about the murky drone affair at Leipzig-Halle airport.
Yet, over the last weeks, within a crowded field of European panic-mongering, Britain has stuck out as especially virulent. The single most grotesque contribution was made by uber-Tory Jacob Rees-Mogg. Comfortably seated against a backdrop that screamed country-squire probity, Rees-Mogg held forth on war within the next few years, ancient Rome (he’s been to Eton, he wants you to know) and, most importantly, “circumstances where people may have to die.” Either that or – so Rees-Mogg’s stern message – decline and fall, as happened to those Romans, who let mercenaries do their fighting and thus lost their empire.
So much to unpack. For one thing, the reference to paying others to fight – and die – must be a Freudian slip. Surely, Sir Jacob cannot have meant to refer to how the West, Britain very much included, has paid the Kiev regime to send its subjects – if need be, after kidnapping them – into the folly of a proxy war meatgrinder to demote Russia. And then, that Roman Empire analogy? Clearly, Rees-Mogg, true to type, is still struggling with the fact that Britain has its imperial collapse well behind it already.
Yet, sour oddball as he is, the arch-conservative – and multimillionaire – Rees-Mogg is perfectly representative of the current British establishment trend. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, for instance, has just used his first UN General Assembly address in New York to blame his country’s misery not on, say, his predecessor and Labour Party comrade Keir Starmer, but on Russia.
Meanwhile, at home, Sky News is rolling out ‘The Wargame’, a bizarre “docu”-fantasy in four parts, built on the premise that the Russians are coming, no, they really, really ARE this time!
Pretending to be a sort of “realistic” account of what a British government would do in case of Moscow launching a series of escalating attacks, this production – from available reviews – is unusually awful shlock. It features has-been politicos doubling as un-reality TV stars, such as Michael Gove and Nicola Sturgeon, and living out their inner Tom Clancy by pretending to be serious, decisive, and, most of all, terribly important to the nation’s survival.
Unintentionally funny, though, as it may be, ‘The Wargame’ clearly has substantial political support and much hype around it. Propaganda can easily look ridiculous and be highly toxic at the same time. Because effective propaganda is, above all, one simple thing: the psychological manipulation of the many by the few. This is such a case. The viewers of ‘The Wargame’ are fed a silly but efficiently dramatized story, with the whole bag of well-worn but powerful tricks: suspense, shock, and, last but not least, a thrilling score.
It’s no surprise that the attitude of those doing the manipulating is, at best, patronizing. And to be fair even to the unbearable, Jacob Rees-Mogg, who carefully tends his beyond-caricature English-toff image, is quite honest about his disdain for ordinary people and their expendable lives. From his always obstinately ill-fitting yet clearly expensively tailored suit to the diction of a terribly bored yet forbearing Eton headmaster, his performance oozes good old upper-class condescension.
When Rees-Mogg tells you that you may have to die, you know he won’t lose sleep over it, because you are you, and he – well, he is something entirely different and, really, much better (and, as it happens, richer, too), of course.
In a Sky News interview, the UK’s Chief of the Defense Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton, has revealed a less excentric as well as more insidious approach to the masses. Referring to a “national conversation on defense,” both he and his interviewer took it for granted that the purpose of such a conversation is to remedy “what the British public hasn’t got, […] haven’t understood.”
What a delicate way to start a “conversation”: let me tell you how damn slow you are and where you need to catch up. Not: Let’s exchange views and respect each other as equal citizens. Indeed, it’s not only very rude – what has happened to English manners? – but positively Orwellian to call such offensively complacent preaching a “conversation.”
Marshal Knighton’s idea of how the British can and must do better was no less revealing: In essence, be more like the Estonians or, at least, the Swedes. Because in Estonia “the threat from Russia” is “part of normal daily conversation,” and in Sweden, they are at least trying to achieve the same single-minded obsessiveness.
There you have it, chums on the homefront: Make an effort, will you now? Learn from the worst, get a grip, and make your whole life turn around the fear we tell you to feel.
And don’t you dare notice that – how embarrassing, really – it is precisely the Estonian authorities who, notwithstanding their generally record-level Russophobia – have just called on everyone in NATO-EU Europe to cool it.
Because, those unpredictable Estonians tell us, the Russia-at-the-gates narrative “has been blown completely out of proportion. For example, Russia makes some adjustments on the other side of the Narva River and now everyone across NATO is losing their heads and hyperventilating over it,” while, in reality, “there is absolutely no reason to believe that Russia is imminently going to launch a military attack on NATO, Estonia, or the Baltic states.” Oops.
Unfortunately, war propaganda is almost immune to its own absurdities, inconsistencies, and plain silliness. Because it is designed to operate not by appealing to reason but to fear, stereotypes, and conformism. A conformism that some British establishment members already openly want to reinforce by locking up any dissenters.
The true weak spot of this warmongering may be its arrogance. There are signs on social media that many Brits do not appreciate their establishment’s latest efforts to scare and mobilize them for senseless war. Let’s hope that the mix of threats and condescension – displayed by a snob as gleefully aloof as Rees-Mogg, an officer-bureaucrat as clumsily tactless as Knighton, and the makers of something as slick as ‘The Wargame’ – rubs much of the country the wrong way. The “elites” are insane and malevolent. Any hope for peace and a return to reason will have to come from below.

Differences are normal: poll panel

"Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution," the panel said in a statement on Wednesday following the newspaper report.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The National Health Insurance premium rate is unlikely to rise next year if wages go up and the government provides additional funding, Health Minister Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said Thursday.
CNA reported that the 2027 National Health Insurance global budget will reach about NT$1.04 trillion (US$32.7 billion), topping NT$1 trillion for the first time. The budget will grow by 5.5%, the upper end of the government-approved range.
Shih expects higher minimum wages, public-sector salaries, and wages in other industries to increase revenue from regular insurance premiums. Supplemental premiums and NT$60 billion in additional government funding are also expected to strengthen the system's finances.

The budget covers hospitals, clinics, dental care, and traditional Chinese medicine. Representatives of the four sectors and premium payers agreed on the 5.5% growth rate, per Liberty Times.
The increase will add about NT$55 billion to National Health Insurance spending from this year. It is the third consecutive year that the system has adopted the upper end of the projected growth range, per UDN.
Addressing concerns that much of the annual budget negotiation is settled before the formal meeting, Shih defended advance discussions as necessary for efficiency. Trying to resolve every issue in one meeting would make the process more difficult, he added.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The PCB industry is expected to post combined domestic and overseas output of NT$1.14 trillion (US$35.83 billion) this year, the Taiwan Printed Circuit Association said Thursday.
Q2 output reached NT$279.1 billion, up 27.9% from a year earlier, while first-half output rose 23.9% to NT$524.7 billion, per CNA. The TPCA said output this year has been stronger than in the previous two years.
The association said demand for AI servers, high-speed networking equipment, and memory is boosting demand for high-end PCBs, including IC substrates, high-layer-count boards, and high-density interconnect boards. Tight supplies of high-end materials and rising raw material costs have also pushed PCB prices higher.
The TPCA expects combined output to rise 24.5% year on year in the second half to NT$611.8 billion, according to UDN. Growing AI applications and emerging uses such as AI glasses and satellite communications are expected to support demand.
The industry still faces risks from rising component costs, tight supplies of key materials, geopolitical tensions, and uncertainty over returns on AI infrastructure investments, the TPCA said. Changes in supply and demand could also affect growth in the second half.
Despite the risks, the association expects AI infrastructure investment to continue expanding. Continued shortages of high-end materials are expected to support PCB prices and shipment volumes, it added.

Personal hardship and online isolation predict support for white nationalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:00:25 UTC
21:00:25 KST

About 5 percent of white American adults express support for the core ideas of the white nationalist movement, with rates rising to over 13 percent among young white men. The research indicates that personal hardships and isolated online social lives predict this support, rather than changing local racial demographics. The findings were published in Nature.
White nationalism is an ideology based on the belief that white people are under threat in the United States and that the white race must ensure its survival. According to this worldview, white people should hold more political and economic power than other groups, maintain a demographic majority, and treat white culture as superior to all other cultures. The movement operates through informal online networks, paramilitary groups, and public rallies. Until recently, public opinion researchers had not directly measured how many Americans explicitly endorse these exact principles.
Previous research has shown that white Americans hold distinct in-group racial identities, which sets the stage for understanding their political behavior. For instance, a 2019 study showed that many white Americans possess a strong sense of white racial solidarity. Other studies have explored what might cause these group-based attitudes to turn hostile.
A 2014 study indicated that learning about the country’s growing non-white population tends to make white Americans feel threatened and adopt more conservative views. Additionally, a study covered by PsyPost in 2020 found that people holding extreme white identitarian attitudes tend to score lower in personality traits related to politeness and openness to new experiences.
“We observed white nationalist ideas becoming more visible in American public life—in marches and rallies, on the internet and social media, and even in election campaigns,” Patrick J. Egan, a professor of politics and public policy and director of the Berkley Institute for Civil Discourse & Civic Solutions at New York University, told PsyPost.
“That led us to wonder the extent to which white nationalism appeals to the broader public, and who is most likely to support it,” Egan explained. “It turned out no academic study had directly measured support for the white nationalist movement before, and so we decided to investigate these questions ourselves.”
Egan and his colleagues suspected that explicit support for white nationalism might actually be driven by personal economic hardship or online radicalization, rather than local demographic changes. They also wanted to measure support directly by providing respondents with an accurate definition of the movement, reducing the chance that people would misunderstand the label.
To explore this, the researchers conducted three national surveys of non-Hispanic white adults in the United States. In the first study, conducted in 2021, the team surveyed 3,227 people using an online panel matched to national demographics. To test whether people truly understood what white nationalism meant, the researchers ran an experiment. Half of the participants were asked if they supported the movement, while the other half were given a short, factual description of its core beliefs about white power and cultural superiority before being asked the same question.
Providing the definition increased expressed support from 3.8 percent to 7.6 percent. When people were informed about the movement’s actual goals, their answers aligned more closely with their other racial attitudes, such as their sense of white identity and their opposition to minority groups holding power. This suggests that some white Americans agree with the movement’s ideas but are unfamiliar with the term white nationalism until it is explained to them.
Using the fully informed responses, the researchers then looked for demographic predictors. They found that support for white nationalism was 15 percentage points higher among people without a high school diploma compared to those with postgraduate degrees. It was also higher among conservatives, Republicans, frequent church attenders, people who believe in political conspiracies, and those who feel disconnected from politics entirely.
The researchers then tested the competing theories about what drives these beliefs. They found evidence supporting the idea that social and economic strain plays a role. People who had experienced three or more personal hardships in the past year, such as job loss or divorce, were 4 percentage points more likely to support white nationalism than those who experienced none. Living in a county with high levels of social distress, measured by poverty and unemployment rates, also predicted higher support.
However, the researchers found no evidence that changing local demographics drive white nationalist support. Living in a county with a large non-white population or a rapidly shrinking white population was not associated with endorsing the movement. The researchers note that these findings challenge the common assumption that everyday exposure to racial diversity fuels white nationalist grievance.
“One finding that is somewhat unexpected is that white people living in areas that are becoming more racially diverse were not more likely to support white nationalism,” Egan said. “This is in contrast to what we would expect from status-threat theories, which hold that demographic change can spark backlash and resentment.”
“Of course, we don’t have causal evidence in either direction here: our null findings regarding status threat may in part stem from suppressor bias introduced by whites’ residential sorting into preferred ethnoracial environments,” he added. In other words, if white Americans who dislike diversity simply move to neighborhoods that match their preferred racial makeup, it could mask the true relationship between demographic changes and nationalist views.
The study also explored the role of the internet. General social media use did not predict support for white nationalism. Instead, the nature of a person’s social ties mattered. Support was 13 percentage points higher among respondents who said all three of their closest friends were people they only knew online, compared to those whose closest friends were all known in real life.
In 2024, the researchers conducted a second study to confirm these patterns using a probability-based sample of 2,114 non-Hispanic white adults. This method is generally considered more accurate for estimating how common a belief is in the general population. This second survey replicated the main demographic findings, including the strong link between lower education, lower income, and higher support for white nationalism.
Based on this second sample, the researchers estimated that 4.9 percent of white American adults support the white nationalist movement once its tenets are explained to them. Support was highest among young men. The data showed that 13.5 percent of white men aged 18 to 29 endorsed the movement. The researchers noted that young men today spend vast amounts of time online and face unique social and economic challenges, potentially making them more receptive to grievance narratives.
A third survey, involving 2,548 white adults in late 2024 and early 2025, was designed to rule out statistical errors. The researchers tested whether respondents were just clicking a button to agree with whatever the survey asked, a phenomenon known as acquiescence bias. They also checked if asking about racial attitudes earlier in the survey primed people to express more extreme views. The results held up against these checks, confirming that the measurement of white nationalist support was robust.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that exposing white Americans to news about a growing non-white population did not actually increase their feelings of racial threat or worsen their attitudes toward minorities. The new study builds on this by showing that even real-world, local demographic trends fail to predict explicit support for white nationalism.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relies on observational data taken at specific points in time, meaning it cannot strictly determine cause and effect. Unmeasured factors, such as underlying personality traits or mental health challenges, might make someone more likely to experience personal hardships and also more susceptible to extreme political views.
The connection between online friendships and white nationalism is also complex. While isolated people might fall into online extremism, it is equally possible that holding extreme, unconventional political views makes it difficult for someone to maintain offline friendships. This dynamic could force individuals to seek out like-minded communities entirely on the internet.
Finally, the researchers noted that their study focuses strictly on ideological agreement rather than behavior. “We want to emphasize that we are only asking about endorsement of white nationalist views,” Egan noted. “We do not measure organizational affiliation with the white nationalist movement, nor do we measure support for its tactics.”
“We hope that researchers—whether that be ourselves, or other scholars—use our measure on future surveys to determine whether support for white nationalism is changing over time,” Egan said. “This will help us know if the rising visibility of white nationalism in the US is being accompanied by rising support for its ideas in the mass public.”
The study, “Predictors and prevalence of support for white nationalism in the United States,” was authored by Patrick J. Egan, James Bisbee, and Joshua A. Tucker.

Do any coffee-flavoured drinks come close to the real thing?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:00:16 UTC
21:00:16 KST

My family has benefited hugely from charities that support healthcare, so it is with extra zeal that I’ll be drinking coffee with a slice of cake tomorrow to mark this year’s Macmillan Coffee Morning. In anticipation, I’ve been tasting some coffee-flavoured drinks.
I should preface this by saying that, when it comes to coffee, I am a creature of habit and, almost 30 years into my relationship with the stuff, I know what I like: short-ish, strong, preferably made in a moka pot and only a tiny splash of milk. I’m less faithful to brands, though I do rate Union’s House Roast, which is bold, crowdpleasing, not too bitter and sold in most big supermarkets. Much as my partner has tried to seduce me to the trendy charms of filter coffee, this leopard can’t seem to change her spots.
So imagine my feelings when I lined up the cast of products to taste for this column. Canned lattes! Coffee-flavoured protein drinks! Instant coffee 2.0! I’ll start with the first group, because the market is now teeming with examples (many of them in extra-unsustainable packaging). All the big players are there – Starbucks, Nescafé, Califia Farms – and all with the three-quarters (or more) milk to one quarter (or less) coffee ratio typical of a latte. The difference is that these drinks all have added sugar or sweeteners, thereby turning your morning coffee into a liquid pudding. If they contain dairy milk, it tends to be UHT (not a taste I like), although some use lactose-free or plant-based milks. The best of the bunch was Grind’s Iced Vanilla Oat Latte: less milk (57%), more coffee (40%) and less sugar, too.
As far as I could tell, Emmi’s Caffe Latte High Protein is no higher in protein than any of the rest, so it strikes me that the brand may simply be jumping on what’s becoming a rather hackneyed bandwagon catering to a health-anxious and possibly appetite-suppressed crowd. Yfood’s This Is Food, meanwhile, made me quickly wonder: “Is it?” This ready-to-drink, coffee-flavoured “complete meal” with 30g protein per bottle and more than 20 ingredients is a sorry substitute for a food, and it certainly isn’t coffee.
Cold brew – that is, coffee that has been steeped in cold water for an extended period for a softer, more naturally sweet result – takes a fair while to make, so I can see the point in buying it off the shelf: Tesco and Nescafé both make inoffensive unsweetened cold-brew concentrates that are a good option for an Indian summer. And, much to my surprise, I rather enjoyed the next-gen flavoured instant coffees by Little’s and Beanies, especially the former’s glazed cinnamon number. But as much as Union from my moka? Come off it.
Four coffee drinks worth your attention
Grind Iced Vanilla Oat Latte £2.25 (250ml) Ocado. The best example of this dubious genre: a not-too-sweet, good-quality cold brew blended with oat milk.
Tesco Finest Cold Brew Coffee £4.50 (500ml). A cold brew concentrate to which you just add water. Would be nice with a slice of citrus.
Little’s Glazed Cinnamon £4 (50g) Ocado. The doughnut vibes are more in the aroma than the taste, but it’s a scent that could seduce non-coffee drinkers.
Union House Roast £7.50 (200g) Ocado. You can’t beat a home brew, and this balanced, slightly chocolatey all-rounder is my food shop stalwart.
