Why is Iran threatening regional airports, and what could be the impact?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:10:42 UTC
20:10:42 KST

Why is Iran threatening regional airports, and what could be the impact?
Tehran hints retaliation as Georgia and Azerbaijan suspend Iranian flights amid mounting US sanctions on airlines.
Iran has threatened neighbouring countries with retaliation if they enforce new United States sanctions designed to stop Iranian airlines from operating internationally, raising the prospect of further disruption to air travel across a region already affected by nearly seven months of the US-Israel war on Iran.
“I urge all our neighbouring countries not to get involved in the United States adventure. This adventure will very soon end in failure,” Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Iranian state media.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iran’s president brings receipts of US strikes on civilians to the UNGA
- list 2 of 3US threatens to ground Iranian airlines worldwide from Wednesday
- list 3 of 3Can the US ban Iranian airlines worldwide – and what would it mean?
The warning came as Iranian carriers cancelled a number of international flights after the US threatened airports and aviation service providers with secondary sanctions if they continued doing business with it. On Thursday, the all Iranian flights to and from the United Arab Emirates were cancelled, the Iranian Students’ News Agency reported.
Azerbaijan and Georgia had on Wednesday confirmed suspending Iranian flights, while flights to Baghdad and Muscat have also been halted. Meanwhile, several connections to Turkiye and China have continued, but many flights to these countries have been cancelled, too.
So, what has Iran said, can it carry out its threats against neighbouring countries, and how could this potentially affect the travel industry in the region?
What has Iran said?
Rezaei warned on Wednesday that Tehran would retaliate against neighbouring countries that cooperate with the US restrictions.
“If a country cooperates with or embarks on adventures with the United States, its airports will no longer be able to operate flights” to Iran, Rezaei told Iranian state television. Rezaei said Iran would ensure airports in countries stopping Iranian flights “cannot function”.
The warning is part of a broader Iranian attempt to deter countries from participating in Washington’s campaign of economic pressure, which has heightened since the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28.
What is the backdrop to this threat?
The immediate trigger to this threat from Rezaei is Washington’s attempt to isolate Iran’s aviation industry.
The US Department of the Treasury earlier this month announced sanctions against Iran’s remaining airlines as well as foreign companies and intermediaries accused of helping them operate.
The measures expanded longstanding restrictions on Mahan Air to cover 27 Iranian airlines and also suspended authorisations that had allowed a number of aviation links with Iran. The US accuses Mahan Air of having links to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent then warned that airports and companies servicing Iranian aircraft risk being cut off from the US financial system.
He said they could not provide Iranian carriers with fuel or landing services, or sell them tickets, without risking US penalties.
“Rezaei’s warning is essentially an attempt at coercive deterrence directed at Iran’s neighbours,” Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow at the US-based Center for International Policy, told Al Jazeera. “Tehran is signalling that it will not regard compliance with US aviation sanctions as a neutral commercial decision, but as participation in Washington’s pressure campaign against Iran.”
“It also shows how the US-Iran confrontation is increasingly pulling third countries into the conflict,” she said.
Can Iran actually do this?
Iran has not publicly explained what action it could take to prevent airports in neighbouring countries from functioning, and Rezaei did not specify whether Tehran’s response would be diplomatic, economic or military.
Iran cannot legally decide whether an airport in another sovereign country accepts Iranian aircraft. Likewise, the US does not have the authority to simply close another country’s airspace.
But Washington can make servicing Iranian aircraft financially risky by threatening local fuel suppliers, ground handlers, ticketing companies and other businesses with secondary sanctions.
“The important point is that Rezaei left the threat deliberately ambiguous,” Mortazavi said. “He did not specify how Iran would make neighbouring airports unable to operate. But the message is clear: if neighbouring states help Washington isolate Iranian aviation, Tehran is threatening to impose reciprocal costs on their aviation sectors.”
And Iran demonstrated, in the opening months of the current war with the US and Israel, that it could bring air travel in the Gulf to a near-halt. After it launched missiles and drones at Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman and Jordan, starting February 28, all of these countries partially or entirely closed their airspace in the early days of March.
They restarted limited operations slowly and one by one: Emirates was the first to start a few flights out of its Dubai hub on March 3, with Abu Dhabi-based Etihad following on March 6, and Qatar Airways the following week. The planes that took off or landed in those early days of the war were accompanied by military jets.
Gulf carriers took months to restore their schedules to normal. The International Air Transport Association estimates their airlines in the the Middle East are on track to post a collective $4.3bn loss in 2026.
The World Travel & Tourism Council estimated in March that the conflict was costing the region about $600m a day in international visitor spending. At about the same time, Tourism Economics forecast international travel to Gulf countries could fall by 25 percent in 2026 due to the war.
Iranian projectiles – either directly or after interception – also hit the Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Kuwait and Bahrain airports.
Wolfgang Pusztai, a security and defence analyst and former Austrian defence attache, told Al Jazeera that he did not expect Iran to attack regional airports this time around. “It is extremely unlikely that Iran will attack these airports,” Pusztai said.
He argued that the immediate practical impact of the US measures could also be limited because Iran retains aviation links with countries that may be less likely to enforce Washington’s restrictions.
“I don’t think that Turkiye will stop working, cooperating with them, or Pakistan or China,” he said. “And moreover, as I said, there are other carriers serving Iran from outside, so the practical impact will be limited.”
Pusztai said the greater effect may instead be psychological, particularly for Iranians who can immediately see the consequences when international flights disappear.
“This will certainly contribute to the perception of the Iranians of increasing isolation, and this is probably the reason for this tough reaction from the side of Iran,” he said.
Unlike restrictions on financial institutions or other secondary sanctions, disruptions to flights are immediately visible, Pusztai said. “Such an air blockade is definitely seen immediately.”
He also cautioned against expecting aviation sanctions alone to force Tehran to change course.
“Will it be enough to break the will of the country? Absolutely not. Absolutely not,” Pusztai said, describing the restrictions instead as another element of Washington’s effort to increase pressure on Iran.
How will this impact the travel industry?
The most immediate effect is on Iranian travellers. International flight capacity from Iran was already 49 percent lower in August 2026 than a year earlier, according to aviation analytics company Cirium.
The latest restrictions have left only a handful of Iranian-operated international routes and pushed thousands of travellers towards land crossings with countries including Turkiye and Armenia.
The effects can spread beyond passengers, experts say, as measures could threaten thousands of jobs in the Iranian aviation industry and related sectors including tourism and hospitality.
For neighbouring countries, further escalation could add another layer of uncertainty to the travel industry in the region, which has seen tourism battered amid ongoing fighting between the US and Iran.
Passenger traffic at major hubs like Dubai International Airport dropped by 31 percent in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year.

Swiss Senate moves to weaken journalistic source protection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:10:26 UTC
20:10:26 KST

Swiss Senate moves to weaken journalistic source protection
The Swiss Senate has tabled a motion calling on the government to relax the protection of journalistic sources. This would make it easier to prosecute breaches of official secrecy.
Under the criminal code, journalists are not required to disclose their sources of information for investigative purposes.
Exceptions to this right to refuse to give evidence apply in cases of serious criminal offences or where the information is necessary to save people’s lives or protect them from physical harm.
The motion, which was adopted by the Senate by 34 votes to 10, seeks to limit source protection to media professionals for whom it is directly necessary to safeguard media freedom.
Protection against seizure is also to apply only to media professionals, and not to those who breach confidentiality.
The motion will now be referred to the House of Representatives.

BRUSSELS — EU officials warned Thursday that a U.S. plan to ban diesel exports for 90 days could have a significant impact on European markets and said the bloc was in talks with the Trump administration to wave it off the ban.
"The European Union views with concern the report that the U.S. plans to ban diesel exports, including to the European Union," Olof Gill, a spokesperson for the European Commission, the EU's executive arm, told reporters in response to a question for POLITICO. "Any disruption would risk negatively impacting both sides."
In this light, "high level contacts between the European Union and the U.S. administration are ongoing," and the EU expects "close partners to consult each other before taking measures that affect shared markets," he added.
Advertisement
Gill declined to share details on the content of the diplomatic talks but said "there are strong voices — also there — that believe any proposed ban of this nature would be a very bad idea indeed."
The EU's imports of U.S. diesel have increased in recent months to make up for imports lost due to the conflict in the Middle East, and the bloc currently imports more than half of its diesel from America. Prices and supply have been further affected by strikes on Russian oil refineries.
The United States is now the world’s largest exporter of diesel and has been setting new records for exports this year, according to ClearView Energy. Taking that supply out of global markets would have far-reaching effects on the European and global economy.
“Given the precarious situation that Europe currently finds itself in, any further restrictions on fuels available to the EU at this stage could quickly become very serious,” said a person in the industry who closely follows the market situation and was granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive situation openly.
The planned ban, first reported by POLITICO, would last 90 days amid growing domestic concerns over rising fuel prices. However, the move has drawn vociferous opposition from the U.S. oil sector, which has warned the ban would significantly tighten global supply. Trump's energy secretary, Chris Wright, also opposes the ban.
Anna-Kaisa Itkonen, a Commission spokesperson, added that Brussels was "monitoring the markets and security of supply very, very closely, together with our member states." She said the EU was a "big U.S. diesel importer" and remains a "solid and attractive market to the United States."
Advertisement
While seeking to boost the share of renewables in the bloc, the EU has also touted its pledge to invest $750 billion in U.S. energy products by 2028 under the U.S.-EU trade deal. Asked whether the EU would rethink this commitment — and the broader increase in U.S. fuel imports — Itkonen said the U.S-EU energy trade was "mutually beneficial" while highlighting the EU's longer-term commitment to weaning off fossil fuels entirely.
She added that private companies were responsible for much of the increase in imports.
"It's no secret, of course, that the United States is a major supplier to us as regards to diesel oil as well as [liquefied natural gas]. This is clearly part of our diversification strategy since 2022," she said. But "these are very often contracts between companies so we will not have the full breakdown of those to share here in any case."

Russia’s Global Recruitment Pipeline: How Russia Hunts the World’s Poor to Feed Its War in Ukraine – Part 2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:09:00 UTC
20:09:00 KST

You can find Part 1 here.
If Africa is one front in this campaign, South Asia is arguably the largest.
CNN has reported estimates of up to 15,000 Nepali citizens recruited for Russia’s war, with Nepal’s foreign minister confirming at least 14 deaths and formally asking Russia to return hundreds of citizens.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Sri Lanka’s government has acknowledged around 280 citizens recruited to fight on both sides of the war, while UN Special Rapporteurs formally raised allegations with Moscow in July 2025 documenting Sri Lankans trafficked and forcibly conscripted through false job offers.
India’s Central Bureau of Investigation identified at least 35 citizens duped into travelling to Russia through recruitment agents, and the government has put the total figure recruited at 91 in a formal parliamentary statement. High-level diplomatic engagement has since secured Russian commitments to stop recruiting Indian nationals.
An Associated Press (AP) investigation published in early 2026 found Bangladeshi men lured with promises of civilian work and then coerced, under threat of violence or imprisonment, into front-line logistics and casualty-recovery tasks. Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters has said Russia formally agreed to stop recruiting from Sri Lanka, Nepal, India, and Pakistan after those four countries alone had sent at least 1,794 fighters combined.
Latin America, the former USSR, and now Indonesia
Cuba’s foreign ministry says it launched a crackdown on trafficking networks after discovering in 2023 that its citizens were fighting in Ukraine. Citizens of Cuba, Colombia, and Brazil have since turned up in testimony gathered by the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and Amnesty alike.
Ukraine Pushes Forward in 4 Frontline Sectors as Russia Struggles for Gains
Two Chinese nationals were captured fighting for Russia in the Donetsk Oblast in April. And the pipeline keeps finding new markets. In August 2026, Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service said that it had documented at least eight Indonesian citizens recruited through the same false-job, fast-passport model already tested for years on Nepal, Cuba, Kenya, and India – describing the approach as a scheme already validated on “dozens of other countries” now simply redeployed on a new one.
Even Russia’s own neighbors are treated as a recruiting pool rather than an ally’s citizenry.
Independent media tallies of intercepted recruitment data have logged 86 recruits from Tajikistan, 71 each from Uzbekistan and Belarus, 64 from Kyrgyzstan, 59 from Kazakhstan, 19 from Turkmenistan, and 12 from Moldova. Citizens of formally friendly or allied post-Soviet states, pitched with the same “become a new Russian” citizenship offer used everywhere else.
Why Russia needs all of them
The reason for this global hunt for recruits is not a mystery: Russia’s own losses in Ukraine are staggering, and it is running out of Russians willing to replace them.
According to Ukraine’s General Staff, cumulative Russian personnel losses (killed and wounded) since Feb. 24, 2022 have reached approximately 1,519,650 as of Sept. 21, 2026 – daily losses through September running consistently above 1,300 and briefly spiking past 1,900 in a single day.
Independent Western estimates are more conservative but still place Russian casualties in the region of 1.2 million, part of combined battlefield losses on both sides that analysts now put close to two million people.
This is precisely why foreign recruits are so valuable to Moscow and so disposable in its eyes. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has described their fate bluntly: “Most of them are immediately sent to the so-called ‘meat assaults,’ where they are quickly killed. Most mercenaries do not survive more than a month.”
Untrained, unable to communicate in Russian, and with no support network on the ground, foreign recruits are disproportionately used to open assaults ahead of trained units – absorbing the first, heaviest casualties, so that experienced Russian soldiers do not have to.
What happens when they don’t come home
A WhatsApp correspondence obtained for this story, with a contact representing several Ugandan families of recruits killed or missing in Russia’s war, shows exactly what these families face once the fighting is over for their relative – whether he survived it or not. The identity of the contact is withheld for their protection. The number that opened the exchange is a Uganda-registered line. The exchange opened with the question at the center of every one of these cases:
Contact: “Some families went to Russia for the repatriation of remains and compensation but unfortunately they got nothing. How can the families get help in this case?”
The reply did not soften the reality:
Ukrainian side: “This comes as no surprise – this is Russia, after all. They have no interest in returning foreign prisoners of war, or in paying them compensation, or providing assistance to their families in the event of their death. No such cases have yet been recorded. At present, the only way forward is to publicize these stories in the media so that they gain public attention. Perhaps then, the Russian Federation will take some action to meet the needs of these families. Alongside this, it is necessary to take the matter to an international court, but this requires evidence that their relative signed a contract providing for payments in the event of death, and so on. But Russia will deny everything, it will be difficult to prove. In any case, publicity is needed.”
The Ukrainian side then asked the only question that matters in court or in print:
Ukrainian side: “Tell me, do these families have any documents from the Russian government? Any replies or refusals regarding the payment of funds? You do realize that mere words are just words. To substantiate claims in the media or in court, evidence is required.”
The contact then described documentation that, unusually, had already reached government level:
Contact: “We have a few examples of contracts, visas, and letters from the Ministry of Defense Department of Sub Saharan Africa.”
Contact: “Family traveled to Russia but no remains available nor compensation.”
Asked to clarify whether those letters had come from African defense ministries writing to Moscow, the contact corrected the address:
Contact: “This is a department in Russia defense that handles African cases, unfortunately when families get to Russia they are denied access to a facility. I don’t know how this issue can be addressed.”
Ukrainian side: “Do you mean the Russian Federation’s African Corps?”
Contact: “I will share a copy, it’s confidential.”
The files that followed were not Africa Corps letterhead. They were the embassy covering letters and the Russian foreign ministry notes on Benon, Mutesigensi, and Mwesigwa.
The reply confirmed the scale of the wider machine rather than answering the Africa Corps question directly:
Ukrainian side: “On the Russian side, the participation of foreign nationals from more than 130 different countries has already been confirmed. They lure these people to Russia under false pretenses, where they are forced or tricked into signing contracts with the Russian Armed Forces. And then, after a week of training, they are sent straight into hell.”
The contact raised a second, less-documented layer of harm – families already grieving being targeted a second time by people posing as fixers:
Contact: “How can we get help? From what I see I think there are cartels trying to swindle compensations and there is also a big challenge with accountability. Majority of our people are missing on all lists, we tried to check on Ukrainian chat bot ‘I want to find.’”
Ukrainian side: “To make sure your people aren’t deceived by scammers or others, just remember that Russia does not pay any compensation to foreign citizens.”
Ukrainian side: “Yes, this is the bot for the Coordination Headquarters on the Treatment of Prisoners of War.”
When pressed further, the Ukrainian side was explicit about what it can and cannot do. It can gather information on missing foreigners, but cannot extract payment or accountability from Moscow:
Ukrainian side: “We do not disseminate or publicize any sensitive information, but we do collect, study, and analyze it. We strive to help families searching for their relatives – there are tens of thousands of them around the world – given Russia’s extensive influence and capabilities. We are working to counter the recruitment of foreign citizens into the ranks of the Russian Armed Forces. This will benefit both your people and ours.”
The contact’s response captured the grievance driving families toward any channel willing to listen:
Contact: “They don’t have information about our people, and Russia doesn’t give any accountability at all, it’s been eight months of no communication.”
Ukrainian side: “Yes, because we gather this information bit by bit.”
At that point, the contact shared two scanned documents bearing the letterhead of the Embassy of the Republic of Uganda in Moscow: a three-page disappearance file on Kamusiye Benon and a two-page death notice on Alex Mutesigensi and Baker Mwesigwa. They were formal diplomatic instruments, not informal testimony, showing that Kampala’s own mission has already engaged Moscow on paper over specific citizens. The contact then described the practical burden families carry even before they learn about an outcome:
Contact: “Make research please, the poor families struggle to raise money for tickets, visas, document legalization, hotels, but when they get to Russia, they aren’t getting addressed.”
The final substantive reply is, in effect, the bluntest available summary of where every one of these families currently stands, regardless of nationality:
Ukrainian side: “We will look for information about your citizens, but that is all we can do. We understand you and your efforts to uncover the truth, but I must emphasize once again that this is how the Russians treat everyone. Therefore, I cannot help you obtain compensation, since Russia is a terrorist state, and you will receive nothing from them. However, we can draw public attention to this issue, and then the international community will put pressure on Russia and perhaps force them to pay all reparations, as well as compensation to the families of those who died because of their actions.”
The contact’s closing message pointed to the one avenue Uganda itself has offered so far, and its evident limits:
Contact: “Our ambassador says compensation is possible but we don’t have a clear process. I think families should be allowed to interface with the responsible Russian ministries handling compensation.”
That is the trap inside the notes themselves. Russia writes that payments are “provided for.” The ambassador forwards the invitation to come and collect. The families sell assets for tickets and certified translations. Then, they say, the door stays closed: no remains, no money, and a second market of fixers offering to “process” a compensation that does not arrive.
Main takeaway
Every recruitment pitch described above – from Kampala to Kathmandu, Jakarta to Dushanbe – sells the same three things: fast money, a fast passport, and a job nowhere near a battlefield.
Every documented outcome delivers the same three things instead: a Russian-language contract no one explains, a front-line assignment inside weeks, and – for hundreds already confirmed dead and thousands more unaccounted for – silence.
Russia’s own notes to Uganda speak of payments “provided for by legislative and other regulatory legal acts.” No country’s ministry of defense has produced a single confirmed case of those payments reaching a foreign recruit’s family. No embassy correspondence reviewed for this story, or in the wider reporting cited here, describes Russia returning a body without months or years of pressure, if at all.
The gap between the loud promise and what a person actually ends up receiving is not an accident here. It is an iron pattern, repeating itself in every documented case.
But there is a deeper dimension to this cynical calculation. Russia’s Ministry of Defense has kept official casualty figures under wraps since September 2022, and the one number the Kremlin ever gave at the start of the full-scale invasion, independent researchers openly describe as a several-fold undercount. Instead, a joint project by the BBC’s Russian Service and Mediazona painstakingly rebuilds the list of Russian dead from obituaries, state death payments to families, and fresh cemetery records.
As of Sept. 21, 2026, they had confirmed the names of at least 258,989 dead Russian service members, not an official government tally, but names gathered from obituaries, payouts, and grave records. Foreigners among them number 1,285, plus 2,304 fighters from North Korea, for a combined total of 3,589 as of July 2026.
The investigators themselves caution that this is only the beginning: foreign recruits are far less likely to leave behind the kind of trace – a local obituary, a regional-government payment, a relative’s social media post – that the entire counting method depends on.
In the end, for Russia’s war machine, a foreign recruit is not simply someone who will later, quietly, not get paid. He is a convenient, expendable resource whose loss is almost impossible for anyone to count.

Starlink base station providing communications for Ukraine set on fire in Poland

20:08:16 KST

A fire broke out on Wednesday evening on the grounds of the Starlink satellite communications ground base station in Masovia (Poland), which provides internet connectivity for Central and Eastern Europe, including Ukraine, RMF24 reports.
"Late Wednesday evening, the owner of the plot hosting the telecommunication infrastructure elements called the emergency services hotline. He reported that an antenna fire had occurred. The power generator was also damaged. Firefighters arrived at the scene and managed to extinguish the blaze. According to preliminary findings by the services, a switchboard may have been deliberately set on fire. The second scenario to be considered is a short circuit in the electrical grid," the report states.
The police were called to the scene. The Internal Security Agency and the Central Bureau of Police Investigation were notified of the incident.
Police crime scene investigators are continuing to record evidence at the site of the fire. Preventive service officers are also patrolling the village.
According to Minister of Digitalization Krzysztof Gawkowski, much indicates that the fire was a deliberate attempt to disrupt the station's operation.
"The operator of this station is Exatel, a state-owned telecommunications operator that is one of the elements ensuring internet security and providing network access, including for Ukraine," Gawkowski stated.
He explained that a potential shutdown of such stations would cause disruptions in internet access and, consequently, in the operation of systems such as ATMs.
"Sometimes we do not realize that it is precisely such a telecommunication repeater that determines whether there will be internet access in a given part of Poland or Europe, including Ukraine," he emphasized.

US Democrats tee up pre-election war powers vote as some Republicans break with Trump on Iran

Unknown Publisher

US Senate rejects Democratic-led resolution to curb Trump's Iran war powers
WASHINGTON, Sept 24 - The US Senate on Thursday narrowly rejected a resolution demanding President Donald Trump end the war in Iran or seek congressional authorization, as Democrats sought to put Republicans on the defensive over the unpopular conflict before November's midterm elections.
With polls showing Trump's Republicans struggling to keep their slim congressional majorities on November 3, more of them have been edging away from the war, which has pushed up food and fuel prices.
However, Thursday's Senate vote was 50-49 against the resolution, largely along party lines. Four Republicans — Senators Susan Collins of Maine, Rand Paul of Kentucky, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska — voted in favor.
Tillis, who is leaving the Senate in January, was the only Republican to vote in favor of a war powers resolution for the first time. Republicans in competitive reelection races, including Jon Husted of Ohio, Dan Sullivan of Alaska, Roger Marshall of Kansas, Pete Ricketts of Nebraska and Darline Graham of South Carolina stuck with Trump.
One Democrat, John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, voted against the resolution, which passed the House of Representatives in July.
The vote was largely symbolic. The Trump administration has not changed policy in response to previous war powers votes. Thursday's vote took place two days after Trump threatened that he could "annihilate the Islamic Republic" in a UN speech.
Democrats see the votes as a way to put Republicans on the record on a conflict that has become increasingly unpopular with voters. Only 34% of respondents in a Reuters/Ipsos poll this week said they approved of the strikes on Iran.
The Senate has considered Iran war powers resolutions 14 times — voting in favor only twice — since US and Israeli forces began bombing Iran on February 28. The House has held six votes, with three in favor of ending the conflict.
Only one has passed both the House and Senate, and the White House ignored the result.
The US Constitution says that only Congress, not the president, can declare war, and Democrats have argued that Trump may have pulled the country into a long conflict by failing to spell out a clear strategy.
Republicans say Trump's actions are within his rights as commander-in-chief.
SHIFTS IN TIGHT RACES
A small number of Republicans have, however, broken ranks on the war.
In the House, seven Republicans voted with Democrats to pass a war powers resolution last week. Three of the seven — Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa and Nancy Mace of South Carolina — voted against party leaders on the issue for the first time.
Nunn and Miller-Meeks face competitive reelection races in November, when all 435 House seats and 35 of 100 Senate seats are up for grabs. Mace is not seeking reelection after a failed campaign for South Carolina's governor.
And two Republican Senate candidates called on Monday for a swift end to the war, the latest sign that vulnerable candidates are trying to put some distance between themselves and Trump.
Both Mike Rogers in Michigan and Ashley Hinson in Iowa had previously backed Trump's authority to strike Tehran.
Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the House's Democratic leader, suggested Republicans were calling for an end to the war only because they face tough races.
"It's interesting to me that several of them who are in tight races and on the verge of losing, including in places like Iowa or Michigan or Wisconsin, are all now starting to say the war needs to end," Jeffries told a news conference on Wednesday. REUTERS

Survey reveals Swiss transport habits and annoyances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:05:41 UTC
20:05:41 KST

Survey reveals Swiss transport habits and annoyances
Almost half of all Swiss people regularly get annoyed with other road users, according to a traffic survey commissioned by insurance group Axa.
Around 26% of road users surveyed get annoyed by others several times a week, and 23% even do so every day, as this year’s Axa Mobility Survey revealed.
Stressed, aggressive or agitated driving can be dangerous. Luca Genovese from the AXA Centre of Excellence for Mobility was quoted in a press release on Thursday as saying that drivers who are less focused make more mistakes whilst driving.
Motorbike, bicycle or e-bike riders feel less safe more often, according to the survey. Three out of four cyclists or e-bike riders shared the fear of being involved in an accident caused by other road users.
Axa concluded that, generally speaking, the fear of other road users predominated amongst all respondents, rather than fear of their own abilities.
Looking for mistakes
Traffic jams, congested roads and other drivers’ mistakes: these are the top three annoyances for motorists. They find it particularly annoying when others tailgate (63%), get distracted (59%), fail to use their indicators (57%) or drive at a snail’s pace (51%).
Those travelling on foot or by bike are more likely to fear speeding or reckless driving. What they have in common is frustration with cyclists and e-bike riders.
More
How to behave on a Swiss train
It’s not just on the road; other people can also be a problem on public transport: almost three-quarters complain about people talking loudly on the phone or using media without headphones. But litter left behind (68%), feet on the seat cushions (55%) and overpowering odours (53%) also put people in a bad mood whilst travelling.
Those who mainly cycle are more often satisfied than other road users. Car drivers also expressed satisfaction with their main mode of transport. Public transport users would prefer to travel by car, whilst unhappy pedestrians would prefer to use public transport.
Overall, half of the population stated that their daily commute was at least a little stressful and exhausting – those who travel frequently by public transport are most likely to feel this way.
Treading on others’ toes
Around half of the Swiss population stated that they base their choice of transport on environmental friendliness – 15% do so to a significant extent. Four in ten respondents occasionally feel guilty about not doing so.
At the same time, as many as 70% of those surveyed believe that others should make their travel habits more environmentally friendly. But only 52% are themselves prepared to do so.

Back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:04:51 UTC
20:04:51 KST

One day, I’m posting here about how to address AI risks, the next, Daily Nous suffers from a “critical error” and goes down for over a week. Coincidence? Or evidence that the AI’s thought I was onto something?
Yes I know it was the former… probably.
What happened? Daily Nous and its server were hacked. This isn’t the first time the site has had problems. A month earlier, the site was subject to what looks like some kind of attack. And at several times over recent years, various types of malware have infected the site, causing assorted difficulties. I employ security and clean-up services, but they face an increasing number and variety of threats. Meanwhile, the site has been aging—it’s over 14 years old—with some of its components becoming outdated, mutually incompatible, and difficult or impossible to update. It had slowed down a bit, too.
So when this last hack occurred, my technical consultant, John Hunt, recommended the site be rebuilt: taken apart, inspected piece by piece, problem elements fixed or replaced if necessary, and then put back together again, with even more security. “But what if we have to replace all of the pieces?” I asked. “Will it still be the same blog?”
I wish I could say that the reason it has taken so long to get DN up and running again is that we were distracted by the metaphysics of blogular identity over time. But what really happened is that we just did what John recommended. And by “we” I mean mostly John. At the start of the process we thought it would only take a few days, but as it continued, various further issues were discovered that needed addressing.
The result is not really a redesign of the site. It should look roughly the same as it did before (despite that we had to ditch the original “theme”–the code that gave the site its look). But there are some functional improvements, and the site should run a little faster than it used to.
We haven’t finished putting everything back on the site just yet. Some posts that had embedded videos or spreadsheets may be missing them, for example. The Heap of Links is, fittingly enough, disordered at the moment. The ad placements aren’t quite right. Some settings may still have to be properly adjusted. And we may yet notice some mistakes we need to correct.
So things aren’t perfect yet, but, as you may have noticed over the years, I subscribe to the idea that one shouldn’t let the perfect be the enemy of the blog.
You’ve all been quite patient. Thanks for that. And it seems you’ve all been quite cooperative, making barely any news while the site has been down, which I also appreciate. Or did I miss something? Let me know.

Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun’s Regular Press Conference on September 24, 2026

CGTN: We’ve noted that the fifth Global Digital Trade Expo (GDTE) opened in Hangzhou this morning under the theme “Meet the AI Future at GDTE.” Premier Li Qiang attended and addressed the launching ceremony. Can you share more information on that?
Guo Jiakun: This morning, the fifth GDTE opened in Hangzhou. Premier Li Qiang attended and addressed the launching ceremony. Leaders including Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers of Kyrgyzstan Adylbek Aleshovich Kasymaliev attended and addressed the launching ceremony. Other leaders including Director General of the UN Industrial Development Organization Gerd Müller addressed the event via video link. Over 1,200 representatives from various sectors of close to 50 countries and regions and relevant international organizations attended the launching ceremony.
In response to questions such as where global trade is heading amid the trend of digitalization, what should the world do to capitalize on that trend, and what role can China play, Premier Li Qiang shared three observations. First, the need to grasp the new changes and new trends in global trade through digital trade. Flourishing digital trade provides new impetus and opportunities. The world economy faces broad prospects as well as new development gaps. Market matching becomes more convenient while at the same time, new trade barriers emerge. Global trade can accelerate growth through innovation, but without sufficient protection of relevant rules. Second, openness is essential to enable better development of global trade in the digital era. Amid economic globalization, the international community needs to engage in sincere coordination. We need to enhance digital connectivity for more free trade, bridge the digital divide for more universally beneficial trade, and improve digital governance for more orderly trade. Third, China will make greater contribution to global digital trade. We will keep expanding digital consumer demand and share market opportunities with countries around the world. We will continue to strengthen support for the digital industry and empower global digitalization. China’s technology advancement follows an open-source approach such as in the field of artificial intelligence to build “digital ladders” accessible to all countries. We will continue to improve the environment for digital development and offer China’s solutions to setting up well-rounded international rules.
Foreign leaders noted in their remarks that the the GDTE provides an invaluable platform for countries to have discussions on cooperation, jointly promote development and share outcomes. They appreciated China’s effort of sharing development outcomes and expressed hopes to work with China to bridge the digital divide, build a fair, safe and secure global digital trade order for good and for all, and provide new impetus for the sustainable development of the world.

‘We have nothing’: DRC displacement crisis worsens as fighting continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:03:04 UTC
20:03:04 KST

A cry of panic erupts across the camp as several shelters are engulfed in flames. Women rush to pull their children and meagre possessions away from the blaze. The young men of the camp quickly tear down the neighbouring shelters to form a firebreak.
Thousands of displaced civilians are living in the Muganwa camp, close to the lakeside town of Kalemie, the provincial capital of Tanganyika in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (the DRC). Their shelters are made with little more than sticks and dried palm leaves.
It is the dry season, and a spark from a charcoal cooking fire has destroyed the homes of several families.
The people here have fled heavy fighting between the Congolese army and the March 23 rebel group (M23), which is supported militarily by neighbouring Rwanda. More than a year has passed since the governments of the DRC and Rwanda signed a peace accord mediated by the United States, but violence has continued unabated, and the M23 continues to hold swathes of land across the provinces of North and South Kivu.
The impact of war is now felt here in a third province, Tanganyika, which borders South Kivu.
Furaha Kahisa, a mother of six, watches as the fire dies down. She made her journey here in early 2025, travelling more than 250 miles (400km) on foot with her young children. “I came from Minova on the South Kivu-North Kivu border, and fled as militias defeated by M23 looted my village,” she says. “We fled to Goma [capital of North Kivu], but knew the M23 would arrive shortly after the militias ran away, so we moved quickly and reached South Kivu.”
The family could hear fierce fighting behind them as the advancing M23 seized the provincial capitals of Goma and Bukavu. “What I witnessed at home made me fear we would never escape if we were attacked again,” says Kahisa. Instead of waiting for renewed attacks, she decided to take her family as far south as possible along Lake Tanganyika.
To reach Muganwa camp, she spent nearly three more weeks on the road, relying on the kindness of strangers in roadside villages, who gave her cassava to feed the children.
Kahisa decided to settle in the camp, even though conditions there are dire: a single muddy stream is the sole source of water for drinking and washing for hundreds of people.
Nearly 100,000 displaced civilians arrived in Tanganyika between November 2025 and February 2026 alone, during an M23 offensive against the lakeside town of Uvira in South Kivu. The town was recaptured by government forces this January, but fighting has continued ever since in the nearby mountains of Fizi.
Many civilians and soldiers fled the fighting in Uvira by boat. “The wind was very strong,” says Jeanne Sikitu. “It took a week of sailing. We suffered … I could not even count how many of us were in that boat under the sun,” she says. “We had nothing to eat on the journey, because we fled our village with nothing when the gunfire approached.”
Those fleeing the M23 frontline to arrive in Tanganyika find themselves in a place that has itself experienced years of insecurity. The province is now home to an estimated more than 330,000 displaced civilians, including the new arrivals, staying in several camps including Muganwa and Mulicha.
Many of these are victims of ethnic clashes. A local grouping of militias, the Biloze Bishambuke, has attacked other ethnic groups, pillaged communities and stolen cattle in the nearby hills for more than a decade, and in Tanganyika’s forests a conflict has simmered between the Twa and Luba communities since it resumed in 2016.
Josephine Salima lives in a shelter in Muganwa camp, just a short walk across the sand from Kahisa’s family. Unlike Kahisa, however, she was born in Tanganyika province and has lived at the camp since fleeing raids by the Biloze Bishambuke on her village, Matete, in late 2025. “They beat my pregnant daughter,” she explains. “We had no choice but to flee.”
In many of the displacement sites dotted across the province, survivors of these conflicts can now be found cohabiting, sharing resources and awaiting aid.
Rose Mukalay, a 55-year-old farmer, fled from South Kivu in February 2025. “Two thousand, three hundred of us arrived here by boat,” she says. “The local village chief gave us this space, where we met others who already fled the Twa war.” She was recently elected president of the Mulicha displacement site, which means she must seek out the administrators of the territory to negotiate access to local schools for displaced children, and oversee attempts to raise whatever income she can for the two communities sheltering there.
“We cannot help ourselves if we have nothing,” says Mukalay. “So we are sharing the work of harvesting palm oil for the farmers here, and planting our own fields.”
In the past five decades, Mukalay has seen generations of conflict along the lake. She remembers when another Rwanda-backed group, the Rally for Congolese Democracy (RCD), attacked her region in the late 1990s, during the height of the second Congo war. “Even when the RCD were advancing, we could endure,” she says. But her fear during that conflict, which killed more people than any since the end of the second world war, doesn’t compare to what she is going through now.
“With the M23 arriving, everything has worsened,” she says. “We would rather go hungry than hear gunshots each night.”

France succeeded in its push to remove Usmanov from the EU sanctions list on Tuesday, and on Wednesday, Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev signed a decree pardoning Ryan, among others, and the French national left Baku shortly after.
Thursday’s French statement does not make any reference to the Usmanov case, but it describes a “patient and demanding dialogue” and calls Ryan’s presidential pardon a “humanitarian gesture which French salutes.”
The apparent diplomatic, possibly historic breakthrough towards what Paris now calls “a step towards normalisation” between France and Azerbaijan coincides with the unfolding peace and reconciliation process between Armenia and Azerbaijan after decades of war over Karabakh.

Lebanon arrests IS operative tasked with assassinating Pope Leo
Lebanese authorities have arrested a prominent Islamic State (IS) group operative who was allegedly tasked with assassinating Pope Leo XIV during the pontiff’s visit to the country last year, according to local media reports.
The suspect, a Syrian national known as Al-Daameesh, allegedly began preparing the attack during the pope’s three-day visit to Lebanon in late 2025, carrying out field surveillance and monitoring areas along his planned route to identify potential vulnerabilities in security arrangements.
The alleged plot was ultimately thwarted by the heavy security presence and measures put in place during the visit, Lebanese broadcaster MTV reported, citing sources.
Lebanese Army Intelligence arrested Al-Daameesh in the northern region of Batroun, it said, adding that he had since been handed over to the Military Tribunal. It was not clear when he was arrested.
Al-Daameesh reportedly began his militant career with the Nusra Front, an Al-Qaeda affiliate, before later joining IS, where he had served as the group’s "deputy governor of Aleppo".
He was previously detained by the former Syrian regime and spent three years in prison.
Following the collapse of the Assad regime in December 2024 and the opening of prisons by rebel forces, he reportedly escaped detention and entered Lebanon illegally.
Sources told MTV that after settling in Lebanon, Al-Daameesh re-established contact with his commanders and began receiving orders directly from an IS emir.
IS and other militant groups carried out a series of attacks in Lebanon following the outbreak of the Syrian civil war in 2011, including suicide and car bombings targeting residential areas, particularly Beirut’s southern suburbs.
Sunni extremist groups, some of which pledged allegiance to IS, also fought several battles with the Lebanese army during that period, including in Tripoli and Sidon.
While the groups never established a territorial foothold in Lebanon, unlike in Syria and Iraq where they seized large swathes of territory, IS and Nusra fighters remained entrenched along the Lebanon-Syria border for years before being driven out by the Lebanese army and Hezbollah in 2017.
Lebanese authorities have announced several arrests of senior IS operatives and other members in recent years.

A specific narcissistic trait predicts aggression in socially anxious individuals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:00:17 UTC
20:00:17 KST

People with high social anxiety are typically expected to avoid conflict, yet some display surprisingly high levels of aggression. A recent study published in Aggressive Behavior suggests that a specific personality trait, narcissistic self-centeredness, helps explain this paradox. The research shows that when high social anxiety combines with a high degree of self-centeredness, individuals are much more likely to react to social threats with hostility rather than avoidance.
Social anxiety is commonly understood as an intense fear of negative evaluation in social situations. Psychologists historically viewed it as a condition defined by withdrawal and inhibition. Under this perspective, individuals who experience intense social anxiety try to protect themselves by shrinking away from potential embarrassment. They tend to suppress their emotions and avoid interactions that might lead to perceived failure.
Recent research has challenged this view by revealing that some socially anxious people respond to social threats with anger. The scientific literature contains contradictory findings on this topic. Some research links social anxiety to aggressive outbursts, while other studies find no such association.
Psychologists Reyihangu Tuerxun and Yanan Li, alongside their colleague Lixia Cui from Capital Normal University in China, aimed to resolve these contradictory findings. They suspected that aggression in socially anxious people is not uniform. Instead, it might depend on specific underlying personality traits.
The research team focused on a concept called vulnerable narcissism. Unlike grandiose narcissism, which involves overt arrogance and exhibitionism, vulnerable narcissism is characterized by fragile self-esteem, constant feelings of shame, and an extreme sensitivity to how others evaluate them.
Vulnerable narcissism contains two primary components. The first is a general hypersensitivity to rejection, and the second is a high degree of self-centeredness. Many socially anxious people are highly sensitive to rejection.
Self-centeredness brings a unique cognitive layer to the equation. Highly self-centered individuals tend to interpret minor social slights not just as awkward failures, but as direct, intolerable attacks on their self-worth. The researchers proposed that this specific appraisal of ego-threat shifts a person’s behavioral reaction from quiet avoidance to active, defensive hostility.
Psychologists evaluate aggression through several different lenses. The research team focused specifically on two distinct subtypes known as reactive and proactive aggression. Reactive aggression is an impulsive, angry response to a perceived provocation or threat, often happening in the heat of the moment.
Proactive aggression is a more calculated and instrumental behavior. People use proactive aggression deliberately to assert dominance, secure social resources, or intimidate others. The researchers wanted to see if self-centeredness was related to these specific types of aggression in different ways.
To investigate these dynamics, the researchers recruited 872 university students in China. Participants completed a series of online questionnaires designed to measure their levels of social interaction anxiety, social phobia, vulnerable narcissism, and both proactive and reactive aggression. After verifying the data with attention checks, the team analyzed the responses using two distinct statistical approaches.
First, the researchers used a technique called latent profile analysis. This statistical method groups individuals into naturally occurring categories based on their shared characteristics. By feeding the participants’ survey scores into the model, the team identified seven distinct personality profiles within the sample. These profiles ranged from individuals with low anxiety and low narcissism to those experiencing moderate and high levels of both traits.
One specific group, making up nearly ten percent of the participants, displayed high levels of both social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism. The researchers labeled this the vulnerable-defensive profile. When looking at the aggression scores, this vulnerable-defensive group reported the highest levels of both reactive and proactive aggression across all seven profiles.
The team then compared this vulnerable-defensive group to another specific profile: students who had high social anxiety but low vulnerable narcissism. Both groups experienced similarly high levels of social anxiety. However, the group with high vulnerable narcissism reported notably higher rates of reactive aggression and overall aggression.
This comparison indicates that a high level of self-centeredness acts as a distinguishing factor. It separates those who retreat from social threats from those who push back.
The analysis also revealed a large group of students who carried moderate levels of both social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism. This group made up nearly a quarter of the sample. Their aggression scores fell just below the highly vulnerable-defensive group. This finding suggests that multiple psychological vulnerabilities can stack up, resulting in elevated hostility even when neither trait reaches extreme levels individually.
Following the profile grouping, the researchers conducted a second analysis using moderated regression. This statistical technique looks at the entire sample as a continuous spectrum. It tests whether one variable changes the strength of the relationship between two other variables. In this case, the team tested whether self-centeredness changed the link between social anxiety and the two forms of aggression.
The regression analysis showed that self-centeredness did alter the relationship between social anxiety and proactive aggression. As self-centeredness increased across the participant pool, the positive association between social anxiety and calculated, proactive aggression grew stronger. Highly self-centered individuals with social anxiety were more willing to use deliberate aggression to protect their social standing.
When the team ran the same continuous analysis for reactive aggression, the interaction was not statistically significant. A gradual increase in self-centeredness across the general population did not smoothly predict higher reactive aggression.
The researchers note that this seemingly contradictory result actually highlights a threshold effect. Reactive, explosive aggression seems to occur primarily when both social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism reach extreme levels simultaneously, as seen in the vulnerable-defensive profile. It operates like a tipping point rather than a gradual incline.
The study relies entirely on cross-sectional data, meaning all measurements were taken at a single point in time. This design makes it impossible to determine the sequence of events. While self-centeredness might lead to aggression, aggressive behaviors could also lead to further social rejection, which in turn might heighten anxiety and defensive personality traits.
The data also comes entirely from self-reported questionnaires. Participants might alter their answers to appear more socially acceptable, which is a known issue when asking people to report their own aggressive behaviors. Proactive aggression, in particular, is often underreported in survey research.
The participant pool consisted entirely of university students. The findings might not reflect the psychological dynamics of older adults, clinical populations, or individuals from different cultural backgrounds. Expanding the demographic scope will help determine how universally these personality profiles apply.
Future studies could track individuals over time to see how the relationship between anxiety, narcissism, and aggression develops. The researchers also recommend incorporating different methods of measuring aggression, such as peer reports or behavioral observations. Finally, future work could look at passive aggression, a subtle form of hostility that may be particularly common among socially anxious individuals.
The study, “Aggression in Social Anxiety: Narcissistic Self-Centeredness as a Differentiator in Person-Centered and Variable-Centered Analyses,” was authored by Reyihangu Tuerxun, Yanan Li, and Lixia Cui.

‘First there’s the gruelling task of trying to charge my laptop’: a day in the life of a university lecturer in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:00:17 UTC
20:00:17 KST

It is time for Mahmoud Seydam’s online lecture on museum architecture. He squats in front of the step he calls a table and opens his laptop.
“Is Mohammed the only one here?” He pulls out his phone and types into the students’ chat group that the lecture is about to start. There are two students now. Mahmoud decides to wait a little for the others to join.
“Today, we have a simple presentation: an overview of museum design.” He asks his students to imagine the museum as honey in a glass. “The museum is a beautiful interior space. It becomes an element that attracts people.”
The internet connection drops out and halts the lecture.
Mahmoud, head of engineering sciences and applied arts at the University College of Science and Technology in Khan Younis and a lecturer at al-Aqsa University, does not seem frustrated. He is used to this.
In his usual calm and professional tone, he records a voice message to his students: “Hello everyone … There seems to be an internet problem, so I will record the lecture, upload it to YouTube and send you the link.”
This is what a day in the life of a university lecturer in Gaza looks like.
Daybreak
 Sleep itself is a struggle. Sleeping isn’t easy while living in tents. Anxiety dominates everything … because there’s no sense of stability.
You compare how your life was before the war to your current life and, psychologically, you’re unable to accept this reality. You’re living in a tent, which doesn’t protect you from anything and doesn’t provide any privacy. You can’t even do your work peacefully because of the noise.
Not to mention the anxiety about an emergency occurring. There was a strike on the tents around us before. There’s fear for the children, of harm to any member of the family. There’s anxiety about being displaced again. We were displaced more than 15 times, including from a place that was uncomfortable, unstable and didn’t support human life, to one that was even worse, sometimes abandoning all our belongings just to save our lives. We slept for three or four nights on the street, on the pavement.
You feel anxious at night. I wake up around dawn, pray and open my mobile phone. I make a cup of coffee and sit outside the tent to respond to messages from students and colleagues that came overnight. I preserve some of my phone’s battery specifically for this task. It’s easier for me to send them voice notes than to type. This is how I start my day.
Morning
The morning tasks begin with fetching water. Mahmoud grabs a plastic container and walks to where the water truck stops. His children – three sons and a daughter, studying engineering, nursing and computer science – often help out. He brings the water back to the tent and pours it into their tank, then into buckets of different sizes and colours in front of their tent.
 We use these buckets to store some of the water for daily use to make it last as long as possible, because the tank only holds 200 litres.
We don’t have any other tanks. They were all destroyed when our house was bombed. And the water doesn’t reach us every day.
In displacement, we face things we didn’t expect in life. The tent constantly needs repairs. Plus, there is the gruelling task of trying to charge my mobile phone and laptop to start my day and do my work.
Sometimes we have breakfast; sometimes we don’t. Currently, there is flour and we knead and bake in the tent, but the bread spoils from the heat and then there is no breakfast. Meals are not regular, but if I get absorbed in work, I forget about food.
Afternoon
Mahmoud starts to set up for the day’s lecture. As soon as he plugs his laptop into the power strip, the system shuts down. He has learned basic solar energy technology to manage these recurring breakdowns. He grabs the broom, steps on to a plastic chair and cleans the dust off the solar panels on top of the tent. He records the museum design lecture and then it is time to set off for the Scholars Without Borders offices, the college’s temporary headquarters.
 Not everything is online; there are meetings and student issues for which you need to be present. The distance to Scholars Without Borders is about 6km.
I usually go on foot because of how difficult transportation is: the roads are rough and everything is packed with tents and carts. Today, I used a cart pulled by an old car – it’s the kind that is usually pulled by a horse or a donkey – and then a rundown tuk-tuk. It takes me an hour to get there.
Being in these circumstances and still being able to carry on, to give my all – frankly, I find it incredibly difficult. The basic necessities of life must be in place for a person to be able to excel in their work. People don’t even have the bare minimum for life right now.
The application and practical side of learning has become extremely difficult. Most sessions are online. Most of the basic tools and materials needed for the learning process have become difficult to access or simply unavailable.
From the early stages of the war, we noticed that the universities were deliberately targeted. The university has a certain symbolic significance. It brings together all the future talent and potential, whether among students or the teaching staff.
At one point, we were displaced in an area between Rafah and Khan Younis, where my university was visible from a distance. I saw with my own eyes the military strikes against the university buildings and facilities. When the ceasefire was broken, a video emerged showing the demolition of all of the university buildings, a complete levelling of the site.
We continue with a certain degree of patience and perseverance.
Evening
 Before the war you could take your family out to eat in a restaurant.
As an architect, I was also quite interested in archaeological and heritage sites, and I’d pop into some of the shops selling antiques to have a look around.
All of this is lost now. There is no time for leisure; we can barely secure the bare necessities. Our life runs like a machine. Every day is just like the next.
My parents and two siblings live in tents nearby, a 10-minute walk. My parents – because of the war, illnesses and old age – have been really affected. It’s a responsibility, so almost every day I visit them to see if they need anything.
I sometimes sit outside my tent and talk with others to unwind after the long day. Then I resume my communications with students. This doesn’t stop until I sleep.
From the moment you wake up until you go to sleep, you’re barely able to keep up with anything other than the tasks you have to do.

Tom Watson’s move to Palantir is the latest sign of how far the rot has spread in UK politics | Clive Lewis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:00:17 UTC
20:00:17 KST

Whatever is said about Tom Watson, the former deputy leader of the Labour party has a knack for landing headlines. In the past he did it at the expense of the rich and powerful – from News International, over phone hacking, to the Home Office, over its mass surveillance of our data. But his latest headline – that he has joined Palantir as a senior vice-president – has been at the expense of public confidence in the political class.
His new appointment is more than just a private career choice. It sends yet another signal to a weary public about just how far the rot in our democracy has spread.
Now, the former scourge of mass surveillance finds a surveillance company “the most interesting … on the planet”. It’s quite a journey, and one not many of us will want to take with him. Palantir does do work of real consequence. That’s rather the point. Watson says some criticism of Palantir is propaganda. Some of it is also true, which is the part he will find harder to square.
Palantir is a company built on surveillance and military targeting. Its co-founder Peter Thiel wrote in 2009 that he no longer believed freedom and democracy were compatible. He sees technology as an alternative to politics, a way to change the world without having to persuade voters, and backs private “startup cities” run by chief executives. This attitude runs through the company’s DNA. Palantir’s co-founder and chief executive, Alex Karp, has boasted that its work is there “to scare enemies and on occasion kill them”. Its software is used to target people for ICE raids in the US, and civilians in Gaza. This isn’t just another global corporation with some unsavoury corners to its business.
I can’t parse Watson’s mind or motivation. Palantir probably doesn’t hire a former deputy leader for his coding skills. But does it hire access? Access to networks across party and government, and to the doors behind which Palantir would fight to keep a £330m NHS England contract and legally challenge Sadiq Khan’s block on a £50m Metropolitan police contract?
Watson won’t be alone. He will join more than 30 former UK officials at a company that Peter Mandelson’s former lobbying firm, Global Counsel, counted as a client. Mandelson accompanied Keir Starmer to Palantir’s Washington office in 2025, while still retaining a stake in Global Counsel. The MoD has since signed a major partnership with Palantir. And none of this will have broken a single law. The rules on jobs for former ministers last only two years and have no legal force. Therein lies the problem.
Whether it’s Tony Blair and his relationship with Oracle, Mandelson and Global Counsel or Nick Clegg and his time at Meta, the section of the political class meant to oppose vested interests and promote public service appears to have switched sides.
According to the Institute for Public Policy Research’s latest findings, the main political parties, including Labour and the Liberal Democrats, have been accepting donations from wealthy individuals at an accelerating pace. The research found 72% of all £1m-plus donations from individuals since records began in 2001 had come since 2019. Sadly, none of this can be described as an aberration. Rather, it’s how the system increasingly works. Now politicians’ proximity to wealth and the “elites” who own it has fostered a growing public mistrust. One need only listen to Danny Dyer at a rally last week, calling for public ownership of water, to get a feel for that sentiment. These examples are all symptoms of the growing proximity between political power and the wealth it is supposed to hold to account.
In the recent Robin Cook memorial lecture I gave, I termed this malaise the “integrity gap”: the widening gulf between what governments and politicians say and what people believe. Every flagrant act deepens public cynicism about politics, and about the democracy that depends on public trust. This is a fact of which those around Trump are well aware. They know every allegation of presidential corruption erodes people’s willingness to defend democracy.
Thiel understands this implicitly. His vision for our society is simply not compatible with a progressive worldview. That is why a former Labour deputy leader lending his name to Palantir matters so much.
The integrity gap will not close with better messaging. It will close only when politicians show whose side they are on. That means revolving-door rules with the force of law, and a regulator with teeth. It means capping political donations and ending second jobs in the House of Commons, while abolishing the House of Lords altogether. And it means public ownership and democratic control of the things firms such as Palantir want to run, from our health data to our water.
Those who sell access to power have made their choice. Those who oppose Thiel’s vision need to make theirs, and act on it. It’s time to pick a side.
- 
  Clive Lewis is the Labour MP for Norwich South
